text: From Wall Street to Wisconsin, financial brokers applaud Trump's directive. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump took decisive action to dismantle a retirement advice regulation that wealth managers from Wall Street to Wisconsin have been lobbying against for the past six years. This significant measure, originating from the Obama administration, is known as the fiduciary rule, which mandates that brokers and financial advisors prioritize the best interests of retirement savers. This regulation limits their capacity to earn commissions and to market certain higher-fee products. Wall Street contends that it could disadvantage consumers by increasing compliance expenses and thus fees, and compel them to eliminate Main Street clients as well as small businesses that provide 401(k) plans. Trump's executive order instructs the Labor Department to assess whether the rule requires modification or repeal. Both advocates and detractors are preparing to present their arguments. However, the industry seems to have the upper hand, as Trump officials have indicated intentions to generally reduce regulations and specifically criticized the fiduciary rule. The Chamber of Commerce, among various trade organizations that have launched lawsuits to overturn the regulation, praised Trump's action. "We anticipate prompt measures from the Department of Labor to implement this delay and reassess policy and legal aspects," stated the Chamber. Stocks of banks with significant wealth management operations surged on Friday, with Bank of America (BAC.N) rising by 2.5 percent, Morgan Stanley (MS.N) increasing by 5.5 percent, and Wells Fargo (WFC.N) climbing over 2 percent. Insurance companies, whose annuity product sales were threatened by the rule, also experienced gains, with Prudential (PRU.N) up 1.9 percent and Metlife (MET.N) gaining 1 percent. "Everyone will be relieved that the DOL's haste to finalize it before the administration change has been postponed," remarked Judi Carsrud, director of government relations for the National Association of Insurance Financial Advisors (NAIFA), which has opposed the regulation for years. NAIFA intends to pursue a "very straightforward" solution, such as a "legislative approach" that instructs retirement account advisors to act in the best interests of their clients—a benchmark that Carsrud believes the group’s members already satisfy. The Obama administration indicated that conflicted advice costs American families $17 billion annually, a figure that the industry claims is exaggerated. However, there is consensus regarding the substantial costs firms would incur to comply with the new rule, with the Labor Department estimating this could reach as much as $31 billion over the next decade. Banks have begun adjusting their practices, with Bank of America announcing this week that it would more transparently disclose the fees it imposes on clients of its Merrill Lynch wealth management division. Bank of America Corp had already started reducing “transactional” accounts that charge clients a commission for each trade, rather than a flat fee based on assets. Morgan Stanley (MS.N) has opted to maintain such accounts but is implementing changes that will enable advisors to operate within the rule’s limitations by developing new contracts, retraining advisors, and upgrading supervisory software. Swiss bank UBS UBSN.VX embraced Trump's directive and expressed support for establishing a fiduciary rule under the Securities and Exchange Commission, which could extend to all advisors, not merely retirement advisors. Wells Fargo stated it would continue collaborating with regulators to ensure enhanced standards of care for investment clients. text: Greek law enforcement faces limitations: EU court favors women. LUXEMBOURG (Reuters) - Police forces within the European Union are prohibited from implementing universal height criteria for recruits, as this practice discriminates against women, the highest court in the EU declared on Wednesday, rejecting a position from the Greek administration. The government in Athens had supported a minimum height standard of 1.70 meters (5 feet 7 inches) for individuals seeking admission to the Greek police academy after a female applicant raised concerns about gender discrimination when her entry was denied in 2007 due to her short stature. However, the European Court of Justice determined that such a universal requirement lacked justification. The court noted that certain police duties, such as traffic management, do not necessitate specific physical traits, and even for roles that do require physical fitness, assessments could be designed to be less discriminatory toward women. In Greece, women represent 13 percent of the police force. In comparison, France has 18 percent, having eliminated a 1.60-meter height requirement in 2010, while England and Wales have 29 percent, having done away with minimum height standards for both genders 27 years ago. Until 1990, women in England were required to be at least 1.60 meters tall to become police officers, which is 3 centimeters shorter than the requirement for men.

text: The U.S. electric vehicle tax credit will remain intact in the Republican tax bill. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A revised Republican tax proposal unveiled late on Friday does not remove the $7,500 tax credit for electric vehicles, contrary to what Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives had previously suggested. This decision aligns with the Senate version passed last month, which also retained the credit. Eliminating this incentive could have negatively impacted automakers such as General Motors Co (GM.N), Volkswagen AG (VOWG_p.DE), Tesla Inc (TSLA.O), and Nissan Motor Co (7201.T). Under the existing legislation, consumers can receive a $7,500 tax credit to help offset the costs of plug-in electric vehicles. This tax credit begins to phase out when a manufacturer sells 200,000 plug-in vehicles. Once an automaker reaches that sales threshold, the $7,500 tax credit remains available for at least three additional months before it gradually diminishes. Consumers can currently claim the credit until the manufacturer sells 200,000 plug-in vehicles. Electric vehicles are generally more expensive due to their high-cost batteries compared to gasoline-powered cars. The Electric Drive Transportation Association expressed satisfaction in a statement late Friday regarding the retention of the credit, stating, "The credit supports innovation and job creation while helping drivers access advanced vehicle technology." Earlier this week, over 50 automakers and various companies and organizations sent a letter to Congress advocating for the preservation of the credit, including Ford Motor Co (F.N), BMW AG (BMWG.DE), GM, and Uber Technologies Inc. Former President Barack Obama had consistently suggested increasing the electric vehicle tax credit to $10,000 and transforming it into a point-of-sale rebate, but Congress did not pass this proposal. Automakers are under obligations from California and several other states to produce an increasing number of zero-emission vehicles and have indicated that these credits are vital for compliance with the regulations.

text: Senator Susan Collins, a moderate Republican from Maine, has announced her intention to continue serving in the U.S. Senate instead of pursuing a gubernatorial campaign. This decision comes after she played a vital role in halting her party's attempts to repeal the Affordable Care Act earlier this year. The four-term senator gained national recognition this summer as one of three Republican senators who voted against a bill aimed at repealing the law commonly known as Obamacare in July, a decision that displeased President Donald Trump. On Friday, Collins expressed that staying in the Senate would enable her to advocate for significant reforms in the U.S. healthcare system. Although she voted against major healthcare legislation with other Senate Republicans in 2009, Collins acknowledged the necessity for urgent improvements, criticizing the manner in which repeal initiatives were approached over the summer. "When dealing with an issue that impacts millions of Americans, we must comprehend the repercussions of our actions, rather than voting on bills in the early hours that have not undergone substantial hearings," stated Collins, 64, while addressing business leaders in Rockland, a city located in the midcoast region of Maine. "We need to cease allowing partisanship to be the pre-existing condition that hinders meaningful healthcare reform." She emphasized the urgent need to stabilize insurance markets, advocating for the establishment of high-risk pools. Additionally, Collins proposed that employers should be mandated to provide healthcare coverage exclusively for individuals who work 40 hours a week or more, raising the threshold from the current 30 hours. For several weeks, Collins had publicly entertained the possibility of running to succeed Governor Paul LePage, a staunch conservative who was first elected in 2010 with strong backing from the populist Tea Party movement. State statutes prevent LePage from seeking a third term. Collins and LePage represent the two extremes of the Maine Republican Party. According to a seasoned political analyst from Maine, Collins’ independence has rendered her an increasingly influential figure in Washington. "She is at the core of nearly every significant policy discussion and major vote in the U.S. Senate," remarked Mark Brewer, a political science professor at the University of Maine. "She remains a crucial player on any issue she chooses to prioritize." Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell praised her decision: "Her choice to stay in the Senate is significant not only for the residents of Maine, whom she serves exceptionally well, but also for the nation at large."

text: Multinational corporations are facing unexpected challenges due to a Republican excise tax proposal. WASHINGTON/LONDON (Reuters) - The tax legislation introduced last week in the U.S. Congress by Republicans may disrupt the global supply chains of major multinational firms by imposing a 20-percent tax on cross-border transactions that these companies routinely engage in between their affiliated business units. According to tax experts, European multinationals, many of which currently incur minimal U.S. taxes on their U.S. profits owing to tax treaties and the rerouting of U.S. earnings to their home countries or other low-tax areas, could be particularly adversely affected if the proposed tax is enacted. Some analysts warned that the initiative could violate international tax treaties, the World Trade Organization regulations, and other global norms that prevent the double taxation of profits if the new tax does not consider the income taxes that have already been paid in other nations. This proposed tax, which is embedded within the extensive 429-page legislation endorsed by President Donald Trump, surprised corporate tax strategists and left them racing to comprehend its implications and objectives, as well as the likelihood of Congress voting on it. Reuters reached out to seven multinational firms and four industry associations. None were willing to provide direct comments regarding the proposal, with most indicating they were still assessing the comprehensive tax package. This proposal forms part of a wide-ranging tax reform initiative introduced by House Republicans on Thursday, which aims to reduce overall tax burdens and streamline the tax code. The future of these proposed reforms remains uncertain, with numerous weeks, and potentially months, of debate and vigorous lobbying ahead. The overall House package has faced backlash for potentially increasing the federal budget deficit and disproportionately benefiting wealthy individuals and large corporations. Nevertheless, experts noted that the corporate tax segment includes several ambitious proposals deserving of further examination. They pointed out that the 20 percent excise tax is one such measure aimed at addressing the issues associated with transfer pricing, wherein multinationals establish the prices of goods, services, and intellectual property that continuously transfer among their domestic business units. According to global standards, these prices should be comparable to those found in the open market. However, if a foreign parent company charges inflated prices to its U.S. affiliates, it can lower its U.S. tax obligations and effectively shift profits to a jurisdiction with lower tax rates, thereby decreasing the overall tax liabilities of the entire corporation. "It is evident that there is a transfer-pricing concern, and action should be taken," stated Steven Rosenthal, a senior fellow at the Tax Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank based in Washington. "I would characterize this 20-percent excise tax as a blunt tool to tackle the issue. The drawback of blunt instruments is that they may sometimes hit the intended target and at other times affect unintended targets," remarked Rosenthal, who previously served as legislative counsel at Congress’s Joint Tax Committee. Under the proposed legislation, U.S. business entities that import goods, pay royalties, or incur other tax-deductible, non-interest fees to foreign parent companies or affiliates as part of their operations would either be subjected to a 20-percent tax on these transactions or must agree to categorize the amounts as income linked to their U.S. operations and therefore liable for U.S. taxes. As suggested, the new tax regulation would only apply to businesses with payments exceeding $100 million from U.S. units to foreign affiliates. The rule is set to take effect only after 2018. European companies that market foreign-manufactured products in the U.S. through local distribution channels could be among those significantly impacted, as noted by Michael Mundaca, co-director of the national tax division at the accounting firm Ernst & Young. Such firms may face the prospect of being taxed on these transfers twice—first through the excise tax in the United States and subsequently in their home countries, where they are already taxed, and where the new U.S. tax would not be recognized without amendments to bilateral tax treaties. text: Trump: Following taxes, healthcare, infrastructure and welfare reforms are next. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump indicated that he intends to address the issues of healthcare, infrastructure, and welfare reform shortly after the Republicans finalize their tax overhaul, which the party has committed to completing by year’s end. "We will be presenting plans regarding healthcare, infrastructure, and welfare reform, which is urgently needed in this nation, soon after taxes," he remarked to reporters at the White House before a meeting with his Cabinet secretaries.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday said he plans to take up  healthcare, infrastructure and welfare reform issues soon after Republicans’ tax overhaul is finalized, which the party has pledged to complete by the end of the year. “We’ll be submitting plans on healthcare, plans on  infrastructure and plans on welfare reform, which is desperately needed in this country, soon after taxes,” he told reporters at the White House ahead of a meeting with his Cabinet secretaries.

text: Trump announces additional sanctions against North Korea. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Thursday, President Donald Trump declared that the United States plans to impose further sanctions on North Korea. In recent weeks, tensions have heightened regarding Pyongyang's missile and nuclear arsenal, despite significant pressure from global powers. "We will be putting more sanctions on North Korea," Trump stated when asked during a meeting with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani. Regarding Afghanistan, Trump mentioned that the U.S. military is focusing more on leading than on engaging in combat.

We will be putting more sanctions on North Korea,  Trump said in response to a question at a meeting with Afghan president Ashraf Ghani. On Thursday, spokesperson Josh Earnest informed reporters in Washington that he was questioned about a New York Times article, which claimed Obama urged Democratic supporters to back candidate Hillary Clinton at the fundraiser held in Austin, Texas, the previous weekend.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama did not specify a candidate preference in the race for the Democratic presidential nomination at a Democratic National Committee fundraising event, White House spokesman Josh Earnest told reporters on Thursday. Earnest was asked about a New York Times report that said Obama told Democratic donors to rally behind candidate Hillary Clinton during the fundraiser in Austin, Texas last weekend.

text: China expresses support for Myanmar's initiatives to improve the circumstances in Rakhine. BEIJING (Reuters) - Wang Yi, China's Foreign Minister, stated that China appreciates the actions undertaken by the Myanmar government to improve the situation in Rakhine state. Wang shared these remarks on Thursday in New York during a discussion held alongside the annual United Nations General Assembly with officials from Myanmar, as reported by a statement from the Foreign Ministry. Over 400,000 Muslim Rohingya individuals have sought refuge in Bangladesh after fleeing Rakhine due to a counter-insurgency campaign by Myanmar's military, which was launched in response to militant attacks on security personnel. U.N. representatives have characterized Myanmar's approach as ethnic cleansing.

text: A Japanese cosmetic surgeon, who has faced criticism for his admiration of Nazis and downplaying Japan's wartime actions, has successfully bid $275,000 for a memoir written by Emperor Hirohito that details the country's descent into World War Two. Katsuya Takasu, a frequent presence on Japanese television, has been condemned by the Simon Wiesenthal Center, a Jewish human rights organization, for breaching all standards of decency by labeling the Holocaust and the Nanjing massacre as fabrications. In October 2015, Takasu stated on Twitter, "I think both Nanjing and Auschwitz are fabrications." He acknowledged that there was no doubt regarding the persecution of Jews but also commended the contributions of Nazi scientists to various fields, including science and medicine. In a conversation with Reuters on Thursday, Takasu explained that he purchased the handwritten memoir, referred to as the "Emperor's Monologue," because he believed it contained important messages for both the Japanese populace and the royal family, asserting it should remain in Japan. The document recounts events from the 1920s, including Hirohito's expressed intention not to contest future cabinet decisions. Its public release in 1990 generated significant controversy, reviving discussions about the emperor's accountability for the war. The narrative was dictated to one of Hirohito's aides in 1946, during Japan's occupation by Allied forces following its defeat, as the emperor faced potential war crimes charges that ultimately did not materialize. In a phone interview, Takasu claimed that his social media comments had been deliberately misconstrued. "The criticism comes from individuals who have selectively highlighted some of my tweets and maliciously interpreted them; it is a misunderstanding," he remarked. "If you examine all my tweets, it is clear that I oppose Nazism. However, I do hold in high regard the remarkable medical advancements of that time." Nevertheless, Takasu expressed his belief that the casualty figures from both the Holocaust and the Nanjing massacre had been inflated, a viewpoint often found among Japanese ultra-nationalists. China asserts that Japanese soldiers killed 300,000 individuals in Nanjing from December 1937 to January 1938, while an Allied tribunal estimated the death toll to be around half that amount. "What I intended to convey was that while it is claimed that six million or seven million were killed in the Holocaust, could it not be several tens of thousands instead?" Takasu questioned. "It is claimed that 300,000 were killed in the Nanjing massacre, but could that not be just 6,000 to 7,000 people? That is what I meant by fabrication." The memoir concludes with Hirohito's assertion that had he opposed the war decision, it would have led to a civil war that would have been far worse, resulting in Japan's destruction, as noted on the auction house Bonhams' website. Scholars argue that Hirohito's accountability for the war has never been thoroughly investigated in Japan, mainly due to the decision by U.S. occupying forces to keep the emperor as a symbol of a newly democratic state. When asked about Hirohito's accountability for the war, Takasu expressed that he believes the late emperor was absolved when he stated he would sacrifice his life for the Japanese people. "At the moment the emperor made that statement, he bore no guilt," he added.

text: President Barack Obama criticized Donald Trump’s intention to ease Wall Street regulations during a visit to Elkhart, Indiana, on Wednesday. This trip came three weeks after he first visited the city at the start of his presidency, which has since bounced back from its economic downturn. Obama’s comments in Elkhart indicated the themes he is likely to address on the campaign trail this autumn against the presumptive Republican presidential candidate. While he did not directly name Trump, he expressed strong disapproval of the billionaire’s policy ideas, especially his commitment to roll back significant parts of the Dodd-Frank financial regulations in the U.S. "How is it that someone would suggest we relax regulations on Wall Street? Have we genuinely forgotten what transpired eight years ago?" Obama remarked, sounding frustrated. "The idea that you would support anyone who would permit them to revert to the practices that nearly shattered our economy is illogical. It doesn't matter if you are a Republican, a Democrat, or an independent, why would you do that?" As he prepares to leave office in January, Obama is keen for a Democrat to take his place to maintain his legacy regarding the economy, healthcare reform, and climate change. By visiting Elkhart, he aimed to showcase the effectiveness of his policies despite pushback from Republicans. His earlier trip to the city in early 2009 coincided with efforts in Congress to approve an approximately $800 billion economic stimulus initiative. In 2009, Elkhart’s unemployment rate peaked at 19.6 percent, according to the White House; it currently stands at about 4 percent. Indiana’s Republican Governor Mike Pence asserted that the city recovered not due to Obama’s policies, but despite them. "I believe the residents of Elkhart... have revitalized our economy in spite of the burdens imposed by higher taxes, mandates, and increasing regulations from Washington, D.C.," he wrote in an opinion editorial for "The Elkhart Truth." Although Obama has yet to endorse former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in her campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination against Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, he has shown his willingness to support the eventual nominee. He acknowledged Clinton’s husband, former President Bill Clinton, by pointing out that deficits decreased during both of their administrations, and he criticized Republicans for blaming the economic struggles of the middle class on the poor, minorities, feminists, and immigrants. "The primary narrative that Republicans have been presenting regarding the economy is not backed by the facts. It simply isn’t," Obama stated to a largely supportive audience at a local high school.

text: In an effort to recover, Trump intensifies his criticisms of Clinton. MANHEIM, Pa. (Reuters) - On Saturday, Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump wrapped up a challenging week for his campaign by heightening personal assaults on Democrat Hillary Clinton, questioning her endurance and asserting that she ought to be imprisoned due to her management of classified emails. Following a week marked by widespread backlash over a public dispute with a former beauty queen, Trump aimed to regain momentum with a strongly negative attack on his rival in the upcoming Nov. 8 election, as the second presidential debate against her approaches in a week. Concurrently, the New York Times revealed it had acquired documents indicating that Trump reported a $916 million loss on his 1995 income tax returns, a deduction so substantial that it might have enabled him to avoid paying federal income taxes for several years. Trump has declined to disclose his tax records, claiming he is undergoing a federal audit. During a rally in Manheim, Pennsylvania, Trump expressed skepticism about Clinton's capability to fulfill the presidential role, particularly after her recent bout of pneumonia. He attempted to revive a strategy he had used against former Republican competitor Jeb Bush, whom Trump labeled as “low energy.” Clinton kept her pneumonia diagnosis confidential until she was witnessed nearly collapsing while entering her vehicle at a ceremony commemorating the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks in New York. Listing various global issues, Trump remarked, “She’s supposed to tackle all of these matters yet she can’t make it 15 feet to her car. Give me a break.” “People, we require stamina, we need energy, we need individuals who can negotiate deals,” Trump stated. Trump frequently urges audiences who chant “lock her up” regarding her use of a private email server during her tenure as U.S. secretary of state from 2009 to 2013 to instead assist him in defeating her. However, on Saturday, Trump conveyed to thousands of supporters that Clinton’s management of classified emails and the deletion of 33,000 emails she categorized as personal meant that “she should be in prison, let me tell you.” Trump continued his remarks by expressing doubts about Clinton’s loyalty to her supporters and laughed, “I don’t even think she’s loyal to Bill, to be honest. And why should she be, right? Why should she be?” In 1998, Clinton’s spouse, former President Bill Clinton, became embroiled in a scandal involving former White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Trump was generally perceived as having lost his initial presidential debate with Clinton last Monday, although he references online polls that indicate he emerged victorious. Since the debate took place, Trump has been attempting to regain his balance, becoming entangled in a back-and-forth exchange with former Miss Universe Alicia Machado, whom Trump had criticized for her weight gain.

text: The U.S. Senate addressed a technical glitch on Thursday that had delayed a new sanctions package targeting Russia, but lawmakers indicated that the measure could still encounter resistance in the House, potentially leading to further postponements. The Countering Iran’s Destabilizing Activities Act, which encompasses the sanctions against Russia, was passed by the Senate with a strong 98-2 vote on June 15. Many lawmakers expressed hope that the legislation would be enacted promptly to deliver a firm message to Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of President Donald Trump’s upcoming meeting with him in Germany next week. However, the Senate's progress was impeded when House Republican leaders claimed it breached a constitutional stipulation requiring that revenue-affecting legislation must originate in the House, a situation referred to as a “blue slip” violation. Since then, lawmakers from both chambers have been engaged in disputes over the matter. Democrats have accused House Republicans of attempting to derail the bill to appease Trump following concerns raised by administration officials. In response, House Republican leaders maintained that their objection was purely procedural. "The speaker has made it clear that we will address sanctions once the House receives it," stated AshLee Strong, a spokesperson for Speaker Paul Ryan. The Senate managed to resolve the procedural concern on Thursday. Nevertheless, this delay implies that the House will not hold a vote until after the G20, due to Congress’ recess scheduled for next week. "This is now going to serve as a referendum on the Republican leadership; if they choose to align with the president’s leniency towards Putin and the Russians, that will become part of their legacy," remarked Representative Eliot Engel, the leading Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Engel, along with Republican committee chairman Ed Royce, has expressed a desire for the swift passage of the sanctions. Some Republican members in the House have expressed hesitations. Representative Pete Sessions, from Texas, a state pivotal to U.S. energy interests, indicated he sought guarantees regarding the bill's impact on businesses. Representative Mark Meadows mentioned he would review the bill thoroughly after consulting with ambassadors from Italy, Germany, and Britain, who raised energy-related issues. "It could potentially face challenges. However, it’s too soon to determine," Meadows noted. The proposed legislation aims to codify sanctions that were previously enacted through executive orders by former President Barack Obama. It includes sanctions targeting the mining sector and other industries, as well as individuals in Russia implicated in cyber attacks or in supplying arms to the Syrian government. Additionally, it establishes a review protocol that mandates Trump to obtain Congressional consent prior to lifting sanctions on Russia.

text: Six individuals were killed following an ambush targeting the president of the High Court of Justice in Mali. On Tuesday, in central Mali, the defense ministry reported that five soldiers from Mali's military and one civilian lost their lives during an attack on a convoy carrying Abdrahamane Niang. The identity of those responsible for the ambush remains uncertain; however, the high-profile nature of the target and the military casualties underscore the worsening security conditions in Mali, attributed to the expanding influence of jihadist organizations operating across the nation’s vast desert regions. The convoy was en route from the towns of Dia to Diafarab in the Mopti region, situated approximately 500 kilometers (311 miles) northeast of the capital city, Bamako, at the time of the assault. The army successfully rescued Mr. Niang and his spouse. The statement indicated that there were six fatalities: five members of the Malian army and the driver of Honorable Niang, while also mentioning additional injuries. Further specifics regarding the ambush were not provided. The proliferation of jihadist groups, some associated with al Qaeda and Islamic State, continues to undermine stability in Mali, four years post the French military intervention that curbed an Islamist uprising that began in 2012. Currently, around 4,000 French troops are still deployed as part of Operation Barkhane, collaborating with approximately 10,000 U.N. peacekeepers stationed in Mali. Nonetheless, attacks targeting peacekeepers, humanitarian workers, and the Malian armed forces are frequent. Earlier this month, four U.S. Special Forces soldiers were killed in neighboring Niger by militants believed to be affiliated with a local Islamic State group operating from Mali. The G5 Sahel, an anti-terrorism taskforce composed of troops from Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Chad, and Mauritania, is set to initiate its first joint operations this month aimed at combating Islamists in the Sahel.

text: Syrian rebels are looking for action from President Donald Trump regarding the establishment of safe zones in their nation, while Damascus remains unresponsive. BEIRUT (Reuters) - Syrian insurgents have called on President Trump to honor his commitment to create safe zones within their country, yet experts are skeptical that he will take such a step, which could entangle Washington further in conflict, accelerate Syria's disintegration, and provoke a clash with Russia. Trump stated during an ABC News interview on Wednesday that he "will absolutely do safe zones in Syria" for individuals escaping violence, asserting that Europe erred by allowing millions of Syrian refugees to enter. Opponents of President Bashar al-Assad have long sought safe zones to shield civilians who have escaped government airstrikes and assaults on areas held by rebels. However, reflecting the doubts surrounding the announcement, insurgent representatives expressed only measured hope. "We haven’t seen any tangible outcomes from (U.S.) statements made six years ago. Therefore, we are waiting for action before anything else," remarked Fares al-Bayoush, a rebel leader in northwestern Syria. Qatar, which supports the rebels, expressed approval of Trump’s remarks and "stressed the necessity of establishing safe havens in Syria and implementing no-fly zones to guarantee civilian safety." There was no immediate response from Damascus, but it is expected to reject such a proposal as Assad has pledged to restore control over all of Syria. Iran, which supports various militias in Syria, including Lebanon’s Hezbollah, would also oppose any U.S. military involvement. Russia indicated that it had not been consulted about Trump’s initiative, cautioning that it should not "exacerbate the situation with refugees" and that Washington should consider "all the consequences." The establishment of safe zones would represent a significant alteration in U.S. foreign policy. Former President Barack Obama was resistant to an idea that would necessitate a commitment to defend such zones against the Syrian regime or its foreign allies, including Russia. Trump seems to view safe zones as a method to reduce the influx of refugees, which he perceives as a potential threat to U.S. security. However, there are no clear solutions regarding how the United States would circumvent the issues that have previously hindered the establishment of safe zones in Syria, such as the challenges associated with governing such an area in a conflict zone populated with armed factions. "At this point, this is largely within the realm of political maneuvering," stated Yezid Sayigh, a senior fellow and Syria specialist at the Carnegie Middle East Center in Beirut. "I don’t believe it is indicating imminent U.S. intervention." Trump might direct the State Department and Pentagon to devise a plan that would also establish "safe areas" in nations surrounding Syria, where millions of refugees are currently residing. The Syrian authorities are hoping Trump will terminate U.S. support for the rebels opposing Assad and shift U.S. strategy solely toward combating Islamic State, possibly in collaboration with Russia. Trump has signaled that he intends to pursue both objectives. Nearly six years of conflict have transformed Syria into a fragmented landscape, with some regions under Assad's control, others held by rebel factions, and additional areas governed by Kurdish forces or Islamic State militants. Previous discussions regarding safe zones in Syria have concentrated on areas held by rebels in the northwest, stretching from Idlib province to the Euphrates River. Regions in the southwest near the Jordan border have also been considered. However, complications have increased since the Syrian opposition initially called for safe zones, particularly following the deployment of Russia’s air force to Syria. Defending a safe zone from attacks by the Syrian government or its allies, backed by Russia and Iran, would almost certainly escalate tensions, which is one of the reasons Obama had previously avoided this route, Sayigh noted. Another significant challenge would be determining how to enforce the area to maintain its neutral status as a safe zone, he added. While much of Trump’s policy regarding Syria remains ambiguous, Syrian Kurds, who have typically steered clear of conflict with Assad, appear poised to remain integral to U.S. strategy. The Syrian Kurdish YPG militia controls extensive territories in northeast Syria, where they have largely avoided confrontation with the government.

text: Rebranding Hillary: Democrats aim to enhance Clinton's image. PHILADELPHIA (Reuters) - During her initial presidential campaign in 2008, Hillary Clinton faced a stinging remark from rival Barack Obama, who described her as "likable enough" before he secured the Democratic nomination and ultimately the presidency. Fast forward eight years, with her party’s nomination to follow Obama firmly secured, the topic of her likability, honesty, and trustworthiness continues to overshadow her quest to become the first female president of the United States, competing against Republican Donald Trump in the election on November 8. This week’s Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia is partially an initiative to reintroduce her to American voters, more than half of whom, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling, have an unfavorable opinion of her. She has faced criticism for years: Clinton can come across as stiff in public, struggling to convey the compassion her supporters insist she possesses privately, leading some voters to feel she is not providing straightforward answers to challenging questions. Clinton is aware of this issue, according to her aides. "She understands she must work to gain people’s trust," stated Jennifer Palmieri, her communications director. "She also recognizes there are no magical phrases that can instantly earn that trust." Throughout Monday and Tuesday at the convention, multiple speakers took to the stage to share testimonials about her, including her husband, former President Bill Clinton, who filled his primetime address on Tuesday with stories and intimate moments from the lives of America’s most recognized political duo. Jason Collins, a gay basketball player, recounted the support she extended when he publicly came out; a grandmother shared how her daughter’s struggle with addiction motivated Clinton to tackle the drug crisis. A series of individuals provided behind-the-scenes accounts of the former first lady, U.S. senator, and secretary of state, illustrating instances where she drove through severe weather to attend a funeral, organized birthday celebrations, and visited survivors of the September 11, 2001, attacks. Clinton’s public persona, which has seen ups and downs over her 25 years in the spotlight, took a hit following a contentious Democratic primary, ongoing controversy regarding her use of a private email account during her tenure as the top U.S. diplomat, and continuous Republican jabs at “crooked Hillary.” According to Reuters/Ipsos polling, 55 percent of Americans view Clinton unfavorably. Trump has an even lower approval rating, with 61 percent holding an unfavorable opinion of him. Many Americans believe both candidates have issues with honesty. The poll indicates that 59 percent of Americans do not consider her “honest and truthful,” while 53 percent feel the same about Trump. Republican strategist John Feehery asserted that it may be too late to improve Clinton’s image. "You have only one decade to make a first impression," he remarked. Instead, he suggested that a more effective strategy would be to focus on undermining Trump, given his negative perceptions exceed her own. Clinton’s campaign seems to be adopting this approach, airing an advertisement featuring clips of Trump, as children watch, in which he uses profanity, disparages Mexican immigrants as rapists and drug dealers, and mocks a journalist with disabilities. Clinton, 68, has been a target for conservative criticism for over two decades, and at the Republican convention in Cleveland last week, attendees chanted “Lock Her Up” and displayed signs proclaiming “Hillary for Prison.” For many of Clinton’s Democratic supporters, the low polling figures are attributed to these persistent attacks, along with a significant element of sexism directed at a woman in pursuit of power. “When someone is constantly attacking you, it will eventually take its toll,” remarked Richard Trumka, head of the AFL-CIO labor federation. “I’ve stated this publicly: Hillary Clinton needs to perform at an A+ level to achieve a C-.” For Democrats, this week presents what may be their best opportunity before the election.

text: U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis announced on Thursday that he had signed orders to deploy more troops to Afghanistan, marking the most significant action taken by President Donald Trump’s administration in addressing America’s protracted conflict. While Mattis did not disclose the exact number of troops involved, the reinforcements are intended to assist in combating Taliban militants and other extremist groups. "Yes, I have signed orders, but it is not finalized. I have signed some of the (orders for) troops that will be sent, and we are in the process of identifying the specific units," Mattis informed reporters. He indicated that he would withhold details on the troop count until he briefs Congress the following week; however, U.S. officials have informed Reuters that Trump has authorized Mattis to deploy approximately 4,000 additional personnel to Afghanistan. "It involves more advisers, and additional enablers, such as fire support," Mattis explained. He noted that no additional forces had yet been deployed and that it could take "a couple of days" before they arrive. Following a protracted review of his Afghanistan strategy, Trump last week committed the U.S. to an indefinite engagement in the region and vowed to intensify operations against Taliban insurgents. As of Wednesday, the Pentagon reported that roughly 11,000 U.S. troops are currently stationed in Afghanistan, which is significantly more than previously acknowledged. Mattis added that the composition of U.S. forces in Afghanistan would begin to change in accordance with Trump’s directives. Even with an increase of several thousand troops, U.S. military presence in Afghanistan would still remain considerably lower than its peak of over 100,000 in 2011, a time when Washington faced immense domestic pressure to reduce its involvement in the expensive conflict. Some officials have expressed skepticism to Reuters regarding the effectiveness of sending additional troops, arguing that any politically acceptable number would be insufficient to alter the current situation, let alone establish stability and security. To date, more than 2,300 American service members have lost their lives, and over 17,000 have sustained injuries in Afghanistan. The security landscape in Afghanistan has worsened for both U.S. forces and the Afghan government in recent years. As of February 20, the U.S. military assessed that the Afghan government controlled or had influence over nearly 60 percent of the country’s 407 districts, reflecting a nearly 11 percentage-point decline from the same period in 2016, based on data from the U.S. Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction. Earlier this month, the Taliban communicated with Trump in an open letter, asserting that the military conditions in Afghanistan were "far worse than you realize" and that deploying more troops would be counterproductive. The Taliban, which aims to reinstate strict Islamic law, has been engaged in an insurgency against the Western-supported Afghan government since being ousted in a U.S.-led invasion following the September 11 attacks in 2001. Those attacks were orchestrated by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden from a sanctuary in Afghanistan.

This crackdown has raised concerns among Turkey's Western allies and human rights organizations, who argue that President Tayyip Erdogan is leveraging the coup as a justification to suppress dissent. The government asserts that the actions taken under the emergency rule established post-coup are essential due to the security threats confronting Turkey.

text: The United States and Israel have finalized a historic military assistance agreement worth $38 billion, marking the largest military aid package in the history of U.S. support. Announced on Wednesday, this landmark deal will provide Israel with military aid over the next ten years. According to a senior U.S. official, the agreement will enable Israel, a key ally in the Middle East, to enhance the capabilities of most of its fighter jets, boost the mobility of its ground forces, and reinforce its missile defense systems. Although this package represents the most extensive military aid ever provided by the U.S. to any nation, it comes with concessions from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as indicated by officials from both nations. These concessions include Israel's commitment to refrain from requesting additional funding from Congress beyond what is secured annually in this new arrangement, and to gradually eliminate a special provision that permitted Israel to allocate a portion of its U.S. aid to its own defense sector rather than exclusively on American-made military equipment. The prolonged negotiations that stretched over nearly ten months highlighted the ongoing tensions between President Barack Obama and Netanyahu, particularly regarding last year's U.S.-brokered nuclear agreement with Iran, Israel's principal adversary, which Netanyahu opposed. Additionally, the U.S. and Israel have had disagreements regarding the Palestinian situation. Nevertheless, Netanyahu, representing the right-wing perspective, opted to establish a new agreement with Obama, who will be leaving office in January, instead of waiting for potentially more favorable conditions from the upcoming U.S. administration, as suggested by officials from both sides. This new agreement allows him to bypass uncertainties related to the next president, whether it be Democrat Hillary Clinton or Republican Donald Trump, while also enabling Israel's defense sector to strategize for the future. Obama’s administration aimed to finalize a new deal before the conclusion of his presidency, viewing it as a crucial aspect of his legacy. Critics from the Republican party have accused him of being insufficiently attentive to Israel's security needs, a charge that the White House has firmly rejected, asserting that he has been overly stringent with Netanyahu. The $38 billion memorandum of understanding spans U.S. fiscal years 2019-2028, succeeding the existing $30 billion MOU established in 2007, which will conclude at the end of fiscal year 2018. In a written statement, Obama expressed, "Prime Minister Netanyahu and I are confident that the new MOU will significantly enhance Israel's security in what continues to be a perilous region." The agreement was formalized at the State Department, with U.S. Undersecretary of State Thomas Shannon and Jacob Nagel, acting head of Netanyahu’s national security council, signing the document. As outlined in a White House “fact sheet,” the agreement encompasses: - annual payments of $3.3 billion in foreign military financing - $500 million annually for funding Israeli missile defense, marking the first time this amount has been officially included in the aid agreement. - A phase-out of a long-standing arrangement that has allowed Israel to use 26.3 percent of the U.S. aid for its domestic defense industry rather than solely for American-made weapons. - The removal of an established provision that has permitted Israel to allocate approximately 13 percent of the U.S. aid for military fuel purchases. - The funding will enable Israel to modernize “the lion's share” of its fighter jets, including the acquisition of additional F-35 Joint Strike Fighters. Israel is slated to receive 33 F-35 aircraft, with the first two set to be delivered in December.

text: A fatal air strike struck the government-controlled Qusur area of Deir al-Zor city in eastern Syria, resulting in over a dozen fatalities, as reported by Syrian state television and a war monitoring group on Monday. According to state TV, the air raid was conducted by jets from a U.S.-led international coalition engaged in the fight against Islamic State, claiming it resulted in the deaths of 14 civilians and left 32 others injured. However, a representative from the coalition stated on Tuesday that they had not executed such an air strike, noting that their only operation in the recent weeks occurred in September on the opposite side of the Euphrates River from the city. The British-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the war monitoring organization, indicated that the identity of the aircraft involved in the strike remains unknown, but reported that at least 22 individuals were killed. The Syrian military, with support from Russia, Iran, and Shiite militias, is engaged in combat against Islamic State in Deir al-Zor city and in the surrounding rural areas. Both Syrian and Russian air forces have been targeting Islamic State positions in that region. The U.S.-backed coalition has been carrying out air strikes against Islamic State to assist the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), an alliance of Kurdish and Arab militias located to the east of Deir al-Zor across the Euphrates River. In recent months, the competing offensives supported by the U.S. and the Syrian army against Islamic State have encountered confrontations as they have advanced against the jihadists to reclaim territory in eastern Syria. Both the U.S. and Russia have indicated they maintain communication to avert potential conflicts or violence between the two military operations.

State television said jets from a U.S.-led international coalition battling Islamic State carried out the air strike and that it killed 14 civilians and wounded 32 others.  A spokesman for the coalition said on Tuesday it had not carried out such a raid, and that its only strike in the vicinity in recent weeks took place in September across the Euphrates from the city. The war monitor, the Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, reported that it was not known which aircraft carried out the strike, but that at least 22 people were killed.  The Syrian army, backed by Russia, Iran and Shi ite militias, is fighting Islamic State in the city of Deir al-Zor, as well as in parts of the surrounding countryside.

text: LONDON (Reuters) - The UK is optimistic about quickly reaching an agreement on a transitional framework for its exit from the European Union, as stated by Prime Minister Theresa May's spokesperson on Tuesday, despite ongoing significant disagreements regarding the Brexit timeline. The UK is pursuing a so-called implementation phase lasting approximately two years after its departure from the EU in March 2019, during which access to the EU single market would remain largely the same while new arrangements are established. Businesses are eager to receive the specifics of such an arrangement promptly to eliminate uncertainty regarding the trading regulations they will encounter post-Brexit. Regarding the general outline of an implementation period, we believe that reaching an agreement can be accomplished swiftly, the spokesperson mentioned. However, he did not elaborate on the anticipated timeline for finalizing such an agreement. We are determined to achieve this implementation period, confident that we can do so, and our main focus is to ensure certainty for businesses, he added. On Monday, May caused some confusion among businesses by indicating that any implementation period would only be finalized once an agreement was made regarding the future trading relationship between the UK and the EU. This contradicted earlier expectations that a transitional arrangement would be established well ahead of any trade agreement. It also underscored the existing disparity between the UK and the EU concerning the timeline for reaching a trade deal. The UK is aiming for an ambitious trade agreement with the EU to succeed the current arrangement at the conclusion of the implementation period. The UK is convinced that its existing strong connections with the EU will facilitate an agreement by October 2018. Conversely, the EU's chief negotiator, Michel Barnier, indicated that negotiating a trade agreement would require three years, suggesting that if discussions commence in December, the deal would be ready by the conclusion of a transition period extending to December 2020. In response to a question about whether the UK still believes it could secure a trade agreement by the end of next year within the two-year exit framework, May's spokesperson affirmed: Yes. An EU official, commenting on the timeline put forth by the UK, remarked that the bloc aims to establish a framework for its future relationship by this time next year, ensuring that a withdrawal treaty could reflect that future in accordance with the Article 50 legal exit process. However, the official noted that the EU will only engage in negotiations regarding the specifics of a free trade agreement after the UK has officially exited in March 2019, due to the EU's regulations that prohibit negotiations on trade agreements with its own member states. Article 50 stipulates that the withdrawal agreement must consider our future relationship, thus we will know the terms of our partnership with the EU by the time of our exit, a spokesperson for May stated in response to the EU official's position. However, regarding the specifics, those are open to negotiation, and I cannot anticipate those details.

text: SEOUL/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - South Korea stated on Tuesday that U.S. President-elect Donald Trump’s "clear warning" to North Korea indicates his recognition of the urgent threat presented by North Korea’s nuclear program and his commitment to a policy of sanctions against the reclusive nation. On Sunday, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un claimed that his country, which possesses nuclear capabilities, was nearing the test launch of an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), raising concerns that parts of the United States could be within its range. Trump dismissed this assertion by tweeting, "It won’t happen." The South Korean Foreign Ministry remarked that Trump’s statement, his first reference to the North Korean nuclear dilemma since the November U.S. elections, could be seen as a "clear warning" to North Korea. Ministry spokesperson Cho June-hyuck noted at a briefing, "Through our proactive engagement, President-elect Trump and U.S. officials are evidently cognizant of the seriousness and urgency of the North Korean nuclear threat. They are holding a firm position regarding the necessity for sanctions on North Korea and for strong collaboration between South Korea and the United States." The U.S. State Department acknowledged that North Korea persists in its pursuit of nuclear and ballistic missile technology. "At this moment, we do not believe he has the capability to equip one of these (missiles) with a nuclear warhead... but we are aware that he continues to aspire to possess such capabilities, and the programs are advancing in that direction," State Department spokesperson John Kirby informed reporters. While Trump has not yet specified a policy for North Korea, he expressed during the U.S. election campaign a willingness to engage in dialogue with its leader, Kim, if the opportunity arises. Trump’s spokesperson Kellyanne Conway indicated on ABC’s "Good Morning America" that the president-elect was "putting North Korea on notice through this tweet and other statements that this won’t happen." "As the president of the United States, he seeks to position himself between them and their missile capabilities, which experts suggest could potentially reach Seattle almost immediately," Conway stated. She added that Trump had not disclosed how he might react to North Korea’s nuclear weapons and missile initiatives and "won’t before he’s inaugurated." "We are aware that there are potential sanctions," Conway mentioned. "They haven’t always been effective. I believe China must play a significant role in this matter as well." Trump has criticized China regarding this issue. On Monday, he stated that China has profited from its economic relations with the United States but has not utilized its influence to assist in controlling North Korea. In response, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Geng Shuang asserted that China has been advocating for the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. "China’s contributions in this regard are clearly evident," Geng told a news briefing. "As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, we have actively engaged in relevant discussions concerning the North Korean nuclear situation and have collectively passed several resolutions with other parties. This demonstrates China’s responsible stance." When asked about Trump’s perspective that China was failing to help contain North Korea’s nuclear ambitions, State Department spokesperson Kirby replied, "We would not concur with that evaluation." The United States has long rejected North Korean requests for dialogue, insisting that disarmament must precede any negotiations. In response to two North Korean nuclear tests and various missile tests last year, the United States and its ally South Korea have implemented increasingly stringent sanctions. The U.N. Security Council enacted new sanctions against North Korea at the end of November following Pyongyang’s fifth and largest nuclear test to date in September. A fully developed North Korean ICBM could pose a threat to the continental United States, which lies approximately 9,000 km (5,500 miles) away from North Korea. ICBMs have a minimum operational range of about 5,500 km (3,400 miles), although some are designed to exceed that distance.

text: The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday seemed inclined to decide that property owners have the right to challenge the federal government in court regarding the necessity of permits under a national water protection legislation in a case concerning a company's intentions for a peat mine in Minnesota. The court listened to a one-hour argument in a matter weighing property rights against environmental regulations, specifically the significant 1972 U.S. Clean Water Act. A majority of the eight justices appeared to be in favor of Hawkes Co Inc, a company based in North Dakota, which is contesting an Obama administration determination that its land contains wetlands. According to the law, property owners are required to obtain permits in such cases. Determining whether a specific piece of land is subject to the law's authority is crucial for developers and other landowners since such a designation initiates a protracted and costly permitting procedure. Attorneys for Hawkes contended that the company ought to have the opportunity to dispute the necessity of undergoing the permit process. Justices from both liberal and conservative backgrounds voiced concerns about the current system's strain on property owners. Chief Justice John Roberts, a conservative, remarked that applicants who ignore a government determination requiring a permit do so at "great practical risk." Liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg described the process as "very arduous and very expensive." Furthermore, Liberal Justice Stephen Breyer mentioned that the government's conclusion that Hawkes required a permit is "perfectly suited for review in the courts." The only justice expressing support for the government was liberal Elena Kagan, who raised worries about how a ruling in favor of property owners could affect actions by other government entities, such as the Securities and Exchange Commission. Advocates for property rights noted that the permitting process can extend for two years and incur costs as high as $270,000, with owners facing fines of up to $37,500 per day for noncompliance. Business organizations, including the National Association of Home Builders and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, along with 29 states, submitted court documents opposing the Obama administration in this case. This litigation follows the justices' unanimous decision in 2012, which allowed property owners facing enforcement actions under the Clean Water Act to seek court intervention before being compelled to comply or incur financial penalties. Last year, the Obama administration established a new rule that clarifies the extent of federal jurisdiction over water bodies. A federal appeals court suspended the rule after it was contested by 18 states. Following the February death of Justice Antonin Scalia, only eight justices participated in the case. A decision is expected by the end of June.

text: Paul Manafort, the former campaign manager for President Donald Trump who has been indicted, allocated nearly $1 million on eight rugs over a span of two years and over $1.3 million on clothing purchased from retailers in Beverly Hills, California, and New York City. His extravagant lifestyle, including residences in Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Hamptons, Arlington, Virginia, and other locations, was outlined in an indictment submitted to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, which was disclosed on Monday. The indictment from Justice Department Special Counsel Robert Mueller indicated that Manafort "utilized his concealed overseas wealth to lead a luxurious lifestyle in the United States." Prosecutors uncovered transactions involving payments made by Manafort for four Range Rovers and a Mercedes-Benz that they claimed were illegally funded from overseas to evade U.S. income taxes, according to the 31-page court document. They also discovered evidence that he purchased a condominium in a renovated red-brick structure in the affluent Soho area of New York for $2.85 million, also funded by overseas money, predominantly from Cyprus. On Monday, Manafort and his associate Rick Gates entered not guilty pleas to charges of money laundering and other offenses in connection with an investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. Both Manafort and Gates maintained a composed demeanor during the court proceedings on Monday. Greg Andres, a federal prosecutor on Mueller’s team, noted that determining the net worth of Manafort and Gates presented challenges, complicating the process of establishing suitable bail conditions. Andres mentioned that Manafort declared a wide range of net asset values on various financial documents, estimating them between $20 million and $100 million. In contrast, Gates reported assets ranging from $2 million to $30 million. A federal judge mandated house arrest for both individuals, setting an unsecured bond of $10 million for Manafort and $5 million for Gates. On Monday, Manafort’s attorney Kevin Downing stated that there was no proof that his client had colluded with the Russian government during his tenure with the Trump campaign. The indictment did not mention either Trump or his campaign. Manafort managed the Trump campaign from June to August 2016 before stepping down amid allegations of receiving millions in illegal payments from a pro-Russian political party in Ukraine. The indictment claimed that both Manafort and Gates earned tens of millions of dollars from their work in Ukraine and laundered funds through numerous U.S. and foreign entities to conceal payments from American authorities. The indictment detailed that he spent $849,215 at a men's clothing store in New York and $520,440 at another in Beverly Hills. Furthermore, he paid $5,434,793 for a residence in Water Mill, New York, situated in Long Island’s Hamptons, including $820,240 for landscaping. Aerial images of the property reveal gardens, a swimming pool, a tennis court, a basketball court, and a putting green along with a sand trap on 2.37 acres (0.96 hectare). A seven-bedroom brownstone in Brooklyn that he acquired for $3 million was characterized in a real estate listing as "dripping with detail - perfectly intact crown moldings and medallions, gold leafed carved window detail, five marble mantels, and original Lincrusta paper wall covering."

text: EU summit venue closed for another week due to toxic fumes. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - The location that hosts EU summits, which had to shift locations last week due to toxic fumes, will remain closed for an additional week as investigations aim to address the issue. Fumes emanating from the drains have necessitated the evacuation of the Europa Building, also referred to as The Egg, on two occasions this month, including prior to the EU leaders' summit held on Thursday and Friday. This new facility was inaugurated in January amid debates regarding its cost of 321 million euros ($378 million). In the interim, staff and meetings will be relocated to the adjacent Justus Lipsius building until the situation is rectified. text: TALLINN (Reuters) - This month, European Union nations are set to discuss intensifying pressure on Poland regarding concerns about its democracy, according to sources. This discussion represents the next phase in a process that might lead to a formal condemnation of its government for being anti-democratic. The Law and Justice (PiS) party, which governs Warsaw, has enacted reforms impacting the judiciary and media that critics within the EU argue have undermined democratic principles. PiS counters these critiques, claiming that Brussels is exceeding its authority and insists that it has substantial support for its reforms among Poland's population of 38 million, a leading economy in former communist eastern Europe. Following over a year of escalating pressure from the European Commission, the executive body on Wednesday requested the bloc's 28 EU affairs ministers to address its concerns on September 25, the day following Germany’s national elections. The Commission's deputy leader, Frans Timmermans, will brief the ministers on his ongoing but unsuccessful attempts to convince Warsaw to alter its stance, as per the sources. German Chancellor Angela Merkel has added her voice to the increasing calls for stronger measures against Poland and has discussed the issue with the Commission's president, Jean-Claude Juncker. If Warsaw maintains its firm position, it could ultimately jeopardize receiving substantial EU funding, which is contributed by its wealthier counterparts, a discussion that is intensifying within the bloc. Currently, the EU possesses limited mechanisms to act. However, it could invoke Article 7, which would require the other 27 EU nations to officially declare that the rule of law is at risk in Poland—an unprecedented move in the history of the EU. Timmermans has established a definitive boundary by stating that Article 7 proceedings would commence if Warsaw begins to dismiss judges from the country’s Supreme Court as part of the judicial reform. This conflict underscores Warsaw's increasing isolation within the EU since the eurosceptic PiS took power in 2015 and highlights a growing east-west divide within the bloc. Initiating Article 7 would be a significant embarrassment for Poland, yet its regional ally Hungary—led by Viktor Orban, who also has a history of conflicts with Brussels—has indicated it would veto any sanctions against Poland under this punitive framework. In the west, there is a rising frustration over the escalating disputes with Warsaw, which also involve issues related to migration and environmental policies, leading some to express renewed skepticism about the 2004 EU enlargement that incorporated eight former communist nations into the union. Meanwhile, in Poland, opposition parties are raising alarms that PiS is abandoning core EU values and could ultimately threaten Poland's EU membership, which has brought the nation billions of euros and secured its place in the western sphere following decades of communism enforced by Moscow after World War Two. Nevertheless, PiS has effectively gathered its supporters around the narrative of defending Poland’s national interests against EU mandates, similarly to how Orban has framed his own confrontations with the bloc to his electorate. The immediate consequence is that Warsaw is losing political clout within the EU and is finding it more challenging to influence the bloc's policies, despite being the sixth most populous state and the fifth largest after Britain's exit.

text: BARCELONA - Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy has called on the people of Catalonia to participate in large numbers in the upcoming election scheduled for December, aiming to restore stability to a region that has faced challenges in its efforts to separate from Spain. During his first trip to Barcelona since the Spanish government implemented direct rule over Catalonia and dismissed its separatist leaders, Rajoy emphasized that the election on December 21 would protect the economy and prevent businesses from relocating away from this economically pivotal area. "We want a substantial turnout to initiate a new political chapter characterized by tranquility, normalcy, coexistence, and respect," Rajoy remarked to the Catalan branch of his conservative People's Party (PP). "It is imperative that we promptly restore normalcy to Catalonia... to alleviate social tensions and avert economic damage." Despite the opposition to the early election enforced by Madrid as a means to address the political deadlock, the two main pro-independence parties, PDeCAT, associated with ousted leader Carles Puigdemont, and the ERC, have confirmed their participation. Nonetheless, they were unable to come to an agreement to present a united front, which could undermine the separatist coalition's prospects of securing a majority in the regional parliament. The far-left pro-independence CUP party, whose backing was crucial for Puigdemont's administration, decided on Sunday to contest in the forthcoming election. The enforcement of direct rule by Madrid has deepened divisions between political entities, both in regional governance and at the local level. On Sunday, the party led by Ada Colau, the Mayor of Barcelona, voted to terminate its governing alliance with the Catalan Socialist Party (PSC), citing the latter’s support for the enforcement of direct rule. A poll conducted for the newspaper El Pais indicates that around 54 percent of Spaniards view Madrid's management of the Catalan crisis positively, while only 28 percent of Catalans share this perspective. On Saturday, 750,000 individuals marched through Barcelona, advocating for the release of separatist leaders currently held in pre-trial detention.

text: On Thursday, President Barack Obama emphasized the necessity for Congress to put aside political differences and take action to secure further funding to fight the Zika virus before financial resources are depleted. At a news conference held at the Pentagon, Obama stated, "Our experts at the CDC, the folks on the front lines have been doing their best in making due by moving funds from other areas, but now the money we need to fight Zika is rapidly running out." He cautioned that if Congress does not allocate additional funds, the development of a vaccine for the virus could face delays and encouraged Americans to reach out to their legislators to urge them to address the matter. The concern regarding Zika, which can lead to a birth defect known as microcephaly characterized by a smaller head size that can result in significant developmental challenges for infants, has intensified since Florida officials identified the initial indications of local transmission in the continental United States last week. Zika funding remains in limbo six months after Obama requested the Republican-controlled Congress to approve $1.9 billion in emergency resources. On Thursday, 41 Democratic U.S. senators sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and House Speaker Paul Ryan, calling for lawmakers to return from their summer break to vote on emergency funding to combat the virus. However, Ryan accused Democrats of hindering the funding process and claimed that the Obama administration had not effectively utilized the available funds to curb the spread of the mosquito-borne virus. Congressional records show that Congress has interrupted its own recesses at least eight times since 1998, with the most recent instance occurring in 2013 when lawmakers returned early to discuss military action in Syria. The latest exchanges of blame suggested a slim likelihood that lawmakers would shorten their seven-week summer hiatus for a vote on Zika funding. A compromise proposal of $1.1 billion was unsuccessful after House Republicans attached provisions that would impose restrictions on abortion and defund portions of Obama’s notable 2010 healthcare legislation. Senate Democrats, who blocked this proposal twice prior to Congress’s departure from Washington last month, are insisting that Republicans agree to a new funding plan that eliminates those stipulations, which Republicans have rejected. In an opinion piece published in the USA Today newspaper, Ryan expressed, "We need the White House and Senate Democrats to drop politics and put the public’s health first. We hope for a change of heart, and soon." Don Stewart, a spokesperson for McConnell, encouraged Democrats to permit the current bill to pass through unanimous consent during a brief session on Friday.

text: Merkel sees no justification for resignation; aims to establish a stable government. BERLIN (Reuters) - On Monday, German Chancellor Angela Merkel expressed that she found no grounds to resign following the breakdown of negotiations concerning a three-party coalition government, asserting that her conservative faction would approach any forthcoming elections with greater unity than before. In an interview with German broadcaster ZDF, Merkel indicated her willingness to serve an additional four years as chancellor, emphasizing the necessity of conveying a message of stability for Germany, Europe, and the globe. When queried about the potential for another grand coalition with the Social Democrats, Merkel stated she would await the party's feedback after their discussions with President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Wednesday. However, she remarked that any calls for her resignation would not be a constructive way to initiate a new coalition. She expressed disappointment regarding the pro-business Free Democrats' decision to withdraw from the coalition discussions but did not anticipate the party reversing its stance.

text: Switzerland is willing to step in as a mediator to assist in addressing the crisis in North Korea, as stated by Swiss President Doris Leuthard on Monday. Leuthard mentioned that Swiss military personnel are stationed in the demarcation area separating South Korea from North Korea, and she highlighted her nation’s longstanding tradition of neutral and discreet diplomatic efforts, shared with Sweden. This history includes Switzerland advocating for U.S. interests in both Iran and Cuba. However, she emphasized that both China and the United States must accept their responsibilities, cautioning against excessive reactions following North Korea's sixth and most significant nuclear test. According to Leuthard, sanctions have not significantly influenced Pyongyang's decision to relinquish its weapons programs, despite the hardships faced by its citizens. "I believe it is truly time for dialogue," she remarked during a news conference held in Berne. "We are prepared to fulfill our role as a mediator. Speaking in Brussels, the envoy, Anthony Gardner, cautioned the incoming U.S. president against the irrationality of supporting the disintegration of the EU, suggesting that Farage may have created a false narrative that other nations would likely exit the bloc following Britain’s departure. Gardner, who has overseen U.S.-EU relations for the past three years, made these candid remarks during a press briefing held on Friday, just a week before Trump has mandated that all individuals appointed by Obama must resign. In light of Trump’s positive reception of the British decision to leave the EU and Farage's perceived influence within Trump’s circle, Gardner remarked: “For us to be the cheerleaders of Brexit and to be encouraging Brexit Mark 2, Mark 3, is the height of folly.” He noted that Farage, who serves as an EU lawmaker and is an ally of Trump, had recently contacted him to arrange a meeting. Gardner expressed that Farage's perspectives were completely contrary to his own and believed that Farage had provided misleading information to Trump’s transition team regarding the EU’s situation. Reflecting on the inquiries made to EU institutions by Trump’s aides in recent weeks, Gardner stated: “That was the one question that was asked - basically, ‘What’s the next country to leave?’. Which is kind of suggesting that the place is about to fall apart.” He characterized this as indicative of a widespread misperception, one that Farage seems to be promoting in Washington, describing it as a caricature. Gardner asserted that it would be deeply misguided for the United States to treat the EU as “dysfunctional” and instead concentrate solely on traditional allies like Britain and Germany. “We should not depart from 50 years of foreign policy with regard to the EU,” he emphasized. “We should not become the cheerleaders for Brexit, particularly if Brexit appears more likely to be a hard, disorderly unmanaged Brexit.” He further stated, “A hard Brexit or a fragmentation of the European market would be very bad news for American business,” adding, “They’ve understood it ... and we need to make the case.” Gardner called on both Europeans and the new U.S. administration to maintain a united front on sanctions against Russia in response to the situation in Ukraine, noting that Trump has expressed a desire for improved relations with Moscow after taking office next Friday.
