text: Libyans exchange jewelry for medical care as the crisis worsens. TRIPOLI (Reuters) - In a square located behind Libya's central bank, black market traders, some armed, transport small plastic bags filled with dollars and larger ones with dinars in and out of numerous informal exchange locations. These traders procure food and other products from abroad at the official exchange rate and then sell them at a higher unofficial rate, reaping considerable profits; others earn similarly large amounts by smuggling subsidized fuel out of the country. Meanwhile, in the narrow streets of the old city, common citizens are selling their jewelry or dollars hidden away at home as the impact of six years of post-dictatorship turmoil becomes increasingly evident. "I haven't received a salary in four months," stated Fatima, 40, from the southern city of Sabha, as she traded three small gold charms to cover her sister Hasina's diabetes treatment, who remarked, "We feel powerless; there’s nothing else we can do." Other indicators of increasing poverty include elderly women pleading with drivers for money on the streets of Tripoli and families lining up for charitable food distributions. The United Nations has estimated that approximately 1.3 million individuals in Libya require humanitarian aid this year. The situation deteriorated further in the past fortnight as the black market dinar rate, which has been at historic lows for a long time, dropped again, exacerbating inflation that is already between 25-30 percent. The central bank has held the audit bureau and the U.N.-backed government accountable for limiting letters of credit that finance essential supplies to a fractured nation where a lack of security and smuggling operations have destabilized the broader region. Officials have encountered questionable requests - one attempting to import tuna valued at $120,000, which exceeds the nation's annual consumption, according to a Libyan entrepreneur who chose to remain unnamed due to fears of retaliation from Libya's influential armed groups. Only $2.5 billion of the anticipated $7.4 billion in credit has been distributed, the trader mentioned, causing the dinar to drop from roughly 8.5 to 9.25 against the dollar in the black market. Its worth has plummeted by over 600 percent since early 2014. The economy ministry was not immediately reachable for commentary regarding a complicated credit system that flows through commercial banks, where the audit bureau had recorded previous abuses and insufficient oversight. "We are facing an extremely dire economic and financial scenario," stated Central Bank Governor Sadiq al-Kabir during a rare press conference on Tuesday. "All parties, whether legislative or executive, share equal responsibility." Traders and economists assert that political instability is a significant factor undermining the currency, with U.N. discussions aimed at negotiating an agreement between conflicting factions currently halted. Libya is struggling to finance food imports and safeguard its foreign reserves, which the World Bank predicts will reach $67.5 billion by year’s end, down from $123.5 billion in 2012. International experts contend that the only viable solution is to devalue the dinar from the official exchange rate of 1.37 to the dollar, but reaching a consensus on an economic plan in a country dominated by armed groups with competing governments and no budgets is a challenging endeavor. A powerful or well-connected minority benefiting from a thriving shadow economy has little motivation for change. The central bank did not provide comments on devaluation, but economists and diplomats indicate that the bank is hesitant to devalue without a strategic plan to address the ensuing shock. This year, Libya has managed to increase oil production to around 1 million barrels per day, but output remains significantly below pre-2011 uprising levels that led to the ousting of Muammar Gaddafi. Revenues, which typically account for about 80 percent of gross domestic product, are primarily used for salaries, including those of armed factions that were added to the state payroll for their involvement in the uprising. Subsidies include an annual fuel subsidy exceeding $4 billion, among the most generous globally.

text: Demonstrators across the country are expressing their opposition to the influence of substantial financial contributions in U.S. politics. BOSTON/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Protesters identifying as conservative and independent, drawing inspiration from the presidential campaigns of Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders, poured fake donations into Boston Harbor on Friday, part of approximately 30 coordinated protests nationwide aimed at addressing the issue of money in politics. In Washington, law enforcement apprehended 142 individuals from a more progressive group known as Democracy Spring, including 12 who shackled themselves within the Capitol Rotunda to draw attention to the sway of special interests and to criticize legislation that makes voting more challenging. This week, nearly 1,000 participants in Democracy Spring have been arrested in Washington. The week-long demonstrations in Washington, along with Friday's nationwide events organized by the activist group Represent.Us, have resonated with the voter dissatisfaction evident during the presidential campaign. "There are numerous perfectly legal ways to bribe a politician, from super PACs (political action committees) to lucrative job offers and campaign donations," stated Charlotte Hill, the communications director for Represent.Us. The organization, which advocates for anti-corruption measures in various American cities, claims it does not support or oppose any presidential candidate. Represent.Us announced plans to hold events in 33 cities. Trump, a wealthy Republican, and Sanders, who identifies as a democratic socialist seeking the Democratic nomination, have both criticized the impact of significant campaign contributions during their unexpected bids for the presidency. "It is irrelevant whether you are conservative or progressive. Two hundred and forty-three years after the original Boston Tea Party, Americans across the political spectrum continue to grapple with taxation without representation," remarked Dan Krassner, political director of Represent.Us. Approximately 40 activists participated in a symbolic reenactment of the Boston Tea Party at the location where American colonists once discarded tea into the harbor in protest of British taxation. Activists from Represent.Us threw a pile of wooden crates into the water, symbolizing campaign donations. In Washington on Friday, Democracy Spring participants attached themselves to scaffolding in the Capitol Rotunda. "We the people insist on a democracy that is free from the corrupting influence of big money and voter suppression," the demonstrators chanted together. text: A rescue package for Puerto Rico moved closer to a complete House vote on Wednesday, as U.S. lawmakers expressed their support for a strategy aimed at alleviating the territory's severe debt and stimulating economic growth. This development suggests that the proposal could reach the House of Representatives for a vote in the coming days. The House Natural Resources Committee approved the initiative with a vote tally of 29-10, keeping most of the provisions favored by House Speaker Paul Ryan unchanged. The initiative would grant authority to a federal oversight board to negotiate with creditors and determine the recovery amounts for the approximately $70 billion that investors have lent to the island. According to a statement from Ryan's office on Wednesday, taxpayer funds will not be used for this rescue, thereby avoiding a bailout. Puerto Rico's Governor, Alejandro Garcia Padilla, commended the legislation for its provisions aimed at tackling insolvency, safeguarding essential services, and promoting economic growth. Nevertheless, he reiterated his concerns regarding the extensive powers granted to the oversight board. "Puerto Ricans are Americans and our democratic rights need to be protected, just like those of American citizens living on the mainland, and the oversight provisions do not meet that obligation," he stated, urging Ryan to modify the bill before it is presented to the full House for voting. According to the proposal, creditors will be barred from suing Puerto Rico while the oversight board is operational, and all of the island's creditors may experience losses, despite recent lobbying efforts by Wall Street groups. Among the Republicans who voted on Wednesday, more than half supported the rescue initiative, although a vocal minority cautioned that it could diminish investor interest in municipal bonds and compel issuers to provide higher yields. "Taxpayers across the country will have to pay ... as markets adjust to this new world," warned Congressman Tom McClintock from California. text: The White House has proposed to revive the Yucca Mountain nuclear waste facility. This project has faced years of delays due to legal challenges and local opposition. This initiative indicates that President Donald Trump may believe that solutions for nuclear waste could prolong the operational lifespan of current U.S. nuclear power plants and accelerate advancements in next-generation nuclear facilities, which proponents argue are safer than older reactor designs. "I will collaborate closely with you and the members of this committee to find solutions to this issue." text: MILWAUKEE (Reuters) - A federal court ruled on Monday that the Republican manipulation of district maps in Wisconsin was unconstitutional, aimed at disadvantaging Democrats to secure victories in the state elections of 2012 and 2014. The decision by the United States District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin, made with a 2-1 vote, concluded that Act 43, which involved the redistricting approved by the Republican-controlled legislature in 2012, contravened the U.S. Constitution, according to court documents. "The discriminatory impact cannot be accounted for by Wisconsin's political geography, nor is it backed by any legitimate state interest," the court stated in its judgment. This case does not affect Donald Trump’s win in Wisconsin during the presidential election on November 8, where he defeated Democrat Hillary Clinton. Wisconsin Attorney General Brad Schimel announced he intends to appeal, which would escalate the case to the U.S. Supreme Court. A ruling from the Supreme Court regarding gerrymandering—the practice of altering electoral boundaries for political gain—could have significant consequences nationwide, as similar cases from Maryland and North Carolina progress through lower courts. Richard Hasen, an expert in election law at the University of California, Irvine, commented on his blog, "This is a significant win for those advocating for judicial limitations on partisan gerrymandering. However, it remains uncertain what the Supreme Court will decide on this matter." Since 2010, Republicans have significantly increased their dominance in state legislatures, holding control of both chambers in a record 32 states, as reported by the New York Times. Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos stated, "Republicans achieve electoral success due to superior candidates and a message that resonates with voters." A group of twelve Wisconsin voters contended in their lawsuit that the Republicans redrew the maps in 2011 to fragment Democratic voters, preventing them from attaining a majority in various districts, and to concentrate Democratic voters in certain areas, ensuring they win by large margins while diminishing the overall votes of Democrats across the state, as noted in the ruling. Although Democrats garnered 51 percent of the statewide vote in 2012, they secured only 39 out of 99 Assembly seats. In the 2014 elections, Republicans received a similar percentage of the statewide vote yet won 63 seats, resulting in a 24-seat gap, according to the judges. The Wisconsin case was based on a novel metric for evaluating the discriminatory impact of gerrymandering. The "efficiency gap" analysis revealed that the redistricting in Wisconsin led to a greater waste of votes for Democrats compared to Republicans. Barry Burden, director of the Elections Research Center at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, explained to the New York Times that this measure provides judges with "a clear benchmark for determining what is permissible."

text: According to Hurriyet newspaper, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has urged the mayors of three key cities to step down, which includes the well-known mayor of Ankara, the capital. This request was reported on Thursday as part of his efforts to rejuvenate his ruling party in anticipation of the 2019 elections. Erdogan's remarks represent his most direct call for a change among long-serving politicians, many of whom hold national recognition, following the rejection by voters in several cities of an April referendum that would have granted him extensive powers. Although Erdogan narrowly succeeded in the referendum aimed at altering the constitution to establish an executive presidency, voters in 17 of Turkey's 30 largest cities opposed the amendment. Since that time, Erdogan has emphasized the necessity for renewal within local governance and the ruling AK Party, referring to indications of 'metal fatigue' within the administrations. The newspaper reported that a request had been made for the resignation of the mayor of Balikesir, located in northwestern Turkey. Similarly, this request was communicated to (Ankara Mayor) Melih (Gokcek), as well as regarding Bursa, he was quoted as saying. Bursa is situated in northwestern Turkey. In the past month, the mayor of Istanbul has resigned, along with the mayor of Duzce city in northwestern Turkey. Additionally, the mayor of Nigde city in central Turkey stepped down on Wednesday. However, Gokcek, who has held the position of Ankara mayor since 1994 and has won five consecutive elections, has yet to resign, despite rampant speculation that he would do so. text: Obama expresses hope for swift reconciliation within the Democratic Party following a challenging primary. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Wednesday, President Barack Obama conveyed his hopes that the rifts among Democrats would begin to mend in the upcoming weeks, now that his former Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton, has secured the party’s nomination for the presidential election scheduled on November 8. "I hope that over the next few weeks we can come together," Obama remarked in his initial public comments following Clinton's primary victories on Tuesday in California and other locations, which solidified her lead over competitor Bernie Sanders after a lengthy and intense campaign. "During primaries, things can get a bit ouchy," Obama shared with NBC late-night host Jimmy Fallon during a taping of "The Tonight Show," set to broadcast on Thursday. Sanders, who has yet to concede the contest, is expected to meet with Obama at the White House on Thursday at 11:15 a.m. (1515 GMT). Subsequently, at a fundraising event held in the Central Park West residence of Kenneth Lerer, a venture capitalist and head of BuzzFeed, Obama stated he was "not overly concerned" about any "bruised feelings" stemming from the primary. "We just concluded - or sort of concluded - our primary season," Obama acknowledged, correcting himself as the audience of about 60 Democratic donors, who contributed up to $33,400 to attend, chuckled nervously. "I am worried about us undertaking the essential, hands-on work of mobilizing voters, especially among young individuals and low-income communities," Obama noted. When inquired whether he believed Sanders, a senator from Vermont, should promptly withdraw from the race, White House spokesman Josh Earnest affirmed that the senator had "more than earned the right to determine the path of his own campaign." The official vote on Clinton’s nomination will take place at the party’s convention in Philadelphia at the end of July. Obama informed Fallon that "having a contested primary was beneficial for the Democratic Party" and commended Sanders for the "significant energy and fresh ideas" he contributed to the campaign. "He challenged the party and pushed them. I found it made Hillary a stronger candidate," Obama remarked. The White House has indicated that Obama, who enjoys widespread popularity among Democrats, will serve a unifying function on the campaign trail. "My primary role in this process will be to remind the American public that this is a serious job. This is not reality TV," Obama told Fallon, alluding to presumptive Republican nominee and real estate mogul Donald Trump, who gained fame through a reality television series.

text: Trump's nominee for the head of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services stated on Tuesday during a congressional hearing that he does not endorse the privatization of Medicare, while also defending his ethical track record. Addressing the Senate Committee on Finance, one of the two committees overseeing the health department, Representative Tom Price expressed that his stance aligns with President Donald Trump's, who has indicated his desire to protect the federal health program for seniors. "I want to assure the Medicare beneficiaries of this nation that they need not worry," he remarked. "We are eager to help them obtain the necessary care and coverage." text: LOME (Reuters) - On Thursday, security personnel in Togo discharged live rounds and tear gas at demonstrators, resulting in injuries to at least seven individuals as they attempted to disperse tumultuous protests against the family dynasty that has ruled for 50 years in the West African center for banking and transport. Since August, activists have been rallying against President Faure Gnassingbe's unwillingness to provide a definitive timeline for his departure and to permit opposition parties to thrive in the only nation in the region that has yet to implement presidential term limits. A Reuters photographer observed armed paramilitary gendarmes driving into the crowd in trucks and unleashing clouds of tear gas. In the Lome district of Be, surrounded by dilapidated structures and palm trees, protesters erected barricades, ignited tires, and hurled stones at security personnel. "We have treated seven individuals with bullet wounds thus far," reported a physician at the Social Medical Centre in Be, where some were being bandaged. This former French colony, with a population of 8 million, hosts several major corporations, including Ecobank and regional airline ASKY, and has seen extensive port enhancements as the president aims to establish the resource-deficient nation as a commercial hub. However, a legacy of oppression and power monopolization by a single family - Faure assumed control in 2005 following the death of his father, Gnassingbe Eyadema, who had been in power for 38 years - jeopardizes its stability. Opponents of Gnassingbe argue that the reforms introduced last month, as a reaction to the protests in August, will still enable him to govern the West African nation until 2030.

text: Macau's predominantly pro-democracy opposition made minor advancements in the legislative elections, as observers noted indications of public discontent with the pro-Beijing administration following a deadly typhoon that struck the Asian gambling center a month prior. Results from Sunday’s voting, revealed on Monday, indicated that the opposition secured five seats in the 33-seat legislative assembly, one more than the previous election held four years ago, according to reports from local media. The political environment in Macau has historically been influenced by pro-establishment, pro-Beijing, and casino industry interests, and any progress made by the opposition is seen as a positive step. Only 14 of the legislative seats were filled through direct elections, a significantly lower percentage compared to neighboring Hong Kong, which, as another former colony of China, has fought more vigorously for and achieved greater democratic liberties than Macau, which transitioned from Portuguese to Chinese governance in 1999. Twelve additional seats are filled through indirect elections in smaller constituencies, while another seven are appointed by Macau's Beijing-supported leader, Fernando Chui, making it nearly impossible for the opposition to ever achieve a majority. Among the successful candidates was 26-year-old pro-democracy advocate and vocal government critic Sulu Sou, who now becomes Macau's youngest lawmaker ever. Sou played a pivotal role in leading one of Macau's largest anti-government demonstrations three years ago, when approximately 20,000 individuals protested against a proposal offering substantial compensation to outgoing officials. Subsequently, Macau’s leader, Chui, retracted the proposal. The appeal from the intelligence leaders aimed to exert pressure on lawmakers who seemed to have abandoned the initiative this week to enact legislation that would renew for several years the NSA's warrantless internet surveillance program, which is set to end on December 31. That initiative collapsed late Wednesday due to objections from a considerable coalition of Republicans and Democrats advocating for stronger privacy protections within the program, which primarily targets foreign nationals but also captures communications from an unspecified number of Americans. In place of this, House Republicans introduced a temporary funding bill on Thursday that proposes extending the surveillance law until January 19. This law, referred to as Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, is deemed crucial to national security by U.S. intelligence entities. In a joint statement, Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats, Attorney General Jeff Sessions, along with the leaders of the NSA, FBI, and CIA, stated, 'There is no substitute for Section 702,' emphasizing that not renewing this authority would facilitate foreign adversaries in 'planning attacks against our citizens and allies without detection.' Section 702 permits the NSA to gather extensive digital communications from foreign suspects residing outside the U.S. However, the program inadvertently collects communications from Americans for various technical reasons, such as when they interact with a foreign target living abroad. These communications can then be searched without a warrant, including by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Some legislators from both parties are advocating for the complete elimination or partial restriction of the U.S. government's capacity to examine data of Americans gathered under Section 702 without prior warrant approval. The intelligence leaders also condemned the current proposal to temporarily prolong the program, arguing that short-term extensions 'fail to provide certainty and will create needless and wasteful operational complications.' U.S. officials have recently acknowledged that the end-of-year deadline may not be significant due to the belief that the program can legally continue until April because of its annual certification process. text: LONDON (Reuters) - The Islamic Revolutionary Guards of Iran have taken into custody at least 30 individuals holding dual nationality over the last two years, predominantly on charges of espionage, as reported by lawyers, relatives, and diplomats. This figure is double that which has previously been reported by local and international outlets. This increase is notable compared to 2015, when an international agreement concerning nuclear matters raised expectations for improved relations with Western countries. Prior to that, the number of dual nationals detained at any given moment was typically in the low single digits. Furthermore, this trend reveals that the majority of those apprehended recently—19 out of the 30—hold European citizenship. In contrast, earlier detainees were primarily Iranian Americans. Relatives and legal representatives of those detained claim that the Guards are leveraging these individuals as pawns in diplomatic negotiations and aiming to deter European companies from pursuing business opportunities in Iran following the government's agreement with global powers to alleviate sanctions. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps possesses extensive business interests while also serving as Iran's most formidable security organization, frequently criticizing the government for awarding contracts to foreign entities. The Guards have not responded to numerous requests for comment. The Iranian government directed Reuters to the judiciary, which also failed to respond to repeated inquiries. Iranian officials have previously denied taking hostages for ransom, accusing Western nations of fabricating charges against Iranians. Relatives of dual nationals held in Iran, along with their attorneys and Western diplomats, provided details such as names, arrest dates, and charges, on the condition that neither they nor the detainees would be identified due to concerns about possible repercussions. Iran typically does not announce arrests or charges and does not recognize dual nationality, which limits the rights of these individuals to consular support as outlined in the U.N. Vienna Convention. According to the sources, the detainees have not engaged in any espionage activities and were apprehended solely due to their dual citizenship. They expressed their willingness to disclose information because they feel left in the dark by both Iranian authorities and Western governments. Several governments maintain that keeping a low profile is in the best interest of the detainees. "This very much informs our strategy," stated a source from the UK government. Dutch Foreign Ministry spokesperson Daphne Kerremans indicated that revealing the identities of detainees could jeopardize their safety. Some relatives only speak out after their initial hopes have been dashed. Vida Mehrannia, the wife of Ahmadreza Djalali, a Swedish-based Iranian scientist who was arrested in 2016 after attending a conference in Tehran, chose to voice her concerns in February. "We were all optimistic that he would be released shortly. He was calling us from prison, stating that he had not been formally charged. They told him he would be freed after answering a few questions," she recounted via telephone from Stockholm. "I made the case public to the media after nine months when he faced threats of a death sentence from a prosecutor and began a hunger strike," she continued. Djalali received a death sentence in October on espionage allegations. Swedish Foreign Minister Margot Wallstrom remarked at that time: "We will emphasize that this will impact our relationship with the EU, especially at a time when Iran and the EU need to collaborate, particularly regarding the nuclear deal we have with Iran." The agreement to lift sanctions in exchange for limits on Iran's nuclear activities was international in scope, although significant U.S. restrictions remained. Official confirmations of new arrests occasionally arise through indirect means. Records from a European Parliament session in June 2017 indicated that three Dutch-Iranian nationals were imprisoned in Iran. However, only one of these cases has been disclosed. When asked about the two unidentified cases, Dutch Foreign Ministry spokesperson Kerremans informed Reuters that those individuals were detained in November 2012 and January 2016, stating that governmental actions were primarily directed at ensuring honesty.

text: New York City has discreetly initiated the removal of certain deteriorating yellow nuclear fallout shelter signs that were affixed to numerous buildings during the 1960s, citing that many of these are misleading artifacts from the Cold War that no longer indicate operational shelters. These small metal signs are remnants of the fears surrounding the nuclear arms race between the United States and the former Soviet Union, which led U.S. President John F. Kennedy to establish the shelter program in 1961 across various cities in the nation. Featuring a simple design of three interconnected triangles within a circle, the signs became a symbol of that period. While some residents may hardly take notice of them today, for others, they serve as an unsettling reminder that although the danger has evolved and lessened, it has not completely disappeared. Despite the Cold War having concluded long ago, North Korea continues its efforts to develop nuclear-capable missiles that could reach the United States, amidst aggressive rhetoric from both Washington and Pyongyang. A nuclear detonation is now perceived as being even less probable than it was during the Cold War. However, in the event of a catastrophe, city officials and experts in disaster preparedness advise that the signs, which still exist in large numbers, should be disregarded. Following a nearby nuclear explosion, any survivors relying on the signs to guide them to safety from radioactive fallout after rushing outside would likely find themselves facing locked doors or perhaps forcing entry into what has now become a building's laundry facility or bike-storage zone. The maintenance of the shelter system, which once included federal funding to equip shelters with food and water, ceased many years ago. The decision to remove some signs from public school buildings, a move that has not been reported previously, aims to reduce potential confusion, according to the city’s Department of Education. Michael Aciman, a spokesperson for the department, confirmed that any shelters designated for fallout in the city’s schools are no longer operational and mentioned that the department plans to complete the removal of the signs from school walls by approximately January 1. Although many of the tens of thousands of fallout shelter signs installed throughout the city by the federal government’s Office of Civil Defense have disappeared as older buildings have been renovated or torn down, city officials assert that this marks the first organized effort to take them down. The Office of Civil Defense was ultimately disbanded in the 1970s, merging into the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Aciman did not disclose whether the U.S. government was consulted, given that the signs are technically federal property. However, FEMA indicated it had no objections. "FEMA does not have a stance on the signs," wrote Jenny Burke, a FEMA spokeswoman, in an email on Tuesday. Although the agency does not keep records of old shelter locations, she added that as part of an ongoing planning initiative, the agency is researching to recover records from the Office of Civilian Defense. The city’s removal process appeared somewhat random: on one street in Brooklyn, a sign on a school photographed by Reuters this month was taken down, while another school a few blocks away still had its sign in place, albeit with a missing screw. As a history enthusiast, Jeff Schlegelmilch appreciates the signs enough that he has placed a replica on his office door at Columbia University’s National Center for Disaster Preparedness, where he serves as deputy director. "I enjoy seeing the signs, but as a disaster planner, they need to be removed," he stated. "At best, they are ignored; at worst, they are misleading and could cost lives." There is a growing consensus now, from the federal government downwards, that designated shelters are an outdated notion, and updated contingency plans have been widely implemented since the al Qaeda attacks on the United States on September 11, 2001, Schlegelmilch noted. "If a nuclear explosion were ever to occur, though..."

text: WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Friday, Donald Trump identified U.S. Senator Mike Lee as a possible nominee for the Supreme Court, reaching out to an ally of his former opponent Ted Cruz in what appears to be a move to reassure conservative Republicans who have shown hesitance toward the Republican presidential candidate. Lee was named in a newly released list of 21 prospective Supreme Court justices that Trump would contemplate for the court should he win against Democrat Hillary Clinton in the election scheduled for November 8. "This list is definitive and I will select only from it when appointing future justices of the United States Supreme Court," Trump stated in a press release. This announcement was made on a day when neither candidate had any public engagements, as they were both preparing for the first presidential debate set for Monday. The list that Trump revealed encompassed 10 new names alongside 11 conservative jurists from a previous list that the New York businessman had shared in May. Thomas Lee, Mike Lee’s brother and an associate justice on the Utah Supreme Court, was part of the initial list and continues to be included in Trump’s updated list. By mentioning Mike Lee, Trump appeared to be extending a gesture toward Senator Cruz from Texas, a conservative who vigorously contested Trump for the Republican presidential nomination and has yet to endorse him. Trump's outspoken style and his proposals that diverge from certain conservative traditions, such as his support for free trade agreements, have caused some concern among traditional conservative Republicans. Mike Lee, in response, expressed gratitude for being considered. "At this moment, I am concentrating on my responsibilities in the Senate, where I am well-positioned to uphold the Constitution by opposing government overreach. Both lists I have reviewed from the Trump campaign are excellent.  "While my brother and I may have differing opinions on which list is superior, they are both outstanding," he joked. The passing of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia on February 13 resulted in a tie on the court, with four justices leaning right and four leaning left. Democratic President Barack Obama has put forth Merrick Garland, who serves as the chief judge of the U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington, for nomination, but the Republican-led U.S. Senate has declined to move forward with his confirmation. Trump articulated that his list was founded on individuals who would adhere to constitutional principles on the court. The threat of Republicans losing court control to the Democrats has been one of his primary themes at campaign rallies. Others included in Trump’s list are Keith Blackwell, a justice on the Supreme Court of Georgia; Charles Canady, a Florida Supreme Court justice; Neil Gorsuch, a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit; and Edward Mansfield, a justice on the Iowa Supreme Court. text: MIDWAY ATOLL (Reuters) - On Thursday, President Barack Obama went snorkeling in the vibrant blue waters surrounding Midway Atoll, a distant coral reef that highlights contemporary global climate issues as well as the United States' influence in the Pacific since its World War Two triumph in that area. The purpose of the visit was to convey the importance of safeguarding at-risk species and environments from the detrimental impacts of climate change. Additionally, it coincided with Obama's trip to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and other global leaders during his final tour of Asia, where he has been attempting to realign U.S. defense and trade strategies towards this region. "It’s a signal, it’s a message saying the United States is committed to staying in the Pacific, and not sort of backing away," remarked naval historian Tom Hone, who has researched the Battle of Midway. As he traveled around the island in an 18-golf-cart motorcade accompanied by Secret Service agents, aides, and media crews, Obama paused to observe several endangered green sea turtles lazily swimming ashore to bask on the white sandy beach. "When I was young, we used to see these turtles all the time. You hardly ever see them coming ashore like this, just soaking up the sun," Obama noted, reflecting on his childhood in Hawaii, located over 1,100 nautical miles to the southeast. With just five months left in his presidency, Obama has aimed to inspire greater awareness about climate change among Americans. According to Reuters/Ipsos polling conducted from July 24 to August 21, fewer than 5 percent of American voters consider the environment to be the most pressing issue facing the nation, and 35 percent believe climate change will not influence their voting decisions in the November 8 election to select Obama's successor. This island visit complements Obama's previous trip to Alaska last year, where he trekked on a retreating glacier. "These aren’t ‘photo ops’ - I think these are genuine chances to help the American populace comprehend," stated Carol Browner, a former administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency who provided climate-related advice to Obama during his initial term. "He can draw attention like no one else can," Browner added. Last week, Obama announced a fourfold expansion of the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, establishing it as the largest marine monument globally, thereby protecting the offshore area from commercial fishing and drilling activities. "This will be a valuable resource for future generations," Obama declared, his dress shirt unbuttoned an extra notch in the sweltering heat. "This is sacred ground," he remarked near a beach where young soldiers sheltered under pillboxes, waiting for Japanese fighter aircraft during the World War Two Battle of Midway, one of the most analyzed confrontations in military history. "If it weren't for the bravery and valor of those aviators, the tide in the Pacific battle might not have shifted in our favor," he commented. In June 1942, U.S. forces, alerted by code-breakers regarding a Japanese naval attack, sank four Japanese aircraft carriers and a heavy cruiser in a major air and sea confrontation. Obama’s motorcade rolled over a tarmac riddled with shrapnel remnants from the battle, passing by old hangars and a “bone yard” filled with scrap metal, discarded office chairs, and broken appliances. Large bags contained some of the 20 tons of plastic waste that wash ashore on the island annually, with 5 tons originating from the stomachs of albatrosses, which mistakenly feed the plastic to their chicks, often with fatal consequences. Young tern fledglings curiously approached his group, which tripled the island's typical human population of roughly 35. "Watch the burrow!" shouted Miel Corbett, a spokeswoman for Fish and Wildlife Services, as a visitor narrowly missed stepping on the underground home of the bonin petrel. Approximately one million of these birds emerge from their nests each evening at dusk. Remnants of the island's previous existence as a significant naval base still exist, although many have deteriorated. Due to budget constraints, visitors have been prohibited since 2012.

text: Connecticut has decided to halt pay increases for managers within state agencies due to recent forecasts indicating that the state’s financial condition may be significantly worse than earlier assessments, according to top officials on Monday. This decision to cancel raises serves as an initial sign of the negative impact of the state’s financial crisis. Additional budget cuts are anticipated this year as officials grapple with a budget shortfall that could reach up to $900 million in the upcoming fiscal year. While the amounts in question are notably high-profile, they are mainly symbolic. The cancellations will impact 1,950 employees and result in savings of $12.74 million over a period of two years. This amount does not account for pay freezes in the judicial branch. Connecticut has had to revise its revenue predictions downward due to the underperforming stock market affecting capital gains tax revenue, which is crucial to the budget. The state also faced pushback when it attempted to increase taxes. Earlier this year, General Electric relocated its headquarters out of Connecticut. "We have a responsibility to the taxpayers of Connecticut not to proceed with managerial raises at a time when numerous state programs will experience cuts and when many state positions are likely to be eliminated," stated Ben Barnes, secretary of the Office of Policy and Management. This letter was also signed by Brian Durand, chief of staff to Democratic Governor Dannel Malloy. A report released last week by the non-partisan Office of Fiscal Management indicated that the deficit might be as much as $900 million in the next fiscal year, which starts on July 1. An earlier projection from Barnes’ office estimated the deficit at $570 million. Most of the raises, which had already been delayed twice, were scheduled to be granted on Friday but will now be indefinitely suspended.

This law enables Moscow to compel foreign media to label the news they provide to Russian audiences as being produced by 'foreign agents' and to reveal their funding sources. The law was made available on the online legislative database of the Russian government on Saturday, indicating that it took effect immediately upon publication. Russia's action against U.S. media is part of the ongoing repercussions from accusations that Russia interfered in the previous year's U.S. presidential election to benefit Donald Trump. Last week, the Russian Justice Ministry released a list of nine U.S.-supported news organizations that may be impacted by these new regulations. text: The president of Poland and the ruling political party have come to an agreement regarding judicial reforms, as stated by a parliamentary deputy on Friday. This development moves them closer to settling a disagreement that has persisted for over three months. Since July, the government and President Andrzej Duda have been in talks, following Duda's unexpected veto of a legislative proposal supported by the Law and Justice (PiS) party aimed at overhauling the Polish judicial system. 'We have reached a preliminary agreement... I am optimistic that we can discuss the project in parliament by late November,' remarked PiS parliamentary deputy and negotiator Stanislaw Piotrowicz on Friday. The legislation that Duda vetoed would have led to the immediate removal of all sitting Supreme Court judges unless they received approval from the justice minister. Additionally, parliament would have acquired the authority to appoint most members of the National Council of the Judiciary, which would suggest future candidates to lead the Supreme Court. By enabling parliament to effectively control the appointment and dismissal of senior judges, these proposals raised concerns within the European Union, of which Poland is a part. The EU expressed that such changes would undermine judicial independence and pose a threat to the rule of law. The suggested compromise would still allow parliament to appoint members of the National Council of the Judiciary, but this would necessitate a three-fifths majority in the lower house, according to Piotrowicz. Opposition parties would also have the opportunity to propose judges. If candidates did not secure approval, they could be selected by a simple majority, he added. The PiS argues that the judicial system requires reform due to its slow pace, inefficiency, and lingering communist-era mentality. Duda's veto of certain aspects of the reforms and his suggested limitations on the authority over the court system resulted in a deadlock that could have hindered the party's ambitions to reform not only the judiciary but also the media and electoral system. The compromise revealed today still awaits endorsement from the president and the PiS leadership.

text: The U.S. State Department is set to restart news briefings during the week of March 6, as announced by a spokesperson on Friday. This decision follows a six-week pause under Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, which had left American diplomats uneasy and led to confusion internationally regarding U.S. stances on important matters. Historically, these briefings have been broadcast live and occurred daily, attracting significant attention from both allies and adversaries seeking insight into U.S. responses to major global crises and events. However, they have been suspended since President Donald Trump took office on January 20, marking an unprecedented situation in at least the last three transitions between parties, as indicated by online records of briefing transcripts. The final televised briefing at the State Department took place on January 19, the last complete day of Barack Obama’s presidency. These question-and-answer sessions enable journalists to inquire about the specifics of U.S. foreign policy and the actions of diplomats in other countries. "We are committed to responding to media inquiries and breaking news continuously." Toner did not specify whether the briefings would occur daily or if they would all be broadcasted. These mixed messages have sparked uncertainty in foreign capitals regarding who truly represents the Trump administration and what policies it intends to implement. The lack of communication from the State Department during the chaotic first month of Trump's presidency has also instilled concerns among both current and former American diplomats that the department is being marginalized and is less equipped to influence U.S. foreign policy.

text: SEC Chair Mary Jo White on Monday rejected requests from Senate Republicans to postpone the implementation of new regulations concerning everything from derivatives to mutual funds until after President-elect Donald Trump assumes office. In a correspondence addressed to the leading Republicans on the Senate Banking Committee, Chairman Richard Shelby and Mike Crapo of Idaho, White emphasized that it was "incumbent" upon the SEC to "display a spirit of firm independence" in executing its regulatory responsibilities "without fear or favor." White's letter, dated December 12 and reviewed by Reuters, was a response to a request made last month by Shelby and Crapo asking the SEC to halt rule adoption until Trump had an opportunity to evaluate the agency's agenda. Congressional Republicans have been urging federal agencies to slow down their rulemaking efforts. Trump has pledged to eliminate numerous regulations established during the Obama administration, including the Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform legislation. White, who is an independent, is expected to resign from her position at the conclusion of Democratic President Barack Obama’s term in January. The Senate did not confirm Obama’s two nominees for vacant commissioner positions at the SEC prior to its adjournment last week, which will leave the SEC with just two commissioners - one from the Democratic party and one from the Republican party - after White's departure next month. Even before her exit, she may still face challenges in getting the rules approved if she cannot secure a quorum of commissioners to reach a consensus. Trump has yet to disclose a nominee for SEC chair; however, many individuals working on his financial regulatory transition team, including former SEC Commissioner Paul Atkins, have openly criticized several of the SEC’s regulations and the Dodd-Frank Act overall. In her letter on Monday, White presented Shelby and Crapo with a comprehensive list of all the rules that are currently prepared for a vote. Among these rules are derivatives reforms required by Dodd-Frank, such as capital and margin requirements for swap dealers, alongside a more contentious rule that would restrict how mutual funds and exchange-traded funds utilize derivatives to amplify returns. The letter did not specify when the SEC might hold a vote on the rules, which could occur in an open meeting or in a private session. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment on the timing of the vote. "I am not oblivious to the concerns raised in your letter and have deliberated carefully on what influence, if any, the election should exert on the Commission's ongoing work," White stated. She also noted that she had verified that the SEC "historically has continued its work during similar post-election phases." To bolster her argument, White included footnotes in her letter referencing earlier remarks made by Republican SEC Commissioner Mike Piwowar, who is set to become the acting chair in January, expressing his support for finalizing new derivatives regulations. This is not the first occasion the SEC has encountered backlash regarding its attempts to finalize rules prior to a transition in leadership at the regulator. In 2005, a federal appeals court sided with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in a legal conflict with the SEC concerning controversial rules that mandated the majority of mutual fund board directors to be independent. The court returned the rule to the SEC with instructions to consider its costs. The then-SEC Chairman William Donaldson quickly arranged a meeting, and the SEC re-adopted the rule just one day before his resignation, asserting that the rule would not impose excessive costs. The rule was later overturned once again, with the court reprimanding the SEC for its failure to adhere to appropriate rulemaking procedures. Even if White manages to finalize the rules in the upcoming weeks, Congress may still have the ability to revoke them once Trump takes office on January 20. According to law, Congress can vote to overturn regulations within 60 legislative days of their finalization - a process that may be easier under a Republican-dominated Congress.

text: Hong Kong aims to implement legislation that would penalize individuals who boo the Chinese national anthem as quickly as possible, an official announced on Wednesday. Critics argue that this initiative undermines the autonomy and freedoms of the city, which is governed by China. In recent years, certain football fans in Hong Kong have expressed their discontent by booing the national anthem during World Cup qualifiers and other matches, paralleling a recent protest in the United States where football players kneel during the national anthem, a practice criticized by U.S. President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, the Asian Football Confederation issued a warning to the Hong Kong Football Association regarding the behavior of fans who booed the national anthem during a match in October. A law in China stipulates that disrespecting the national anthem could lead to imprisonment. While this law is already in effect in China, it has not yet been applied to Hong Kong. Patrick Nip, the Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs in Hong Kong, stated that the city has a constitutional obligation to comply with the actions taken by China’s largely ceremonial parliament. This law will be incorporated into the annex of Hong Kong’s mini-constitution, known as the Basic Law, and will be presented to the city’s 70-member legislature. "We will do it as soon as possible," Nip assured lawmakers, mentioning that there would be a process for consultation. Hong Kong, a former British territory, returned to Chinese sovereignty in 1997 under a framework known as "one country, two systems," which guarantees the city a high degree of autonomy, including an independent judiciary. However, China's increasing influence over Hong Kong's affairs has fueled tensions and widespread protests, including the 2014 Occupy civil disobedience movement that obstructed major roads in the city for 79 days to urge China to permit full democracy. Nip indicated that no decisions have been made regarding prison sentences, but the government intends to refer to existing laws concerning the desecration of China's national flag, which carry a maximum penalty of three years. Some critics expressed that this initiative would further diminish Hong Kong's autonomy and is another example of China's tightening control. "If a country (China) weren’t employing totalitarian and autocratic methods to create pressure, I believe many more Hong Kong residents would show respect for the national anthem," stated Dennis Kwok, a lawmaker from the Civic Party. In recent years, Hong Kong supporters have booed the national anthem at various football matches featuring the Hong Kong team, with an upcoming Asian Cup qualifier against Lebanon being another potential point of contention. "Some inappropriate conduct... must be addressed," Nip remarked, without providing specific details. Chinese authorities have sought to promote greater patriotism in Hong Kong while denouncing the efforts of democracy advocates to distance the city from Beijing by embracing local culture and core values, with some even advocating for independence from China. "In recent years, incidents of disrespect toward the national anthem have taken place in Hong Kong, challenging the bottom line... and igniting anger," said Zhang Rongshun, who leads a legislative affairs commission within China’s parliament, the National People’s Congress, as reported by the official Xinhua news agency. "It is urgent and crucial to enforce the National Anthem Law in Hong Kong to prevent and manage such offenses."

text: The EU has called on Spain to engage in dialogue with Catalan separatists, denouncing violence while simultaneously advocating for unity. This appeal came on Monday, following an incident where Spanish police clashed with individuals attempting to vote in an independence referendum in Catalonia. The European Commission issued a carefully worded statement, wading into a contentious issue that it has previously avoided, acknowledging the potential risks to stability in both Spain and the eurozone. The Commission expressed confidence in Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy's capacity to handle this domestic situation, while also urging for discussions and reminding Madrid of its obligation to uphold citizens' fundamental rights. "We urge all relevant parties to swiftly transition from confrontation to dialogue. Violence should never be a political tool," the Commission stated through its chief spokesman, Margaritis Schinas, right before Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont requested EU mediation. When pressed by journalists, Schinas refrained from explicitly stating that the EU condemned the actions of the Spanish police, even though their conduct at polling stations on Sunday largely astonished fellow Europeans and led to public pressure that prompted other governments, including Germany and France, to advocate for increased dialogue. Later on Monday, Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker communicated with Rajoy after having been in touch over the weekend, although the EU spokesman did not confirm whether the Union would engage in mediation, a rare move for Brussels within one of its member states. According to aides, Juncker conveyed the Commission's perspective while also adopting a receptive stance. Donald Tusk, the former Polish prime minister who presides over summits of EU national leaders, stated after his conversation with Rajoy that he supported the Spanish premier's constitutional arguments but urged him to seek solutions to avoid further escalation and the use of force. The Commission's statement also aligned with Madrid's stance that the vote, which Catalan leaders claimed demonstrated overwhelming support for independence, was unconstitutional under Spain's legal framework. Historically, Brussels has offered minimal or no support to separatist movements within the European Union, whether they are from Catalonia, Scotland, Flanders, or elsewhere. "Now is the time for unity and stability, not for division and fragmentation," the statement emphasized. Any region seeking to separate would need to exit the EU and then reapply for membership, the statement added. Even this process would only be feasible if the separation were amicable. This situation differentiates Scotland, which conducted a referendum agreed upon with London in 2014, from Catalonia, where Spain's Constitutional Court has indicated that the 1978 constitution prohibits secession. Despite the reluctance of other European nations to publicly engage in the dispute, there is an increasing concern in Brussels regarding how the conservative government in Madrid has managed the tensions with Barcelona, rekindling feelings tied to the 20th-century civil war and dictatorship. As images of heavily armed Spanish police striking women on the ground shocked Europe on Sunday, a few governments, including those of Scotland, Slovenia— which emerged from the violent disintegration of Yugoslavia— and Belgium, where successive devolution attempts have prevented a definitive split between French- and Dutch-speaking communities, voiced their concerns. On Monday, Berlin joined the calls for dialogue, cautioning against a "spiral of escalation." Germany's BDI industrial federation warned that the separation of this highly industrialized region from Spain would result in significant harm for both parties.

text: Following years of conflict, the FARC rebels in Colombia are launching their political party. BOGOTA (Reuters) - The left-wing FARC guerrilla group in Colombia is unveiling its political party at a conference that commenced on Sunday, marking a significant move in its shift towards a civilian organization after over 50 years of conflict and the first opportunity to present policies to doubtful voters. The six-day gathering in Bogota, attended by FARC members who have surrendered more than 8,000 weapons to the United Nations during their demobilization process, is anticipated to wrap up on Friday with a platform that the party will promote in the upcoming elections next year. According to the 2016 peace agreement with the government aimed at ending its involvement in a conflict that has claimed the lives of more than 220,000 individuals, most of the fighters from the group officially recognized as the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia received amnesty and were permitted to engage in politics. It remains uncertain whether the rebels will receive support from Colombians, many of whom harbor disdain for them. The FARC's somewhat outdated Marxist rhetoric is perceived by many as a relic from its inception in 1964; however, proposals for reforms concerning intricate property laws may resonate with rural voters who face challenges as subsistence farmers. The peace agreement, which was narrowly rejected by less than 1 percent in a referendum before being revised and implemented, guarantees the FARC's party 10 automatic seats in Congress until 2026, although the group may pursue additional seats in elections. In a scene that would have seemed unimaginable just a few years prior, FARC representatives arrived by bus in the heart of the capital, escorted by police on motorcycles. "From this moment on, we will evolve into a new, entirely political entity that will conduct its activities through legal avenues," stated FARC leader Rodrigo Londono, also known by his alias Timochenko, to hundreds gathered at the event center in Bogota. "We face numerous challenges and obstacles ahead," Londono continued. "Nothing in politics comes easily." He also emphasized that rural improvements would continue to be a priority for the party. Many attendees donned conference t-shirts emblazoned with the phrase "A new party for a new country" and carried branded tote bags. An artwork featuring the likenesses of Cuban revolutionary figures Fidel Castro and Ernesto Che Guevara, the late Venezuelan president Hugo Chavez, and Jesus Christ was showcased. Initially, the party will be named the Revolutionary Alternative Force of Colombia, maintaining the FARC initials in Spanish. Legislative and presidential elections are set to occur in 2018. It is still uncertain in which contests the FARC will field candidates. "I believe the FARC will aim for regional consolidation, leveraging their presence and influence in specific provinces," remarked Catalina Jimenez, a political science professor at Externado University. "On a national scale, they require a significant number of votes they currently lack." The FARC has expressed openness to forming coalitions, the group announced this week. Historically, leftist parties have faced challenges in conservative-leaning Colombia due to internal divisions, despite achieving some success in urban elections. Widespread corruption scandals are likely to be a major concern for the crowded slate of candidates in the 2018 presidential race. Campaigns are also expected to emphasize initiatives aimed at improving the everyday lives of Colombians, many of whom express an urgent need for enhanced security, public education, and healthcare services. The FARC contends that the government led by President Juan Manuel Santos, which allocates a regulated amount of funding to each political party, should assist with the expenses of the conference, considering the rebels have relinquished their assets as reparations for war victims. However, while the peace agreement is a cornerstone of Santos's legacy, the government has questioned the authenticity of the FARC's reported $324 million asset list. This week, the government announced the formation of a commission to verify that the FARC has accounted for all profits potentially earned through extortion, ransom, and drug trafficking, asserting that the group must adhere to the same regulations as any other political party.

text: Democrats criticize Trump's selection for Education Secretary. (Corrects in 6th paragraph to clarify rules) By Lisa Lambert WASHINGTON (Reuters) - During a confirmation hearing on Tuesday, Democrats scrutinized the qualifications of billionaire Betsy DeVos for the position of U.S. Education Secretary, expressing skepticism about whether President-elect Donald Trump’s choice will gain approval from the full Senate. DeVos's nomination to lead an agency responsible for policy affecting young children and universities, as well as overseeing a $1 trillion college financial aid program, has provoked outrage among Democrats who fear that the Michigan Republican aims to dismantle public education. Teachers unions, which are a significant support base for the party, are strongly against DeVos, who is known for her philanthropic efforts and investment background. “Do you think if you were not a multi-billionaire, if your family had not made hundreds of millions of dollars in contributions to the Republican party, that you would be sitting here today?” inquired Independent Bernie Sanders from Vermont, who recently campaigned for the Democratic presidential nomination. Democratic Senators have expressed their opposition clearly in recent days through letters, speeches, and notably during the hearing. Next Tuesday, the Education Committee is expected to approve forwarding her nomination to the full Senate during an executive session. Afterward, Democrats might try to block the nomination on the Senate floor. Since nominations other than those for the Supreme Court only need a simple majority vote, they cannot employ a filibuster and would have to persuade some Republicans to vote against the nomination alongside them. Former Senator Joe Lieberman, the Democratic candidate for vice president in 2000, gave DeVos a complimentary introduction at the hearing, but other members of the party were diverse in their criticism. Minnesota’s Al Franken was taken aback that DeVos was unaware of a significant education issue concerning the measurement of student achievement by proficiency versus growth. Connecticut’s Chris Murphy was disappointed when DeVos failed to denounce the presence of guns in schools. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who advocates for stringent financial regulations, asked whether DeVos or her children had ever attended public schools, taken out student loans, or received federal financial assistance known as Pell grants. “You have no experience with financial aid,” Warren concluded when DeVos responded with a “no.” Many were troubled by DeVos’s refusal to commit to enforcing rules regarding sexual assault, for-profit colleges, and equitable access for students with disabilities, instead stating she would review the policies. Overall, Democrats focused on how DeVos plans to handle her investments and businesses within the education sector, including an online charter school, while serving as the most influential public figure in that field. They also persistently questioned whether she intended to redirect funds to charter schools that operate independently from school districts and are often managed by corporations, as well as whether she would harm public schools. “I have major concerns with how you have spent your career and fortune fighting to privatize public education and diminish investments in public schools,” remarked Patty Murray from Washington, the committee’s senior Democrat. DeVos worked to reassure them that she supports taxpayer-funded education. She also stated her intention to provide parents with choices regarding their children’s schooling, treat all students fairly, and respect state decisions concerning education. The hearing, which had been postponed from the previous week due to missing financial disclosures, commenced at 5 p.m. (EST). Committee Chairman Lamar Alexander allocated only five minutes for questions from each member. Democrats protested, arguing that since DeVos had not completed the necessary ethics paperwork, they lacked crucial information and required additional time. Alexander mentioned that the Office of Government Ethics would deliver a letter outlining resolutions for her potential conflicts of interest by Friday. Committee Republicans unanimously supported DeVos, praising her advocacy for vouchers that families may use.

text: The House of Representatives has approved a measure on Wednesday to allocate $622.1 million to manage the proliferation of the Zika virus, a sum significantly less than what President Barack Obama requested and also lower than what has been proposed in the Senate. The bill was passed by the Republican-led House with a vote of 241 to 184, primarily along party affiliations, leading to a potential clash with both the Republican-dominated Senate and the Democratic administration of Obama. The White House has indicated its intention to veto the House measure, deeming it "woefully inadequate." The administration has asked for $1.9 billion. On Tuesday, the Senate took steps toward anticipated approval of $1.1 billion on Thursday to combat the mosquito-borne Zika virus, which is associated with birth defects. Unlike the Senate's proposal, the House bill stipulates that the $622.1 million must be completely offset by cuts in other areas of spending. Numerous conservative Republicans in the House are reluctant to approve Zika funding that would increase federal budget deficits, while Democrats and some Republicans in the Senate advocate for addressing the issue as an emergency that wouldn’t require reductions in spending. House Republicans contend that their legislation, along with $589 million that the Obama administration has already redirected from unused Ebola funds to Zika, would ensure sufficient financial resources through September 30, which marks the end of the current fiscal year. It remains uncertain how long it will take for the Senate and House to reconcile their differences after both pass their individual bills. U.S. health authorities have determined that Zika infections in pregnant women can result in microcephaly, a birth defect characterized by an abnormally small head size that can lead to significant developmental challenges in infants. The World Health Organization has asserted that there is a strong scientific agreement that Zika may also cause Guillain-Barre syndrome, a rare neurological condition that induces temporary paralysis in adults. In the previous year, Brazil reported a rise in cases of microcephaly, and the virus has been rapidly spreading throughout the Americas, with fresh cases being documented in warmer regions of southern U.S. states such as Florida. The Obama administration claims that it requires these emergency funds to assist state and local governments in eliminating the mosquitoes that transmit the virus and to advance the development of a vaccine.

text: U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry expressed concerns on Tuesday regarding the risks posed by authoritarian populism, while indirectly criticizing Donald Trump’s extensive use of Twitter, which he argued enables the president-elect to evade responsibility. In his most direct remarks about Trump following the presidential election on November 8, Kerry indicated that the Cabinet nominees of the president-elect were receiving leniency from Congress for not providing tax returns and other necessary documentation prior to their Senate confirmation processes. "Every country in the world better ... start worrying about authoritarian populism and the absence of substance in our dialogue," Kerry stated at a forum in Washington. "If policies are going to be crafted in 140 characters on Twitter, and all reasonable standards of accountability are being overlooked, and people are indifferent, we have a problem," he remarked. He pointed out that during the campaign between Trump and Democratic rival Hillary Clinton, climate change was notably neglected as an issue, exemplifying the lack of substance in political discussions. Kerry compared the scrutiny he faced during his vetting for secretary of state, including the paperwork he had to submit, to the exceptions he claimed were being made for Trump’s Cabinet nominees ahead of their confirmation hearings. In December, Bob Corker, the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, stated that they had not requested tax returns from Rex Tillerson, Trump’s nominee for secretary of state, which Corker noted was consistent with established practice. Although Tillerson, the former chairman and CEO of ExxonMobil Corp (XOM.N), has not provided tax returns, his financial disclosure and ethics agreement have been publicly released. Kerry, who previously served as a senator and was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2004 before becoming President Barack Obama’s secretary of state in 2013, remarked, "It is quite astonishing when you consider the hurdles I had to clear regarding submitted documents, provided documentation, and tax returns. ... Suddenly that’s not deemed as crucial." When asked whether he thought Trump’s nominees were receiving "a free pass," Kerry laughed and sidestepped the inquiry. Walter Shaub, director of the federal Office of Government Ethics, expressed his "great concern" in a letter to senators last week about the hearing timelines for Trump nominees who had not finalized the ethics review process, stating it would be "cause for alarm if the Senate were to proceed with hearings on nominees whose reports OGE has not approved." With just 10 days remaining before Trump assumes office, Kerry mentioned that there had been minimal high-level interactions between current State Department officials and Trump’s transition team. Discussing the transition at a forum hosted by the nonpartisan U.S. Institute of Peace, Kerry remarked, "It’s going pretty smoothly because there’s not an enormous amount of it." "There are some individuals who have been in the building for a while, but quite frankly, I believe there has not been much high-level communication at this moment," said Kerry. He noted that he had not yet met with Tillerson but anticipated doing so shortly. According to the State Department, Kerry and Tillerson had a phone conversation last month. A spokesperson for the Trump transition team declined to comment on Kerry’s statements. Tillerson’s Senate confirmation hearing is set for Wednesday and is expected to draw significant attention, particularly because of concerns surrounding his ties to Russia from his tenure as ExxonMobil’s top executive. Trump has advocated for improved relations with Russia, while some Republican colleagues in Congress are calling for a tougher stance in response to what U.S. intelligence agencies have determined was interference by the Kremlin in the presidential election.

text: DENPASAR, Indonesia (Reuters) - In Bali, Indonesia, authorities have apprehended an Australian, an American, and a Malaysian for drug-related offenses, marking yet another instance of foreigners violating some of the strictest narcotics laws worldwide. The three individuals, arrested in distinct incidents, were presented to the media during a briefing while wearing orange prison uniforms, their faces hidden by balaclavas, accompanied by armed police officers. It remains uncertain whether any of these individuals, who were referred to only by their initials, may face capital punishment if found guilty. According to the customs office, methamphetamine and ecstasy were discovered concealed in a plastic bottle and another container within the Australian's luggage upon his arrival on a flight from Bangkok on Monday. "Based on the inspection results, our officers uncovered five packages containing clear crystals weighing 19.97 grams and 14 tablets totaling 6.22 grams," stated Himawan Indrajono, the head of Bali Airport's customs office. The Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it is offering consular support to the Australian man detained in Bali but declined to provide additional comments in response to emailed inquiries about the arrest. The execution by firing squad of two Australians in 2015, along with six other drug offenders from various countries, caused tensions between Jakarta and Canberra. President Joko Widodo has advocated for an 'uncompromising' offensive against narcotics, instructing law enforcement to shoot drug traffickers who resist arrest. text: China's largely ceremonial parliament is reviewing the possibility of imposing prison sentences of up to three years for individuals who show disrespect towards the national anthem or flag in public spaces, according to state media reports on Tuesday. Since assuming the presidency in 2013, Xi Jinping has introduced new laws aimed at safeguarding China from internal and external threats, while also leading a significant crackdown on dissent and freedom of expression. In September, China enacted a law that allows for up to 15 days of police detention for those who ridicule the national anthem, 'March of the Volunteers,' a legislation that also applies to the Chinese regions of Hong Kong and Macau. The parliament is currently assessing an amendment to China's Criminal Law that would introduce criminal punishments for disrespecting the national anthem, which includes deliberately altering the lyrics or melody, as reported by Xinhua. Stricter penalties would also be applicable to acts of desecration against the national flag or emblem, such as burning, defacing, or trampling it in public, which had previously been subject to a maximum of 15 days of detention. A proposed amendment has been presented for discussion during a bi-monthly session of the standing committee of parliament, which commenced on Monday. Offenders may face penalties of up to three years in prison, as outlined in the draft, the report noted. It remains uncertain when the amendment will be finalized, though it may happen by the end of the week when the standing committee concludes its current session. The National Anthem Law, effective from October 1, will also be included in an appendix of Hong Kong's Basic Law, or mini constitution, according to Xinhua, though it is not yet clear if this will encompass the three-year prison sentences. The national anthem legislation has raised concerns in Hong Kong, where residents have grown anxious about China's perceived infringement on the city's autonomy, particularly following incidents such as the disappearance of booksellers who were later found in mainland Chinese custody. In 2015, Hong Kong soccer fans booed the Chinese anthem during a World Cup qualifier match, resulting in FIFA imposing a fine on the territory’s football association. text: India has put a hold on applications for the commercial release of a genetically modified mustard variety developed locally, as indicated by a document from the environment ministry made public on Tuesday. This decision comes in the face of strong opposition from activists and political figures against genetically altered food. The mustard variety was set to be the first transgenic crop permitted for commercial farming in the country. However, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) of the environment ministry has postponed approval, despite a technical clearance granted last year by a panel overseen by the ministry. "Following the receipt of numerous representations from various stakeholders, issues regarding the environmental release of transgenic mustard are being held for further examination," the GEAC noted in the minutes of a meeting published on the environment ministry's website, which was marked as "confidential and restricted circulation." Currently, cotton is the sole genetically modified crop permitted for sale in India's second most populous nation, where agricultural land is diminishing. Monsanto Co, a U.S. firm, holds a dominant position in the cotton seed market in India and frequently encounters pushback from local businesses regarding its dominance. On July 31, the environment ministry informed parliament that the GEAC had recommended GM mustard for "consideration for environmental release and cultivation." A spokesperson from the environment ministry referred Reuters to the head of the GEAC, Amita Prasad, whose office indicated she was unavailable. Another GEAC representative listed on the ministry's website, Madhumita Biswas, did not respond to inquiries for comments. The decision regarding the mustard variety marks a disappointment for Deepak Pental and his team at Delhi University, who have dedicated years to the development and testing of this variety. Pental, who previously acknowledged the challenges in obtaining approval for GM foods, refrained from commenting on Tuesday. There is significant opposition to GM foods from activists and political figures in India, fueled by concerns regarding food safety and biodiversity. Some experts have also raised doubts about the assertion that GM crops yield higher productivity compared to conventional varieties. The Hindu nationalist organization Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, which translates to "national volunteer organization" and is the ideological foundation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party, also stands against GM foods and advocates for the promotion of indigenous varieties. Even the prior administration, which was led by the opposition Congress party, imposed a moratorium on GM eggplant in 2010, after a panel of experts had given it the green light, effectively causing a stalemate in the regulatory system until Modi revitalized it.
