text: INDIANAPOLIS (Reuters) - The backing of Republican evangelicals, who are wary of Donald Trump's more moderate views as he reveals his social opinions, may play a pivotal role in his campaign for the presidency. Trump, a businessman from New York without prior public office experience, has found some support among evangelicals in states like South Carolina. However, ahead of the nominating event in Indiana on Tuesday— a conservative Midwestern state that has favored Republican candidates in nine of the last ten presidential elections— there are indications of a decline in support for him. At 69 years old, Trump has adopted positions on issues such as Planned Parenthood and LGBTQ rights that have raised questions among Christian conservatives, particularly in states like Indiana where they represent a significant voting demographic. An NBC/Wall Street Journal/Marist poll has Trump leading in Indiana with 49 percent, while his closest competitor, U.S. Senator Ted Cruz from Texas, has 34 percent, and Ohio Governor John Kasich trails with 13 percent. Previous surveys from Indiana had suggested a tighter contest, with Trump only marginally ahead of Cruz. A victory for Trump in Indiana could be vital for his nomination prospects and would indicate his ability to unite evangelical voters. Cruz, 45, highlights his Christian beliefs during his campaign, claiming that Trump is not a genuine Republican. A recent advertisement from Cruz portrays Trump and Democratic frontrunner Hillary Clinton as fundamentally similar. It states, "Both endorse the Obamacare individual mandate. Both advocate for taxpayer funding of Planned Parenthood. Both support allowing transgender men to use girls’ restrooms." Trump has commended Planned Parenthood clinics for assisting millions of women, despite opposing funding for their abortion services. He supports the right for transgender individuals to utilize the restroom they deem suitable. If evangelical support wanes, there is a risk they might abstain from voting in the general election on November 8, potentially allowing Hillary Clinton, the leading Democratic candidate, or her competitor, U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders, to win. Bob Vander Plaats, a prominent evangelical leader in Iowa, expressed concern, stating, "The worry is many may choose to stay home. You cannot win without our base." Trump has irritated some social conservatives by criticizing North Carolina's contentious law that mandates transgender individuals to use bathrooms corresponding to their birth gender. Pastor Shan Rutherford of Greenwood, Indiana remarked, "The restroom issue resonates deeply with many people," adding that he was initially attracted to Trump's message but was deterred by his views on social matters and his abrasive behavior during the campaign. Rutherford, who supports Cruz, mentioned that if the election were to boil down to Trump against Clinton, he might abstain from voting. According to the Pew Research Center, 45 percent of registered Republican voters nationwide identify as "born-again" or "evangelical," and only 44 percent perceive Trump as a religious individual, while 76 percent view Cruz in this light. Cruz has criticized Trump over his position on the North Carolina bathroom law, to which Trump has responded that issues regarding transgender individuals in bathrooms have not caused significant problems and should be determined by the states. Cruz contends that permitting adult men in bathrooms with young girls is "opening the door for predators." Recently, Cruz received an endorsement from Indiana Governor Mike Pence, a social conservative who previously signed legislation that critics argue could allow business owners to refuse services to same-sex couples. Trump has expressed his support for laws preventing companies from dismissing employees based on their sexual orientation, although he has also criticized last year's Supreme Court ruling that legalized same-sex marriage. Cruz has utilized his father, Rafael Cruz, an evangelical minister, as a campaign surrogate in Indiana.

text: Challenges accumulate for unfortunate community close to the center of the Mexican earthquake. HUAUTLA, Mexico (Reuters) - Yesenia Vergara took her two daughters and fled her residence in the remote Mexican village of Huautla at the end of last month when the swollen river waters surged through her window, inundating her home with debris, rocks, and mud. Merely two weeks later, Mexico's deadliest earthquake in a generation struck another devastating blow to her modest riverside dwelling, which was financed by money her husband sent back from the United States.  "This is the end of the world, I thought. Now is the time that God has called us to be judged," Vergara recalled, reminiscing about the moment the quake hit in the early afternoon last Tuesday.  "The village was just getting back on its feet and now another tragedy has come," she expressed. The epicenter of the 7.1 magnitude quake, which has resulted in nearly 300 fatalities thus far, flattened numerous structures in Mexico City, igniting a frantic search for survivors. The tremor occurred 70 km (45 miles) from Huautla, a picturesque community located amidst the verdant mountains of Morelos state.  While the Mexican capital has been inundated with enthusiastic volunteers amid a surge of support, the villages in Morelos and Puebla states situated near the epicenter have attracted significantly less attention.  A growing group of kind-hearted individuals aimed to change that on Friday, spreading out across the states' backroads, wading through knee-high streams to provide food, water, and medical supplies to remote communities high in the mountains.  This effort has far exceeded the government's response, with the volunteers' patriotic actions uplifting a shaken nation. It has also created a stark contrast to the increasingly politicized reactions to the quake, which sparked a virtual competition among political parties attempting to outdo one another with contributions to relief efforts.  "We feel very grateful," Vergara remarked about the volunteers. "But also very disappointed with the government."  Although the quake did not demolish any buildings in Huautla, Mayor Miguel Medina stated that 10 families out of roughly 1,000 residents were evacuated due to damage to around 100 structures.  By Friday afternoon, Vergara noted that no one had come to assess the significant cracks threatening her home, forcing her and her young family to seek refuge at her mother's house.  Fortino Garcia, a 48-year-old taxi driver from Cuernavaca, was among eight individuals who traveled from Mexico City to provide aid to the local villages.  While he approved of the government's response to the earthquake, he condemned politicians who he claimed were attempting to exploit the tragedy by affixing stickers with their names or party logos on supplies gathered by volunteers.  "Many politicians are unfortunately using this to campaign," he stated in Huautla's central square, after delivering diapers, sanitary products, and water.  A growing discontent regarding the distribution of aid by local officials was evident as residents accused them of selectively choosing higher-quality donations of clothing and food while leaving the less desirable items for the villagers.  In a storage facility in the heart of the village where hundreds of women were queuing for food and water, Medina denied any wrongdoing by himself or his staff, asserting that the aid came from all corners of the globe.  "People from other countries have come to give us their little grain of sand," he said. "We are very surprised and thankful."  Nonetheless, rumors of official misconduct circulated on every street corner.  Like much of Mexico, crime and violence in Huautla had surged dramatically over recent years, according to a shopkeeper who wished to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. She reported that some villagers armed themselves last month and positioned themselves at the town's entrance to deter outsiders.  In July, she recounted, an elderly woman was killed when she interrupted a burglary in her home, an event that was previously unheard of in this tranquil farming community.

text: The Senate may cast a vote on an updated healthcare bill next week. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, U.S. Senate Republicans announced their intention to present their healthcare reform to the Senate floor in the upcoming week following an extensive internal party dispute. However, it was still uncertain if they possessed sufficient votes to pass the legislation or what its final form would be. With his reputation as a strategic leader at stake, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell outlined a timeline for the Senate to consider legislation aimed at fulfilling President Donald Trump’s campaign commitment to dismantle the Affordable Care Act of 2010, commonly referred to as Obamacare. Departing from traditional Republican views on tax cuts, sources from the Senate indicated that the legislation would likely maintain some taxes imposed on the affluent under Obamacare. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether a revised bill set to be revealed on Thursday morning will be able to appease both moderate and hardline conservatives within the Republican majority, who expressed their opposition to a draft presented last month for very different reasons. With Trump urging action from the Senate before the August recess, McConnell has delayed the Senate's scheduled August break by two weeks to provide senators with additional time to address the measure that would repeal significant aspects of Obamacare while also pursuing other legislative objectives. McConnell’s announcement led to a rebound in stock prices during afternoon trading on Wall Street following an earlier decline, raising hopes that a shorter recess could signal progress on the stalled Republican legislative agenda. A somber atmosphere persisted among some Republicans regarding the healthcare issue, as party leaders seemed compelled to resolve healthcare matters to shift focus to other priorities, which include raising the U.S. debt ceiling. “I believe we have now narrowed it down to the key decision points, and we just need to make those decisions,” Senator John Thune, a junior member of the Republican leadership, shared with reporters. Leaders were still attempting to “determine how we reach 50” votes, he mentioned. Republicans, who control 52 seats in the 100-member Senate, would require 50 votes to pass the legislation, with Vice President Mike Pence available to cast the tie-breaking vote. “I am quite pessimistic” regarding the chances for Republican healthcare legislation, stated Chuck Grassley, a senior senator, during an interview with Fox News on Tuesday. Another Republican senator, Lindsey Graham, is working on his own healthcare plan and is expected to unveil it this week, as indicated by a Graham aide. McConnell stated that the intention was to vote on the healthcare legislation next week, and he expressed hope to receive a new analysis of the bill from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office at the beginning of the week. He did not disclose any of the anticipated modifications to the draft, which he had postponed action on last month due to insufficient support. However, Senate sources indicated that it is probable that two taxes from Obamacare affecting the wealthy would be retained - a 3.8 percent net investment tax and a 0.9 percent payroll tax that contributes to Medicare funding - which may attract moderates who are hesitant about the idea of reducing taxes for the wealthy while cutting benefits for the underprivileged. “Clearly, that’s the direction many of our members prefer, which is to retain some of those (taxes) and utilize those revenues to allocate elsewhere in the bill,” Thune remarked, while emphasizing that no decisions have been finalized. Additionally, Republicans might keep Obamacare’s limit on corporate tax deductions for executive compensation within the health insurance sector, according to one Senate source. It was uncertain whether the bill would incorporate a proposal from conservative Republican Ted Cruz that would permit insurers to provide basic low-cost healthcare plans that do not adhere to Obamacare regulations. Cruz contends that this would aid in reducing premiums, but critics argue it would enable insurers to offer less comprehensive plans that may lack essential health benefits while also charging higher rates for more extensive, Obamacare-compliant options.

text: Over 300 scientists have expressed their concerns regarding Donald Trump's position on climate change. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, a group of prominent scientists cautioned against the Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump's promise to withdraw the United States from the Paris climate agreement if he wins the election in November. The 375 members of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, which includes 30 Nobel laureates, stated in an open letter that a U.S. exit from the accord would significantly hinder the development of international strategies aimed at mitigating the effects of climate change. "It is therefore very troubling that the Republican nominee for President has proposed the U.S. disengagement from the Paris Accord," the letter stated. "A 'Parexit' would send a distinct message to the global community: 'The United States is indifferent to the worldwide issue of human-induced climate change. You are left to fend for yourselves.'" Notable signatories include biologist E.O. Wilson, physicists Stephen Hawking and Claude Canizares, astrophysicist Simon D.M. White, along with Nobel laureates Thomas Steitz, Michael Levitt, and William Daniel Phillips. The National Academy of Sciences is a private organization of scholars that provides scientific and technological advice to the United States. The individuals who signed the letter clarified that they did so in their personal capacities and not as representatives of the Academy or their respective institutions. In December in Paris, nearly 200 nations agreed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and maintain global temperature increases to "well below" 2 degrees Celsius. This month, the United States and China, the two leading carbon emitters, ratified the agreement. Trump is scheduled to address a natural gas industry conference in Pennsylvania on Thursday. A spokesperson for Trump did not reply to a request for comments. Trump has characterized human-induced climate change as a fabrication created by the Chinese and has indicated that he would withdraw from the Paris agreement if elected. He has pledged to overturn much of the climate change initiatives implemented by President Barack Obama’s administration, which includes regulations aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The platform of the Republican Party also challenges the legality of Obama’s executive order that ratified the Paris agreement. Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton is a firm advocate of the Paris accord.

Netanyahu, who has endorsed Trump's decision, is scheduled to meet with Macron on Sunday prior to a gathering with European Union foreign ministers in Brussels on Monday. On Friday, France stated that the United States had marginalized itself in the Middle East by recognizing Jerusalem as Israel's capital. French Foreign Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian commented on French television that the U.S. action was contrary to international law. He remarked, 'Trump says he has a project. text: Putin observes as Russia escalates military exercises that have alarmed the West. MOSCOW (Reuters) - On Monday, President Vladimir Putin watched over Russia's largest military drills in years, during which his troops successfully fended off a simulated enemy and initiated a tank-led counterattack, part of a training operation that has unsettled Western nations. NATO representatives claim they are observing the Zapad-2017 (West-2017) exercises with calm assurance, yet many express concern regarding what they perceive as Moscow assessing its capacity for warfare against the West. Russia maintains that the drills focus on a strictly defensive scenario. Putin, serving as the commander-in-chief of Russia's military, was situated in a command center alongside his defense minister and the chief of the General Staff, utilizing binoculars to watch the simulated battle unfold amid a chilly drizzle. The Russian leader has attended similar displays before, occasionally wearing military attire, using these events to enhance his image as a strong protector of his nation's interests on the global stage. On this occasion, the 64-year-old president, who is largely anticipated to seek re-election in March, donned a dark suit and appeared at ease as the firing range in the Leningrad region was momentarily converted into a combat zone. Tracer rounds illuminated the gloomy skyline, battle tanks maneuvered through the muddy landscape, shells detonated, helicopters launched missiles, aircraft roared overhead, and hundreds of paratroopers along with armored vehicles descended from the skies. The paratroopers, deployed behind enemy lines in the simulation, then engaged in combat with what the defense ministry referred to as illegal armed formations. The overarching Zapad military exercises, which commenced on September 14 and are scheduled to conclude on September 20, are being held in western Russia, the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, and Belarus, a Russian ally that borders both Ukraine and NATO member countries Poland, Latvia, and Lithuania. Moscow states that nearly 13,000 Russian and Belarusian military personnel are participating, along with around 70 aircraft and helicopters. It claims to be deploying nearly 700 units of military equipment, which includes close to 250 tanks, 10 ships, and various artillery and rocket systems. However, NATO officials assert that they believe the drills involve more personnel than Russia has revealed and have raised concerns about what they describe as a lack of transparency regarding the exercises, an accusation that Russia denies. As part of the same maneuvers, Russia announced on Monday that it successfully test-fired a ballistic missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, hitting a target located at a firing range in Kazakhstan approximately 480 km (300 miles) away. Moscow asserts that it is the West that poses a threat to stability in Eastern Europe due to NATO's deployment of a 4,000-strong multinational force in the Baltics and Poland, while the U.S. Army has sent 600 paratroopers to the Baltics during the Zapad exercises. As a precautionary measure, the United States has also temporarily assumed control of the airspace over Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, which lack sufficient air forces and air defense systems.

text: According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Tuesday, fewer than one-third of Americans are in favor of Donald Trump’s tax reduction plan. This comes as the U.S. president seeks Republican support on Capitol Hill for his proposal, which aims to lower tax rates for both individuals and corporations. With the midterm congressional elections of 2018 approaching, the survey revealed that over two-thirds of registered voters believe that addressing the U.S. federal budget deficit is more crucial than providing tax cuts for the wealthy or corporations. Critics and independent analysts argue that Trump’s plan would exacerbate the deficit and contribute to the national debt, which currently stands at $20 trillion, while Republicans maintain that the proposed tax cuts would be compensated by economic growth leading to increased tax revenue. Among the Republicans surveyed, 63 percent indicated that deficit reduction should take precedence over tax cuts for corporations, and 75 percent said it should take precedence over tax cuts for wealthy individuals. Democrats are against Trump’s proposal, which was introduced on September 27, claiming it is unjust towards the poor and working-class citizens. The proposal is still only a nine-page outline, developed in secrecy by Trump’s administration along with congressional leaders, and formal legislation is being crafted. Congressional leaders and Trump are working to secure backing for the plan from rank-and-file Republicans who were not involved in its drafting. Trump, who has not yet achieved a significant legislative victory since his inauguration in January, aims to have his plan passed into law before the year concludes, a timeline that some policy experts consider unrealistic. More than half of the adults polled expressed agreement that "cutting taxes for the poor is more important than reducing the federal deficit," with 68 percent of Democrats and 47 percent of Republicans supporting this view, according to the survey. The poll conducted from October 20-23 indicated that just 15 percent of registered voters believe Congress should prioritize tax reform over other matters. Approximately a quarter of respondents, including 23 percent of Democrats and 30 percent of Republicans, concurred that Congress should keep working on healthcare legislation. Among those adults aware of the "tax reform plan recently proposed by congressional Republicans," only 28 percent expressed support, while 41 percent opposed it, and another 31 percent said they were unsure. The poll showed that opinions on Trump’s plan were significantly polarized along party lines, with 56 percent of Republicans and only 9 percent of Democrats in favor of it. Of those familiar with the plan, 14 percent believed it would lower their taxes, while 30 percent thought it would raise their taxes. Another 35 percent felt their taxes would remain unchanged, and 20 percent were unsure of how it would affect them. The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online in English across all 50 states, gathering responses from 1,862 individuals, including 1,079 who acknowledged awareness of the Republican tax plan. It has a credibility interval of 3 percentage points, indicating its accuracy.

text: BENGHAZI, Libya (Reuters) - Prominent individuals from various political factions in Libya denounced remarks made by British Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson on Thursday regarding the removal of deceased individuals from the city of Sirte. On Tuesday, Johnson informed Conservative Party members that British investors had a "brilliant vision" to transform Sirte, previously a stronghold for Islamic State, into a future Dubai, contingent on the clearance of bodies. Lawmakers from Libya's House of Representatives (HOR), representing political and military groups in the eastern region, deemed the statements unacceptable. The HOR's foreign affairs committee released a statement requesting a clarification from the British prime minister and an apology to the Libyan populace. During a meeting with the British ambassador in Tripoli, the leader of Libya's U.N.-backed government, which has been rejected by the HOR, also sought clarification. "Some aspects of (Johnson's) statement are unacceptable," stated Fayez Seraj, the head of the U.N.-supported administration. Johnson's comments prompted calls for his resignation from political rivals in Britain. He accused them of politicizing the issue, asserting on Twitter that his remarks pertained to the clearing of booby-trapped bodies of Islamic State fighters. Local Libyan forces, supported by U.S. air strikes, battled for over six months last year to expel militants from Sirte, which had been transformed by Islamic State into its most significant base outside the Middle East. The coastal city, home to approximately 80,000 residents, suffered extensive damage during the conflict and is currently facing challenges in its recovery efforts. Since 2014, the HOR has operated from eastern Libya following a conflict in Tripoli that resulted in the establishment of rival parliaments and administrations in both the capital and the east. Its collaboration is deemed vital for advancing a new U.N. initiative aimed at stabilizing Libya and concluding the turmoil that began after the NATO-supported uprising that ousted Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

text: TransCanada Corp, the second largest pipeline operator in Canada, announced on Friday that it will reach a final investment decision regarding its Keystone XL project by December, as it reported profits that exceeded expectations. This December deadline marks the first instance where the company has publicly indicated a timeline for the investment decision since U.S. President Donald Trump granted approval for Keystone XL in March, overturning a previous decision made by Barack Obama. According to Paul Miller, the executive vice president and president of liquid pipeline at TransCanada, the investment decision will depend on the demand from shippers and regulatory developments in Nebraska, the U.S. state through which the project will run, which he discussed during a conference call following the release of quarterly earnings. "Our evaluation of these elements will significantly influence our investment decision as we approach the November-December period," he remarked. Although TransCanada enjoys "good support" from its current shippers, including those who left after the rejection of Keystone XL in 2015, the company is actively searching for new participants and is aiming for a "significant" level of commitment, although Miller did not provide specific numbers. On Thursday, TransCanada initiated an open season to gather additional commitments for Keystone XL. This expansion aims to enhance the capacity of the existing Keystone system that transports oil from Alberta, Canada's oil-producing province, to the Gulf of Mexico. Additionally, on Friday, TransCanada revealed plans to invest around C$160 million ($129 million) to increase the capacity of the Canadian natural gas mainline, which could assist producers who have lost an export route following the recent cancellation of the Pacific NorthWest project. This week, Malaysian state-owned Petroliam Nasional Bhd [PETR.UL], commonly known as Petronas, declared the cancellation of its Pacific NorthWest liquefied natural gas terminal in British Columbia, Canada, due to declining commodity prices. TransCanada, which invested at least C$500 million to construct the pipeline linking gas wells to the terminal, stated it expects to be reimbursed this year for expenses related to the project. On Friday, the company reported profits bolstered by strong performance in its U.S. natural gas and liquids pipelines divisions. Revenue from the U.S. natural gas pipelines unit more than doubled to C$879 million. The net income attributable to shareholders increased to C$881 million, or C$1.01 per share, for the second quarter ending June 30, up from C$365 million, or 52 Canadian cents per share, during the same period the previous year. On an adjusted basis, the company reported earnings of 76 Canadian cents per share, surpassing analysts' forecast of 69 Canadian cents per share, according to Thomson Reuters I/B/E/S. Overall revenue grew nearly 17 percent to reach C$3.22 billion.

text: A federal judge confirmed a North Carolina statute on Monday that mandates voters to present specific types of photo identification at polling stations, marking a significant victory for Republicans in an election year who assert that the measure is essential for preventing fraud. This case examined a pivotal element of extensive voting restrictions enacted following the 2013 U.S. Supreme Court decision that determined North Carolina and other historically discriminatory states no longer required federal approval for modifications to voting laws impacting minorities. In a 485-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Thomas Schroeder in Winston-Salem supported Republican Governor Pat McCrory and other state officials by rejecting challenges to the law, stating that North Carolina “has provided legitimate state interests for its voter-ID requirement and electoral system.” Judge Schroeder noted, “In sum, plaintiffs have failed to show that any North Carolinian who wishes to vote faces anything other than the ‘usual burdens of voting.’” The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, along with individual voters backed by the U.S. Justice Department, contended that the law disproportionately affects African-Americans and Hispanics, who are statistically more likely than whites to lack acceptable forms of identification. Democrats contend that voter ID laws enacted by Republican-led state legislatures are aimed at voters who typically favor the Democratic party. Advocates for these laws argue that they are designed to combat voter fraud. The trial in Winston-Salem was one among several closely monitored voting rights disputes nationwide, coinciding with the ongoing battle between Democrats and Republicans for the White House in November. Governor McCrory, facing a challenging re-election campaign this year, remarked in a statement: “This ruling further affirms that requiring a photo ID in order to vote is not only common-sense, it’s constitutional.” The law in North Carolina necessitates that voters present approved identification, such as a driver’s license or passport, prior to casting their ballots. Voters who claim a “reasonable impediment” in obtaining such identification are permitted to submit a provisional ballot. Judge Schroeder also upheld measures that removed a week of early voting, abolished same-day registration, and barred the counting of out-of-precinct ballots. He indicated that the plaintiffs did not demonstrate that black or Hispanic individuals had fewer opportunities than others to engage in the electoral process and highlighted that North Carolina is one of only two states, alongside South Carolina, to offer voters the “reasonable impediment” provision. Opponents of the law announced their intent to file an appeal. William Barber, president of the North Carolina State Conference of the NAACP, referred to the law’s “restrictive provisions” as “an affront to democracy” and pledged to persist in the battle against “regressive and discriminatory voter suppression tactics.”

text: A suspected drone strike by the U.S. on Thursday hit a hideout of the Haqqani militant group in Pakistan, resulting in the deaths of four individuals, according to officials. If verified, this incident would mark the fourth U.S. drone strike within Pakistan since President Donald Trump took office in January. Two intelligence officials from Pakistan and a local government representative reported that an unmanned aerial vehicle released two missiles on a compound that housed militants led by a prominent commander, Abdur Rasheed Haqqani. Initially, villagers informed authorities of an explosion in the Upper Kurram region, one of the officials noted, adding, "We later received information from our informant that it was a U.S. drone strike aimed at the Haqqani group." It remains uncertain whether the commander was among those who died, the officials mentioned, requesting anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the matter. Trump’s revised strategy for the Afghanistan conflict advocates a more stringent approach towards Pakistan in dealing with militants like the Haqqani network, which is known to operate from within Pakistani borders. Following the review of Afghan policy, the U.S. has been urging Islamabad to take decisive measures against Haqqani network militants, who are infamous for utilizing Pakistani territory to carry out assaults against American-led NATO forces in Afghanistan. Islamabad refutes these claims and instead holds Kabul accountable for failing to remove militants that exploit Afghan land for attacks on targets in Pakistan. Pakistan has been grappling with a severe Islamist insurgency for over a decade. On Wednesday, gunmen targeted a minority Shiite Muslim mosque in Islamabad, the capital city, resulting in two fatalities. The mosque attack was claimed by Lashkar-e-Jhangvi al-Alami, a Sunni sectarian organization associated with the militant group Islamic State.

TAIPEI (Reuters) - The self-governing island's representative at a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders stated on Monday that Taiwan has no plans to instigate issues in the Taiwan Strait. James Soong made these remarks following his discussions with journalists in Danang, Vietnam, over the weekend, where he noted having productive conversations with both U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Rex Tillerson during informal intervals between summit activities. "We do not wish to create issues in the Taiwan Strait, and we do not want to give the impression to the U.S., China, Japan, and all observers that we are instigators. The entire world does not desire Taiwan to act as a provocateur," Soong expressed when asked about his dialogues with Trump and Tillerson. "We aspire to resolve relevant issues through peaceful means." Additionally, Soong mentioned having a "natural interaction" with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Relations between Beijing and Taipei have deteriorated since President Tsai Ing-wen's election last year. China is concerned that she aims for Taiwan's formal independence, which is a non-negotiable issue for Beijing. In her defense, Tsai asserts her commitment to maintaining peace with China while upholding Taiwan's democracy and security. Since Tsai assumed office, China has halted regular dialogue with Taiwan and intensified military drills around the island. It has also increased diplomatic pressure by securing the allegiance of two more of Taiwan's diminishing diplomatic partners. At the summit, Soong, who leads the China-friendly People First Party, highlighted that Tsai has continuously expressed her desire for peaceful relations and stability with China. Earlier this month, Xi informed Trump in Beijing that Taiwan represents the most critical and sensitive aspect of Sino-U.S. relations.

text: On Thursday, U.S. Senate Republican leaders unveiled an updated version of their healthcare legislation. This new draft maintains significant taxes on affluent individuals and permits insurance companies to provide plans that do not meet the Obamacare requirements mandating coverage for specific health services. Additionally, the bill retains the limit imposed by Obamacare on corporate tax deductions for executive compensation within the health insurance sector. text: CHICAGO (Reuters) - On Wednesday, former U.S. President Barack Obama revealed the design plans for his presidential center in Chicago, which he envisions as a training hub for upcoming leaders. The Obama Presidential Center will be constructed in Jackson Park, a 500-acre (200-hectare) area located on the South Side of Chicago. This park originally served as the venue for the 1893 World’s Fair. The development will consist of three structures—a museum, a forum, and a library—arranged around a central plaza. According to a statement from the Obama Foundation, the museum, which will be the tallest among the three buildings, will include public spaces, offices, and classrooms alongside exhibition areas. "Our aim is for this to become the world’s leading institution dedicated to training young individuals in leadership, empowering them to effect change in their communities, nations, and globally. That is our mission," Obama remarked during the design presentation in Chicago. Since departing from office in January, Obama has gradually begun to re-engage with the public. Last month, he hosted an event at the University of Chicago, marking his first significant public appearance after leaving the White House. The project is expected to take approximately four years to finish, according to Obama, although educational initiatives are set to commence this year. On Wednesday, he announced his intention to contribute $2 million to a local summer jobs program. Obama, who spent his childhood in Hawaii and attended college in New York and California, has a residence and spent the majority of his political career prior to the presidency in Chicago—initially as a community organizer, followed by his roles as an Illinois state senator and a U.S. senator. Chicago was selected over proposals from New York City and Hawaii to host the library. Last year, Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects Partners from New York and Interactive Design Architects from Chicago were appointed to lead the design efforts for the center. Residents of Chicago’s South Side, which encompasses several impoverished and crime-affected areas, are hopeful that the library will bring job opportunities and investment. However, some small business owners fear they might be displaced if rental costs rise. Obama stated that the center has the potential to be a transformative project for the community.

text: Trump and the intelligence chief provide contrasting accounts regarding a conversation about the Russia dossier. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. intelligence chief James Clapper and President-elect Donald Trump presented differing perspectives on a phone call they had concerning a dossier filled with unverified, sensational claims connecting Russia to Trump, who is currently engaged in a verbal conflict with the intelligence agencies he will oversee in just eight days. As a political newcomer, businessman Trump has been at odds with U.S. intelligence agencies for several months, contesting their assessments that Russia employed hacking and other methods to influence the 2016 presidential election in his favor. On Wednesday, he acknowledged this point but initiated a new confrontation, responding to media reports of unverified claims that he was involved in a compromising situation in Russia by accusing intelligence agencies of employing tactics reminiscent of Nazi Germany. Clapper further stated that he did not think the leaks originated from U.S. intelligence agencies. Clapper emphasized to Trump that the report was not generated by U.S. intelligence agencies and that they had not assessed the credibility of the information. He refrained from declaring the document as false. Conversely, Trump implied in a tweet on Thursday that Clapper had concurred that the report was inaccurate. "James Clapper called me yesterday to condemn the false and fictitious report that was illegally circulated. Made up, phony facts. Too bad!" Trump tweeted. Democratic Congressman Adam Schiff, a critic of the Republican Trump, was asked by CNN on Thursday morning to comment on Trump’s interpretation of Clapper’s statement that the document was false. "Unfortunately, you cannot depend on the president-elect’s tweets or statements about what he is being told in intelligence briefings. text: The White House is anticipated to communicate with the Pentagon in the near future regarding the implementation of a ban on transgender individuals serving in the military, as indicated by a memo stating that the defense secretary might have the authority to decide on the removal of service members based on their deployment capacities, a U.S. official disclosed on Wednesday. According to a report first published by The Wall Street Journal and validated by the official, the two-and-a-half-page document from the White House allocates six months for Defense Secretary Jim Mattis to fully execute the ban. Furthermore, it instructs the Defense Department to refuse entry to transgender persons and halt funding for medical treatment plans for those currently in service, as reported by the Journal, citing U.S. officials. Mattis is likely to focus on 'deployability'—referring to the capability to operate in combat zones, engage in training exercises, or spend extended periods aboard ships—as the primary legal grounds for deciding whether to remove service members from military service, the Journal noted. On July 26, President Donald Trump tweeted that the U.S. government 'will not accept or allow transgender individuals to serve in any capacity' in the armed forces, marking a reversal of previous Pentagon policy. Earlier this month, five transgender military members, including veterans from the Iraq and Afghanistan conflicts, filed a lawsuit against Trump, arguing that the ban was enacted without consulting senior military leaders. The lawsuit names Trump, Mattis, and other military officials, including Joseph Dunford, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, as defendants. Dunford indicated in a memo the day after Trump’s tweets that there would be no policy alterations until Mattis received a formal directive from the president. text: A U.S. appeals court has permitted Democratic state attorneys general to defend subsidy payments to insurance companies under the Obamacare healthcare law, which is a vital funding element for the statute that President Donald Trump has threatened to eliminate. On Tuesday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit accepted a motion submitted by 16 attorneys general, led by California’s Xavier Becerra and New York’s Eric Schneiderman. Frustrated by his and his Republican counterparts' inability to fulfill campaign promises to repeal and replace Obamacare, President Donald Trump has indicated he may halt the so-called cost-sharing subsidy, or CSR, payments. A statement from the White House noted, “The President is working with his staff and his cabinet to consider the issues raised by the CSR payments.” These subsidies assist low-income Americans with out-of-pocket medical expenses. The origins of this case trace back to President Barack Obama’s administration, initiated by the Republican-led House of Representatives seeking to prevent the federal government from making subsidy payments to insurers for individual plans established by the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare. The order from the court allows Democrats who support the law to participate in the legal proceedings, empowering them to obstruct a settlement or appeal a decision that would stop the payments. They are also permitted to submit briefs and their legal representatives can engage in oral arguments. Schneiderman expressed, “The court’s decision is good news for the hundreds of thousands of New York families that rely on these subsidies for their health care. It’s disturbingly clear that President Trump and his administration are willing to treat them as political pawns.” Becerra stated, “If Donald Trump won’t defend these vital subsidies for American families, then we will.” The three-judge panel, composed entirely of Obama appointees, indicated in its ruling that the states had demonstrated “a substantial risk that an injunction requiring termination of the payments at issue here ... would lead directly and imminently to an increase in insurance prices, which in turn will increase the number of uninsured individuals for whom the states will have to provide health care.” Furthermore, the court order added, “In addition, state-funded hospitals will suffer financially when they are unable to recoup costs from uninsured, indigent patients for whom federal law requires them to provide medical care.” Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan, remarked that the decision is significant as it complicates any potential settlement for the Trump administration. “Allowing the states to intervene will increase the pressure on the administration to keep making the cost-sharing payments,” he noted, while acknowledging that the administration still has the option to cease the payments. Trump has consistently threatened to stop the payments to insurers, which total approximately $7 billion this year, referring to them as a “bailout.” In their court filing from May, the attorneys general referenced Trump’s own statements promising to let Obamacare “explode” as part of their rationale for intervening. Currently, the case is on hold at the request of both parties. It was expected that the case might be dismissed due to the Republican-controlled Congress's plans to repeal the Obamacare law. However, since that effort failed last week, the significance of the court case has increased. Anthem Inc, a U.S. health insurer, is retracting its offerings in 16 of 19 pricing regions in California where it provided Obamacare options this year, partly due to the uncertainty regarding the payments, state officials reported on Tuesday.

text: The U.S. Senate has approved Rex Tillerson to be the secretary of state under President Donald Trump. This decision was made on Wednesday, securing an essential role in the Republican administration's national security framework, despite apprehensions regarding Tillerson's connections to Russia as the former CEO of Exxon Mobil Corp. The voting outcome, primarily along party lines, was the narrowest in over fifty years. A total of 56 senators voted in favor of Tillerson, while 43 opposed him. All Republican senators supported Tillerson, along with four Democrats: Senators Heidi Heitkamp, Joe Manchin, Mark Warner, and independent Angus King. Democratic Senator Chris Coons abstained from voting. In contrast, Tillerson’s predecessor, John Kerry, received a confirmation vote of 94 to 3, and Condoleezza Rice, the last Republican-nominated secretary of state, was confirmed with an 85-13 vote. Senate Democrats attempted to postpone the confirmation vote for Tillerson due to President Trump’s executive order prohibiting immigration from seven predominantly Muslim nations and temporarily suspending refugee admissions. They claimed they needed more time to question Tillerson about the implications of the order signed by Trump on Friday, which triggered protests and confusion at airports nationwide and caused uncertainty for travelers globally. However, with Republicans holding 52 of the 100 Senate seats, they have successfully confirmed all six Trump nominees that have been brought to vote. Senators had voiced concerns regarding Tillerson’s connections to Russia following his extensive tenure with the oil company. Some criticized him for not committing to abstain from any Exxon Mobil-related issues for the entirety of his time as secretary of state, opting instead for the one-year recusal mandated by law. At 64 years old, Tillerson concluded his role as chairman and CEO of Exxon Mobil at the end of 2016, having spent four decades with the firm. Supporters of Tillerson among Republicans and others expressed confidence in his capability to serve as an effective leader in the role of the nation’s top diplomat, pointing to his experience managing a massive corporation that operates across six continents. They emphasized the necessity of swiftly finalizing Trump’s national security team to tackle international challenges and provide reassurance to allies regarding the new president’s "America First" approach to foreign policy.

text: The United States has prolonged certain sanctions relief for Iran in accordance with the 2015 nuclear agreement, as announced by the State Department on Thursday. However, the administration has not yet reached a conclusion regarding the future of the deal itself. President Donald Trump, who is required to make a decision by mid-October that could jeopardize the agreement, stated that Iran is breaching the spirit of the 2015 accord, which allowed Iran to receive sanctions relief in exchange for limiting its nuclear activities. In a demonstration of Trump's intent to increase pressure on Iran, which contends it has not violated the agreement, the U.S. Treasury issued new sanctions related to cyber activities and other measures against seven Iranian individuals, two Iranian organizations, and two entities based in Ukraine. "We are not going to stand for what they are doing," Trump remarked to reporters aboard Air Force One. Nevertheless, he refrained from indicating whether he would choose not to recertify the agreement. In October, Trump must determine whether to validate that Iran is adhering to the agreement, referred to as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). If he opts against this, Congress will have a 60-day window to decide on reinstating the sanctions that were lifted under the deal. The potential for the U.S. to backtrack on the agreement has raised concerns among several key allies involved in the negotiations, particularly as the world deals with another nuclear issue regarding North Korea's development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles. Republican Senator Bob Corker, chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the author of the legislation granting Congress the authority to review the Iran deal, mentioned that he and the White House are preparing for a potential policy shift. He also acknowledged the importance of collaborating with allies. "I think it’s crucial that... we take actions that, as much as possible, keep all of our allies united," Corker told Reuters. text: Trump aims to coerce Mexico into financing the border wall. WASHINGTON - On Tuesday, Donald Trump suggested that he would compel Mexico to cover the expenses for his proposed border wall by threatening to halt remittances sent by undocumented immigrants, which he described as "welfare" for impoverished families in Mexico that their government fails to provide. The campaign for the Republican presidential candidate stated in a memo that if he wins in November, Trump would employ a U.S. anti-terrorism statute to terminate these money transfers unless Mexico made a one-time contribution of $5 billion to $10 billion toward the wall. Trump's commitment to erecting the wall has become a prominent feature of his platform aimed at illegal immigration in the U.S., bolstering his position as the leading candidate for the Republican nomination in the election on Nov. 8. The actual cost of a wall along the nearly 2,000-mile (3,200-km) U.S.-Mexico border remains uncertain, and Mexico has firmly asserted that it will not comply. The memo expanded on a concept Trump proposed in August, where he mentioned confiscating all remittances associated with "illegal wages." It indicated that upon taking office, a Trump administration would introduce a regulation requiring firms like Western Union Co WU.N to verify that customers were legally present in the United States. Should Mexico consent to fund the wall, Trump would retract the proposed regulation, it stated. "It’s a simple choice for Mexico," his campaign remarked, noting that the nation receives approximately $24 billion annually in remittances from Mexicans residing in the U.S., the majority of whom are in the country unlawfully. "It (remittances) functions as a de facto welfare system for low-income families in Mexico. There is no substantial social safety network offered by the government in Mexico," it noted. According to the World Bank Remittances project, the money flow from the U.S. to Mexico in 2014, the last complete year for which data is available, was close to $24 billion, though it is unclear how much of that comes from Mexicans living in the country illegally. President Barack Obama, a Democrat, characterized the idea of blocking remittances as impractical and potentially counterproductive. "The idea that we’re going to keep track of every Western Union transaction being sent to Mexico, you know, good luck with that," he told reporters. He added that if Mexico's economy were to collapse, it would only lead to an increase in immigration to the United States. Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto seemed to disregard the proposal as mere campaign talk. "The (Mexican) Presidency has no comment on any opinion expressed in the heat of the electoral process to choose candidates for the U.S. presidency," stated the president’s office in a text message to Reuters. Any initiative to target payments sent back by individuals living in the United States could have a devastating financial impact in Mexico, the top recipient of U.S. remittances. Trump's suggestion could also influence banks and companies involved in wire transfers, including MoneyGram International Inc (MGI.O) and PayPal Holdings Inc’s (PYPL.O) Xoom. These companies did not respond to inquiries for comments. Besides his wall initiative, Trump has accused Mexico of dispatching rapists and drug traffickers to the United States. Both Democrats and numerous Republicans have consistently condemned his remarks as incendiary; however, his statements have been warmly welcomed by his supporters, particularly within the white working-class demographic. In the memo, initially reported by The Washington Post, Trump's campaign reiterated its vow to target visas. It also mentioned the possibility of imposing trade tariffs or enforcing current trade regulations as a means to compel Mexico to pay. Trump supporter Benjamin Proto, a lawyer from Connecticut, recognized that the remittance strategy was not realistic but commended the candidate for "exploring different approaches." The memo surfaced as Republican contender Ted Cruz appeared poised to defeat Trump in Wisconsin's primary on Tuesday, a victory he would hope to use as a stepping stone to position himself as the leading alternative to the New York billionaire.

text: Turks turn to social media amid gold trader sanctions trial. ANKARA (Reuters) - This week, allegations against Turkey's political and financial elite have captivated the nation, yet various newspapers have chosen to highlight courtroom drama and fashion instead, leaving many Turks craving substantial updates. "Casual chic on the 2nd day," proclaimed HaberTurk newspaper's headline following the main witness Reza Zarrab's testimony in a New York courtroom, where he asserted that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan sanctioned a transaction designed to assist Iran in circumventing U.S. sanctions. On the trial's second day, Zarrab appeared in a casual white shirt and dark blazer rather than a prison uniform, according to HaberTurk. Similar to other outlets, HaberTurk deftly avoided delving into the core matters at hand. Since a failed coup last year, Erdogan has overseen a crackdown on various sectors, including the judiciary and media, resulting in numerous journalists being incarcerated. He has also frequently pursued legal action against individuals he perceives as having insulted him. Zarrab is aiding U.S. prosecutors in their criminal case against a Turkish bank executive accused of facilitating money laundering for Iran. The executive has entered a plea of not guilty. Erdogan, who has led Turkey for nearly 15 years, has yet to address the courtroom allegations but has previously dismissed the case as a politically motivated effort to destabilize the Turkish government. He claims that the U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom Ankara blames for the failed coup and refers to as FETO, is also behind the legal proceedings. The pro-government newspaper Star labeled the trial as "American Theater" on its front page. The Zarrab plot trial is portrayed as a political spectacle orchestrated by FETO in collaboration with judges, prosecutors, and experts described as Neo-cons and adversaries of Turkey. The limited or skeptical reporting on the case has prompted inquisitive Turks to flock to Twitter, where hashtags like #Zarrabcase and #Zarrabkonusuyor (Zarrab is speaking) became leading topics late on Wednesday and Thursday. Since the trial commenced this week, there have been hundreds of thousands of tweets, retweets, and responses featuring Zarrab-related hashtags on Twitter. "You can’t see it on television or in newspapers here. They either cut the feeds or do not mention it at all," remarked Oguzcan Gundogmus, a 24-year-old PhD student, while enjoying tea in central Ankara. The court proceedings have resonated in public spaces. "Spill the beans, my son!" an elderly protester called out to Zarrab during a women's demonstration in Istanbul last weekend. Yet, the majority of the attention has shifted online. The number of followers for journalists tweeting from inside the courtroom surged over the last two days, increasing more than twenty-fold in certain instances. One court reporter’s tweets are being translated into Turkish in real-time and have garnered a following of 10,000 thus far. In court, Zarrab admitted to bribing several Turkish officials as part of his operation. "I’m surprised the government hasn’t banned Twitter yet. My friends and I stay up late and follow the case there; we even make popcorn as if it’s a movie night and refer to the case as ‘Lord of the Bribes,’" shared Mehmet Baglar, a 34-year-old engineer.

text: President Donald Trump on Thursday put forward the nomination of R. Alexander Acosta, a former member of the National Labor Relations Board, to take on the role of U.S. secretary of labor. This announcement came just a day after Trump's initial selection withdrew from consideration. Acosta, who currently serves as the dean of the Florida International University College of Law in Miami, represents Trump's first Hispanic nominee. With a long-standing career in public service, Acosta has held three positions that required presidential appointment and Senate confirmation, and he is anticipated to have a smooth confirmation process. Senator Lamar Alexander, the chair of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, which will evaluate the nomination, remarked, "Mr. Acosta’s nomination is off to a good start because he’s already been confirmed by the Senate three times." Acosta was appointed to the NLRB by former Republican President George W. Bush, who also designated him as assistant attorney general in the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department. Subsequently, he became the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where he pursued high-profile cases against individuals like Jack Abramoff and the Swiss bank UBS, leading to fines exceeding $750 million related to a tax-avoidance scheme. Acosta also previously worked as a law clerk for Samuel Alito from 1994 to 1995 when Alito was a judge on the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. In a statement, Acosta expressed gratitude, saying, "I thank the President and his staff for their confidence in me and I am eager to work tirelessly on behalf of the American worker." During his tenure at the NLRB, Acosta authored numerous opinions. According to those acquainted with his work, he is regarded as a meticulous and prudent public servant whose career path hinted at a potential future as a federal judge. Given his previous vetting by the U.S. Senate, it is improbable that any unforeseen issues will arise regarding his background that could jeopardize his nomination. The selection of Acosta, a conventional Republican conservative, is interpreted by some as an indication that Trump was compelled to abandon a more aggressive stance on labor issues. Trump's initial selection for labor secretary, Andrew Puzder, the CEO of CKE Restaurants Inc., was a vocal critic of matters like overtime pay and minimum wage increases, even suggesting the advantages of robots compared to human employees. Puzder withdrew his name from consideration on Wednesday, amid worries that he would not secure sufficient Senate votes for confirmation. "This is the humbling of Donald Trump," stated Seth Harris, a former Acting Labor Secretary during the Obama administration, who mentioned that Puzder would have acted as a "radical disruptor," a role Acosta is not expected to fulfill. Acosta has consistently advocated for the civil rights of Muslims who experienced backlash following the September 11, 2001 attacks in the U.S. During a congressional hearing in 2011, he commended the Justice Department's actions against civil rights violations, asserting that they reassured Muslim Americans that "their government would protect their rights." Some progressive organizations have already voiced their discontent regarding Acosta's appointment, with Allied Progress accusing him of mismanaging the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice during his leadership. An internal report from the Justice Department in 2008 criticized Acosta for not addressing the actions of a staff member who engaged in inappropriate politicized hiring. Nevertheless, the reaction from union groups, who had strongly opposed Puzder, was notably more tempered on Thursday. "Unlike Andy Puzder, Alexander Acosta’s nomination deserves serious consideration," commented AFL-CIO President Richard Trumka. "In one day, we’ve gone from a fast-food CEO who routinely violates labor law to a public servant with experience enforcing it."

text: The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum expressed deep concern on Monday regarding "hateful speech" at a white nationalist event that took place over the weekend, and a restaurant issued an apology for accommodating the group after a woman tweeted a photo of herself performing a Nazi salute. The National Policy Institute, a think tank associated with the alt-right movement that encompasses neo-Nazis, white supremacists, and anti-Semites, organized a meeting at the federally owned Ronald Reagan Building on Saturday. The alt-right movement gained prominence during the U.S. presidential election. President-elect Donald Trump faced backlash for appointing Steve Bannon, the former head of a website tied to the alt-right, as his chief strategist in the White House. On Monday, Trump's transition team released a statement asserting that Trump has consistently condemned racism, as reported by CNN. "President-elect Trump has continued to denounce racism of any kind and he was elected because he will be a leader for every American," said Bryan Lanza, a spokesman for the Trump-Pence Transition, in a statement. The Saturday gathering attracted numerous protesters who obstructed traffic around the building in demonstration against the event. A video recorded by The Atlantic from within the conference depicted Richard Spencer, the leader of the National Policy Institute, exclaiming, "Hail Trump, hail our people, hail victory!" while some attendees raised their arms in a Nazi salute. The Holocaust Memorial Museum remarked in a statement, "The Holocaust did not begin with killings: it began with words." The museum urged all American citizens, as well as religious and civic leaders and officials from all levels of government, to confront racist ideologies and divisive hateful rhetoric. Some participants from the nationalist meeting later assembled for a banquet at Maggiano’s Little Italy restaurant located in northwest Washington. Protesters gathered at the location, leading the restaurant to shut down for the safety of its staff and customers, as stated in a Facebook apology from management. The restaurant clarified that the reservation was made last-minute under a different name, so the staff was unaware that the National Policy Institute was dining there and had no knowledge of the group's beliefs. "After the event, an attendee tweeted a photo in which she made a 'Seig Heil salute' in support of Hitler and white supremacy. This display of support for Hitler is profoundly offensive to us, as our restaurant welcomes teammates and patrons from all races, religions, and cultural backgrounds," the Facebook post read. The restaurant extended its apologies to the local community and announced it would donate $10,000, the profits from its sales on Friday, to the Washington office of the Anti-Defamation League, a Jewish civil rights organization. The Ronald Reagan Building, the largest structure in the U.S. capital, is federally owned but operated by Trade Center Management Associates, a division of Drew Co., a real estate development firm based in Boston. The company defended its decision to permit the nationalist group to utilize the venue, stating in a release that its contract stipulates that unless there is a security risk posed by an organization or individual requesting space, the building is available for rental. The agenda for the National Policy Institute’s Saturday meeting included an analysis of the 2016 election and strategies for expanding the alt-right. The nonprofit Southern Poverty Law Center, which monitors hate groups, characterized Spencer as an "academic racist" who advocates for the establishment of an Aryan homeland. Last week, Twitter Inc suspended multiple accounts linked to the alt-right, including Spencer’s, following the company's announcement that it would enhance certain features to better address cyberbullying.

text: The Trump administration and prominent Republicans in the U.S. Congress are reportedly just weeks away from finalizing key elements of a tax reform plan, which is anticipated to shape the legislation expected in September, according to an administration official who spoke to Reuters this week. Facing pressure from business organizations and grassroots Republicans, Trump officials and congressional leaders still have to determine the extent of tax rate reductions and whether the proposed package should add to the federal budget deficit, sources from both the administration and Congress indicated. Additionally, a decision regarding the border adjustment tax (BAT) proposal from House Republicans, designed to enhance exports while discouraging imports, may also be reached in the next two to three weeks, as per the administration official. President Donald Trump has committed to prioritizing tax reform. However, after being in office for 20 weeks and dealing with various distractions, he has yet to present a tax bill to Congress. Anticipations for the legislation have repeatedly diminished, shifting from spring to summer and now to after the U.S. Labor Day holiday. Nevertheless, stock prices have increased since Trump's election victory in November, with companies and affluent Americans preparing to earn more in 2018, betting on forthcoming tax reductions. The leader of the House Freedom Caucus, a group of approximately thirty-six conservatives capable of hindering legislation, urged Republicans on Friday to recognize the lack of agreement on the BAT and to produce a tax proposal by the end of July. Trump and his Republican counterparts made a commitment during last year’s election campaign to address the most significant tax reform since the Reagan administration in 2017. However, this plan has been delayed due to internal conflicts regarding the repeal of Obamacare and investigations into potential connections between Trump’s campaign and alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election. This week, the Business Roundtable, a significant lobbying entity representing CEOs, sent a letter to Trump and congressional leaders advocating for a transition from discussion to action concerning tax reform. The unnamed administration official noted that there is widespread consensus among those involved in the discussions on the necessity to reduce taxes, streamline the tax code, eliminate tax incentives, cease taxing U.S. companies’ overseas profits, and bring back an estimated $2.6 trillion in corporate profits held abroad. However, several crucial details remain unresolved. Additional meetings are expected to take place among U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, White House economic advisor Gary Cohn, Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, House Speaker Paul Ryan, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Kevin Brady, and Senate Finance Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, along with their respective staff, according to the official. Following their third meeting on Tuesday, officials had yet to determine whether to implement full expensing for corporations, as indicated by the administration official. This policy would permit companies to deduct the cost of capital investments like equipment immediately, allowing them to reinvest that money into their operations. The official stated that the goal of these discussions is to reach an agreement on a framework by mid-year and to release legislation shortly after Congress’s extended August break. A significant choice awaits regarding the House Republicans' BAT, which is aimed at increasing exports while helping to fund reforms and discouraging firms from relocating assets, profits, and jobs overseas. The BAT, which proposes taxing imports while exempting export revenues from taxation, has faced opposition from many Republicans and criticism from the administration. Congressional and administration officials are exploring alternatives to the BAT that could minimize the erosion of the federal tax base, including implementing certain rules and a minimum corporate tax. The determinations regarding the BAT, revenue neutrality, and expensing will play a crucial role in whether Congress can reduce the corporate income tax to 15 percent, as Trump desires, or to 20-25 percent, as outlined in the House Republicans’ tax proposal.

text: DANANG, Vietnam (Reuters) - On Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump delivered a firm trade message during a gathering of Asia-Pacific nations in Vietnam, asserting that the United States could no longer accept ongoing trade violations and would demand fair and equitable policies. Trump stated that the United States was prepared to enter into bilateral agreements with any nation in the Indo-Pacific region, but only based on mutual respect and benefits. He mentioned, "When the United States engages in trade with other nations or peoples, we will now expect our partners to adhere to the rules faithfully," while speaking at the coastal resort of Danang. He added, "We anticipate that markets will be equally accessible on both sides and that private investments, rather than government planners, will guide investment decisions," during his address prior to a summit of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders. Trump arrived in Vietnam from China, marking the fourth stop on his 12-day tour of Asia. Addressing the trade imbalance between Asia and the United States is central to Trump's "America First" policy, which he claims will safeguard American workers. The contrast between Trump's and China's strategies became more pronounced following remarks by Chinese President Xi Jinping in a subsequent speech, where he stated that globalization is an unstoppable trend and expressed support for multilateral trade agreements. Although China maintains the largest trade surplus with the United States, Vietnam is also among the countries the Trump administration aims to address regarding trade surpluses. APEC, which has historically supported free trade, has been shaken by the shifts initiated by Trump. After Trump withdrew from the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) trade agreement early in his presidency, the remaining 11 member nations have faced challenges in generating momentum to sustain it. Leaders from TPP countries are scheduled to meet on Friday after discussions among ministers concluded in confusion on Thursday, with Japan's economy minister stating that they "agree in principle," while his Canadian counterpart disputed that claim. Trump departed from the "Pivot to Asia" strategy of the Obama administration early on, raising concerns among some traditional allies that he might permit China to extend its rising influence. Danang is located along the South China Sea, a significant security concern in the region, where China's neighboring countries contest its extensive claims over most of the waterway, asserting that these claims have no legal foundation. Trump emphasized that the future of the region relies on maintaining freedom of navigation and overflight, which includes open shipping routes. He also highlighted territorial expansion alongside issues like drug trafficking, human smuggling, and terrorism as significant problems. Vietnam has emerged as one of the most outspoken critics of China's assertions in the South China Sea and its development of artificial islands. In a potential challenge to China's ambitious Belt and Road initiative, Trump stated he would encourage the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank to finance infrastructure projects and would reform U.S. development finance institutions. He asserted that this would "offer robust alternatives to state-directed initiatives that come with numerous conditions." "Above all, we seek friendship and we do not aspire for dominance," he remarked. While addressing a meeting in conjunction with the summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, Trump frequently referred to the Indo-Pacific region and emphasized India's significance in his address. Danang holds a notable place in the history of U.S.-Vietnam relations: it was where the first U.S. ground troops arrived in 1965 during the escalation of a conflict that would endure for another decade before the communist triumph. Danang was near some of the fiercest fighting, and its air base served as the route for many Americans of Trump's generation heading to the war. Trump himself did not serve, having received five deferments, one of which was for bone spurs in his heel.

Ankara (Reuters) - Iran and Turkey will work together to confront the disintegration of Iraq and Syria to ease tension in the crisis-hit region, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani said on Wednesday after meeting with his Turkish counterpart in Tehran.  We want security and stability in the Middle East ... the independence referendum in Iraq s Kurdistan is a sectarian plot by foreign countries and is rejected by Tehran and Ankara,  Rouhani told a joint news conference with Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan.

text: The Belgian prosecutor has announced that they will review the arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont. On Friday, Eric Van der Sypt, the federal prosecutor, stated that Belgian officials have received the arrest warrant from Spain concerning the ousted Catalan leader and will assess it prior to presenting it to a judge. "We will examine it, and we may present it to an investigative judge tomorrow or the day after," Van der Sypt informed Reuters. These remarks came shortly after Spain issued the warrant citing sedition and additional charges against Puigdemont, who relocated to Brussels following the dismissal of his government due to a declaration of independence.
