BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Belgian authorities have received Spain s arrest warrant for ousted Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont and will examine it before handing it over to a judge, federal prosecutor Eric Van der Sypt said on Friday.  We will study it, we will give it to an investigative judge maybe tomorrow or the day after tomorrow,  Van der Sypt told Reuters. The comments came just hours after Spain issued an arrest warrant on sedition and other charges for Puigdemont, who went to Brussels after his government was sacked over a declaration of independence.

text: The Democratic leader of the U.S. Senate, Harry Reid, has rejected the Zika funding proposal put forth by House Republicans. In a statement from Washington, Reid criticized the $1.1 billion funding agreement announced on Wednesday as an inadequate response to the Zika virus threat. He stated, "A narrowly partisan proposal that cuts off women’s access to birth control, shortchanges veterans and rescinds Obamacare funds to cover the cost is not a serious response to the threat from the Zika virus."
source_text: U.S. Senate Democratic leader dismisses Republicans' Zika funding proposal. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid said an agreement announced on Wednesday by House of Representatives Republicans on $1.1 billion in new funding to fight the Zika virus was not a serious response to the threat. “A narrowly partisan proposal that cuts off women’s access to birth control, shortchanges veterans and rescinds Obamacare funds to cover the cost is not a serious response to the threat from the Zika virus,” Reid said in a statement.

text: Hashtag politics: Merkel seeks to connect with Germany's youth. BERLIN (Reuters) - After a dozen years in office, Chancellor Angela Merkel is positioning herself as more than merely Germany's Mutti, engaging in online campaigning to attract younger voters and secure their backing well beyond the upcoming elections this month. Merkel, whose nickname translates to 'Mummy,' appears to be on track for a fourth term with substantial support from older Germans. However, the 63-year-old, who unlike some of her Western counterparts does not have a personal Twitter profile, aims to rally almost 3 million first-time voters to her conservative CDU party on September 24. To achieve this, Merkel has taken questions from four YouTube vloggers, participated in Europe’s largest gaming convention, and established a walk-in campaign hub in Berlin’s trendy startup area. Diana Kinnert, a 26-year-old who contributed to proposals aimed at modernizing the CDU, noted that political parties ought to leverage new communication methods to engage young individuals who feel alienated by 'sterile' politics in the long run. "It would be unfortunate if it ended up being just election noise," Kinnert, who sports tattoos and a baseball cap, remarked to Reuters at the walk-in center. The CDU, which is not expected to secure an overall majority in parliament, relies on the youth vote to bolster Merkel’s position in the coalition negotiations that will follow the election. To some confusion, the party has launched a Twitter hashtag #fedidwgugl. Far from being a result of a malfunctioning keyboard, it stands for the CDU campaign slogan: Fuer ein Deutschland In Dem Wir Gut und Gern Leben (For a Germany in which we can live well and gladly). Consequently, the Berlin walk-in center, where themed spaces bring the CDU manifesto to life, is dubbed the #fedidwgugl House. In Britain, young voters turned out in large numbers in June to support the opposition Labour party, removing the ruling Conservatives’ majority and demonstrating how youth can influence government outcomes despite their smaller numbers. With German society aging rapidly, older demographics continue to dominate the country's political agenda. There are more than twice as many eligible voters aged over 60 compared to those under 30. The CDU captured the highest youth vote share in 2013, but its support is still heavily tilted toward older voters. In the previous election, two-fifths of its supporters were over 60, while only 5.4 percent were under 25. Kinnert, who has shared posts on Instagram wearing a T-shirt that says 'Keep Calm and Vote for Angie,' asserts that Merkel is constantly learning and remains forward-thinking despite her long time in power. One of Merkel's key goals is the digitization of Germany's industry. She maintains Facebook and Instagram profiles and has made efforts to demonstrate her familiarity with social media, even if it sometimes appears awkward. When asked about her preferred emoji during the YouTube conversation, Merkel replied that it was a smiley: "If things are good, even one with a little heart," she joked. Merkel’s principal opponent, Social Democrat leader Martin Schulz, has also embraced the digital space. This week, he faced questions on YouTube regarding issues such as cannabis legalization, animal rights, and expanding broadband access. While the CDU faced ridicule for the confounding #fedidwgugl hashtag, the media buzz attracted attention to the CDU's platform. Campaigning through new media also resonates with older voters who wish the best for their children and grandchildren, noted Stefan Marschall from Düsseldorf’s Heinrich Heine University. Merkel is the only chancellor that most first-time voters remember, which allows the CDU to present her as a stable figure during the turbulent times of Donald Trump and Brexit. A June opinion poll by Forsa revealed that 57 percent of 18 to 21-year-olds supported Merkel, compared to 53 percent of the general populace. Only 21 percent of young voters backed Schulz. Forsa's managing director Manfred Guellner stated that younger Germans have become more conservative than their counterparts in other nations: "Young people here are pragmatic."

text: India prohibits 'unruly' travelers from flying for a period ranging from three months to over two years. NEW DELHI (Reuters) - The Indian government has announced new regulations that prevent unruly passengers from flying for a minimum duration of three months and potentially up to more than two years, depending on the severity of the offense, according to a statement released on Friday. A no-fly list for disruptive passengers has been created by the federal authorities following an incident where a lawmaker confessed to assaulting an employee of the state-owned airline, Air India. These revised rules will also apply to international airlines, the government noted in its announcement, stating that unruly conduct has been classified into three categories: verbal, physical, and life-threatening. The no-fly policy is designed to ensure the safety of fellow passengers, crew members, and the aircraft itself, rather than solely addressing security threats, the government explained.

The new rules will be applicable to foreign carriers as well, the government said in a statement, adding that unruly behavior has been categorized in three levels - verbal, physical and life threatening.  The concept of no-fly is based on safety of other passengers, crew and the aircraft, and not just on the security threat,  the government said.

text: The Senate is divided over a proposal aimed at preventing a government shutdown. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A covert struggle in Congress to avert a U.S. government shutdown became public on Thursday when Republicans unveiled a temporary funding bill that Democrats swiftly dismissed. The federal fiscal year concludes on September 30, and it is essential for Congress to enact a spending bill by that date to keep the government operational. In recent years, lawmakers have rarely managed to agree on a complete federal budget, opting instead for temporary funding solutions. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell concluded weeks of arduous discussions by putting forward a continuing resolution intended to finance government agencies from October 1 through December 9 at an annual expenditure rate of slightly more than $1 trillion. This measure also allocates $1.1 billion to fight the growing Zika virus, provides $500 million for flood relief in states including Louisiana, and supports U.S. military operations abroad with an annual budget of $74 billion. "There have been widespread requests for a straightforward continuing resolution. That’s what I’ve just proposed," stated McConnell, a Republican from Kentucky, who characterized the proposal as a result of bipartisan discussions. Democrats promptly criticized the resolution as "a Republican-only bill" that would not assist Flint, Michigan, in dealing with lead-contaminated water and would maintain a ban on the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission from mandating public companies to disclose political expenditures. "We Democrats cannot support that," remarked Senator Barbara Mikulski, the leading Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee. White House spokesperson Josh Earnest informed the press that plans were already in motion for a systematic government shutdown should Congress fail to reach an agreement on a funding proposal. McConnell excluded a measure supported by Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump and his former adversary in the White House race, Senator Ted Cruz, which would have prevented the U.S. government from transferring oversight of the internet’s technical management to an international group of stakeholders on October 1. Additionally, the proposal lacked provisions that would have allowed the U.S. Export-Import Bank to authorize loans or guarantees exceeding $10 million. Both Republicans and Democrats had aimed to incorporate such a provision, but it became too contentious for the essential funding resolution. A senior aide to the Republicans indicated that the Senate could start voting on the funding legislation as soon as Monday.

text: Zika virus sexual transmission research is commencing despite a deadlock in U.S. Congress regarding funding. (Reuters) - Determining the duration for which men infected with Zika can sexually transmit the virus, which may lead to severe birth defects and significant neurological issues, could take several years. Health authorities are advising couples to avoid unprotected sexual activity for six months following a male partner's infection. This unusual recommendation stems from a single instance where Zika was found to survive for 62 days in semen, potentially impacting millions. The serious dangers posed by Zika and its possible spread are pushing U.S. health officials to advance research, even amid funding challenges in Congress. A study examining the risk of sexual transmission is an example of research that public health officials assert cannot be delayed by political issues. By reallocating funds designated for other initiatives, the U.S. National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases has begun enrolling men infected with Zika in Brazil and Colombia to investigate how long the virus remains transmittable in semen. Although the study may take years to finalize, preliminary findings could assist public health officials in refining their sexual health recommendations. "We are taking a risk, but it is necessary," stated Dr. Anthony Fauci, the director of the U.S. institute, in an interview. "We cannot wait until we have all the funding before proceeding." Public health officials are concerned about Zika's ability to spread, which could enhance its reach. The virus is mainly transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which also spread dengue and chikungunya viruses. However, at least 10 nations, including the United States and France, have documented Zika infections in individuals who had not traveled to affected areas but whose sexual partners had. This potential for sexual transmission could allow Zika to establish a presence beyond the warmer regions that favor its mosquito vector. To safeguard women who are pregnant or planning to conceive, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has advised couples to avoid unprotected sex for six months—three times longer than the 62 days the virus was shown to survive in semen in one British case study. The World Health Organization has recently released similar recommendations. However, such stringent advice is not ideal, according to Dr. Anne Schuchat, a deputy director at the CDC, who commented in an interview, "Advising people to abstain from sex until we provide further information is not a very fulfilling recommendation. We seek to gain a better understanding of the sexual transmission risk." In Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory where over 2,100 infections have been recorded this year, health officials are distributing Zika protection kits that include insect repellent and condoms, along with their guidance. However, the recommendation to avoid unprotected sex has not been well received, according to Dr. Chris Prue, a behavioral scientist at the CDC who has investigated the public's response. "Condom use is not favored in many areas," she noted. "There are personal and religious considerations and numerous other individual factors involved." On Tuesday, U.S. lawmakers remained at an impasse over funding to combat the Zika virus, as Senate Democrats blocked a Republican proposal they claimed was insufficient to meet the challenge of the virus and detrimental to other health priorities. It remains uncertain when Congress will address President Barack Obama's request for $1.9 billion. Meanwhile, the White House has redirected over $500 million intended for other programs to urgent Zika efforts, including initiatives that would miss critical scientific opportunities if not acted upon promptly. One of these studies will track children born to mothers infected with Zika to identify any developmental disabilities that were not apparent at birth. Additional priority projects include the development of vaccines and mosquito control efforts. One ongoing study will evaluate whether the risk of transmission is higher from men exhibiting Zika infection symptoms, such as fever and rash, compared to those who do not show symptoms.

text: Paul Ryan has been re-elected as the speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, U.S. Representative Paul Ryan secured another term as speaker as a Congress controlled by Republicans commenced a new session. The congressman from Wisconsin was chosen with a tally of 239 to 189. Ryan first took on the role of speaker in October 2015, following the retirement of his predecessor John Boehner, who stepped down after facing multiple uprisings from House conservatives.

The Wisconsin congressman was elected on a vote of 239-189. Ryan was first elected speaker in October 2015, after his predecessor John Boehner retired following repeated revolts by House conservatives.

text: Soccer icon George Weah is set to compete against Vice President Joseph Boakai in the upcoming presidential run-off in Liberia. MONROVIA (Reuters) - The former soccer player secured victory in the initial round of Liberia's presidential election, garnering 38.4 percent of the votes, which places him 10 points ahead of Vice President Boakai, who will challenge him next month, according to the electoral commission's announcement on Thursday. The citizens of Liberia are gradually coming to terms with the possibility that Weah, the only African to have received the FIFA World Player of the Year and the Ballon d'Or awards, could succeed Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ellen Johnson Sirleaf as their president. At 51 years old, Weah has been a senator representing the opposition Congress for Democratic Change since 2015, after returning to his home country following an international soccer career to engage in politics. He previously lost to Johnson Sirleaf in the 2005 presidential election as a political newcomer. The confirmed final results indicated that Boakai, who is affiliated with Johnson Sirleaf's ruling Unity Party, received 28.8 percent of the votes, leaving the two leading candidates significantly ahead of a large number of primarily lesser-known contenders. Charles Brumskine, a lawyer who claims the election was manipulated despite observers deeming it fair, finished in third place with 9.6 percent of the vote. Known affectionately by his supporters as King George, Weah enjoys immense popularity among the younger population and those who feel marginalized, particularly in the impoverished areas of the coastal city Monrovia. Many of these individuals believe they have not reaped the benefits of Liberia's recovery following the war, which has negatively impacted Boakai's standing. However, Weah has yet to present substantial policy proposals and will encounter significant challenges in fulfilling the lofty expectations amid a tough economic situation characterized by declining prices for Liberia's primary exports. Johnson Sirleaf, a former finance minister who had worked for Citibank and the World Bank while in exile after fleeing during a coup, received the Nobel Prize in 2011 for her efforts in restoring peace after a civil war that lasted 15 years and concluded in 2003. Numerous Liberians attribute to her the establishment of the necessary conditions for this election to facilitate Liberia's first democratic transition of power in seventy years. Nevertheless, she has struggled to effectively address corruption and alleviate poverty for millions. The economy was severely impacted by an Ebola outbreak, and a reduction in iron ore prices exacerbated the situation. Furthermore, inadequate road infrastructure continues to leave much of rural Liberia isolated during the rainy season, and outside of the main urban areas, few Liberians have access to electrical grids.

text: A federal appeals court in the U.S. has denied New Jersey Senator Robert Menendez's request to dismiss a corruption case against him. On Friday, the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Democrat's argument that the U.S. Constitution provided him immunity from prosecution. The court ruled that prosecutors are permitted to continue with charges alleging that Menendez received campaign contributions and gifts, such as a stay at a villa in the Caribbean and private jet rides from his affluent friend, Florida eye doctor Salomon Melgen, in return for advocating for Melgen’s interests using his official position. "Members of Congress should not be considered 'super-citizens' free from criminal accountability," stated Circuit Judge Thomas Ambro on behalf of a three-judge panel from the Philadelphia-based court. This ruling indicates that the case may eventually proceed to trial, which could hinder the Democrats' ambitions to regain control of the U.S. Senate following the election on November 8. Should Menendez, 62, be compelled to vacate the position he has held since 2006, New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a Republican, would be able to appoint a temporary successor according to state law. The senator has vowed to remain in his role while he defends himself, although he has relinquished his position as the senior Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Abbe Lowell, Menendez's attorney, stated that the senator plans to petition the entire appeals court to reconsider Friday's ruling, and if necessary, to escalate the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court. Lowell expressed confidence that the legal process will ultimately demonstrate that Senator Menendez has consistently acted lawfully. "The Senator is optimistic that he will be exonerated," he remarked in a statement. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Justice, Peter Carr, opted not to comment. In an indictment revealed in April 2015, Menendez faced allegations of accepting bribes from Melgen in exchange for intervening in various issues for his friend. Prosecutors noted that these accusations included a dispute over $8.9 million in Medicare billing, as well as a contract issue with the Dominican Republic where Menendez urged the State Department to step in. Menendez and Melgen have both entered not guilty pleas regarding the charges outlined in the 22-count indictment. In September of the previous year, U.S. District Judge William Walls in Newark, New Jersey dismissed four bribery counts but upheld the majority of the government’s case. In his appeal, Menendez contended that his actions were safeguarded by the Constitution's "speech or debate" clause, which offers significant protection to congressional members against prosecution for actions performed as legislators. However, Ambro stated that Menendez’s conduct essentially constituted lobbying for a specific party and thus fell outside the constitutional "safe harbor." He noted that there is "a sufficient basis for the district court’s conclusion that the predominant purpose of the challenged acts was to pursue a political resolution to Dr. Melgen’s disputes." Ambro added that it was not related to true legislative oversight or the influence of broader policy matters. Lowell had argued that Judge Walls should have concentrated on the actual content of the meetings in question, asserting that the records indicated "high-level policy discussions" occurred. Ambro mentioned that Menendez is still able to claim that his efforts were aimed at affecting policy, and the government must bear the burden of proof at trial to demonstrate the contrary. "The evidence supporting Senator Menendez will undoubtedly robustly present his position during the trial," the judge stated. The ruling issued on Friday took place one month after the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bribery convictions of former Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell. The Supreme Court ruled that typical political activities such as arranging meetings or contacting public officials generally do not constitute grounds for criminal charges. The 3rd Circuit primarily concentrated on the speech or debate clause and did not reference the McDonnell case. Lowell indicated that this case raises significant questions.

text: PHOENIX (Reuters) - Authorities deployed pepper spray to disperse demonstrators outside a rally held by U.S. President Donald Trump in Phoenix, Arizona, on Tuesday, after being targeted with rocks and bottles, according to police reports. While police have not provided a count of the protesters, local Arizona news outlets reported that the number was in the thousands. It remains unclear whether the pepper spray was directed at supporters or opponents of Trump, or both. "Individuals in the crowd began launching rocks and bottles at law enforcement," stated Sergeant Jonathan Howard, a spokesman for the Phoenix Police Department. "In response, police utilized pepper balls and OC (oleoresin capsicum) spray to disperse the crowd and halt the assaults," he added. During the demonstration, four individuals were taken into custody, as reported by Phoenix Police Chief Jeri Williams in a press briefing. "We had tens of thousands of individuals downtown peacefully exercising their first amendment rights," Williams noted. "Unfortunately, a very small number of people opted for criminal behavior." Authorities urged the crowds to clear the area. Many protesters left, while numerous officers in riot gear, equipped with shields, attempted to remove the remaining demonstrators from the central area. The Phoenix Fire Department reported treating 56 individuals for heat exhaustion and dehydration at the convention center, with twelve people requiring hospital care.

text: The director of the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) defended the agency during a congressional hearing on Wednesday amidst a wave of criticism from Republican lawmakers. The scrutiny ranged from the agency's management of the Wells Fargo accounts scandal to Cordray's personal job performance. Appearing before the House Financial Services Committee, Richard Cordray was evasive when questioned about his plans to complete his term, which is set to end in July 2018. Republican members of the committee and others have called for President Trump to dismiss him, and there is speculation that Cordray may run for governor of Ohio in 2018. Cordray, who has been in charge of the agency since 2012 when he was appointed by former President Barack Obama, has not resigned since President Donald Trump took office. He refrained from confirming whether he intends to serve until the end of his term, stating, "I have no insights to provide" in response to a related inquiry. According to the Dodd-Frank law that established the CFPB, the president can only remove Cordray for specific reasons. However, long-time Republican adversaries argue that Cordray's regulatory decisions present sufficient grounds for his dismissal. "Given the damage inflicted on consumers, Richard Cordray should be removed by the president," remarked Jeb Hensarling, Chairman of the House Financial Services Committee. Hensarling pointed out that the CFPB has not completed regulatory projects required by Congress, such as creating rules for financial institutions to gather data on credit applications from minority and women-owned businesses. Republicans asserted that the agency failed to identify misconduct at Wells Fargo & Co, depending on outside investigators and media reports to reveal extensive issues regarding improper account openings. "The CFPB was asleep at the wheel!" exclaimed Ann Wagner, a Republican from Missouri. She indicated that the earliest the committee found evidence of the CFPB investigating Wells Fargo was in May 2015, after the bank had informed the regulator that the Los Angeles City Attorney was already pursuing a civil case. Nevertheless, the CFPB played a significant role in the announcement of a high-profile $185 million multi-agency settlement in September 2016. Cordray contended that Wagner was "conflating" issues and stated that the oversight efforts "became exponential over time." The CFPB imposed a $100 million fine on the bank in an enforcement action in collaboration with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the City and County of Los Angeles. The investigation was initiated following a 2013 investigative report by the Los Angeles Times.

text: At least 15 individuals lost their lives due to flash floods along the Greek coastline. MANDRA, Greece (Reuters) - On Wednesday, flash floods resulted in the deaths of at least 15 people, rendered many homeless, and caused significant damage to infrastructure in Greece after a torrential downpour overwhelmed two coastal towns situated west of Athens. In what locals described as an unprecedented level of devastation, an overnight downpour led to flash floods in the industrial areas of Nea Peramos and Mandra, located at the base of a mountain just west of Athens. Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras announced a national mourning period. "These are very difficult moments for Greece. We are living a great disaster," he stated during a public address. "Support measures for affected households and businesses will be implemented immediately and without delay," he added, although he did not provide further details. Residents reported being awakened on Wednesday morning by a surge of rainwater and mud entering their homes. text: Challenges are significant for Merkel in negotiations for a three-party 'Jamaica' coalition. BERLIN (Reuters) - Angela Merkel, Germany's conservative chancellor, may have secured her fourth consecutive national election victory, yet she is confronted with a considerable obstacle in her attempts to establish a three-party coalition among parties with differing political ideologies. Although her bloc garnered the highest number of votes, it fell to its lowest result since 1949, and equally important for government formation, her current coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), announced their intention to enter opposition after dropping to 20.7 percent in forecasts, a post-war record low. Merkel herself suggested that she has only one alternative to govern. The term 'Jamaica' refers to the coalition between her conservative bloc, the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP), and the environmentalist Greens, based on the fact that the flag of the island features the black, yellow, and green colors of the three parties. Current projections show the conservatives, made up of Merkel's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), at 33.0 percent, the FDP at 10.6 percent, and the Greens at 8.9 percent—sufficient for a functional majority. However, this type of alliance, which has not been tested at the federal level, failed in January 2012 in the western state of Saarland after just over two years, although it has been attempted again since May in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein. At the national level, it would need to navigate significant differences regarding EU reform, taxation, energy, and immigration. Both the Greens and FDP, wary of alienating their voter base with necessary compromises, have downplayed the chances of forming such a coalition. Nevertheless, the allure of sharing governance in Europe’s largest economy will be a strong motivating factor. They may also feel a responsibility to prevent the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD)—which has raised troubling echoes of Germany's Nazi history with its anti-Islam and anti-immigrant rhetoric—from becoming the leading opposition party. The AfD capitalized on voter dissatisfaction stemming from Merkel’s decision in 2015 to allow approximately one million migrants, primarily fleeing conflict in the Middle East, to enter the country, resulting in them receiving 13 percent of the vote and becoming the third-largest party, marking the first far-right presence in the national parliament in over fifty years. "It will be very difficult, but we all have a duty to our country. We don’t want new elections," remarked conservative Interior Minister Thomas de Maiziere, warning that such a scenario could further empower the AfD. A final coalition agreement might focus more on demonstrating Germany's dedication to democratic principles than on achieving a wide-ranging policy consensus, particularly given the stark ideological divide between the pro-business FDP and the left-leaning Greens. Cem Ozdemir, co-leader of the Greens, stated that his party would not engage in "anti-European populism" in a coalition with the conservatives and FDP. Although the low-tax, deregulation-focused FDP traditionally supports Europe, its young leader, Christian Lindner, has dismissed proposals from French President Emmanuel Macron for greater eurozone integration. "We want to change the trajectory for our country, and if it becomes clear during discussions that these objectives can be achieved, then of course we will be open to it, but if not, it would be our responsibility to move into opposition," Lindner noted. He also mentioned that the annexation of Crimea by Russia in 2014 might need to be accepted as a permanent provisional arrangement, a stance that seems difficult for Merkel to agree to. The Greens are focused on climate policy and are advocating for a commitment to phase out coal power by 2030, which would pose challenges for the other parties to accept. Additionally, refugee policy will be contentious, particularly as the FDP and Merkel's Bavarian partners, the CSU, advocate for stricter immigration controls compared to the Greens. Holger Schmieding, an economist at Berenberg, suggested that in the distribution of ministries within a Jamaica coalition, Wolfgang Schaeuble, who has been the conservative finance minister since 2009, may have to relinquish his position to the FDP.

text: Robo-advisers remain unfazed by the commotion surrounding the U.S. fiduciary rule. NEW YORK (Reuters) - While traditional Wall Street firms have been troubled by the implications of a significant U.S. regulation concerning retirement guidance, their younger counterparts from Silicon Valley have maintained a nonchalant attitude. The debate centers on the timing and manner in which the federal government will enact the so-called "fiduciary rule" that was issued by the U.S. Labor Department last year. This regulation, intended to safeguard retirees by removing conflicts of interest for the brokers compensated for advising them, was scheduled to take effect in April but is currently facing opposition from the Trump administration. The implementation of the rule is now projected to be postponed by 180 days, resulting in considerable uncertainty about its future. Major wealth management firms and insurance companies that would be most impacted by the rule have expressed relief at indications that the new administration may seek to rescind it. They have vigorously contested the rule both in court and in Congress, claiming it would increase compliance and technology expenses while limiting brokers’ capacity to collect commissions and market certain high-fee products. Detractors argue that the extra costs would drive brokerages to abandon less affluent clients in favor of wealthier individuals. Conversely, startups that provide digital wealth management services have taken a different stance, asserting that the rule would be advantageous for retirees and their own operations. The reasoning is that investors neglected by larger firms may turn to digital providers, which present transparent, lower-cost options. In discussions following Trump’s directive to the Labor Department to reassess the rule earlier this month, leaders at "robo-advisers," which utilize algorithms to manage investor funds, dismissed the rule’s influence on their enterprises. They noted that while the rule could accelerate a broader transition of investor capital to "robo-advisers," this trend was already gaining traction. "An expansion of the fiduciary rule would be beneficial for our business, but it does not influence our overall success," stated Andy Rachleff, CEO of Wealthfront, one of the foremost robo-advisers that engages directly with investors. Wealthfront’s rival Betterment has urged Democrats in recent weeks to oppose attempts to delay or weaken the rule. Nevertheless, Betterment’s Associate General Counsel Seth Rosenbloom remarked that any alterations in regulation would have minimal effect on the company’s expansion. "We are disappointed that it seems like ... the rule might be eliminated, postponed, or diminished," said Rosenbloom. "However, we are hopeful that the focus on this issue will lead to better-informed investors over time." Among robo-advisers servicing brokerages, Mike Sha, co-founder and CEO of the robo-adviser SigFig, expressed that he did not foresee the rule’s postponement affecting their business or partnerships whatsoever. The wealth divisions of Wells Fargo & Co and UBS Group AG utilize SigFig’s technology and provide its online investment tools to their customers. Robo-advisers account for a minor fraction of the wealth management sector, managing approximately $200 billion in client assets in 2016, as reported by consulting firm A.T. Kearney. It anticipates that this figure will skyrocket to $2.2 trillion by 2020. Disrupting the fiduciary rule could hinder that growth for certain companies. For example, last week, LPL Financial Holdings indicated that if the rule were delayed, it might take a more gradual approach in implementing some compliance initiatives, which include its robo-adviser and other new technologies. However, the movement towards more affordable digital solutions started prior to the formal establishment of the rule, primarily propelled by consumer demand for enhanced digital options. Analysts believe that this trend is unlikely to be halted regardless of the rule's status. "All forecasts indicate there is tremendous demand for digital advice and solutions," stated Kendra Thompson, a managing director in the financial services group at the consulting firm Accenture. She noted that the rule serves as "an accelerator for digital, not an originator."

text: U.S. President Donald Trump asserted on Thursday that he had not obstructed the FBI's investigation into purported Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and confirmed that he had not recorded his discussions with former FBI Director James Comey. Comey was overseeing the inquiry into claims that Russia attempted to influence the election in favor of Trump and whether Trump associates collaborated with Moscow when the president dismissed him on May 9, igniting a political uproar. Fox News released a partial transcript of the interview on Thursday. The former FBI chief testified to a Senate committee that Trump had requested he drop an investigation into former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn's alleged connections to Russia. Earlier on Thursday, Trump declared he had not made and did not have any recordings of his conversations with Comey, following his suggestion last month that he might possess tapes that could challenge Comey's account of events. Lawmakers probing claims of Russian interference in the U.S. election had sought any such recordings from the White House. Shortly after dismissing Comey, Trump alluded to the possibility of tapes in a Twitter message. Allegations of connections to Russia have loomed over Trump during his first five months in office, diverting attention from efforts by his Republican colleagues in Congress to reform the U.S. healthcare and tax systems. Trump has privately informed aides that the mere suggestion of tapes compelled Comey to be truthful in his recent testimony, according to a source familiar with the matter. text: Austria has committed to consulting with Rome regarding its proposal to extend citizenship to the German-speaking population in northern Italy. On Tuesday, the newly formed coalition government in Vienna announced its intention to move forward with the citizenship plan, which could potentially reopen historical grievances. The initiative for dual citizenship in the Alto Adige region of northern Italy was part of a 180-page coalition agreement released over the weekend by Chancellor Sebastian Kurz's conservative People's Party and the far-right Freedom Party (FPO). After World War One, Austria relinquished control of Alto Adige to Italy. In the 1920s, the fascist regime of Benito Mussolini attempted to settle thousands of ethnic Italians in the area, yet German speakers continue to outnumber Italians by approximately two to one. The two communities have separate educational institutions and typically patronize different bars and eateries. Nevertheless, the region benefits from significant autonomy and substantial financial support from Rome, which has helped mitigate secessionist sentiments among the population. Kurz emphasized that the initiative, long advocated by the FPO, aims solely to foster collaboration between European nations. "This is certainly something we intend to pursue in close partnership with Italy and the government in Rome," Kurz stated at a joint press conference with FPO leader and Vice Chancellor Heinz-Christian Strache after their cabinet's inaugural meeting. Italian officials have strongly criticized Austria’s proposal, labeling it a move toward nationalism that could disrupt the fragile ethnic equilibrium in Alto Adige, also known as South Tyrol. Italy's foreign minister was cited by the ANSA news agency on Monday as saying that addressing this matter would necessitate "a conversation that requires enormous delicacy." However, Kurz played down any potential friction, noting, "We have excellent relations with Rome. I am personally acquainted with the head of government. I also count the foreign minister as a personal friend," said Kurz, who previously served as foreign minister before his government took office. "In our government program, we have addressed a request from South Tyroleans that was articulated by all political factions in South Tyrol and particularly conveyed by the South Tyrolean provincial administration," Kurz remarked. Strache pointed out that Italy has a comparable arrangement for its Italian minorities residing in Slovenia and Croatia. The Italian Foreign Ministry's website details the criteria under which individuals who lost their citizenship when certain territories became part of Yugoslavia may apply for an Italian passport. This issue did not arise during Austria's parliamentary elections in October, which were won by Kurz's party, which adopted a stringent stance on immigration, often aligning with the FPO’s views. Austria received a significant influx of asylum seekers amid Europe’s migration crisis, and both parties vowed to prevent another similar wave. In Austrian Tyrol, the emotional resonance of the issue remains strong, as maps of the province frequently still depict the area to the south now belonging to Italy. This province, a bastion of Kurz’s conservatives, is scheduled to have a local parliamentary election in February. The leader of Alto Adige’s government, Arno Kompatscher, expressed his support for the initiative, provided it is framed within a European context aimed at unifying nations instead of dividing them—a possible nod to any concerns from Italy. "Thus, this has nothing to do with secession or altering borders or any related matters. It pertains instead to this expression of personal ties to Austria, and the discussion should unfold within that framework," he stated during a press conference. Austria and Italy have had several confrontations in recent years over Austria’s warning to implement controls at the Brenner crossing, a crucial transport route along their common border, should there be a notable increase in migrants arriving from Italy.

Stephan Weil, the prominent premier of Lower Saxony, indicated that the SPD would seek to see its policies incorporated in exchange for backing any government. Schulz’s suggestions were met with caution by Merkel. 'The (EU's) capacity to act should be our priority now,' she stated at a press briefing in Berlin. 'Thus, I will focus on enhancing cooperation in defense by 2025 and addressing other matters, such as employment and innovation.' Outside the congress venue, SPD youth activists, many of whom are eager for the party to pursue a distinct path after spending eight of the last twelve years in centrist coalitions, distributed red cards stating 'No Grand Coalition.' 'Merkel leads this country without a clear direction,' one speaker remarked at the conference. 'She lacks a plan for Europe and governs the country week by week. Schulz, who had initially suggested that his party should enter opposition after facing repercussions for being part of the previous grand coalition under Merkel, expressed remorse for his party's poor electoral performance. Schulz criticized European efforts to support large banks while failing to adequately address high youth unemployment rates. 'When states are unable to balance their budgets, they encounter severe penalties from Brussels. If we can mobilize billions for bank bailouts, yet struggle for meager amounts to support jobs for young individuals, then this is certainly not the Europe I envision.' His comments reflected a more critical stance toward large corporations than that of French President Emmanuel Macron, who advocates for deeper euro zone integration and pro-business reforms under an appointed euro zone finance minister. He specifically targeted American tech giants Apple, Facebook, and Google, asserting that a strong Europe is necessary to ensure compliance with regulations and safeguard workers’ rights amid changing circumstances.

BERLIN (Reuters) - Germany s Social Democrats (SPD) voted on Thursday to hold talks with Chancellor Angela Merkel s conservatives on forming a government after their leader made an impassioned plea for a free hand to work for a social  United States of Europe . The vote clears the way for talks that could resolve the impasse into which Europe s economic powerhouse was plunged after Merkel and the SPD shed support in a September election, greatly complicating the parliamentary arithmetic. Martin Schulz urged reluctant center-left SPD members to be open to Merkel s overtures to renew the coalition that has governed for the past four years, saying the party had a responsibility to revive social democracy in Germany. A new  grand coalition  with the reluctant SPD is Merkel s best hope of extending her 12 years in power after talks with two smaller parties failed, giving the smaller SPD greater leverage in any negotiations.

text: Janet Reno, the first woman to hold the position of U.S. attorney general, has passed away at the age of 78. (Reuters) - Known for her straightforward demeanor, Reno served for eight years as the inaugural female U.S. attorney general and authorized the tragic 1993 raid on the Branch Davidian cult's compound in Texas shortly after taking office. She died on Monday in Miami due to complications related to Parkinson’s disease, as reported by her goddaughter, Gabrielle D’Alemberte. Reno was diagnosed with the progressive central nervous system illness in 1995. During her tenure from 1993 to 2001, under President Bill Clinton, she was the top law enforcement official in the United States, making her the longest-serving attorney general of the 20th century. Among her significant actions was the federal agents' seizure of 6-year-old Cuban shipwreck survivor Elian Gonzalez from his relatives in Miami in 2000, in addition to initiating the substantial antitrust lawsuit against Microsoft Corp in 1998. "Janet Reno was an American original, a public servant whose intellect, integrity and fierce commitment to justice helped shape our nation’s legal landscape," President Barack Obama stated. Clinton remarked on Monday, "As attorney general throughout my entire presidency, Janet dedicated herself to improving community safety, protecting the vulnerable, and finding the appropriate balance between pursuing justice and preventing the misuse of power." The former prosecutor from Miami was chosen by Clinton after his first two selections encountered difficulties, and she was known for her independent attitude and blunt communication style, which sometimes caused friction with the White House. Reno faced complaints from the White House about her perceived lack of team spirit and her propensity to appoint numerous special prosecutors to investigate various cases, including the Whitewater affair related to the finances of President Clinton and First Lady Hillary Clinton. Just 38 days into her role as attorney general, Reno approved the FBI raid on April 19, 1993, that resulted in the deaths of approximately 80 individuals, including many children, at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas. Federal agents had previously attempted to serve a warrant to the cult leader, David Koresh, who claimed to be the Messiah, for stockpiling weapons. In the resulting gunfight, four agents and six cult members lost their lives, which led to a 51-day standoff. After negotiations failed, Reno authorized the raid following reports of child abuse within the compound. The raid on the heavily armed cult culminated in a fire that consumed the site. "I made the decision. I’m accountable. The buck stops with me," a somber Reno stated at a subsequent news conference. Reno took a personal stake in the political controversy surrounding Elian Gonzalez, the young survivor whose mother drowned while attempting to flee Cuba. She engaged with the boy and his Miami relatives, who fought to prevent his return to communist Cuba, as well as his father and grandmothers, who wished to raise Gonzalez in Cuba. Reno contended that Elian should be with his father and acted after the Miami relatives disregarded a U.S. government order to surrender him. She sanctioned armed agents to retrieve the boy from his relatives’ home during a predawn raid in April 2000, reuniting him with his father, who subsequently took him back to Cuba. This raid provoked outrage among members of Miami’s Cuban exile community, who labeled her a "witch" and a pawn of Cuban President Fidel Castro. In 1998, Reno’s Justice Department filed a significant antitrust lawsuit against Microsoft. Two years later, a federal judge mandated the breakup of the software giant for failing to comply with a ruling that it had engaged in illegal monopolistic behavior. The case concluded in 2001 under the administration of President George W. Bush, Clinton’s Republican successor, with terms perceived as favorable to Microsoft. Reno appeared alongside Clinton following the 1995 truck bombing of the Oklahoma City federal building, which resulted in 168 fatalities, and vowed to pursue the death penalty for those responsible. Convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh became the first federal prisoner executed since 1963 in 2001.

text: The United States has partially restarted the issuance of visas in Turkey as of Monday, after what it claimed were assurances regarding the safety of its personnel at diplomatic missions following several detentions. The Turkish embassy in Washington quickly stated it would follow suit, although it refuted any claims of providing assurances. The embassy characterized the U.S. decision as a positive step, particularly noting its timing just before a visit to the U.S. by Turkey's Prime Minister Binali Yildirim. Despite this move, the U.S. embassy expressed ongoing concerns about the detention of two locally employed staff members at its missions in Turkey, as well as the situation of U.S. citizens detained under a state of emergency that has been in effect since last year's failed coup. The suspension of all non-immigrant visa services by the U.S. was triggered by the arrest of a long-serving employee at the U.S. consulate in Istanbul a month prior, which prompted the U.S. to evaluate staff security in Turkey. Following the U.S. announcement on October 8, Turkey indicated it would take reciprocal action, with President Tayyip Erdogan later expressing his frustration, accusing Washington of jeopardizing a longstanding partnership with Ankara. The U.S. embassy stated it had received initial high-level assurances from the Turkish government that no further local employees of its mission in Turkey were under investigation, and that local staff would not face detention or arrest for carrying out their official responsibilities. However, shortly afterward, the Turkish embassy contended that no such assurances had been provided and that any legal actions regarding U.S. mission employees would be decided by Turkey's judiciary. The personnel involved, employed by the U.S., are under judicial scrutiny not due to their official roles, but because of serious accusations against them, the statement said. The embassy also remarked that a mention of security conditions of U.S. missions in Turkey in its statement was deemed unusual and did not represent the reality. The partial resumption of visa services, reported earlier by Reuters, contributed to a strengthening of the lira, which rose to 3.8356 against the dollar from a previous rate of 3.8708. In May, a translator at the U.S. consulate in the southern province of Adana was arrested, and more recently, a worker from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) was detained in Istanbul, both facing allegations of connections to the failed coup of the previous year. The U.S. embassy has asserted that these accusations are unfounded. Turkish officials have indicated that police are seeking to interrogate a third employee based in Istanbul, whose wife and daughter were detained over supposed ties to the network of Fethullah Gulen, a cleric based in the U.S. whom Ankara accuses of orchestrating the coup attempt; they have since been released. Turkey has expressed discontent over what it perceives as U.S. hesitance to extradite Gulen, who has resided in Pennsylvania since 1999. U.S. officials have stated that courts require adequate evidence to approve his extradition. Gulen has denied any involvement in the coup attempt. Erdogan has also criticized the U.S. following charges against a former Turkish economy minister and the ex-leader of a state-run bank for conspiring to breach U.S. sanctions on Iran by illicitly transferring hundreds of millions of dollars through the U.S. financial system on behalf of Tehran. These charges are part of an ongoing case against Reza Zarrab, a prosperous Turkish-Iranian gold trader who was arrested in the U.S. last year for sanctions evasion. Zarrab, who is set to go on trial this month, has pleaded not guilty. Erdogan has accused U.S. prosecutors of having ulterior motives in this case, citing references to himself and his wife in court documents. In their statement, the Turkish embassy expressed serious concerns regarding legal matters involving its citizens in the United States.

text: U.S. Congress ensures healthcare benefits for coal miners. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. government along with coal companies will be obligated to provide healthcare for retired coal miners, ensuring that benefits continue for workers even amid potential bankruptcies of coal companies, following a fiscal spending agreement reached by Congress on Sunday for 2017. The measure to secure healthcare benefits for the United Mine Workers was part of a deal finalized late on Sunday, which encompasses approximately $1 trillion in federal funding aimed at preventing a government shutdown later this week. As of April 30, around 22,600 coal miners and their families were at risk of losing their healthcare benefits, which were in jeopardy due to the industry's struggles and companies attempting to recover from bankruptcies. "This permanent resolution to safeguard these benefits is a triumph for our miners, their families, and their widows," remarked Congressman Evan Jenkins, a Republican from West Virginia representing coal-producing regions. Members of the UMWA have made numerous trips to Washington over the past several months to implore lawmakers to safeguard their benefits, which they assert is a government responsibility. The Krug-Lewis agreement, facilitated by President Harry Truman in 1946, ensured health and pension benefits for coal miners. However, the agreement reached on Sunday did not provide a long-term solution for the miners’ pension funds, which are also facing termination. Lawmakers from both parties remain optimistic about passing the Miners Protection Act, which aims to reallocate funds from the Abandoned Mine Land fund to the union’s pension plan to avert insolvency. Democratic Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia has been collaborating with the UMWA as well as Democratic and Republican lawmakers to advance the bill. Should Congress be unable to transfer those funds, the financially-strapped $5 billion federal Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp, which backs failed private-sector pension programs, would take on the responsibility of covering the plans. Manchin expressed that there exists a "sacred bond between worker and country" and emphasized his "increased determination to fulfill our complete obligation and secure pension benefits for retired miners as well."

text: Tourism decline in Bali town due to Indonesia volcano. AMED, Indonesia (Reuters) - A Balinese town that was once filled with vacationers has seen a significant decrease in tourists following alerts that Mount Agung, located nearby, may erupt at any moment. This situation highlights the increasing economic impact that the active volcano has on Indonesia. Since authorities raised the alert level for Mount Agung to the highest status last month, many hotels, dive resorts, and restaurants in the surrounding areas have experienced a downturn in business. An operator of a dive center in Amed, situated approximately 15 km (9 miles) from the volcano and just outside the designated danger zone, reported a substantial number of cancellations from guests. "If (the situation) lasts for nine months or more... then we will have no option but to shut down due to insufficient funds to sustain operations and pay our staff," stated Helene Rabate, a Spanish national managing the center. The local cafes and restaurants are mostly vacant, and few tourists are present at the typically busy dive centers in this coastal town. The last eruption of Agung occurred in 1963, resulting in over 1,000 fatalities. Since that event, tourism has significantly changed towns like Amed from tranquil fishing and agricultural communities. Restaurant proprietor Wayan Widarti has noticed a sharp decline in patrons. "It might be worse than the Bali bombing because there’s unpredictability regarding when (the eruption) might occur and how long we will have to wait," she remarked, referencing the 2002 nightclub bombing that resulted in 202 deaths and led to a drop in visitors to the resort island. Renowned for its surfing, beaches, and temples, Bali welcomed nearly 5 million tourists last year, accounting for more than half of all foreign visitors to Indonesia. Tourism is a vital part of Bali's economy and ranks as Indonesia's fourth-largest source of foreign currency after natural resources such as coal and palm oil. Indonesian policymakers have been striving to stimulate an economy that has been growing at around 5 percent for several years, making any prolonged impact on tourism particularly concerning. Officials in Indonesia have reassured that Bali is still safe for tourists, though there have been cancellations in areas farther from the volcano due to fears that ash clouds could interfere with air travel. Some tourists remain in the vicinity at a secure distance from the volcano. "We intend to... simply adhere to security directives... and take a fast boat to evacuate if an eruption occurs," shared Arlin Shiu, a traveler from Hong Kong who is visiting with a companion. Disaster management authorities have established an exclusion zone extending up to 12 km, which has led to over 140,000 residents evacuating to nearby villages. Bali governor I Made Mangku Pastika stated that for individuals residing in safe zones, there is no necessity to evacuate, adding that temporary evacuation centers are being challenged by the influx of thousands of additional evacuees. text: Four men accused of espionage were executed by Somalia's Islamist al Shabaab insurgency on Monday in a public display that highlighted the group's authority over large areas of the southern part of the country, even as the government prepares for a military campaign against them. The individuals were apprehended several weeks prior and were executed today following a court verdict and their admissions of guilt regarding spying, according to Mohamed Abu Abdalla, the al Shabaab governor for the Jubba regions, who spoke via phone. Of the four, two were alleged to have been spying for the Ethiopian government, while the other two were accused of working for Somali government intelligence. The executions took place in Buale, the capital of Middle Jubba, an area predominantly under al Shabaab's control located south of the capital, Mogadishu. The government did not respond to requests for comments. Al Shabaab's influence in the Horn of Africa has diminished since they were expelled from the capital in 2011 by African Union peacekeeping forces. Nevertheless, they continue to dominate extensive rural territories. The group seeks to dismantle the fragile, U.N.-supported government and enforce a stringent interpretation of Islamic law. text: 'Expats return home': Residents of Amsterdam upset about surge in visitors. AMSTERDAM (Reuters) - Last month, Dutch lawmakers celebrated winning the bid to host the European Medicines Agency, but not all in the capital are pleased with the anticipated arrival of high-earning pharmaceutical professionals. Locals and media in Amsterdam, already frustrated by the influx of tourists flocking to the city's stag-do strip clubs, are becoming increasingly annoyed about another category of visitors - white-collar expatriates. A headline from the newspaper NRC Handelsblad read, A Nice Brexit Trophy, But Can The City Handle It?, in reference to the decision to relocate the regulatory agency from London to Amsterdam following Britain's exit from the EU. The EMA is expected to bring approximately 900 employees, which supporters view as a significant economic advantage. Critics, however, argue that it's merely another group of affluent foreigners inflating rent and property costs. National broadcaster NOS stated, Home Buyers Will Pay The Price For Drugs Agency In Amsterdam. On social media, many lamented the loss of the city's vibrant and unconventional spirit, which they believe has been stifled by the bureaucratic presence of the EMA. The gentrification of Amsterdam has been underway for over a decade. Marketing efforts have concentrated on the city's canals, the Anne Frank House, and museums featuring masterpieces from Van Gogh and Rembrandt. Legislative actions have aided in this rebranding, such as closing one-third of the city's brothels in 2008 and initiating a program to shut marijuana cafes near schools in 2011. According to Amsterdam Marketing, the number of overnight visitors nearly doubled from 2011 to 2016. The city, now home to 850,000 residents, welcomes over 6 million international tourists annually. This surge has paralleled a rise in the population of affluent expatriates, with numbers increasing from 39,000 in 2009 to 77,000 in 2015, based on data from the city's statistics office. Reinier van Dantzig, leader of the largest faction in the city parliament from the centrist D-66 party, remarked, Amsterdam has always been an open city. He noted that immigrants played a crucial role in the city’s 17th-Century golden age and continue to contribute to the current economic growth. He expressed his difficulty in understanding those who perceive newcomers wishing to become Amsterdammers as a threat, stating, I believe they enhance our community. He mentioned that the city is developing housing for an additional 70,000 residents, with provisions for affordable apartments for low and middle-income families. However, for Danielle van Diemen, a fifth-generation resident of Amsterdam, this effort comes too late. She remarked, The city is being shaped by a blend of Western foreigners who believe Amsterdam is still edgy, but that is no longer the case, highlighting a squatting ban that took effect in 2010. She further stated that the divide between wealthy expatriates who do not speak Dutch and locals is nearly insurmountable. Therefore, she stated, expats should return home and leave the city to us. Bert Nap, a resident near the city center, expressed, I feel like a stranger in my own neighborhood. We have lost all our bakers and local shops to businesses catering to tourists, he added, reflecting sentiments heard across Europe’s popular travel destinations. An April survey by the apartment-search site Nestpick ranked Amsterdam as the top city globally for millennials, citing its tolerance, nightlife, and burgeoning startup environment. Jan Rath, a sociology professor at the University of Amsterdam, noted, These individuals possess qualifications, skills, and connections, which means they compete for housing and employment with those lacking such qualifications. He suggested that what is occurring... could be seen as a population replacement. The skyrocketing real estate prices have led to challenges for unskilled workers, regardless of whether they are native Dutch or immigrants from Turkey and Morocco. Statistics Netherlands (CBS) reports that 40 percent of young couples depart the city within four years.

text: A woman in France has been sentenced to prison for providing financial support to her son who was killed while fighting in Syria. On Thursday, a French court declared Nathalie Haddadi, a 42-year-old mother of three from eastern France, guilty of terrorism financing after she sent money abroad to her radicalized son, Belabbas Bounaga, who later traveled to engage in combat in Syria. The court imposed a two-year prison term on her. This case may set a significant legal precedent in France. Haddadi, who identifies as a non-practicing Muslim, stated that she had no knowledge that her son would use the funds to join Islamist militants. However, the presiding judge accused her of dishonesty, asserting, "Without your substantial help, he would not have been able to reach Syria so easily and fight with Islamic State. You financed a terrorist organization." Bounaga, who was radicalized in prison between 2014 and 2015 after being convicted of drug offenses and other crimes, left France to stay with his father in Algeria after his release. He lived there for six months before moving to Malaysia. During his time in those countries, Haddadi transferred several thousand euros to him, including multiple transfers in April 2016 after he underwent medical treatment in a Malaysian hospital. Shortly thereafter, he arrived in Syria. Although the judge did not require Haddadi to begin her sentence immediately, it remains possible for her to avoid serving the entire term. Outside the courthouse, Haddadi expressed her feelings, stating, "What was I supposed to do? Ignore him because he did stupid things when he was younger," referring to the money she claimed was intended for his medical expenses. In August 2016, she received a call from Syria informing her that Bounaga had died as a "martyr" at the age of 21. The two-year sentence exceeded the 18-month request made by the prosecutor. The court also found Bounaga's younger brother and his close friend guilty of the same offense. Earlier this month, in an interview with the Le Parisien newspaper, Haddadi expressed her concerns that her radicalized son would attempt to travel to Syria after his prison release in 2015, and she criticized the authorities for their lack of assistance in helping her "save him" at that time. After her sentencing, she stated, "I strongly condemn terrorism." Haddadi's attorney mentioned that she has filed an appeal against the ruling. According to France's interior ministry, 18,500 French citizens were identified as radicalized last month, marking a 60 percent rise compared to two years ago. It was estimated that approximately 700 individuals were fighting in Iraq and Syria by mid-2016. Haddadi's lawyer noted that other parents of radicalized youths could face similar legal repercussions from French courts. "This battle does not solely belong to Mrs. Haddadi but affects all parents of sons who were radicalized in prison and are at risk of prosecution by authorities who hold them accountable for their children's circumstances," said Herve Denis, Haddadi's attorney, to Reuters.

text: Support is increasing for another grand coalition in Germany. BERLIN (Reuters) - It is expected that members of the Social Democrats (SPD) in Germany will likely endorse a renewed alliance with Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservatives if the party leadership presents a persuasive proposal, as stated by a member of the party's executive committee on Saturday. Niels Annen of the SPD, in a conversation with the Passauer Neue Presse newspaper, urged for prompt action to establish a new German government in light of various global crises and mentioned that a grand coalition remains a possibility that should not be dismissed. On Friday, SPD leader Martin Schulz consented to discussions with Merkel regarding the revival of their outgoing coalition government, although he noted that no decisions had been finalized and that party members would ultimately determine the outcome of any agreement. He implied that participating in governance could assist the SPD in realizing its political objectives and communicated to the party's youth division, which opposed another grand coalition at a party conference, that he anticipated their loyalty and collaborative spirit. Annen expressed that the SPD must listen to the unsuccessful chancellor regarding her vision for the prospective government before committing to another four-year partnership with conservatives. The center-left SPD had pledged to enter opposition after experiencing its poorest performance in 70 years during the election in September, but faced significant pressure, including from German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, to reconsider its stance and help prevent a disruptive repeat election in Europe’s largest economy. Schulz remarked that party leaders agreed to engage in discussions out of a sense of duty to Germany and Europe following Merkel's failed attempt to form a government with two smaller parties that fell apart on Sunday. Germany is in urgent need of a stable and dependable government. A grand coalition might be a viable option, and we should not rule it out, Annen conveyed to the newspaper, emphasizing that the SPD was dedicated to what benefits the country. He appreciated the intention to present any coalition agreement to members for a vote and stated that the party should persist in its restructuring initiatives following the setback in the September election. Annen highlighted citizens' insurance and improved protections for renters as matters to negotiate with conservatives. SPD deputy leader Ralf Stegner informed the Funke newspaper group that Schulz would maintain his leadership position, indicating that he still enjoys robust support within the party. text: Israel has given the green light for the construction of 176 new homes for Jewish settlers in East Jerusalem. JERUSALEM (Reuters) - On Wednesday, Israeli officials authorized a significant increase in a Jewish settler enclave located within a Palestinian neighborhood in East Jerusalem, granting building permits for 176 additional housing units. The construction was confirmed by a spokeswoman for the Jerusalem municipality, who stated that it received approval from the city’s planning committee. The Palestinians quickly denounced the initiative as a breach of international law. This new construction will nearly triple the existing number of settler homes in the Nof Zion settlement, which currently consists of 91 residences and is encircled by Palestinian homes in the Jabel al-Mukaber area. This region lies within territory that Israel seized and subsequently annexed during the 1967 Middle East conflict, which the Palestinians view as integral to the state they aspire to establish in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip, with East Jerusalem as its capital. "We are unifying Jerusalem through actions on the ground," stated Jerusalem Mayor Nir Barkat concerning the expansion of the settlement. Israel's assertion of Jerusalem as its undivided capital has not gained international acknowledgment, and numerous countries consider the settlements established on occupied land as illegal and as impediments to any prospective land-for-peace agreement. Israel contests this view. Wasel Abu Yousif, a member of the Palestine Liberation Organization, described the development plans in Jabel al-Mukaber as a provocation against the international community's calls to cease settlement expansion. Just last week, Israel disclosed the approval of several hundred more homes for settlers in the West Bank, prompting backlash from Palestinians and the European Union. Peace negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians have been stalled since 2014, with settlement expansion being one of the key issues that contributed to their breakdown. Approximately 500,000 Israelis reside in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, regions that are home to over 2.6 million Palestinians. BEIRUT (Reuters) - Militias in Syria that receive backing from the U.S. announced the establishment of a joint military center with the Iraqi army aimed at securing their mutual border area following the expulsion of Islamic State militants. On Sunday, leaders from the SDF, which is a coalition of Kurdish and Arab militias, convened with Iraqi military officials to discuss strategies for safeguarding the Syrian-Iraqi border near Deir al-Zor province and the ultimate elimination of Daesh fighters in that region, as stated by the SDF. Daesh is the Arabic term for Islamic State. The two parties resolved to create a joint coordination center to ensure border security, as indicated in the statement. The military campaign concentrated on taking control of land east of the Euphrates River, which divides the oil-rich province. Meanwhile, Iraqi forces regained the final territories still held by Islamic State along the Syria border on Saturday and secured the western desert. This event signified the conclusion of the conflict against IS, three years after they captured approximately one-third of Iraq’s territory. The Iraqi forces that battled IS consisted of the army, air force, police, elite counter-terrorism units, as well as Shiite and Sunni paramilitary groups and Kurdish Peshmerga fighters. They received crucial air assistance from the U.S.-led international coalition. Syrian government troops and their allies, supported by Russian air capabilities, have taken control of most remaining parts of Deir al-Zor province, primarily on the western bank of the Euphrates, while the SDF operates on the eastern side. To minimize the risk of clashes between the two opposing campaigns against Islamic State, Russia and the United States established a communication channel. Colonel Ryan Dillon, a spokesperson for the coalition, mentioned that Iraqi security forces and the SDF had connected at their shared border area on Sunday. "A secure international border safeguards Iraqis (and) Syrians from the remaining Daesh movement into (and) across the region as terrorist fighters/leaders attempt to escape the battlefield," he tweeted.

text: Although he made a commitment, the Trump Organization is not monitoring all earnings from foreign nations. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The businesses owned by President Donald Trump have stated that it would be "impractical" for customers representing foreign governments to disclose their identities, which raises concerns about how Trump intends to uphold his promise to donate all profits derived from foreign governments to the U.S. Treasury. The Trump Organization distributed a brochure to the general managers of each hotel, golf course, social club, and winery under Trump’s ownership or management, indicating that it would only donate earnings from patrons who announce they represent foreign governments. This brochure was submitted to the House of Representatives Oversight and Reform Committee in reply to a request for clarification regarding how the Trump Organization was meeting the commitment Trump made in January. "Implementing a policy that mandates all guests to identify themselves would infringe on personal privacy and lessen the guest experience associated with our brand," the brochure stated. The Trump Organization, along with Trump’s attorney, Sheri Dillon, and the White House, did not provide comments upon being approached for their opinions. Dillon had declared at a press conference in January that Trump would voluntarily contribute all profits from foreign government payments made to his properties to the Treasury. Payments made by foreign governments to Trump’s businesses have faced criticism from experts in constitutional law and ethics who argue that these payments violate the U.S. Constitution’s prohibition against the president receiving "emoluments" from foreign governments. In this context, emoluments are typically interpreted as valuable gifts or funds. On Wednesday, seven Democratic members of the House Judiciary Committee sent a letter to the Republican president requesting a comprehensive account of "any benefits or rewards, financial or otherwise" that he has received from foreign governments since his inauguration on January 20. The governments of Kuwait and Azerbaijan have already held events at the Trump International Hotel located in Washington, D.C. In March, the Government Accountability Office announced it would investigate whether Trump has remitted any payments to the U.S. Treasury from profits accrued at his hotels. The brochure from the Trump Organization identified additional entities through which foreign governments might operate, including state-owned enterprises in aerospace, defense, banking, finance, healthcare, and energy. Those entities "may not be easily recognizable as foreign government entities, and thus may not be factored into our profit calculation for donation," the brochure stated. Elijah Cummings, the leading Democrat on the congressional committee that received the brochure, responded by stating that the Trump Organization’s approach to identifying payments from foreign governments was inadequate. Cummings asserted that foreign powers could still provide unconstitutional emoluments to Trump via entities that are funded and controlled but not overtly associated with foreign governments. "Such payments would remain unmonitored and concealed from the American public," Cummings wrote.

text: The Justice Minister of Ukraine, Pavlo Petrenko, expressed on Thursday his willingness to consider modifications to recent legal reforms due to worries that they might facilitate corruption and potentially halt investigations into the shooting of demonstrators leading up to the 2014 revolution. This Eastern European nation, currently embroiled in a conflict with Russia over the annexation of Crimea, enacted amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code last week that anti-corruption advocates argue significantly restrict the timeframe for investigators to resolve crimes and bring cases to court. Petrenko mentioned that he had not yet reviewed the final draft of the extensive reforms but acknowledged awareness of the issues raised. 'If there are any aspects hindering the investigation process for both historical and new cases, I will propose changes to the parliament and the president,' Petrenko stated during an interview in Sydney, where he was participating in a legal industry conference. The new legislation still awaits approval from President Petro Poroshenko. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine indicated in a statement last week that the updated law could require investigators to submit a criminal case to the court within six months, extendable to 12 months with judicial approval. According to the law enforcement agency, corrupt officials might gain an advantage, considering the intricate nature of investigations that may involve international cooperation. Additionally, there are concerns that this legislation might hinder prosecutions for offenses committed during the Euromaidan protests in 2013 and 2014, where over 100 demonstrators advocating for closer ties with Europe lost their lives. This popular uprising, driven by issues of corruption and Ukraine's relationship with Russia, led to the ousting of then-president Viktor Yanukovych. More than three years later, Ukraine continues to grapple with serious corruption allegations, with Transparency International ranking the country 131st out of 176 nations in its World Corruption Perception Index earlier this year. On Thursday, Petrenko emphasized the nation's commitment to overhauling its judicial framework, which includes the selection of more than 100 Supreme Court judges through a competitive process aimed at eliminating corruption. 'Are all these individuals perfect? I believe not, as the country is not perfect,' Petrenko remarked. 'You cannot find ideal individuals from Mars or the moon and place them in these roles; however, those appointed have undergone an objective, transparent, and entirely public competition.' Ukraine is also a beneficiary of an aid-for-reforms initiative from the International Monetary Fund.
