text: "You are the light" - Duterte sings at Trump's behest. MANILA (Reuters) - President Rodrigo Duterte performed a popular Filipino romantic song during a dinner event in Manila attended by leaders from across Asia, later clarifying that it was at the request of U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump and Duterte were among 19 leaders present at a lavish gala in the Philippine capital on Sunday, which took place prior to an annual summit. At one moment, Duterte grabbed the microphone to sing Ikaw (You), partnering with local pop star Pilita Corrales. A translated verse of the song begins: You are the light in my world, a half of this heart of mine. "Ladies and gentlemen, I sang without an invitation, at the command of the commander-in-chief of the United States," Duterte stated later, as reported by the ABS-CBN news outlet. Duterte, often referred to as the Trump of the East due to his bold demeanor, is scheduled to meet the U.S. president on the sidelines of the summit on Monday. The United States and the Philippines, its former colony, have been strategic partners since World War Two. However, their relationship has been tested by Duterte's anti-U.S. comments and his interest in strengthening ties with Russia and China. Since Duterte assumed office last year, more than 3,900 Filipinos have lost their lives in a declared war on drugs. His administration claims that police actions are in self-defense, but opponents argue that extrajudicial killings are occurring without accountability. Last week, Duterte mentioned he would tell the U.S. president to "lay off" if human rights were brought up during their meeting. They enjoyed a four-course Filipino-Asian fusion meal curated and prepared by Chef Jessie Sincioco, who also created the menu for Pope Francis during his visit to the Philippines in 2015.

text: ROME (Reuters) - On Thursday, the Italian Chamber of Deputies granted final approval to a controversial electoral law that is anticipated to disadvantage the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement in the upcoming election next year. The legislation, which has the backing of the ruling Democratic Party (PD) along with mainstream center-right opposition parties, was passed in a secret ballot with a vote tally of 375 in favor and 215 against, and it will now proceed to the Senate for additional discussion. An election is scheduled to take place by May 2018. Analysts suggest that the newly implemented system is unlikely to produce a definitive parliamentary majority, as opinion polls indicate a three-way split among the center-left, center-right, and 5-Star parties. However, the 5-Star Movement has opted not to join any coalitions and claims that the reform could result in a loss of at least 50 seats in the next parliament, significantly diminishing its chances of gaining power. The party, which leads in many opinion polls, has conducted two days of street demonstrations against what it perceives as efforts by mainstream rivals to undermine its electoral prospects. "You are manipulating the foundations of our democratic system and rigging the rules before the game starts," 5-Star leader Luigi Di Maio addressed the parliament prior to the vote. Smaller left-wing and right-wing parties are also opposing the bill, which receives support from the center-right Forza Italia (Go Italy!) and the right-wing Northern League. President Sergio Mattarella has called for revised voting regulations, asserting that the current system is too disparate between the upper and lower houses, which could potentially lead to contradictory majorities. text: 'Fully committed' NATO endorses new U.S. strategy on Afghanistan. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - On Tuesday, NATO allies expressed their support for President Donald Trump's decision to increase troop levels in Afghanistan as part of a revised U.S. strategy that he indicated would necessitate additional forces and financial contributions from America's allies. After campaigning for the presidency last year with a promise to swiftly withdraw from Afghanistan, Trump changed his stance on Monday, vowing to intensify military operations against Taliban insurgents, stating: 'Our troops will fight to win.' U.S. officials disclosed that he had approved plans to deploy approximately 4,000 more U.S. troops, supplementing the nearly 8,400 already stationed in Afghanistan. However, his address did not establish specific criteria for successfully concluding the war that began with the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan in 2001, which he recognized had demanded an 'extraordinary sacrifice of blood and treasure.' 'We will request our NATO allies and global partners to back our new strategy, with increased troop commitments and funding that align with our own. We are confident they will,' Trump remarked. This statement indicated he would exert additional pressure on U.S. allies, who have already been shaken by his ongoing demands for increased contributions to NATO and his prior characterization of the alliance as 'obsolete' - although he has since stated this is no longer his view. NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg remarked in a statement: 'NATO remains fully committed to Afghanistan, and I look forward to discussing the way forward with (Defense) Secretary (James) Mattis and our Allies and international partners.' NATO has 12,000 troops in Afghanistan, and Stoltenberg mentioned that 15 nations have committed more forces. Britain, a prominent NATO member, described the U.S. commitment as 'very welcome.' 'In my conversation with Secretary Mattis yesterday, we concurred that despite the challenges, we must maintain our course in Afghanistan to aid in strengthening its fragile democracy and mitigating the terrorist threat to the West,' stated Defense Secretary Michael Fallon. Germany, which has faced significant criticism from Trump regarding its defense spending levels, also expressed support for the new U.S. strategy. 'Our ongoing commitment is essential on the path to stabilizing the country,' a government spokeswoman remarked. In June, European allies had previously pledged additional troops but had not disclosed specific numbers, waiting for the Trump administration to present its strategy for the region. Nearly 16 years after the U.S.-led invasion - which was a reaction to the Sept. 11 attacks orchestrated by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden from Afghanistan - the nation continues to grapple with a weak central government and a Taliban insurgency. Trump acknowledged that he shared the frustration of the American populace who were 'weary of war without victory,' but cautioned that a hasty withdrawal would create an opportunity for groups like Islamic State and al Qaeda to exploit.

Speaking at the Milken Institute Global Conference in Beverly Hills, California, and following the announcement of plans to reduce taxes for individuals and corporations to 15 percent, Mnuchin emphasized that tax reform and easing regulations will contribute to economic expansion. His remarks followed the release of government data indicating a modest economic growth rate of 0.7 percent over the past three months. "Our tax plan represents our approach to a jobs bill," Mnuchin remarked during an interview on stage with journalist Maria Bartoromo. He conveyed to CNBC, on the sidelines of the conference, that the tax proposal was intentionally broad to allow the administration to negotiate with lawmakers on a viable plan for Congress. Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic adviser at Allianz, remarked that while stock market optimism is at an all-time high, geopolitical challenges are a genuine concern.

text: WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, U.S. House Republicans put forward a proposal to delay or suspend various taxes associated with former President Barack Obama’s healthcare legislation, including a tax on medical devices and the “Cadillac” tax affecting high-end health insurance plans. This initiative marks another effort by Republicans to dismantle elements of the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, following multiple failed attempts by the congressional majority to repeal the law this year. Additionally, both House and Senate Republicans are nearing the conclusion of tax reform discussions, which include a suggestion to eliminate Obamacare’s individual mandate that imposes a tax penalty on individuals who do not secure health insurance. A representative from the House Ways and Means Committee indicated that these additional healthcare tax rollbacks would not be included in the larger tax reform legislation. There is a possibility that Republicans might attempt to combine the healthcare tax measures with a critical government funding bill that is anticipated to be passed by December 22, when current funding expires. However, to achieve this, Senate Republicans, who possess a narrow majority, would require support from Democrats to navigate procedural obstacles. In a statement, House Ways and Means Chairman Kevin Brady unveiled five new bills sponsored by Republicans aimed at providing targeted relief from Obamacare taxes, expressing his eagerness to “advance legislation in the weeks ahead.” One of the proposed bills seeks to retroactively eliminate penalties associated with Obamacare for employers that did not provide health insurance to their employees over the past three years, as well as for the upcoming year. This legislation would also postpone the Cadillac tax on high-cost employer-sponsored plans for an additional year, which is slated to be enforced in 2020. Labor unions are against this tax due to the fact that their members frequently receive more lavish healthcare plans, and they worry it would lead to increased expenses. Another proposed bill aims to suspend the tax on medical devices, like pacemakers and artificial hips, for five years. This tax was initially enacted in January 2013 as a funding source for Obamacare, which has expanded medical coverage to millions of Americans who were previously uninsured. The medical device tax has strong adversaries across both political parties, and manufacturers have actively campaigned against it. Additional proposals included in the package would halt a tax on health insurers for two years, as well as provide two years of relief from a tax on over-the-counter medications.

Trump, who pledged to repeal and replace Obamacare during his campaign, which he has labeled a "disaster," has referred to the subsidies as a bailout for insurance companies. By statute, health insurers are still required to provide discounts on deductibles, co-pays, and other out-of-pocket expenses, even if the government ceases to reimburse them. Insurers argue that they do not benefit from these subsidies. Anticipating Trump's actions, insurers proposed increased monthly premium rates for 2018 to recover the lost funds. In nearly all states, they submitted two sets of premium rates: a lower rate contingent on the continuation of the subsidies and a higher rate if the funding were to be eliminated. A California court is scheduled to review on Monday a plea from Democratic attorneys general to maintain the subsidies until a legal challenge to Trump's decision is settled. text: US Restores Funding for Bomb Clearance in Cambodia. PHNOM PENH (Reuters) - On Wednesday, the United States initiated a tender worth $2 million aimed at assisting in the removal of unexploded ordnance in Cambodia, following a recent announcement from the government’s mine clearance agency that its financial support from the U.S. had been halted. This year, relations between Cambodia and the United States have deteriorated, with the Cambodian government alleging American involvement in a scheme orchestrated by detained opposition leader Kem Sokha to overthrow Prime Minister Hun Sen. Washington has dismissed these claims as unfounded. Last week, the U.S. announced a reduction in aid for the upcoming election and indicated that additional measures would follow the dissolution of the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP) by the Supreme Court at the government’s request. The U.S. embassy announced that it is now accepting proposals for a one-year grant of $2 million intended for surveying and clearing unexploded bombs in eastern Cambodia, a region that experienced extensive U.S. bombing during the Vietnam War. "The United States has been involved in humanitarian demining efforts in Cambodia for over 20 years and remains dedicated to addressing our wartime legacy," stated Ambassador William Heidt. "We seek the most qualified national and international specialists." The value of the contract aligns with the funding amount that the Cambodian Mine Action Centre had indicated was previously reduced from the financial support received from the United States via Norwegian People’s Aid. Huy Vannak, undersecretary of state at the Interior Ministry, expressed appreciation for the commitment to addressing the war’s legacy. Shortly thereafter, China, which is currently Cambodia's closest ally, promptly offered assistance with demining efforts. As Cambodia's largest donor and investor, China has taken on an increasingly significant role as Western nations have criticized actions against the opposition, civil society, and media in the lead-up to next year’s elections. Although it has not yet taken any measures, the European Union highlighted last week that Cambodia's access to duty-free imports, crucial for its garment sector, is contingent upon upholding human rights. On Wednesday, Hun Sen informed garment workers that they would bear the consequences - not him - if that access were to be revoked. In 2016, European Union nations accounted for roughly 40 percent of Cambodia's exports, predominantly in clothing. "It’s important to understand that if there is any reduction in orders, it is entirely due to a group of individuals from the opposition party," Hun Sen remarked to garment workers in Phnom Penh. "Hun Sen will survive, but workers, you will perish," he added. The prime minister accused exiled opposition leaders of attempting to instigate sanctions. Thus far, they have stated they would refrain from advocating for trade restrictions due to the potential adverse effects on the livelihoods of around 700,000 garment workers. Despite the political unrest, Cambodia's economy has shown resilience. The World Bank reported on Wednesday that it anticipates the economy will expand by 6.9 percent next year, compared to a projected growth of 6.8 percent in 2017, despite potential risks including uncertainties surrounding the election.

text: Leaders from the Balkans have expressed their endorsement for Serbia's aspiration to join the European Union. SOFIA (Reuters) - On Tuesday, the prime ministers of Bulgaria, Greece, and Romania voiced their support for Serbia's application to join the EU, asserting that the integration of the western Balkans is essential for ensuring regional peace and stability. Serbia, previously viewed as an outcast in the western Balkans due to its pivotal involvement in the conflicts that ensued after Yugoslavia's disintegration in the 1990s, aims to finalize its EU membership negotiations by 2019. "We all recognize that Serbia's rightful place is within the European Union," stated Bulgarian Prime Minister Boyko Borissov following a summit in Varna by the Black Sea, which included Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, Romanian Prime Minister Mihai Tudose, and Serbian President Alexander Vucic. Borissov indicated that the three EU member states plan to expedite the process to promote peace and stability both in the Balkans and across Europe. Bulgaria is set to assume the six-month rotating EU presidency in January, with Romania to follow in 2019. However, many Serbs remain doubtful about joining the EU, perceiving Western European nations as strong proponents of the 1999 NATO bombings that aimed to cease the killings and displacements of ethnic Albanians in the former Kosovo province, where numerous civilians lost their lives. Vucic accused the European Union of applying double standards by not acknowledging the Catalan independence referendum while largely accepting Kosovo's separation. "We support Spain, as it is our friendly nation," Vucic remarked. "Yet the European Commission has reacted differently regarding Kosovo, which was detrimental to my people and my nation." Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia was recognized by Washington and most EU countries, but it was rejected by Belgrade and its allies. Vucic pointed out that Kosovo achieved independence without conducting a referendum, whereas Catalonia... is denied similar treatment. "At times, we, the Serbs, wonder why we have been subjected to such double standards?" Serbia's stance concerning Kosovo has been a significant obstacle in its pursuit of EU membership. Brussels has stated that Serbia must enhance its relations with the authorities in Pristina and cease its efforts to obstruct their ambitions to join international organizations.

text: When Donald Trump advises his supporters against making donations, they tend to heed his advice. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Trump often expresses to his followers that he is wealthy enough to finance his presidential campaign without external funds. His supporters appear willing to respect this, as indicated by financial reports released on Sunday. The businessman from New York’s pursuit of the Republican party's presidential nomination has attracted large audiences, yet the donations have been minimal, as shown by reports submitted to the U.S. Federal Election Commission. In the final quarter of 2015, he garnered merely $2.6 million from contributors. The majority of this amount, approximately three-quarters, originated from merchandise sales, such as baseball caps with his campaign motto “Make America Great Again.” Only around $540,000 was contributed by individuals donating more than $200. In contrast, most of his Republican competitors have accumulated significantly larger amounts. His closest competitor, Senator Ted Cruz, raised $20.5 million, while former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, who was initially a leading candidate but has seen a decline in his polling numbers, collected $7 million. Nevertheless, Trump continues to maintain a lead in all national polls as Iowa voters prepare for the nominating event on Monday. The primary source of funding for Trump's presidential campaign stems from $12.6 million in loans he provided to his campaign in 2015. Some of these funds have been redirected back to his businesses: his largest campaign expense in the last quarter of 2015 was $826,590 paid to TAG Air, Inc., which operates his private aircraft, for transporting him between campaign locations and his residences in New York and Florida. Following that, his second most significant expenditure was $478,000 allocated to Wizbang Solutions, a firm specializing in printing and design, and $411,000 went to a consulting agency that gathers signatures for candidates to qualify for state election ballots. He is the sole billionaire in the race, though a few of his opponents are millionaires. Supporters nationwide frequently comment that his financial autonomy is appealing to them, as they believe he is not susceptible to being influenced by special interest groups. Trump’s financial disclosures indicate that his fundraising is not the only aspect that distinguishes him from other contenders. During the last quarter of 2015, Trump expended $6.9 million. In comparison, his far-off opponent for the Republican nomination, retired neurosurgeon Ben Carson, spent $27 million. Cruz's expenses totaled $15.5 million. Moreover, Florida Senator Marco Rubio, who is currently viewed as the most viable establishment alternative to Trump, spent $14.8 million in the fourth quarter, which is approximately $2 million more than Trump’s total expenditures for the entire year of 2015. text: Trump reignites feud with U.S. sports community. SOMERSET, N.J. (Reuters) - On Sunday, President Donald Trump reignited his conflict with the sports community, reiterating his call for National Football League owners to dismiss players who engage in protests during the national anthem of the U.S. In a tweet sent early in the morning, Trump proposed that fans might boycott NFL games to pressure teams into disciplining players who protest the anthem. "If NFL fans refuse to attend games until players cease disrespecting our Flag & Country, you will witness swift change," Trump stated on Sunday. "Fire or suspend!" In another tweet, Trump remarked that the "league should support" fans who are frustrated with the protests. Trump is spending the weekend at his Bedminster, New Jersey, golf club and did not participate in any public events on Saturday. On that same day, NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell commented that Trump’s initial remarks on the issue, which were made during a political rally in Alabama on Friday, demonstrated an "unfortunate lack of respect" for the NFL and its athletes. During the rally, Trump referred to any protesting football player as a "son of a bitch" who should be dismissed from their job. "Wouldn’t it be great to see one of these NFL owners, when someone disrespects our flag, say, 'Get that son of a bitch off the field right now ... He is fired'," Trump declared on Friday while supporting Alabama Senate Republican candidate Luther Strange. Trump later tweeted on Saturday that if NFL players sought "the privilege" of high salaries, they "should stand for the National Anthem. If not, YOU’RE FIRED. Find something else to do!" Former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick sparked a contentious national conversation in 2016 after he refused to stand for pre-game performances of the "Star Spangled Banner." Instead, Kaepernick took a knee to protest police brutality against African-Americans. Several players have since engaged in similar forms of protest prior to games. Goodell, as commissioner, is accountable to NFL owners, some of whom have previously supported Trump. Woody Johnson, the owner of the New York Jets and a significant donor to Trump’s presidential campaign, was confirmed by the Senate last month as Trump’s choice to be U.S. ambassador to Britain. The union representing professional football players also countered Trump’s remarks, asserting that it would defend the players' right to freedom of expression. The White House has not yet replied to a request for comments regarding this issue. Players from the National Basketball Association also responded to the president's comments on Saturday after Trump had a dispute with one of the NBA’s biggest stars. In an early morning Twitter message on Saturday, the president withdrew a White House invitation to Stephen Curry, who indicated he would "vote" against the anticipated visit from the NBA champion Golden State Warriors. "Going to the White House is deemed a tremendous honor for a championship team. Stephen Curry is hesitating, so the invitation is rescinded!" Trump tweeted. Curry addressed a press conference in Oakland, California, stating: "It’s beneath the leader of a country to go that route." "It’s not what leaders do," he added. The Golden State Warriors, based in Oakland, released a statement indicating that they had planned to meet to discuss the potential visit at the earliest opportunity on Saturday morning. "We acknowledge that President Trump has made it clear that we are not invited," the team stated. LeBron James defended Curry, contesting Trump’s claim that a visit to the White House is an honor. "Going to the White House was a great honor until you showed up!" James, a well-known supporter of Hillary Clinton during the 2016 presidential elections, tweeted. Singer Stevie Wonder seemed to reference Kaepernick and other athletes' protests when he took a knee on stage during a performance at the Global Citizen Festival in New York City on Saturday. "Tonight, I’m taking a knee for America," Wonder expressed to the audience as his son, Kwame Morris, assisted him down. Wonder then lowered his other leg to assume a kneeling position.

text: A federal appeals court determined on Wednesday that a New Hampshire law from 2014, which forbids voters from taking selfies with their ballots on election day, constitutes an unconstitutional violation of free speech rights. The law in the New England state aimed to prohibit this practice, which has gained popularity among voters wishing to demonstrate support for their preferred candidates, on the grounds that it could revive vote-buying scandals that plagued numerous U.S. states in the 19th century. In that same year, three residents of New Hampshire, including an individual who wrote in his dog’s name to express his dissatisfaction with the options in the 2014 Republican primary for the U.S. Senate, filed a lawsuit against the state, asserting that the law infringed upon their rights to free expression, as guaranteed by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. A federal court in New Hampshire ruled in their favor; however, the state subsequently appealed and presented its arguments in Boston just two weeks ago. The appeals court quickly dismissed the state’s reasoning. Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch stated in the court's ruling, "The statute’s purposes cannot justify the restrictions it imposes on speech." Lynch further explained that New Hampshire's claim that ballot selfies might lead to vote selling or coercion by employers fell short, primarily because the state lacked evidence of such occurrences. "The legislative history of the bill does not contain any corroborated evidence of vote buying or voter coercion in New Hampshire during the 20th and 21st centuries," she noted. Additionally, she remarked that "Digital photography, the internet, and social media are not unknown quantities — they have been ubiquitous for several election cycles, without being shown to have the effect of furthering vote buying or voter intimidation." Lynch also pointed out that there are already several federal and state laws in New Hampshire that prohibit vote buying or selling, allowing prosecutors to address allegations of election tampering, even if selfies were allowed. Other states, such as nearby Rhode Island, have enacted laws that explicitly permit ballot selfies, partly arguing that this trend has encouraged younger voters to express their enthusiasm for the democratic process.

text: Republicans revise U.S. healthcare legislation, enhance benefits for senior citizens. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - House Republicans in the U.S. are currently making adjustments to their healthcare reform bill to offer more substantial tax credits for older Americans and introduce a work requirement for the Medicaid program aimed at low-income individuals, House Speaker Paul Ryan mentioned on Sunday. Ryan indicated that GOP leaders still intended to present the healthcare legislation for a vote on the House of Representatives floor this Thursday. During an appearance on the "Fox News Sunday" television program, he stated that they were addressing issues raised by rank-and-file Republicans regarding the bill. The Republican Party remains significantly split over the healthcare reform, which represents President Donald Trump’s inaugural major legislative effort. This initiative seeks to fulfill his campaign promise to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, widely known as Obamacare, which is the hallmark healthcare initiative of his Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama. Democrats argue that the Republican proposal could leave millions without health insurance and negatively impact the elderly, impoverished, and working families, while providing tax reductions for the wealthy. "We believe we should provide even greater assistance than the current bill does" for lower-income individuals aged 50 to 64, Ryan, the leading Republican in Congress, stated regarding the proposed health insurance tax credits in the legislation. Furthermore, Ryan mentioned that Republicans were drafting modifications that would enable federal block grants to states for Medicaid and allow states to enforce a work requirement for able-bodied Medicaid beneficiaries. Trump informed reporters during a short exchange aboard Air Force One that he had discussions concerning healthcare reform in Florida over the weekend and that the campaign to promote the proposal was progressing well. He has been reaching out to lawmakers to secure votes for the bill and garnered support from a dozen conservative legislators on Friday following an Oval Office meeting where the president backed a work requirement and the block-grant strategy for Medicaid. Trump is scheduled to meet Ezekiel Emanuel, a health policy advisor under Obama who played a role in developing the Affordable Care Act, at the White House on Monday, along with Ryan and Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price. Block grants would allocate a fixed sum of money to states for Medicaid and grant them flexibility in their spending choices. However, there is no assurance that funding would match future needs. While Ryan expressed that he felt "very good" about the bill’s chances in the House, a prominent conservative lawmaker, Representative Mark Meadows, disclosed on the C-Span "Newsmakers" program that there were presently 40 Republican "no" votes in the House. Although Republicans hold a majority in the chamber, they cannot afford to have more than 21 members dissent for the bill to succeed. Meadows, along with two other Republican critics of the bill, Senators Mike Lee of Utah and Ted Cruz of Texas, convened at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday to negotiate with the president’s team in efforts to amend the bill, Cruz mentioned to CBS’ "Face the Nation." North Carolina Republican Meadows asserted that the proposed modifications to the Medicaid program would be insufficient if they left the decision to the states regarding the implementation of a work requirement. Price acknowledged the challenging negotiations, stating to ABC’s "This Week": "It’s a fine needle that needs to be threaded, there’s no doubt about it." The healthcare legislation would encounter considerable obstacles in the Senate even if it clears the House. Senator Tom Cotton, a conservative Republican from Arkansas, remarked that the bill would not lower premiums for individuals in the private insurance market. "It’s fixable, but it’s going to take a lot of work," Cotton asserted on CNN’s "State of the Union." Moderate Republicans have also voiced their concerns about the bill, which often differ from those of conservatives. Speaking on NBC’s "Meet the Press," Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine expressed apprehension that the bill would adversely affect older Americans.

text: Macron: France prepared to bolster forces in Sahel combating Islamists. PARIS (Reuters) - On Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron indicated that France is prepared to enhance its military presence if necessary to support African troops in their fight against Islamist militants in the Sahel region. France has been aiming to eventually withdraw from the inadequately monitored scrublands of the Sahel, adjacent to the Sahara to the north, which has become a hub for the recruitment and training of Islamist fighters, with the assistance of a newly established regional African force. The G5 Sahel, which commenced official operations in November, consists of soldiers from Mali, Niger, Chad, Burkina Faso, and Mauritania who will monitor the area in partnership with 4,000 French troops that have been stationed there since intervening in 2013 to address an uprising in northern Mali. "France is prepared, not just to sustain, but if necessary, to increase its involvement in the area because, in my view, the battle against terrorism in the Sahel is crucial," he articulated during a joint press conference with his Nigerien counterpart Mahamoudou Issoufou. "The struggle is not yet concluded... it is vital not only to maintain but also to enhance our responsiveness on the ground, to innovate further, and to concentrate our efforts on the areas identified as most vulnerable," he continued. While in Niger, Macron also revealed an additional funding of 10 million euros aimed at promoting girls' education, a key initiative advocated by President Issoufou to mitigate migration. This amount is in addition to the 15 million euros that France has already allocated to support education in Niger. In mid-December, Paris committed to investing 400 million euros from 2017 to 2021 to assist Niamey.

text: Nigeria is set to commence a mass trial of over 1,600 individuals suspected of connections to Boko Haram, with proceedings expected to start behind closed doors on Monday. This represents the largest legal inquiry into the eight-year-long militant Islamist insurgency. The conflict has resulted in more than 20,000 fatalities and displaced two million people in northeastern Nigeria, contributing to what the United Nations has described as one of the worst humanitarian crises globally. Last month, Nigeria's ministry of justice announced that the trial of approximately 1,670 detainees at the Kainji detention facility would take place at that location in the central Niger state, with four judges overseeing the proceedings. A representative from the ministry has not responded to inquiries to confirm whether the trial has commenced. A military spokesperson refrained from commenting, stating that any questions should be directed to the judiciary. The ministry indicated that after the Kainji trials conclude, an additional 651 individuals alleged to have links to Boko Haram, currently held in prisons in Maiduguri, the capital of Borno state, would also face trial. Clement Nwankwo, a human rights attorney in Abuja, stated that open trials would serve as a more effective deterrent and emphasized the importance of public awareness regarding the ongoing situation and the nature of the crimes committed. Nwankwo expressed concerns that the closed nature of the trials makes it difficult to assess their fairness. He noted that the Nigerian authorities have not been particularly thorough in investigating and prosecuting suspects, warning that a feeling of injustice could foster resentment among families, potentially leading to future radicalization. Conversely, Fatima Akilu, who led the government’s counter-violent extremism program during the previous administration, argued that confidentiality was essential to encourage the participation of witnesses and judges, given the absence of a witness protection program in Nigeria. Akilu, who served in the Office of the National Security Adviser from 2012 to 2015, remarked that many witnesses were fearful of coming forward. She further explained that judges and witnesses had faced death threats in past trials. text: Suspected U.S. drone attacks result in 31 fatalities along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border. PARACHINAR/PESHAWAR, Pakistan (Reuters) - On Tuesday, two suspected U.S. drone strikes claimed the lives of 11 individuals in the mountainous region along the Pakistan-Afghanistan frontier, following a prior attack a day before that resulted in 20 deaths, according to sources from both the government and militant groups. These strikes occurred shortly after a Canadian-American couple held captive by the Taliban were rescued from the northwestern area of Pakistan, marking a rare positive development in the often tense relations between the United States and Pakistan. On Friday, U.S. drones were spotted in the vicinity where American Caitlan Coleman, her Canadian spouse, Joshua Boyle, and their three children, all born during their captivity, were liberated after being abducted by the Haqqani network while hiking in Afghanistan back in 2012. Four unmanned aerial vehicles launched six missiles during Monday’s attack, with an additional four missiles deployed in two strikes on Tuesday, as reported by Baseer Khan Wazir, the highest administrative official in the Kurram Agency, which is part of Pakistan’s turbulent Federally Administered Tribal Areas. The drones targeted Taliban hideouts, resulting in at least 31 fatalities over the span of two days, Wazir stated, noting that all three assaults occurred on the Afghan side of the border. “Yesterday, 20 individuals were killed, primarily from the Afghan Taliban, and today’s assaults resulted in 11 additional fatalities,” Wazir informed Reuters. Taliban sources indicated that 18 members of the Pakistan-based Haqqani militants, who are allied with the Taliban, perished in Monday’s strike, while six were killed in one of Tuesday’s attacks. “There were some mud-built houses being utilized by the mujahideen (Afghan Taliban fighters),” mentioned a Taliban member, who requested anonymity. He added that no significant militants were present in the area when the drones targeted two or three distinct compounds. Another Taliban source claimed that two commanders died in Monday’s strike. Witnesses reported hearing the drones and observing smoke billowing before they saw 20 makeshift coffins being transported from the site. Local residents noted that the strikes occurred within 300 meters (yards) of the Pakistan side of the border. “Drones are frequently seen hovering over this border region, but it was the first instance of four drones being observed simultaneously,” stated Kurram resident Gulab Sher.

Typically, these joint trainings occur every two years, but they were also called off in 2011 after the Arab Spring revolt that resulted in the ousting of Egypt's long-standing leader, Hosni Mubarak. text: The European Commission announced on Monday that it has received unanimous approval from all 28 member states of the European Union to complete negotiations for a free trade agreement with the United States. This statement came shortly after Germany's economy minister, Sigmar Gabriel, declared that talks had "de facto failed". Gabriel, representing Germany, the largest economy in the EU, stated on Sunday that discussions regarding the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership (TTIP) had collapsed due to Europe's refusal to accept certain U.S. demands. In response to Gabriel's comments, a spokesperson for the European Commission remarked, "The ball is still rolling" on TTIP. Margaritis Schinas mentioned at a press conference, "Although trade negotiations require time, progress is being made right now in the ongoing TTIP discussions." The White House also challenged Gabriel's assertion, affirming its goal to finalize a deal by the year’s end. White House spokesman Josh Earnest informed reporters in Washington, "It’s going to require the resolution of some pretty thorny negotiations, but the president and his team are committed to doing that." In Berlin, leading industry groups in Germany criticized Gabriel’s statements and called on the government to demonstrate stronger support for free trade agreements. Ulrich Grillo, head of the industry association BDI, expressed astonishment that Gabriel, who also serves as vice chancellor and leader of the co-governing Social Democrats, had labeled the TTIP talks a failure while negotiations were still in progress. Senior officials from other industry organizations such as VDMA and the Auto Industry Association VDA also voiced opposition to Gabriel’s comments, indicating rising divisions within Chancellor Angela Merkel’s governing coalition ahead of the upcoming elections next year. After three years of negotiations, numerous differences remain unresolved, particularly regarding food and environmental safety, with critics arguing that the agreement would grant excessive power to large multinational corporations, undermining the interests of consumers and workers. Proponents of a comprehensive U.S.-EU free trade agreement believe it would yield economic benefits for both sides of the Atlantic. EU trade ministers are scheduled to deliberate on this matter in Bratislava on September 22. Schinas stated that the Commission remains prepared to conclude the agreement by the year's end but not at the cost of "Europe’s safety, health, social and data protection standards, or our cultural diversity." In a separate commentary regarding Gabriel’s statements, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Linas Linkevicius expressed his belief that reaching a deal would be advantageous for both the EU and the United States. He stated, "It would be better for all sides to agree. Of course, not at the expense of our interests. We must defend our interests, but we also need to negotiate and finalize this agreement. It would be a significant boost for economies, jobs, and trade." The June decision by Britain to exit the EU has further complicated the situation, although Schinas emphasized that Brussels continues to negotiate on behalf of all 28 bloc members, including London.

text: A U.S. appeals court on Wednesday engaged in discussions regarding President Donald Trump's effort to demonstrate the legality of his latest travel ban aimed at individuals from six Muslim-majority nations. The hearing at the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Seattle took place just two days after the U.S. Supreme Court permitted the implementation of Trump’s travel ban while the legal battle over its ultimate legitimacy continues. This ban affects individuals from Chad, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Syria, and Yemen who wish to enter the United States. The Republican president has asserted that the travel ban is essential for safeguarding the U.S. from terrorism. However, the state of Hawaii has contested this in court, with a federal judge in Honolulu ruling that it overstepped Trump’s authority under immigration law. Additionally, Trump’s ban also includes individuals from North Korea and specific government officials from Venezuela, though lower courts had previously allowed these provisions to be enforced. The same panel of three judges from the 9th Circuit that had limited an earlier version of Trump’s ban heard the arguments on Wednesday. Some judges seemed more hesitant about the notion of blocking the president’s policy. Judge Michael Daly Hawkins inquired of Hawaii’s attorneys whether Trump’s latest order is more valid than earlier iterations. He noted that the current ban is founded on particular findings that certain foreign governments fail to provide adequate information to thoroughly vet immigrants. "Would you trust Kim Jong Un to confirm this person’s identity, allowing them entry?" Hawkins posed. Judge Ronald Gould remarked that the court would deliver a decision "as soon as practicable." Trump initially imposed a travel ban targeting several Muslim-majority countries in January, which resulted in turmoil at airports and large-scale demonstrations. He subsequently issued a revised version in March after the initial ban was blocked by federal courts. That version lapsed in September following a protracted legal struggle, leading to the introduction of the current iteration. The ban does include some exceptions; individuals from each targeted nation can still apply for visas for tourism, business, or educational reasons, and any applicant may request an individual waiver. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals is scheduled to hear a different challenge to the ban on Friday, with the U.S. Supreme Court anticipated to ultimately resolve the matter in the coming months.

text: Trump, seeking to counteract financial disadvantages, intensifies his attacks on Clinton. WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - This week, Donald Trump elevated his use of scandalous allegations against Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton to a level not seen in modern U.S. presidential elections, demonstrating the Republican's unconventional strategy. The presumptive nominee of the Republican Party is striving to improve his standing and counter a significant edge that Clinton is expected to hold leading up to the presidential election on November 8: a substantial campaign fund that she and her supporters plan to utilize to unleash a wave of criticisms against him. Trump is employing the same approach he consistently used during the Republican nomination battle against contenders like Ted Cruz: making provocative assertions that U.S. television networks cannot help but cover, providing him with hours of complimentary media exposure and forcing his opponents to defend themselves. This tactic may already be proving effective. Trump has drawn significant attention with his most recent attacks on Clinton. He has transformed historical events into headlines that resemble a continuous feed in the 24-hour news environment of cable television and the internet. Corey Lewandowski, Trump's campaign manager, indicated that the strategy is sound. "Clearly, she’s going to have massive amounts of money," Lewandowski told Reuters. "The difference is Mr. Trump has financed his campaign. What we’ve managed to accomplish in this campaign cycle is to generate earned media based on Mr. Trump’s ability to speak plainly, being genuine and authentic, and I believe that drives the news cycle." Among Trump's latest accusations is a claim of rape against former President Bill Clinton from the 1970s and the suicide of a former aide to the ex-president in 1993—events that the campaign ties to Hillary Clinton. An online video released by Trump features various women alleging that the former president committed rape or made unwanted sexual advances. Trump has accused Hillary Clinton of assisting in silencing these women. The Clintons and their supporters have dismissed these allegations as unfounded and politically motivated. In an interview with The Washington Post, Trump also insinuated that the Clintons could have played a role in the 1993 demise of Vince Foster, a former aide to Bill Clinton and a friend of Hillary Clinton, despite more than five investigations, including one led by Republican special prosecutor Kenneth Starr, concluding that Foster died by suicide in a Virginia park. Trump was referencing theories that have circulated over the years in tabloid media, on various internet platforms, and in literature produced by the adversaries of the Clintons. On Wednesday, Trump's campaign inadvertently sent an email to a reporter at Politico disclosing that the Republican plans to next focus their attacks on Clinton regarding Whitewater, a real estate controversy that troubled Bill Clinton’s administration. No evidence of wrongdoing by the Clintons has ever been substantiated. These assaults have placed Hillary Clinton in a difficult position. Trump "just continues to dominate news cycle after news cycle," commented Republican pollster Kellyanne Conway, who managed the Super PACs that supported Senator Ted Cruz during the primary and fiercely criticized Trump. "Clinton is dedicating less time to campaigning on future issues and more time clarifying past events than she would probably prefer." This relentless attack places Clinton in a challenging situation. To date, she has chosen to disregard Trump’s personal assaults, and her campaign has provided general rebuttals. However, Clinton risks the possibility of this negative barrage undermining her public image and irrevocably harming her chances in the general election. "I have dealt with a lot of tough situations in my life, but I don’t envy the challenges facing the Clinton campaign right now. Trump has completely altered the political landscape," stated Jim Manley, a Democratic strategist who supports Clinton. "What they cannot afford is to stoop to his level. He possesses absolutely no morals or principles. Engaging him on that level is a total waste of time." Clinton’s campaign and the Super PACs backing her will not be without funding.

text: The United States referred to Myanmar's military actions against the Rohingya community as "ethnic cleansing" on Wednesday and issued a warning of targeted sanctions against those deemed responsible for what it described as "horrendous atrocities." U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson stated, "The situation in northern Rakhine state constitutes ethnic cleansing against the Rohingya," in a declaration that he had previously refrained from using during his visit to Myanmar, also known as Burma, the prior week. He added, "The United States will also pursue accountability through U.S. law, including possible targeted sanctions" against individuals accountable for the alleged offenses, which have forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee into neighboring Bangladesh. The U.S. adjusted its position partly to increase pressure on Myanmar's military and civilian authorities, who have shared power for the last two years under a precarious arrangement following decades of military governance, to confront the ongoing crisis. Human rights observers have accused Myanmar's military of committing atrocities, including murders, mass rapes, and arson against the stateless Rohingya during what were termed clearance operations following attacks by Rohingya militants on 30 police stations and an army facility on August 25. Since the crackdown initiated in response to the insurgent assaults, more than 600,000 Rohingya Muslims have escaped from Rakhine state in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, primarily heading to neighboring Bangladesh. Tillerson remarked, "These abuses perpetrated by certain members of the Burmese military, security personnel, and local vigilantes have inflicted severe suffering and compelled hundreds of thousands of men, women, and children to abandon their homes." While reiterating U.S. condemnation of the insurgent actions, he stated, "No provocation can justify the horrendous atrocities that have ensued." Myanmar's government, which is two years old and led by Nobel Peace Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi, has faced significant international condemnation for its handling of the crisis, even though it lacks control over the military leaders with whom it shares power. A senior U.S. official informed reporters during a conference call, "It’s not a situation that is completely under her authority, but certainly we are counting on her to demonstrate leadership and to collaborate through the civilian government with the military to address the crisis." The term "ethnic cleansing" lacks a formal definition in both international and U.S. law and does not inherently imply specific repercussions, according to a second senior U.S. official on the call. Murray Hiebert, a Southeast Asia analyst at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, stated that the State Department's application of the term and the threat of sanctions "will likely have limited to no impact on the ground." He added, "It is likely to foster greater distrust between the United States and Myanmar’s military and government and push them closer to China, Russia, and its more authoritarian neighbors in Southeast Asia." The U.S. announcement coincided with a U.N. tribunal's conviction of former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic for genocide and crimes against humanity related to the massacres of Bosnian Muslims and ethnic cleansing campaigns, resulting in a life sentence. The second U.S. official mentioned that Washington was evaluating whether genocide or crimes against humanity had occurred in Myanmar, which would breach international law, but no conclusion had been reached, and that assessment would require time. "Ultimately, it’s a court that must make that decision, as we’ve just witnessed with the verdict against Mladic," he stated. A high-ranking U.N. official referred to the military actions in September as a classic instance of "ethnic cleansing," yet the United States had refrained from using the term until Wednesday. Washington has attempted to balance its desire to support Myanmar's civilian government, where it vies for influence with China, alongside its aim to hold the military accountable for its abuses. U.S. officials are also concerned that the maltreatment of the Rohingya Muslim minority could exacerbate tensions.

text: U.S. bombers conduct drills over Korean peninsula following North Korea's recent missile launch. SEOUL/TOKYO (Reuters) - On Thursday, South Korean and Japanese aircraft participated in exercises alongside two supersonic U.S. B-1B bombers over and around the Korean peninsula, just two days after North Korea significantly escalated tensions by launching a missile over Japan. The drills, which included four U.S. stealth F-35B jets along with fighter jets from South Korea and Japan, concluded the annual U.S.-South Korea military exercises that primarily centered on computer simulations. General Terrence J. O'Shaughnessy, Commander of Pacific Air Forces, who made an unexpected trip to Japan, stated, "North Korea's actions pose a threat to our allies, partners, and homeland, and their destabilizing actions will be addressed accordingly." He emphasized that this intricate mission clearly illustrates our unity with allies and highlights the increasing cooperation to defend against this shared regional threat. North Korea has been pursuing the development of a nuclear missile capable of striking the United States and has recently threatened to launch missiles near Guam, a U.S. Pacific territory. On Monday, North Korea, which perceives the military exercises as a pretext for invasion, escalated its confrontation with the United States and its allies by firing an intermediate-range missile over Japan. On Thursday, the country's official news outlet, KCNA, criticized the military exercises in a traditionally forceful manner, labeling them as "the reckless act of those startled by the missile test," which it referred to as "the first military operation in the Pacific." President Donald Trump, who has cautioned that the U.S. military is "locked and loaded" in response to potential provocations from North Korea, expressed his anger regarding the recent missile test, asserting on Twitter that "talking is not the answer" to the crisis surrounding North Korea's weapons programs. U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis quickly emphasized on Wednesday that a diplomatic resolution remained achievable, but on Thursday, he told reporters he concurred with Trump that Washington "should not be engaging in discussions right now with a nation that is launching missiles over Japan, an ally." White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders reiterated during a regular briefing on Thursday that all options - diplomatic, economic, and military - are still available. Japanese Defense Minister Itsunori Onodera communicated with Mattis via telephone and agreed to continue applying pressure on North Korea in a visible manner, according to Japan's defense ministry. Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe mentioned that he and visiting British Prime Minister Theresa May concurred on the need to urge China, North Korea's sole significant ally, to take further action to restrain North Korea. May and Abe also talked about the possibility of implementing a new U.N. Security Council resolution regarding North Korea, as stated by a British government source. The U.N. Security Council, which consists of 15 members, condemned the missile launch over Japan on Tuesday as "outrageous" and demanded that North Korea cease its weapons programs. However, the U.S.-drafted statement did not threaten new sanctions. Japan has been pressing Washington to propose new sanctions through the Security Council, which diplomats indicated could affect North Korean laborers abroad, oil supplies, and textile exports. Nonetheless, diplomats anticipate opposition from Russia and fellow veto-wielding member China, especially considering that new measures were only announced on August 5 after North Korea tested its first two intercontinental ballistic missiles in July. A U.S. travel ban prohibiting Americans from visiting North Korea will be implemented on Friday, a measure announced following the death of a U.S. student shortly after his release from a 15-year prison sentence in the country, where three other Americans remain detained. China reiterated its call on Thursday for all parties to exercise restraint. Defense ministry spokesperson Ren Guoqiang stated during a monthly briefing that China would never permit war or chaos on the Korean peninsula, which is its immediate neighbor, and that military options were not viable. China strongly insists that all parties maintain restraint and composure.

text: CHICAGO (Reuters) - On Tuesday, Illinois Governor Bruce Rauner declared his veto of a $5 billion increase in the income tax rate, a central component of a recently approved bipartisan budget framework aimed at resolving the state's unprecedented fiscal deadlock, which he shared through social media. The Republican governor stated, "I just vetoed Speaker Madigan’s 32 percent permanent income tax increase," in messages posted on his Facebook and Twitter platforms, referencing Democratic House Speaker Michael Madigan, the primary architect of the legislative package. The updates did not indicate whether he had also acted on the spending and borrowing provisions that were part of the comprehensive package.

A treaty was signed by the two nations on Thursday outlining the conditions for the repatriation process. They plan to initiate the return of the Rohingya within two months to alleviate the strain on the refugee camps that have expanded rapidly in the Cox's Bazar region of Bangladesh. However, human rights advocates have raised concerns about Myanmar, also referred to as Burma, fulfilling its commitments under the agreement, with some calling for independent oversight. "The notion that Burma will now embrace them back into their charred villages is absurd," remarked Bill Frelick, the refugee rights director at Human Rights Watch. "Rather than participating in a public relations facade, the international community must assert that no returns will occur without international monitors to guarantee safety, a cessation of the notion of confining returnees in camps, the restoration of land, and the reconstruction of destroyed homes and communities." Over 600,000 Rohingya sought refuge in Bangladesh after the military in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar initiated a severe counterinsurgency in northern Rakhine State following assaults by Rohingya militants on an army base and police stations on August 25. The United Nations and the United States have characterized the military's actions as ethnic cleansing, and rights organizations have accused the security forces of committing atrocities, including mass rape, arson, and murder. Nevertheless, China has supported Myanmar during this crisis and has obstructed a more robust international response. On Friday, Chinese President Xi Jinping addressed the matter in Beijing with Myanmar's military chief, Min Aung Hlaing. Although Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's civilian leader, has stated that the repatriation of the largely stateless Muslim minority would be contingent on residency and would be "safe and voluntary," there are worries that the country's autonomous military might hinder the process. The memorandum of understanding signed between Myanmar and Bangladesh on Thursday indicated that a joint working group would be formed within three weeks to prepare for the return of the refugees. However, it provided minimal details regarding the criteria for return and the potential involvement of the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR. The agency expressed concerns that the conditions in northern Rakhine are not conducive to the safe and sustainable return of Rohingya, with some refugees still fleeing Myanmar, as stated by spokesman Adrian Edwards to reporters. "It is crucial that international standards are upheld, and we are prepared to assist," he noted, adding that the UNHCR has yet to review the repatriation agreement signed by both nations. "It is vital that individuals do not end up being forced back into confinement and ghettos." Human rights monitors pointed out that other significant issues not covered in the separate announcements from the two governments included the safeguarding of Rohingya from further violence, pathways to address their legal status, and whether they would have the opportunity to return to their previous homes. A spokesperson for Suu Kyi was not immediately reachable for comments on Friday and had previously declined to address these concerns when approached by Reuters late on Thursday. Charmain Mohamed, the director for refugee and migrant rights at Amnesty International, stated that the United Nations and the international community "have been entirely marginalized," and asserted that discussion of returns was "premature" while the influx of Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh continues. text: BAGHDAD (Reuters) - On Thursday, Iraqi forces declared that they had seized the Islamic State's final stronghold in northern Iraq, forcing the militant organization into a position near the Syrian border as its self-proclaimed caliphate continues to diminish. The offensive led to the capture of the town of Hawija and its surrounding regions by U.S.-backed Iraqi government troops along with Iranian-supported Shi'ite paramilitary groups known as Popular Mobilisation. Some clashes occurred to the north and east of Hawija where the militants were encircled. Following the fall of Hawija, which is located close to the Kurdish-controlled oil city of Kirkuk, the only territory still held by Islamic State in Iraq is a corridor along the western border with Syria, where the group is also facing setbacks. The recapture of Hawija is seen as a significant victory for the Iraqi government, which is concurrently grappling with a different crisis in the northern part of the country, where the Kurdish minority recently voted overwhelmingly in favor of independence for their autonomous region. In Hawija, state television broadcast images of Iraqi forces hoisting flags in one of the town squares while Humvees patrolled deserted streets strewn with car wreckage, buildings pockmarked with bullets, and shattered shop fronts. (Graphics on 'Iraqi Kurds' independence push' - here) A statement from the joint operations commander, Lieutenant-General Abdul Ameer Rasheed Yarallah, stated, "The army’s 9th armored division, the Federal Police, the Emergency Response division and Popular Mobilisation liberated Hawija." Thick plumes of black smoke billowed from areas surrounding Hawija due to oil wells ignited by the militants to evade aerial detection. The capture of Hawija brings Iraqi forces into direct interaction with Kurdish Peshmerga fighters who oversee Kirkuk, a multi-ethnic area claimed by both Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG). Kirkuk became a potential flashpoint last month when the KRG included the city in its referendum concerning Kurdish independence in northern Iraq. "We don’t desire any aggression or confrontations, but federal authority must be established in the disputed regions," Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi stated during a press briefing in Paris alongside French President Emmanuel Macron. Macron expressed willingness to mediate between the Iraqi government and Kurdish regional authorities, vowing to maintain a military presence in the area until Islamic State was fully defeated. In response to the independence vote, the Iraqi government imposed sanctions; however, Abadi acknowledged the Kurds' aspirations, provided they were articulated in alignment with the constitution. The referendum's outcome has sparked concerns both domestically and internationally regarding the potential for ethnic conflict in Iraq, which could undermine the fight against Islamic State. Turkey, currently engaged in a decades-long battle against its own Kurdish militants, has taken the lead in opposing the Iraqi Kurds' aspirations for independence. Intensifying his rhetoric on the matter, President Tayyip Erdogan stated that Turkey would soon close its border with northern Iraq and restrict its airspace following the referendum. He further noted that Turkey, Iran, and Iraq would collectively decide to halt the flow of oil from northern Iraq, a crucial source of revenue for Iraqi Kurdistan. On Wednesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose nation has significant energy interests in Kurdistan, remarked that it would not benefit anyone to cut off oil supplies from the region. Nonetheless, Erdogan asserted that if a decision is reached regarding the cessation of oil exports in the area, it will be made by Turkey. Together, Turkey, Iran, and the Iraqi central government will execute this decision. Erdogan's position has received support from Iran. Following discussions with Erdogan in Tehran on Wednesday, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei stated that Iran and Turkey should work together to prevent the Iraqi Kurds from declaring independence. Relations have been strained between Shi'ite Iran and predominantly Sunni Turkey, yet both nations share concerns regarding the independence vote.

text: On Tuesday, Israel's Supreme Court annulled a law that allowed Jewish religious seminary students to be exempt from military service, inciting anger among ultra-Orthodox lawmakers who may threaten the stability of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition. A group of nine justices determined that certain provisions of the conscription law granting exemptions to seminary students were both unreasonable and unconstitutional, and mandated that the government address the issue within a year. For many years, the exemption for seminary students on religious grounds has generated tension within Israeli society, where the majority of Jewish individuals are summoned for military duty at the age of 18. The ultra-Orthodox community argues that their Torah studies are essential for the ongoing survival of the Jewish nation and are concerned that young men in the military might interact with women and less religious segments of society. Nevertheless, several hundred ultra-Orthodox men have enlisted in specialized units that accommodate their religious requirements. In 2014, legislation was introduced to replace previous arrangements that had lapsed, driven by Yair Lapid's secular, centrist Yesh Atid party, which advocated for a fair distribution of national responsibilities. This law provoked outrage among ultra-Orthodox parties, which re-entered Netanyahu's government in 2015 after Lapid's party moved to the opposition, resulting in a dilution of the legislation. The Supreme Court's decision saw eight of the nine justices agree that the law ought to be repealed, with Supreme Court President Miriam Naor stating that the latest compromise made to satisfy ultra-Orthodox parties significantly undermines equality and infringes upon the constitutional right to human dignity. Since Israel's establishment in 1948, ultra-Orthodox politicians have actively opposed the conscription of individuals from their community, who constitute approximately 10 percent of Israel's 9 million populace. Netanyahu's administration, which holds 67 out of 120 seats in the Knesset, includes ultra-Orthodox parties, yet two other significant factions are resistant to any further leniency regarding conscription laws. Aryeh Deri, the leader of the ultra-Orthodox Shas party and Israel's Interior Minister, reacted to the ruling by asserting that the justices were entirely disconnected from our heritage and traditions and from the populace. He urged seminary students to persist with their biblical studies, stating: 'Do not lose hope, continue to engage in Torah study; we will remain steadfast and do everything to rectify this situation.' Lapid, who has been identified in opinion polls as a potential contender to Netanyahu in forthcoming elections, held a press conference to commend the court's ruling, claiming it had issued a judgment that would ensure equality across communities. 'This is why we entered politics. Conscription for all, work for all. Benjamin Netanyahu can no longer evade accountability. Military service is a requirement for everyone, not just for those who lack a party in his coalition,' Lapid remarked.

text: Experts indicate that U.S. President Donald Trump’s tax reduction proposal will spur growth, but it will not be sufficient to compensate for the trillions of dollars in revenue losses, and the increasing deficits might even negate some of the economic benefits. This assessment was made on Wednesday. The fundamental tenets of the proposal, which was introduced on Wednesday, are heavily dependent on a method known as "dynamic scoring," which is a budget analysis approach that presumes tax reductions will enhance economic activity, thereby resulting in increased revenues. These assumptions have been central to Republican tax philosophy since Ronald Reagan employed them to rationalize significant tax reductions in 1981, which were criticized at that time as "voodoo economics." On Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin stated that Trump’s proposal would "pay for itself with growth" and the elimination of certain deductions and credits. According to the information available thus far, Maya MacGuineas, the president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB), mentioned that the plan could contribute an additional $3 trillion to over $5 trillion to the federal deficit over the next five years. "No credible dynamic score is going to demonstrate that this bill is funded," MacGuineas stated. "The growth impacts, which are genuine and significant, add only decimal points to growth, not whole percentage points." Her organization estimates that in order to finance the proposal, the U.S. would need to maintain a growth rate of 4.5 percent annually, a level that has not been sustained since the late 1960s and early 1970s. Mnuchin has expressed his expectation that the proposal will elevate sustained U.S. growth above 3 percent, but CRFB’s projections suggest that even achieving this rate would necessitate substantial increases in productivity, and that a rapidly retiring baby-boom generation poses challenges to attaining high growth rates. Doug Elmendorf, the former director of the Congressional Budget Office, which provides cost estimates for legislation, remarked that he perceives minimal likelihood of Congress identifying "politically acceptable" offsets to fund the proposal, and the escalation in borrowing could hinder Trump’s objectives. "The resulting rise in the deficit will dampen economic activity, counteracting at least some of the stimulative effects of reduced tax rates," Elmendorf noted, who is currently the dean of Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government. The elevated federal debt burden will "crowd out" private capital, inhibiting long-term economic activity, Elmendorf added. Congressional Republicans aim to leverage budget procedural rules that permit a 51-vote threshold in the Senate to enact tax reform, which would restrict the tax cuts to a duration of 10 years. However, if the proposal leads to deficits in the years following the first decade, it could also encounter another procedural stipulation that may necessitate 60 votes in the Senate. Tax reductions that lapse after a decade could trigger another fiscal crisis in the U.S., similar to the situation in 2012 when tax cuts established under George W. Bush expired. "What the Trump Administration has suggested is not enduring tax reform, but a decade-long tax reduction and the establishment of an unprecedented fiscal cliff in 2028," remarked Chris Krueger, a political analyst at Cowen and Co in Washington, in a communication to clients.

text: OSLO (Reuters) - Supporters assert that the threatened withdrawal of the U.S. from a 2015 global agreement aimed at combating climate change could potentially have beneficial effects, marking a shift from previous pessimism regarding the future of a deal that took two decades to finalize. The Paris Agreement necessitates a consensus for all decisions, indicating that the exit of a non-compliant United States would facilitate emitters like China and the European Union in shaping the specifics of a trillion-dollar transition away from fossil fuels. President Trump has labeled human-induced climate change a hoax and has made a campaign promise, which he has yet to fulfill, to "cancel" the agreement, expressing his desire to support the domestic fossil fuel sector. In an effort to reverse environmental regulations established during Barack Obama’s presidency, Trump plans to sign an executive order on Tuesday designed to simplify energy production for companies in the United States. Christiana Figueres, a key figure in the crafting of the agreement and former U.N. climate chief in Paris, remarked, "There will be some advantages for other countries and there will also be extraordinary disadvantages," if the U.S. ultimately withdraws from Paris. "It’s not a black and white scenario," she noted. Figueres expressed that the most favorable scenario for both the United States and other countries would involve Washington remaining committed to the agreement and significantly reducing greenhouse gas emissions. She also mentioned that the investment outlook for renewable energy sources like solar power is more promising than that for coal. Concerns have long existed that the departure of the world’s leading economy could diminish other nations’ motivation to reduce greenhouse gas emissions under an agreement endorsed by a wide range of countries, including China, Saudi Arabia, and various African nations. However, a competing perspective is emerging that suggests the Paris Agreement might actually benefit from the U.S. withdrawal. Johan Rockstrom, director of the Stockholm Resilience Center at Stockholm University, stated, "The Achilles heel of the Paris Agreement is that it’s built on consensus." He added, "It’s very difficult to have a negative giant in the room" capable of blocking all decisions, and he has recently shifted his opinion to consider that a U.S. exit could prove more advantageous than his earlier view that it would represent a "big failure." The Paris Agreement imposes few binding commitments, allowing all nations to establish their own climate change objectives without facing penalties for non-compliance. Governments have set a deadline of 2018 to finalize a rule book for the Paris Agreement, detailing how countries will report and monitor their emission reductions. Thoriq Ibrahim, the Environment Minister of the Maldives and chair of the Alliance of Small Island States, which fears the impacts of rising sea levels, called for ongoing U.S. involvement in Paris. He stated, "The closer you look at it, the clearer it becomes that it (the Paris Agreement) also promotes important strategic, economic, and security benefits as well." Norwegian Prime Minister Erna Solberg also expressed that it would be preferable for the United States to remain part of the agreement, though she remarked, "But I don’t think that it’s the end of the Paris Agreement if the United States decides to leave." Oliver Geden from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs disagreed, asserting that a U.S. withdrawal would severely weaken the Paris Agreement and render any decisions largely insignificant without the world’s largest economy. He predicted, "The momentum could fade away pretty soon." Nevertheless, nearly 200 nations concurred after Trump’s election in November that there is an "urgent duty" to address an "alarming and unprecedented" rate of global warming. Stephanie Pfeifer, the head of the Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change, which manages 18 trillion euros ($20 trillion) in assets, commented, "The pace and scale of change already underway in the global economy is remarkable and irreversible." She noted, "Renewables have already overtaken coal as a global power source, electric vehicles are the growth segment."

text: Factbox: Contents of the Senate's 'skinny repeal' healthcare legislation. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Thursday evening, Senate Republicans unveiled their 'skinny bill' aimed at rolling back certain aspects of Obamacare, just hours prior to a scheduled vote on the proposal. Numerous Republican lawmakers expressed reluctance to see the eight-page bill enacted, delaying their support until they received commitments from House Speaker Paul Ryan that both chambers could establish a special committee to draft new legislation. Senate Republican leaders indicated that the bill serves as a means to uphold the seven-year commitment to repeal and replace Obamacare, which was also a significant campaign pledge from President Donald Trump. Earlier in the week, the Senate was unable to pass two significant pieces of legislation intended to repeal or substitute the healthcare law after dedicating months to both efforts. The Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, provided insurance coverage to 20 million Americans who were previously uninsured and is regarded as the hallmark domestic accomplishment of former Democratic President Barack Obama. Republicans argue that the law is excessively expensive and constitutes inappropriate government intrusion into healthcare. Here’s an overview of what the 'skinny' repeal bill, officially named the Health Care Freedom Act, entails: The bill abolishes the Obamacare penalty for individuals who do not obtain health insurance. Additionally, it eliminates a penalty, for a duration of eight years, on employers with over 50 employees who fail to offer health insurance. The legislation also nullifies a 2.3 percent excise tax on the sale of medical devices, effective until December 31, 2020. Should it be enacted, this repeal would be positively received by manufacturers like Medtronic Inc and Abbott Laboratories Inc. The Senate bill effectively cuts funding to Planned Parenthood for one year by disallowing Medicaid, the government health insurance program catering to the poor and disabled, from reimbursing the women's healthcare provider, the majority of whose patients rely on Medicaid. In contrast to earlier efforts to devise legislation for repealing or replacing Obamacare, the skinny bill does not terminate the law's Medicaid expansion or alter the federal health program.
