text: Boris Johnson provides PM May with counsel on Brexit while showcasing loyalty. MANCHESTER, England (Reuters) - British Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson publicly gave Theresa May unsolicited advice on achieving a successful Brexit on Tuesday, subtly probing the limits of the prime minister's diminished authority while affirming his loyalty. Along with his public displays of support for May, he utilized media interviews and articles prior to the Conservative Party Conference in Manchester to present his vision for an ambitious Brexit. After commending May for securing a snap election in June, which resulted in her party losing its parliamentary majority, Johnson, in his principal address, asserted that her senior ministers were collectively united behind "every syllable" of her Brexit strategy articulated last month in Florence. "The entire nation owes her a debt for her determination in leading Britain forward, as she will, towards a commendable Brexit agreement, grounded in that Florence speech, of which I assure you, the entire cabinet stands united behind every syllable," Johnson stated. However, just hours later, the individual who spearheaded the primary leave campaign during the 2016 referendum concerning Britain's EU membership told supporters at a different event that there was excessive negativity surrounding Brexit. He then elaborated on his perspective regarding how the UK’s departure should be structured, suggesting that Britain may require distinct regulations on various matters, including data and bioscience. "I campaigned with the slogan... Take Back Control... I believe that the prime minister shares this belief very strongly," Johnson conveyed to the audience. "If you’re going to pursue this, do it effectively. Do it in a manner that secures a favorable outcome for the UK," he added. "We desire an agreement that ensures we are not merely trapped in a rigid rotational orbit around the EU." Johnson, who is commonly seen in Britain as harboring intense political ambitions beneath a humorous facade, has cast a shadow over the party conference that May intended to utilize to regain some authority after her electoral miscalculation. Arriving with his signature tousled blonde hair and searching through a suit jacket pocket, Boris energized Conservative members but was cautious to refrain from making any direct appeal to succeed May. Prior to Johnson's address, May had consistently faced inquiries from journalists regarding whether she would dismiss Johnson after he seemed to undermine her Brexit strategy by articulating his own vision. She has evaded these questions. The European Parliament heavily criticized the British government's approach to Brexit negotiations on Tuesday, voting against the commencement of discussions regarding future trade and denouncing chaos within May’s team. A German ally of conservative Chancellor Angela Merkel, Manfred Weber, stated that infighting within the British cabinet jeopardized a deal and urged May to remove Johnson. Nevertheless, Johnson also injected a rare burst of energy into Manchester where Conservative ministers lined up to portray the opposition Labour Party as perilous Marxists while failing to propose any notable new policies. "To me, that exemplified true leadership: motivating, inspirational. What defines a good leader? It’s someone who can achieve that," remarked Vanessa Churchman, a local government official from the Isle of Wight in southern England. "Everyone departing from here will feel inspired." At prior party conferences, Boris, as he is affectionately called in Britain, also consistently overshadowed then-prime minister David Cameron, although after the referendum ended Cameron’s career, Johnson withdrew from the leadership contest when a colleague broke a pact to support him. While Johnson enjoys popularity among party members, numerous Conservative lawmakers are frustrated that he has eclipsed May with what they characterize as unhelpful and disloyal remarks. May, the reserved daughter of a vicar, possesses a presentation style that contrasts sharply with Johnson’s flamboyant on-stage persona. She is set to conclude the conference on Wednesday.

text: Holocaust survivors inspire with a song of hope at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate. BERLIN (Reuters) - On Wednesday, two elderly Holocaust survivors collaborated with a younger Israeli performer to deliver songs of hope at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate, coinciding with a troubling rise in anti-Semitism in Germany. Saul Dreier, a 92-year-old drummer, and Reuwen 'Ruby' Sosnowicz, an 89-year-old accordion player, accompanied Gad Elbaz at a location that once served as a platform for Adolf Hitler's anti-Semitic addresses. 'I don’t want to cry. If I can be 92 and be here after what I endured - there are no words,' Dreier expressed to Reuters at the conclusion of a long and emotional day. 'This is a miracle. I lost 30 people in my family,' he shared with an audience of approximately 80 attendees before the performance. Dreier mentioned that recent reports of neo-Nazi demonstrations in the United States and Germany made him feel ill and triggered memories of the atrocities committed by the Nazi regime, which claimed the lives of 6 million Jews. 'It’s very frightening. Young people must ensure that it never happens again.' Both men, who reside in Florida, established their 'Holocaust Survivors Band' in 2014 and have since performed for enthusiastic crowds in cities ranging from Warsaw and Las Vegas to Washington, D.C. Elbaz remarked that the event in Berlin aimed to encourage younger generations to remain alert to the threats posed by anti-Semitism. 'This is about reviving history and illustrating to our generation the importance of remembering where we came from, what we have endured, and ensuring it never occurs again,' he stated. Organizers intend to produce a music video featuring footage from the performance of one of the pieces, 'Let the Light Shine On.' Shani Ramer, 48, who was born in Israel but was raised and currently resides in Berlin, expressed that the concert brought back memories of her relatives who were lost. 'It touched my heart,' she noted, appreciating the concert's hopeful message. 'It conveys that we are still here. No one will kill us now.' Abida Ali, a Muslim tourist from Pakistan visiting Germany, participated in the lively atmosphere, dancing alongside other onlookers to the cheerful music. Ali remarked that she had not faced any discrimination during her stay, despite wearing a headscarf. 'It's just a small fraction of people who are violent,' she commented. 'There is hope. Everyone truly desires peace.' A survey conducted by Bielefeld University last year revealed that 78 percent of Jews living in Germany feel that anti-Semitism has increased, either somewhat or significantly, over the past five years.

text: New York City’s budget chief is cautioning the state: We are not a 'piggy bank.' NEW YORK (Reuters) - The fiscal overseer of New York City has indicated that the city is likely to experience significantly larger budget shortfalls in the upcoming years than what the mayor has anticipated, advising state lawmakers against viewing the city as a mere "piggy bank." As both the state and the city finalize their budgets, forthcoming decisions will impact New York City. "Some legislators from upstate simply don’t understand," stated New York City Comptroller Scott Stringer during his evaluation of the city budget on Wednesday. "They perceive New York City as their piggy bank." Stringer expressed concern regarding rushed, late-night budget decisions that may strip the city of essential resources. His remarks signal a rising irritation with state legislators who imply that the city is financially robust due to a more vigorous economic recovery compared to other areas of the state. New York State Governor Andrew Cuomo has had a strained relationship with New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio, convincing his fellow Democrat the previous year to contribute $2.5 billion to the city’s public transit system, which is managed by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, a state entity. There have also been proposals in the state capital suggesting that the city should take on a greater share of healthcare expenses and contribute more towards the city's university system. New York State lawmakers are known for their "vampire" budget sessions that extend into the early morning hours to meet the budget deadline at the beginning of the state’s fiscal year on April 1. Stringer noted that while next year's budget remains balanced, the total projected deficits for fiscal year 2020 are $1 billion greater than the estimates provided by the mayor’s office. "Budget monitors and rating agencies have all commended this administration’s financial responsibility and emphasis on safeguarding against economic uncertainty – and investors concur," commented Amy Spitalnick, a spokesperson for de Blasio. The mayor’s office highlights that Stringer anticipates an additional $900 million in tax revenue for this financial year and the following one, using this as evidence of the city’s prudent revenue estimates. Stringer argued that the mayor should not have factored in $731 million from taxi medallion sales through 2020, asserting that the taxi industry is currently in turmoil. The city has already lowered its expectations for income from taxi medallion transactions, but Stringer has been more assertive in eliminating it from future years. He also mentioned that certain taxes may be lower than the mayor's predictions and that expenses related to overtime, healthcare, and homeless shelters could be higher.

text: President Barack Obama nominated Merrick Garland to the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday, opting for a moderate judge in hopes of winning over resistant Senate Republicans, who quickly dismissed the Democratic president's choice. A fierce political battle is on the horizon regarding this nomination, which is likely to play a significant role in the already heated campaign for the U.S. presidential election on November 8. The leaders of the Republican-controlled Senate have pledged not to conduct confirmation hearings or a vote for any nominee put forth by Obama. Garland, aged 63, has been chosen to succeed the long-serving conservative Justice Antonin Scalia, who passed away on February 13. A fellow Chicagoan, Garland is the chief judge of the prominent U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and has previously garnered praise from both sides of the aisle as a former prosecutor. In a bid to advocate for Garland's Senate confirmation, the administration is sending him to Capitol Hill on Thursday for discussions with Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont, the senior Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, and then with Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid from Nevada. These meetings are designed to bolster Senate support for Garland and attract media attention. Securing a lifetime appointment to the Supreme Court necessitates Senate confirmation. The announcement made by Obama triggered a wave of responses from various organizations that will either support or oppose the nomination. The UAW, which represents workers in the automotive, aerospace, and some agricultural sectors, described Garland as "a distinguished, moderate judge with more federal judicial experience than any other Supreme Court nominee in history." Chris Cox, the Executive Director of the National Rifle Association, stated, "A basic analysis of Merrick Garland’s judicial record shows that he does not respect our fundamental, individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense." Republicans, anticipating a member of their party will win the presidential election, are insisting that Obama keep the seat vacant and allow the incoming president, who will take office next January, to make the appointment. Billionaire businessman Donald Trump is currently leading the Republican candidates for the nomination, while Obama’s former secretary of state, Hillary Clinton, is the leading contender for the Democrats. Obama urged Republican senators to provide Garland with a fair hearing, asserting that not doing so would not only represent a failure of the Senate's constitutional responsibility but would also indicate a broken process for nominating and confirming judges. He warned that such actions would damage the Supreme Court's reputation and erode trust in the American legal system. "Our democracy will ultimately suffer as well," Obama remarked while introducing Garland during a ceremony in the White House Rose Garden. The passing of Scalia resulted in the nine-member Supreme Court being evenly divided between four liberal and four conservative justices. Obama's nominee has the potential to shift the court toward the left for the first time in decades, potentially influencing decisions on contentious matters such as abortion, gun rights, capital punishment, and political financing. Obama emphasized that the Supreme Court should transcend political disputes and maintain that independence. He noted that given the extreme polarization of U.S. politics, "this is precisely the time when we should play it straight, and treat the process of appointing a Supreme Court justice with the seriousness and care it deserves." Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell from Kentucky quickly reaffirmed that the Senate would not entertain the president's nomination. A spokesperson for McConnell indicated that the senator had communicated with Garland via phone and would not engage in a "perfunctory meeting" with him. John Cornyn, the second-highest-ranking Senate Republican from Texas, added, "This person will not be confirmed, so there’s no reason to go through some motions and pretend that it will happen, because it’s not going to happen."

text: The tax oversight panel in the U.S. House of Representatives is set to conduct public hearings in the upcoming weeks as it prepares to introduce legislation aimed at overhauling the U.S. tax code, according to congressional aides on Wednesday. The decision to hold hearings was made during a meeting that lasted an hour between House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Kevin Brady and 15 Democratic members of the panel, as reported by a House Democratic aide. There were no specifics provided regarding the timing of the hearings, which tax reform topics would be covered, or whether the entire Ways and Means Committee would take part. "We had a positive and open discussion, and I appreciated the opportunity to engage in a two-way dialogue," stated Brady, a Republican from Texas, after the meeting. The committee, led by Republicans, is anticipated to present tax reform legislation this spring in preparation for a vote on the House floor during the summer. Staff members of the committee have been working on drafting a bill based on a House Republican framework that aims to significantly reduce taxes for both businesses and individuals. On Wednesday, House Speaker Paul Ryan indicated that the House, Senate, and White House, all under Republican control, "aren’t on the same page yet on tax reform." Earlier this week, Brady announced the bipartisan gathering, mentioning that the focus would be on simplifying the U.S. tax code for individuals and preventing U.S. corporations from relocating production and research operations abroad, which are two key Republican goals. "It was clear from this meeting we share the same fundamental goals on tax reform, particularly regarding growth and simplicity," a Republican committee aide noted. Brady emphasized his aim to incorporate a border adjustment tax provision into the tax reform legislation, according to aides. This policy, proposing a 20 percent tax on imports, has led to divisions within the business sector and has faced criticism from Republicans in both the House and Senate. The meeting on Wednesday was the first occasion that Brady met with the Democratic members of the committee to discuss the House Republican tax reform initiative, aides reported. However, the bipartisan spirit was disrupted by the distribution of a letter from committee Republicans to President Donald Trump, urging the dismissal of John Koskinen as commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service. Koskinen was appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama. "Democrats raised this letter with Republicans during the meeting, pointing out how this kind of partisan action undermines the potential for bipartisanship on other issues, such as collaborating on tax reform," the Democratic aide stated.

text: Three fatalities occurred as Storm Ophelia struck Ireland. LAHINCH, Ireland (Reuters) - On Monday, Tropical Storm Ophelia impacted the southern coastline of Ireland, resulting in three deaths, uprooting trees and power lines, and generating waves reaching 10 meters (30 feet) in height. According to Ireland's Electricity Supply Board, over 360,000 homes and businesses were left without power, with an additional 100,000 outages anticipated by nightfall, marking this as an extraordinary event that would affect all regions of the country for several days. Approximately 170 flights were canceled from the two primary airports in Ireland, Dublin and Shannon. Two individuals tragically lost their lives in different incidents when trees fell onto their vehicles: a woman in her 50s in the southeast and a man on the east coast. A third victim, a man in his 30s, died while attempting to remove a downed tree using a chainsaw. The storm, which was downgraded from hurricane status overnight, is being regarded as the most severe to strike Ireland in fifty years. The Irish National Meteorological Service reported that it made landfall after 10:40 a.m. (0940 GMT), with wind speeds reaching up to 190 kph (110 mph) at the southernmost point of the nation. Coastal flooding was expected. "This storm remains very active and there are still extremely hazardous conditions in various areas of the country. Do not be misled into thinking it has subsided," cautioned Sean Hogan, chairman of Ireland's National Emergency Coordination Group, during an announcement on national broadcaster RTE. The military was deployed to reinforce flood defenses, public transportation services were suspended, and schools throughout Ireland and Northern Ireland were set to remain closed for a second consecutive day on Tuesday. Hogan indicated that hundreds of roads were obstructed by fallen trees. Social media images captured roofs being torn from buildings, including at the Cork City soccer club’s Turner’s Cross stadium, where a stand's roof had collapsed. Prime Minister Leo Varadkar urged the public to remain indoors. The transport minister stated that driving was unsafe. The storm winds were predicted to peak between 1600 GMT and 1800 GMT in Dublin and Galway, two of Ireland's most populated cities, and later in the northern regions on the same day. The meteorological service in Britain issued an Amber Weather Warning for Northern Ireland from 1400-2100 GMT, indicating that the storm posed a risk to life and was likely to lead to transport disruptions, power outages, and loose debris. It was expected to shift towards western Scotland overnight, with significant weather anticipated in other western and northern areas of the United Kingdom. British media have drawn comparisons between Ophelia and the Great Storm of 1987, which brought hurricane-force winds to parts of the United Kingdom exactly 30 years prior. The Irish government indicated that this storm might be the most severe since Hurricane Debbie, which resulted in 11 fatalities in Ireland in 1961. It passed near a golf course in western Ireland owned by U.S. President Donald Trump, who has been considering a wall to safeguard its greens from coastal erosion. Climatologists noted that similar storms in the past have altered the shape of sections of the Irish coastline.

text: HOUSTON (Reuters) - On Monday, a shareholder resolution was submitted by an activist investor in Chevron Corp that demands the oil company assess the practicality of ceasing its operations in Myanmar. This follows a significant crackdown on the minority Rohingya Muslims, which the United States has characterized as ethnic cleansing. The resolution was presented last week by Azzad Asset Management, an Islamic finance firm, and urges Chevron's board to evaluate how it might mitigate risks associated with collaborating with governments involved in genocide or crimes against humanity. A similar resolution was introduced at the previous Chevron shareholder meeting, receiving backing from 6 percent of those who voted. Since the end of August, over 600,000 Rohingya Muslims have fled to southern Bangladesh as a result of a military campaign by Myanmar security forces responding to militant attacks in Rakhine State. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and officials from the United Nations have condemned the crackdown as a genocidal act. Myanmar has rejected allegations of committing atrocities against the Rohingya. Chevron, which ranks as the second-largest oil producer in the U.S., operates in Myanmar through its subsidiary, Unocal Myanmar Offshore Co Ltd. The company is involved in projects that include a minority stake in natural gas production and a pipeline, as detailed on its website. On Monday, Chevron spokeswoman Melissa Ritchie stated to Reuters that the company values the ongoing discussions with shareholders regarding this crucial issue of violence in Rakhine State, Myanmar. She added that they will continue collaborating with other U.S. firms and the government to advocate for the importance of U.S. investment in Myanmar and the necessity to cultivate a business atmosphere that honors human rights. Chevron has the choice to either accept the proposal or request the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to permit it to block the resolution. Should Chevron decide to block it, Azzad would then have the opportunity to appeal to the SEC. The annual meeting of Chevron is scheduled for the upcoming spring. This resolution comes in the wake of the arrest of two Reuters journalists by Myanmar authorities last week. text: Hillary Clinton, the Democratic candidate for president, has urged the pharmaceutical firm Mylan NV to voluntarily reduce the price of its EpiPen, a medication for severe allergies, which has surged in cost by over 400 percent in the last ten years. "That’s outrageous - and it’s just the latest troubling example of a company taking advantage of its consumers," Clinton stated. "It’s wrong when drug companies prioritize profits over patients, increasing prices without providing justification for their value." Throughout the primary, Clinton often asserted her commitment to combating pharmaceutical companies, as part of her effort to address critiques regarding her close connections to the insurance sector. She has unveiled a plan that she claims will reduce drug expenses for consumers. Mylan spokesperson Nina Devlin did not respond to questions regarding Clinton’s remarks about the company. Mylan purchased the EpiPen in 2007, and the price escalated from $100 in 2008 to its current price of $600. Mylan's stock fell by more than 5 percent to $43.15 on the Nasdaq. "The price of EpiPen is outrageous," remarked Robert Weissman, president of the advocacy group Public Citizen. "Mylan is endangering lives and exploiting the nation." Weissman argued that the U.S. price of EpiPen should be significantly reduced, indicating that it can be found for as low as $112 in Canada. He also noted that many other pharmaceutical manufacturers routinely increase prices of their prescription medications by 10 percent or more annually, calling for U.S. legislation to curb such "price spikes." The White House adopted a more measured approach in addressing rising drug prices, opting not to comment on an individual company's decisions. "I will note, however, that pharmaceutical companies that frequently attempt to present themselves as the creators of life-saving drugs often damage their reputation significantly by being greedy and raising prices in a manner that victimizes consumers," White House spokesman Josh Earnest stated during a news briefing. Clinton is joining a bipartisan coalition of legislators advocating for investigations into the price hikes of EpiPens, which are prefilled injections of epinephrine (adrenaline) used during severe allergic reactions that, if untreated, could lead to death. Republican Senator Chuck Grassley, who chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee, reached out to Mylan earlier this week for an explanation regarding the price increase. Senator Amy Klobuchar, the leading Democrat on the committee’s antitrust subcommittee, requested an investigation by the Federal Trade Commission. On Wednesday, Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democratic Senator Claire McCaskill asked Mylan to provide a briefing for the Senate to clarify the price changes. Grassley and Klobuchar, along with Democratic Senators Patrick Leahy and Richard Blumenthal and Republican Senator Ron Johnson, wrote to the Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday to inquire about its approval process for alternatives to the EpiPen. "Given the significance of this issue, it is essential to comprehend the FDA’s role in relation to EpiPens and its approval of generic versions that might promote competition and lower prices if introduced," the senators stated. "We have reached out to every member of Congress who has sent us a letter, and we look forward to meeting with them and addressing their inquiries as soon as possible," Devlin said. In January, Clinton criticized Valeant Pharmaceuticals International Inc for raising the price of a heart medication. Following a blog post from Clinton’s campaign targeting Valeant, the company's stock price dropped. In March, she released a campaign advertisement promising to focus on the company specifically. Clinton also condemned Turing Pharmaceuticals in the fall of 2015 after public outrage increased when it decided to raise the price of an antiviral drug commonly used by AIDS patients and pregnant women.

text: It's entirely his doing: Italy's left fixated on Renzi, not adversaries. ROME (Reuters) - With national elections approaching, the left in Italy appears determined to orchestrate its own downfall as Democratic Party (PD) leader Matteo Renzi faces criticism from prospective allies. The PD suffered a significant setback in a recent Sicilian regional election, finishing a distant third behind a center-right coalition and the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement in a race seen by many as a precursor to a national election expected by May. Despite a weekend poll indicating a decline of six percentage points for the PD over the last six months, it remains embroiled in a tight contest against 5-Star and a center-right coalition that features four-time Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia (Go Italy!). The economy is currently expanding at its fastest rate in seven years and the number of migrant arrivals has significantly decreased, two circumstances that the ruling PD hopes will attract moderate and progressive voters who would never align with Berlusconi and are cautious of the untested 5-Star. However, a faction of left-wing lawmakers who broke away from the PD earlier this year blame Renzi for steering the party too far right and turning it into his own personal domain; thus far, they have declined to reconcile. Former Prime Minister Massimo D'Alema, who spearheaded the notable split, seizes every opportunity to criticize Renzi. Pietro Grasso, the President of the Senate and a former anti-mafia magistrate who left the PD unexpectedly last month, remarked that 'the PD doesn’t exist anymore.' The PD and its possible allies could remain significant players post-election if they can unite in targeting their opponents instead of Renzi during the limited time remaining before the vote. The 42-year-old Florentine, known for his quick speech, has not made things easier for himself. Just last month, he had a confrontation with the most favored member of his own party - Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni. Just days prior to the expiration of Bank of Italy Governor Ignazio Visco's term, Renzi unexpectedly blindsided Gentiloni with a parliamentary motion suggesting that the premier not renew the central banker’s six-year mandate. The PD accused Visco of inadequately addressing banking crises that cost taxpayers as much as 23 billion euros ($26.8 billion) this year in rescue operations for failing banks. To mitigate a conflict with President Sergio Mattarella, who officially appoints Bank of Italy leaders and supported Visco, Gentiloni disregarded Renzi's request. The Visco situation has created a division within the party, according to a PD lawmaker from Sicily who preferred to remain anonymous. 'Two power structures are clashing, one external to the current Italian establishment and one internal. Renzi is positioned on the outside.' Using a soccer metaphor, a government source and PD member told Reuters that the Visco situation has shown Renzi to be increasingly unpredictable. 'Three years ago, Renzi was the Diego Maradona of Italian politics,' the source stated, 'but now he resembles Antonio Cassano, a temperamental Italian soccer star whose explosive demeanor created issues on the field. Like Maradona, he was somewhat difficult to manage, but that was acceptable because the team was winning,' the source continued. 'Now, however, he’s more akin to Cassano, whose erratic personality outweighed his skills and negatively impacted his team.' Under the new electoral framework, Renzi and other party leaders will personally select their candidates for the upcoming vote next year. While many within the PD are silent publicly, the dissenters who have separated from the party are openly expressing their views. 'The reunification of the center-left necessitates a shift in policy and leadership,' D'Alema stated last week. Laura Garavini, a PD lawmaker aligned with Renzi, informed Reuters that internal conflicts within the party continue. 'The expectation was that after the split, they would fade away, but they haven’t,' she remarked. Another point of contention on the left has been Renzi's pact with center-right opponents last month to enact a proportional electoral law that benefits pre-election coalitions, inciting anger from the PD splinter group that is unwilling to participate.

text: Clinton claims she depended on State staff for decisions regarding classification. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Hillary Clinton refuted a harsh evaluation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation that labeled her as "extremely careless" with classified governmental information, asserting on Friday that she relied on the judgment of her team at the U.S. State Department. After insisting for over a year that she did not send or receive classified information through her unauthorized private email account, she admitted in a series of interviews on Friday that she may have inadvertently done so, just three days after the FBI determined that this occurred at least 110 times. Clinton, the likely Democratic presidential nominee, stated she "certainly did not believe" she was managing classified information via her email account at the time, but stressed that she followed the guidance of her subordinates regarding whether information was classified. "I did not have a basis for second-guessing their conclusion," Clinton said in a CNN interview, expressing her "highest regard" for her former colleagues. "These are seasoned diplomats, they possess expertise in dealing with classified materials," she mentioned in a separate PBS Newshour interview. "They were not careless, and the materials they transmitted were not considered classified by them." Clinton, who held the position of the department’s highest authority on classification during her four-year leadership, did not address the FBI’s finding that she herself sent information on subjects deemed ‘top secret’, the most sensitive classification, through a private server located in her basement. "I have stated, and I reiterate, that it was a mistake to utilize personal email and I regret that," she remarked in another ABC interview. Mishandling classified information is illegal, and although FBI Director James Comey indicated on Tuesday there was evidence that Clinton or her aides might have violated these laws, he noted that there was insufficient evidence of criminal intent to warrant prosecution. In an atypical 15-minute statement detailing the FBI’s results, Comey ended up disappointing both Republican and Democratic factions. While Clinton’s Republican adversaries have expressed outrage at the decision not to pursue criminal charges, Clinton and her team have contested some of Comey’s criticisms that challenge her claim of possessing better judgment than Donald Trump, the presumptive Republican presidential candidate. Comey characterized her and her staff as "extremely careless" and stated that any "reasonable" government employee should have recognized that such information should not be shared in emails. He mentioned that her server was inadequately secured, leaving open the possibility that it may have been hacked by hostile nations. When asked if she concurred with being labeled as "extremely careless," Clinton responded to CNN that she did not agree, adding that Comey had "clarified" his statements. The nature of the clarification Clinton referred to was not clear. In more extensive remarks before lawmakers on Thursday, Comey again highlighted the carelessness and "real sloppiness" of Clinton and her staff, suggesting that she did not seem "particularly sophisticated with respect to classified information."

text: Cruz's triumph in Iowa may indicate a decline in Big Corn's sway. NEW YORK (Reuters) - The success of U.S. Republican presidential hopeful Ted Cruz on Monday in Iowa, a state abundant in corn production, might signify a significant setback for the nation's disputed biofuels initiative, highlighting its diminishing power over politicians, even within the agricultural core of the U.S. Cruz, a conservative senator hailing from Texas and a vocal critic of the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), managed to defeat billionaire Donald Trump in the Iowa caucuses, which are the initial contests in the series of state-by-state selections to determine party nominees for the election set for November 8. Cruz secured 28 percent of the votes, while Trump garnered 24 percent, marking a victory that included winning Kossuth County, the largest corn-producing county in the state. This outcome posed a challenge to corn farmers in the leading ethanol-producing state, who have been advocating vigorously to maintain the policy that has been in place for over a decade. The RFS mandates the inclusion of ethanol and other biofuels in the nation's fuel supply, aiming to lessen U.S. reliance on foreign oil, promote cleaner domestic energy sources, and enhance rural economies. Cruz has shifted his stance to favor a gradual elimination of renewable fuel requirements, rather than the immediate repeal he sought in 2013. Nevertheless, Cruz's Iowa victory, achieved without the endorsement of the ethanol and corn lobby, may lead to questions regarding the necessity for candidates to secure its support in the future, potentially undermining a significant foundation of backing for the lobby's objectives. "The dialogue within Congress will change immediately in the morning, as Republicans comprehend they can oppose the mandate and still achieve victory," remarked Michael McKenna, a Republican strategist and energy lobbyist, regarding a Cruz win. For some constituents, issues such as terrorism and healthcare outweigh the ethanol sector in the state. "The clear takeaway from Iowa is that any political leverage ethanol previously held in the state is now a thing of the past," stated George David Banks, Executive Vice President of the American Council for Capital Formation. The RFS has faced intensified scrutiny from oil companies, which argue that the volumes mandated by Congress are unrealistic. Environmental advocates also challenge the advantages of corn-based ethanol, which constitutes the majority of an 18-billion-gallon biofuels sector. Efforts to amend or abolish the program have not succeeded. A repeal amendment attached to a Senate energy bill under discussion this week is anticipated to be dismissed, should it be brought to a vote. Prior to the caucuses on Monday, certain equity traders had minimized the significance of the vote for U.S. ethanol producers, suggesting it was premature in the election timeline to impact individual stocks meaningfully. Shares of Green Plains Inc and Pacific Ethanol Inc dropped over 4 percent in light trading on Tuesday morning, trailing behind the broader stock market. BB&T reduced its price forecast for Green Plains on Tuesday. Further emphasizing the bleak outlook for ethanol margins on Tuesday, Archer Daniels Midland disclosed earnings that fell short of expectations, attributing this to poor biofuels pricing. The company's shares fell nearly 8 percent to $32.73, heading towards its worst daily decline in 4-1/2 years. Iowa, being the leading state in ethanol production, continues to be a bastion of support for the program. The sector contributes over $4.9 billion, or 3.5 percent, to the state's gross domestic product. Ethanol has already integrated into the transportation fuel infrastructure, making up around 10 percent of blended gasoline, with some analysts suggesting that the majority of Iowa voters still back the RFS. Eric Branstad, the Iowa director for the pro-RFS organization, America’s Renewable Future, stated on Monday night that while Cruz’s stance could be detrimental to the state’s economy, "We feel optimistic about our results." "The overwhelming majority of our candidates and the vast majority of caucus-goers recognize the economic, national security, and environmental advantages of the RFS," Branstad conveyed in a statement.

text: The legal confrontation between the Obama administration and North Carolina regarding a law that restricts bathroom access for transgender individuals intensified on Monday, as both parties filed lawsuits against one another, accusing each of infringing on civil rights and governmental overreach. The complaint from the U.S. Justice Department requested that a federal district court in North Carolina rule that the state is in violation of the 1964 Civil Rights Act and mandate the cessation of the enforcement of the ban. Earlier that same day, Pat McCrory, the Republican governor of North Carolina, along with the state's secretary of public safety, initiated legal action against the agency in a separate federal court located in North Carolina, alleging “baseless and blatant overreach.” Known as HB 2, the bathroom law, which was enacted in March, forbids individuals from utilizing public restrooms that do not align with their biological sex. This legislation has placed North Carolina at the forefront of a national discussion concerning equality and privacy, potentially leading to an extended and expensive legal struggle with the federal government. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, Americans are split on the issue of restroom use for transgender individuals, with 44 percent asserting that restrooms should be used according to biological sex, while 39 percent believe they should be utilized according to one's identified gender. By enacting this law, North Carolina became the first state in the nation to prohibit individuals from using public restrooms or changing facilities that do not correspond to the sex indicated on their birth certificate. On Monday, U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch stated that the department “retains the option” to reduce federal funding to North Carolina unless the state relents. “None of us can stand by when a state engages in legislating identity and demands that a person pretend to be something or someone they are not,” Lynch remarked during a press conference, likening the law to the racial discrimination statutes from the Jim Crow era and restrictions on same-sex marriage. Lynch indicated that the department is observing other U.S. jurisdictions that have enacted or are contemplating laws similar to North Carolina’s but refrained from disclosing whether the agency intends to take any action against them. Josh Earnest, a spokesperson for the White House, described the North Carolina law as “mean-spirited,” while McCrory maintained in his complaint that it constitutes a “common sense privacy policy.” Republican representatives in North Carolina argue that this law prevents men from impersonating transgender individuals to gain access to women's restrooms. According to an analysis conducted by attorneys at the University of California, Los Angeles Law School, North Carolina risks losing $4.8 billion in funding, primarily educational grants, if it does not retract the law. The Justice Department's lawsuit identifies the state of North Carolina, McCrory, the North Carolina Department of Public Safety, and the University of North Carolina system as defendants. The 17-campus University of North Carolina system asserts that it takes federal non-discrimination laws very seriously but is also required to comply with state laws such as HB 2. “In these circumstances, the University is truly caught in the middle,” stated UNC President Margaret Spellings. McCrory informed reporters that the state felt compelled to enact this law after the Charlotte city council approved an ordinance permitting transgender individuals to access bathrooms based on their gender identity in both public and private facilities. “We’re taking the Obama administration to court. They’re bypassing Congress, attempting to rewrite law & policies for the whole country, not just NC,” McCrory tweeted. Republican leaders in North Carolina’s state legislature also filed a lawsuit against the U.S. government concerning the law on Monday, just hours after McCrory's suit. Additionally, the law is being contested in federal district court by opponents, including the American Civil Liberties Union.

text: Planned Parenthood receives a temporary stay after the healthcare bill is withdrawn. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Planned Parenthood, the nationwide health organization poised to lose federal funding due to extensive healthcare reform legislation, interprets the bill's withdrawal on Friday as a short-term relief rather than a definitive end to the threats against its operations. Officials from the organization, which has long been a target for those opposed to its abortion services, predict additional efforts by Republicans to limit its involvement in federally funded public health initiatives, which comprise a significant portion of its financial support. In a significant defeat for Republican President Donald Trump, leaders of the U.S. House of Representatives retracted the healthcare bill after a revolt from moderate Republicans and the party's most conservative members left them lacking enough votes. Democrats stood firmly against it. Planned Parenthood executives will convene in Washington next week to devise their strategy for the upcoming battles in what they perceive as a prolonged struggle. "It’s one good night’s sleep, and then we have to see what they are going to cook up," stated Chris Charbonneau, chief executive of Planned Parenthood of the Great Northwest and the Hawaiian Islands, during a phone conversation. "They’re trying to find some means to attach some Planned Parenthood defunding to." Numerous Republicans are opposed to the organization, some based on religious beliefs, due to its provision of abortion services, despite the fact that it does not receive any federal funding or reimbursements for abortions, as dictated by federal law. The federal support it obtains mainly comes from reimbursements through Medicaid and the Title X Family Planning grant program for care provided to low-income patients. Abortion opponents have asserted that Republican leaders have vowed for years to terminate federal reimbursements for Planned Parenthood, and that voters would persist in holding them accountable. Prior to his victory in the presidential election in November, Trump also pledged to cut funding for Planned Parenthood and worked to advance the healthcare bill. "I’m confident the Republicans in Congress and the president will proceed to defund Planned Parenthood," remarked Joe Pojman, executive director of the anti-abortion Texas Alliance for Life. He added that the issue "is so dear to the electorate who put the Republicans and president in office," following the bill's retraction. Conversely, Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association, expressed his approval of the bill's withdrawal and noted that the renewed attention on Planned Parenthood may complicate future attempts to restrict its funding. "I think in many ways it’s going to be harder for them to go after Planned Parenthood, not that they won’t," he mentioned in a phone interview. "I hope people recognize that Planned Parenthood did more than abortions, that they recognize it has a broader portfolio," he added, highlighting services like cancer screenings that the organization offers. The proposed American Health Care Act (AHCA) aimed to repeal several components of the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, which Democratic President Barack Obama enacted in 2010. Charbonneau and other Planned Parenthood representatives pointed to a widespread public backlash against the AHCA as a reason why its moderate Republican supporters were unable to find a compromise with members of the conservative Freedom Caucus, who insisted on a complete dismantling of Obamacare. "The irony is that the Freedom Caucus, which is very pro-life and against Planned Parenthood, allows P.P. to continue if they stop this plan!" Trump tweeted on Friday morning. Public opinion surveys indicated that the AHCA was unpopular among Americans, including those who identify as Republican, and that there was significant public backing for funding some of Planned Parenthood's initiatives. In a Reuters-Ipsos poll conducted last month, almost half of 5,459 American adults surveyed indicated that Planned Parenthood should receive federal funding.

text: Exclusive: Trump states U.S. seeks equitable treatment in climate agreement. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Thursday, President Donald Trump expressed his concerns that the United States was being treated unfairly under the Paris Climate Agreement, revealing to Reuters that he would make an announcement in approximately two weeks regarding whether the U.S. would continue its participation in the accord. The Republican Trump, who was elected in November, had promised during his campaign to withdraw from the Paris agreement within 100 days of taking office, as part of a larger initiative to eliminate the environmental regulations established by the Obama administration, which he argued were detrimental to the economy. He has since indicated a willingness to remain in the agreement if the U.S. can secure more favorable conditions. Numerous large American companies and several Republican lawmakers have encouraged him to maintain the U.S. involvement in the deal to safeguard American industrial interests abroad. In an interview with Reuters, Trump, who will reach the 100-day milestone of his presidency on Saturday, stated that he would reveal his decision “in about two weeks,” but voiced his concerns that China, India, Russia, and other nations were contributing too little to assist poorer countries in combating climate change through the agreement's Green Climate Fund. “It’s not a fair situation because they are paying virtually nothing and we are paying massive amounts of money,” he remarked. When asked for a preview of his potential decision, he responded: “I can say this, we want to be treated fairly.” An administration insider informed Reuters previously that officials from the Trump administration were likely to convene in May to determine whether to maintain U.S. participation in the climate agreement, following an initial meeting on Thursday at the White House. The advisory group, which comprises Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, Energy Secretary Rick Perry, and national security adviser H.R. McMaster, is expected to make a decision ahead of a Group of Seven summit scheduled for May 26, according to the source. Both Tillerson, the ex-CEO of Exxon Mobil Corp, and Perry have expressed that the nation should remain part of the agreement. McMaster reportedly shares this perspective, as stated by an external source. Among the critics of the agreement are Environmental Protection Agency head Scott Pruitt, who previously served as the attorney general of the oil-rich state of Oklahoma, and White House chief strategist Steve Bannon. Nearly 200 nations reached the Paris agreement to mitigate climate change by reducing carbon dioxide emissions and investing in clean energy initiatives. Corporations like BP Plc and Microsoft Corp have advocated for the United States to remain in the agreement to maintain their competitive edge. A collective of nine Republican lawmakers on Thursday urged Trump to adhere to the pact while advocating for a reduction of the U.S. commitment to lower greenhouse gas emissions. Congressman Kevin Cramer from the oil-producing state of North Dakota, along with eight other Republican representatives, sent a letter to Trump encouraging him to leverage the country’s “seat at the Paris table to defend and promote our commercial interest, including our manufacturing and fossil fuel sectors.” If the United States is to continue its involvement in the 2015 agreement, Washington should propose a new pledge for emissions reductions that “does no harm to our economy,” according to the correspondence from Cramer, who was an advisor to Trump on energy and climate matters during the 2016 presidential campaign. Trump's Democratic predecessor, former President Barack Obama, had committed to a 26 percent to 28 percent reduction in U.S. greenhouse gas emissions from 2005 levels by the year 2025. The majority of scientists assert that global efforts must focus on reducing greenhouse gas emissions to mitigate the impacts of climate change, which include rising sea levels, extreme heatwaves, and severe storms and droughts. The Republican lawmakers also stated that Washington should keep its position on the Green Climate Fund but refrain from making additional contributions to it. Obama had pledged $3 billion to the fund in 2014 and contributed $1 billion, with the final $500 million payment made during his last days in office.

text: Frankfurt is set to evacuate thousands as a massive World War II bomb is defused. FRANKFURT (Reuters) - Officials in Frankfurt have cautioned that the financial capital of Germany could come to a standstill on Monday if residents do not follow evacuation orders to facilitate the disarming of a large World War II bomb. On Sunday, around 60,000 individuals will be evacuated in the largest such operation in Germany since the war, as authorities disable the British bomb found at a construction site this week in the affluent Westend neighborhood of Frankfurt, where numerous wealthy bankers reside. During a press conference convened on Friday, fire and police leaders stated they would resort to force and detention if necessary to ensure the area is cleared of residents. An uncontrolled detonation of the bomb could potentially devastate an entire city block, warned Frankfurt fire chief Reinhard Ries to reporters. This bomb contains over 1.4 tonnes of explosives, he noted. The danger lies not only in the shrapnel but also in the pressure it generates, which could destroy all structures within a 100-metre (yard) radius. The HC 4000 bomb is believed to have been dropped by the Royal Air Force of Britain during the 1939-45 conflict. While such discoveries are not uncommon, it is rare for unexploded ordnance to be both this large and situated in such a critical location. The mandatory evacuation zone, which extends 1.5 km (approximately a mile) from the bomb, encompasses police headquarters, two hospitals, transport systems, and Germany's central bank, which holds $70 billion in gold reserves. On Friday, officials urged Frankfurt's citizens to vacate the area by 8 a.m. on Sunday, emphasizing that the operation could last a minimum of 12 hours. Police indicated that they could not commence defusing the bomb until they were certain that everyone had exited the area. They plan to ring doorbells and utilize heat-sensing technology from helicopters above to locate any remaining individuals, they stated. Roads and transport systems, including parts of the underground, will be shut down during the operation and for at least two hours post-defusal, to facilitate patient transfers back to hospitals without traffic interference. Air traffic from Frankfurt airport might also face disruptions if an easterly wind occurs on Sunday, air traffic control informed Reuters on Friday. Additionally, small private aircraft, helicopters, and drones will be prohibited from entering the evacuation zone, they added. Residents of Frankfurt can spend the day at designated shelters established at the trade fair and the Jahrhunderthalle convention center, according to police. Furthermore, most museums will provide free admission to Frankfurt residents on Sunday, with some opening their doors earlier than usual, as stated on the city’s website.

text: The United States has requested that the United Nations Security Council impose sanctions on 10 vessels for transporting prohibited goods from North Korea, as per documents reviewed by Reuters on Tuesday. JOHANNESBURG (Reuters) - Grace Mugabe, the First Lady of Zimbabwe, has refuted allegations of assaulting South African model Gabriella Engels with an electric cable in a hotel suite in Johannesburg last month, asserting that a 'drunken and unhinged' Engels was the one who attacked her with a knife. In a deposition dated August 17, which has not been previously reported and was exclusively reviewed by Reuters, Mugabe challenged the account of 20-year-old Engels, presenting herself as the aggrieved party after stepping in to assist her adult sons, Chatunga and Robert Junior, who were reportedly involved with a drunken young woman. The statement indicated that Grace Mugabe, 52, who is a potential successor to her 93-year-old husband as Zimbabwe's president, is contemplating filing charges of attempted murder. A representative group for Engels dismissed these claims as falsehoods. According to the model, a furious Mugabe entered the room where she was with two friends waiting to meet Chatunga on August 13 and began attacking her with an electric cable. Images taken by Engels' mother shortly after the incident displayed wounds on the model's head, along with bruises on her thighs. In her deposition, Mugabe characterized Engels' account as 'malicious allegations' and claimed she had been assaulted after arriving to assist her sons. Concerned for their well-being, she went to their hotel suite, the statement mentioned. Upon her arrival, Ms. Engels, who was intoxicated and irrational, allegedly attacked Dr. Grace Mugabe with a knife when asked to leave the hotel. It continued that security had no alternative but to remove Ms. Engels from the hotel suite. The statement also claimed that Engels had been involved in a confrontation with other women at Johannesburg's Taboo nightclub the night prior, suggesting that this might have been the source of her injuries. Afriforum, an Afrikaans civil society organization representing Engels, rejected both claims. 'Gabriella never attacked Grace Mugabe in any manner and she was not involved in the altercation at Taboo,' Afriforum stated. 'It is evident that Grace Mugabe is urgently attempting to evade accountability for her aggressive conduct by fabricating lies to wrongfully depict the victim in this situation as the aggressor.' South Africa provided Grace Mugabe with diplomatic immunity, enabling her to avoid immediate prosecution for assault; however, Engels and Afriforum have contested this ruling, asserting that Mugabe was not in South Africa for official business. They further contended that assault is a 'serious crime' that is not protected by diplomatic immunity statutes. The choice to allow Grace Mugabe to return home ignited controversy in South Africa, prompting the opposition Democratic Alliance to pursue legal action to annul the immunity. According to intelligence documents from Zimbabwe reviewed by Reuters, Robert Mugabe sought to persuade his South African counterpart, Jacob Zuma, to resolve the matter amicably and outside of court, but was hindered by Engels' refusal to accept a settlement. 'He is trying to avoid the humiliation of his wife facing the court,' one document dated August 30 stated. 'The issue he is confronting is that the woman who was assaulted is rejecting any monetary offer and solely desires justice against Grace.' Gerrie Nel, the Afriforum lawyer - recognized for prosecuting South African athlete Oscar Pistorius for the shooting of his girlfriend - noted last month that Engels had been offered cash but had declined it. The intelligence report is part of a larger collection of hundreds of documents from Zimbabwe's Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO) dating back to 2009. Reuters has not confirmed the original author or intended recipient of these documents. The report from August 30 indicated that Mugabe was 'changing his stance' regarding the case and was now supporting Grace while accusing Engels of wrongdoing. 'Mugabe wishes for people to cease criticizing his wife and using derogatory names,' it stated. 'Mugabe is asserting that his wife acted out of anger, similar to how any other woman might respond.'

text: The United States has imposed sanctions on 13 organizations from China and North Korea, as stated on Tuesday. According to Washington, these entities have been aiding in the circumvention of nuclear restrictions imposed on Pyongyang and have been facilitating trade in commodities such as coal. This announcement from the U.S. Treasury came just a day after President Donald Trump reinstated North Korea on the list of state sponsors of terrorism on the official website. The new restrictions highlight the Trump administration's efforts to disrupt commerce between China and North Korea, which is perceived as crucial in deterring Pyongyang's aspirations to create a nuclear-capable missile that could reach the United States. Treasury Secretary Steven T. Mnuchin remarked, "This designation will impose further sanctions and penalties on North Korea and related persons, and supports our maximum pressure campaign to isolate the murderous regime." The latest sanctions included the blacklisting of three Chinese firms: Dandong Kehua Economy & Trade Co., Dandong Xianghe Trading Co., and Dandong Hongda Trade Co. The Treasury Department reported these companies collectively engaged in over $750 million in trade with North Korea over nearly five years, ending on August 31. Their involvement included the trading of coal, iron ore, lead, zinc, silver ore, lead metal, ferrous products, as well as notebook computers. Additionally, Sun Sidong and his business, Dandong Dongyuan Industrial Co., were also blacklisted. A report from the Washington think tank C4ADS in June identified this firm as part of a web of Chinese companies that handle a significant portion of trade with North Korea. U.S. officials have consistently targeted firms and individuals from Dandong, a Chinese city adjacent to North Korea, in efforts to diminish Pyongyang's primary revenue from exporting natural resources like coal. In Beijing, foreign ministry spokesperson Lu Kang reiterated China's stance against unilateral sanctions imposed by other nations, stating that China is capable of investigating any violations of its laws or international responsibilities itself. "If other parties wish to cooperate effectively with China on this issue and are genuinely informed on certain matters, they can certainly share intelligence with China and collaborate to appropriately address the matter," Lu stated during a daily press briefing on Wednesday. The immediate effect on the listed companies is expected to be minimal, as trade between China and its isolated northern neighbor has significantly decreased since the United Nations enforced a ban in September on North Korean exports of coal, iron, iron ore, lead, lead ore, and seafood. In February, China also banned coal imports from North Korea. According to Anthony Ruggiero, a North Korea specialist at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, financial regulations are not strictly enforced in the Dandong region, leading to an influx of companies eager to profit from selling to North Korea. The new sanctions also target various North Korean firms that send laborers to countries like Russia, Poland, Cambodia, and China. U.S. authorities indicated that they are aiming to cut off the revenue North Korea generates from labor exports. Beyond targeting sources of weapons technology, these restrictions mark the first instance where the United States has sought to directly affect North Korea's everyday consumer trade, according to Peter Harrell, a sanctions expert at the Center for a New American Security. "We are sanctioning companies involved in ordinary trade," Harrell stated. "That’s the logical next step." The sanctions are intended to further isolate Pyongyang, as noted by Heather Nauert, a spokeswoman for the State Department, who expressed confidence that targeting additional Chinese companies would not hinder Beijing's cooperation regarding North Korea. "I don't think it jeopardizes anything," she said. "I believe the world has united on this issue. We maintain a good relationship with China, and that’s not going to change."

text: Former California Democratic state Senator Leland Yee was sentenced to five years in prison on Wednesday due to conspiracy charges arising from a corruption investigation that included bribery, weapon trafficking, and money laundering, according to federal prosecutors. The 67-year-old Yee entered a guilty plea for the conspiracy charge following his arrest in 2014 during a crackdown that involved alleged organized crime figures in San Francisco, the city he represented in the state legislature. Prosecutors had requested an eight-year sentence for Yee, whose guilty plea in federal court in San Francisco last July signified the conclusion of his lengthy political career, which featured two terms on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors and subsequent elections to both the California Assembly and Senate. Yee was the third California state senator to face charges in 2014 within separate criminal cases. All three ultimately resigned, resulting in a significant loss of a two-thirds legislative majority for the Democrats.

text: Lawsuit initiates new chapter in Obama immigration legal battle. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Thursday, immigration advocates launched a challenging effort to revive a segment of U.S. President Barack Obama’s initiative aimed at protecting millions of immigrants from deportation by submitting a lawsuit that disputes the nationwide scope of a court order that obstructed it. With favorable judicial outcomes, the attorneys pursuing the lawsuit claim it has the potential to dismantle rulings that halted Obama’s November 2014 initiative across the country. Had the White House program been fully enacted, it could have permitted up to four million individuals lacking legal immigration status to gain work permits. The lawsuit was submitted in federal court in New York on behalf of Martin Batalla Vidal, 25, a Mexican immigrant who has resided in the United States since the age of seven and has reaped the benefits of the program. He was initially granted a three-year work permit, which has since been revoked following a Texas judge's ruling in February 2015 that blocked Obama’s initiative. Texas and 25 additional states had contested it. Vidal remains eligible for a two-year work permit under a previous program, which has not faced legal challenge and was not impacted by the injunction. Vidal’s attorneys at the National Immigration Law Center assert that a victory for him could have significant consequences, as it could aid in the potential reinstatement of Obama’s program for up to 60 percent of prospective applicants in regions of the country not affected by the Texas ruling. The Texas judge’s decision was affirmed on appeal. On June 23, the Supreme Court reached a 4-4 stalemate on the matter, thus maintaining the appeals court's ruling. The court currently lacks one justice following the passing of Justice Antonin Scalia in February. The Supreme Court is deliberating whether to revisit the case once it has a complete set of justices.

text: President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that he intends to collaborate with the U.S. Congress to secure grants and loans aimed at aiding the reconstruction of Puerto Rico, which suffered extensive damage from Hurricane Maria a month prior. The U.S. territory, already burdened by debt due to years of economic downturn, is facing storm-related destruction that some estimates suggest could reach as high as $95 billion. It has requested the federal government to make exceptions to regulations that generally require states and local governments to contribute to recovery costs. Trump did not specify the amount of financial assistance the government might provide to the financially troubled territory, which is home to 3.4 million U.S. citizens. "I have given my blessing to Congress, and Congress is working with you and your representatives on developing a plan and a payment strategy and how it will be financed. Because we are discussing some significant figures," Trump stated to Puerto Rico Governor Ricardo Rossello during the opening of a meeting in the Oval Office. Last week, Trump and some of his senior aides indicated that there might be limitations on the extent of help Puerto Rico could receive from Washington. However, the president’s comments on Thursday were largely supportive. The hurricane devastated the island's power infrastructure, causing destruction to homes, roads, and other essential facilities. The bankrupt territory is still facing challenges in delivering basic services, such as access to running water. An oversight board tasked with addressing Puerto Rico’s debt crisis has warned that the island’s government could exhaust its funds by the end of the month without assistance. Trump highlighted that the repayment of federal loans and other debts related to the storm incurred by Puerto Rico would take precedence over the repayment of the island’s existing $72 billion debt. "Any funding provided by individuals—whether public or private—will seek to be in the first position," Trump remarked. "We’re going to come before—well before—any current debt that exists on the island," he added. When asked whether the process would be simpler if Puerto Rico were a state instead of a territory, a sensitive political topic on the island, Trump refrained from commenting. "That question will get me into trouble," he replied to a journalist. While in Washington, Rossello also conferred with Senate leaders. A Senate vote is anticipated in the upcoming days on an aid package that proposes $18.7 billion for the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which has been assisting Texas, Florida, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands in recovering from three major hurricanes. Some senators are advocating for additional funds to be incorporated into that package, as Senator John Thune, a member of the Republican leadership, mentioned to the press. Senator Marco Rubio, a Republican from Florida who has been actively engaged in discussions about the aid, expressed earlier on Thursday his desire to modify the bill so the island could gain quicker access to funds. Congress is projected to deliberate on another aid package by the end of December; however, Rubio cautioned that this timeline may be too late for the island, which currently lacks tax revenue. "From experience, I know that as we move further away from these hurricanes, the urgency diminishes," Rubio stated. Rossello has requested the federal government’s authorization to utilize disaster aid for a wide range of expenses. He has also appealed to the White House and Congress for a minimum of $4.6 billion in block grants and other funding types. "The reality is that we still have much more to do for the people of Puerto Rico, and that’s why we’re meeting," Rossello noted. "This situation is far from resolved."

text: Numerous U.S. Democrats express doubt regarding the potential to restore relations with Netanyahu. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Benjamin Netanyahu’s inaugural visit to Washington during the Trump administration presents an opportunity to mend ties with Democrats that have deteriorated over years of frosty relations under the Obama presidency. However, many members of the party believe that significant improvement is unlikely due to the Israeli prime minister’s strong alignment with Republicans. "There’s a considerable amount of fence-mending that needs to occur between the Netanyahu administration and many Democrats who feel that he has unnecessarily politicized the U.S.-Israeli relationship," stated Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, in a phone interview. The nadir of relations occurred in March 2015 when Netanyahu bypassed the White House and State Department to organize a speech before the Republican-controlled Congress to contest the international nuclear agreement with Iran that President Barack Obama was negotiating at the time. More than 55 Democratic lawmakers from both the Senate and House, led by the Congressional Black Caucus, boycotted the speech in protest of what they perceived as an affront to Obama, the first African-American president of the United States. Despite nearly seventy years of bipartisan backing for Israel in Congress, tensions between Netanyahu and congressional Democrats have persisted, with Congress utilizing its spending authority to ensure Israel remains the largest annual recipient of U.S. military aid. Following Trump’s inauguration last month, Netanyahu tweeted his commendation of Trump’s proposal to construct a wall to prevent individuals from Mexico from entering, which Democrats view as a costly and racially charged slight toward a U.S. neighbor and ally. Additionally, numerous Democrats are apprehensive about Netanyahu’s advocacy for new settlements on territories claimed by Palestinians and express concern over remarks from certain members of his government opposing the establishment of a Palestinian state. Democrats have criticized congressional Republicans for leveraging Israel as a divisive issue, notwithstanding robust Democratic backing for initiatives like the $38 billion military aid agreement signed by the Obama administration in September. Aides accompanying Netanyahu did not reply to requests for comments on Tuesday. Nevertheless, upon his departure for Washington, Netanyahu emphasized his intention to engage with congressional leaders from both parties, indicating a potential shift towards rebalancing. "The partnership between Israel and America has consistently been exceptionally robust. It is poised to become even stronger," Netanyahu informed reporters.

text: The U.S. military will postpone indefinitely its prohibition on older varieties of cluster bombs that was set to take effect on January 1, 2019, according to officials. They argue that advancements in munitions technology have not progressed sufficiently to substitute for outdated stockpiles. Cluster bombs, which can be delivered via aircraft or artillery, disperse smaller explosive devices over a broad area, but these devices sometimes fail to detonate and can be challenging to locate and remove, potentially causing civilian casualties long after wars have concluded. The military had aimed to shift to cluster munitions that detonate at a rate of at least 99 percent, significantly minimizing associated risks. However, with just over a year remaining before the implementation of the ban, a Pentagon representative informed Reuters that technological advancements in safety had not developed enough to allow for the replacement of current stockpiles with safer alternatives. Reuters has obtained a copy of the policy memo and verified the updates with Pentagon sources. The memo states, "While the Department aims to deploy a new generation of more reliable munitions, we cannot jeopardize mission success or increase the risk of military and civilian casualties by relinquishing the best available capabilities." The memo is anticipated to be signed by Deputy Defense Secretary Patrick Shanahan on Thursday and refers to cluster munitions as "legitimate weapons with clear military utility." The announcement of this new policy has drawn significant backlash from Congress and human rights organizations. Senator Patrick Leahy, a Democrat who has been instrumental in advocating for restrictions on cluster bomb usage, remarked that the Pentagon is effectively "perpetuating the use of an indiscriminate weapon that has demonstrated high failure rates." Senator Dianne Feinstein labeled the decision as "unbelievable." Human Rights Watch contested the assertion that the military requires these weapons, noting that aside from a single strike in Yemen in 2009, the U.S. military has not deployed them since 2003 in Iraq. Mary Wareham, the arms division director at Human Rights Watch, stated, "We condemn this decision to reverse the long-standing U.S. commitment not to utilize cluster munitions that fail more than 1 percent of the time, leading to deadly unexploded submunitions." Pentagon spokesman Tom Crosson acknowledged that it has been years since the military employed a significant quantity of cluster munitions, and the new Pentagon policy stresses the eventual transition to safer alternatives. Nonetheless, it remains uncertain when the Pentagon will be obliged to cease using its existing stockpiles, as there will also need to be not only advanced weaponry but also adequate supplies of new cluster munitions for U.S. inventory. The updated policy prohibits the Pentagon from acquiring any additional cluster bombs that do not conform to the new standards outlined in the memo. The revised guidelines expand the definition of which munitions meet safety criteria beyond the 99 percent detonation rate. According to the new policy, the Pentagon indicates that bombs equipped with advanced self-destruct or deactivation technology would also be permissible for future purchase. Such munitions must satisfy a set of requirements, including a mechanism to render submunitions inoperable within 15 minutes after being armed. Additionally, the Pentagon's policy forbids the acquisition of arms that are banned under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, which strictly prohibits the use of such munitions, while exempting certain types that the Pentagon claims it would still categorize as cluster munitions.

text: Trump intensifies claims of a 'rigged' election, which Republican attorneys contest. GREEN BAY, Wis./WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Monday, Donald Trump, the Republican presidential candidate, referenced studies that he claimed indicated widespread voter fraud, asserting that the election on November 8 was 'rigged' against him, despite Republican lawyers declaring his claims baseless. Trump, a businessman from New York embarking on his initial campaign for office, has aimed to stir concerns about a compromised election as he has seen a decline in polls compared to Democrat Hillary Clinton. 'They even want to attempt to rig the election at the polling location,' Trump expressed at a rally in Green Bay, Wisconsin. 'Numerous cities are corrupt, and voter fraud is quite prevalent.' Trump pointed to research from Pew Trusts conducted in 2012, which recommended improvements to the voter registration system due to approximately 24 million inaccurate registrations. (bit.ly/1HN4uTF) He also mentioned a 2014 article by two political scientists in the Washington Post, which suggested that votes from non-citizens might have influenced Democratic wins in several closely contested elections in 2008, though the authors conceded that their study's sample size was limited. (wapo.st/1pX17Bf) Many studies have indicated that voter fraud is exceedingly rare in U.S. elections. Republican campaign attorney Chris Ashby warned that Trump's allegations could incite unrest and were 'unfounded' and 'dangerous.' 'By claiming an election is rigged, you’re telling voters, your supporters, that their votes are insignificant,' Ashby stated in an interview. 'I believe some of Donald Trump's remarks could provoke unrest at polling places.' Some members of the Republican Party have advised Trump to retract his claims. Early voting and mail-in voting have already commenced in numerous states. Mark Braden, a partner at Baker and Hostetler and former chief counsel for the Republican National Committee, asserted that any form of election manipulation at the national level 'is simply impossible,' pointing to the various systems that would complicate and hinder such an effort. 'Our system fundamentally relies on each side monitoring the other,' Braden remarked in an interview. 'Our system depends on local volunteer involvement. It has operated very effectively because we have individuals who engage in the process and fulfill these roles.' Trump also seized on the release of Federal Bureau of Investigation documents on Monday, which he claimed indicated 'felony corruption.' The documents included a statement from an FBI official asserting that a senior State Department official attempted to persuade the bureau in 2015 to retract its claim that an email from Clinton’s private server contained classified material.
