text: Lebanon has scheduled its first parliamentary election in almost ten years for May 6 of next year. This election could significantly alter the political dynamics in a nation currently experiencing tensions between Saudi Arabia and Iran. On Friday, Interior Minister Nohad Machnouk signed a decree to officially set the election date, enabling the vote to finally proceed. Since the last election in 2009, the vote has been delayed three times, with politicians citing reasons such as security issues, political turmoil, and disagreements over the electoral law. The coalition government led by Prime Minister Saad al-Hariri, which took office a year ago, reached an agreement on the new election law in June; however, finalizing the date was stalled due to discussions among officials regarding technical aspects and the registration of Lebanese citizens living abroad. Since the previous election, the political landscape in Lebanon has undergone significant changes. Hariri's Saudi-backed, pro-Western political coalition has fragmented. Over the past year, he has presided over a power-sharing government that includes the heavily armed, Iran-supported Shiite group Hezbollah, which is not favored by his Saudi allies. Last month, Hariri triggered a political crisis by announcing his resignation while in Riyadh, during which he criticized both Hezbollah and Iran. He remained abroad for two weeks before returning and ultimately rescinded his resignation the following week. Lebanon's electoral system is intricate, designed to uphold civil harmony in a country that has experienced numerous civil wars since its independence in 1943, involving various religious groups such as Sunnis, Shiites, Christians, and Druze. The parliament consists of 128 seats, with 64 designated for Christians across seven denominations and 64 for Muslims, divided equally between Sunnis and Shiites. The nation is organized into districts that elect several lawmakers based on strict religious quotas. The president is required to be a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim, and the speaker of parliament a Shiite Muslim, ensuring representation of the three largest groups in the parliament. The global community has consistently emphasized the necessity for Lebanon to conduct elections on schedule to restore faith in its institutions and preserve stability. Machnouk announced that Lebanese citizens abroad will have the opportunity to cast their votes on April 22 and 28.

On Monday, May met with leaders from GlaxoSmithKline (GSK.L), Vodafone (VOD.L), HSBC (HSBA.L), and several other major firms to gather their expectations from discussions regarding the UK's future relationship with the EU post-Brexit. text: (Reuters) - The legal reasoning provided by President Donald Trump’s personal attorney regarding the president’s tweets about former U.S. national security advisor Michael Flynn has been met with skepticism from legal analysts. In an effort to clarify a Trump tweet from Saturday, attorney John Dowd informed Reuters on Sunday that he composed and “bollixed up” the president’s message in which Trump stated he dismissed Michael Flynn for lying to the FBI, rather than merely misleading U.S. Vice President Mike Pence. Some observers have suggested that the tweet indicated Trump was aware Flynn had committed a crime and attempted to obstruct justice by, among other actions, firing then FBI director James Comey. Dowd refuted the claim that Trump was aware Flynn had lied to the FBI but introduced new uncertainties by offering additional details regarding the January meetings in which former Acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates cautioned White House Counsel Don McGahn that Flynn posed a security threat due to his dishonesty about discussions with former Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak. Dowd stated that Yates informed McGahn that Flynn had told the FBI the same information he had shared with Pence, but did not indicate that Flynn was at risk of criminal prosecution. He claimed that McGahn communicated the conversation to Trump in that manner. “You may conclude that’s a lie, but the Department of Justice, that had the power to charge, did not,” Dowd stated. “The first time the president knows for a fact this guy lies was when he was charged.” However, several attorneys remarked that, irrespective of whether Yates explicitly mentioned that Flynn had lied to the FBI, the White House counsel ought to have recognized that possibility and relayed it to the president. “It’s not every day that the acting attorney general comes over to the White House with that sort of message,” remarked Alex Whiting, a former federal prosecutor currently teaching at Harvard Law School. “It had to have been obvious to McGahn that Flynn probably lied to the FBI whether Yates said it or not.” Michael Gerhardt, a law professor at the University of North Carolina, described Dowd’s argument as “a stretch” but acknowledged that there could be a “bit of credibility” in the notion that McGahn might have been waiting for more details before alerting the president regarding Flynn’s criminal exposure. Neither Yates nor McGahn were available for comments on Monday. Dowd also turned down requests for further commentary on Monday. Yates’ testimony in May before a Senate committee, where she stated she declined to answer McGahn’s inquiry about Flynn’s FBI interview, seems to contradict Dowd’s account. A source familiar with the situation indicated that Yates never asserted that Flynn informed FBI agents the same information he relayed to Pence. Dowd maintained his version of events. Last Friday, Flynn entered a guilty plea to a charge of lying to the FBI that was filed by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is conducting an investigation into alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election and potential obstruction of justice by the Trump administration. Russia has denied any interference in the 2016 U.S. election, and Trump has rejected any claims of collusion between Russia and his campaign. On Sunday, Dowd also contended that Trump could not be guilty of obstruction of justice since “he’s the chief law enforcement officer of the U.S.” Former prosecutor Robert Ray acknowledged there is some validity to the argument that Trump could not obstruct justice by dismissing Comey because he had the authority to do so. Nevertheless, several other attorneys disputed Dowd’s remarks, recalling that former President Richard Nixon faced impeachment for obstruction of justice preceding his resignation during the Watergate scandal. “It’s a patently absurd argument,” remarked Andrew Wright, a former White House attorney under President Barack Obama. “The president as the chief executive sits on top of the org chart, but he has to take care to ensure that the law is upheld.”

text: Thirteen individuals, including some civilians, lost their lives during a clash involving Colombia's ELN rebels and dissidents from the now-dissolved FARC guerrilla group, according to the nation’s ombudsman on Tuesday. The confrontation occurred on November 27 in the Narino region of southwestern Colombia, an area notorious for drug trafficking activities. This region is known for its cultivation, processing, and smuggling of coca, the raw material for cocaine. A peace agreement was reached last year with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), which marked the end of nearly five decades of conflict. However, a variety of dissident factions from FARC, ELN rebels, right-wing former paramilitaries, and criminal organizations remain operational in Colombia, vying for dominance over lucrative illegal mining and drug trafficking routes. In Narino, ELN members launched an assault on the Rural Resistance, as reported by ombudsman Carlos Alfonso Negret. The Rural Resistance consists of FARC dissidents who declined to demobilize after the peace accord. Negret informed reporters that his office conducted a visit to the site and confirmed that gunfire erupted between the group known as Rural Resistance and the ELN. The crossfire resulted in the deaths of 13 individuals. The report and Negret did not clarify how many of those deceased were civilians. This year, over 11,000 fighters and supporters from the FARC surrendered their arms as part of the peace agreement. The group has retained its initials in its new form as a political party. However, Negret stated that approximately 800 former guerillas opted not to demobilize, while other security analysts and think tanks estimate the number of dissident ex-FARC members to be between 700 and 1,300. The ELN and the government initiated their inaugural bilateral ceasefire in October, which is part of ongoing peace negotiations taking place in Ecuador. This ceasefire is scheduled to continue until January 9 and has the potential to be prolonged. According to Negret, the recent incident constituted a breach of this ceasefire. It marks the second violent event that has overshadowed the ceasefire, following the ELN's admission of responsibility for the killing of an indigenous leader in the troubled Choco province.

Pryor, who was the attorney general of Alabama at that time and currently serves on a federal appeals court, is among the 11 conservative judges that presumptive Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump has suggested he might nominate to the Supreme Court, should he win the election. "A constitutional right that safeguards 'the choice of one’s partner' and 'whether and how to engage sexually' must logically extend to actions such as prostitution, adultery, necrophilia, bestiality, possession of child pornography, and even incest and pedophilia," Pryor stated in a legal document submitted to the Supreme Court. Pryor has a history of contentious comments, as do several others included in Trump's selection. However, many possess solid conservative judicial credentials that would likely resonate with Republicans in the Senate, which has the authority to confirm Supreme Court nominees, and have avoided incendiary language. Unveiled on Wednesday, Trump’s list featured judges who have shown support for various conservative initiatives, aged between 41 and 58, and primarily originating from states governed by conservatives and Republicans. All of the eleven nominees, comprising eight men and three women, are white. The release of this list appears to have eased the concerns of some conservatives who were uncertain whether Trump would appoint a true conservative to the Supreme Court, which has an opening following the February passing of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia. "I’ve heard nothing but positive feedback regarding this. Individuals in the Senate believe this will alleviate a lot of concerns," remarked Republican Jeff Sessions of Alabama, a significant Trump ally in the Senate. The Republican-controlled Senate has declined to consider President Barack Obama’s nominee, Merrick Garland, arguing that the victor of the November 8 election, which will determine Obama’s successor, should have the opportunity to fill the position. Some judges on Trump’s list have issued rulings against abortion and birth control rights. text: A commission in South Africa has recommended an increase in state funding for higher education, suggesting that it should be raised by approximately one-third to a minimum of 1 percent of the nation's gross domestic product, according to a report released on Monday and commissioned by the presidency. This recommendation comes as a senior official from the Treasury resigned after reports indicated he expressed concerns about presidential meddling in the budgeting process. Additionally, state-owned power company Eskom is reportedly encountering significant liquidity challenges. South Africa is heavily dependent on foreign investors to cover its substantial budget and current account deficits. Investor anxiety is heightened as crucial credit rating evaluations are set for this month, coinciding with the African National Congress (ANC) preparing to choose Zuma's successor as party leader in December. On Monday, the presidency announced that Zuma would address the findings of the higher education report once the ministers had reviewed it. The commission was established by Zuma early last year in response to student protests advocating for free education. Following the announcement of the report's impending publication, the rand and benchmark bonds experienced a decline, though they showed little change after the report was officially released. Currency traders and analysts noted that the market was awaiting the presidency's reaction to the report, with some indicating that the recommendations posed economic risks. Senior economist Nicky Weimar from Nedbank warned, "If we continue to exhibit this trend of increasing budget deficits, we are certainly headed towards downgrades." Last year, South Africa's GDP was approximately 4.3 trillion rand ($296.6 billion), meaning an increase in government spending on higher education by 0.25 percent of GDP would equate to about $750 million in additional spending. The commission also suggested that all university students should receive funding through a cost-sharing mechanism, where the government would back income-contingent loans provided by commercial banks. If a student does not achieve a specified income level, the state would take on the responsibility of repaying the tuition loan, according to their advice. Implementing these strategies could complicate the Treasury's efforts to manage a projected budget deficit exceeding 4 percent of GDP for the 2017/18 fiscal year. Nevertheless, such measures would likely be popular among younger individuals and ANC supporters, many of whom feel discontented that South African society remains significantly unequal more than twenty years after apartheid ended in 1994. The next national election in South Africa is scheduled for 2019, and the ANC has experienced a reduction in its electoral majority in recent elections. Moreover, concerns have arisen in South African markets regarding the potential threat to the independence of financial institutions. Local media outlet Fin24 reported on Monday that Treasury Deputy Director-General Michael Sachs had resigned the previous week after voicing his concerns about Zuma's interference in the budgeting process. The Treasury confirmed Sachs's resignation, stating only that he wished to serve the public sector in a different role. Earlier this year, international rating agencies downgraded South Africa's debt following Zuma's abrupt dismissal of the well-regarded finance minister Pravin Gordhan. S&P Global and Moody's are anticipated to reassess the country's ratings on November 24, with attention focused on whether they will lower its local-currency rating to junk status after Gordhan's successor, Malusi Gigaba, presented bleak medium-term budget predictions last month. Downgrades to sub-investment grade may trigger forced sales of up to $12 billion in South African bonds, adding further strain on the rand, which is already trading at a twelve-month low against the dollar. On Monday, South Africa's debt insurance costs reached a four-month high, indicating an increased likelihood of rating downgrades.

NEW YORK (Reuters) - Advocates for gun safety are channeling tens of millions of dollars into Maine and Nevada to back ballot initiatives that would require background checks for firearm sales, aiming to achieve state-level successes after numerous unsuccessful attempts in Congress. Everytown for Gun Safety, the gun control organization established by billionaire former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, is spearheading the effort, contributing significant financial resources to three of the four initiatives. The organization plans to allocate $25 million across the nation for this cause, which is nearly equivalent to the amount the influential National Rifle Association has spent on television advertisements for Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump. The Second Amendment of the U.S. Constitution safeguards the right to possess firearms, and any attempts to limit that right are vigorously opposed by gun rights supporters, who wield considerable influence within the Republican Party. Success for gun control groups in Maine and Nevada would result in half of the U.S. population residing in states with enhanced background checks, including private sales that do not involve licensed dealers. Proponents of gun control argue that this would represent a significant and symbolically important milestone. Detractors of the proposals contend that the laws are poorly crafted, would have minimal impact on crime, and would penalize responsible gun owners. A poll conducted by the University of New Hampshire in late October indicated that 52 percent of Maine residents are in favor of the measure, while 43 percent oppose it. In Nevada, two polls from late October revealed a 16-point margin and a 25-point margin in favor of the initiative, respectively. text: ANKARA (Reuters) - On Monday, Turkey called in the U.S. ambassador to express its discontent regarding the treatment of Turkish security officials during President Tayyip Erdogan's recent visit to the United States, according to the foreign ministry. A confrontation occurred between demonstrators and Turkish security forces outside the residence of the Turkish ambassador while Erdogan was in Washington for discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump. Turkey attributed the unrest to protesters associated with the militant Kurdistan Workers Party, while the police chief in Washington labeled the occurrence a "brutal attack" on peaceful demonstrators. In a statement, the U.S. State Department described the actions of Turkish security personnel during the incident as "deeply disturbing." "A formal request has been made for U.S. authorities to carry out a comprehensive investigation into this diplomatic incident and to provide the required explanation," the foreign ministry stated. It noted that the security lapses experienced during Erdogan's visit to Washington were due to the "inability of U.S. authorities to implement adequate precautions at every phase of the official agenda," while asserting that these incidents would not diminish what was otherwise a "very successful" visit. Authorities reported that 11 individuals were injured, which included a Washington police officer, and two individuals were taken into custody for assault, with at least one of the arrested being a protester. Last week, Washington stated that it was expressing its utmost concern to Turkey regarding the brawl. The nature of Comey’s dealings with Trump is pivotal to the ongoing inquiries into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and the potential collusion between Trump’s associates and Russia. Warner refrained from elaborating on the investigation's progress or offering a timeline for its conclusion. "I would have thought we would have made more progress, but I never anticipated the administration would terminate Jim Comey. You can’t fabricate this kind of situation," he remarked. text: The chief aide to U.S. Vice President Mike Pence is departing from the Trump administration, and a seasoned Republican political strategist will take over, according to an announcement from Pence’s office on Thursday. Josh Pitcock, who has been serving as Pence’s chief of staff, is set to be replaced in August by Nick Ayers, who previously acted as Pence’s chief strategist during the presidential campaign. text: Moscow has called for an urgent meeting of the United Nations ceasefire task force in Geneva to address the U.S. missile strikes on Syria, as reported by the RIA news agency, citing a diplomatic source on Friday. These gatherings are led by U.N. Syria envoy Staffan de Mistura and were established in early 2016 with the support of both the U.S. and Russia. They serve as a platform for diplomats to discuss violations of Syria's fragile ceasefire. According to the source, Moscow is seeking to hold this meeting in Geneva today at 1500 GMT to deliberate on "the situation on the ground in relation to the U.S. missile strike on Syria's Shayrat airbase." Earlier on Friday, the United States launched cruise missiles at the airbase, which President Donald Trump indicated was the origin of a lethal chemical weapons assault. Russia has strongly condemned these strikes.
source_text: Russia calls emergency U.N. task force meeting on Syria strikes. MOSCOW (Reuters) - Russia has demanded an emergency meeting of the United Nations ceasefire task force in Geneva to discuss U.S. missile strikes on Syria, the RIA news agency quoted a diplomatic source as saying on Friday. Such meetings are chaired by U.N. Syria envoy Staffan de Mistura and were set up in early 2016 with joint U.S.-Russian backing. They are a forum for diplomats to talk about breaches of Syria’s shaky ceasefire. Moscow wants the meeting to be held in Geneva today at 1500 GMT, the source told RIA, adding that the task force would discuss “the situation on the ground with connection to the U.S. missile strike on Syria’s Shayrat airbase.” The United States fired cruise missiles earlier on Friday at the base from which President Donald Trump said a deadly chemical weapons attack had been launched. Russia has sharply condemned the strikes.

text: LONDON (Reuters) - On Sunday, Britain and Germany reaffirmed their commitment to the nuclear agreement with Iran following the U.S. decision to withdraw its certification of the accord, according to a spokeswoman after a conversation between Prime Minister Theresa May and German Chancellor Angela Merkel. The spokeswoman stated that both the UK and Germany are steadfast in their dedication to the deal. Additionally, they concurred that the international community must unite to counter Iran's destabilizing activities in the region and to seek solutions regarding concerns over Iran's ballistic missile program.
source_text: Britain, Germany committed to Iran nuclear deal: May's office. LONDON (Reuters) - Britain and Germany agreed on Sunday they remained committed to the nuclear deal with Iran after a U.S. decision to decertify the agreement, a spokeswoman said after a call between Prime Minister Theresa May and German Chancellor Angela Merkel.  They agreed the UK and Germany both remained firmly committed to the deal,  the spokeswoman said in a statement.  They also agreed the international community needed to continue to come together to push back against Iran s destabilizing regional activity, and to explore ways of addressing concerns about Iran s ballistic missile program.

text: A U.S. District Court judge announced on Friday that she would lift house arrest for former Trump campaign manager Paul Manafort, provided he meets specific conditions, indicating her satisfaction that the $10 million he agreed to forfeit would be available should he fail to attend court sessions. In her ruling, Judge Amy Berman Jackson stipulated that to be released from home confinement, Manafort must sign documents consenting to the forfeiture of four properties, which include two in New York, one in Alexandria, Virginia, and his residence in Florida. He will face restrictions such as a curfew and electronic GPS monitoring, but he will be permitted to travel from his home in Alexandria to his residence in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, once he fulfills the required conditions. Manafort faces charges related to conspiring to launder money and neglecting to register as a foreign agent while working for the former pro-Russia President of Ukraine, Viktor Yanukovych. He is currently being prosecuted by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, as part of the investigation into allegations of Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and potential collusion with the Trump campaign. Should the forfeited properties fail to generate the $10 million, the judge mentioned that Manafort’s wife, Kathleen, has placed $5 million in an account, and his daughter Andrea Manafort Shand has contributed $2 million in another account to cover any shortfall. These assets are not to be accessed without a court order. Once in Florida, Manafort must remain within the designated area unless he is traveling to Washington for court appearances or meetings with his legal counsel, as specified in the order. He must obtain approval for any other domestic travel and is prohibited from leaving the country.

text: The ethics committee of the U.S. House of Representatives has initiated an extensive investigation into potential sexual harassment and discrimination involving the chamber’s 434 lawmakers and their staff. On Friday, the committee requested a comprehensive array of documents from the congressional office responsible for handling employment disputes. Susan Brooks, the Republican chair of the committee, alongside Theodore Deutch, its leading Democrat, sent a letter to the office asking for the immediate sharing of all records concerning "any claims of sexual harassment, discrimination, retaliation or any other employment practice." This fall, Capitol Hill has been shaken by allegations of possible sexual misconduct among lawmakers, with public discontent growing over the use of taxpayer money to resolve harassment lawsuits against them. Notably, Representative John Conyers, a Democrat from Michigan, is facing increasing pressure to resign due to allegations of sexual harassment, claims that have not been verified by Reuters. Reports from U.S. media indicate that Conyers utilized public funds to settle a claim involving a woman, and the ethics committee is currently looking into whether he "used official resources for impermissible personal purposes." Conyers has admitted to settling with a former staff member regarding her harassment claims, although he has denied any wrongdoing. In a separate incident, Texas Republican Representative Joe Barton recently announced that he would not run for re-election following the emergence of a nude photo of him online. The committee has refrained from making any comments beyond the initial letter. There is growing pressure on the committee to enhance its enforcement of congressional regulations. The last disciplinary action taken was on August 1, when it found Representative Ben Ray Lujan had violated a rule concerning campaign communications, although no sanctions were imposed. In addition to addressing disputes and enforcing employment laws for over 30,000 individuals employed by Congress, the compliance office also allocates public funds to confidentially settle claims against lawmakers. A bipartisan coalition of lawmakers is advocating for changes to this practice through legislation that would mandate prompt public disclosure of settlement amounts. In a letter sent on Friday to House Administration Committee Chair Gregg Harper, the compliance office indicated that since 2013, it has disbursed settlements for two claims, one involving allegations of sex discrimination and the other concerning sexual harassment. It allocated $84,000 for one instance of sexual harassment and $7,000 for a case involving both sex and religious discrimination. Politico reported that the harassment settlement was made on behalf of Texas Republican Blake Farenthold. "While I fully support increased transparency regarding claims against members of Congress, I am unable to confirm or deny whether the settlement was related to my office, as the Congressional Accountability Act prohibits me from answering that question," Farenthold stated. In 2014, Farenthold’s former communications director, Lauren Greene, filed a lawsuit against him, claiming a hostile work environment, gender discrimination, and retaliation, as indicated by court documents. Farenthold and Greene reached a mediated resolution in 2015 to avoid expensive litigation; however, the specifics of the settlement were kept confidential, as stated at the time, with Farenthold denying any wrongdoing.

(In the 13th paragraph of the December 18 article, it is corrected to note that a distinct attack occurred in June, impacting FedEx computers.) By Dustin Volz WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Trump administration has officially accused North Korea of initiating the WannaCry cyberattack, which severely disrupted hospitals, banks, and various businesses worldwide earlier this year. The attack was extensive and incurred billions in costs, with Tom Bossert, President Donald Trump’s homeland security adviser, stating in an article published on Monday night in the Wall Street Journal that North Korea is directly accountable. Bossert commented that North Korea has engaged in particularly harmful activities, largely without repercussions, for over a decade, and its malicious actions are increasingly severe. He described WannaCry as indiscriminately reckless. A senior administration official indicated that the White House was anticipated to issue a more formal statement assigning blame to Pyongyang on Tuesday. The U.S. government has assessed with a very high level of confidence that the hacking group known as Lazarus Group, operating on behalf of the North Korean government, executed the WannaCry attack, according to the official, who requested anonymity to discuss the details of the government’s investigation. Security researchers and U.S. officials widely believe that Lazarus Group was behind the 2014 cyber intrusion at Sony Pictures Entertainment, which resulted in lost files, leaks of corporate communications online, and the resignation of several high-ranking studio executives. Representatives from the North Korean government were not immediately available for comment. The nation has consistently denied any involvement in WannaCry and has labeled other claims regarding cyberattacks as a smear campaign. According to the administration official, Washington’s public denunciation does not involve any indictments or naming specific individuals; rather, the intention behind this shaming is to hold Pyongyang accountable for its actions and to undermine their capacity to conduct further attacks. This accusation comes amid rising concerns over North Korea’s hacking abilities and its nuclear weapons program. Numerous security researchers, including those from the cybersecurity firm Symantec, along with the British government, have already concluded that North Korea was likely behind the WannaCry attack, which rapidly spread across the globe in May, infecting over 300,000 computers in 150 nations. At the time, it was regarded as unprecedented in scale, as WannaCry incapacitated British hospitals, resulting in thousands of patients needing to reschedule appointments, and disrupted infrastructure and businesses globally. Initially, the attack appeared to be a ransomware scheme, where hackers encrypt a targeted computer and demand payment to restore access to the files. However, some experts later suggested that the ransom threat may have served as a smokescreen to conceal a more destructive agenda. Additionally, a separate but analogous attack in June, referred to as NotPetya, targeted Ukraine and other countries, resulting in approximately $300 million in damages for international shipper FedEx. Some researchers believe that WannaCry may have been unintentionally released by North Korea while hackers were still developing the code. The senior administration official refrained from commenting on whether U.S. intelligence could determine if the attack was intentional. The official remarked, "What we observe is an ongoing pattern of North Korea’s misconduct, whether through destructive cyberattacks, hacking for financial gain, or targeting global infrastructure." WannaCry was enabled by a vulnerability in Microsoft’s Windows software, which was identified by the U.S. National Security Agency and subsequently utilized by the NSA to create a hacking tool for its own operations. Following a significant security breach at the NSA, that hacking tool, among others, was made publicly available online by the Shadow Brokers, a mysterious group known for regularly posting cryptic taunts directed at the U.S. government.

text: Germany's Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel refuted a claim on Saturday regarding his aspirations for the finance minister position. According to Reuters, the Social Democrat, whose party has consented to engage in discussions with Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservatives about establishing a coalition, denied the report. text: YANGON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, two Reuters reporters who have been in detention in Myanmar for the last fortnight were ordered to remain in custody for an additional 14 days as investigations continue regarding claims that they violated the country's Official Secrets Act. Judge Ohn Myint approved the 14-day extension for journalists Wa Lone, aged 31, and Kyaw Soe Oo, aged 27, at the request of law enforcement, who subsequently transported them to Insein prison in Yangon. Prior to this, they were held in a police facility. During their appearance at Mingaladon court, Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo were permitted to see their families and legal counsel for the first time since their arrest. The two journalists had been involved in Reuters' reporting on the crisis in Rakhine state, where an estimated 655,000 Rohingya Muslims have fled due to intense military actions against militants, according to the United Nations. They were taken into custody on December 12 after being invited to a dinner with police officials. The Ministry of Information has alleged that they unlawfully obtained information with the intent to share it with international media, facing charges under the Official Secrets Act from the British colonial era, which carries a potential maximum prison term of 14 years. The journalists stated that they had not faced any mistreatment while detained. "The situation is okay," Wa Lone remarked following the hearing. "We will handle this as best we can because we have done nothing wrong. We have not breached media laws or ethics. We will keep striving to do our best." A spokesperson for Reuters expressed that the two should be released. "These journalists are being detained for merely performing their duties and have not committed any wrongdoing. Approximately 100 journalists, lawyers, and farmers protested in Pyay, located 290 km (180 miles) north of Yangon, demanding the release of the two journalists, as reported by one of the demonstrators. Members of the Protection Committee for Myanmar Journalists sat in chains in a public square in the town's center, inscribing the names of the two arrested reporters on their hands, a common gesture of solidarity in Myanmar for those imprisoned. Their attorney, Than Zaw Aung, who has been engaged by Reuters, reiterated that the two were simply fulfilling their responsibilities as journalists. "They are facing accusations while performing their duties in the media," he told reporters. Lieutenant Colonel Myint Htwe, a senior officer with the Yangon Police Division, stated, "We took action because they committed the crime. It needs to be resolved in court." Only the journalists' lawyer and family members, along with police and government attorneys, were permitted entry into the courtroom. "I would like to ask the government to consider their release." Nyo Nyo Aye, the sister of Kyaw Soe Oo, mentioned that her brother asserted he had not committed any wrongdoing. "I believe he can return home soon," she said.

text: The global perception of the United States has significantly declined under President Donald Trump, according to a survey conducted by the Pew Research Center. Five months into Trump's presidency, the study, which encompassed 37 countries, indicated that U.S. favorability ratings dropped to 49 percent from 64 percent at the conclusion of Barack Obama’s two terms in office. The declines were notably more pronounced among some of America's closest allies, such as its neighbors Mexico and Canada, as well as European partners like Germany and Spain. Trump, who assumed office in January, promised to prioritize 'America First'. Since taking office, he has initiated plans to construct a wall at the U.S.-Mexico border, declared intentions to exit the Paris climate agreement, and criticized nations including Canada, Germany, and China for perceived unfair trade practices. During his inaugural foreign visit in early June, Trump was warmly welcomed in Saudi Arabia and Israel, but encountered a lukewarm reception from European allies, where he faced disputes regarding NATO funding, climate change, and trade issues. Currently, only 30 percent of Mexicans express a favorable opinion of the United States, a decrease from 66 percent at the end of the Obama administration. In Canada and Germany, favorability ratings fell by 22 points, landing at 43 percent and 35 percent, respectively. In several European nations, the ratings were reminiscent of those observed at the end of George W. Bush's presidency, particularly following his controversial 2003 Iraq invasion. The Pew report highlighted that 'the decline in favorability ratings for the United States is widespread,' noting that the positive perception of the U.S. has drastically fallen across a variety of regions, including Latin America, North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa. The survey, which gathered responses from 40,447 individuals between February 16 and May 8 of this year, revealed even greater skepticism towards Trump personally, with only 22 percent expressing confidence in his judgment on global matters, in contrast to 64 percent who placed their trust in Obama. Both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping received higher confidence ratings, at 27 percent and 28 percent, respectively, while German Chancellor Angela Merkel achieved the highest rating among the four leaders surveyed, at 42 percent. The countries exhibiting the least confidence in Trump were Mexico, at 5 percent, and Spain, at 7 percent. The only two nations where confidence ratings improved compared to Obama were Russia, which saw an increase to 53 percent from 11 percent, and Israel, which rose by 7 points to 56 percent. Worldwide, 75 percent of participants characterized Trump as 'arrogant,' 65 percent labeled him as 'intolerant,' and 62 percent deemed him 'dangerous.' Additionally, a majority of 55 percent considered him a 'strong leader.' The survey indicated broad disapproval of Trump’s key policy initiatives, with 76 percent opposing his proposal to construct the border wall with Mexico, 72 percent against his withdrawal from significant trade agreements, and 62 percent opposed to his travel restrictions on certain majority-Muslim countries. Conversely, the survey revealed that 58 percent of respondents held a positive view of Americans in general. Furthermore, in numerous parts of the world, a majority or plurality of respondents anticipated that U.S. relations would remain relatively unchanged despite Trump’s presidency.

text: As U.S. President Donald Trump prepares for his trip to the Philippines, he receives significant approval from American veterans. SUBIC, Philippines (Reuters) - Trump is well-known for stirring controversy, facing intense criticism both domestically and internationally. However, in Subic, a town in the Philippines, he is regarded as a hero. Once the site of one of the largest U.S. naval bases globally, Subic serves as a retreat for retired military personnel who are excited about Trump's visit and believe that the polarizing businessman can do no wrong. "Trump, I support him wholeheartedly," stated Mike McCarthy, a former master chief of the U.S. 7th Fleet, while enjoying a drink in one of the American-themed bars that populate Subic's main street, which features names like "Alaska," "Crazy Horse," and "Rolling Stone." He expressed his views on Trump's opponents, saying, "They won’t let him govern, but he’s smarter than them, always a step ahead." Trump will arrive in Manila, the capital, on Sunday to attend a summit of Asian leaders, wrapping up a tour that has included visits to Japan, South Korea, China, and Vietnam. "He’s just approaching things differently, with his tweeting and strong rhetoric. But where has he made a mistake so far?" McCarthy remarked. Originally from Florida and a resident of Subic for ten years, McCarthy noted that Trump’s regard for veterans makes him very popular among them and within military circles. "If he invited me to meet him in Manila, I would go immediately," he added. Trump is scheduled to meet with Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, aiming to strengthen relations that have been strained by Duterte's unpredictable anti-U.S. stance and his desire for closer ties with Russia and China. Attending the summit alongside Trump will be leaders such as Chinese Premier Li Keqiang, Russian Premier Dmitry Medvedev, and representatives from Japan, South Korea, India, Australia, New Zealand, and ASEAN member states. For security, the Philippines will deploy nearly 60,000 police and military personnel. The Philippines has long been a crucial defense partner for the U.S. Despite the closure of the base in 1992, Subic has continued to see a steady influx of retirees and visits from U.S. naval vessels for repairs, resupply, and training exercises. Approximately 220,000 Americans, many of whom are military veterans, reside in the Philippines, with an additional 650,000 visiting annually, according to figures from the U.S. State Department. Subic has retained its American ambiance, featuring bars that offer military discounts and eateries serving a wide range of dishes from baby-back ribs, buffalo wings, and steaks to burgers named "shotgun" and an omelet called "the sheriff." The town is also home to tattoo shops, liquor stores advertising bourbon whiskey, and a Harley Davidson repair shop catering to the easy-rider motorcycles that have been a staple in this community of 100,000 residents, located about a three-hour drive north of Manila. Veteran James Goodman, 51, has operated six bars throughout his 13 years in Subic. His current establishment, "Sit-n-Bull," includes bar games, live sports, and rock music that competes with the lively conversations of tattooed patrons in tank tops. The bar's walls showcase vehicle license plates from Florida, Ohio, California, and Nevada, alongside a neon-lit USA sign in red, white, and blue. A guitar hangs next to a wooden carving of a Native American and a schedule for American Football playoffs featuring hot dog promotions. "I’m very pleased that Donald Trump is coming here; I believe he and President Duterte will have a good rapport," said Goodman, who hails from New Jersey. "He’s for the American people... His business partner Ronn Oliver, 54, who manages a nearby restaurant bearing the same name, commented that veterans respect Trump and are aware of his astuteness. "He needs to garner more support, so people..."

text: The trial of the alleged mastermind behind the Benghazi assault commenced in Washington. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Monday, federal prosecutors initiated their case against Ahmed Abu Khatallah, asserting that he was the architect of the 2012 attack on a U.S. diplomatic facility in Benghazi, Libya, which resulted in the deaths of U.S. Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. Khatallah has been in custody since 2014, following his capture by a U.S. military and FBI team in Libya, and subsequently transported over a 13-day period to the United States aboard a Navy ship. In his opening remarks at the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, federal prosecutor John Crabb stated that Khatallah harbors a profound hatred for America and played a significant role in the orchestration of the assault on the U.S. diplomatic mission on September 11, 2012. He noted that while Khatallah did not ignite the fires or discharge the mortars, he would be shown to be just as culpable as those who did. Khatallah, facing charges that include murder and providing material support to terrorists, sat at the defense table dressed in a white shirt and wearing headphones that facilitated an Arabic translation of the proceedings. Defense lawyer Jeffrey Robinson contended that his client was not involved in planning the attack, claiming, "The evidence is going to show that Mr. Abu Khatallah did not participate in the attack." The session on Monday featured distressing testimony from Special Agent Scott Wickland, who recounted efforts to rescue Stevens and State Department employee Sean Smith as they crawled through thick, black smoke while flames engulfed the mission. "Initially, I had my hand on the ambassador and we were crawling," he recounted. "I was breathing through the last centimeter of air at ground level... and I was shouting to the others, 'Come on! We can make it!' And within that 8 meters, they vanished." Crabb, the prosecutor, also provided a preview of additional testimonies that the jury would hear from witnesses alleging they overheard Khatallah discussing his role in the attack. One witness, who was later compensated with $7 million to assist in luring Khatallah to the location of his capture, is expected to tell jurors that he heard the defendant proclaim he "would have killed all of the Americans that night," according to Crabb. Additionally, Crabb presented grainy video footage from the attack night, showing images of over half a dozen individuals believed to be Khatallah's associates. Khatallah was visible in one video as armed militia entered a room containing closely guarded maps and other documents. Robinson asserted that his client went to the mission out of curiosity about the events unfolding and cautioned others to stay away from the gunfire. He further claimed that some of the government witnesses "are individuals who lie." The trial, which will continue on Tuesday, is anticipated to extend over several weeks.

text: The Supreme Court's emissions decision will not hinder the push for clean energy. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - According to state regulators and utilities on Wednesday, the transition in the U.S. power sector towards reduced coal usage and an increase in natural gas and renewable energy will remain on track despite the Supreme Court's ruling against the Obama administration's carbon emissions restrictions. On Tuesday, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 5-4 to halt the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) initiative to limit carbon emissions from coal plants until a legal dispute is resolved. Although some states may delay their efforts to comply with the EPA’s Clean Power Plan, several experts expressed optimism that the rule will hold up against legal challenges when the D.C. circuit court delivers its ruling this summer. "In a way we are really just postponing the inevitable," remarked Vicki Arroyo, executive director of the Georgetown Climate Center. Even in the 27 states that filed lawsuits to challenge the rule, officials had already been developing compliance strategies. The majority of states indicated they would persist in decarbonizing their energy sources. Utilities nationwide have started a significant transition from coal-fired electricity towards cleaner and more affordable options like natural gas and renewable sources such as wind and solar. "We fully expect that many of these states will continue their efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions under their own legal authorities," stated Bill Becker, director of the National Association of Clean Air Agencies. States such as California, Colorado, and New York voiced their disapproval of the Supreme Court’s ruling and pledged to advance their clean energy initiatives regardless of the delay in the EPA regulation. Conversely, states like Montana and North Dakota, which participated in the lawsuit against the EPA, welcomed the relief that the stay provides. Nevertheless, even opponents of the rule asserted they would continue to diversify their energy portfolios. Colorado’s Democratic Governor John Hickenlooper mentioned that the state would maintain its compliance efforts to avoid being at a disadvantage if the courts uphold some or all aspects of the Clean Power Plan. Even though Colorado challenged the EPA's plan, the governor supports it, while the state’s Republican attorney general disagrees on the legality and economic implications of the rule. Montana's Democratic Governor Steve Bullock opposed the EPA regulation, indicating that the state would pause the efforts of a group tasked with developing compliance options, but emphasized the need to "address climate change and embrace Montana’s energy future." He expressed his commitment to ensuring that this is done on the state’s own terms. For North Dakota, a coal-producing state with one of the highest emission reduction targets under the rule, regulators and utilities will continue exploring methods to reduce emissions from power plants, according to state health department head Dave Glatt. He noted that the EPA plan did not provide the state "a sufficient amount of time to have reasonable solutions" and committed to "look at reasonable steps forward." Coal-fired electricity generation has been declining in most states. In 2015, more than 15,000 megawatts of coal-fired power plants were shut down by generators, marking the highest amount in any single year, primarily due to low gas prices reducing power costs. It became financially unfeasible to upgrade older coal plants to comply with existing federal clean air regulations. Ohio regulators indicated on Wednesday that they were uncertain how the state would react to the court ruling, but the major utilities in the state are already moving away from coal. American Electric Power Co Inc (AEP.N) will persist in generating more electricity using natural gas and renewable resources, as prices for these have significantly decreased, according to spokeswoman Melissa McHenry. She added that the five-year extension of federal renewable energy tax credits has motivated AEP to incorporate more renewable energy into its portfolio. "It makes sense that we are sticking to our current plans, and will be positioned to respond to the courts’ ultimate decision on the future of the Clean Power Plan," she stated. text: An arrest warrant for former Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont would be 'normal' if he does not testify, according to the Supreme Court. MADRID (Reuters) - The president of Spain's Supreme Court indicated on Thursday that if Puigdemont, who has been ousted, fails to show up in court, the typical course of action would be to issue an arrest warrant. Supreme Court President Carlos Lesmes stated that when an individual does not appear after being summoned by a judge to give testimony, it is standard practice in Spain, as well as in any other EU nation, to issue an arrest warrant. On Wednesday, Puigdemont announced that he would disregard a court directive to return to Spain to face charges related to the region's bid for independence. He did not attend a High Court session on Thursday.

text: As Donald Trump's representative to Congress, Mike Pence may encounter a significant hurdle - his superior. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Soon after Donald Trump secured victory in the U.S. presidential election in November, Vice President-elect Mike Pence made a visit to the nation's largest manufacturing lobby, situated six blocks from the White House, to discuss Trump’s legislative priorities. According to Aric Newhouse, NAM’s senior vice president of government relations, the dialogue at the National Association of Manufacturers was constructive, featuring a lot of mutual exchange. The business organization believed that Pence was conversing in their terms and anticipated progress on longstanding objectives, including tax code simplification and the repeal of Obamacare, President Barack Obama’s hallmark legislation aimed at expanding health insurance coverage to more Americans. However, in the past week, Trump has introduced uncertainty regarding some of his legislative goals. He voiced criticism over a crucial component of his Republican Party’s tax strategy, referred to as the border adjustment tax. Additionally, he appeared to blur the clarity of his commitment to repeal Obamacare by advocating for healthcare coverage for all. While NAM was not overly concerned, this incident underscores the difficulties Pence, 57, will face as he acts as the primary representative to Capitol Hill for Trump, who will be inaugurated as the 45th U.S. president on Friday. Pence has spent twelve years as a congressman starting in 2001, establishing many personal connections, particularly among conservatives. While he is not widely recognized on Capitol Hill as a negotiator, lawmakers, aides, and lobbyists describe him as friendly and an effective communicator who treats both allies and adversaries with respect. Nevertheless, the NAM situation illustrates that Pence's greatest challenge in securing agreements in Congress might be Trump himself. This is because those negotiating with Pence may not always be certain if he is conveying his boss's views. Pence and Trump are quite different in their approaches. While Trump tends to be confrontational and seeks the spotlight, Pence, who was most recently the governor of Indiana, is composed and steady, characterized by both Republicans and Democrats as articulate and positive. Few vice presidents in contemporary U.S. history have played as significant a role in legislative matters as Pence is expected to. Former Vice President Dick Cheney negotiated agreements and persuaded lawmakers for President George W. Bush, but Pence’s role may encompass even more. During Trump's initial 100 days in office, Pence will be “leading the charge” on several initiatives in Congress, including revising Obamacare and reforming the tax code, senior Trump advisor Kellyanne Conway informed Reuters. “He has the confidence and the approval to proceed with this from President Trump,” Conway stated. “He is a crucial participant in every serious dialogue and key decision, particularly regarding the legislative agenda,” she added. Although Pence seems to be included in Trump’s inner circle, it remains uncertain who has the closest relationship with the new president or whether they will align with Pence’s views. Even with Republicans in control of both Congressional chambers, Pence will require considerable political skill to unite the party’s occasionally unruly members behind Trump’s agenda once it is fully outlined. The party remains fragmented, ranging from the conservative Tea Party faction to moderate Republicans. Numerous Republicans oppose Trump on matters like free trade and express concerns he might be overly inclined to increase spending, potentially leading to larger budget deficits. In the 1990s, while in his home state of Indiana, Pence sharpened his communication abilities as a talk radio personality. However, his understated demeanor sharply contrasted with many conservative radio commentators. He has humorously labeled himself “Rush Limbaugh on decaf,” in reference to the renowned right-wing talk show host known for his provocative remarks. Pence, who was raised in a Catholic environment and later embraced evangelical Christianity, occasionally led Bible study sessions in his House of Representatives office. Texas Representative John Carter participated in these gatherings.

text: The theft incident at the fire-damaged Grenfell Tower complicates the laborious efforts of the police. LONDON (Reuters) - While already engaged in the daunting task of searching through the wreckage for human remains at Grenfell Tower, the London social housing structure where approximately 80 individuals lost their lives due to a fire, law enforcement must now also look into alleged thefts from the apartments of survivors. Situated in one of London’s wealthiest boroughs, Grenfell Tower was home to a low-income, diverse community and was devastated by a fire that swiftly consumed the entire building in the early hours of June 14. This disaster has sparked a nationwide discussion regarding social disparities, the neglect of underprivileged communities, and whether fire safety regulations were insufficient or disregarded. Authorities are undertaking a criminal investigation into the fire, which could result in manslaughter charges; however, police officials indicated on Tuesday that any legal actions might take several months due to the investigation's extensive nature and complexity. "The scale of it is something that I personally have never encountered in policing," remarked Commander Stuart Cundy, who oversees the Grenfell operations. Ongoing efforts to recover all human remains from the tower include officers meticulously searching devastated apartments and sifting through tons of debris using sieves to locate fragments of teeth, bones, or tissue. "It is a really harrowing scene," stated Detective Superintendent Fiona McCormack, who leads the search and recovery efforts. Sixty victims have been officially identified, and Cundy mentioned that the ultimate death count would likely be slightly under 80. The building remains unstable, and each room must be secured individually with steel bars to ensure safety for investigators. Due to non-operational elevators, workers are required to transport equipment and materials all the way up the tower. The catastrophe has elicited a wave of emotional responses, with contributions of money and clothing streaming in from across Britain, although there have also been a few instances of individuals attempting to exploit the tragedy. McCormack noted that police were examining one confirmed theft involving a significant amount of money taken from one of the less damaged units at the base of the tower, along with three additional suspected thefts of residents' belongings. These incidents were uncovered when former residents were allowed to enter their flats to retrieve cherished possessions and bid farewell to their homes. Stuart expressed the shock of the officers involved. "All of us here, whether working directly on Grenfell Tower or in any other capacity, are deeply disappointed that something like this could occur in the wake of such a catastrophic event," he said. Additional alarms, cameras, and lighting have been installed, and access procedures to the site have been tightened. Police are also looking into eight instances of suspected fraud involving individuals who falsely claimed to have been affected by the fire to obtain funds provided by the government for survivors and grieving families. Two individuals have been charged with fraud, one is on police bail, and five others are under investigation. The criminal investigation into the fire itself is being conducted by hundreds of officers and is concentrating on four key areas: the construction of Grenfell Tower, its refurbishment, its management, and the emergency response to the fire. "I will seek to identify and address any offenses that emerge during that investigation," stated Detective Chief Inspector Matt Bonner, who oversees the criminal inquiry. text: Legislation in Oklahoma is set to address the punishment for sexual offenses. OKLAHOMA CITY (Reuters) - Next week, lawmakers in Oklahoma will consider a bill designed to guarantee that sexual crimes are prosecuted in cases where victims were either intoxicated or unconscious at the time of the incident. In March, the highest criminal court in Oklahoma determined that the state’s laws regarding rape do include instances of sexual assault where victims were incapacitated. However, the court indicated that the law regarding forcible sodomy, which also covers oral sex, does not encompass these situations. This decision stemmed from a case involving a Tulsa teenager accused of sexually assaulting a girl who had lost consciousness after drinking. A lower court judge had previously dismissed the case last year. On Friday, Oklahoma Representative Scott Biggs, a Republican, announced that he would be introducing legislation to clarify the definition of forcible sodomy to explicitly include victims who are unconscious. Biggs stated that the bill has significant support and is anticipated to be reviewed by the Oklahoma legislature soon. "The judges made a significant mistake, but if they require further clarification, we are willing to provide it by amending the statute," Biggs remarked in an interview. The ruling from the state’s highest criminal appeals court noted: "Sodomy cannot occur where a victim is so intoxicated as to be completely unconscious at the time of the sexual act of oral copulation." Furthermore, it remarked, "we will not extend a statute beyond the reasonable interpretation of its wording to justify prosecuting someone for an offense." The March ruling largely went unnoticed until this month when the public interest news organization Oklahoma Watch highlighted it, leading to significant public reaction. The 2014 case involved two high school students who were socializing with friends while consuming alcohol and marijuana. The boy claimed that the oral sex was consensual, while the girl asserted that it was not, as reported by Oklahoma Watch, which also noted that the teen’s DNA was discovered on the girl. "Sadly, legal professionals often get bogged down by semantic debates, despite the fact that most of us understand the law's intent," Biggs stated. "I cannot emphasize enough how remorseful I am for the victim and how she was denied justice," he further added.

text: BANGKOK (Reuters) - As Thailand gets ready to conduct the elaborate funeral for its esteemed King Bhumibol Adulyadej next week, hotels in the bustling old town of Bangkok, which is popular among international travelers, are fully booked, according to the hotel association on Monday. The funeral service for King Bhumibol, who passed away on October 13 last year after reigning for seventy years, will take place over five days next week, primarily at the Grand Palace and Sanam Luang, a public square located in the historic district. Approximately 250,000 mourners are anticipated to participate in the funeral, which will showcase gold-tipped pavilions specifically constructed for this occasion, and October 26, the day designated for the cremation, has been established as a national holiday. Many Thais hoping to be present for the cremation believe that having nearby accommodations would be more practical, which is why nearly all hotels have already been reserved, stated Supawan Tanomkieatipume, president of the Thai Hotels Association, in an interview with Reuters. A survey by Reuters of three hotels along Khao San Road, the main thoroughfare of the Banglamphu backpacker district, revealed that there were no available rooms. "We are fully booked during the royal cremation," commented Preechaya Amngeun, 23, a guest services representative at the Ibis Styles Bangkok Khaosan Viengtai, which is part of the French hotel group Accor. "About 80 percent of our guests are Thai. The remaining 20 percent are international tourists." The tourism sector in Thailand, which contributes to 12 percent of the country's GDP, has been one of the few bright spots for an economy that has faced challenges since the coup in 2014. text: SYDNEY (Reuters) - Papua New Guinea's Immigration Minister Petrus Thomas announced that on Monday, authorities would initiate actions to forcibly evacuate approximately 450 men who are currently residing in an abandoned Australian detention facility lacking food and running water. For over 13 days, hundreds of men have barricaded themselves within the Manus Island center, resisting efforts by both Australia and Papua New Guinea to shut down the site, expressing concerns for their safety if relocated to transit centers. Thomas stated in a press release late on Sunday, "We will be taking steps with relevant authorities to move the residents based on serious exposure to health risk for the food of everyone that is remaining." As of 5:00 p.m. (0700 GMT) on Monday, several asylum seekers within the center informed Reuters via email that the government had not yet taken action to remove the men. An asylum seeker inside the facility mentioned on Monday that the water supply had been compromised after Papua New Guinea workers entered the location and drained rainwater collected in tanks and bins. "Immigration came and bored holes in the water tanks where we had been collecting rain water," he stated, requesting anonymity due to fears of retaliation from Papua New Guinea authorities. "They also demolished the well we built." Two weeks ago, running water and electricity were cut off to the center following the withdrawal of Australian security personnel, and the camp was officially closed on October 31. A Papua New Guinea Court had ruled the center illegal. The United Nations has issued warnings about a potential humanitarian crisis among the asylum seekers, who primarily come from Afghanistan, Iran, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Syria. Australia has utilized this center, along with a facility on the small Pacific island of Nauru, to detain asylum seekers who attempt to reach its shores via boat. The Australian government asserts that boat arrivals will never be allowed to enter Australia, even if they are recognized as refugees, as this would encourage human trafficking in Asia. Under a refugee swap arrangement, the United States has consented to accept up to 1,250 asylum seekers from Manus and Nauru, in exchange for Australia agreeing to take in refugees from Central America. text: U.S. Defense Secretary cancels trip to Afghanistan due to inclement weather. ABU DHABI (Reuters) - The defense secretary for U.S. President Donald Trump announced that he had to call off a visit to Afghanistan on Sunday because of poor weather conditions, but stated he was assessing the future course of the war following talks with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani and the leading U.S. commander. "We’re currently gathering our thoughts," Defense Secretary Jim Mattis told journalists in Abu Dhabi during his first visit to the Middle East. U.S. General John Nicholson, who heads U.S. and international forces in Afghanistan, mentioned earlier this month that the NATO-led contingent in Afghanistan had sufficient personnel to conduct counterterrorism operations, but experienced a "shortfall of a few thousand" for its primary function of advising Afghan security forces. Mattis indicated that he had a lengthy video-link conversation with Nicholson on Sunday, yet did not reveal his stance on deploying additional U.S. military forces there. Additionally, Mattis stated he had an extensive discussion with Ghani "at length" prior to departing Munich, Germany, on Saturday. Thus far, Trump has provided little guidance on whether he will authorize an increase in troop numbers for Afghanistan, where approximately 8,400 U.S. soldiers remain deployed more than 15 years after the fall of the Islamist Taliban regime. "He’s awaiting my evaluation and the feedback from the intelligence community, and he’s receptive to my recommendations on the matter," said Mattis. "But first, I need to clarify my position." Afghan government forces govern no more than two-thirds of the nation's territory and have encountered difficulties in managing the Taliban insurgency since the majority of NATO troops withdrew at the end of 2014. The government is also facing challenges from other militant groups, especially from the Islamic State’s branch in Afghanistan. The Islamic State took responsibility for a suicide bombing that claimed the lives of at least 22 individuals on February 7 outside the Supreme Court of Afghanistan. Several provincial capitals have been under duress from the Taliban, and Afghan government forces have experienced significant casualty rates, with over 5,500 killed in the initial eight months of 2016. "The Afghan security forces have paid a tremendous cost to keep the Taliban pressured. However, they managed to achieve that," said Mattis. "And the Taliban finds itself in a more precarious situation today, even though I do not equate that with success on our part."

The letter, spearheaded by Representative Eliot Engel, who is the leading Democrat on the committee, asserted, "The exodus of talent from the State Department jeopardizes the institution and weakens American leadership, security, and interests globally." text: Some schools in Syria are removing references to Assad, but tensions regarding the Kurdish population are escalating. HAZIMA, Syria (Reuters) - The few schools that escaped destruction or sabotage by the Islamic State around Raqqa, once a stronghold of the group in Syria, are alive with the sounds of children learning for the first time in several years. In Hazima, a village located north of Raqqa, teachers recently conducted spontaneous alphabet lessons for crowded classrooms on a summer day just before the new school term began.   "Right now, the most important thing is to get children into class," stated teacher Ahmed al-Ahmed, beside a hole in the staircase left by a mine explosion that injured a colleague. The extremist organization Islamic State had closed this school and many others throughout northern Syria after taking control of the area in 2014, three years into the civil war. Instead of education, it indoctrinated children in extremist ideologies within mosques. However, following the group's expulsion from most of the territory it controlled around Raqqa by a U.S.-supported military coalition known as the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), a rising discussion about education has arisen, highlighting the ethnic tensions anticipated to emerge. The curriculum being taught in SDF-controlled regions, which consists of Arab militias but is primarily led by the Kurdish YPG, raises many questions about the governance of predominantly Arab regions in northern Syria as they integrate into the Kurdish framework. This year, schools in the Raqqa area will implement a new curriculum that utilizes old textbooks while omitting the Baathist principles of President Bashar al-Assad, a decision reached by both Arab and Kurdish educators. Yet, an official from the SDF has suggested the immediate introduction of Kurdish language classes in Raqqa's schools, a proposal that has caused local officials to react with disapproval. Unlike other SDF-controlled areas where Kurdish has been taught for years, there are currently no plans to include the language in mostly Arab Raqqa. Officials assert that broad consensus would be necessary, indicating worries that a hasty introduction could lead to unrest.  "We wouldn’t object to Kurdish being taught. However, if it’s forced upon the schools, then problems will arise," Ahmed remarked. The YPG has maintained control of regions in northeast Syria since the beginning of the six-year conflict, regions that now operate under a self-governing authority opposed to Assad, who controls the main population centers in the west and is also advancing against the Islamic State, along with Turkey, a rival of the YPG that shares a border with Syria. Officials predict that Raqqa will likely join this administration. All ethnic groups are represented in the local governing bodies managing predominantly Arab areas that were captured by the SDF during their campaign against IS fighters; however, critics argue that Kurds have a disproportionate influence on decision-making. Interviews conducted by Reuters with SDF officials and local authorities indicate that resentment towards Kurdish dominance is growing regarding educational policies. A high-ranking SDF advisor and liaison with the U.S. coalition expressed his belief that Kurdish would be taught to Kurdish students in the Raqqa area this year, following the established model for other schools within SDF territory.  "No one has opposed this ... every (ethnic) group has the right to learn in its own language," Amed Sido communicated via the internet. Officials from the newly-formed Raqqa Civil Council, the local governing body, were surprised by this suggestion.  "No, that won’t happen without discussions with us and an agreement in the council," Ammar Hussein, an official from the education committee, stated at their office in the town of Ain Issa.  Currently, classes are conducted in Arabic, with additional lessons in English and French. Echoing the sentiments of several council members, he indicated that Kurdish would only be taught if families expressed interest, there were sufficient qualified instructors, and the Arab-Kurdish council approved the initiative.  "If the community agrees ... there won’t be any objection," remarked Ali Shanna, another member of the education committee.  However, a former Kurdish educator privately criticized Shanna’s viewpoints.  "I dislike that perspective. It’s ignorance; it’s akin to the mindset of Daesh (Islamic State)," commented the teacher, who had previously faced imprisonment under Assad for writing a Kurdish-language journal.

text: The Pentagon has put forward a defense budget proposal of $582.7 billion for 2017, which focuses on rising threats from Russia, China, and Islamic State militants. However, this proposal is already facing criticism from Republican lawmakers who argue it does not sufficiently support the U.S. military. President Barack Obama’s final budget aims to increase funding for the fight against Islamic State forces to $7.5 billion in the fiscal year 2017, representing a 50 percent increase from the $5 billion allocated this year. Of this amount, $200 million is designated for combating militants in northern and western Africa. The proposal also intends to increase funding to counter Russian aggression in Europe fourfold, in light of its annexation of Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula and frequent strategic bomber missions near NATO airspace. The funding to enhance the U.S. military presence and training in Europe is set to rise from $800 million this year to $3.4 billion. This budget indicates a strategic transition as Washington shifts its focus from the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan to a new era of competition with major powers such as Russia and China, as well as challenges from smaller adversaries including Iran and North Korea, according to officials. "This budget signifies a critical turning point for the Department of Defense," Defense Secretary Ash Carter stated. "While we contend with current conflicts, we must also prepare for potential challenges that may arise in the next 10, 20, or 30 years." Overall, the administration is proposing a base Pentagon budget of $523.9 billion for the fiscal year commencing on October 1, alongside $58.8 billion earmarked for war expenditures and overseas operations. The base budget reflects an increase of approximately $2.5 billion compared to this year, while war funding remains relatively stable, officials indicated. This spending plan aligns with a congressional budget agreement reached last year, which established funding parameters for the Pentagon for 2016 and 2017. Nevertheless, Republican lawmakers have voiced their discontent with the war funding proposal, contending that the $59 billion figure in the budget agreement was intended as a minimum, not a maximum, and that the president should have requested additional funds. "This request falls short of addressing the national security threats we confront," remarked Senator John McCain, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, in a statement. Congressman Mac Thornberry, chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, accused the administration of engaging in "budgetary games." McCain pointed out that by aiming for the lowest level of war funding in the budget deal, the president has left the Pentagon with $17 billion less than it projected it would require for 2017 in last year’s budget. To compensate for the budgetary shortfall, the Pentagon has reduced more than $5 billion by revising its expectations regarding fuel costs and inflation rates, according to Pentagon Comptroller Mike McCord. Additionally, procurement funding has been decreased to $112.1 billion, which is a 6 percent reduction from this year’s figures. These cuts will primarily affect planned aircraft acquisitions, including the reduction of five F-35 Joint Strike Fighters and several types of Army helicopters, as indicated in budget documents. While procurement spending is being cut, the Pentagon plans to increase investment in research and development by 4 percent, raising it to $71.8 billion, as it aims to create new technologies to maintain a military advantage. The department has allocated $16.8 billion for its classified military intelligence accounts. Furthermore, it has decided to postpone until 2022 the controversial retirement of the A-10 close air support aircraft, which is currently in use against Islamic State forces. The decision to retain the aircraft will incur a cost of $3.4 billion over the next five years. The budget also continues the trend of reducing the size of the U.S. Army, which will decrease to 460,000 soldiers in 2017 from the current force of 475,000. In addition, the president’s budget includes funding for a new polar icebreaker vessel, with a budget of $150 million, to ensure year-round access to the Arctic for Coast Guard operations.
