text: According to a report released on Thursday by the U.N. Human Rights Committee, Australia needs to modify its migration legislation. The committee, which consists of 18 independent experts responsible for overseeing compliance with a global human rights agreement, recommended that Australia cease its practice of rejecting refugees and align its laws with international standards. They requested that Australia return in a year to provide an update on the measures it has undertaken to address their concerns. Australia has faced significant criticism from both the United Nations and human rights organizations for its policy of detaining asylum seekers attempting to reach its territory by boat, even when they are recognized as refugees, and for holding them in offshore processing facilities located in Nauru and Papua New Guinea. The U.N. has issued warnings regarding an impending humanitarian crisis at the Manus Island facility in Papua New Guinea, which was shut down on October 31; however, 600 asylum seekers remain unwilling to leave due to fears of violent retribution from local residents if they relocate to transit centers while awaiting potential resettlement in the United States. Vice-chair Yuval Shany of the committee noted that while the recommendations are not legally binding, it seems Australia is not taking its obligations seriously. "We do not dispute Australia’s right to enforce strict policies, particularly regarding resettlement," he stated. "However, they cannot treat asylum seekers as criminals and detain them, nor can they neglect their responsibility to avoid sending them back to perilous situations." He remarked that it is unusual for a developed nation with a commendable human rights history to publicly dismiss the committee's recommendations one after the other, as Australia has done. The government was not immediately available for a response. Earlier, Immigration Minister Peter Dutton reaffirmed on 2GB radio his support for the detention policy, which the government argues is essential to dissuade asylum seekers from attempting dangerous maritime journeys to Australia, asserting that they would not retreat from evictions at Manus. The offshore detention strategies are supported by both the center-right government and the Labor opposition. The U.N. committee urged Australia to reduce the duration of mandatory initial detention, limit overall detention, and ensure that children are not detained except as a last resort and for the shortest possible duration. They also called on Australia to guarantee that the international principle of not returning refugees to danger is enshrined in law and strictly followed. The committee expressed concerns regarding conditions in Manus and Nauru, highlighting serious safety issues and reports of assaults, sexual abuse, self-harm, and suspicious deaths. Furthermore, it suggested that Australia consider shutting down the Christmas Island detention facility, as it is deemed too isolated to provide adequate protection for those held there.

text: U.S. legislators have come to an agreement on Wednesday that will facilitate a vote in the Senate regarding new sanctions against Russia. This vote is set to occur as soon as this week and will also prevent President Donald Trump from lifting sanctions on Moscow without the approval of Congress. Earlier on the same day, Russia issued a warning that it was approaching a point of retaliation against the United States after the House of Representatives supported additional sanctions against Moscow. The European Union expressed concerns that these actions might jeopardize its energy security and indicated its readiness to respond as well. Senator Bob Corker, the Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, stated in a Wednesday evening announcement, "I am pleased to inform you that we have reached an agreement that will enable us to send sanctions legislation to the president’s desk." He noted that the Senate would proceed to approve the sanctions on Russia and Iran that it had initially passed in mid-June, along with sanctions on North Korea developed by the House and incorporated into a bill that received overwhelming support in the House on Wednesday. Prior to the recent agreement, some senators had raised objections to the North Korea provisions, leading to concerns that the sanctions bill, already postponed since mid-June, might extend into September. If the Senate passes the bill as anticipated, it will be forwarded to the White House for Trump’s approval or veto. However, it is expected to have sufficient backing to counter a Trump veto. On Tuesday, the House voted 419-3 to implement new sanctions against Moscow and to mandate that Trump secure approval from lawmakers before easing any punitive measures against Russia. Dmitry Peskov, a spokesperson for the Kremlin, remarked, "This is quite unfortunate news from the perspective of Russia-U.S. relations," adding, "We are discussing an extremely unfriendly act." He indicated that President Vladimir Putin would determine the manner and extent of Moscow's retaliation once the sanctions become law. Russia's deputy foreign minister cautioned that this move was driving bilateral relations into unfamiliar territory, extinguishing hopes for improvement in the near future. Trump, who has been embroiled in a contentious dispute regarding alleged connections between his associates and Moscow, is facing scrutiny regarding accusations that Russia aided in his election victory last year. He has expressed a desire to restore relations with Russia, which are at a post-Cold War low. Trump has denied any collusion between his campaign and Russia. Most observers of the White House anticipate that Trump will reluctantly endorse the new sanctions, given the strong support they have among U.S. lawmakers and his intent to avoid perceptions of being lenient towards Moscow. Representative Ed Royce, the Republican chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, indicated that Trump would have limited options. The Senate had passed a version of the legislation, excluding the North Korea sanctions, on June 15 with a vote of 98-2. Royce expressed on NBC’s Meet the Press Daily on Wednesday, "I believe the president will sign it." This situation has unsettled Russia, which worries that its economy, already weakened by the 2014 Western sanctions related to its involvement in the Ukraine crisis, may now struggle further to recover and expand. Foreign investors might be deterred. The European Union is concerned that new U.S. restrictions could create barriers for its companies operating in Russia and jeopardize the bloc’s energy supply chains. The Kremlin’s alleged interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election is a significant factor driving lawmakers to advocate for these new sanctions. Peskov mentioned that Moscow would hold off on a complete analysis of the sanctions and a decision on how to respond until they become law. Moscow had been hopeful that Trump, who had previously made positive remarks about Putin before assuming the presidency, would strive to mend the U.S.-Russia relationship. However, it has become increasingly frustrated as the allegations of vote meddling have dashed any hopes for improved relations. This month, the Russian Foreign Ministry stated that there were too many American spies operating in Russia under the guise of diplomatic roles.

text: BEIJING (Reuters) - Sources indicate that a prominent ally of President Xi Jinping is anticipated to receive a promotion to the position of vice chairman of China’s Central Military Commission, as Xi reinforces his authority over the military. Zhang Youxia, aged 67, is among the limited number of senior military figures with combat experience and is favored to become one of at least two vice chairmen on the commission, as reported by four sources, including three with direct connections to the leadership. Xi serves as chairman of the commission, which oversees the People’s Liberation Army, in addition to being the nation’s president and the general secretary of the Communist Party of China. Zhang is set to take over the role from Fan Changlong, who is anticipated to retire at the upcoming 19th Communist Party Congress commencing on Wednesday. The other vice chairman, Xu Qiliang, is expected to remain in his position, according to the sources. Both Xi and Zhang hail from the northwestern province of Shaanxi and are offspring of former high-ranking officials who fought alongside each other during the civil war in the 1940s. The Defence Ministry of China did not respond to a faxed request for comment. The party is currently considering a proposal to increase the number of vice chairmen on the military commission from two to four while reducing the number of other committee members, which currently stands at eight, according to some sources. Since taking power in late 2012, Xi has restructured the commission and the military as he tackles corruption and streamlines the armed forces, which number 2 million, making it the largest in the world. Approximately 300,000 troops have been dismissed, and advanced new technologies such as stealth fighters have been developed. Although China has not engaged in warfare for decades, it is adopting a more assertive stance in the contested East China Sea and South China Sea, as well as concerning self-governing Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Two departing members of the commission are presently under investigation for suspected corruption, as per sources who have informed Reuters, though the government has yet to verify this information. This is not the first instance of corruption issues within the military. A previous vice chairman, Guo Boxiong, received a life sentence for graft last year, while another former vice chairman, Xu Caihou, passed away from cancer in 2015 before he could face trial for alleged corruption. Currently, Zhang ranks eighth among the 11 members of the military commission. He is also expected to be elevated to the Communist Party’s 25-member Politburo, one of its elite ruling entities, according to three sources. One source with connections to the leadership noted that Xi and Zhang’s fathers - Xi Zhongxun and Zhang Zongxun - were close associates. Both fathers fought together in the civil war that concluded in 1949, resulting in the Communist victory and the establishment of the People’s Republic of China. Both men ascended to significant roles within the government and military. The next generation of both families also shares a close relationship, the source added, referring to Xi and Zhang. Born in Beijing, Zhang Youxia enlisted in the army in 1968, advancing through the ranks and joining the military commission in late 2012. He participated in the brief border conflict with Vietnam in 1979, which China initiated in response to Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia the previous year that led to the ousting of the Beijing-supported Khmer Rouge. At the age of 26, Zhang was deployed to the frontlines to confront the Vietnamese, where he excelled and was rapidly promoted, as stated by state media. He also engaged in another border skirmish with Vietnam in 1984. During the confrontation, whether on the offensive or defensive, Zhang Youxia distinguished himself, according to a piece published by the official China Youth Daily in August titled, 'These Chinese generals have killed the enemy on the battlefield.' Another officer recently advanced, Li Zuocheng, who was appointed chief of the Joint Staff Department of the People’s Liberation Army in August, also fought in the 1979 war. Li is also expected to join the ranks of the commission’s vice chairmen, but it remains uncertain if he will also be included in the Politburo, the sources noted.

text: TOKYO (Reuters) - On Saturday, Japanese authorities apprehended three members of a North Korean crew for allegedly stealing a generator from a shelter on an uninhabited island, as reported by public broadcaster NHK. This incident is part of a series of events following a rise in the number of North Korean fishing boats arriving off the coast of Japan. Some of these vessels have been found in distress, while others have been abandoned or discovered with deceased individuals on board, leading to concerns over potential espionage as tensions with North Korea escalate due to its missile and nuclear activities. North Korea has conducted two missile tests over Japan, a nation it has threatened with destruction. Most analysts believe that the wooden boats are primarily manned by fishermen, including military personnel conscripted for fishing duties. There has been no indication that the crew members are seeking asylum. Last month, a boat carrying 10 crew members was located docked at the island near Hokkaido, with several crew members stating they had taken electronic items from the hut, according to NHK. Police have detained three individuals for theft, while the remaining crew members will be directed to the Immigration Bureau, NHK reported. Hokkaido police were not available for immediate comment. A representative from the Japan Coast Guard refrained from making any statements. According to the coast guard, there were 28 incidents of boats either adrift off Japan or stranded on its shores in November, up from only four in the same month last year.

text: LONDON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, British Prime Minister Theresa May faced new efforts to extract concessions regarding her strategy for exiting the European Union, marking the second day of a parliamentary discussion that is intensifying divisions over Brexit. May's position has been undermined by the loss of the Conservative Party's majority in the June elections, and she is encountering resistance from numerous lawmakers, including some from her own party, regarding various aspects of the EU withdrawal bill that necessitate parliamentary endorsement. All proposed amendments to the bill concerning the severance of ties with the EU have been rejected thus far, but a forthcoming debate next month on the specific timing of Britain's exit, and whether a definitive date should even be established, is anticipated to challenge her leadership. May called on lawmakers to collaborate ahead of a discussion on several amendments intended to solidify EU protections across a broad spectrum of issues, from environmental concerns to workers' rights. "We will be leaving the European Union on the 19th of March, 2019, and of course there is a lively debate going on in this place and that’s right and proper, and that’s important," May stated during the weekly prime minister's question time. "We are listening carefully to those who wish to improve the bill and I hope that we can all come together to deliver on the decision that the country took that we should leave the European Union." The debates are expected to extend over several weeks regarding a bill that May considers vital for ensuring that businesses remain confident that no significant legal changes impacting commerce will occur when Britain exits the EU in March 2019. During the first day of discussion on Tuesday, lawmakers crossed party lines, engaging in a tumultuous exchange filled with catcalls, jeers, and allegations of betrayal. The underlying concern for pro-Brexit lawmakers is the possibility that Britain may not actually leave the EU, while pro-EU politicians are apprehensive about the prospect of a no-deal exit. The date of departure has become a central point of contention within parliament, with some lawmakers asserting that pro-Brexit politicians are seeking a firm date within the bill - 11:00 p.m. on March 29, 2019 - to restrict flexibility during negotiations with the EU, which are currently stalled primarily over financial issues. May and her ministers are increasing their engagement with EU officials, looking for strategies to apply pressure on negotiators in Brussels to advance discussions by December, which businesses assert is necessary for making investment choices. On Wednesday, May met with Manfred Weber, a prominent member of the European Parliament and an associate of German Chancellor Angela Merkel, in London, where he conveyed optimism that the challenges in the negotiations could be surmounted. The parliamentary debate adds to the list of challenges for a prime minister who has already lost two ministers due to scandals and is facing demands to dismiss her foreign minister, Boris Johnson, over comments he made regarding a detained Iranian-British aid worker in Iran. She has made attempts to alleviate tensions by offering lawmakers some compromises on the bill, yet she has not succeeded in persuading all of her party members, many of whom have indicated that they will not support the government on at least one of the debates, specifically regarding the "exit day."

text: SANTIAGO (Reuters) - The candidates for the Chilean presidency concluded their campaigns in the heart of Santiago on Thursday, just days ahead of an unpredictable runoff election that will decide if the world's leading copper producer shifts towards the right or continues on its center-left path. On Sunday, voters will select between billionaire conservative Sebastian Pinera and Alejandro Guillier, a senator and journalist representing the center-left. The initial round of voting in November saw an unexpected rise of more radical leftist candidates, which took analysts by surprise, caused market declines, and paved the way for a runoff that is anticipated to be closer than expected. Guillermo Holzmann, a professor at the University of Valparaiso, remarked, "Everything points to a narrow margin of victory. It's an unusual race in that it's been difficult to gauge the electorate." Both Pinera and Guillier are committed to maintaining the long-established free-market economic model in Latin America’s most developed nation. However, candidates with more extreme positions on both ends of the political spectrum performed better than anticipated in November, prompting both candidates to adjust their platforms in an attempt to attract voters from those whose initial choices did not advance. Former Uruguayan president Jose 'Pepe' Mujica, a leftist figure in a region that has largely leaned rightward, came out in support of Guillier. "The conservative right has no future in Chile," Guillier expressed to his supporters. Pinera, 68, a previous president and the candidate favored by the markets, led the first round with 36.6 percent of the vote. He has pledged to stimulate growth by reducing the corporate tax rate and rolling back the tax, labor, and education reforms instituted by outgoing President Michelle Bachelet, which Guillier intends to expand. Speaking at Santiago's Caupolicán theater, he promised a "new and improved treatment of the middle class, older adults, and children." The 64-year-old Guillier, hailing from northern Chile, secured 22.7 percent of the November vote from supporters who aim to protect the advances achieved during Bachelet’s administration for students, women, and workers, including initiatives like reduced university fees and laws that empower unions. To win over leftist voters, Guillier has suggested a reform of the nation’s privatized pension system and a constitutional rewrite. On the other hand, Pinera has attempted to attract centrist voters by advocating for free technical education for the underprivileged and a public pension option. Guillier narrowly surpassed Beatriz Sanchez from the leftist Frente Amplio, who finished in third place. Sanchez garnered support from 20 percent of voters with her promises to tax the "super-rich" to enhance social spending and combat inequality. The 1.3 million voters who backed Sanchez are viewed as crucial in the forthcoming election. In Chile, voting is not mandatory, and voter turnout has been notably low in recent years. "It comes down to how many people stay home, and particularly, how many people stay home on Guillier’s side," noted University of Chile professor Robert Funk.

text: The U.N. aviation organization is advocating for the establishment of a universal drone registry. MONTREAL (Reuters) - The United Nations aviation organization is supporting the development of a comprehensive global drone registry as part of wider initiatives to establish standardized regulations for the operation and monitoring of unmanned aerial vehicles. Although the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) lacks the authority to enforce regulations on nations, it has suggested the creation of the registry during a symposium in Montreal this month, aimed at providing real-time data access, according to Stephen Creamer, the director of ICAO's air navigation bureau. This unified registry would replace several databases with a centralized system that would enable law enforcement to remotely identify and monitor unmanned aircraft, along with their operators and owners. This initiative emerges as drone usage continues to increase in the United States, Europe, and China, raising concerns regarding privacy and the potential for collisions with commercial airliners. "There needs to be some commonality to avoid having five receivers in your police vehicle," Creamer stated in an interview on Thursday. It remains uncertain who would manage such a database, although ICAO could potentially take on that responsibility. However, the proposal might encounter resistance from users, particularly after hobbyists successfully contested the establishment of a U.S. drone registry by the Federal Aviation Administration in court earlier this year. ICAO is set to host the symposium from September 22-23, focusing on topics such as drone registration and tracking, along with geofencing systems designed to restrict operations in certain areas. Experts and companies, including Google, Rockwell Collins (COL.N), and Amazon.com (AMZN.O), are expected to attend the discussions, as indicated in the meeting program schedule. Headquartered in Montreal, ICAO typically formulates standards for international civil aviation, which are adopted by its 191 member countries. It was requested to assist in creating more uniform domestic drone regulations due to the global nature of remotely-piloted aircraft sales and operations. "The manufacturers (of drones) are concerned that Europe might implement one set of regulations, the United States another, and China a third. Consequently, they need to design drones differently for each of these markets," Creamer noted. Parimal Kopardekar, a lead researcher for Unmanned Aircraft System Traffic Management (UTM) at NASA's Ames Research Center in California, expressed his support for the drone industry evolving globally with consistent operational standards. "I believe it is wise for ICAO to pursue harmonization," he remarked via phone. "If you manufacture a drone in one nation, you should be able to utilize it in another nation and the same applies in reverse."

text: Trump promotes tax reform while neglecting to mention aide Cohn. SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (Reuters) - On Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump delivered his inaugural significant speech regarding tax reform, yet in his extensive list of acknowledgments, he failed to mention Gary Cohn, the White House's chief tax advisor who accompanied Trump to the event. Speaking at a manufacturing firm in Springfield, Missouri, Trump reiterated his long-standing proposal to reduce the U.S. corporate tax rate from 35 percent to 15 percent, despite lawmakers thinking they might only manage to lower it to 25 percent. When questioned about the absence of Cohn’s name, White House spokeswoman Sarah Sanders responded to reporters aboard Air Force One, on the way back to Washington from Missouri, stating that it is customary for Trump to acknowledge Cabinet members but not advisors during speeches. Cohn was present on Air Force One with Trump for the Missouri address, where Trump urged Democrats to support his tax reform initiative. He emphasized his intention to reduce taxes and streamline the extensive U.S. tax code for the middle class. However, he provided limited details, and tax reform is expected to be a challenging endeavor in Congress. "We need to decrease the tax rate on American businesses so they can retain jobs in America, generate jobs in America, and compete for workers right here in America," Trump articulated in his first presidential address focused explicitly on tax reform, a central issue during his 2016 campaign. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress agree that tax reform is necessary, but the Republican objective of passing legislation this year faces significant obstacles in Congress, which has already struggled to achieve the healthcare reform that Trump desires. During his speech, Trump did highlight Cabinet members, including Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, and Small Business Administration head Linda McMahon, along with various members of Congress — totaling over a dozen individuals. He even requested his daughter Ivanka Trump, who is a staff member but not a Cabinet member, to stand and be acknowledged during his address at the manufacturing facility in Springfield. "Did I forget anyone?" Trump inquired. Cohn, who was positioned next to the stage during the speech alongside Sanders, has been collaborating closely with Mnuchin for months to formulate Trump’s tax reform strategy. "It’s fairly standard for us not to specifically mention staff," Sanders remarked to reporters afterward. "He often mentions Cabinet members but infrequently acknowledges staff in his speeches." When asked if the omission of Cohn was noteworthy, Sanders replied, "Well, look, Gary is here. The president is present. They are both diligently working and wholly dedicated to delivering tax relief for middle-class Americans. The president has made it abundantly clear that this is a top priority for him and his administration, and Gary is among those leading the effort." Cohn recently voiced criticism of Trump regarding his remarks on the violence that occurred during racially charged protests in Virginia earlier this month. Trump attributed blame for the violence in Charlottesville to "both sides," which involved clashes between white supremacists, neo-Nazis, and anti-racism demonstrators. His comments received backlash from both Republican and Democratic circles. Cohn conveyed to the Financial Times last week that the Trump administration "can and must do better in consistently and unequivocally condemning" hate groups. The former Goldman Sachs executive, who is Jewish, stated that he faced "enormous pressure" to resign due to Trump’s statements. TAX REFORM UNLIKELY BEFORE YEAR-END Analysts and lobbyists outside of Congress are growing increasingly skeptical that legislative action can be achieved by the end of 2017, with some predicting that the final tax legislation might resemble a straightforward tax cut rather than comprehensive reform. "I don’t want to be let down by Congress. Do you understand me?" Trump asserted to enthusiastic applause. He argued that tax reductions for businesses would result in increased wages for workers by fostering economic growth and enhancing the competitiveness of American companies, a claim that Democrats dismiss as merely a continuation of the "trickle-down" economic policies they argue have neglected workers in recent decades.

text: U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to include a stop in China during his upcoming trip to Asia in November, according to a U.S. official on Tuesday. This visit will occur against the backdrop of rising tensions regarding North Korea’s nuclear activities. The United States and its allies have expressed increasing urgency for China, which is North Korea’s primary ally and trading partner, to exert more influence on its isolated neighbor to persuade it to reduce its nuclear weapons and missile programs. During their meeting in April in Palm Beach, Florida, Chinese President Xi Jinping extended an invitation to Trump to visit China. The two leaders also met informally during the G20 summit in July. In November, Trump is scheduled to participate in the U.S.-ASEAN summit and the East Asia summit in the Philippines, as well as the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Vietnam. The Chinese foreign ministry has yet to respond to a request for comment from Reuters regarding Trump’s prospective visit. Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported unnamed diplomatic sources indicating that Trump is also contemplating a visit to Japan and South Korea as part of his Asian itinerary in November. In February, Trump accepted an invitation from Prime Minister Shinzo Abe to visit Japan by the end of the year. A Japanese Foreign Ministry official stated, "The February agreement is still valid. General Assembly in New York. Citing unnamed government sources, the newspaper stated that the meeting involving Trump, Abe, and South Korean President Moon Jae-in could occur on September 21 and would aim to enhance cooperation in response to provocations from North Korea. Despite being dismissed by Trump last month, Bannon reported during a private lunch in Hong Kong that he still "speaks with President Donald Trump every two to three days," according to the Wall Street Journal.

text: South Africa's Supreme Court has significantly increased Oscar Pistorius' murder sentence, more than doubling it on Friday. The court agreed with the prosecutors' assertion that the initial six-year prison term for the shooting death of his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, was excessively lenient. The celebrated athlete, who is a double amputee famously known as the 'Blade Runner' due to his carbon-fiber prosthetics, was absent during the announcement of his new sentence of 13 years and five months. Although Steenkamp's family did not attend the proceedings, they expressed approval of the revised sentence, which is the minimum 15 years mandated for murder, taking into account the time Pistorius has already served, and stated it demonstrated that justice can prevail in South Africa. 'This is an emotional thing for them. They feel that their faith in the justice system has been reaffirmed today,' said Tania Koen, a spokesperson for the family, to Reuters. Advocacy groups in a nation plagued by elevated rates of violent crime against women claim that Pistorius, 31, received favorable treatment in comparison to non-white individuals and those lacking his wealth or fame. Barry Steenkamp, the father of the deceased model, mentioned to SABC television that the family could now move forward with their lives. 'From the very beginning, I said justice had not been served; now it has,' he stated. In the same interview, her mother, June Steenkamp, commented: 'We felt that we didn’t have justice for Reeva with that overly lenient sentence, but now we have justice for her.' Carl, Pistorius’ older brother, expressed his feelings on Twitter, stating: 'Shattered. Heartbroken. Gutted.' The athlete's legal representatives were unavailable for comment. Pistorius was imprisoned in July of the previous year after being found guilty on appeal of murdering model and law graduate Steenkamp on February 14, 2013, by firing four shots through a locked bathroom door. The case drew international attention. Initially, he was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to five years in prison. This conviction was elevated to murder by the Supreme Court in December 2015, and his sentence was extended to six years by trial judge Thokozile Masipa in July of the previous year. Masipa noted in court that while the Steenkamps had endured a significant loss, the life and career of the 'fallen hero' Pistorius were also in shambles, and that a lengthy sentence would not serve justice. Pistorius' appearance during the trial without his prosthetics elicited gasps from those in the courtroom. In a sharp rebuke, the appeals court stated that Masipa's decision had improperly strayed from the mandated minimum sentence of 15 years for murder. 'The six-year sentence is shockingly lenient, to the extent that it trivializes this serious offense,' remarked Judge Willie Seriti, who delivered the unanimous court ruling. 'In my opinion, there are no substantial and compelling circumstances that could justify straying from the prescribed minimum sentence.' Seriti also criticized Pistorius, stating that his apology to the family of the victim during the hearing failed to show any genuine remorse and that he does not grasp the seriousness of his actions. State prosecutors, led by advocate Andrea Johnson, argued during the appeals hearing this month that there were no mitigating factors that could warrant Pistorius' six-year sentence. Defense attorney Barry Roux contended that Pistorius did not intentionally kill Steenkamp and that the appeal should be dismissed. Roux had previously claimed during the July 2016 trial that Pistorius' disability and mental anguish following the incident should be considered as factors for reducing his sentence. Pistorius reached the semi-finals of the 400 meters at the 2012 London Olympics and won two gold medals in the Paralympics. Even while incarcerated, he has remained in the news; in August, he was granted temporary release to attend his grandmother's funeral and spent a night in the hospital due to what local media reported as a suspected heart attack. In August 2016, the athlete denied allegations of attempting to take his own life.

text: Frankfurt will require the evacuation of 60,000 individuals to safely dispose of a British World War II bomb. FRANKFURT (Reuters) - Approximately 60,000 residents of Germany's financial hub, Frankfurt, are set to be ordered to vacate their residences on Sunday, as a significant World War II bomb found at a construction site is rendered safe, according to police reports. The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, Frankfurt's Goethe University, and at least two hospitals are also included in the evacuation, marking one of the most extensive evacuations in Germany's post-war era. The 1.4-ton HC 4000 bomb, which was released by the British air force during World War II, was located at a construction site on Wismarer Strasse in Frankfurt's affluent Westend, an area known for its wealthy bankers. Bomb disposal specialists who assessed the situation indicated that the large-scale evacuation could be postponed until the weekend. "We are still coordinating the details of the evacuation plan," stated a spokeswoman for Frankfurt police on Wednesday.

text: Trump to endorse Palestinian 'self-determination' during Middle East visit: advisor. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Donald Trump plans to show support for Palestinian "self-determination" on his upcoming trip to the Middle East this month, a senior advisor stated on Friday, indicating that Trump is receptive to a two-state solution regarding the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, despite not having publicly accepted the concept thus far. The statement from U.S. National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster followed just nine days after Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas visited the White House, where Trump committed to pursuing a significant peace agreement but refrained from explicitly reaffirming the ultimate aim of Palestinian statehood, a longstanding principle of U.S. policy. In anticipation of Trump’s inaugural foreign journey, McMaster also mentioned that he would leverage a stop in Saudi Arabia, his initial destination, to motivate Arab and Muslim allies to take "bold new actions" against those associated with Iran, the Islamic State, al Qaeda, and the government of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad “who foster chaos and violence.” Trump’s travels, starting late next week and also including visits to Israel and Rome, are designed to "send a message of unity" by visiting sacred sites of Christianity, Judaism, and Islam, McMaster informed reporters. Trump’s discussions with Israeli and Palestinian leaders, which are currently scheduled to take place separately, will be closely observed to see if he begins to outline a coherent strategy to revive the long-stalled negotiations. Many experts are doubtful about Trump’s likelihood of achieving a peace agreement that has eluded his predecessors. In his discussions with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Trump intends to "reaffirm America’s unwavering bond with the Jewish state" and express to Abbas "his aspiration for dignity and self-determination for the Palestinians," as stated by McMaster, a distinguished Army general with substantial experience in the Middle East. Trump is anticipated to meet Abbas, the Western-supported leader of the Palestinian Authority, in Bethlehem within the West Bank, according to Palestinian sources. Palestinians expressed disappointment when Trump did not mention a two-state resolution during a joint appearance with Abbas on May 3. Trump faced international backlash in February when, during a news conference with Netanyahu, he seemed to step back from a long-standing U.S. commitment to Palestinian statehood, stating he would leave the decision to the involved parties. The establishment of an independent state is not only the goal of the vast majority of Palestinians but has also been the aim of numerous U.S. administrations and the global community. When asked if Trump would bring Netanyahu and Abbas together in one room during the visit planned for May 22-23, McMaster indicated that it would depend on the president and the other leaders. "The final arrangements aren’t confirmed yet," he remarked.

text: Clinton's outreach director for the Asian-American community is departing from the campaign. (Reuters) - The individual in charge of Democratic presidential hopeful Hillary Clinton’s outreach to Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders is leaving the campaign to take a position with the Colorado Democrats, a campaign representative confirmed on Saturday. Lisa Changadveja's exit comes prior to Democratic nominating events in states with a significant percentage of Asian American voters, including Washington later this month and California in June. "She played a crucial role in establishing our AAPI program, and these initiatives will persist with events planned for the upcoming weeks," campaign spokesperson Xochitl Hinojosa stated in an email to Reuters. "We anticipate announcing a new Director of AAPI Outreach shortly." Changadveja informed campaign supporters of her decision to leave in an email dated March 18, expressing her "strong belief in the campaign’s dedication and capability to keep engaging our community as we progress through the primary and get ready for the general election." "I will be departing from Hillary for America as I have recently accepted a new position with the Colorado Democratic Party," she mentioned in the email, which was reviewed by Reuters. Changadveja did not respond promptly to requests for comments. Minority groups have been critical voting demographics for the Clinton campaign, aiding her in securing victories against Bernie Sanders, the U.S. senator from Vermont who is her primary opponent for the Democratic nomination for the presidential election on November 8. Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders comprise approximately 6 percent of the U.S. population, a statistic that excludes individuals of mixed race, as reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. They constitute nearly 15 percent of California's population, where the nominating contest occurs in June, and about 9 percent of Washington state, which is set to hold its Democratic caucus on March 26. Asian Americans are also among the fastest-expanding ethnic groups in the United States, at times surpassing the growth rate of the Latino population, according to the Census. A study conducted by the University of California, Los Angeles last year projected that the Asian-American electorate will increase to 12 million voters by 2040. Changadveja became part of the Clinton campaign in September, as indicated on her LinkedIn profile. Previously, she held the position of LGBTQ and AAPI director for Ready for Hillary, a Super PAC that backed Clinton's presidential aspirations, according to her profile.

text: Trump introduces new elements to his immigration proposals, but legal uncertainties continue. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Donald Trump, the Republican presidential hopeful, has suggested suspending immigration from regions known for terrorism, which may have a legal justification; however, his claim that this should be part of a wider prohibition on Muslim immigrants renders it constitutionally problematic, according to legal experts. This fresh angle in Trump's anti-Muslim discourse emerged following a shooting rampage at a Florida nightclub by an American-born individual whose parents are Afghan immigrants. In a passionate address on Monday, he elaborated on his proposed temporary prohibition on Muslims entering the U.S., promising that if he were to win the presidency, he would cease immigration from any part of the globe that has a "proven history of terrorism" against the United States or its allies. He further accused the Muslim-American community of widespread complicity in incidents like the Orlando shooting, which was perpetrated by a shooter swearing allegiance to the Islamic State, and warned of "significant consequences" for those who do not report suspicious activities by their neighbors. Numerous legal authorities indicated that Trump's plan for a religion-based ban would likely fail to meet the standards set by U.S. constitutional protections of religious freedom, due process, and equal protection, suggesting that it would be likely overturned by the courts if he attempted to enforce it through presidential order. Nevertheless, a restriction on immigrants from certain nations does have some historical precedent and could potentially be upheld. Some view this new proposal as similar to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which was employed for years to curb the influx of Chinese laborers and is regarded as a dark chapter in America’s immigration history. However, Trump's comprehensive immigration strategy would extend beyond that, targeting not only a nation or geographic area but also specific religious groups, a move that no recent U.S. president has undertaken. "This is an outlandish proposal to construct a Fortress America and raise the drawbridges," remarked John Bellinger, a former legal adviser to the Bush administration. President Barack Obama subtly criticized Trump on Tuesday, stating that such notions signify a "dangerous" mindset. However, U.S. presidents possess considerable authority over immigration issues, and some conservative legal scholars asserted that the success of any proposed ban would depend on how narrowly Trump defines it. They pointed out that, for example, Democratic President Jimmy Carter prohibited Iranian nationals from entering the United States during the 1979 Iran hostage situation. "If a Trump administration were to halt immigration from specific countries instead of certain religions, it would not breach the Constitution," stated John Yoo, a law professor at the University of California Berkeley and a former Justice Department official who counseled the George W. Bush administration on interrogation techniques used on terrorism suspects. Herman Schwartz, a law professor at American University in Washington, indicated that if Trump adhered to his plan for a temporary ban on Muslim immigrants, it would raise significant constitutional issues and "demonstrates his uncertain grasp of the legal realities." In his speech on Monday in New Hampshire, Trump displayed little inclination to retract his demand for a ban on Muslims entering the United States, a stance he initially articulated in December following a mass shooting linked to the Islamic State in San Bernardino, California. The discussion surrounding the legality of Trump's proposals is complicated by the ambiguity of his statements and uncertainties regarding how broadly he would enforce any immigration restrictions if elected. While legal scholars assert that presidents hold the authority to prohibit immigrants from particular countries, the U.S. does not currently impose bans on immigration from any specific nation. Officials do provide enhanced scrutiny to individuals entering from nations such as Syria and Iran. Under the broadest interpretation of Trump's statements, immigration could be restricted not only from predominantly Muslim countries but also from U.S.-allied nations in Europe and Asia that have experienced militant attacks.

text: Federer edges past Tiafoe challenge to progress. NEW YORK (Reuters) - The world’s third-ranked player, Roger Federer, faced a first-round challenge from Frances Tiafoe but ultimately secured a 4-6 6-2 6-1 1-6 6-4 win against the young American in front of an enthusiastic audience at the U.S. Open on Tuesday. Federer showed more relief than joy when Tiafoe’s forehand went into the net on match point, allowing him to continue his pursuit of a 20th grand slam title. "We had a good fight," Federer remarked during a post-match interview. "It was thrilling, and this is the reason I came to New York, to experience these emotions," he added with a chuckle. The 19-year-old Tiafoe made a statement by breaking Federer in the very first game of the match and exclaimed a loud "Come on!" after landing a forehand winner that secured him the opening set. Federer, who has claimed victory at this year's Australian Open and Wimbledon following a six-month hiatus last year, eventually found his rhythm after breaking Tiafoe to establish a 3-1 advantage in the second set, going on to win nine of the following ten games. Nonetheless, his previous form faltered during a 23-minute fourth set, as his serve faltered and the precision of his reliable one-handed backhand vanished. Federer expressed confidence in Tiafoe's potential for a successful career. "He is a fantastic player with a promising future ahead of him," he stated regarding the 19-year-old. While he celebrated the victory, the inconsistent performance raised concerns about the condition of the 36-year-old Swiss star, who had missed the Cincinnati Masters earlier this month due to back issues. He admitted he had been anxious about his back prior to the match but mentioned he felt "much, much better." "This victory will boost my confidence significantly," he commented. Due to rain, the quick 2-hour and 35-minute five-set match took place under the closed roof of Arthur Ashe Stadium, amplifying the cheers from the lively crowd. Federer will next face either Slovenian Blaz Kavcic or Russian Mikhail Youzhny.

text: Republican lawmakers appeared to struggle with their party's nominee Donald Trump's rhetoric this week in Congress, leading to some awkward interactions. As they hastily entered elevators, hurried past reporters, and disregarded inquiries or, in some cases, attempted to respond, the discomfort was palpable. Just days following his controversial remarks about a Mexican-American judge, Trump sent shockwaves through the party once more by reiterating his demand for a halt on Muslim immigration after a gunman who declared his allegiance to Islamic extremists took the lives of 49 individuals at a nightclub in Florida. Furthermore, Trump, a former reality television figure, ventured into two contentious areas for social conservatives by supporting the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) community and proposing that the nation might require new gun control measures. For lawmakers used to polished talking points and predictable queries, the week resulted in a chaotic mix of awkward reactions and terse, tight-lipped answers. Senator John Barrasso from Wyoming walked away when questioned about Trump's support for the LGBT community, stating: “I don’t know what the latest is. I haven’t read anything. I haven’t been watching.” Florida Senator Marco Rubio, who previously opposed Trump during the presidential primaries, had to fend off two inquiries about Trump before he could declare his consideration for re-election – a choice that could influence whether Republicans maintain control of the Senate in the upcoming election on November 8. Senator Ted Cruz, another primary competitor, declined to directly address Trump's speech that intensified his stance on Muslims, while Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Burr described it as “an OK speech” before entering an elevator and refusing to answer any further questions. The challenge posed by Trump is evident even to experienced Republicans. "I’m spending my days commenting on everything that Donald Trump says," expressed John McCain, the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee. Orrin Hatch, the Senate's longest-serving Republican, shifted from rejecting Trump's remarks on Muslims to questioning the legality of his suggested immigration ban, ultimately expressing confusion over the billionaire's response to the Orlando shootings. Trump's controversies have also overshadowed House Speaker Paul Ryan's introduction of a policy agenda, a campaign document intended to align Trump's views more closely with mainstream party principles. When asked on Thursday if he was troubled by having to address Trump's statements, Ryan described Trump as “a different kind of candidate...(in) a different kind of year.” When queried about how many more times he would be required to do so, Ryan replied: “I don’t know the answer to that question either.” In a somewhat ironic message directed at his critics within the Republican leadership this week, Trump stated: “Be quiet, just please be quiet. Don’t talk. Please be quiet. Just be quiet.” Ryan's reaction? “...You can’t make this up sometimes,” he remarked. As a political outsider who has never held an elected position, Trump has also indicated that he might not require much assistance from his Republican counterparts in Congress. “We have to have our Republicans either stick together or let me just do it by myself. I’ll do very well,” he mentioned in a CNN interview. “A lot of people thought I should do that anyway, but I’ll just do it very nicely by myself.”

text: The transition team for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under U.S. President Donald Trump is significantly comprised of individuals from the oil industry and pro-drilling organizations, as revealed by a list of the newly formed 10-member team reviewed by Reuters on Monday. The email identifies at least three former researchers linked to think tanks funded by billionaire industrialists Charles and David Koch, along with a former lobbyist for the mining sector. Numerous members of this team have publicly expressed opposition to U.S. initiatives aimed at addressing climate change, which was a primary focus of the EPA during former President Barack Obama’s administration. The composition of the team has heightened expectations that Trump will fulfill his commitment to reduce U.S. environmental regulations to encourage drilling and mining activities. This team is tasked with preparing the agency for new leadership and replaces the original EPA transition group selected by Trump following the November election but prior to his inauguration. Oklahoma Attorney General Scott Pruitt, Trump’s nominee to lead the EPA, is currently awaiting Senate confirmation. The email states, "We are looking forward to working with the career professionals at the EPA to make this transition work as well as possible, and to carry out the Agency’s mission to protect public health and the environment." It continues, "While transitions are always hard, straightforward honest communication combined with respect for each other will make the process work much better." Charles Munoz has been appointed in the email as the White House liaison for the new EPA team. He was a key organizer for Trump during his campaign in Nevada and was instrumental in establishing the state chapter of Americans for Prosperity, a political advocacy organization financed by the Kochs. Another member of the team, David Schnare, is an environmental scientist and lawyer who dedicated 33 years to the EPA as a staff member. Recently, Schnare served as legal counsel at The Energy & Environment Legal Institute, which has received financing from the Koch brothers-associated Donors Trust fund. The institute aims to address "onerous federal and state governmental actions that negatively impact energy and the environment." Schnare has also been affiliated with the Center for Environmental Stewardship at the Thomas Jefferson Institute for Public Policy, which has received partial funding from the Charles Koch Foundation. George Sugiyama, who was part of the initial EPA transition team, is included in the new group as well. He previously served as chief counsel for Republican Senator Jim Inhofe of Oklahoma, who is known for his skepticism regarding climate change. Prior to his role with Inhofe, Sugiyama lobbied on behalf of the National Mining Association. David Kreutzer is also retained from the initial team. Kreutzer was a senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, which is funded by foundations associated with Koch Industries and other energy companies. He has criticized Obama’s climate change initiatives as costly and unjust to specific industries, advocating instead for increased drilling in the Arctic. Doug Ericksen, a current Washington state senator, is the new EPA team’s communications director and previously served as Trump’s deputy campaign director for the northwestern state. Ericksen holds a degree in environmental science and chairs the state senate’s energy and environment committee, opposing the climate policies of Washington state’s Democratic Governor Jay Inslee, including greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. Holly Greaves will manage budget-related matters for the transition team. She previously held the position of senior audit manager at KPMG and worked at Ernst & Young in an advisory services role. Additional team members include Justin Schwab, the legal advisor for the EPA team, who has experience at the law firm Baker Hostetler. Also named is Washington State Senator Don Benton, a Republican with a background running a county environmental department, alongside Patrick Davis, a Republican political figure.

South Sudan descended into civil war in late 2013, just two years after it achieved independence from Sudan, and approximately one-third of its 12 million inhabitants have been displaced. The unrest originated from a dispute between President Salva Kiir and his former deputy Riek Machar, who is currently detained in South Africa, and ultimately resulted in violence along ethnic lines. "We are requesting $1.72 billion to maintain life-saving support and protection for 6 million individuals who are most in need in South Sudan," stated Alain Noudehou, the U.N. Humanitarian Coordinator for South Sudan, during a press briefing. Noudehou emphasized that humanitarian support is essential for those experiencing the repercussions of displacement, food scarcity, malnutrition, violence, and economic hardship. Since the onset of the conflict, around 4 million people have been compelled to leave their homes, with nearly 1.9 million internally displaced and about 2.1 million having sought refuge in neighboring nations, he noted. The ongoing conflict has also resulted in a reduction of crude oil production, which is a critical source of foreign currency, and the resulting instability has hindered food cultivation. Present at the press conference was South Sudan's Humanitarian Affairs Minister Hussein Mar Nyuot. "I believe that if we do not secure the required amount ($1.72 billion) and if donors do not respond, even greater crises will unfold in South Sudan. This could mean that 2018 might be even more challenging than 2017," he warned.

text: The Minnesota Senate may cease its operations and implement employee furloughs starting December 1 due to a funding disagreement with Governor Mark Dayton, as revealed by the Republican leader of the chamber on Wednesday. Senate Majority Leader Paul Gazelka indicated that his chamber will deplete its funds by next month unless the state courts reinstate the funding for the legislature that Dayton vetoed. He mentioned that the Senate intends to request specific funds from the Legislative Coordinating Committee to maintain operations until January 12. "We do not take the suspension of operations of the Minnesota Senate lightly – this is not a game – but we find ourselves with no alternative today," Gazelka stated. The chamber's staff comprises numerous attorneys, analysts, researchers, and assistants who support committees and legislative work. The office of the Democratic governor held Gazelka accountable for the looming shutdown. "Despite having nearly $45 million in available state funds for his operations, he and other legislative leaders are opting to lay off their own personnel instead of acknowledging that they have misled the courts, the media, and the public about their actual financial circumstances," said Matt Swenson, the assistant chief of staff to the governor. In May, Dayton vetoed funding for the Republican-led legislature as part of the state’s new two-year budget to compel lawmakers to amend tax policies that he argued could jeopardize the state's financial health. This action sparked a legal confrontation with lawmakers, who asserted that the removal of nearly $130 million in funding was unconstitutional. Although a judge from the Ramsey County District Court ruled in favor of the legislature in July, the state Supreme Court confirmed on September 8 that the governor's actions were constitutional. Nevertheless, the high court expressed concerns regarding the legislature's ability to function without funding and mandated mediation between the two parties, which ultimately reached a deadlock. Gazelka emphasized the necessity for the court to intervene once more. "After the start of the new year, the residents of Minnesota will lack representation in the legislative branch, not to mention the distress caused to our employees," he remarked. In a court document submitted in September, the House of Representatives indicated that it expected to exhaust its funds by February 1.

He added that the Senate plans to seek certain funds from the Legislative Coordinating Committee which would keep the chamber operating through Jan. 12. “We don’t take the suspension of operations of the Minnesota Senate lightly – this is not a game – but we really have no other choice today,” Gazelka said in a statement. text: An international organization responsible for monitoring compliance with nuclear test bans reported that it detected an unusual underwater sound last week close to the last known location of an Argentine submarine that has gone missing. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO), which is headquartered in Vienna, operates a global system of listening posts that include hydrophones—devices designed to capture sound waves in the ocean. According to a statement from the CTBTO, two of its monitoring stations picked up this unusual signal, and the organization is relaying this information to Argentine officials who are overseeing the search for the ARA San Juan, a submarine that had 44 crew members aboard when it disappeared a week ago. Earlier on Thursday, a spokesman for the Argentine navy indicated that the strange sound detected near the submarine's last known position in the South Atlantic could be indicative of an explosion; however, the CTBTO expressed more caution regarding this interpretation. 'It may be consistent with an explosion, but we cannot confirm this,' stated Mario Zampolli, a hydroacoustic engineer with the CTBTO, in remarks to Reuters. He concurred with the navy spokesman’s characterization of the signal as unusual and brief, noting that its origin is likely non-natural. 'We are also able to determine the timing of the event at that location, which occurred approximately three and a half hours after the last reported contact the submarine had, according to the information available in the news,' he explained. Zampolli also mentioned that the monitoring stations that recorded the signal are situated in both the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, indicating their considerable distance from each other.

text: A senior advisor to Ted Cruz, a candidate for the Republican presidential nomination, criticized Donald Trump’s campaign on Sunday, asserting that it is adopting a "banana republic approach" by claiming that the party's rules for selecting a nominee are biased against him. Ken Cuccinelli, who serves as the delegate operations manager for the Texas senator, expressed this viewpoint during an appearance on ABC’s "This Week," stating that the Trump campaign is contesting the delegate selection process "because they’re getting beat on the ground." On Sunday news programs, Cuccinelli exchanged barbs with Trump’s campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, and Ohio Governor John Kasich, the third Republican candidate, over the delegate selection process. Trump continues to lead in the pursuit of becoming the Republican Party’s nominee for the general election scheduled for November. However, it is still uncertain if the billionaire businessman will secure the required 1,237 delegates to win the nomination on the first ballot at the party’s convention in Cleveland, which will take place from July 18-21. The next significant contest is the New York state primary on Tuesday, where 95 delegates are available. Polls indicate that Trump, a native New Yorker, is well ahead of his competitors, with Cruz and Kasich lagging behind. The most recent CBS News poll, published on Sunday, revealed that Trump is leading in New York with 54 percent support, compared to 21 percent for Cruz and 19 percent for Kasich. On the Democratic side, Hillary Clinton, who previously served as a senator from New York and as U.S. secretary of state, along with Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, will also be appealing to New York voters on Tuesday. Polling suggests that Clinton remains the favorite, although Sanders, who hails from New York City and is seeking an upset victory to maintain his campaign's relevance, has been closing the gap recently. Trump has been increasingly frustrated as Cruz's campaign has outmaneuvered him in the intricate process of securing delegates, which are not merely assigned based on popular votes. During a press conference in Staten Island, New York City, on Sunday, he reiterated his claim that the system is "crooked." He remarked, "You’re basically buying these people," in reference to convention delegates, and added, "I could put them in the best planes and bring them to the best places in the world." However, he stated he was not inclined to attract delegates in that manner, calling it undemocratic. The rules governing delegate selection differ from state to state. Cuccinelli stated that Cruz has been "winning elections. And when we win, Trump whines." He described Trump’s tactics as a "banana republic approach." He continued, "They have a media campaign. But Ted Cruz has built a grassroots campaign." On "Fox News Sunday," Lewandowski highlighted Florida, where Trump achieved a significant primary victory. Nevertheless, Trump is only guaranteed the support of 69 of the 99 delegates from that state, as the chair of the state Republican Party is authorized to appoint 30 delegates. "Ted Cruz performs well in areas where party bosses determine those rules and the public is not able to vote," Lewandowski remarked. Additionally, Paul Manafort, a senior Trump advisor specializing in delegate selection, mentioned to ABC that the campaign plans to contest the outcomes in Missouri and Colorado. However, throughout several interviews on Sunday, Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus repeatedly rejected the notion that the delegate selection rules are unfairly biased against Trump. Kasich mocked Trump and his campaign for alleging that the delegate selection rules are manipulated and that a "dirty trick" allowed Cruz to secure victory in Colorado’s nominating contest without a statewide vote. Kasich, speaking with CNN, advised Trump to "act like you’re a professional. Be a pro." (This story corrects New York state poll numbers in 7th paragraph)

text: Cruz's tax proposal would significantly reduce U.S. revenue and benefit the wealthy: analysis. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - An analysis released on Tuesday by a nonpartisan research organization indicates that the tax plan put forth by Republican presidential hopeful Ted Cruz would decrease federal revenues by $8.6 trillion over a decade, substantially increasing the national debt. Cruz's proposal, which was revealed in November, aims to establish a flat 10 percent tax rate on individual income, primarily favoring high-income families, as per the study conducted by the Tax Policy Center based in Washington. "The plan would lower taxes for most income brackets, with the highest-income households reaping the largest benefits and the poorest receiving the least," stated the Tax Policy Center. The value-added tax suggested by Cruz, a Texas senator who secured a victory in the Republican Iowa caucuses last month, would only account for 70 percent of the tax cut expenses, according to the center. Cruz is aligned with the conservative Tea Party movement, which played a significant role in causing a 16-day government shutdown in September 2013 due to his resistance to a spending proposal aimed at dismantling the healthcare legislation known as Obamacare. The TPC analysis highlighted that high-income taxpayers would experience an average tax reduction of approximately $6,100 in 2017, representing about 8.5 percent of their after-tax income, while individuals earning over $3.7 million would benefit from an average reduction of nearly 29 percent, translating to more than $2 million. "Households situated in the middle of the income spectrum would gain an average tax cut of $1,800, or 3.2 percent of their after-tax income, whereas taxpayers in the lowest income quintile would see an average reduction of $46, or 0.4 percent of after-tax income," the TPC reported. The proposed changes would "enhance incentives to work, save, and invest," but the resulting decrease in revenue would necessitate unprecedented reductions in government spending to prevent borrowing that could elevate interest rates and deter private investment, it noted. text: U.S. House Republicans are in conflict over gun control measures. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, a fractured Republican Party engaged in a dispute regarding gun control legislation that was pieced together after the mass shooting in Orlando last month, casting doubt on U.S. House Speaker Paul Ryan’s capacity to secure passage of the measure. Democrats have criticized the gun control initiative proposed by Republican leaders as insufficient, while a notable faction of around 40 conservative House Republicans declared their opposition as well, arguing that the proposal does not adequately safeguard gun purchasers. According to a statement from the conservative Freedom Caucus, the legislation fails “to do enough to address the threat of radical Islamic terrorism.” The group also raised concerns about “the inclusion of gun control provisions that fail to adequately protect due process.” With the Republican leadership’s proposal facing criticism from both liberal and conservative sides, it remains uncertain whether Ryan can gather the 218 votes needed for approval in the House of Representatives. Last month, the Senate was unable to pass any of the various competing Republican and Democratic gun control proposals put forth in response to the June 12 shooting at a gay nightclub in Orlando, which resulted in 49 fatalities and 53 injuries. During the Senate discussions, Democratic lawmakers organized a sit-in on the House floor to urge Republican leaders to advance legislation that would expand background checks for gun purchases and prevent individuals on terrorism watch lists from buying firearms. The Republican leadership’s bill, introduced last Friday, would allow the government three days to persuade a judge that a gun sale should be prohibited. Ryan stated on Wednesday that he planned to bring it to the floor for a vote either this week or the next, though he acknowledged that many lawmakers were seeking modifications. “The last thing we’re going to do is rush something to the floor that we don’t have right,” Ryan remarked. Representative Matt Salmon from Arizona, a member of the Freedom Caucus, expressed his disapproval of Ryan moving forward with the bill without it first going through the relevant committees. Salmon mentioned that Ryan informed House Republicans in a private meeting that he was hastening the legislation to the House floor because “there are members that need to have this vote” for political reasons in battleground districts that could swing either Republican or Democratic in the elections on November 8. Meanwhile, Democrats continued to exert pressure on Ryan for votes on their more comprehensive gun control initiatives. Representative John Larson of Connecticut, a leader of the Democrats’ sit-in, indicated that his fellow Democrats intend to support Republican mental health legislation that could help prevent certain mass shootings. Larson expressed hope that it would be perceived as a gesture of goodwill toward Republicans for progress on gun control. A large number of gun control advocates gathered outside the House chamber in oppressive heat on Wednesday morning, with 91 individuals clad in orange t-shirts positioned on the steps leading to the House, demanding action. They symbolized the 91 individuals who, according to government data, lose their lives each day in the United States due to gun violence. Many of these fatalities result from suicide.

text: The Czech government has resigned, paving the way for election victor Babis. PRAGUE (Reuters) - The center-left government led by Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka resigned on Wednesday, allowing billionaire Andrej Babis, who emerged victorious in last month's elections, to assume control ahead of an EU summit scheduled for December. The cabinet approved its resignation, which will be presented to the president today, Sobotka informed reporters following a routine governmental meeting. Sobotka's coalition government was the first in 15 years to successfully complete a full four-year term and oversaw significant economic growth that resulted in the lowest unemployment rate in the EU and the fastest wage increases in a decade. Nevertheless, frustrated by the status quo, voters turned to anti-establishment candidates, penalizing traditional political parties in the elections. Babis's ANO party, promising to combat political corruption and manage the state with a business approach, reaped the most benefits from this shift, despite being part of the outgoing administration alongside Sobotka's Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats. ANO has not managed to persuade any of the other eight parliamentary parties to join a coalition. Instead, Babis is pursuing a minority government, which President Milos Zeman is expected to appoint on December 13, enabling Babis to assume power immediately. This timing would allow him to participate in the EU leaders' summit on December 14-15, which will primarily focus on the ongoing negotiations regarding Britain's exit from the EU. Many parties have distanced themselves from Babis, a businessman with a net worth of $4 billion, ranked as the second richest Czech by Forbes, due to police allegations that he unlawfully received a €2 million EU subsidy a decade ago for a farm and convention center by concealing ownership. He asserts that he has done nothing wrong. As a member of parliament, he is protected from prosecution, although the outgoing parliament voted to suspend that immunity, which will reactivate with the new parliament. Some lawmakers who previously voted to allow him to be prosecuted have suggested they might maintain his immunity, thereby postponing any legal actions for this parliamentary term. So far, only the small Communist party has indicated that it might consider tolerating Babis's minority government, but its 15 votes are insufficient to guarantee success in a confidence vote within the 200-seat Chamber of Deputies, where ANO occupies 78 seats. Early votes in the new parliament have shown ANO aligning with the Communists and the far-right, anti-EU, and anti-NATO SPD party, although the latter has thus far stated it will not support or tolerate Babis in a confidence vote. Once Babis is appointed prime minister, he would retain the position even if he were to lose a confidence vote, pending discussions regarding an alternative solution.

text: A coalition of black pastors in Chicago chose to boycott Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s yearly Martin Luther King breakfast on Friday, expressing their dissatisfaction with his management of police shootings. One pastor did attend but disrupted the event with protest chants before being removed. A small group of religious leaders joined demonstrators who obstructed an entrance to the Hyatt Hotel, the venue for the breakfast, vocalizing calls for Emanuel to resign. However, hundreds of African-American leaders from Chicago participated in the breakfast, which was initiated in the 1980s by Harold Washington, the city’s first black mayor, to commemorate civil rights figure King. Bishop Edgar Mullins, the pastor of the Grace Family Worship Center and one of the participants in the boycott, remarked, “This boycott is not in opposition to Harold Washington nor Martin Luther King Jr. This boycott stands for the very cause that they stood for, it was through protesting that achievement was made. To sit by and do nothing is to endorse what is going on.” Local news outlets captured footage of Rev. Matthew Ross disrupting the breakfast, chanting “16 shots and a cover-up,” alluding to the fatal police shooting of Laquan McDonald in 2014, before being escorted out by security personnel. The issue of police killings, predominantly involving men of color, has sparked protests across the United States over the last year and a half. In Chicago, a surge of protests concerning police killings, especially of young black men, has compelled Emanuel to dismiss his police chief and consent to a federal investigation of the police department. The city has also changed its earlier stance on withholding video footage of police shootings. On Thursday, officials released surveillance footage depicting the police shooting of 17-year-old Cedric Chatman in January 2013. Attorneys representing his family assert that the video contradicts police claims that Chatman, a carjacking suspect, was armed with a dark object that he pointed at officers. Alderman Anthony Beale, representing the ninth ward, was among the black leaders who attended the breakfast on Friday. He stated he was present to pay tribute to King’s legacy, which facilitated the possibility of protests. “Either you’re part of the problem or part of the solution. I choose to be part of the solution ... Now is a golden opportunity for us to put real change in this city,” he declared.

text: Trump reorganizes transition team, seeks loyalists for Cabinet. NEW YORK/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President-elect Donald Trump rearranged his transition team once more on Tuesday, removing a national security specialist and lobbyists from his close circle as he neared the announcement of two devoted Wall Street supporters for significant economic roles. Trump, a Republican outsider who achieved an unexpected election win last week, also resolved a paperwork issue that had briefly delayed his transition after assigning his Vice President-elect Mike Pence to oversee the process. "A very organized process is underway as I determine Cabinet and various other positions," Trump tweeted following a dinner outing with his family at 21 Club, a restaurant in Manhattan, while his motorcade discreetly departed from reporters assembled outside his residence. "I am the only one who knows who the finalists are!" Trump asserted. At the forefront of his considerations for top economic roles are campaign finance chair and seasoned Wall Street figure Steve Mnuchin for treasury secretary, along with longtime supporter and billionaire investor Wilbur Ross for commerce secretary, as stated by Trump ally and activist investor Carl Icahn. Nevertheless, a prominent Republican moderate was removed from the transition planning. Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative from Michigan who had been speculated as a potential CIA director candidate, unexpectedly exited the transition team. Rogers had collaborated with New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, who was suddenly replaced by Pence as the head of the transition team on Friday. This restructuring had stalled discussions about the transition with the White House. Pence was required to sign a memorandum of understanding, which the White House received on Tuesday evening. According to a White House spokesperson, the Trump team still must submit additional paperwork before detailed briefings on a department-by-department basis can commence. The team is expected to provide a code of conduct and verify that its transition team members do not have any conflicts of interest. Further modifications are anticipated. Pence and Rick Dearborn, the executive director of the transition team, are "eliminating any lobbyists," a transition aide noted. "This is to assure that President-elect Trump’s pledge to prohibit lobbyist involvement is being honored at all levels of the transition," the aide mentioned. Trump, who had criticized adversaries for being influenced by industry interests throughout his campaign, faced backlash from his regular opponent, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, for including lobbyists in his transition team. "According to public disclosures, your transition team and prospective cabinet comprise over twenty Wall Street elites, industry insiders, and lobbyists making decisions that could significantly affect their clients or employers," Warren stated in a letter. Trump has less than 70 days until his inauguration on January 20 to finalize his Cabinet members and other senior appointments. Ultimately, he will need to fill about 4,000 vacant positions. Wall Street is closely observing Trump's selections for treasury chief, as Republicans hold majorities in both houses of Congress, giving Trump a clearer opportunity for tax and financial regulatory reforms. Mnuchin refrained from commenting to reporters at Trump Tower regarding Cabinet selections but indicated that the team was "ensuring we pass the most substantial tax bill, the most significant tax changes since Reagan." A stream of advisers was seen entering and exiting Trump’s building on Tuesday, including U.S. Senator Jeff Sessions from Alabama, who is considered a potential candidate for secretary of defense or attorney general. U.S. Senator Ted Cruz from Texas, who competed against Trump for the Republican presidential nomination, also visited for a meeting, informing reporters he was "eager to fight hard to truly fulfill the promises we made" during the election. Bloomberg later reported that Trump was contemplating nominating Cruz as attorney general. Rogers was removed from the team partly because Trump’s advisers felt he did not adequately pursue Democratic preside.
