In the U.S., the expected sharp shift in environmental policy contributed to a more than 7 percent rise in Caterpillar's shares on Wednesday, fueled by optimism that a Trump administration would revitalize coal mining and infrastructure investment. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Following a setback on U.S. healthcare legislation, the White House cautioned defiant conservative lawmakers that they ought to support President Donald Trump’s agenda or risk being sidelined in future legislative battles, including tax reform. Economic growth is anticipated to be more subdued without fiscal stimulus, and U.S. equity index futures dipped to a six-week low on Sunday. Trump was unable to persuade the Freedom Caucus members despite extensive outreach efforts. text: COPENHAGEN (Reuters) - On Tuesday, Danish authorities revealed that the dimensions of a headless female torso discovered along the coastline in Copenhagen may suggest it belongs to a Swedish journalist who perished following a submarine excursion with the Danish inventor of the vessel. Police indicated that divers were continuing their search in the vicinity and were looking into reports of additional body parts that might have been seen in Copenhagen harbor. Peter Madsen, the Danish inventor, has been accused of murdering Kim Wall, the Swedish journalist, in his homemade submarine. "We are dealing with a torso from which the arms, legs, and head have been intentionally severed. The size of the torso does not rule out the possibility of it being Kim Wall, but we are still uncertain," stated Copenhagen police spokesperson Jens Moller in a video announcement. Madsen previously informed a court that she had died as a result of an accident aboard the submarine and that he had disposed of her body at sea, altering his earlier claim that he had let her off alive in Copenhagen. Police are conducting DNA analysis to determine the identity of the torso, which was discovered on Monday by a cyclist passing by, with results expected on Wednesday morning, Moller mentioned. This unusual case has captured the attention of both Danish and Swedish media and has sparked global interest. Madsen faces charges of manslaughter in connection with Wall, who has been unaccounted for since he took her out to sea in his 17-meter (56 feet) submarine on August 10. He refutes the allegations. He was rescued the following day after his UC3 Nautilus sank in the narrow strait separating Denmark and Sweden. Authorities found no other individuals in the wreckage. Madsen, who is an entrepreneur, artist, submarine designer, and aerospace engineer, appeared before a judge on Saturday for initial questioning. The proceedings are closed to the public to safeguard ongoing investigations, according to police.

text: Anthem Inc, a U.S. health insurance provider, is scaling back its Obamacare plan offerings in California, reducing its presence in 16 out of 19 pricing regions where it had provided options this year, according to state officials on Tuesday. This decision, effective for 2018, will result in Anthem offering Obamacare coverage in only three pricing regions that include 28 counties within California. This constitutes just 41 percent of its current enrollment, amounting to approximately 108,000 consumers, which leaves around 153,000 consumers without access to Anthem's Obamacare plans, as stated by state officials. Anthem attributed this reduction partly to the uncertainty regarding whether the Trump administration would continue the subsidies that help keep costs manageable, among other factors that have contributed to an overall lack of predictability. text: The United States has initiated a campaign to decrease its reliance on imported critical minerals. On Thursday, U.S. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke announced this initiative, highlighting the risks to national security and the economy posed by dependence on foreign sources for minerals essential for smartphones, computers, and military equipment. Following a directive from President Donald Trump, Zinke, in collaboration with Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, is set to produce a list within 60 days of non-fuel minerals that are susceptible to supply chain interruptions and are crucial for manufacturing. Additionally, a strategy will be formulated to reduce the U.S.'s reliance on international suppliers. The policy aims to pinpoint new domestic sources for critical minerals, enhance local exploration, mining, and recycling efforts, provide miners and producers with electronic access to superior geological and mapping data, and simplify the leasing and permitting processes for new mining operations. "The United States must not remain reliant on foreign competitors like Russia and China for the critical minerals needed to keep our economy strong and our country safe," Trump stated. This order follows a report released earlier this week by the Interior Department and the U.S. Geological Survey, which highlighted the U.S.'s dependence on foreign competitors for specific minerals. The report pinpointed 23 out of 88 minerals that are vital for U.S. national defense and the economy, as they are integral to products ranging from batteries to military equipment. The identified minerals included rare earth metals, lithium, graphite, among others. Although the report did not provide policy recommendations, Zinke mentioned that he would utilize the findings to prioritize research in specific mineral deposit areas on federal lands and formulate policies to encourage mining activities. Twenty of the 23 critical minerals the United States depends on are obtained from China. A significant portion of the world's lithium is produced in Australia and Chile, with the majority of global reserves located in vast salt flats within the lithium triangle of Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina. For instance, lithium exports from Chile were nearly $600 million in 2016, accounting for about 40 percent of the global market by volume, as reported by the Chilean development agency Corfo. Leading lithium producers in the region include SQM, Albemarle, and FMC Lithium.

text: The leader of the Philippines has announced a unilateral ceasefire for the Christmas period. MANILA (Reuters) - President Rodrigo Duterte of the Philippines has instituted a 10-day ceasefire with communist insurgents to enable citizens to enjoy a Christmas season free from worry, just two weeks after peace discussions with the rebels were officially terminated. According to presidential spokesperson Harry Roque, Duterte has instructed the military and police to halt offensive operations from December 24 to January 2 to alleviate public concern during this festive period. Roque expressed his hope that the Maoists and their political representatives would reciprocate with a similar act of goodwill. There was no prompt response from the communist rebel faction, whose senior leaders and negotiators have been in exile in The Netherlands since the late 1980s. Upon taking office last year, Duterte revived a stalled peace initiative and released several communist leaders as a sign of goodwill, but he has recently called off negotiations due to an increase in rebel attacks. He has consistently expressed his anger at what he perceives as the deceitfulness of the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) and its armed faction, the New People’s Army (NPA). He has categorized them as a terrorist organization and has terminated the three-decade-long peace process. The estimated 3,000 rebel fighters have engaged in a long-standing guerrilla warfare in rural areas for almost 50 years, a conflict that has resulted in the deaths of over 40,000 individuals and hindered development in resource-abundant regions of the Philippines. These guerrillas have targeted mining operations, plantations, construction sites, and telecommunications firms, demanding 'revolutionary taxation' to fund arms procurement and recruiting efforts. On Tuesday evening, Duterte stated that his sole intention was for Filipinos to have a Christmas free of stress. 'I do not want to add more strain to what people are now suffering,' he remarked to journalists.

text: Cyril Ramaphosa has emerged victorious in the contest for leadership of the African National Congress, yet he did not successfully seize complete control of South Africa's ruling party from President Jacob Zuma. The faction loyal to Zuma continues to hold sway within the ANC's newly formed National Executive Committee (NEC) and their influence was evident during conference discussions on contentious issues like land expropriation and nationalization. Ramaphosa's partial triumph could hinder his ability to address deep-rooted corruption and execute reforms aimed at revitalizing economic growth, which he emphasized during his campaign for the ANC's top position. This situation may also weaken his prospects of removing Zuma from the presidency before the conclusion of his second term in 2019. Such a scenario could dishearten investors who have heavily invested in the belief that Ramaphosa, a 65-year-old former leader of a trade union and affluent businessman, would successfully revitalize Africa's most industrialized nation. The rand has fluctuated since Ramaphosa's election as investors analyze his level of influence. Darias Jonker, director for Africa at Eurasia Group, noted that Ramaphosa's lack of a strong majority in the NEC, compounded by the enduring presence of Zuma supporters, would impede his ability to pursue his agenda. Zuma's ten-year tenure has significantly damaged the ANC's reputation both domestically and internationally as economic growth has nearly ground to a halt. He has managed to survive multiple votes of no confidence, and analysts suggest he has solidified his grip on the ANC through political patronage. The newly announced NEC of the ANC, revealed in the early hours of Thursday, is approximately evenly divided between the factions of Ramaphosa and Zuma. The party's six most influential officials, disclosed on Monday, also reflect this division. Zuma stated on Thursday that there were no clear winners or losers in the leadership elections at the ANC conference. Should Ramaphosa attempt to unseat Zuma from his position, he would require the backing of the NEC, which includes his primary opponent in the ANC race, former cabinet minister Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma, who is also Zuma's ex-wife and favored successor. Other notable members of the NEC include staunch Zuma allies, Finance Minister Malusi Gigaba and Energy Minister David Mahlobo, who would staunchly support the 75-year-old leader. Two particularly contentious policy resolutions passed at the ANC conference on Wednesday called for land expropriation without compensation and the nationalization of the central bank. Dlamini-Zuma was one of the strongest proponents of both policies. The land expropriation from white farmers in Zimbabwe had a severely detrimental effect on food production, and any discussions regarding nationalization in South Africa are enough to alarm investors, especially since leftist factions within the ANC have also advocated for state ownership of mines and banks. A senior source within the ANC informed Reuters that the Ramaphosa faction would aim to limit the push for full state ownership of the Reserve Bank to the resolutions accepted at the conference. The Reserve Bank indicated that altering its ownership framework could lead to increased economic uncertainty and could be expensive. Although land expropriation without compensation is not expected to become standard practice immediately, the ANC's call to amend the constitution as a preliminary step in that direction could undermine already fragile investor confidence. Analyst Anne Fruhauf from consultancy Teneo remarked that such rhetoric will now need to shape Ramaphosa's speeches and will exacerbate concerns about property rights at a time when the economy requires precisely the opposite signals. Land issues are particularly sensitive in South Africa, where the ANC faces pressure to tackle significant racial disparities more than twenty years after the end of white minority governance. The opposition Democratic Alliance criticized the ANC's demand for land expropriation on Thursday, asserting that it neglects to address broader property rights issues affecting the poor.

text: SEOUL (Reuters) - On Monday, President Moon Jae-in of South Korea and Prime Minister Shinzo Abe of Japan came to an agreement to advocate for more stringent United Nations sanctions against North Korea following Pyongyang's sixth nuclear test that occurred the previous day, as stated by a spokesman from South Korea's presidential office. SEOUL (Reuters) - South Korea s President Moon Jae-in and Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe agreed on Monday to pursue stronger United Nations sanctions against North Korea after Pyongyang s sixth nuclear test a day earlier, South Korea s presidential spokesman said. text: Jalal Talabani, the former president of Iraq, was laid to rest in his native Kurdish region on Friday. His presidency, which followed the downfall of Saddam Hussein, represented a significant moment for the historically marginalized Kurdish population. The coffin of Talabani, who passed away at the age of 83 on Tuesday in Germany, was transported back to Sulaimaniya, his hometown in northern Iraq, aboard an Iraqi Airways plane, as reported by Iraqi and Kurdish television. A 21-gun salute honored the coffin, which was adorned with the Kurdish flag featuring a golden sun, colored in red, white, and green. A military band performed both the Iraqi national anthem, 'Mawtini' (my nation), and Chopin's funeral march. The presence of the Kurdish flag on the coffin incited protests from media outlets aligned with Shiite political factions supportive of the Iraqi government. Al-Etejah TV even interrupted its programming due to the coffin not being covered with the Iraqi flag. The aircraft that returned Talabani's body was granted a special exemption from a ban on international flights to the Kurdish region, which had been imposed by the Iraqi government in response to a recent Kurdish independence referendum. An important figure in the Kurdish pursuit of self-determination, Talabani assumed the presidency in 2005, becoming the first individual to occupy the position after Saddam Hussein's removal in a U.S.-initiated invasion. While the presidency holds limited authority, appointing a member of the Kurdish minority to the role was a significant gesture of unity for Iraq, as the constitution aimed to distribute power among various ethnic and religious communities. The prime minister, representing the Shiite Arab majority, wields executive power. Talabani resigned from the presidency in 2014 following extensive rehabilitation after suffering a stroke in 2012. His successor, Fuad Musum, who is also of Kurdish descent, officiated the airport ceremony on Friday. Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi, who has been insisting that the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) annul the results of the independence vote from the previous week, was absent from the funeral. The central government was represented by Interior Minister Qasim al-Araji. A spokesperson for the government expressed strong discontent due to the absence of the Iraqi flag on Mam Jalal's coffin, despite the national anthem being played. Talabani was affectionately known as Mam, meaning 'uncle' in Kurdish. Tens of thousands converged along the route from the airport and around the Sulaimaniya Grand Mosque, where prayers for the deceased were conducted, while holding images of Talabani and waving the green flags of his Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) party. The funeral procession, consisting of a dozen SUVs, had difficulty navigating through the dense crowds from the mosque to his burial site on a hill that overlooks Sulaimaniya, situated close to the Talabani family residence. The Dabashan hill was packed with attendees as he was interred in the early evening. At the airport ceremony, Masoud Barzani, the leader of the Kurdish regional government and Talabani's long-time rival in the autonomy movement, sat between President Masum and Talabani's wife, Hero. Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif, the most senior foreign official present, reiterated Tehran's position labeling the independence vote as a 'strategic mistake,' according to Iranian media. Talabani had been too unwell to voice his opinions regarding the independence referendum. His PUK party expressed only a half-hearted endorsement. In contrast to Barzani, Talabani maintained favorable relations with Iran and the Iranian-backed Shiite factions that govern in Baghdad. The Baghdad administration, alongside Iran and Turkey, firmly opposed the referendum, and Washington, a long-standing ally of the Kurds, had also cautioned against holding it. Kurdish media and social platforms were filled with grievances concerning the flight ban instituted by Baghdad, which they claimed hindered greater international engagement at the funeral. Talabani was born in 1933 during a time when the region was under British mandate and studied law at B.

text: President Barack Obama’s initiative to relax certain aspects of a visa regulation prompted notable opposition from members of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the U.S. Congress on Wednesday. This regulation, which was implemented in late January, mandates that nationals from 38 nations who were previously able to enter the United States for a duration of up to 90 days without a visa must now secure one if they have traveled to Iran, Iraq, Sudan, or Syria after March 1, 2011. Ed Royce, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, stated on Wednesday that he aimed to include Libya in the list of nations subjected to these restrictions. During a session of the House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee, lawmakers expressed significant apprehension regarding the exemption of certain travelers visiting Iran from the new visa limitations, particularly those engaged in business activities. "The law does not provide for this authority. In fact, Congress clearly rejected the waivers that the White House requested," asserted Chairman Michael McCaul, a Republican. The visa limitations were enacted due to concerns that individuals from the primarily European nations within the Visa Waiver Program could easily enter the United States, even if they had, for instance, visited regions like Syria, Iran, or Iraq, which are known for militant activity. The attacks in Paris on November 13 heightened worries regarding such travel. Some of the attackers from the Islamic State, who were responsible for the deaths of 130 individuals that day, possessed European passports that would have permitted them effortless access to the United States. text: On Monday, Turkey called on the United States to reconsider its suspension of visa services following the apprehension of a U.S. consulate employee, an event that significantly heightened tensions between the two NATO partners and caused a decline in Turkey's currency and stock market. The relationship between Ankara and Washington has been marred by conflicts regarding U.S. backing of Kurdish militants in Syria, Turkey's demands for the extradition of a cleric residing in the U.S., and the indictment of a former Turkish minister in a U.S. court. However, the recent detention of a Turkish staff member from the U.S. consulate in Istanbul represented a new low in relations. Turkey alleged that the employee had ties to Fethullah Gulen, a U.S.-based cleric whom Ankara holds responsible for a failed military coup in July 2016; Gulen has denied any involvement with the coup. The U.S. embassy in Ankara denounced Turkey's allegations as unfounded and announced on Sunday evening that it was suspending all non-immigrant visa services in Turkey while it evaluated the Turkish government's commitment to the safety of its missions and personnel. Shortly thereafter, Ankara declared that it would implement similar measures for U.S. citizens applying for visas to Turkey. The U.S. ambassador indicated that the duration of the visa service suspension would rely on discussions between the two nations regarding the reasons behind the detention of local staff in Turkey. In a written statement late Monday, Ambassador John Bass mentioned that the length of the suspension would also be contingent on the Turkish government's assurance of safeguarding U.S. facilities and personnel in Turkey. He clarified that this action did not constitute a visa ban for Turkish citizens, as valid visas could still be utilized and applications could be submitted outside of Turkey. Bass noted that the U.S. Embassy had not been informed about the rationale behind the arrest of its Turkish employee last week nor the evidence against the individual, stating that he had not been granted sufficient access to the employee's attorney. Justice Minister Abdulhamit Gul remarked that if the U.S. had genuine security concerns regarding its missions in Turkey, measures would be taken to resolve them. However, he added, if the matter pertained to the detention of the consulate employee, it was a decision made by the Turkish judiciary. "Trying a Turkish citizen for a crime committed in Turkey is our right," Gul told A Haber television. The Turkish foreign ministry summoned a U.S. diplomat to request the lifting of the visa services suspension, arguing that it was creating unnecessary tensions, and President Tayyip Erdogan also expressed his disapproval of the U.S. decision. "For the (U.S.) embassy in Ankara to make and enforce such a decision is troubling," Erdogan stated at a news conference during a visit to Ukraine. According to the state-run Anadolu news agency, another employee of the U.S. consulate had been called to provide testimony regarding his wife and daughter's alleged connections to Gulen, which reportedly surfaced during the questioning of Metin Topuz, the staff member who was arrested last week. This diplomatic conflict unsettled investors, leading to a 3.4 percent drop in the lira, which was priced at 3.7385 against the dollar after having been reported at a high of 3.9223 overnight. The primary BIST 100 stock index decreased by as much as 4.7 percent, ultimately closing down 2.73 percent at 101,298 points. Shares in airlines were particularly affected, with national carrier Turkish Airlines experiencing a 9 percent decline. The central bank stated it was closely monitoring the ongoing situation. "This appears to be a very serious situation," remarked Timothy Ash, a strategist at Blue Bay Asset Management. He added that the central bank would need to act swiftly to reassure the market and potentially increase interest rates, a move that Erdogan has opposed. Turkey's foremost business association, TUSIAD, cautioned that the conflict would negatively impact bilateral economic, social, and cultural relations, urging for a calm resolution to the disagreements. The dispute with the United States coincides with significant strains in Turkey's relations with Germany, another important ally, along with Turkish military operations.

text: Factbox: Trump appoints individuals for security and legal roles. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Republican President-elect Donald Trump revealed his choices for key security positions on Friday, which include the head of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), his national security adviser, and the attorney general. A spokesperson from Trump's transition team informed Reuters that he has selected retired General Michael Flynn as his national security adviser, U.S. Senator Jeff Sessions for the role of attorney general, and U.S. Representative Mike Pompeo to oversee the CIA. The official confirmed that all three have accepted the roles. Below are details regarding his picks: Sessions, aged 69, was the first U.S. Senator to back Trump's presidential campaign and has remained a close supporter. A conservative from Alabama, he is currently serving his fourth term in the Senate, where he is part of the Senate Judiciary Committee, which supervises federal courts, immigration, crime, and terrorism issues. Coming from a background as the son of a country-store proprietor, he is a former Army Reserve captain who held the position of U.S. Attorney for Alabama’s Southern District during the administration of former President Ronald Reagan and subsequently served as Alabama’s Attorney General. Although the Senate confirmed him for his U.S. Attorney role in 1981, he faced rejection for a federal judgeship in 1986 when a Senate committee did not advance his nomination due to allegations of racially insensitive comments, which he has denied. To head the Justice Department as attorney general, Sessions needs to gain confirmation from the U.S. Senate, but he only requires majority support in the chamber, which is under Republican control. Sessions has consistently adopted a stringent position on immigration, opposing any pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. While serving during the George W. Bush administration, he criticized a bipartisan initiative aimed at establishing a guest-worker program for illegal immigrants, which was supported by Bush. NATIONAL SECURITY ADVISER: RETIRED LIEUTENANT GENERAL MICHAEL FLYNN Flynn, aged 57, was an early endorser of Trump and currently holds the vice chairman position on his transition team. A former director of the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA), he started his career in the U.S. Army in 1981 and took part in deployments to Afghanistan and Iraq. He subsequently worked within the Office of the Director of Intelligence. Initially a registered Democrat, Flynn became the head of the DIA in 2012 under President Barack Obama but retired a year earlier than planned, according to media reports, and emerged as a strong critic of Obama’s foreign policy. He later established his own consulting business, which has faced scrutiny due to its connections with a Turkish businessman. He stated to the Wall Street Journal on Thursday that he would cut ties with the firm in order to serve Trump. Flynn has expressed that the U.S. ought to collaborate more closely with Russia on global security matters. In an August interview with the Washington Post, he defended a paid speech he gave for state-run Russian Television. Pompeo, aged 52, is a third-term congressman representing Kansas who is a member of the U.S. House Select Intelligence Committee, which supervises the CIA, the National Security Agency (NSA), and cybersecurity. Pompeo also served on the House Select Committee on Benghazi, which investigated the 2012 assault on a U.S. compound in Libya. A California native, he graduated at the top of his class from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point and served as a platoon leader in the U.S. Army before departing the military as a captain to enroll in Harvard Law School. In 1996, he relocated to Kansas to start an aircraft parts company. The decision of the firm to establish a factory in Mexico was criticized when Pompeo later ran for office. He defended his actions, claiming that the company had generated jobs in the state. His connections to Koch Industries, owned by billionaire conservative benefactors Charles and David Koch, have also attracted scrutiny. He was re-elected in the November 8 election, securing 61 percent of the vote, as per Kansas’s unofficial election results available online. Pompeo has been vocal in his criticism of former U.S. intelligence contractor Edward Snowden, who disclosed sensitive information.

text: Amid the 2016 presidential election campaign. (Reuters) - For the multitude of photographers documenting the 2016 U.S. presidential race, capturing the personalities, the atmosphere, and the essence of the election often entails shifting focus away from the speaker at the podium. "The audience, the voters and the candidate are equally important," remarked Brian Snyder, a Reuters photographer with over 20 years of experience. "The candidates rely on the voters and vice versa. Any visual representation of that dynamic makes for an excellent campaign photograph in my view." Consider, for instance, the scene of enthusiastic young Bernie Sanders supporters Snyder captured at Bronx Community College in New York as they waved to the U.S. senator from Vermont. Sanders garnered significant backing from young voters during his challenging campaign against the eventual presumptive Democratic nominee, Hillary Clinton. Or take note of the tree outside a rainy Sanders rally in Buffalo, New York, adorned with umbrellas left to dry after the Secret Service barred supporters from bringing them inside. "I’m sure one person initiated it, then another thought it was a clever idea, and before you know it, there were 30 umbrellas," Snyder recounted. "It was just one of those amusing occurrences." Longtime Reuters photographer Mike Segar characterized his experience covering this year's U.S. presidential campaign as "strangely fun." Having reported on five presidential elections during his 23-year tenure at Reuters, Segar noted that this campaign was unique, particularly with New York businessman Donald Trump, who emerged as the presumptive Republican nominee, taking center stage. "The nature of the Trump campaign alters everything for everyone," Segar stated. He also mentioned that the increased security surrounding Trump has influenced how photographers depict the campaign. Segar captured an image of one of his meals while covering a Clinton rally: ground beef served on a bed of plain spinach in a tinfoil takeout container. "I aimed to provide viewers with a different perspective on what we encounter daily," Segar said with a chuckle. "Your images don’t always need to reflect the most groundbreaking moments of the campaign, but they should engage people's interest." Reuters photographer Lucas Jackson expressed that he consistently seeks unique perspectives at rallies. In one of his shots, young reporters are observed fixated on the screens of their Macbook laptops during a Sanders rally in Pennsylvania. "Typically, cameras are aimed at the candidate," Jackson remarked. "I’m always on the lookout for ways to provide context."

text: Disagreements within Italy's right-wing benefit its adversaries as election campaigning kicks off. ROME (Reuters) - The head of Italy's far-right Northern League announced on Thursday that he was halting interactions with his primary political partner, former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, due to a conflict regarding the strictness of judicial sentences for murderers and rapists. This public dispute over law enforcement has pleased opponents of the right just as election campaigning intensifies ahead of what is likely to be a national vote in early March. "I have consistently stated that the (right) does not exist as a coalition," remarked Luigi Di Maio, who is the prime ministerial hopeful from the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement. "We are drawing closer to governance." The right-wing coalition, which encompasses Berlusconi's Forza Italia! (Go Italy), is leading in the polls, with the 5-Star Movement in the second position. Analysts forecast that no party will secure a clear majority, which raises concerns about political turmoil in the euro zone's third-largest economy. Matteo Salvini, the leader of the Northern League, has frequently clashed with Berlusconi, but his frustration peaked this week after lawmakers from Forza Italia opposed measures aimed at preventing courts from granting sentence reductions for murder and rape. "We are receiving numerous calls and emails from individuals who are angry and disillusioned by Forza Italia's shocking choice to defend rapists and murderers," Salvini was reported as saying by AGI news agency. "For our part ... we are ceasing all our communications and discussions with Forza Italia and Berlusconi until there is a formal clarification," he continued. Berlusconi has vowed to engage with Salvini soon, expressing confusion over why his party members rejected the reform. Support for the right bloc has been steadily increasing in recent months, coinciding with Berlusconi's return to prominent politics following years embroiled in sex and financial controversies. Nonetheless, he has struggled to bridge the gaps between himself and Salvini, who has driven the Northern League toward the far-right spectrum of European politics, aligning with Marine Le Pen’s National Front in France. While the right is determined to campaign collectively in the upcoming election, the ruling centre-left Democratic Party (PD) has distanced itself from its traditional leftist allies, who have declined to form any electoral coalition. "(The right) will engage in debates before, during, and especially after the election, but on election day, they will act as if they are unified to gather a few additional seats," PD leader Matteo Renzi posted on Facebook on Thursday. "This is sheer hypocrisy because everyone is aware of the reality but chooses to ignore it."

text: Trump criticizes Clinton on trade, claims he should be declared the winner. TOLEDO, Ohio; WINSTON SALEM, N.C. (Reuters) - On Thursday, U.S. Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump took aim at Democrat Hillary Clinton regarding her trade policies, asserting that if she were in charge of trade agreements, the nation should simply "cancel the election" and declare him the winner. Addressing his supporters in Toledo, Ohio, Trump remarked that the North American Free Trade Agreement, enacted by Clinton’s spouse, former President Bill Clinton, resulted in the loss of thousands of jobs in Ohio to Mexico, a trend he promised to end if he secures the presidency on Nov. 8. "We should just cancel the election and just give it to Trump, right?" he stated. "What is the purpose of having it? Her policies are so detrimental." Trump expressed his belief that Clinton would push for the approval of the 12-nation Trans Pacific Partnership, an Asian trade deal championed by President Barack Obama, which she has now turned against. These comments from Trump emerged as the New York businessman attempts to stabilize his fluctuating polling numbers amid various controversies and self-created issues. He has faced difficulty managing the repercussions of the emergence of a 2005 "Access Hollywood" video that captured the former reality TV star discussing groping women and attempting to seduce a married woman, recorded just months after his marriage to his third wife, Melania. On Thursday, Trump claimed that it was "certainly illegal" for NBC to unveil the tape and suggested he might consider legal action against the network post-election. Following the video's release, multiple women have accused Trump of groping them or kissing them without consent, allegations he has labeled as "absolutely false." The latest average from RealClearPolitics polls indicates Clinton holds a nearly 6-point national lead over Trump, bolstered by diminishing support among women for his campaign. Trump has, without substantiation, attributed his declining poll numbers to a rigged election and asserted that the media has manipulated opinion polls to enhance Clinton’s standing. Many studies indicate that voter fraud in U.S. elections is exceedingly uncommon, and several prominent Republicans have criticized Trump’s assertion that the electoral system is flawed. While Trump campaigned in Ohio, a plane carrying his running mate, Indiana Governor Mike Pence, slid off the runway upon landing at New York City’s LaGuardia Airport on Thursday night, with no injuries reported, according to the Pence campaign. On Thursday, Clinton made her inaugural joint campaign appearance with one of her strongest supporters, first lady Michelle Obama, at a rally in North Carolina aimed at motivating young individuals and women to vote. Clinton, who previously served as first lady and lost the 2008 Democratic nomination to then-U.S. Senator Barack Obama before becoming his secretary of state, commended Michelle Obama for advocating for the rights of girls and women around the globe, sharply contrasting her Republican opponent. "I wish I didn’t have to say this. ... But indeed, dignity and respect for women and girls is also on the ballot in this election," Clinton expressed to an audience of around 11,000. "And I want to thank our first lady for her articulate, powerful defense of that fundamental principle." Michelle Obama’s vehement criticism of Trump following the leaked 2005 video, where he made lascivious comments and boasted about groping women, was regarded by many as one of the most significant rebukes of the New York businessman throughout the campaign. Without directly mentioning Trump, Obama continued her critique in North Carolina, asking the audience which candidate they preferred to represent their daughters from the White House. "We desire a president who takes this role seriously, and possesses the temperament and maturity to perform it effectively. Someone who is composed. Someone we can trust with the nuclear codes," Obama stated. "I would not be here misleading you: I firmly believe that Hillary Clinton will be that president," she concluded. text: KAMPALA (Reuters) - A proposal aimed at amending Uganda's constitution to enable President Yoweri Museveni to remain in power past the age of 75 sparked chaotic scenes in parliament on Monday, resulting in the expulsion of six members of parliament. Currently 73 years old, Museveni has been in control of the East African nation for 31 years. The existing age limit in the constitution would prevent him from running for president again in 2021. On Monday, lawmakers began discussing a bill introduced by a supporter of Museveni, which seeks to eliminate the requirement that a presidential candidate must be under 75 years old. Opposition activists and human rights organizations argue that this would pave the way for him to hold the presidency indefinitely. The proposed bill has faced criticism from religious leaders and even some members of Museveni's National Resistance Movement (NRM) party, and it requires the approval of two-thirds of all voting members to pass. Nevertheless, the NRM is anticipated to gather sufficient votes easily. Protests against this initiative have been met with arrests, tear gas, and live ammunition, resulting in at least two fatalities in October. The debate on Monday occurred amidst significant police and military presence at parliament. Following a surge of jeering and heckling within the chamber, the six lawmakers were suspended for one session and instructed to leave for undermining the authority of the speaker as well as disrupting the decorum of the house, as stated by parliament spokesman Chris Obore to Reuters. The MPs had been heckling speaker Rebecca Kadaga and disregarded her requests to take their seats, according to Obore. Proceedings in the house were adjourned for several hours after the MPs were removed and later resumed in the afternoon to review a report from a parliamentary committee that had conducted public consultations on the bill. A majority report from the committee endorsed the plan to eliminate the age limit and suggested extending the presidential term from five to seven years. Some committee members disagreed and produced a minority report. 'It is our belief that the proposal...only aims to promote life presidency and undermine contemporary constitutional practices,' stated MP Monicah Amoding, who presented the minority report. Throughout the largely contentious debate, members frequently shouted down one another and expressed disdain. Opposition MPs, who were the majority in the debate, attempted unsuccessfully to delay the proceedings. The speaker adjourned the session to Tuesday after reporting a malfunction with the chamber's microphones. In late September, lawmakers engaged in physical altercations in parliament over two consecutive days as those opposing the bill sought to filibuster but ultimately lost. A minimum of 25 MPs against the proposed constitutional change to extend Museveni's time in power were forcibly removed on the speaker's orders due to their participation in the fighting. Initially, Museveni garnered widespread international backing for his adoption of market-oriented reforms and restoration of political stability after years of chaos in the East African country. However, he has increasingly faced scrutiny in recent years over a variety of human rights abuses, corruption, and his reluctance to relinquish power. Advocates for democracy have voiced concerns about the resurgence of a trend among leaders in the region to amend laws, postpone elections, or employ other strategies to prolong their time in office. Similar actions in Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo have led to instability.

text: A tunnel collapse might have resulted in the deaths of 200 individuals following North Korea's nuclear test, according to a report from Japanese broadcaster TV Asahi. The incident reportedly occurred at the nuclear test site in North Korea after Pyongyang conducted its sixth atomic test in September. TV Asahi, referencing unnamed sources familiar with the incident, shared this information on Tuesday. Reuters has been unable to confirm this report. Approximately 100 workers were impacted by the initial collapse, which is said to have happened around September 10, as per the broadcaster. Additionally, a subsequent collapse during the rescue efforts raised concerns that the number of fatalities could surpass 200. TOKYO (Reuters) - A tunnel at North Korea s nuclear test site collapsed after Pyongyang s sixth atomic test in September, possibly killing more than 200 people, Japanese broadcaster TV Asahi said on Tuesday, citing unnamed sources familiar with the situation. Reuters has not been able to verify the report. About 100 workers at the Punggye-ri nuclear site were affected by the initial collapse, which took place around Sept. 10, the broadcaster said. A second collapse during a rescue operation meant it was possible the death toll could have exceeded 200, it added. Experts have said a series of tremors and landslides near the nuclear test base probably mean the country s sixth and largest blast on Sept. 3 has destabilized the region, and the Punggye-ri nuclear site may not be used for much longer to test nuclear weapons.

text: New Jersey's Governor Chris Christie is experiencing a decline in his approval ratings, as indicated by a statewide poll. According to findings from Fairleigh Dickinson University, which were published on Wednesday, Christie's approval rating has dropped to 27 percent, down from 33 percent prior to his endorsement of Republican frontrunner Donald Trump. The decline is particularly pronounced among individuals without party affiliation, where approval plummeted to 18 percent from 34 percent. Only 29 percent of respondents believe New Jersey is moving in the right direction, while 59 percent disagree. Fairleigh Dickinson noted that this rating represents the lowest recorded during Christie's time in office. Christie has faced criticism for spending considerable time out of state while pursuing the Republican presidential nomination. Following his withdrawal from the race, he was anticipated to re-engage in New Jersey politics; however, his endorsement of Trump has led him back onto the campaign trail. The latest poll conducted by Fairleigh Dickinson's PublicMind took place from February 24 to 28 and surveyed 694 randomly selected registered voters in New Jersey via telephone. (Reporting by Edward Krudy; Editing by Lisa Von Ahn) This piece was partially funded by SAP and was independently produced by the Reuters editorial team. text: According to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the public debt of the United States is projected to reach 150 percent of the nation’s economic output by the year 2047 unless there are modifications to the existing tax and spending regulations. This forecast, released on Thursday, significantly surpasses the record level recorded shortly after World War II. The latest estimates indicate a sharper increase in debt over the next 30 years compared to last year’s long-term predictions by the non-partisan budget analysis organization, potentially complicating support among some Congressional members for a tax reform initiative that relies partially on increased deficits. Previously, the CBO had anticipated that public debt would rise to 141 percent of gross domestic product by 2046, while the historical peak occurred at 106 percent of GDP in 1946. According to the CBO, this record level of debt is expected to be achieved by 2035. For this year, the CBO estimates that the public debt will be around 77 percent of GDP in 2017, with projections of 89 percent in 2027 and 113 percent in 2037. These new projections operate under the assumption that the Affordable Care Act, also referred to as Obamacare, which House Republicans were unable to replace last week, will remain in effect for the foreseeable future. The anticipated growth in debt reflects the CBO's evaluations regarding the increasing expenses associated with an aging population over 65, rising interest expenses, and expectations of slower economic growth due to diminished productivity growth assumptions. It is expected that average annual deficits will be 8.6 percent of GDP from 2038 to 2047, compared to the 2.9 percent projected for 2017 and 4.0 percent for the period from 2018 to 2027. These long-term projections build upon the CBO’s earlier assumptions included in its ten-year budget outlook from January, which indicated decreasing deficits for the next two years, followed by growth afterward. By 2047, net interest costs are expected to account for 6.2 percent of GDP, in contrast to 1.4 percent in 2017 and approximately 1.2 percent in 1967, as reported by the CBO. However, a significant variable in the CBO's 30-year projections is the real interest rates. The CBO assumes that real interest yields on 10-year Treasury notes will average 1.5 percent over the next 30 years, increasing to 2.3 percent by 2047. A potential rise in interest rates, along with varying assumptions regarding productivity and the growth of healthcare costs, could lead to notably different scenarios, according to the CBO. The CBO noted that its debt-to-GDP ratio might fluctuate between 85 percent under conditions of low rates and strong growth, and 244 percent if faced with weaker growth and elevated rates.

Mark Garnier, a junior minister for international trade, allegedly told secretary Caroline Edmondson to purchase two sex toys and referred to her as sugar tits, according to the Mail on Sunday. Garnier explained to the newspaper that the remark stemmed from a light-hearted exchange concerning a television program, asserting that his request for the toys was merely good-humored high jinks. Edmondson, in her remarks to the newspaper, contested Garnier's version of events, including his claim that the interactions were merely high jinks. This report follows an article in another British publication, the Sun, on Friday, which detailed a pervasive culture of sexual harassment among parliamentarians and their staff. Garnier was not available for immediate comment to Reuters through his parliamentary or constituency offices. Following the Sun's report, May's spokesperson stated on Friday that any form of unwanted sexual conduct is completely unacceptable and that any minister who behaves inappropriately will face significant consequences. Health Minister Jeremy Hunt mentioned on Sunday that May had instructed officials to investigate whether Garnier, whose position does not include a seat in the cabinet immediately surrounding May, violated the code of conduct for government ministers. "These reports, if accurate, are clearly entirely unacceptable," Hunt told BBC television. "The Cabinet Office will conduct an investigation to determine if there has been a breach of the ministerial code in this specific instance, but as you know, the facts are disputed." May, in a letter made public to the media, also sought the advice of John Bercow, the Speaker of the House of Commons, on Sunday regarding changes to the culture within that institution. "I believe it is crucial that individuals working in the House of Commons are treated with respect and fairness, as would be expected in any contemporary workplace," May stated in her letter. She expressed that measures like a disciplinary procedure proposed by the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority and a voluntary code of conduct offered by the Conservative Party to its members do not suffice. After facing considerable backlash for this analogy, Gove, a cabinet minister, expressed regret for what he termed a clumsy attempt at humor. The Sun reported on Friday that women in Westminster's political sphere have formed a WhatsApp group to share their experiences with harassment and to alert others about possible offenders. May's spokesperson stated on Friday that the Prime Minister was unequivocal in her response to the reports concerning Harvey Weinstein in recent weeks, affirming that any unwanted sexual behavior is entirely unacceptable, a principle that holds true in every aspect of life, including politics.

text: UK's Brexit minister expressed optimism about reaching a favorable agreement despite recent challenging discussions. WASHINGTON/LONDON (Reuters) - On Friday, Britain's Brexit minister addressed a business gathering in Washington, sharing his hope that the negotiations to exit the European Union would yield a beneficial outcome for both parties, although he acknowledged that the talks were becoming somewhat strained. David Davis had returned on Thursday from Brussels, where EU representatives cautioned that to this point, the advancement in their negotiations had not met the necessary criteria to progress to talks about their future relationship. "I am a determined optimist," Davis stated to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. "Because I fundamentally believe that a good deal is in the interests of both the UK and the EU and the whole of the developed world." Davis faced pressure from Myron Brilliant, the head of international affairs at the U.S. Chamber, to outline a clear Brexit strategy for the 7,500 U.S. businesses operating in the UK—one that featured "predictable transition periods" to reduce disruptions for companies. Thus far, negotiations have focused on Britain's financial commitments to the EU, with the EU insisting that this bill must be settled before discussions can advance to topics such as international trade. Davis refrained from commenting on whether Britain would consider paying for access to the single market during any transitional phase post-Brexit, noting that London was carefully reviewing the exit bill from the EU. "It is getting a bit tense. I rule nothing in, nothing out," Davis remarked. He indicated that Britain aims to finalize a free-trade agreement with the United States once the transition period with the EU concludes. However, he warned that any agreement involving two major economies like Britain and the U.S. would be "quite complex." Davis seemed to aim for a distinction between Britain's aspirations for global free-trade agreements and the protectionist approach championed by U.S. President Donald Trump, who has attempted to impose trade tariffs and has expressed intentions to withdraw from the North American Free Trade Area to support domestic industries. Davis mentioned that Britain would advocate for further liberalization in services and engage with international organizations such as the World Trade Organization. Trump has indicated that the United States might contemplate disregarding WTO rulings. As Britain navigates its exit from the EU, it has been actively seeking closer ties with the United States, with Prime Minister Theresa May becoming the first foreign leader to meet President Donald Trump following his inauguration in January. At that time, she urged Trump to revitalize the "special relationship" between the two nations and has expressed hopes of securing a trade agreement with the U.S. shortly after Brexit to demonstrate that Britain can thrive outside the EU. Nonetheless, she has faced criticism from opposition lawmakers for attempting to align closely with Trump, whose erratic policy positions on trade and other global obligations have raised concerns about whether the U.S. will adhere to its international commitments.

text: The Chinese minister cautions against the allure of Western values. BEIJING (Reuters) - A high-ranking Chinese official has warned that Western nations are attempting to impose their cultural and political ideals on others, enticing them to forsake their own traditions. The propaganda chief of China stated on Friday that the nation must adhere to its own course. Since taking office five years ago, Chinese President Xi Jinping has overseen an extensive crackdown on civil society, tightening government oversight over social interactions, media, and the internet. Xi has committed to advancing what the ruling Communist Party calls core socialist values, which encompass patriotism, traditional Chinese culture, the rule of law, harmony, and prosperity, among others. Huang Kunming, who was appointed to his position following the significant party congress last month that further solidified Xi's authority, expressed in the official People’s Daily that there is an escalating clash of values globally. He noted that certain Western nations exploit their technological supremacy and long-held dominance in discourse to promote what they term 'universal values.' Huang refrained from naming these countries, but he indicated that they aim to entice individuals into glorifying the West and conforming to its expectations, thereby diluting or possibly abandoning their own cultural identity. He emphasized that China’s distinct cultural heritage, unique historical path, and national circumstances necessitate the safeguarding of its values rooted in its culture. Huang asserted that by fostering core socialist values, the Chinese populace can maintain its dignity within the global community. China has consistently opposed what it perceives as efforts to impose Western ideals, such as competitive multi-party democracy and the separation of powers, and the Communist Party does not tolerate any challenges to its authority. Prior to the party congress, the state-run news agency Xinhua criticized Western democracy as being fractious and adversarial. While China’s constitution recognizes the party's enduring leading role in governance, it does permit the existence of various other political parties under a framework referred to as a multi-party cooperation system. However, all these parties remain subordinate to the Communist Party. Activists advocating for pluralism frequently face imprisonment, and dissent against China’s authoritarian regime is routinely suppressed.

text: Austrian political leader resigns from parliament amid sexual assault allegations. VIENNA (Reuters) - The repercussions of the Harvey Weinstein scandal reached Austria on Saturday, as one of the nation's most prominent politicians announced his decision to resign from his parliamentary seat following a sexual assault claim. Peter Pilz, a veteran 63-year-old leftist lawmaker, has been a well-known figure in Austrian politics for many years, gaining recognition for his opposition to arms deals with nations accused of human rights violations and for spearheading investigations into corruption, including one this year involving Austrian fighter-jet acquisitions. Recently, he achieved a significant political milestone by departing from the Greens this summer to establish his own party, Pilz List, which not only outperformed the Greens in last month's parliamentary elections but also surpassed the 4 percent threshold required for parliamentary representation, a mark the Greens narrowly missed. The weekly publication Falter reported on Saturday that Pilz had allegedly groped a female employee of the center-right European People’s Party during a conference in the Alps four years prior. The article included her account of the event, in which she stated that Pilz was 'relatively drunk' at the time. Pilz, known for his vibrant personality in Austrian politics and his penchant for singing rock songs like 'Wild Thing' at political gatherings, claimed he could not recall the incident. 'Not remembering is no excuse,' Pilz stated at a news conference, adding that the editor-in-chief of Falter had assured him that the report was well-researched. 'In light of these allegations, which I take very seriously, even though I do not recall, I will not assume my mandate in the upcoming parliament. I will not attend the swearing-in ceremony on Thursday,' he announced. Following the Weinstein scandal and the subsequent resignations due to inappropriate conduct, including that of British Defence Minister Michael Fallon this week, Austrian media began questioning whether there were other unreported instances of sexual harassment by prominent Austrians. U.S. film producer Weinstein is facing accusations from numerous women who allege he sexually harassed or assaulted them, with incidents reportedly dating back to the 1980s, including three who claimed they were raped. Weinstein has denied engaging in any non-consensual sexual acts. Pilz expressed his intent to uncover all relevant facts concerning the allegations against him. However, he also dismissed separate claims made by a former colleague, who accused him of sexually harassing her on multiple occasions. That allegation was first reported by Austrian media on Friday. Pilz indicated that he would continue to support his party's efforts in parliament 'from the outside,' although he did not explicitly state that he would resign as party leader. A representative for Pilz was unavailable for immediate comment.

text: Gerry Adams: The IRA figure who played a crucial role in securing peace in Northern Ireland. DUBLIN (Reuters) - As the prominent representative of the Irish Republican Army during its violent campaigns, and later as a peacemaker and established politician, Gerry Adams has been a pivotal character in the 50-year evolution of Northern Ireland from sectarian conflict to a more stable situation. On Saturday, Adams expressed his decision to resign as the head of the Irish nationalist party Sinn Fein, while the dream of a united Ireland remains out of reach. The party he will leave behind stands as not only the leading Irish nationalist entity in the British-administered region but also possesses sufficient strength in the Irish Republic to potentially participate in its government as well. Throughout the 1970s and 80s, during the peak of the IRA's bombing efforts to end British governance in Northern Ireland, Sinn Fein acted as the political arm of the IRA. Since taking over leadership in 1983, Adams became, for many in the UK and Northern Ireland, the public face of the IRA. This resulted in him being despised by pro-British unionists and the British authorities, while simultaneously being celebrated by Irish nationalists. However, when the opportunity for political advancement emerged, he demonstrated a willingness to negotiate, collaborating with the late former IRA leader Martin McGuinness to rally support from the IRA and the Roman Catholic community for a 1998 agreement with the pro-British Protestant majority. The Good Friday agreement provided the province's Catholics with a share in governance and significantly brought an end to a conflict that resulted in approximately 3,600 fatalities, many caused by Irish republican factions such as the IRA, as well as pro-British unionist paramilitary groups and British security forces. Since that time, Adams has played a key role in transforming Sinn Fein into the leading Irish nationalist political party in Northern Ireland, overseeing its 2007 agreement to collaborate with its long-standing opponent, the Democratic Unionist Party, and recently working towards restoring power-sharing after its collapse in January. On Saturday, Adams also revealed that he would not seek re-election to the Dublin parliament, where he has served since 2011, elevating Sinn Fein from the margins to the status of the third-largest party in the Irish Republic and its primary leftist force. Adams was born into a Belfast family deeply entrenched in revolutionary politics, with several relatives having engaged in armed republican activities. At the age of 20, he left his position as a bartender to defend fellow Catholics against what they perceived as an antagonistic British regime, advocating for Northern Ireland's separation from the United Kingdom to join the Irish Republic. Like his father, Adams was interned - held without trial - due to suspicions of being a senior IRA leader. He has consistently denied being a member of the IRA, although allegations from former IRA members claiming his involvement in its campaign of assassinations have plagued him throughout his career. From 1988 to 1994, Adams was prohibited from speaking on British media. Despite his large glasses and red-tinged beard being easily recognizable, his voice remained unheard as broadcasters employed actors to voice his statements. John Major, a former British Conservative prime minister and one of the key figures in the peace process in Northern Ireland, once remarked that the idea of engaging in discussions with Adams made him feel nauseous. Nevertheless, at that time, Adams was navigating a precarious political situation - balancing between IRA hardliners who insisted that only a continuation of violence would expel Britain from the island, and moderates who believed negotiations were the way forward to achieve a united Ireland. In October 1997, he re-emerged from the political isolation when he shook hands with new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair during their initial meeting. Sinn Fein had garnered 17 percent of the votes in Northern Ireland's elections, securing Adams a seat in the British parliament, although he declined to take it. text: U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry criticized Carnival Corp on Thursday for prohibiting Cuban-Americans from participating in its scheduled cruises to Cuba and urged the Cuban government to modify its regulations to permit them. In an interview with CNN en Espanol and the Miami Herald, Kerry stated, "Carnival needs to not discriminate." However, those born in Cuba are permitted to fly to the island. "American citizens, Cuban Americans have a right to travel, and we should not be in a situation where the Cuban government is forcing its discrimination policy on us," Kerry remarked. ZINANA, Iraq (Reuters) - After hearing gunfire near his residence for the first time, Abu Riwar quickly gathered his wife and six children into their vehicle and drove to a distant village located 120 km (75 miles) away. "We departed with only the clothes on our backs and nothing more," stated Abu Riwar, a member of the Kurdish security forces from the ethnically diverse town of Tuz Khurmato, which was taken over last month by Iraqi soldiers and Iran-supported Shiite militias. "If the militias discovered I was Peshmerga, they would have killed me." Instead, they set his house ablaze, as recounted by his neighbors who recorded the incident. Tuz Khurmato, previously a disputed area outside the Kurdish region of northern Iraq but maintained by Kurdish forces known as Peshmerga, was reclaimed last month by the central government in a swift operation intended to penalize the Kurds for holding an independence referendum deemed illegal by Baghdad. The majority of Tuz Khurmato's 50,000 Kurds—approximately half of the city's mixed population—escaped the Iraqi advance to Kurdish-controlled villages and towns in the surrounding countryside, according to Mayor Shalal Abdul. The mayor himself sought refuge in Zinana, 120 km east of Tuz Khurmato, where he shared information with Reuters. Most residents have no intention of returning home, citing ongoing reports of assaults. "We cannot manage if this continues," stated the chief of police in Zinana, who added that both the government and humanitarian organizations have been slow to react. Families have occupied school facilities, residences, and the hospital, but we cannot leave them on the streets. The United Nations reported that over 180,000 individuals were displaced due to the Iraqi government's offensive on disputed territories last month. Aid organizations indicate that a significant number of the displaced are Kurds, although some members of other minorities, including certain Sunni Arabs and Turkmen from Tuz Khurmato, have also fled. Prior to Baghdad's military action, Tuz Khurmato was co-administered by Kurdish forces, local law enforcement, and the Iran-aligned Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) paramilitaries, who were allied with the Shiite Turkmen community in the town. Although Turkmen and Kurds collaborated to expel Islamic State militants in 2014, the town's delicate coalition quickly deteriorated, resulting in open conflicts. Tensions rose between the communities in the lead-up to the Kurdish independence vote. In Zinana, displaced Kurds recounted to Reuters their experiences of mistreatment at the hands of the Shiite paramilitaries that took control of Tuz. One individual presented a video he recorded, showing the mangled body of a relative. Family members claimed the victim had been shot while in his car, forcibly pulled out alive by paramilitaries, and then run over by a tank. "He was crushed to death right before my eyes, by those monsters," expressed Abu Alan, the relative who captured the footage. "He was a good man from a respectable family." A video circulating online, seemingly depicting the same event, shows a tank driving over a body while uniformed paramilitaries look on. The paramilitaries denied any allegations of wrongdoing. "Joint patrols by the PMF and government forces are ensuring the security of the town to prevent any attacks against Kurds," declared Ali al-Hussaini, a spokesperson for the PMF in northern Iraq and a leader of the largest armed group, the Badr Organisation. "It is our responsibility to maintain safety in Tuz for all communities." The mayor, who is gathering testimonies and evidence of abuse, reported that seven individuals died during the town's capture, including the man crushed by the tank and three other civilians. He also mentioned being aware of three women and one man who had been sexually assaulted. Reuters was unable to verify these allegations. According to the mayor, over 1,000 businesses and 2,000 homes were either looted, set ablaze, or destroyed. He shared with Reuters images depicting residences and storefronts in Kurdish areas that had been blown up and scorched, with their belongings being taken away by individuals in military uniforms. Other photographs displayed paramilitaries seated in the mayor's office.

text: GENEVA (Reuters) - On Friday, the United Nations made a plea to the Saudi-led military coalition for the complete removal of the blockade on Yemen, warning that as many as eight million individuals are at a critical risk of famine. Earlier in the week, the coalition slightly relaxed its blockade to allow humanitarian aid to enter the ports of Hodeidah and Salif, as well as to facilitate U.N. flights into Sanaa. However, the amount of aid being delivered only addresses a small portion of Yemen's requirements, given that nearly all food, fuel, and medicine are imported. The coalition, which receives support from the United States and other nations, initiated the blockade on November 6 after Saudi Arabia intercepted a missile launched from Yemen aimed at its capital, Riyadh. A second missile was intercepted on Thursday. While the blockade has seen some relaxation, it has not been completely lifted. "It is essential for it to be entirely lifted to prevent a horrific humanitarian disaster that could cost millions of lives, something the world hasn’t witnessed in decades," stated U.N. humanitarian chief Mark Lowcock. Yemen's population stands at 25 million, with twenty million in need of aid, and approximately seven to eight million currently teetering on the edge of famine, he remarked as he unveiled the U.N.'s 2018 humanitarian appeal. Lowcock avoided answering reporters' inquiries on whether the Saudi-led blockade constitutes a breach of international law, although he noted that the United Nations has consistently urged all conflict parties to fulfill their obligations. "I am not a legal expert, but it is evident that international humanitarian law necessitates the facilitation of unobstructed access for aid organizations, which I have been advocating for both publicly and in private discussions," he said. U.N. officials often hesitate to criticize conflict parties out of concern for losing access or funding. Saudi Arabia has been a significant contributor to aid initiatives for Yemen. Others have been more outspoken. Jan Egeland, a former U.N. aid chief, labeled the blockade as "illegal collective punishment," while Alfredo Zamudio, director of the Nansen Center for Peace and Dialogue in Norway, expressed to Reuters his belief that the International Criminal Court should investigate whether it constitutes a war crime. At the event in Geneva on Friday, Helle Thorning-Schmidt, head of Save the Children International, remarked: "What we have observed in Yemen represents a clear violation of the rules, and it is evident that the obstruction of aid has also become a tool of warfare." The coalition entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 after the Iran-aligned Houthi group and its allies compelled President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to seek refuge in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh views the Houthis as a proxy for Iran, its chief adversary in the region. The ongoing conflict has resulted in over 10,000 fatalities, displaced more than 2 million individuals, and sparked a cholera outbreak, pushing the nation to the brink of famine.

text: (Reuters) - The potential consequences of President Donald Trump dismissing Attorney General Jeff Sessions could lead to significant political and legal repercussions, as stated by lawmakers and legal experts on Tuesday. Trump has been vocally criticizing an investigation into possible connections between his 2016 campaign and Russia, targeting Sessions in a manner that has led to speculation about the president's desire to replace the attorney general. Should Trump’s ultimate goal involve firing Robert Mueller, the special counsel directing the Russia investigation, it could result in a contentious legal and political confrontation. Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine, expressed to CNN on Tuesday that he anticipated his fellow lawmakers would resist any attempts by Trump to substitute Sessions with a loyalist, particularly if it seemed intended to undermine Mueller’s inquiry. “The senators are going to be very skeptical about this,” remarked King, who often aligns with Democrats. “I expect you would see a special prosecutor pass with veto-proof majorities in both houses. And the investigation would carry on.” Trump, who previously terminated James Comey as the head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation while it was investigating potential Russian ties, was questioned about Sessions during a news conference on Tuesday and stated, “Time will tell. Time will tell.” These comments came after Trump posted on Twitter, labeling Sessions as “weak” and “beleaguered.” On Tuesday, Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell informed reporters in a Capitol corridor that Sessions is “doing a fine job.” Republican Richard Shelby conveyed to reporters that Sessions, who was once his fellow senator from Alabama, is “not the president’s lawyer; he is the attorney general of the United States.” The following outlines the legal framework surrounding the dismissal of Justice Department officials, including Mueller, who was appointed by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein due to Sessions' recusal from the Russia investigation. What are the possible grounds for dismissing Mueller? According to Justice Department regulations, a special counsel may only be removed for “misconduct, dereliction of duty, incapacity, conflict of interest, or for any other good cause.” Do Trump’s allegations that Mueller is conducting a “witch hunt” and that he is conflicted qualify as “good cause?” Likely not. No court has ever defined “good cause” in this context. However, Andrew Wright, a former associate counsel in the Obama White House and a professor at Savannah Law School, noted that Mueller has an exemplary reputation and there is no evidence he has overstepped his authority. Wright added that campaign contributions from members of Mueller’s team to Democrats do not represent a conflict of interest. Could Trump remove Mueller directly? Probably not. Regulations from the Department of Justice dictate that only the attorney general or acting attorney general can terminate a special counsel. Trump has criticized Rosenstein for appointing Mueller and, due to Sessions' recusal, Rosenstein holds the exclusive power to dismiss Mueller. However, some constitutional scholars suggest that Trump might have the legal authority to directly fire Mueller. Saikrishna Prakash from the University of Virginia Law School stated that special counsel regulations may conflict with the president’s extensive powers under the Constitution to remove officials from the executive branch. “I don’t know if that regulation is constitutional,” he expressed. If Trump were to dismiss Sessions or if Sessions were to resign, could Trump select an attorney general who would fire Mueller? Typically, the president nominates an attorney general who requires Senate confirmation. If Trump were to pursue this route, the Senate would likely interrogate any nominee about their plans regarding Mueller’s termination, according to Prakash. “The Senate is going to want assurances that this individual will act independently of the White House and not be a sycophant,” he stated. How else could Trump appoint an attorney general who he believes would take action against Mueller?

text: The Trump administration is contesting the interpretation of a travel ban ruling. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Monday, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump opposed the inclusion of grandparents from six predominantly Muslim nations, asserting in a court document that the government's understanding of how to enact its temporary travel ban aligns with U.S. immigration law. The U.S. Supreme Court reinstated parts of Trump’s executive order from March 6, which prohibited entry for individuals from Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen for 90 days, a measure that had faced challenges from lower courts. The Supreme Court allowed the ban to proceed but with limitations, stating it does not apply to anyone who has a credible “bona fide relationship” with someone in the U.S. Trump claimed that the ban was essential for preventing terrorist threats. However, opponents, including various states and advocacy groups for refugees, initiated legal action to halt the ban, questioning its justification on security grounds and alleging it discriminates against Muslims. Following the Supreme Court's decision, the administration clarified that a “bona fide relationship” is limited to immediate family members: parents, spouses, siblings, and children. This means that grandparents, grandchildren, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and cousins from the six nations would remain barred. The government’s definition, according to lawyers from the Department of Justice, “closely aligns with the categorical determinations outlined by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act,” as stated in court documents on Monday. The filing from the government followed a request from the State of Hawaii last week to U.S. District Judge Derrick Watson in Honolulu, who initially ruled to block the ban, for clarification regarding the Supreme Court’s ruling. Hawaii argued that the government’s interpretation of “bona fide relationship” was overly restrictive. The government contended that Hawaii, along with refugee organizations that submitted a “friend of the court” brief in support of the state, were attempting to impose “broader, more flexible rules.” The refugee organizations claimed that their efforts to help resettle refugees, a process that can take years of coordination with the U.S. government, constitutes a “bona fide” relationship with a U.S. entity. According to the Supreme Court ruling, any refugees with such relationships should be exempt from the three-month ban on refugees included in the executive order. However, the administration argued that individuals with job offers from U.S. companies and international students are fundamentally different from refugees receiving assistance from U.S. resettlement agencies. “A refugee’s relationship with the agency derives from the government, not from an independent connection between the refugee and the resettlement agency,” the government stated in its brief. “In fact, resettlement agencies usually do not have any direct interaction with the refugees they assist prior to their arrival in the United States.” The government asserted that adopting the organization’s interpretation would render the refugee provisions in the executive order “largely meaningless.” The State Department has indicated that U.S. refugee resettlement will proceed as normal until July 6, around the time when the 50,000 cap for the fiscal year set by Trump’s executive order is expected to be met. Late Thursday, just before the ban took effect, the government altered its stance on fiancés, stating they could also be eligible for exceptions. The court filing detailed a frantic 72-hour effort to “coordinate among multiple government agencies and provide comprehensive guidance” on how to carry out the Supreme Court’s ruling. The implementation of the narrowed version of the ban was relatively calm on Friday, in contrast to January when Trump initially enacted a broader version of the order, which led to protests and disruption at airports nationwide and globally.
