text: A bipartisan initiative in the Senate aimed at strengthening the Obamacare insurance marketplaces is projected to reduce the U.S. deficit by $3.8 billion over the upcoming decade, according to a nonpartisan analysis released on Wednesday. The legislation, put forward last week by Republican Senator Lamar Alexander and Democratic Senator Patty Murray, seeks to reinstate subsidies for private insurers for two years, assisting low-income individuals in purchasing insurance. These subsidies were halted by President Donald Trump earlier this month. Additionally, the bill offers states greater flexibility to modify certain provisions of the 2010 Affordable Care Act, which is a landmark legislative success of Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) had previously projected that various Republican attempts to repeal and replace Obamacare could lead to over 20 million individuals losing their health insurance. Conversely, the CBO stated on Wednesday that reinstating the subsidies as proposed in the Alexander-Murray bill would not lead to a significant change in the number of insured individuals. The CBO further indicated that this legislative fix would not affect health insurance premiums for 2018 since they have already been established. Insurers reported an average premium increase of 20 percent to compensate for the loss of federal subsidies. The CBO anticipates that health insurance premiums for 2019 will be lower with the insurer payments reinstated compared to without them. While the Alexander-Murray proposal aims to decrease the federal deficit, the CBO had earlier determined that the elimination of these subsidies, known as cost-sharing reductions, would increase the federal deficit by $194 billion over a ten-year period. Without these subsidies, premiums would rise, necessitating the government to allocate more funds for financial assistance to low-income Americans. Approximately 20 million Americans secured insurance through Obamacare, which played a significant role in reducing the U.S. uninsured rate to an all-time low; however, Republicans have criticized it as an unnecessary government intrusion into a healthcare system that constitutes one-fifth of the U.S. economy. It remains uncertain if the Alexander-Murray bill will be put to a vote in Congress. Trump has expressed conflicting views on the matter, first showing support last week and then opposing it. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell indicated he would not advance the bill without Trump’s endorsement. Trump has characterized the insurer payments as a “bailout” and has pledged to let Obamacare “implode.” "It does not bail out insurance companies, it does benefit consumers, it does benefit taxpayers to the tune of $3.8 billion," Alexander stated on the Senate floor on Wednesday. Insurers claim they do not gain from the subsidies but instead pass them directly to consumers to lower deductibles, co-payments, and other out-of-pocket healthcare costs for low-income individuals. Trump, who vowed to eliminate Obamacare during his campaign, has expressed frustration over the failure of a Congress controlled by his own party to pass a repeal and replacement measure, and has taken actions that circumvent lawmakers to undermine the law. House Speaker Paul Ryan has indicated his disapproval and stated on Wednesday that his chamber would not address the issue or attempt to pass broader Republican legislation to repeal and replace Obamacare this year. With substantial Democratic support and backing from a dozen Republican senators, the Alexander-Murray bill has enough support to surpass the 60 votes required for passage in the 100-member Senate, provided McConnell allows it to be voted on. On Tuesday, two influential Republicans from the House and Senate introduced an alternative Obamacare fix that is more conservative and seems to respond to many of the Trump administration’s concerns regarding the Alexander-Murray proposal. This alternative was presented by Republican Senator Orrin Hatch, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, and Republican Representative Kevin Brady, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee.

text: According to U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, banks that engage in business with North Korea will not be permitted to operate within the United States. This announcement was made on Thursday in New York and is part of a new sanctions directive designed to impede Pyongyang's nuclear and missile initiatives. He emphasized that foreign financial institutions are now informed that they must choose between conducting business with the United States or North Korea, but they cannot do both. text: (Reuters) - On Tuesday, Democrats celebrated significant victories in Virginia's statehouse and successfully ousted Republicans from various state and local positions throughout the United States, marking the party's first substantial wave of wins since Donald Trump became president a year earlier. As the November 2018 elections approach, Democrats need to strategize on how to leverage this momentum, as control of the U.S. Congress and numerous statehouses hangs in the balance. Across the nation, Democratic triumphs highlighted a grassroots resistance to Trump, energizing the party's base, while independent and conservative voters seemed disillusioned with the unpopular Republican leadership in Washington. This year, Democrats secured gubernatorial victories in Virginia and New Jersey, but the wins in legislative and local races across the country may provide more insight into the party's position after a year under Trump's administration. In Virginia, the unexpectedly substantial Democratic gains in the statehouse surprised even the most hopeful party supporters in a state that has been leaning Democratic in recent years but remains a key target for both parties in national elections. "This is beyond our wildest expectations, to be honest," remarked Catherine Vaughan, co-founder of Flippable, one of several new startup progressive organizations working to revitalize the party at the grassroots level. With a number of races still too close to call, Democrats were nearing a flip, or split, of control in the Virginia House of Delegates, effectively eliminating a two-to-one Republican majority overnight. Democratic Lieutenant Governor Ralph Northam also won against Republican Ed Gillespie by nearly nine percentage points in what was anticipated to be a tighter race for Virginia’s governorship, following Democrat Hillary Clinton's five-point victory in the state during the presidential election a year prior. The losing candidate had used Trump-style campaign strategies that emphasized divisive topics like immigration, though the president did not accompany him on the campaign trail. In New Jersey, a Democratic stronghold, voters chose a Democrat to replace a two-term Republican governor and expanded the party's majorities in the state legislature. Additional wins for Democrats included a Senate race in Washington state, which granted the party complete control of the state government, and in Republican-led Georgia, where Democrats gained three seats in special state legislative elections. "This was the first opportunity for voters to send a message to Donald Trump, and they seized it," said John Feehery, a Republican strategist in Washington, in a phone interview. These gains indicated to some election analysts that Democrats might regain control of the U.S. House of Representatives next year. Republicans currently hold power in both the House and Senate, in addition to the White House. Dave Wasserman, an analyst for U.S. House and statehouse races at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, described the Virginia results as a "tidal wave." Nevertheless, even with Tuesday's victories, Democrats find themselves entirely excluded from power in 26 state governments, while Republicans dominate two-thirds of U.S. legislative chambers. Eager to rebuild, national Democrats have shown a renewed focus this year on legislative contests and races further down the ballot. The Democratic National Committee made successful investments in mayoral elections from St. Petersburg, Florida to Manchester, New Hampshire. "If there's one takeaway from yesterday, it's that we must ensure we're competing everywhere, because Democrats can win," stated DNC Chairman Tom Perez during a media call. Jessica Post, executive director of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, emphasized the necessity for national party leaders to concentrate on local races, even during a congressional election year. text: Ignoring warnings, residents in Mumbai decline to vacate deteriorating structures. MUMBAI (Reuters) - Last week, on a sunny morning following two days of relentless monsoon rainfall, Mohammad Altaf stepped outside his residence for a cigarette when he heard a horrifying crash, accompanied by a massive cloud of dust. The six-story Husainee building, where he had resided for the past month, collapsed, trapping almost 50 individuals. Tragically, thirty-four of them lost their lives, including an infant. "It was unbelievable. I had just come down for a smoke, and in under two minutes, the building was gone," stated Altaf, who claimed he was unaware that the apartment complex had been deemed unsafe by housing authorities in India’s financial center six years prior. Throughout the bustling city, home to 20 million residents, thousands of families inhabit decaying buildings that have been officially marked as uninhabitable - and most are aware of this fact. Housing officials mention that they are unable to enforce evacuations due to lenient laws. This year, the city’s municipal corporation identified 791 buildings as irreparable and too hazardous for habitation, yet nearly 500 of these remain occupied, according to a municipal authority representative. While regulations differ among countries and even states, authorities in many locations possess greater authority to mandate evacuations. Altaf, in his mid-thirties, is single and was sharing the apartment in the Bhendi Bazar area, one of the city's oldest districts, with two colleagues. His two roommates escaped with minor knee and shoulder injuries after leaping from their third-floor apartment. Authorities have yet to ascertain the cause of the collapse, which occurred following several days of heavy rainfall. The 117-year-old building in Bhendi Bazar, a densely populated area filled with narrow streets, shops, and tenements, was classified as unsafe by the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA) in 2011. Nevertheless, it continued to provide shelter for Altaf and his flatmates, along with five other families, a warehouse for a sweet shop, and even a nursery on the ground floor. The building's owner, Hakimmudin Bootwala, stated that seven families vacated by 2014, but others refused to leave despite his requests. One of them had subleased the apartment to Altaf and his associates. "The people were initially my friends and neighbors, and later became tenants," remarked the 73-year-old. "I genuinely urged them to leave. The building had numerous issues, including leaks. The roof was intact, but the walls had grown exceedingly weak and porous." An official from MHADA indicated that there exists a law allowing for the forced evacuation of residents from hazardous buildings, but enforcing it is challenging due to loopholes and legal obstacles. For example, evicting children and elderly individuals could lead to complications, said the housing official, who chose to remain anonymous as he was not permitted to speak with the media. "We disconnect water and electricity supplies to buildings identified as dangerous for habitation, but residents find ways to obtain water and electricity from nearby structures," the official added. MHADA, which conducts regular inspections of buildings older than 30 years, has identified more than 14,000 structures in the city requiring repairs, according to their latest report. Of these, nine thousand, housing nearly 250,000 families, need redevelopment, the housing official stated, noting that the remaining 5,000 are relatively secure due to ongoing maintenance performed by property owners in collaboration with the housing authority. Once regulators determine that a building requires redevelopment, they must appoint a developer to renovate or rebuild the structure in the case of public housing or instruct private owners to hire one. The developer is then obligated to provide residents with alternative accommodation until the renovation is finalized, in accordance with state law in Mumbai. However, residents frequently express concerns that the housing alternatives offered are too small, substandard, or located too far away. Seventy percent of occupants in both privately- and publicly-owned buildings must consent to redevelop their structure.

text: The emergency manager for Detroit Public Schools, Darnell Earley, will resign later this month, as announced by Michigan Governor Rick Snyder on Tuesday. Earley has faced backlash from the teachers' union and African American state legislators due to the deteriorating conditions of the city's educational institutions. According to the governor's statement, Earley will exit the school district on February 29. Having previously overseen Flint and its contaminated water system, Earley has been at the helm of Detroit schools since January 2015. The school district is currently burdened with $3.5 billion in debt, which includes $1.7 billion in bonds secured by property taxes. The district of Detroit Public Schools is experiencing a drop in student enrollment, and significant pension and debt responsibilities have put it at risk of depleting its funds by April. The governor mentioned that if the state Senate quickly approves legislation to reorganize the school district and address its debt, there is a possibility for the system to regain some local governance. However, if the debt issue remains unresolved, Snyder warned that the district could be “virtually insolvent” by April. In a report from November, Earley noted that a bankruptcy filing by Detroit’s school district could transfer the responsibilities for pensions and bonds to state and local governments. The governor, who must authorize any bankruptcy filing for the district, is not expected to support such an action. On Tuesday, Snyder commended Earley for performing a “very good job under some very difficult circumstances,” highlighting his efforts in restructuring the school system, reducing expenses, and striving to stabilize student enrollment. The governor stated he will appoint a transitional leader before the month concludes to implement his strategy for restructuring the district, focusing on both its academic and financial challenges. Last week, the Michigan black legislative caucus urged Snyder to dismiss Earley. Additionally, the union representing Detroit public school teachers filed a lawsuit against the district, seeking Earley’s immediate ouster and the restoration of local control along with a plan to repair the district’s decaying facilities. Ivy Bailey, the interim president of the Detroit Federation of Teachers, referred to Earley’s exit as a “step in the right direction.” While serving as the emergency manager in Flint, Earley oversaw the city’s controversial switch from Detroit’s water supply to the Flint River in April 2014, a decision that was reversed last October when tests revealed elevated lead levels in blood samples from children in Flint. Lead is known to be a neurotoxin that can harm the brain and lead to various health issues. Earley has stated that he should not be held accountable for the water crisis, as the decision was made prior to his appointment.

text: China has stated that the situation in Catalonia illustrates that Taiwan's efforts for independence are likely to fail. BEIJING (Reuters) - A Chinese official remarked on Wednesday that the unsuccessful attempt by Catalonia to declare independence serves as evidence that Taiwan's independence aspirations are also destined to fail, emphasizing that national unity is crucial for all nations. China views secessionist and independence movements around the globe unfavorably, while maintaining a stance of non-interference in the internal matters of other countries. Beijing has expressed its opposition to any actions that would divide Spain. Last month, Madrid took direct control over Catalonia after the Prime Minister dismissed the region's separatist government, which had declared independence from Spain following a failed referendum. This matter is particularly sensitive for China due to the situation of self-governing and democratic Taiwan, which China claims as its territory, although many residents desire to formally declare independence—a red line for Beijing. Ma Xiaoguang, the spokesperson for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, stated that the collapse of Catalonia's independence effort is a positive development. He noted, "The failure of the Catalonia referendum fully shows that protecting national sovereignty and territorial integrity is a paramount national interest for east or west," adding, "Thus, Taiwan independence is doomed to failure." Relations between Beijing and Taipei have deteriorated since Tsai Ing-wen's election as president of Taiwan last year. China is of the opinion that she seeks to achieve formal independence for Taiwan. Tsai asserts that her goal is to preserve peace with China while also safeguarding Taiwan's democracy and security. China has halted a regular dialogue mechanism with Taiwan, increased military exercises around the island, and attempted to limit its international presence by reducing Taiwan's remaining diplomatic allies. This week, Taiwan reported that its environment minister was barred from attending an annual U.N. climate conference in Germany, despite being accredited as a non-governmental participant, due to Chinese pressure. Ma stated that Taiwan was responsible for the strained relations and its lack of participation in events like the climate discussions. "The Taiwan side shouldn’t blame others when they themselves are at fault, and they should sincerely reflect on the situation," he concluded.

'I was ‘grossly generalistic’ last night, and that’s not a good approach. I regret saying ‘half’ - that was incorrect,' Clinton mentioned in a statement following her comments made at a fundraiser in New York the previous evening. However, she added, 'Trump has largely constructed his campaign on prejudice and paranoia,' and insisted, 'I will continue to denounce bigotry and racist language throughout this campaign.' Responses from Republicans and Trump supporters were intense on social media regarding Clinton’s statements made during the LGBT fundraiser, which risked diverting attention from her efforts to depict Trump as unfit for the presidency. Trump, meanwhile, aimed to leverage Clinton’s remarks to launch a similar accusation against her. 'How can she lead our country when she harbors such contempt and disdain for so many wonderful Americans?' a statement from Trump questioned. 'Hillary Clinton ought to be ashamed of herself, and this clearly shows that she is unqualified and incapable of serving as President of the United States,' he continued. During the fundraiser on Friday night, Clinton asserted that Trump had given a platform to hateful rhetoric through his actions as a candidate in the upcoming election on November 8. 'To be grossly generalistic, half of Trump’s supporters can be categorized into what I refer to as the 'basket of deplorables',' Clinton remarked. 'Sadly, there are people like that, and he has elevated their status.' She indicated that while some of these individuals were irredeemable, they did not represent the entirety of America. Clinton added that the other group of Trump’s supporters consisted of people yearning for change who felt let down by the government and the economic situation. 'They don’t agree with everything he says, but he appears to offer them some hope for a better life,' Clinton noted. 'Those are individuals we need to comprehend and empathize with as well.' 'Let me express sincerely: Hillary, they aren’t a basket of anything. They are Americans, and they deserve your respect.' Trump, a businessman from New York who has not previously held political office, frequently makes comments that some find insulting, racist, or inappropriate. On Friday night, he told his supporters in Pensacola, Florida, that Clinton could shoot someone without facing charges. Trump himself tweeted: 'Wow, Hillary Clinton was SO INSULTING to my supporters, millions of amazing, hardworking individuals. I believe this will impact her at the polls!' text: North Korea has labeled the recent U.N. sanctions as an act of war. BEIJING/SEOUL (Reuters) - According to North Korea's foreign ministry, the latest sanctions imposed by the U.N. are equivalent to a complete economic blockade, and the country has threatened to take action against those who supported this measure. On Friday, the U.N. Security Council unanimously enacted new sanctions against North Korea due to its latest intercontinental ballistic missile test, aiming to restrict its access to refined petroleum products and crude oil, as well as its earnings from overseas workers. The resolution intends to prohibit nearly 90 percent of refined petroleum exports to North Korea by limiting them to 500,000 barrels annually and, in a last-minute amendment, requires the repatriation of North Koreans working abroad within 24 months, rather than the initially proposed 12 months. The resolution, drafted by the U.S., also limits crude oil supplies to North Korea to 4 million barrels per year and commits the Council to further reductions if the country conducts another nuclear test or ICBM launch. In a statement released by the official KCNA news agency, North Korea's foreign ministry asserted that the United States is increasingly frantic in its attempts to impose the severest sanctions and exert pressure on the nation due to fear of its nuclear capabilities. The ministry described the new resolution as essentially a total economic blockade of North Korea. "We categorize this sanctions resolution orchestrated by the U.S. and its allies as a serious violation of our Republic's sovereignty, as an act of war undermining peace and stability on the Korean peninsula and in the region, and we categorically reject the resolution," it stated. The ministry warned against the grave error of believing that the U.S. and its allies could halt the victorious progress of the North Korean people, who have successfully achieved the monumental task of completing their state nuclear force, through outdated sanctions. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un announced the completion of the nuclear force on November 29 after the country conducted its largest-ever ICBM test, claiming it puts all of the U.S. within reach. During a meeting with members of the ruling Workers' Party on Friday, Kim stated that the nation has triumphantly achieved the historic goal of finishing its state nuclear force despite facing shortages and numerous challenges due to the despicable anti-DPRK actions of its adversaries. North Korea is officially known as the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). South Korea's foreign ministry responded to Reuters, acknowledging awareness of North Korea's remarks regarding the new sanctions, reiterating its stance that they serve as a serious warning from the international community urging the region to cease reckless provocations and pursue dialogue for denuclearization and peace. The North Korean foreign ministry argued that its nuclear arsenal serves as a self-defensive deterrent and does not violate international law. "We will further strengthen our self-defensive nuclear deterrence to fundamentally eliminate U.S. nuclear threats, coercion, and hostile actions by establishing a practical balance of power with the U.S.," it stated. The ministry cautioned that the U.S. should not forget, even momentarily, the reality of the DPRK, which has quickly become a strategic state capable of posing a significant nuclear threat to the U.S. mainland. North Korea warned that those who supported the sanctions would incur its wrath. "Countries that voted in favor of this sanctions resolution will be held fully accountable for all consequences arising from it, and we will ensure that they pay a heavy price for their actions, now and forever," it declared. Both of North Korea's traditional allies, China and Russia, backed the latest U.N. sanctions. Tensions have been escalating due to North Korea's nuclear and missile programs, which it continues to pursue in defiance of years of U.N. sanctions.

text: BANGKOK (Reuters) - On Saturday, drums and a band accompanied officials dressed in black attire and traditional costumes as they practiced for the funeral procession of Thailand's former King Bhumibol Adulyadej. The cremation is anticipated to take place next week, drawing an expected crowd of 250,000 mourners. Some participants carried a replica of a golden urn, historically used to hold the remains of deceased kings. Currently, the king's body rests in a coffin, but the urn continues to symbolize the monarch's remains. The rehearsal for the procession, projected to last up to five hours, wove through groups of mourners dressed in black within Bangkok's historic district. Many attendees were visibly affected by the somber event, with some displaying gold-framed images of the late king. The military-led government has allocated 3 billion baht (approximately $90 million) for this grand funeral. Preparations have taken nearly a year, involving thousands of artisans who crafted an intricate structure of gold-tipped Thai pavilions in a plaza situated in front of the majestic Grand Palace. King Bhumibol, who passed away on October 13 of the previous year at the age of 87, ruled Thailand for 70 years and is credited by some with revitalizing the monarchy's stature. The monarchy's resurgence in popularity was supported by a powerful public relations campaign; Thai evening news features a daily segment focused on the royals, and the late king was frequently seen in his youth traveling across the nation to meet the underprivileged. This PR effort solidified the king's image as a semi-divine figure among his 68 million citizens. The five-day funeral is expected to see attendance from numerous heads of state, including Bhutan's King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck and Japan's Prince Akishino and Princess Kiko, among others. Analysts suggest that the period following the funeral may bring uncertainty for many Thais, highlighting the king's role as a moral guide and mediator during times of political turbulence. His only son, King Maha Vajiralongkorn, officially took the throne last year, but his coronation will occur only after his father's funeral. The cremation is scheduled for October 26, which has been designated as a national holiday. A number of businesses have announced closures for the entire day or will close at midday. Over 10,000 7-Eleven convenience stores, a common stop for many Thais, will also be closed on that day.

WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - The attorneys representing former national security adviser Michael Flynn have ceased communication with the legal team of U.S. President Donald Trump, marking a potentially significant development in the investigation concerning interactions between Trump’s election campaign and Russia, as stated by sources acquainted with the inquiry on Friday. Flynn’s attorney, Robert Kelner, contacted Trump’s private lawyer, John Dowd, on Wednesday to inform him that the situation had reached a point where they could no longer engage in discussions, two individuals familiar with the conversation relayed to Reuters on Friday. The New York Times was the first to report the cessation of communication between the two legal teams. Flynn, a retired Army general, plays a pivotal role in a federal inquiry spearheaded by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, focused on determining whether Trump associates colluded with purported Russian efforts to enhance his 2016 presidential campaign. It remains unclear if Kelner's call was made after negotiating a plea deal with Mueller for Flynn’s cooperation in the investigation, or if Flynn opted to engage with Mueller, according to two additional sources. "No one should conclude that this indicates anything regarding General Flynn cooperating against the president," Jay Sekulow, another attorney representing Trump, stated on Thursday. Dowd refrained from commenting on the issue on Friday, as did Peter Carr, Mueller’s spokesperson. Kelner also declined to provide any comments. Officials from the White House have similarly chosen not to comment. Flynn’s cooperation, who served as a senior campaign adviser before becoming Trump’s national security adviser in the White House, would represent a significant advantage for Mueller’s investigation. In March, while unsuccessfully seeking immunity for his client to testify before House and Senate investigations related to the matter, Kelner remarked, "Mr. Flynn certainly has a story to tell, and he certainly wants to tell it, should the circumstances permit." Two sources familiar with Mueller’s investigation indicated that Flynn might offer valuable insights into three primary lines of inquiry. These involve: any collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia during the 2016 election; financial crimes, including money laundering, potentially involving Trump aides; and whether Trump attempted to obstruct justice when he dismissed former FBI Director James Comey in May, as Comey was investigating the Trump campaign’s interactions with Russia. Russia has denied any interference in the election. Trump has consistently denied any collusion with Russia by his campaign and has labeled the inquiry as a witch hunt. Two congressional officials engaged in separate investigations into the Trump campaign’s ties with Russia noted that a key area of exploration is whether Flynn or other Trump advisers ever proposed lifting U.S. economic sanctions on Russia in exchange for advantageous business arrangements. Potential arrangements include a suggested commercial nuclear power initiative involving Russian companies that Flynn has worked to promote to prospective clients in the Middle East in recent years, as reported by sources knowledgeable about the project to Reuters. "At this moment, there is no evidence of an effort to negotiate such a deal, but Flynn is among the top individuals who likely would be aware if any such attempt existed," stated one of the congressional officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump terminated Flynn's employment on February 13, following revelations that Flynn had discussed U.S. sanctions on Russia with then-Russian Ambassador Sergei Kislyak in December, the month prior to Trump assuming office, and subsequently misled Vice President Mike Pence about those discussions. Flynn has been under examination by the special counsel in multiple areas, according to sources familiar with the investigation.

Turnout for nationwide mayoral elections, also being held on Sunday, was 47 percent, the national election board said. Three major opposition parties were boycotting the polls, alleging the election authorities were biased towards the socialists.

text: Chad has pulled back hundreds of its troops from neighboring Niger, where they were aiding local forces in the battle against Boko Haram Islamist extremists, according to humanitarian sources and officials. This withdrawal, which took place over the last two weeks, may undermine the broader efforts to combat the militants responsible for the deaths of tens of thousands, causing many others to flee and sparking a humanitarian crisis. There has been no immediate response or clarification from defense officials in Chad. However, this decision follows a month after Chad expressed its discontent over an unanticipated U.S. travel ban affecting its citizens. At that time, Chad cautioned that the ban could have repercussions on its security obligations, which include participation in the U.S.-supported fight against Boko Haram. Locals reported that the troop withdrawal has already impacted the Diffa region of Niger, which has experienced a series of attacks from Boko Haram militants crossing over from their stronghold in Nigeria. Ibrahim Arimi, a resident of the border village of Bosso, mentioned that incidents of banditry had risen since Chadian forces began to depart, and he had relocated to another village for his safety. Lamido Moumouni, a parliament member from Diffa, noted that the local population had started to voice their concerns. "They have come to rely on the forces so there is a perception that security will be lacking," he stated via telephone. At its highest point in 2016, following an assault in Bosso, Chad had stationed 2,000 troops in Niger to assist in countering Boko Haram, although security sources indicate that this number has since declined. Boko Haram has launched attacks on Chad, Niger, and Cameroon from its base in northeastern Nigeria. Its eight-year attempt to establish an Islamist caliphate has displaced millions, with over 200,000 currently residing in Diffa, facing minimal chances of returning to their homes. Many are living in makeshift camps along an incomplete highway amid a desolate savannah with scarce resources. Additionally, Chad's troops are deployed in front-line roles within a peacekeeping mission in northern Mali. Analysts suggest that declining oil revenues following the price collapse in 2014 have diminished Chad's willingness to engage in costly regional security obligations.

text: A Senate committee has endorsed President Donald Trump’s choice to oversee the U.S. government's health programs for seniors and individuals with disabilities, setting the stage for a full Senate vote. The Senate Finance Committee approved Seema Verma with a 13-12 vote to lead the $1 trillion Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Verma owns a healthcare consulting company called SVC and has contributed to the redesign of Medicaid initiatives in various states, including Indiana. She played a role in expanding Medicaid in Indiana, allowing thousands of additional low-income individuals to qualify. These individuals are required to contribute small monthly payments towards their healthcare through health savings accounts, a strategy that could shape the Trump administration's approach to healthcare for low-income populations. During a speech to Congress on Tuesday, Trump advocated for government assistance to help Americans purchase health insurance via tax credits and enhanced health savings accounts. Verma has collaborated closely with Vice President Mike Pence, who, during his governorship in Indiana, honored her with the Sagamore of the Wabash award, typically given to individuals who have provided exemplary service to the state or its governor. Republican Senator Orrin Hatch from Utah remarked in a statement that addressing the issues confronting Medicare and Medicaid necessitates a robust collaboration with the administration. He stated that Verma “will help facilitate that partnership and as we work to repeal and replace Obamacare, she will play a vital role in realigning the focus on patient-centered solutions.” Prior to a preliminary vote on Wednesday, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden from Oregon voiced his concerns that during her confirmation hearing last month, Verma did not adequately respond to inquiries regarding her plans to address escalating drug costs. He also pointed out that while overseeing Indiana’s health program, her firm received payments from businesses supplying services and products to the program. “She was on both sides of the deal,” he noted. Verma has rejected any allegations of misconduct. In a letter dated January 31 to the Department of Health and Human Services, she detailed several measures she would implement to mitigate potential conflicts of interest if she is confirmed as administrator of CMS, including selling her financial stake in SVC Inc within 90 days of her confirmation.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The proposal to sell off 50% of the U.S. emergency oil stockpile to assist in budget balancing has raised concerns among lawmakers from both parties, who fear it could jeopardize the drilling sector and leave the country exposed to supply disruptions. The budget proposal from the White House for 2018, delivered to Congress on Tuesday, suggests generating nearly $16.6 billion by 2027 through the gradual sale of millions of barrels from the reserve, which currently contains around 688 million barrels stored in underground facilities in Texas and Louisiana. The announcement of this proposal briefly caused a drop in oil prices due to worries about market oversupply; however, prices bounced back and ended slightly higher amid hopes that OPEC and other nations would prolong their supply reductions. "We should not be liquidating oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at this time," stated Senator John Hoeven, a Republican from North Dakota, which is a significant oil-producing state. "The SPR should be utilized for emergencies, and selling it now would disturb the markets." The initiative to sell from the SPR is part of a larger proposal from the White House intended to balance the U.S. budget, serving as a foundation for policy discussions with Congress, which will ultimately create its own version. The fate of the SPR proposal during the budget discussions may hinge in part on Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski from Alaska, who is on the appropriations committee and chairs the energy panel of the chamber. In 2015, during Congress's consideration of selling a limited quantity of oil from the reserve to finance a transportation bill, Murkowski was against the notion, arguing that the reserve should not be treated like an ATM. On Tuesday, Murkowski did not specifically comment on the SPR plan, but remarked that "a President’s budget is more of a vision than anything else." Attempts to contact Murkowski on Tuesday did not succeed. Conversely, Murkowski’s Democratic counterpart on the energy committee expressed worries that selling off half of the reserve would contradict the original intent of the facility, which Congress established in 1975 to safeguard against global oil supply disruptions that could negatively impact the U.S. economy. "We are not going to permit Donald Trump to auction off our energy security to the highest bidder," Senator Maria Cantwell of Washington stated in an email. The Arab oil embargo in the early 1970s caused turmoil at U.S. gas stations and instilled fears of long-term economic damage. Since then, the landscape has changed significantly: U.S. oil production has risen sharply in recent years, and imports from Canada have increased, reducing reliance on some less stable Middle Eastern suppliers. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, U.S. oil imports from OPEC have decreased from over 5.4 million barrels per day in 2008 to less than 3.2 million bpd in 2016. Richard Newell, a former head of the EIA, pointed out that the proposal could lead the United States to breach its commitment as a member of the International Energy Agency to maintain reserves equivalent to 90 days’ worth of oil imports. Currently, the SPR holds an amount sufficient for about 145 days’ worth of oil imports. "There are various scenarios in which lowering the SPR to the suggested levels would breach our IEA treaty commitments," he remarked. Legislators from both parties have also indicated that releasing oil from the SPR could suppress crude prices and negatively impact drilling companies that are still recovering from the price collapse of 2014. Trump had campaigned on a promise to revitalize the drilling sector. text: New Jersey Governor Chris Christie on Tuesday put forward a proposal to change the state's education funding structure, suggesting that all public school districts receive a uniform rate of $6,599 for each student. Dubbed the "Fairness Formula" in his policy announcements on Tuesday, Christie assured that funding for students with special needs would persist despite any potential changes to the formula. In New Jersey, schools are financed through property taxes, which are among the highest in the country due to what Christie described as an "unaffordable and broken school funding formula supported by special interests and misguided Supreme Court rulings." He mentioned plans to travel across the state this summer to discuss the proposal. Currently, the amount of state funding allocated to school districts varies significantly, with some receiving under $3,000 per student while others get as much as $28,000. Implementing such a change would be challenging, as it would require approval from a Democrat-controlled legislature that has previously turned down earlier proposals for education formula modifications from Christie, a Republican. "Governor Christie’s proposal is unconstitutional and detrimental to our most vulnerable children," Assembly Speaker Vincent Prieto stated on Tuesday, emphasizing that Christie has yet to fully fund schools according to the existing formula. At present, poorer districts benefit from increased state aid under a formula established by a 1990 New Jersey Supreme Court ruling known as Abbott v. Burke II, which determined that the state’s education funding was inequitable and mandated that low-income "Abbott districts" receive funding equivalent to that of wealthier districts.

text: On Wednesday, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan came to the defense of an Ottoman military leader after the foreign minister of the United Arab Emirates retweeted claims regarding the looting of the sacred city of Medina by Ottoman troops during World War One. Erdogan seemed to be reacting to a tweet from UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahayan, which alleged that in 1916, Ottoman forces commanded by Fakhreddin Pasha pilfered money and manuscripts from Medina. The tweet further asserted that Turkish soldiers kidnapped the city's residents, transporting them to Istanbul. The tweet also stated, "These are Erdogan's ancestors, and their history with Arab Muslims," and was initially shared by an individual claiming to be an Iraqi dentist residing in Germany. Medina, presently part of Saudi Arabia, was under Ottoman control for many centuries until the empire's fall following World War One. While addressing local officials, Erdogan remarked that Fahreddin Pasha did not rob Medina or its inhabitants but rather worked to safeguard the city and its citizens amid wartime chaos. He expressed disdain for those who, in a delusional state, continuously and shamelessly assert that Erdogan's forebears looted sacred artifacts from the city and transported them to Istanbul, claiming that such actions were in fact meant to protect those items from invaders. The UAE, a close ally of the United States, regards Erdogan's Islamist-influenced governing party as an ally of Islamist factions that the UAE opposes throughout the Arab region. Tensions between the two nations escalated further when Ankara supported Qatar after Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, and Egypt imposed sanctions on the Gulf state in June. Two months later, Sheikh Abdullah condemned what he termed the 'colonial' moves of Turkey and Iran in Syria, despite both Turkey and the UAE being opposed to Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. Furthermore, Erdogan's spokesperson, Ibrahim Kalin, also reacted to Sheikh Abdullah's remarks, lamenting that it is regrettable for him to share such propagandistic falsehoods that aim to incite discord between Turks and Arabs. Kalin questioned whether attacking President Erdogan at all costs has become a new trend, expressing his thoughts in a tweet on Tuesday.

text: Britain is hastening its Brexit preparations as divorce discussions are also set to accelerate. LONDON/BRATISLAVA (Reuters) - The UK is intensifying its arrangements for all possible scenarios as it prepares to exit the European Union, while both parties are optimistic that a deal to enhance negotiations aimed at untangling over 40 years of collaboration will soon be finalized. With just 17 months left before the anticipated UK departure, the sluggish pace of negotiations has heightened fears of a no-deal exit, causing concern among business leaders who state that they are running out of time to make investment choices. British and EU negotiators convened in Brussels on Tuesday and agreed to conduct additional divorce discussions on November 9-10. The urgency has prompted the UK government to accelerate its Brexit strategy, hiring thousands of additional personnel and allocating millions to ensure that customs posts, regulations, and systems are operational from day one of Brexit, regardless of whether a future relationship deal is reached. During a meeting with her ministers on Tuesday, Prime Minister Theresa May received updates on plans for the tax and customs authority to recruit an additional 3,000-5,000 workers in the upcoming year and for a 500 million pound ($660.45 million) expenditure for Brexit preparations. "Alongside the negotiations in Brussels, it is essential that we establish our domestic preparations so that we are ready at the moment we exit the EU," stated May’s spokesperson to reporters. The preparatory efforts have seen a notable increase in pace in recent months. Government departments are drafting detailed plans for approximately 300 ongoing programs. May aims to quell dissent from her ruling Conservative Party, which is urging her to abandon discussions that have stalled over the financial settlement Britain should pay to exit the bloc, as well as to intensify negotiations. Brexit advocates are insisting that the UK should exit without a deal if discussions do not progress beyond the matters of the divorce agreement, the so-called Brexit bill, rights of EU citizens, and the border with EU member Ireland by December. On Tuesday, Brexit minister David Davis expressed his belief that the UK would reach some form of basic agreement with the European Union, even in the highly unlikely event that they could not agree on a trade deal. EU chief negotiator Michel Barnier reiterated his commitment in the Slovak capital of Bratislava to accelerate negotiations. "We have clearly proposed three (different dates) for new rounds. In the coming hours or days, we will be collaborating with British delegations to establish the appropriate dates because we need to engage in a very intensive manner to reach this agreement before December," Barnier told reporters, comments which bolstered sterling. The schedule for the new negotiation round will be arranged within hours or days. May’s administration has consistently indicated that it would welcome a speeding up of discussions. Following a high-level meeting in Brussels on October 19-20, Barnier has put forth three additional negotiation rounds before the year concludes. London favors ongoing negotiations. "What does continuous negotiations mean? We are not entirely sure. We are prepared to accelerate, but we need to have something substantive to discuss. We are very willing to increase the frequency of our meetings," stated an EU official. Prior to exiting the EU, May confronts the challenge of securing parliamentary backing for legislation to sever political, financial, and legal connections with the bloc - the EU Withdrawal Bill, which has drawn hundreds of proposed amendments from lawmakers. When asked if May was considering offering a concession regarding a final vote on any agreement reached with the EU, her spokesperson commented that there was "a lot of speculation regarding Brexit." "We’ve always maintained that we will do whatever is necessary," he added.

text: On Saturday, China announced its decision to prohibit certain petroleum exports to North Korea. According to a report by Reuters from SHANGHAI, this action is in line with a resolution from the United Nations Security Council. The Ministry of Commerce released a statement on its official website indicating that starting October 1, exports of refined petroleum products would be restricted, and immediately, the export of condensates and liquefied natural gas would be halted. The statement also mentioned that imports of textiles from North Korea would be banned right away. (The headline has been corrected to specify that some petroleum exports are banned.)

The Ministry of Commerce said in a statement on its website that China would limit exports of refined petroleum products from Oct. 1, and ban exports of condensates and liquefied natural gas immediately. text: At least 17 individuals have lost their lives in a conflict over a gold mine located on the border between Mali and Guinea. CONAKRY (Reuters) - According to a government representative in Guinea, a two-day clash between villagers from Guinea and Mali regarding the control of a gold mine that lies across the shared border resulted in the deaths of at least 17 people. Residents from both nations claim ownership of the area's valuable underground resources, attracting thousands to engage in unregulated, small-scale mining activities near the border. Artisanal gold mining, which utilizes basic tools, serves as a significant income source in both Mali and Guinea, yet it carries many safety hazards, including frequent collapses of mines. Cheick Mohamed Diallo, the prefect of Mandiana in eastern Guinea, reported that there are five fatalities on the Guinean side and 12 on the Malian side. A witness from the Guinean side indicated that the villagers engaged in combat using firearms and edged weapons. Although local resident Cheikh Keita mentioned that the fighting has come to an end, the atmosphere remained tense on Tuesday. A comparable incident took place in February 2015, when miners from Guinea killed three Malian individuals during a dispute over a gold find.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Donald Trump has achieved a significant victory in his campaign against illegal immigration, accomplishing this without the construction of his proposed wall. This success was revealed last week by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which disclosed statistics indicating a 93 percent decrease since December in the apprehension of parents and children attempting to cross the border from Mexico illegally. In December, the number of apprehended parents and children was 16,000; by March, a month typically associated with increased immigration due to milder weather, that figure had plummeted to just over 1,100. This was a noteworthy reduction—more pronounced than the overall 72 percent decline in apprehensions—but according to eight DHS officials interviewed by Reuters, it was not unexpected. Trump has consistently emphasized the necessity of intensifying efforts against all illegal immigrants. However, internally, as per the DHS officials knowledgeable about the department's strategy, his administration has concentrated on one particular group of immigrants more than others: women with children, who represent the fastest-growing demographic among illegal immigrants. This strategic focus has not been previously disclosed. In the time since Trump took office, DHS has implemented a variety of policies designed to deter women from trying to cross the border, including stricter initial requirements for asylum applications and the potential prosecution of parents if they engage smugglers to transport their families across the border. Additionally, the department has proposed measures such as the separation of women and children at the border. DHS Secretary John Kelly stated during a Senate hearing on April 5 that the significant decrease in illegal immigration, particularly among women and children, was a result of Trump's stringent policies. Thus far, it has been the threat of new policies rather than their actual enforcement that has curtailed family migration. Mothers and children are not being separated - and DHS has put the plan on hold; parents have not faced prosecution, and there is no wall across most of the border. Nevertheless, the number of migrants attempting to cross – especially women and children – has seen a sharp decline. When asked for a comment regarding the policy of focusing on women with children, DHS spokesperson Jonathan Hoffman noted the March decline, stating, “Those were 15,000 women and children who did not put themselves at risk of death and assault from smugglers to make the trip north.” The White House opted not to comment and directed Reuters to DHS. For several months, Central Americans had been aware of Trump’s hardline policies. Public service announcements on radio and television depicted grim scenarios regarding the dangers faced by those traveling north. Some of these advertisements were funded by the United States, while others came from United Nations agencies and local governments. One radio advertisement in Honduras featured a mother who lamented, “It’s been a year and I don’t know if she is alive or dead. I’d do anything to have her here with me. Curse the day I sent her north.” The potential for the separation of mothers and children at the border caused particular concern, as Honduran Deputy Foreign Minister Maria Andrea Matamoros explained to Reuters, “That worries any mother that wants to go to the United States with their kid, and being separated drastically changes their plans.” The policies aimed at women and children have their origins in a working group formed by Capitol Hill staffers and others, convened by Trump’s transition team in the weeks following the November 8 election. text: Factbox: Trump controversies: Michael Flynn, the travel ban, and more. U.S. lawmakers, including prominent Republicans, have called for an inquiry. One guest shared a photo on Facebook featuring a man identified as the holder of the "nuclear football," or the codes for nuclear weapons. These occurrences raised alarms about national security, prompting a Republican representative to seek further information from the White House. On January 27, Trump signed an executive order that temporarily barred entry into the U.S. for travelers from seven Muslim-majority nations and all refugees, citing a need to safeguard Americans. The ban incited protests throughout the United States, confusion at both domestic and international airports, and numerous legal challenges. A federal judge in Seattle issued a suspension of the ban on February 3, an order that was later upheld by a federal appeals court in San Francisco. text: Sweet home Chicago: Obama returns to the city where it all began. CHICAGO (Reuters) - On Monday, former U.S. President Barack Obama is set to make his first significant appearance since leaving office, selecting Chicago—the city where his political journey commenced—as the backdrop for his reemergence after a three-month absence from public life. Obama will engage with youth leaders and advocate for community organizing in the same South Side neighborhoods where his activism flourished, ultimately leading him to two terms in the White House that concluded with Donald Trump’s inauguration on January 20. Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who was Obama’s inaugural White House chief of staff, expressed pride that Obama chose Chicago for both his final speech as president and his initial one post-presidency. "I believe it demonstrates both his emotional and intellectual investment in this city, viewing it as his home," he remarked. Obama's ongoing relationship with Chicago holds significance for the city, which harbors global ambitions yet struggles with insecurities about its standing in the world. In the final year of Obama’s second term, Chicago secured its claim to a part of his legacy by outbidding Hawaii and New York for the location of his presidential library. Obama, who maintains a residence in Chicago, was raised in Hawaii. The former president and his wife Michelle are anticipated to relocate from Washington to New York after their younger daughter, Sasha, finishes high school. David Axelrod, a former senior political adviser to Obama, noted that the decision to place the library in Chicago should have alleviated any worries among residents regarding the former Democratic president’s allegiance to the city. However, he indicated that Monday’s gathering serves as another important indication of Obama’s deep connections to Chicago. "He will certainly become more visible in the future," he stated. "This is clearly a reemergence." Reverend Michael Pfleger, a social justice advocate and leader of a significant Roman Catholic church on the South Side, mentioned that a prominent presence from Obama could assist the nation’s third-largest city in tackling some of its pressing challenges. One major concern is the increase in gun violence, which Trump has pointed to as evidence of lawlessness and the shortcomings of the Democratic officials who have governed Chicago for years. "It’s his life, and he’s not holding an elected position at the moment, so he can choose his actions freely," Pfleger commented. "But I would love to see him engage with his hometown of Chicago. He has the potential to make a substantial impact." Civil Rights activist Jesse Jackson stated that Obama could leverage his influential platform to confront glaring disparities in Chicago’s education, housing, and employment sectors, advocating for reinvestments in struggling neighborhoods. The event on Monday is set to occur at the University of Chicago's South Side campus, where Obama previously taught constitutional law. It aims "to inspire and bolster the upcoming generation of leaders focused on strengthening communities," as per an official statement. Since stepping down from office, Obama has maintained a relatively low public profile, enjoying vacations in Palm Springs, California, and the British Virgin Islands, where he engaged in kite-boarding while vacationing with British billionaire Sir Richard Branson. Alongside his wife, who grew up on the South Side of Chicago, the former president recently finalized a two-book memoir deal worth $65 million. He is scheduled to travel to Berlin next month to meet with German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

text: N.J. Senator Menendez aims to have corruption case dismissed. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Bob Menendez, the Democratic Senator from New Jersey, has requested a federal judge to dismiss his corruption indictment, referencing a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that has limited the scope of conduct that may lead to such legal actions. In a court document submitted on Tuesday, the senator's attorneys highlighted the June 2016 Supreme Court ruling that annulled the corruption conviction of former Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell. The ruling determined that political activities, like organizing meetings or making calls to officials, do not constitute 'official acts' as outlined by bribery laws. This landmark decision led the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to vacate the conviction of Sheldon Silver, the former speaker of the New York State Assembly, who has been one of the state's most influential figures for many years. U.S. prosecutors have announced their intention to retry him. Other politicians who have been convicted, such as former New York State Senate Majority Leader Dean Skelos, have also invoked the McDonnell ruling in their appeals following trials. Despite the indictment, Menendez is pursuing a third six-year term in 2018. He is alleged to have accepted campaign contributions, lavish travel, and gifts from a wealthy associate, Florida ophthalmologist Salomon Melgen, in return for advocating for the doctor through his position. Melgen was found guilty in April of a separate Medicare fraud scheme in Florida that reportedly defrauded the healthcare program of up to $105 million. Both he and Menendez have entered not guilty pleas in New Jersey. Menendez previously attempted to have the charges dismissed but that argument was made before the Supreme Court ruling in the McDonnell case. On Tuesday, Menendez’s attorneys contended that the accusations against the senator should be dismissed in light of the Supreme Court's decision. They stated, 'Making calls and holding meetings to discuss these matters, even if to encourage others to take a specific action – something any citizen can do – are not 'official acts' by Senator Menendez under McDonnell.' The U.S. Department of Justice did not provide immediate feedback on the motion as of Wednesday.

text: The U.S. House of Representatives on Friday sanctioned a bill aimed at sustaining a federal insurance initiative for millions of low-income children and expectant mothers, although due to a continuing funding dispute, it may take weeks before additional funds are allocated to the program. The Republican-sponsored measure in the House passed with a vote of 242-174, primarily reflecting party divisions. This legislation would extend the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) for a period of five years. However, Democrats cautioned that this partisan strategy will likely not succeed in the Senate, which could lead to further delays in obtaining funds for a program that has been inactive for over a month. Democratic Representative Frank Pallone expressed concern, stating, "This bill is going nowhere ... the Senate will not take it up, and we will be waiting around until Christmas" to secure funding. The Republicans hold 52 out of 100 seats in the Senate, where a total of 60 votes is required for approval. CHIP, which offers health insurance to approximately 9 million children, has historically enjoyed bipartisan support since its inception two decades ago, but reauthorization of its funding has become contentious recently. Under President Donald Trump and a Congress controlled by Republicans, healthcare matters have turned highly politicized, particularly as Republicans have consistently struggled to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, a key promise of Trump's campaign. The funding for the program expired on September 30, yet most states have sufficient resources to maintain it beyond 2017. Nevertheless, 11 states—including Colorado, California, Utah, Ohio, and Pennsylvania—are projected to deplete their funds by year’s end, as reported by the Kaiser Family Foundation. An additional 21 states expect to run out of funds by the end of March 2018. The House legislation would prolong the program for five years and ensure funding for community health centers for two years. Furthermore, it allocates $1 billion for Medicaid programs in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, which have been severely impacted by recent hurricanes. The bill sparked controversy after Republicans incorporated provisions that would alter the Affordable Care Act, the hallmark domestic policy of former Democratic President Barack Obama. These changes involve cutting funds from the law’s Prevention and Public Health Fund, which addresses various issues including the opioid crisis, and facilitating the removal of individuals from Obamacare plans due to unpaid premiums. On the other hand, Republican Representative Greg Walden highlighted that the bill would prevent Medicaid cuts to hospitals for two years that would have occurred under Obamacare. Democrats have denounced the legislation for requiring the wealthiest one percent of Medicare beneficiaries, those earning over $40,000 monthly, to contribute more to finance health insurance for low-income children.

text: LA PAZ (Reuters) - On Thursday, Bolivian President Evo Morales announced his intention to pursue a fourth term in 2019, motivated by opposition from the United States, which sparked a second day of demonstrations following the constitutional court's removal of term limits. The Morales administration previously dismissed criticisms from Washington, which expressed its significant concern regarding the court's decision made on Tuesday. Morales took this further, stating that the U.S. response actually encouraged him to run. "I was not so determined; now I am determined," he declared at a public gathering in Cochabamba, located in central Bolivia. "I will be a candidate, sisters and brothers, in 2019." The court's ruling is definitive and not subject to appeal. Various groups opposing the ruling protested in multiple cities once again on Thursday, with clashes occurring between opponents and police outside an elections office in Santa Cruz. "Bolivia has a constitution and we should respect it," remarked Olga Flores, a self-identified human rights activist, who was among the several hundred demonstrators enduring the rain in La Paz. Others shouted, "Bolivia said no!" Morales, who has been in office since 2006 and is a former coca farmer, had earlier accepted the outcome of a 2016 referendum in which 51 percent of voters rejected his bid to abolish term limits. He later changed his stance, claiming that while he was open to leaving office, his supporters urged him to continue. The U.S. State Department challenged that assertion, stating, "Twice in the last decade, the Bolivian people have expressed their opposition to the concept of indefinite reelection for elected officials." This statement referenced the approval of the current constitution in 2009 and the 2016 referendum. The Morales administration brushed off the criticism, with the minister of the presidency, Rene Martinez, stating, "It looks like they are trying to tell us who our candidates should be." He accused right-wing political factions in Bolivia of collaborating with the United States and the Organization of American States to hinder Morales from running again. Historically tumultuous Bolivia has experienced relative stability and growth under Morales, the nation’s first indigenous leader. Morales, a staunch opponent of capitalism and a supporter of the beleaguered Venezuelan socialist leader Nicolas Maduro, has approval ratings hovering around 50 percent. In September, Morales' Movement to Socialism party requested that the courts revoke legal restrictions preventing elected officials from seeking indefinite reelection. Morales contends that his initial election occurred under Bolivia’s prior constitution and therefore should not be counted under the now-abolished two-term limit.

A police officer, Major Hussein Osman, stated to Reuters from Beledweyne that the bomber detonated himself inside the restaurant. 'We are behind the attack at the Hiran governor's headquarters. There are casualties. Our target was the employees of the Hiran administration,' declared Abdiasis Abu Musab, the military operations spokesman for al Shabaab. Beledweyne is situated approximately 340 kilometers north of Mogadishu. Local residents reported that clan elders were among those who lost their lives. 'The suicide bomber, wearing an explosive vest, was inside the restaurant when he detonated himself. We were on our way to a meeting in the governor's office when the explosion occurred,' Farah Ali, a local elder, recounted to Reuters. Since 1991, Somalia has been embroiled in conflict, following the overthrow of dictator Siad Barre by clan-based warlords who subsequently turned against one another. Al Shabaab has historically conducted numerous attacks in Mogadishu and other regions of Somalia in an effort to dismantle the Western-backed government and expel African Union peacekeeping forces. The group also seeks to enforce its strict interpretation of Islam throughout Somalia.

text: Democrats intend to leverage the tax legislation to challenge Republicans during the midterm elections. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The tax legislation represents President Donald Trump’s most significant legislative achievement this year; however, Democratic strategists are already strategizing on how to transform it into his most substantial drawback. Their emotional appeal they believe will resonate with voters in next year’s midterm elections: claiming that the legislation is deeply unjust by allocating the majority of advantages to corporations and wealthy individuals. "Be careful what you wish for," Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer remarked in an interview with Reuters on Wednesday regarding Republican leaders. "They desired this, and they should have never wanted it. Now that they have it, they will regret it." Steyer indicated that he will utilize his funds - through his political organization NextGen America - to criticize the Republican tax reform, employing social media and online advertisements targeting younger voters, a tactic that recently aided in the election of Democratic candidate Doug Jones in a Senate race in Alabama and Ralph Northam as governor of Virginia. In November 2018, elections will occur for all 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and for 34 of the 100 Senate seats. Pollsters predict the midterms may present a rare "wave election," where one party regains control of Congress, reminiscent of the Republicans in 2010 and 1994. If Democrats manage to gain two additional Senate seats, they will take control of the chamber. Following the victories in Alabama and Virginia, they are optimistic that they can harness dissatisfaction regarding tax cuts for the wealthy to secure control of the House. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in mid-December, only around 29 percent of voters express approval for the tax bill, while slightly over 52 percent oppose it. No region in the country saw even half of the respondents express support for it. The Democratic Senate Campaign Committee is already airing ads against the tax plan in several crucial states, including Nevada, Arizona, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. The advertisements consist of five-second spots that play before YouTube videos. Viewers, unable to skip the ads, will hear: "The Republican tax scheme provides substantial breaks for corporations but increases taxes on middle-class families." The tax legislation lowers the corporate tax rate to 21 percent and raises the threshold for inheritance taxation. It also reduces the tax rate for the highest earners. Although it lowers tax rates for most other income groups and doubles the standard deduction, the removal of other favored deductions might lead to some taxpayers experiencing a tax increase rather than a reduction. The bill has garnered support from the Republican base, Trump supporters, and the party's financial backers. The stock market has rallied in anticipation of these tax cuts. Democrats plan to highlight provisions such as benefits for commercial real estate owners, contending that the tax bill could generate millions of additional dollars for Trump and his family members. The White House claims Trump will not gain personally, although it concedes that his business might benefit. The Super PAC American Bridge, which backs Democratic candidates, is running digital advertisements in states with Senate contests aimed at women, swing voters, and suburban Republicans, as stated by Joshua Karp, the group's communication director for Senate races. "I believe there are several aspects of this bill that upset nearly all Americans; it is inherently unfair and violates the promise Republicans made to the American public," Karp stated. Republicans argue that Democrats are engaging in unrealistic speculation. Polls indicate that 50 percent of voters believe their taxes will rise, but tax analysts assert that 80 percent will actually pay less tax. Republicans are relying on the notion that voters, upon noticing increased funds in their paychecks, will disregard Democratic rhetoric and possibly even extend their support to Trump. Furthermore, if there are any negative surprises awaiting taxpayers, they will not be filing their first tax returns under the new law until early 2019.

text: As the U.S. budget conflict approaches, Republicans are changing their fiscal narrative. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The leader of a conservative Republican group in the U.S. Congress, who supported a substantial increase in the national debt for tax reductions this month, described himself as a "fiscal conservative" on Sunday and advocated for budget discipline in 2018. Reflecting a significant shift occurring among Republicans, U.S. Representative Mark Meadows, speaking on CBS' "Face the Nation," took a strong stance on federal expenditure, as lawmakers prepare to engage in a struggle over this issue in January. Upon their return from the holiday break on Wednesday, legislators will begin efforts to pass a federal budget amidst a likely connection to other matters, such as immigration policy, all while the November congressional elections approach, where Republicans aim to maintain their Congressional majority. President Donald Trump and the Republicans are seeking a considerable increase in military funding, while Democrats are also advocating for proportional boosts in non-defense "discretionary" expenditures for initiatives that promote education, scientific investigations, infrastructure, public health, and environmental conservation. "The (Trump) administration has already signaled: 'We will increase non-defense discretionary spending ... by around 7 percent,'" Meadows, who chairs the small yet impactful House Freedom Caucus, stated during the program. "Now, Democrats are claiming that’s insufficient; they want a government pay raise of 10 to 11 percent. For a fiscal conservative, I fail to see the justification. ... Ultimately, one exhausts other people's funds," he noted. Meadows was among the Republicans who voted in late December for their party's tax reform, financed by debt, which is anticipated to escalate the federal budget deficit and add approximately $1.5 trillion over a decade to the $20 trillion national debt. "It's intriguing to listen to Mark discuss fiscal responsibility," said Democratic U.S. Representative Joseph Crowley on CBS. Crowley argued that the Republican tax legislation would necessitate the United States borrowing $1.5 trillion that future generations will have to repay to fund tax cuts for corporations and wealthy individuals. "This is one of the least ... fiscally responsible pieces of legislation we have seen passed in the history of the House of Representatives. I believe we will be dealing with the repercussions of this for many, many years ahead," Crowley remarked. Republicans maintain that the tax reform, the largest tax overhaul in the U.S. in over three decades, will stimulate the economy and create jobs. House Speaker Paul Ryan, who also endorsed the tax legislation, recently went beyond Meadows in a radio interview, indicating that welfare or "entitlement reform," as the party frequently refers to it, would be a primary Republican focus in 2018. text: The U.S. Justice Department announced on Thursday that it would investigate a decision made by the Federal Bureau of Investigation to disclose an inquiry into Hillary Clinton’s emails shortly before the presidential election in November, an action she attributes as a contributing factor to her loss. The issue at hand revolved around Clinton’s use of a personal email server for official communications during her tenure as secretary of state under President Barack Obama, which included messages later found to contain classified information. Inspector General Michael Horowitz's office indicated that the review was initiated "in response to requests from numerous chairmen and ranking members of congressional oversight committees, various organizations, and members of the public." Although the FBI eventually opted not to refer Clinton’s case for prosecution, Democrats argued that Comey’s announcement negatively impacted her standing with voters just before the election, facing accusations that his actions were politically motivated. Traditionally, law enforcement entities, including the FBI, refrain from disclosing information about investigations that do not lead to criminal charges. Should the review uncover any evidence of misconduct, involved officials would be subjected to disciplinary measures. In a statement, Comey expressed his commitment to fully cooperate with the investigation and conveyed his appreciation to Horowitz for the inquiry. "He is professional and independent and... I sincerely hope he can share his conclusions and observations with the public because everyone will benefit from a thorough evaluation and transparency regarding this matter." Brian Fallon, speaking for Clinton, remarked to MSNBC on Thursday that Comey’s actions "called for an independent review." Senator Dick Durbin, who ranks as the No. 2 Democrat in the U.S. Senate, commented that Comey’s remarks were not "fair, professional, or aligned with the policies of the Federal Bureau of Investigation." President-elect Donald Trump, set to be inaugurated on January 20, lacks the authority to terminate the probe. However, federal law allows U.S. presidents to dismiss inspectors general of federal agencies, provided they give Congress a written justification for the dismissal 30 days ahead of time. U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch had notified Comey the day before sending the letter that doing so would contradict official Justice Department guidance that directs employees to "never select the timing of investigative steps... for the purpose of affecting any election."
