text: Donald Trump's message following the Orlando tragedy has not resonated well with the Republican establishment. WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - The mass shooting that occurred in Orlando, Florida, has enabled Donald Trump to capitalize on a familiar subject he has leveraged effectively - the danger posed by Islamist extremists and his strategy to restrict Muslim immigration into the United States. This incident may represent a vital opportunity for him to rejuvenate his struggling presidential campaign. However, while grassroots voters may react favorably to Trump's renewed demand for a ban on certain Muslims entering the country, his response to the tragedy displayed little initial evidence of appealing to Republican foreign-policy leaders who have rejected the New York businessman. "It's a missed opportunity to present a different image," stated Peter Feaver, a senior aide at the National Security Council during the George W. Bush administration. "He has reinforced policies I disagree with that won't address the issue." In a speech delivered on Monday in New Hampshire, Trump announced he would halt immigration from nations "where there is a proven history of terrorism" targeting the United States. He claimed radical Muslim immigrants were "attempting to indoctrinate our children into believing how wonderful ISIS (Islamic State) is." Following the deadliest mass shooting in contemporary U.S. history on Sunday, which resulted in 50 fatalities, Trump rapidly altered his speech from a general critique of Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton to a grave caution regarding the threat from Islamist extremists. Although the Islamic State has taken responsibility for the assault, U.S. officials have asserted that Omar Mateen's motivations remain unclear and that he had no known direct ties to the Syria-based organization. Authorities indicated that Mateen was likely radicalized through online channels. Just a week prior, the presumptive Republican presidential candidate's campaign was facing significant challenges. He was being criticized by fellow Republicans for his remarks about a federal judge's Hispanic background, and Clinton was gaining ground in the polls. A renewed emphasis on national security could offer Trump an opportunity to broaden his appeal to both undecided voters and the Republican foreign-policy establishment. While Trump occasionally seems to enjoy being in conflict with the establishment, the dissatisfaction among the party's hawks is not merely a matter of concern. It suggests that if Trump ascends to the presidency, he may struggle to attract skilled, experienced advisors. Max Boot, a prominent conservative at the Council on Foreign Relations, remarked that the Orlando incident "could have opened a door for Trump to unite Republicans against terrorism." However, Boot noted that Trump has instead been "partisan and petty." Boot criticized Trump for implying on Monday that President Barack Obama might empathize with radicalized Muslims and for resurrecting the proposed Muslim ban. "His performance has been consistent with his character," Boot stated, "which is to say disgraceful." Some mainstream Republicans have been unsettled by Trump's promises to dismantle international trade agreements, his insistence that Mexico finance a border wall, and his questioning of fundamental U.S. foreign policy tenets such as security commitments to NATO and allies in Asia. Clinton adopted a markedly different approach in her speech on Monday, advocating for "statesmanship, not partisanship" and "clear, rational discussions" about how to safeguard the United States from terrorist threats. Eliot Cohen, a senior State Department official during the Bush era, characterized Trump's response to the shootings as "opportunistic and superficial" and "not what Americans expect from a president." Lanhee Chen, a senior advisor to Mitt Romney during his 2012 presidential campaign, indicated that Trump may struggle to improve his public image. "While it would generally be true that a significant speech like this could reset the situation, I believe the challenge with Donald Trump lies in who he is fundamentally," Chen stated. Nevertheless, voters may have a different perspective. Trump's rapid ascent within the Republican Party was at least partially attributable to the intense rhetoric he has employed regarding immigrants and refugees.

text: U.N. enhances security as it increases its footprint in Libya. ROME (Reuters) - The United Nations is set to send 150-250 predominantly Nepalese security personnel to Libya to safeguard its facility in the capital, according to U.N. officials on Friday. Supported by Western nations, the U.N. aims to mend divisions between Libya’s competing factions to help stabilize the nation and address militant violence and human trafficking from Libya’s northern coastline. Since 2014, the mission has been operating from Tunis after clashes among rival Libyan groups forced the majority of foreign diplomatic staff to evacuate; however, it has slowly been expanding its presence in Libya and has been preparing for a more comprehensive return for several months. Jean-Pierre Lacroix, U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, informed a news conference in Geneva that the military contingent will likely comprise around 150 guards, most of whom will be from Nepal. "To ensure the safety of our colleagues as they deploy in Tripoli, there will be a guard unit primarily made up of U.N. military personnel from Nepal," Lacroix stated. U.N. envoy to Libya, Ghassan Salame, mentioned in an interview with the Italian publication La Stampa that nearly 250 personnel could be sent in the following weeks. He indicated that deploying the guards to the Tripoli base would enable significant operations in Libya around early October. Salame, who has led the mission since June, remarked, "Deploying the guards to the base in Tripoli will allow us to carry out a substantial portion of our work in Libya." A representative for the mission noted there are currently no intentions to deploy U.N. peacekeepers to Libya. The security situation in Tripoli and other areas of western Libya remains precarious, with armed groups that lack accountability holding sway over the region. Most foreign embassies withdrew their personnel in 2014 amid intense fighting between rival factions that devastated the capital’s airport. This was the most severe conflict since the overthrow of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. Following the NATO-supported uprising that ousted Gaddafi, Libya descended into chaos. A U.N.-endorsed government established in Tripoli last year has faced challenges in asserting its authority and confronts opposition from factions controlling eastern Libya. In July, rival leaders committed in Paris to pursue elections in 2018 along with a conditional ceasefire. Salame stated that constitutional and electoral laws must be drafted to ensure that any election results lead to lasting change. "We must ensure that everyone accepts the final outcome," he asserted. "Let’s not forget that presidential elections would be the first of their kind." Salame also voiced his disappointment regarding the various international initiatives in Libya, where regional and European powers have competed for influence. "I believe the multitude of initiatives and mediations is not beneficial," he expressed. French Foreign Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian conveyed his hope that following his country’s endeavors, a revision of the 2015 U.N.-facilitated agreement that established the Tripoli government could be achieved under Salame’s leadership. Conversations have focused on restructuring the government’s leadership and authority over military appointments. "It appears that efforts are aligning," Le Drian told reporters during his visit to Moscow.

text: Puerto Rico announced on Friday that it will default on $779 million of senior debt, which is backed by the constitution, fulfilling warnings that the territory would prioritize essential services for its residents over payments to creditors. Debt obligations totaling slightly more than $2 billion were due on Friday. Following the signing of a bill by U.S. President Barack Obama on Thursday, Puerto Rico’s finances will soon be overseen by a U.S. federal oversight board, granting the island access to a debt restructuring process and imposing a pause on litigation related to any defaults on its $70 billion debt. "Today, Puerto Rico is safeguarded against creditor actions," stated Garcia Padilla. The General Obligation (GO) debt, which includes debt guaranteed by GO, is a type of debt that no U.S. state has defaulted on for decades. The Government Development Bank (GDB) for Puerto Rico revealed on Friday that the island would have only $95 million in cash remaining by the end of the year, even after the defaults announced. The benchmark 2035 GO bond for Puerto Rico increased by 0.25 points to trade at 67.50 points, which resulted in a yield decrease to 12.519 percent. On Thursday, Garcia Padilla permitted Puerto Rico, under a local debt moratorium law, to postpone a portion of the $2 billion in debt payments due that day. These events mark the lowest point in Puerto Rico's decade-long struggle to evade economic failure, as the island faces challenges from emigration and a staggering 45 percent poverty rate. "Even if the Commonwealth allocated every last cent in the (accounts) to debt service on July 1, it would still owe public debt holders hundreds of millions of dollars," the GDB stated in a press release on Friday. Certain debts expected to be defaulted on, such as the PBA (Public Building Authority) ex-series L bonds, will predominantly be covered by reserve funds held by the trustee bank. If some debt is insured, certain creditors may receive partial payments. The GDB, which serves as Puerto Rico’s primary fiscal agent, noted that the island has merely $200 million in its operating account and an additional $150 million in redirected revenue from recent months meant for other debt payments. Despite maintaining emergency measures such as delaying vendor payments and withholding contributions to an already insolvent pension fund, the GDB warned that the operating account would deplete its cash reserves within 30 to 60 days. Late Thursday, the island’s legislature passed an $8.9 billion budget for fiscal year 2017, which is now pending Garcia Padilla’s approval. These statements, audited by KPMG, revealed that Puerto Rico’s largest public pension has depleted its assets and is now insolvent. text: U.S. Interior Department nullifies coal valuation regulation. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Monday, the U.S. Department of the Interior announced its decision to nullify a rule from the Obama administration that altered the way energy firms assess the value of oil, gas, and coal sales from federal and tribal territories, aiming to safeguard taxpayers. This measure was deemed to have created "confusion and uncertainty" for energy businesses, according to Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke. He stated that a newly established committee focused on royalty policy would suggest alternatives to this regulation and emphasized the commitment to ensuring that every dollar owed is collected. "The repeal of the valuation regulation offers a fresh start to develop effective valuation guidelines," Zinke expressed in a statement. The valuation regulation was introduced by former Interior Secretary Sally Jewell the previous year to address a loophole that allowed companies to evade royalty payments when extracting resources from public lands owned by taxpayers. It mandated that energy companies remit royalties based on sales to the first independent buyer, referred to as an arm's-length sale, as the resources transition to the market. A Reuters investigation in 2012 revealed that coal firms were utilizing affiliated brokers to manage royalty payments on exports to Asia at significantly reduced domestic rates. Zinke indicated that the valuation regulation had raised expenses for coal, oil, and gas companies, which hindered production on federal lands, thereby increasing reliance on foreign oil and gas imports. Industry participants and trade groups launched three lawsuits contesting the Obama-era regulation. Additionally, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a group monitoring taxpayer interests, discovered that taxpayers lost nearly $30 billion in revenue over a span of thirty years due to this loophole. The revocation of the valuation regulation was documented in the Federal Register on August 7 and will take effect on September 6.

text: SAN JUAN (Reuters) - On Thursday, Puerto Rico took the step of permitting a halt on payments regarding its general obligation debt, just moments after U.S. President Barack Obama enacted a law that establishes a federal oversight board empowered to negotiate the restructuring of the island's $70 billion debt. The executive order from Puerto Rico's governor, Alejandro Garcia Padilla, was issued a day prior to when the U.S. territory was scheduled to make $1.9 billion in debt payments on July 1, which included approximately $780 million in constitutionally-backed general obligation bonds. It is still uncertain whether Puerto Rico will partially pay the GO debt or any of the non-GO debt. Garcia Padilla's administration stated, "In these circumstances, these executive orders safeguard the limited resources available to the agencies mentioned in these orders and prevent them from being seized by creditors, which would leave Puerto Ricans without essential services." This rapid sequence of events marks the lowest point in Puerto Rico's decade-long effort to avert economic disaster, combat a 45 percent poverty rate, and address the rampant emigration that worsens the economic downturn. Garcia Padilla invoked the suspension of general obligation payments under a local debt moratorium law that has faced challenges from a creditor lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court in Manhattan. Furthermore, Garcia Padilla declared states of emergency for the island's largest public pension, the Commonwealth’s Employee Retirement System, which is over 99 percent underfunded, and for the University of Puerto Rico along with other agencies. The benchmark 2035 General Obligation bond for Puerto Rico rose by 0.44 points to trade at 67.19 points, resulting in a yield drop to 12.578 percent. In Washington, Obama signed the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management and Economic Stability Act, known as PROMESA, in the Oval Office on Thursday, marking one of the rare bipartisan bills to reach his desk. Obama remarked to reporters prior to signing, "I want to let the people of Puerto Rico know that although there are still some tough work that we’re going to have to do to dig Puerto Rico out of the hole that it’s in, this indicates how committed my administration is to making sure that they get the help they need." The legislation will grant the island access to a bankruptcy-like debt restructuring mechanism but will place its finances under the supervision of a federally-appointed board—a stipulation that has angered many in Puerto Rico, including Garcia Padilla. PROMESA, which the U.S. Senate approved on Wednesday, imposes a stay on litigation in case of a default. Puerto Rico has already defaulted on parts of its debt three times within the past year. This stay is crucial to prevent Puerto Rico's financial restructuring from descending into a series of prolonged and expensive court disputes. The stay is retroactive to December 2015. The oversight board will be equipped to facilitate consensual restructuring discussions or compel Puerto Rico into a court-supervised process similar to U.S. bankruptcy. It will also monitor and ensure the implementation of sustainable budgets. Nonetheless, missed payments are significant for the insurers who are obligated to pay claims should Puerto Rico fail to provide cash to its bondholders. MBIA’s National Public Finance Guarantee insures around $173 million in GO debt due on Friday, while Assured Guaranty covers an additional $184 million, and Ambac provides insurance for $40 million in GO or GO-guaranteed debt due on Friday. Earlier on Thursday, PREPA, the island's heavily indebted semi-public power utility, announced it will fulfill its full payment of $415 million due Friday, as outlined in a restructuring agreement reached with most of its creditors late last year. PREPA had previously been close to collapse with $8.3 billion in debt, but last year it secured an exchange deal with the majority.

text: Cox's Bazar/Yangon (Reuters) - In a desperate bid to escape violence and starvation, thousands of new Rohingya refugees crossed into Bangladesh from Myanmar early on Monday, according to witnesses from Reuters. The refugees, who are hungry, impoverished, and fearful, fled from assaults by Buddhist mobs, which the United Nations has termed ethnic cleansing. Struggling through waist-deep water with children secured to their sides, the refugees recounted to Reuters their journey through thick underbrush and swollen streams during monsoon season, lasting several days. A continuous stream of people entered Bangladesh close to the village of Palongkhali. Many bore injuries, with the elderly transported on makeshift stretchers, while women carried household goods like pots, rice sacks, and clothing atop their heads. "We couldn’t leave our house for the past month because the military was looting from people," stated Mohammad Shoaib, 29, who wore a yellow vest while balancing jute bags filled with food and aluminum pots on a bamboo pole. "They began firing on the village, prompting us to flee to another area. As time went on, conditions deteriorated, driving us toward Bangladesh. Before departing, I returned to my village to check on my home, and the whole village was reduced to ashes," Shoaib added. These refugees joined approximately 536,000 Rohingya Muslims who have escaped from Myanmar since August 25, when coordinated attacks by Rohingya insurgents ignited a brutal military crackdown, with those fleeing accusing security forces of arson, murder, and sexual assault. Myanmar has denied allegations of ethnic cleansing and has labeled the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, the group responsible for the attacks, as terrorists, asserting that they have killed civilians and incinerated villages. On Monday, the European Union announced it would halt invitations to Myanmar's army commander-in-chief and other senior generals due to the excessive use of force by the security apparatus. A statement released following a gathering of EU foreign ministers also called for a comprehensive investigation into credible claims of severe human rights violations and abuses. Not everyone managed to reach Bangladesh safely on Monday. Several kilometers south of Palongkhali, a boat filled with numerous refugees capsized at dawn, resulting in at least 12 fatalities and 35 individuals unaccounted for. According to Bangladeshi authorities, there were 21 survivors. "So far, 12 bodies have been retrieved, including six children and four women," stated police officer Moinuddin Khan. Border guards from Bangladesh informed Reuters that the boat sank due to being overloaded with refugees, who pay exorbitant fees to traverse the Naf River, the natural boundary with Myanmar in the Cox's Bazar area of Bangladesh. This incident occurred roughly a week after another boat sank in the river's estuary, which has turned into a graveyard for many Muslim refugees. Survivors of the treacherous journey reported being forced out by hunger, as food markets in Myanmar's western Rakhine State have been closed and aid deliveries hampered. They also spoke of assaults by the military and Rakhine Buddhist mobs. This surge in refugees will exacerbate the unprecedented humanitarian crisis currently unfolding in Cox's Bazar, where aid workers are struggling to supply food, clean water, and shelter to the displaced. On Monday, the Red Cross inaugurated a field hospital equivalent in size to two football fields, featuring 60 beds, three wards, an operating theater, a delivery suite with a maternity ward, and a psychosocial support unit. Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya had previously been in Bangladesh after fleeing earlier outbreaks of violence in Myanmar, where they have long been denied citizenship and faced restrictions on their movements and access to essential services. The EU's decision to limit further interactions with Myanmar's military leadership follows reports to Reuters that both the European Union and the United States are contemplating targeted sanctions against military leaders. The measures announced by Brussels are primarily symbolic, although the EU indicated that it might consider additional steps.

text: A new investigation by the House into Russia has brought attention to a previously low-key lawmaker. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Representative Mike Conaway’s appointment to lead the House Intelligence Committee probe into the connections between the Trump campaign and Russia has thrust the understated legislator into one of the most controversial topics in both Congress and the nation. His selection received commendations from both Republicans and Democrats. With experience in administration as a committee chairman and a background in sensitive matters from his time as head of the House Ethics Committee from 2013 to 2015, he is seen as a capable choice. "I like him. I hope he can get us back on track," stated Representative Eric Swalwell, a Democratic member of the committee, in a brief chat outside the U.S. House of Representatives. At 68, Conaway maintains affiliations with mainstream Republicans and has longstanding ties to the Bush political dynasty, yet the Texas native was a staunch supporter of Trump during the 2016 election. In that year, Conaway endorsed Trump, pointing to the candidate’s selection of Mike Pence for the vice presidency, his commitment to appoint conservative justices to the Supreme Court, and his own strong opposition to Hillary Clinton, the Democratic nominee. However, in contrast to Devin Nunes, who resigned on Thursday from his role leading the investigation into alleged Russian interference in the U.S. presidential election, including the potential collusion with Trump associates, Conaway was not part of the incoming president’s transition team. Russia has denied these allegations. Compared to other Republican members of the committee, such as Trey Gowdy, the chairman of the House Select Committee that looked into the 2012 attacks on a U.S. diplomatic facility in Benghazi, Libya, Conaway is viewed as less partisan. Democrats have accused Gowdy of conducting a biased inquiry aimed at damaging former Secretary of State Clinton’s 2016 presidential bid. In his statement announcing his decision to step down, Nunes mentioned that Gowdy and another Republican committee member, Tom Rooney, would also take leadership roles in the Russia investigation. According to Fox News, Nunes contacted Conaway on Wednesday night. Nonetheless, some of Conaway’s remarks regarding the Russia investigation have raised concerns. During a committee hearing on March 20, he questioned FBI Director James Comey about whether reporters from the Washington Post had assisted intelligence agencies in crafting their evaluation that Moscow was attempting to support Trump’s election. Additionally, in a January interview with the Dallas Morning News, he appeared to downplay the alleged Russian interference in the election, commenting that it was akin to the Democrats’ use of Mexican entertainers to engage their voters, both being examples of "foreign interference." Even though he also chairs the House Agriculture Committee, Conaway has largely stayed out of the limelight, known more for his close connections to the Bush family than for media attention. Elected to the House for the first time in 2004 and easily winning re-election six times since, Conaway currently holds the position of second-ranking Republican on the intelligence panel. House Speaker Paul Ryan expressed his confidence in Conaway during a press briefing on Thursday. "I am confident that he will oversee a professional investigation into Russia’s actions and follow the facts wherever they may lead," Ryan stated.

text: Japanese businesses largely desire Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's ruling coalition to maintain control in the national election set for this Sunday, according to a Reuters poll. However, approximately two-thirds of those surveyed prefer that the coalition loses some seats. The results indicate that while companies seek political stability, they are hesitant to grant Abe a sweeping victory, fearing it could lead to complacency regarding economic revival. Numerous firms expressed apprehension that a significant win for Abe might prompt him to focus on his long-standing goal of amending Japan's pacifist constitution, potentially sidelining economic policies. A construction company manager commented, "We require political stability, but the primary focus should be on economic measures rather than constitutional revisions," favoring a scenario where Abe's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its ally Komeito maintain a simple majority while losing some seats. On Sunday, voters will cast ballots for representatives in Japan's 465-member lower house, the more influential chamber of the national diet, or parliament. Predictions released last week anticipated that Abe’s coalition could secure about 300 seats, nearing the two-thirds super-majority they held prior to the election call. Additionally, the LDP coalition holds a majority in the upper house, which is crucial for any constitutional amendments. The corporate poll, conducted from September 28 to October 12, revealed that 94 percent of firms wished for Abe's coalition to win the election. Nevertheless, 48 percent preferred that his bloc achieve a narrower majority, while 20 percent hoped for the retention of the 323 seats previously held before the lower house's dissolution last month. Only 7 percent desired an increase in seats for the ruling coalition. "Those anticipating surprises like Brexit and Donald Trump’s presidency will likely face disappointment. This election lacks a single, dominant issue," stated Masaki Kuwahara, a senior economist at Nomura Securities, who analyzed the survey findings. The distribution of votes among opposition parties is expected to benefit Abe's coalition. The campaign has seen the rise of Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike’s new Party of Hope, which supports delaying a proposed sales tax increase set for 2019. The Reuters survey indicated that a slight majority favored Abe adhering to a fiscal balancing objective, while opposing his proposal to allocate revenue from the planned sales tax increase towards education and childcare instead of debt reduction. A manager at a metal products machinery company remarked in the survey, "Abe must be appealing to voters with such a proposal. How will Japan manage the financing of social security services?" When asked about post-election priorities, fiscal consolidation—aimed at addressing the industrial world's highest public debt—was the leading concern, selected by 35 percent, followed by additional fiscal stimulus at 14 percent. Merely 5 percent advocated for further monetary stimulus, reflecting the prevalent belief that easy-money policies are reaching their limits. Only 3 percent indicated that constitutional revision should be a priority. Kuwahara noted that many businesses are apprehensive about a possible public finance collapse, which could threaten the financial system and the wider economy. They also worry that constitutional amendments might send a negative message to Asian countries that endured Japan’s wartime aggression. The survey, conducted for Reuters by Nikkei Research, involved 548 large and mid-sized firms that responded anonymously, with around 230 companies providing views on the election and policy outlook.

text: ADDIS ABABA (Reuters) - Officials reported that at least 61 individuals have died in confrontations among various ethnic groups in Ethiopia's Oromiya region, marking the latest instance of violence that underscores the growing instability in a province that experienced deadly protests in 2015 and 2016. Starting from Thursday, 29 ethnic Oromos lost their lives due to attacks from ethnic Somali assailants in the districts of Hawi Gudina and Daro Lebu, according to regional spokesman Addisu Arega Kitessa. This outbreak of violence provoked retaliatory assaults by ethnic Oromos in another district, leading to the deaths of 32 Somalis who had sought refuge in the area following prior violent incidents. The spokesman stated that efforts are underway to hold the offenders accountable. The triggers for this recent violence remain unclear; however, it followed demonstrations in the town of Celenko in Oromiya, where regional officials reported that soldiers killed 16 ethnic Oromos on Tuesday while attempting to disperse a gathering. "We do not know who ordered the deployment of the military. This illegal act should be punished," remarked Lema Megersa, the president of the region. These clashes are expected to heighten concerns regarding security in Ethiopia, which is the largest economy in the region and a key ally of the West. Lema's remarks also reflect the increasing tensions within Ethiopia's ruling EPRDF coalition, as unrest erupted in the Oromiya region during 2015 and 2016, resulting in hundreds of fatalities. That period of violence compelled the government to enforce a nine-month state of emergency, which was only lifted in August. The unrest stemmed from a development plan for the capital, Addis Ababa, which dissidents claimed amounted to land seizures and escalated into wider anti-government protests concerning political and human rights issues. This involved assaults on businesses, many of which were foreign-owned, including farms dedicated to growing flowers for export.

BOSTON (Reuters) - (Editor’s note: This report includes language that may be offensive to some readers; the final six paragraphs provide no comment from Gattine's representative) Maine Governor Paul LePage, known for his confrontational style, informed a radio host on Tuesday that he was contemplating the possibility of not completing his term in office, following a surge of criticism after he left a vulgar voicemail for a lawmaker. However, the two-term Republican governor, who has the backing of the Tea Party, seemed to retract that statement, tweeting a paraphrase of Mark Twain that stated in part: “The reports of my political demise are greatly exaggerated.” This tweet was sent just hours after he indicated during an interview on Maine’s WVOM-FM radio that he was “considering all options” when questioned about whether he would serve out his term, which is set to end in 2018. LePage's recent remarks were provoked by a comment from state Representative Drew Gattine, who labeled him as racist for attributing the majority of the state's drug issues to black individuals. In response, LePage issued a harsh and profane voicemail to Gattine that has since gained significant attention. “I’m not going to say that I’m not going to finish it; I’m not saying that I am going to finish it,” LePage stated during the radio interview, referring to his tenure. “What I’m going to do right now is take one step at a time. I want to meet with Mr. Gattine and then I want to have a discussion with my team at my office to determine the appropriate steps for moving the state forward.” In the voicemail sent last week, LePage referred to Gattine using offensive language and urged him to make the message public “because I am after you.” A spokesperson for LePage did not respond immediately to inquiries for clarification regarding the governor’s tweet referencing Twain. Gattine's spokesperson mentioned he would refrain from making comments until after his meeting with LePage on Wednesday. LePage has often characterized himself as a straightforward, unrefined politician. “It’s possible it was a mistake,” noted Michael Franz, the chair of the government department at Bowdoin College in Maine, commenting on the radio interview. “My initial thought is that this isn’t serious and that he’s merely trying to express his regret.” LePage, 67, admitted that he lost his temper upon learning that Gattine had characterized his views as racist. He told reporters that he would like to engage in a duel with Gattine, a comment he later clarified was intended metaphorically. “I just want to apologize to the people of Maine, to Gattine’s family, and most importantly to my family,” LePage expressed during the 15-minute interview. “And we will take action.” Some Democratic legislators have called for a special legislative session to censure LePage, who earlier in the year successfully resisted an impeachment attempt. “A half-hearted, partial apology on a radio show does not adequately address the core issue: Maine is facing significant challenges and its government is not functioning,” stated the Democratic leadership in the House on Tuesday. State Senate President Michael Thibodeau and other Republican legislative leaders held a private meeting with LePage late Monday to discuss his future. The governor informed the group that he intended to consult with friends and family about his next steps and would provide them with a response on Tuesday, according to Jim Cyr, a spokesperson for Thibodeau. LePage’s six years in office have been marked by controversial statements. Earlier this year, he asserted that he did not intend to sound racist when he remarked that drug dealers “with names like D-Money, Smoothie, Shifty” were coming to the state to impregnate “white girls.” Last week, during a news conference, LePage likened Maine's attempts to combat heroin dealers to warfare. “Look, the bad guy is the bad guy,” he remarked. “I don’t care about their skin color ... text: U.S. Republicans dismiss Democratic funding proposals aimed at addressing opioid issues. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, Republican members of Congress turned down two Democratic amendments that sought nearly $1 billion in funding for a bipartisan initiative designed to tackle the opioid crisis in America, according to aides. This rejection occurred during a meeting involving negotiators from the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate regarding the legislation and could weaken Democratic backing for the final bill, which might be voted on in the House as soon as Friday. In recent months, both the House and Senate have passed their own versions of the bill. Now, Democratic lawmakers in both chambers are withholding their support for the final iteration of the legislation, as reported by two Democratic aides. The opposition from Democrats may pose a significant hurdle, particularly in the Senate, where 60 votes are required to advance legislation. The two amendments put forth by House and Senate Democrats would have allocated $920 million upfront to fund program grants for states. According to aides, without these amendments, the programs would need to go through a lengthy appropriations process, which could be delayed due to this year's election campaign shortening the congressional session. Republican aides were not available for immediate comment. However, House Republicans are considering a separate health spending bill that would allocate over $581 million to combat opioid abuse. House Democratic Caucus Chairman Xavier Becerra remarked on Wednesday that this is merely the latest example of bipartisan-supported legislation falling short on funding. "It’s becoming a bit of a joke to say we’re concerned and want to do something, when the only thing we’ll do is shell of what it actually takes," he stated.

text: The Philippines has halted its trade activities with North Korea to adhere to a U.N. Security Council resolution concerning the country's ongoing missile tests, as stated by the foreign minister of Manila on Friday. Following North Korea's recent test, which it claimed was an advanced hydrogen bomb, the United States and several other Western nations have urged the United Nations to impose stricter sanctions on North Korea. "We can confirm that we have suspended trade relations with North Korea," Foreign Minister Alan Peter Cayetano informed reporters after a discussion with the U.S. ambassador related to collaboration on an anti-drug initiative. "We will fully adhere to the UNSC resolution, including the economic sanctions." Tensions have risen on the Korean Peninsula as the young leader of North Korea, Kim Jong Un, has intensified the development of weaponry in disregard of U.N. sanctions. This year, North Korea has conducted multiple missile tests, including one that traversed Japan, and executed its sixth and most significant nuclear test on Sunday. The Philippines ranks as North Korea's fifth-largest trading partner, with trade amounting to $28.8 million between January and June of this year, according to the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency, which is state-run. In 2016, North Korea imported $28.8 million worth of goods from the Philippines, marking an 80 percent rise from the previous year, whereas imports from Pyongyang to Manila surged by 170 percent to reach $16.1 million. As per the Philippine Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), the primary exports to North Korea in 2015 included computers, integrated circuit boards, bananas, and women's undergarments. "The U.N. Security Council is quite explicit," Cayetano remarked. "Included in these are the economic sanctions, and the Philippines will comply. We have been in contact with the DTI secretary, and I believe it was yesterday and the day before that we received instructions from the (presidential) palace to support the U.N. Security Council." Cayetano indicated that the trade prohibition extends to raw computer chips originating from the Philippines.

text: Boris Johnson, the British Foreign Secretary, made a light-hearted remark on Tuesday regarding Libya, suggesting that the nation could become a new Dubai if it could remove the dead bodies. This comment marks yet another misstep from the UK's leading diplomat. Speaking to members of the Conservative Party, Johnson stated that Sirte, a Libyan city, could be transformed into the next Dubai by British investors, provided they manage to clear away the corpses. 'They have an excellent vision to develop Sirte, with the assistance of the municipality of Sirte, to make it the next Dubai,' Johnson remarked. 'The only task they need to accomplish is to remove the dead bodies, and then we will be there.' Some party activists laughed at the joke, but the event's chair quickly shifted the topic, stating, 'Next question.' In 2011, Britain and France played a significant role in the military actions that led to the downfall of Muammar Gaddafi. Since then, Libya has plunged into disorder, resulting in numerous casualties. The Islamic State terrorist organization seized control of Sirte in early 2015, establishing it as their primary base outside the Middle East and drawing many foreign fighters to the area. Eventually, the militants were expelled. In a series of late-night tweets, Johnson clarified that he was referencing the removal of booby-trapped corpses belonging to Islamic State fighters. 'It's unfortunate that individuals lacking knowledge or understanding of Libya wish to engage in politics regarding the extremely perilous situation in Sirte,' Johnson expressed. 'The truth is that removing the corpses of Daesh fighters has been complicated by IEDs and booby traps.' When questioned about Johnson's statements, Damian Green, the Deputy of Prime Minister May, commented that all ministers must be cautious with their language surrounding sensitive topics but chose not to criticize the foreign minister. Emily Thornberry, the Labour Party's spokesperson on foreign affairs, condemned Johnson's joke as disgraceful and questioned whether May would take any disciplinary action against him. May's decision to appoint Johnson, who previously compared the aims of the European Union to those of Adolf Hitler and Napoleon ahead of Britain's EU membership referendum, raised concerns in various European capitals. Earlier this year, the UK's ambassador to Myanmar had to interrupt Johnson while he attempted to recite a nostalgic colonial poem by Rudyard Kipling publicly during a visit to the country’s most renowned Buddhist site.

text: Trump admits facing a tough battle in typically Republican Utah. ORLANDO, Fla. (Reuters) - On Thursday, Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump recognized that his campaign was encountering difficulties in Utah, a state that usually solidly supports Republicans, marking a rare moment of uncertainty from him. Trump made these remarks while encouraging conservative Christian evangelicals to rally support for him in several pivotal states where the election on Nov. 8 could be determined, including Ohio, Florida, and Virginia. The affluent businessman from New York has faced several self-inflicted setbacks recently, which have given Democrat Hillary Clinton an edge in the race. "We’re having a tremendous problem in Utah," Trump stated to a gathering of evangelical pastors, attributing it to a "false narrative" surrounding his campaign. He has consistently pointed fingers at the media for misleading tactics. A SurveyUSA poll conducted for the Salt Lake Tribune in June indicated a tie between Clinton and Trump. Other surveys have shown Trump with a lead, but not the substantial advantage that past Republican nominees have had in the state. Trump, who is usually self-assured, rarely apologizes and is reluctant to acknowledge potential challenges. However, during a discussion with the National Association of Home Builders in Miami Beach, he conceded that his previous years before entering politics might be creating issues for him now. "If I had planned for it, I wouldn’t have had such a rocky path," he remarked. "I wouldn’t have spoken to Howard so much." This referred to his numerous appearances on the "Howard Stern Show" radio program, where he is estimated to have been featured more than two dozen times over two decades, often engaging in risqué conversations. Trump, who is trailing Clinton in Virginia—a state that was once Republican but which Democratic President Barack Obama won in both 2008 and 2012—called on evangelicals to assist him there as well. In this context, Trump promised to revise the Johnson Amendment, the 1954 amendment to the U.S. tax code that bars church leaders from engaging in political activities from the pulpit. "If we get those people to vote, we’re going to win in Virginia," he asserted. "If they don’t vote, it’s not going to happen." Trump also remarked, "We need help in Ohio," the state where he hosted his Republican National Convention last month. Ohio Governor John Kasich, who lost to Trump in the Republican primaries, has declined to endorse him. "We’re very close in Ohio, but we need help," Trump stated. A continuous stream of moderate Republicans, such as U.S. Senator Susan Collins of Maine, have pledged not to support him, and a letter opposing Trump was signed by 50 Republican national security experts. This situation reflects divisions within the party regarding Trump’s aggressive rhetoric and positions, as he recently labeled Obama "the founder of ISIS," referring to the Islamic State, and Clinton as "the co-founder." Trump humorously suggested that winning the presidency and performing well might be his only path to salvation. "So go out and spread the words, and once I get in, I will do the thing that I do very well," Trump said with a grin. "I figure it’s probably maybe the only way I’m going to get to heaven, so I better do a good job."

text: Attorney General Lynch has requested to be excluded from consideration for the Supreme Court vacancy. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch has formally asked not to be nominated to fill the Supreme Court position that became vacant following Justice Antonin Scalia's passing last month, according to a statement from the Justice Department on Tuesday. At 56 years old, Lynch was thought to be a potential candidate by Democratic President Barack Obama. She is highly respected within the administration, received support from both parties for her attorney general nomination, and would be the first black woman to occupy a seat on the Supreme Court. "Given the urgent matters facing the Department of Justice, she requested not to be considered for the role," the department indicated in their announcement. In recent weeks, other candidates have surfaced on Obama’s shortlist, including Sri Srinivasan, Jane Kelly, and Paul Watford, all of whom are currently federal appeals court judges. In a Fox News interview last week, Lynch addressed rumors regarding her vetting for the position. "I haven’t had those discussions. I’m very content with my current role," Lynch stated. Justice Department spokesperson Melanie Newman mentioned that while Lynch is extremely appreciative of those who have suggested her as a nominee for the Supreme Court, "she is honored to serve as attorney general, and she is entirely dedicated to fulfilling the responsibilities of the Department of Justice for the remainder of her term." The efforts to fill the vacancy left by Scalia, known as one of the court’s most conservative justices, have sparked a partisan conflict in Washington. Republicans, who hold the majority in the U.S. Senate, are opposed to the court shifting ideologically to the left and have declared they will not conduct a vote on Obama’s nominee. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has asserted that the next Supreme Court justice should be appointed by the victor of the presidential election on November 8.

text: KIEV (Reuters) - Two activists from the Crimean Tatar community, who were released from Russian detention this week, declared on Friday their intention to return to the annexed Crimea and advocate for the release of other political detainees as well as the restoration of Crimea to Ukraine. This group, primarily a Muslim Turkic minority in Crimea, has largely resisted Russian governance since the annexation in 2014. The Kiev authorities report that Moscow has been accused of infringing upon the rights of this community, with 50 of its members still incarcerated on political charges. Ilmi Umerov, who serves as the deputy head of the semi-official Mejlis legislature of the Crimean Tatars, along with fellow leader Ahtem Chiygoz, were released unexpectedly on Wednesday. Umerov informed reporters after returning to Kiev, "Whether they allow me or not, I will go home without fail." He expressed confidence that if the current situation persists, the topic of Crimea will continue to be present in the news, and the process of liberating individuals, gradually reclaiming Crimea, and restoring Ukraine's territorial integrity will proceed. Umerov, who had received a two-year prison sentence in Russia for separatism, attributed his early release to international pressure on the Kremlin. Previously, they had traveled to Turkey to meet with Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, with Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko expressing gratitude for his assistance in securing the release of the two. Supporters of Umerov noted at that time that his two-year sentence effectively represented a death sentence, given his battle with Parkinson's disease. Russian officials refuted claims that the prosecutions were politically motivated. Chiygoz remarked that their release did not feel like true freedom, stating, "Because a release would be the liberation of my people, my land, my homeland, my country." A U.N. human rights report indicates that Russia is perpetrating severe human rights abuses in Crimea, including the imposition of Russian citizenship and the deportation of inmates. Following a pro-European uprising in Kiev that resulted in the ousting of a Moscow-aligned president, Russia annexed Crimea. The region's laws were replaced with those of Russia, yet this annexation has never received international recognition. Traditionally, Crimean Tatars have been pro-Ukrainian, having endured mass deportation to Central Asia under the regime of Soviet dictator Josef Stalin. Since the annexation, they have faced intimidation, home raids, and arbitrary detentions, according to human rights organizations. Moscow asserts that a significant majority of Crimeans voted to join Russia in a legitimate and fair referendum.

text: President Donald Trump’s executive order titled "Buy American, Hire American," issued on Tuesday, has raised uncertainties regarding the enforcement of the order and its potential impact on production and employment, as noted by steel industry executives and analysts. Existing "Buy American" regulations are already part of U.S. law; however, enforcing these laws has proven challenging due to exemptions provided to foreign firms that offer lower prices compared to their U.S. competitors. On Tuesday, Trump initiated a review of federal procurement regulations that favor American businesses to ascertain whether they are genuinely advantageous, particularly for the U.S. steel sector. While his executive order pledges to ensure proper enforcement of these regulations, it lacks specifics on how this will be achieved. Bill Hickey, who is the president of Lapham-Hickey Steel, based in Chicago and operating seven steel mills across the Midwest and Northeast, remarked that discussions surrounding "Buy American" have been ongoing for many years, yet both American and foreign contractors often exploit loopholes to utilize imported steel. "Politicians all say the same things, but ultimately it just doesn’t pan out," Hickey stated, referring to the exemptions associated with existing regulations. Charles Bradford from Bradford Research pointed out that emphasizing "Buy American" for U.S. steel does not consider that certain steel products, such as tin plate and semi-finished goods, are not produced domestically. If not enforced correctly, this could lead to supply issues in a U.S. market where as much as 25 percent of steel was imported in the first quarter of this year. "Those advocating for this are clueless and lack mathematical understanding," Bradford commented. He mentioned that restricting access to goods not manufactured in the U.S. would introduce new challenges for American businesses. Additionally, in the construction sector, there are worries about overly strict definitions of what qualifies as U.S.-made steel products, according to Kenneth Simonson, chief economist of the Associated General Contractors of America. Simonson expressed concerns regarding steel that may have been melted down from scrap sourced from outside the U.S. and the difficulty in tracing its origins. The track record of Trump’s administration has further fueled industry skepticism. Unlike the bold measures promised last year by Trump as a candidate regarding the North American Free Trade Agreement, China, and free trade agreements, the current administration has "not demonstrated much evidence of taking action," said Philip Gibbs, a steel analyst at KeyBanc Capital Markets. "I’m considerably less optimistic than I was three and a half months ago because what I’ve observed from the Trump administration thus far mirrors that of the previous administration," he added. Consequently, Gibbs advised that investors should lower their expectations regarding any significant actions from Trump concerning trade or infrastructure, areas where such an order could indeed have an impact. Investors appeared to be indifferent to the executive order announced on Tuesday. Shares of Nucor Corp increased by 0.2 percent, closing at $57.33, while AK Steel Holding Corp rose by a penny to end at $6.32, and United States Steel Corp fell by 0.5 percent, closing at $28.73. AK Steel did not respond to inquiries for comments. Both Nucor and U.S. Steel expressed support for the president’s executive order. The labor unions also embraced the initiative. The United Steelworkers stated that current practices allow "contractors often to evade the law through loopholes to procure cheap and frequently substandard foreign products, including many from China." Thomas Gibson, the chief executive of the American Iron and Steel Institute, noted in a statement that "Buy American" provisions "are essential to the sustainability of the domestic steel industry and have contributed to the creation of manufacturing jobs and the development of American infrastructure." Veteran steel industry analyst Michelle Applebaum indicated that it is yet to be determined how thoroughly the Trump administration will enforce these measures.

text: Islamic State has taken responsibility for an assault on a television station in the capital of Afghanistan. KABUL (Reuters) - On Tuesday, gunmen posing as police officers fatally shot a security guard and opened fire on personnel at a private television station in Kabul. The Islamic State claimed the attack as its own. Following a sporadic gunfight that lasted approximately two hours, Afghan special forces were able to subdue the attackers at Shamshad TV, a private Pashto-language broadcaster situated near the national stadium. Authorities reported that at least two individuals were killed and 20 others were injured. Abed Ehsas, the news director of Shamshad, informed Tolo News TV, "Individuals dressed in police uniforms came in and initially tossed hand grenades, resulting in the death of one of our guards and injuring another. Others entered our premises and began shooting. Some of our colleagues were struck, though thankfully, many others were able to escape. Some sustained injuries from gunfire, shattered glass, and when they jumped from higher floors." Approximately two hours later, the station, which had replaced its regular programming with a still image during the violence, returned to normal broadcasting, with its newsreader appearing with a bandage on a hand that was injured during the incident. This attack, which highlighted the ongoing insecurity in Kabul, coincided with NATO's announcement of an increase of roughly 3,000 troops to its Resolute Support mission in Afghanistan as part of efforts to overcome the deadlock with Taliban insurgents. Amid the sound of gunfire, a special forces team breached the concrete wall surrounding the compound and entered the site while police cordoned off the nearby streets. At least one attacker was killed during this operation, and another was shot at the entrance to the compound. In a statement released through its news agency Amaq, the Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack without providing any evidence. The group, primarily based in the eastern province of Nangarhar, has claimed several attacks on civilian targets in Kabul, but there remains uncertainty regarding whether all the incidents the group attributes to itself are genuinely its actions. Shortly after the attack commenced, the Taliban's chief spokesman, Zabihullah Mujahid, promptly denied any involvement. While suicide bombings have become a part of life in Kabul, the recent attack on journalists and media professionals was termed an "horrific crime" by the human rights organization Amnesty International. The group stated, "The Afghan authorities must take all necessary measures to safeguard the nation's media, enabling them to operate freely and without fear." Last year, a Taliban suicide bomber killed seven employees of Tolo, Afghanistan's largest private television station. In May, the Islamic State claimed responsibility for a suicide bombing targeting the state broadcaster RTA in the eastern city of Jalalabad. Tuesday's incident occurred roughly three weeks after a series of attacks, including one on a Shiite mosque in the city that resulted in the deaths of over 50 individuals.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga told a news conference that Japan would continue to call on the United States to engage on the issue of climate change.

text: A South African High Court determined on Friday that it lacks the authority to force President Jacob Zuma to establish a commission of inquiry regarding alleged influence-peddling within his administration. The Democratic Alliance (DA), the opposition party, sought the court's intervention to compel Zuma to create a commission, referencing a report from the previous year by an anti-corruption watchdog concerning claims that the Gupta brothers—Ajay, Atul, and Rajesh—had swayed ministerial appointments. Both Zuma and the Gupta siblings have refuted these allegations. The president has challenged the findings in court, asserting that the Public Protector does not possess the authority to mandate him to form such a commission, as this decision rests solely with the president. "To force the President at this juncture would not only equate to denying him a chance to present his case but would also imply that the powers of the Public Protector are beyond question, regardless of the decision’s content, which cannot be accurate," stated Pretoria High Court Judge Motsamai Makume. "It would serve justice better to allow the President a stay of the implementation of the remedial action while awaiting a ruling on the review application." New accusations regarding improper collusion between state-owned enterprises and the Gupta brothers have intensified scrutiny on Zuma and his close ministers. However, the court's decision is seen as a favorable development for the embattled Zuma during a challenging period. Allegations of extensive corruption and the misappropriation of taxpayer resources, referred to locally as "state capture," have undermined investor trust in an economy that slipped into recession earlier in 2017. On Wednesday, thousands of South Africans participated in anti-corruption demonstrations, rallying against Zuma and his influential associates, just three months ahead of the selection of a new leader for the African National Congress. Zuma also managed to overcome a no-confidence vote in parliament in August but has seen a decline in support among several ANC Members of Parliament, highlighting significant rifts within the party that has governed South Africa since apartheid's conclusion in 1994. The DA remarked that it had taken note of the ruling "with interest," indicating that it approached the court to expedite the investigation into influence-peddling claims. "On several occasions, including before the National Assembly, President Zuma has expressed his intention to set up a Commission of Inquiry. However, he has yet to do so," stated James Selfe, the party's federal council chairman, in a press release. "This issue has not been dismissed but is currently on hold pending the outcome of the President's review application, which is scheduled for a hearing at the end of October, where we will also be present in court to continue our pursuit of accountability." Some analysts suggested that the ongoing legal disputes would extend the investigations into the influence-peddling allegations. "The court had its legal responsibilities to fulfill, and this will allow Zuma to avoid executing his political responsibilities," commented Gary van Staden, an analyst at NKC African Economics. "In the end, this is detrimental to addressing state capture. It won't bring resolution to the ongoing issues."

text: MANILA (Reuters) - In an effort to expand its arms market within Southeast Asia, Russia has donated a variety of military supplies, including thousands of assault rifles and helmets, to the Philippines, as the latter seeks to diversify its weaponry. On Wednesday, Manila received approximately 5,000 Kalashnikov rifles, 5,000 steel helmets, around one million rounds of ammunition for those rifles, and 20 army trucks during a ceremony that included President Rodrigo Duterte, who also inspected one of five Russian warships visiting the country. This donation occurred a day after the Philippines and Russia formalized two military agreements, which included a sales contract with Rosoboronexport, a state-owned Russian defense supplier. Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana informed Reuters, "We are looking at acquiring some equipment for humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations, but there are no specifics yet. We are still discussing." Lorenzana clarified that the contract with Rosoboronexport is not a sales arrangement but indicates the Philippines' desire to obtain small arms, vehicles, and specialized equipment for disaster response. However, the United States, the Philippines’ primary arms supplier, expressed no concern regarding the equipment provided by competitors such as China and Russia. U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis remarked to reporters aboard a flight to Bangkok, "I don’t attach very much significance to it, some trucks or guns being dropped off to a country that’s fighting terrorists right now. It’s a sovereign decision by the Philippines," he continued, stating that it is not a major issue and that other nations are extending their support. The arms trade in the region is primarily dominated by the United States and China. Since the year 2000, the U.S. has contributed nearly $1 billion worth of military supplies to the Philippines, which includes everything from surveillance aircraft and drones to small arms. Following a meeting on Wednesday between Lorenzana and his Chinese counterpart, General Chang Wanquan, China has pledged a third shipment of small arms and has already provided around $7 million in small arms to the Philippines. Another senior Philippine official, who requested anonymity due to lack of authorization to speak with the media, stated that these agreements with the Philippines will enable Russia to broaden its arms market in the area. He mentioned that the Philippines is now receptive to the idea of purchasing Russian arms as Manila strengthens its relationship with Moscow, particularly as the military aims to diversify its arsenal while controlling expenses and ensuring quality. "Moscow has been offering to sell arms to us since the mid-1990s, and they are prepared to trade guns for bananas," he added, noting that Russia has been offering fighters, helicopters, and submarines to the Philippines.

text: Italy's leading political factions are set to endorse a new electoral framework this week, which is perceived as disadvantaging the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement in advance of the national election next year. The lower chamber of parliament is scheduled to commence voting on Tuesday regarding an electoral law backed by the primary right- and left-wing parties in the country. In contrast to the existing system, this law would permit the creation of extensive coalitions prior to voting, a development likely to be detrimental to 5-Star, which declines to participate in alliances. "The sole purpose (of the law) is to enable others to unite against us," remarked 5-Star legislator Danilo Toninelli on Sunday, following a parliamentary committee's approval of the new initiative. He added that for the traditional parties, "the key objective is to prevent the 5-Star from succeeding." A national election is anticipated to take place in the first half of 2018, between March and May. Current polls indicate that Matteo Renzi’s governing center-left Democratic Party (PD), which introduced the new legislation, is closely competing with the 5-Star. However, should the PD align with smaller centrist and leftist parties, they would likely outpace the 5-Star, currently led by 31-year-old Luigi Di Maio. The proposed law might particularly benefit Silvio Berlusconi’s center-right Forza Italia (Go Italy!) and the far-right Northern League, both of which support the legislation. In a coalition, polling suggests they could secure the highest number of votes. "The center-right and Forza Italia are gaining momentum," stated Renato Brunetta, the speaker of the lower house representing Berlusconi’s party. Nevertheless, polls indicate that neither Renzi's center-left nor Berlusconi's center-right has sufficient support to govern independently, implying that a right-left coalition might be the sole path to forming a government post-election. The bill could be approved as soon as this week in the Chamber, after which it will be sent to the Senate for ratification. There is a possibility that it could be thwarted by numerous secret votes where lawmakers may deviate from their party's official stance. Secret voting was responsible for the failure of an earlier electoral law proposal in June, which had initially garnered support from the 5-Star Movement. The 5-Star surged into parliament in 2013, capturing nearly 25% of the national vote, but has since faced challenges in broadening its appeal. It has committed to liberating Italy from what it describes as a corrupt political framework. The policies of the 5-Star include implementing universal income support for the impoverished, revising European Union public spending restrictions, and transitioning away from fossil fuels. It now claims that holding a referendum on abandoning the euro, which was once a fundamental aspect of its agenda, is not a pressing concern. The proposed electoral law would allocate nearly two-thirds of parliamentary seats based on proportional representation, while the remaining third would be determined by a first-past-the-post vote for specific candidates. Coalitions would need to achieve 10% of the national vote to enter parliament, whereas parties contesting independently would require only 3%. Party leaders would select the candidates.

A court decision on November 16 will determine whether the CNRP will be dissolved following a lawsuit filed by the government seeking its disbandment. Critics accuse Hun Sen of attempting to establish a one-party state in the nation. Tensions between the two parties have escalated, with Hun Sen issuing threats of conflict if his party does not prevail in the 2018 election. In September, opposition leader Kem Sokha faced treason charges after being accused by the government of conspiring to topple its leaders with support from the United States. Human rights organizations claim that the charges against Kem Sokha are fabricated. Half of Cambodia's opposition members of parliament have fled the nation. Koul Panha, the director of the Committee for Free and Fair Elections in Cambodia, noted that the low registration turnout was partially a result of intimidation and political strife.

text: Forbes estimates Donald Trump's net worth at $3.7 billion, which is $800 million lower than the previous year. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, Forbes magazine reported that the estimated wealth of U.S. Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump stands at $3.7 billion, reflecting a decrease of $800 million compared to last year, primarily attributed to the weakening real estate market in New York. The publication examined 28 assets or categories belonging to the New York entrepreneur and discovered that 18 of them had lost value, including Trump Tower located in Manhattan and the Mar-a-Lago club situated in Palm Beach, Florida. Additionally, the valuation of his property at 40 Wall Street in downtown New York has also dropped, as stated by Forbes, which has been monitoring Trump’s financial status for 34 years. Meanwhile, one asset held stable, and seven others, such as 555 California Street, the second tallest structure in San Francisco, experienced an increase in value, the report indicated. Trump campaign representatives were not available for immediate comment. This report comes as Trump, recognized for his reality television presence as well as his real estate ventures, enters the final phase of campaigning ahead of the election on November 8. As a first-time candidate, Trump has emphasized his business skills in advocating for changes in Washington. He has pledged to abolish trade agreements, negotiate with allies to increase their financial contributions for U.S. defense, and insist that Mexico finance a proposed wall along the southern U.S. border. If he wins, he would become the first billionaire to assume the presidency, according to Forbes. The specifics of Trump's wealth remain undisclosed to the public because he has declined to release his tax returns, breaking a longstanding tradition among U.S. presidential candidates. His opponent, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, reported an income of $10.75 million in 2015, along with her husband, former U.S. President Bill Clinton, as indicated in their tax documents. Clinton and others, including several notable Republicans, have urged Trump to disclose his tax returns, raising concerns regarding his net worth, charitable donations, and business affiliations. Forbes noted that its evaluation did not assign any value to Trump's brand. The magazine also contested Trump's claim made during Monday night’s presidential debate that he reported $694 million in income to the Federal Election Commission from the previous year, stating that Trump conflated revenue with income in that documentation. To date, Trump has contributed $54 million to his presidential campaign. Federal election records reveal that his campaign has also compensated his businesses for office space in Trump Tower and for the utilization of his private jet, among other costs. Politico additionally reported on Wednesday that Trump is contemplating increasing his financial support for his campaign to facilitate an advertising surge, citing three sources close to him. In the midst of his campaign, he executed only one real estate transaction over the past year: the acquisition of a warehouse in Charleston, South Carolina, which was in foreclosure, according to Forbes.

text: As President Donald Trump approaches the conclusion of his first year in office, sources indicate that U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson is anticipated to exit the Trump administration, among various other staff changes. Meanwhile, Kushner, whose influence has diminished within the White House, may receive a ‘face-saving’ exit as he navigates legal challenges tied to a special counsel’s investigation into alleged connections between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia, as stated by one source. White House spokesman Raj Shah commented via email regarding the potential staff changes, saying, ‘This is pure speculation.’ Additionally, lower-level advisers may choose to leave following the completion of Trump’s first year and tax legislation, which could lead to another phase of uncertainty that has occasionally overshadowed Trump’s presidency, which commenced on January 20. The dynamics in the Trump White House can shift rapidly, making it difficult to predict personnel changes, as advisers and Cabinet members who lose favor with the president can regain his trust. Such personnel adjustments are closely monitored globally for insights into how Trump might address various issues, including North Korea and regulatory policies. text: Trump's tax proposal faces a setback in the Senate as Rand Paul considers a 'no' vote. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, Senate Republicans hurried to secure backing for a budget resolution critical to President Donald Trump’s initiative to reform the U.S. tax system, as one Republican fiscal conservative indicated he might oppose the proposal. As discussions commenced in the Senate regarding the fiscal year 2018 budget, Senator Rand Paul raised concerns about spending levels that he claimed would surpass agreed limits by $43 billion, and advocated for reforms in entitlement programs like Medicare and Medicaid. "I will not support the budget if it does not adhere to the spending caps," the Republican senator informed journalists. In a discussion with Trump earlier that day, Paul stated he conveyed to the Republican president: "I’m all in. I want to be supportive. I’m a 'yes' vote. But we have to follow our own rules." Senate Republican staff refuted the claim that the budget resolution breaches federal spending limits established by the Budget Control Act of 2011. Paul argued that the excess spending was related to military operations overseas, which aides noted are exempt from the caps. The budget resolution already had a precarious path toward approval in the Senate, where Democrats oppose the measures and Republicans hold only a 52-48 majority. A 'no' vote from Paul seemed to place the budget just one vote away from failure, jeopardizing Trump's efforts for tax reform. Another fiscal conservative, Senator Ted Cruz, has not revealed whether he would back the measure. However, the prospects for Republicans to advance a budget resolution unexpectedly improved when Senator Thad Cochran returned to the Senate despite health issues and expressed in a statement his eagerness to "engage in the budget and tax cut discussions." Just a day prior, Cochran's office indicated he would be unavailable that week. With Cochran present, Republicans could still pass the measure even with the loss of two votes. The budget resolution is crucial to Trump’s tax reform plans as it would activate a legislative mechanism known as reconciliation, enabling Senate Republicans to pass a tax bill with a simple majority. Without it, a partisan tax bill would require 60 votes in the 100-member Senate and would almost certainly fail. The Republican campaign had gained traction on Monday when two other potential Senate Republican "no" votes - Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski - suggested they were leaning toward "yes." Senator John McCain also expressed his support for the budget resolution. Following their inability to repeal Obamacare earlier this year, Republicans are concerned about facing backlash from voters in the upcoming congressional midterm elections if they do not succeed in passing legislation to reduce taxes for both businesses and individuals. Trump and senior Republicans have put forward a proposal to provide up to $6 trillion in tax cuts over the next decade as part of a reform package they argue will enhance economic growth and create more jobs with higher wages. Democrats, who criticize the Republican proposal as a giveaway to the affluent, are expected to suggest numerous amendments to the budget plan to block tax reductions for the wealthy and mandate legislation that would not increase the federal deficit. "We’re discussing a significant political party now working tirelessly for the top 0.1 percent," Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent aligned with Democrats, told Reuters on Tuesday. Both the Senate and the House of Representatives must concur on a budget resolution. The House has already passed a different version, meaning that House and Senate Republicans will need to negotiate a unified version and approve it before reconciliation can take effect.

text: LONDON (Reuters) - A committee of lawmakers has expressed skepticism regarding Britain's strategy to prevent a hard border between Ireland and Northern Ireland post-Brexit, stating that it conflicts with the nation's intention to exit the European Union's single market and customs union. The Irish border, which will serve as the sole land connection between the EU and Britain after Brexit, has emerged as one of the most challenging matters in a sluggish diplomatic effort that is testing the endurance of politicians, businesses, and investors alike. The EU is urging the UK to propose a method for managing the movement of goods between Ireland and the British province without implementing politically sensitive border controls. The UK government has indicated its desire to leave the EU's customs union, which allows for the free movement of goods, yet it refuses to consider the establishment of border posts or any other infrastructure that could jeopardize two decades of fragile peace in Northern Ireland. "At this point, we cannot envision how exiting the customs union and the single market can align with the absence of a border or any infrastructure," remarked opposition MP Hilary Benn, who chairs the Brexit committee overseeing the negotiations. The British government has claimed it is pursuing a flexible and creative solution for the border that surpasses current EU examples, suggesting the use of technological innovations or a novel type of customs union. However, Irish officials have criticized the ministers for their vague proposals. Progress on the border matter is vital for the UK's ambitions to advance discussions toward trade and future relations, a topic that businesses are keen to gain clarity on as they consider potential relocations. On Thursday, Deputy Irish Prime Minister Simon Coveney stated that "significantly more clarity" is essential ahead of the Dec. 14-15 summit, which could potentially initiate "phase two" negotiations regarding trade. The committee, which formulated its report based on insights from Brexit minister David Davis, emphasized the need for the government to provide additional details about both its immediate strategies for a transition period post-departure and its long-term aspirations for a trade relationship with Europe. Benn stated, "If phase two of the talks commence next month, ministers must progress beyond terms like 'bespoke' and 'special' and clearly articulate what they are actually pursuing."
