text: SAN FRANCISCO (Reuters) - This November, California's ballot will showcase an unprecedented number of local tax and bond initiatives, with more than $32 billion earmarked for education, infrastructure, and services for the homeless. Voters will see approximately 650 local measures, which includes 427 revenue-related proposals. This figure significantly surpasses the amount proposed during any of the past five gubernatorial or presidential elections, as reported by the local government finance consulting firm CaliforniaCityFinance.com. The previous record for local revenue measures was set in November 2014, with 268 proposals. California is among 24 states that grant citizens the right to initiate measures. Voter-approved initiatives are employed to generate funds for designated construction projects, modify tax regulations, or establish new legislation. A surge in bond proposals, both in California and across the nation, follows years of federal reductions in state and local program funding, persistent low interest rates, and ongoing infrastructure demands. Among the largest financial requests from local governments in California are $3.5 billion for the Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART), $1.2 billion for housing and services for the homeless in Los Angeles, and $950 million for affordable housing in Santa Clara County. There are 184 local measures aimed at financing community college and public school projects, amounting to over $25 billion. Michael Coleman, the leader of CaliforniaCityFinance.com, noted that the increase in education bond measures aligns with statewide Proposition 51, which authorizes $9 billion in general obligation bonds for public school infrastructure. Proposition 55 seeks to enhance education funding by extending tax rates for higher income brackets. "Many believe this is the opportune moment to pursue a new school bond," Coleman remarked. "They view it as a coordinated message and the right time to secure matching funds." The election on November 8 will also highlight statewide propositions, with 17 in total addressing topics such as marijuana legalization, the public expense of prescription medications, tobacco taxes, and the death penalty. The rise in ballot measures occurs during an election cycle where the presidential contest is expected to attract significant voter turnout. Additionally, the impact of low voter participation in the November 2014 election has led to a reduction in the signature requirement for a proposition to qualify. Nationwide, 74 citizen-initiated measures are present on state ballots, more than twice the amount certified in 2014, according to Natalie Cohen, a senior analyst at Wells Fargo Securities. A growing sense of populism and dissatisfaction with conventional government has fueled this increase, Cohen noted in a recent report on forthcoming ballot measures. In California, several local measures are responses to state propositions. For instance, Proposition 64 seeks to legalize recreational cannabis, and 37 local measures would impose taxes on marijuana for cities and counties. Thirteen countywide measures are set to finance transportation enhancements. "This reflects a recognized, pent-up need for essential infrastructure repairs," Coleman stated. Eighty-eight measures aim to raise or extend local sales taxes. An additional 39 support parcel taxes for improvements to roads, fire and emergency services, hospitals, and police departments. Parcel taxes are flat-rate taxes on properties that emerged after Proposition 13 significantly restricted property taxes in 1978. Three measures in the Bay Area would levy taxes on sugary drinks.

text: Exclusive: U.S. budget proposal allocates more than $13 billion for a new submarine - sources. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The upcoming five-year budget proposal from the Pentagon is set to request in excess of $13 billion to develop a new submarine designed to carry nuclear ballistic missiles, along with orders for additional fighter jets from Boeing Co (BA.N) and Lockheed Martin Corp (LMT.N), as indicated by sources familiar with the matter. Additionally, the strategy for a new carrier-based unmanned drone will be adjusted to prioritize intelligence gathering and refueling over combat strike operations, according to the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity prior to the budget announcement. U.S. Defense Secretary Ash Carter is expected to outline his funding priorities for the $583 billion defense budget for 2017 on Tuesday, ahead of the official budget unveiling scheduled for February 9. The Pentagon's budget proposal will also emphasize the importance of financing all three components of the U.S. strategic deterrent 'triad' - a new Air Force bomber, a successor to the Ohio-class submarines that house nuclear weapons, and new nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to one source. The Navy's proposed budget for fiscal year 2017 will allocate funds for the procurement of materials necessary for the new submarines, which have long lead times, with construction funding for the initial complete new submarine planned for fiscal 2021, one source revealed. Over the next five years, the Navy is projected to invest more than $4 billion in research and development for the new submarines, along with over $9 billion in procurement expenses, per the sources. General Dynamics Corp (GD.N) will take the lead on the new submarine project intended to replace the existing Ohio-class submarines, partnering with Huntington Ingalls Industries Inc (HII.N). Boeing is expected to secure orders exceeding $1 billion for new aircraft as it aims to sustain production at its St. Louis facility. The Navy plans to request funding for two Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornets as part of its fiscal 2017 war budget, and 14 in the fiscal 2018 budget, according to one source. Navy officials are also anticipated to include a request for an additional 12 Boeing Super Hornets in their annual list of 'unfunded priorities' for fiscal 2017, as noted by one source. These actions are intended to address a shortfall in the number of strike fighters available on aircraft carriers, attributed to delays in the Lockheed F-35 fighter jet program and longer-than-expected maintenance times for the current Boeing F/A-18 jets. The five-year budget plan stipulates that Lockheed will provide a total of 161 F-35 fighter jets to the Navy and Marine Corps - comprising 64 C-model jets that can take off and land on aircraft carriers and 97 B-model jets, which are capable of taking off from shorter runways and landing vertically like a helicopter, according to one source. Furthermore, the proposal modifies the mission scope of a new drone that the U.S. Navy plans to develop, the sources stated. In line with this change, the Navy intends to rename the new drone initiative to the Carrier-Based Air Refueling System, or CBARS, replacing the previous designation of Unmanned Carrier-Launched Airborne Surveillance and Strike (UCLASS), according to one source. While the drones will initially possess limited strike capabilities, additional features may be incorporated in future years, the sources indicated. Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop Grumman Corp (NOC.N), which produces the unarmed X-47B drone tested on U.S. aircraft carriers, and privately owned General Atomics invested tens of millions of dollars in preparation for the earlier bidding process. However, the initiative was suspended in 2014 while awaiting a comprehensive review of intelligence and surveillance programs by the Pentagon.

text: French President Emmanuel Macron emphasized that Turkey is an essential partner for the European Union and that relations should be upheld, despite the country's deviation from the EU trajectory, as stated in an interview with a newspaper released on Thursday. A high-ranking Turkish official indicated that EU nations need to determine whether they wish to have Turkey as a member, although there appears to be a sentiment that they prefer a more distant arrangement rather than a formal union. Macron's statements came in response to German Chancellor Angela Merkel's comments during a television debate on Sunday, where she suggested that the EU should cease membership discussions with Ankara. Macron remarked to Greece’s Kathimerini newspaper that Turkey has indeed moved away from the EU in recent months and has crossed critical boundaries that cannot be overlooked. However, he expressed a desire to prevent a separation, highlighting Turkey's significance in addressing numerous challenges, particularly the issues of immigration and terrorism. The EU is keen to maintain its agreement with Turkey, which has significantly reduced mass migration through Turkish land from conflict-ridden regions. Turkey has previously raised doubts regarding the EU’s commitment to upholding its part of the deal. The relationship between Ankara and the European Union has soured since the attempted coup in July 2016, which led to the detention of tens of thousands across Turkey. Critics contend that President Tayyip Erdogan is exploiting the coup attempt as a justification for targeting political rivals. Turkey, which entered into an association agreement with the EU in 1963, began official negotiations for EU membership in 2005. Nonetheless, several member states, including France, have opposed discussions on particular topics, resulting in only 16 out of 35 negotiation chapters being opened. In remarks to the press in Paris, Turkey’s ambassador reiterated Erdogan’s position that the EU must clarify its stance on membership and rejected the idea of a different special partnership. He stated that integrating Turkey into the EU is a matter for Europe to resolve, not just Turkey. 'Of course we feel deceived,' Ismail Hakki Musa told reporters in Paris. 'They no longer desire marriage; they prefer cohabitation. It’s too late for a privileged partnership, and Europe must now be truthful and earnest.' The latest, Loup Bureau, was apprehended by Turkish border officials at the Iraq border in early August. Musa mentioned that Macron and Erdogan have instructed their respective interior and justice ministers to work towards resolving the issue. 'We need to find a solution without compromising the fundamentals of the Turkish system,' he stated. France’s foreign minister is scheduled to visit Ankara on September 14. 'Dialogue is always beneficial. We acknowledge that there are human rights issues in Turkey.' text: GOMA, Democratic Republic of Congo (Reuters) - On Sunday, clashes in the eastern city of Bukavu between Congolese forces and followers of a renegade colonel resulted in the deaths of seven individuals before the colonel surrendered to U.N. peacekeepers, according to the army. Dieudonne Kasereka, the spokesperson for the Democratic Republic of Congo army in South Kivu province, reported that the confrontations began when police attempted to disarm Colonel Abbas Kayonga, who had been dismissed from his position overseeing anti-fraud initiatives in local mines on Thursday. Kayonga, who was previously part of a rebel faction that had been disarmed and assimilated into the Congolese military, turned himself in at the local U.N. mission base. "He has just surrendered with 17 people at the base of the mission," Kasereka stated via telephone. The fighting resulted in the deaths of two army soldiers and three of Kayonga's bodyguards, along with two civilians who were struck by stray gunfire, he noted. Seventeen members of Kayonga’s faction handed themselves over to U.N. forces, while the army captured nine others, Kasereka added, mentioning that soldiers discovered approximately a dozen heavy weapons at Kayonga’s residence. The security situation in Congo has been worsening since the end of last year, when President Joseph Kabila refused to resign despite the expiration of his mandate. Increasing militia violence in the east—a region long troubled by ethnic tensions fueled by its mineral resources—and in the previously stable central Kasai area has sparked concerns that the country might revert to the complex civil wars experienced at the turn of the century. Those conflicts resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths directly from violence, with millions more believed to have succumbed to famine and disease. South Kivu is rich in gold, tin, and coltan—materials used in mobile phones—which have historically funded rebel factions and military officials. The national electoral commission was anticipated to announce a date for the election to succeed Kabila later on Sunday. Last month, it indicated that the election could not occur until April 2019, raising anxieties about a potential increase in militia violence and civil unrest. During a recent visit to meet with Kabila, U.S. envoy Nikki Haley emphasized that the election must take place in 2018 or risk losing international backing.

In a series of tweets, Trump continued to question the conclusions drawn by U.S. intelligence agencies that indicated Russia was behind a sequence of leaks that embarrassed Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton’s campaign prior to the Nov. 8 election. These tweets led White House spokesman Josh Earnest to inquire, “Who are you going to believe?” Documents taken from the Democratic National Committee and John Podesta, Clinton’s campaign manager, were disclosed to the media ahead of the election. One email revealed that the Clinton campaign had received a question ahead of a town hall meeting. Several lawmakers, including some of Trump’s fellow Republicans, have supported calls for an investigation. text: New Jersey Governor Chris Christie has put a stop to non-essential projects related to roads, bridges, and mass transit as of late Thursday. This decision came after the legislature did not renew the state fund responsible for financing these initiatives. Christie's executive order instructs the state Department of Transportation and New Jersey Transit to create a plan by midnight Saturday to ensure an “orderly” shutdown of projects backed by the Transportation Trust Fund. According to his executive order, projects funded by federal sources will proceed as planned. The state anticipates receiving approximately $906 million in federal transportation assistance, as noted in the annual report from the state treasurer. The ability of New Jersey to borrow for fresh transportation projects ceased on Friday, coinciding with the beginning of the new fiscal year. The trust fund already carries about $16 billion in existing debt for ongoing road projects. Assembly Transportation Committee Chairman John Wisniewski stated that the fund has roughly $80 million remaining and criticized Christie's executive order as “pure theater.” Without new appropriations or bond revenues, the authority lacks the capability to compensate contractors for construction work. The Department of Transportation indicated that Christie’s order affects projects at every phase, including procurement, design, and construction. Approximately one month ago, lawmakers deliberated on the possibility of issuing grant anticipation revenue bonds, known as GARVEEs, as a temporary solution, but the proposal was ultimately not pursued, Wisniewski informed Reuters. The availability of federal funds supporting those bonds is often unpredictable from year to year. “You can’t implement an annual capital program using GARVEE bonds,” he remarked. Christie mandated that the remaining funds in the trust be reserved exclusively for the most crucial projects “to ensure the health, safety and welfare” of the residents of New Jersey, as he stated. Earlier this week, Christie had brokered a late-night agreement with the Assembly to increase the state gasoline tax by 23 cents, bringing it to 37.5 cents per gallon, in order to replenish the fund. In return, the sales tax rate would decrease by 1 percentage point to 6 percent, which could result in an annual budget shortfall of $1.7 billion in the future. However, the Senate concluded its session on Thursday without restoring the program, which is projected to deplete its funds by August. Senators were advocating for their own legislation, which aimed to eliminate the estate tax for affluent residents instead of lowering sales taxes. On Thursday, Christie also removed several items from the legislature’s budget, approving a trimmed-down budget of $34.5 billion for fiscal 2017, which reflects an increase of just 2.1 percent compared to fiscal 2016.

text: A British lesbian has won the right to a spousal visa in a significant ruling by a Hong Kong appeals court on Monday. This landmark decision could pave the way for expatriate same-sex partners to relocate to the financial hub controlled by China. The British individual, referred to as QT, had her application for a dependant visa denied on the basis that she was not considered a spouse, despite having entered into a civil partnership in England. In Hong Kong, marriage is defined strictly as a union between a man and a woman, yet legislation prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation. Since its return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, the former British colony has maintained a high degree of autonomy, including an independent judiciary. In a unanimous ruling from a panel of three judges, the Court of Appeal determined that the immigration director did not adequately explain the indirect discrimination experienced by QT due to her sexual orientation. Although the appeal did not contest the legal definition of marriage, Chief Judge Andrew Cheung noted that societal norms have evolved, and more individuals are unwilling to accept traditional views without critical examination. He remarked, "Excluding a foreign worker's legally married (even if same-sex) spouse or civil partner... from joining the worker is obviously counter-productive to attracting that worker to come to or stay in Hong Kong for employment in the first place." The court directed QT and the Department of Immigration to collaborate on an agreement and present it to the court within a period of 28 days. Advocates for LGBT rights in Hong Kong expressed their approval of the ruling, with the city’s first openly gay legislator, Ray Chan, describing it as a "significant victory for same-sex dependants seeking a visa to reside in Hong Kong." Same-sex marriage was legalized in Taiwan in May, marking a first for Asia. In mainland China, homosexuality was classified as a mental disorder until 2001, though being gay is not considered illegal.

In Chiapas, a southern state renowned for its verdant mountains, I captured images of a small Muslim group comprised of hundreds of primarily indigenous Tzotzil men and women, many of whom transitioned to Islam from Catholicism or other Christian faiths. The Muslim men are easily recognized by their prayer caps, known as kufis, while the women wear hijabs that resemble traditional Maya shawls. Residents indicate that the shift to Islam commenced in the late 1980s, coinciding with the rise of Mexico's Zapatista movement in Chiapas, as various institutions, including Christianity and capitalism, faced heightened scrutiny. The most recent census reveals that approximately 83 percent of the Mexican population identifies as Catholic. Despite Muslims constituting less than 1 percent of Mexico's 120 million residents, a significant number are indigenous, particularly found in and around San Cristobal de las Casas, a highland city that embodies both Maya and Spanish heritage. "When we converted, people looked at us strangely; they perceived us as terrorists and felt frightened by our presence," remarked Mustafa, a member of the nearby Ahmadia community. "However, over time and through our actions, that perspective has evolved," he continued. Umar, an indigenous individual who was formerly an evangelical pastor, embraced Islam in the late 1990s and now acts as a liaison between local Christians and Muslims. "We believe in one God," he stated. "However, we do not venerate saints." Later, I met Mohamed Amin, a 55-year-old who graciously invited me into his home, where he offered cookies and tea. He shared his prayer space, where he engages in prayer five times daily, and introduced me to his family. When he inquired if I believed in God, I replied no, which did not seem to concern him. He proceeded to share the primary motivation behind his conversion to Islam. "I appreciate cleanliness and enjoy changing my clothes," he explained. "This is a clean religion, and that was the initial attraction for me." For a related photo essay, see: reut.rs/2izhpmh

text: Trump narrows search for Supreme Court nominee, to announce conservative pick next week. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Donald Trump, ready to reinstate the conservative majority on the Supreme Court, convened with important senators on Tuesday and committed to revealing his nominee next week, with three judges from U.S. appeals courts among those being closely evaluated. Trump met at the White House with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, and the leading Republican and Democrat on the Judiciary Committee to discuss filling the vacancy on the court left by the death of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia more than 11 months ago. The appointment of a Supreme Court justice for a lifetime term necessitates Senate confirmation. Leonard Leo, a conservative lawyer providing counsel to Trump, stated that the president “has definitely narrowed his focus” and is “looking very seriously” at a shortlist of candidates. The leading contenders include three conservative judges: Neil Gorsuch, a judge on the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals based in Denver; Thomas Hardiman, who is on the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals located in Philadelphia; and William Pryor, a judge on the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta. “Judges Gorsuch, Hardiman, and Pryor have attracted significant attention from the president. He knows who they are. He is well-acquainted with their records. He’s evidently impressed with their qualifications,” Leo remarked. All three were appointed by former Republican President George W. Bush. “I’ll be finalizing my decision this week. We’ll be making an announcement next week. We have remarkable candidates, and we will select a truly outstanding Supreme Court justice,” Trump informed reporters in the Oval Office. The primary candidates all possess strong conservative credentials. Gorsuch participated in a 2013 ruling stating that owners of private companies can object on religious grounds to a section of the Obamacare health insurance law mandating employers to provide coverage for birth control for women. Hardiman authored an opinion in 2013 that endorsed a broad interpretation of the Second Amendment rights. Pryor has been a vocal opponent of the court’s landmark 1973 decision that legalized abortion. Leo mentioned that all three are “very much in the mold of Justice Scalia,” who was one of the court's most conservative members. Following the meeting with Trump, Schumer expressed that he reiterated the idea that the president “should select a mainstream nominee who could gain bipartisan backing” and that Democrats would oppose any nominee they consider outside the mainstream. “I expect what we’re going to receive from the president is a highly qualified, well-credentialed conservative jurist,” McConnell told reporters. Trump is able to appoint Scalia’s successor because the Republican-controlled U.S. Senate, in an action that has little precedent in U.S. history, last year chose not to consider Democratic President Barack Obama’s nominee, appeals court judge Merrick Garland. Obama, who transferred power to Trump last Friday, nominated Garland on March 16, but Republican senators, led by McConnell, denied Garland the usual confirmation hearings and vote. Since Scalia’s passing, the court has been ideologically split with four conservative justices and four liberal justices. A conservative nominee to replace Scalia would restore the court’s narrow conservative majority that had been in place for decades. Trump’s fellow Republicans hold a 52-48 majority in the Senate. Democrats, angered by the rejection of Garland, may attempt to obstruct the nomination through procedural challenges.

text: The German Justice Ministry is calling for a prohibition on Kuwait Airways due to its policy regarding Israeli passengers. On Friday, a high-ranking official from the Justice Department stated that the government ought to withdraw landing permissions for Kuwait Airways, deeming such discrimination unacceptable. Christian Lange, the parliamentary state secretary within the ministry, urged Chancellor Angela Merkel to personally support the initiative to ban Kuwait Airways from operating in Germany. A ruling by a German court on Thursday affirmed the airline's right to deny transportation to an Israeli passenger based on his nationality, a decision that Jewish organizations claimed legitimized anti-Semitic behavior. In a letter to Merkel, Lange noted he had received numerous calls from Jewish community members and individuals in Israel who were appalled by the court's decision, which came only days after Germany solemnly commemorated the anniversary of the November 9, 1938, Nazi pogroms against Jewish people. "We cannot declare 'Never again' at a memorial event while remaining silent when activists in Germany push for a boycott of Israel, or, in this instance, when an airline refuses to transport Israeli citizens," Lange articulated. He emphasized to the Chancellor that it is essential for the German government to demonstrate that it denounces this type of discrimination and hatred, and that it stands with its Israeli allies. The Lawfare Project, the legal organization representing the affected plaintiff, has pledged to contest the court's decision. Brooke Goldstein, the executive director of the group, remarked, "To witness a Jewish individual being barred from exercising his rights in Germany in 2017 is already alarming. To see such discrimination endorsed and validated by a German judge is appalling." Additionally, Deputy German Foreign Minister Michael Roth criticized the airline's stance, revealing to Die Welt newspaper that he had reached out to the Kuwaiti ambassador in Germany regarding the situation. German Transport Minister Christian Schmidt expressed to Bild newspaper that it is intolerable to discriminate against airline passengers based on their nationality, and indicated that the German government would address the issue with the Kuwaiti authorities. "This requires ministerial-level discussions," Schmidt stated in an interview scheduled for publication on Saturday. "We will exhaust all our legal options to prevent this from happening again," he concluded. The airline did not provide an immediate response to an email inquiry for comment.

text: A division within a division: the Catalan valley that remains loyal to Spain. VIELHA, Spain (Reuters) - Should Catalonia proclaim independence from Spain this week, one community in the mountainous northern region may choose to break away from Catalonia itself. The majority of residents in the charming Aran Valley - a semi-autonomous area located in the Pyrenees - wish to remain part of Spain, and this community has the right to self-determination as per a law enacted in 2015 by the Catalan parliament. "We are a small dot on the map and often overlooked," stated Maria Verges Perez, the deputy mayor of Aran’s capital, Vielha, a cluster of stone and slate structures situated on the valley floor surrounded by autumn foliage. "However, we will exercise our right to determine our future." Catalan President Carles Puigdemont is anticipated to announce independence on Tuesday, marking Spain's most severe constitutional crisis since the establishment of democracy in the 1970s. The approximately 10,000 inhabitants of Aran, located along the French border, possess a unique language and culture that sets them apart from the rest of Catalonia, which is itself distinct from the broader Spanish context. The economy of the valley greatly relies on winter sports tourists from both Spain and the EU. Their representatives assert that the 2015 legislation grants them the right to vote on whether they wish to separate from Catalonia - a claim that Catalan officials do not contest. The Spanish government has pledged to obstruct Catalonia's secession. The loss of this region would mean a reduction of 16 percent of Spain’s population and a fifth of its economic production. Despite Madrid's assertion that Spain is indivisible according to its constitution, the Aran Valley illustrates the intricate nature of national identity within such a culturally rich nation. Since the restoration of democracy in the 1970s, Madrid has faced challenges in reconciling the country's diverse regional identities, including its long-standing efforts to suppress separatism in the northern Basque Country, previously led by the militant group ETA. Few in the medieval settlements throughout the Aran Valley believe the community would choose to leave Spain if given the opportunity to vote. "The people here feel quite disconnected from what is occurring in Barcelona," remarked Carlos Barrera, the head of the Aran government, during a rural festival in Salardu village, where locals evaluated robust Pyrenean horses and distributed racks of blood sausages. The valley recorded the lowest voter turnout in Catalonia's October 1 independence referendum, which had been deemed illegal by Spain's constitutional court. The overall turnout in Catalonia was 43 percent, with many individuals favoring remaining in Spain opting not to participate, and 90 percent of those who cast votes supported secession. In Aran, merely 24 percent participated, with 84 percent of that group endorsing independence. The valley’s political ties trace back to agreements established in the 13th century with the Crown of Aragon, which would later merge with the Crown of Castile two centuries later to create what is now Spain. Many residents communicate in Aranese, a dialect of the Occitan language still utilized in certain areas of the Pyrenees and southern France. Two years prior, the Catalan parliament ratified the Law on Aran's Special Status, granting the region authority over its culture, language, and governance, and acknowledging the Aranese people's right to determine their own future. A representative of the Catalan government indicated that Catalonia would honor the Aranese people's decision in any forthcoming referendum. A spokesperson for the Spanish government refrained from commenting on whether Aran could remain part of Spain, asserting instead that Catalonia would never achieve independence. The residents of Aran are among the most vocal critics of the Catalan government, which they claim is disregarding those who wish to remain in Spain and pursuing independence recklessly. In Vielha, a solitary red and yellow Catalan independence flag hanging from an apartment building was the sole indication last Saturday of the separatist enthusiasm permeating many areas of the region, where cities are engulfed in protests sparked by Madrid's violent response to the referendum.

text: Elaine Chao, nominated by Donald Trump to lead the U.S. Transportation Department, endorsed the president-elect’s $1 trillion infrastructure initiative as a "bold vision" during her confirmation hearing on Wednesday, which was characterized by overwhelming support in the Senate. Although some criticisms regarding her environmental stance have been raised, there appears to be no substantial opposition to her confirmation, and she is anticipated to be approved. Chao previously held the position of labor secretary under President George W. Bush from 2001 to 2009, making her the first Asian-American woman to serve in a Cabinet role. She was also deputy secretary of transportation under President George H. W. Bush. Her husband, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, introduced her at the hearing. Bill Nelson, the top Democrat on the committee from Florida, mentioned his wife's friendship with Chao. Chao is expected to play a pivotal role in Trump’s strategy to restore deteriorating U.S. roads and bridges through the proposed $1 trillion fund. The plan includes offering private investors an 82 percent tax credit for their contributions to projects; however, critics have raised concerns about the lack of clarity on how these investors can recuperate their funds without significantly raising costs for users of the infrastructure. Presenting the plan to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, Chao referred to it as a "bold vision" and recognized the importance of addressing how to repay investors. She stated, "For them (partnerships) to be truly effective, there need to be revenue streams that need to be assured." She added, "We all know that the government doesn’t have the resources to do it all." Chao’s nomination comes as she is set to lead a department with extensive responsibilities, including the management of the nation’s airports and highways, oversight of fuel-economy regulations for vehicles, and investigations into auto manufacturers regarding safety recalls of critical components such as airbags. She refrained from expressing views on various topics, including the potential privatization of air traffic control, the safety concerns associated with transporting crude oil by rail, the entry of foreign carriers like Norwegian Air Shuttle into the U.S. market, and the regulation of emerging technologies such as autonomous vehicles and drones. During the hearing, Chao was not questioned about her involvement in corporate boards. She is a board member of Wells Fargo & Co, which has faced challenges since September after agreeing to pay $190 million in fines and restitution to resolve allegations that its employees improperly created up to 2 million accounts without customer consent. Chao immigrated from Taiwan to the United States at the age of 8. Her father, James S.C. Chao, is the founder of the Foremost Group, a global shipping enterprise.

text: A window detached from a U.S. Marines helicopter and landed on a school sports field in Okinawa, Japan, on Wednesday, according to the Marines. This incident marks yet another occurrence that has heightened safety apprehensions on the southern island of Japan. For years, Japan's central government and authorities in Okinawa have been in disagreement regarding the Futenma base. Local residents express concerns about the perceived disproportionate burden they endure to accommodate the U.S. military presence in the country. An official from Okinawa prefecture reported to Reuters that a 10-year-old boy sustained a minor injury, although the precise cause of the incident remains uncertain. At the time, approximately 50 children were present on the elementary school grounds when the window fell from a U.S. CH-53E transport helicopter. Yoshihide Suga, Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary, commented, "Such incidents instill anxiety not only among those at the school but also among the residents of Okinawa, and they must never occur." He added during a routine press conference that the government would take appropriate action following a report from U.S. officials. The U.S. Marines stationed in Okinawa issued a statement indicating that the helicopter promptly returned and reported the occurrence. "We regard this report with utmost seriousness and are investigating the incident's cause in close collaboration with local authorities," the statement read. "This unfortunate event is regrettable, and we apologize for any distress it has caused the community." The Futenma base is located near schools, hospitals, and shops, which raises local concerns about potential air crashes. Additionally, crimes committed by U.S. servicemen have at times sparked anger among residents. Okinawa Governor Takeshi Onaga has spearheaded efforts to relocate the base off the island, while the central government has suggested moving it to a less densely populated area known as Henoko. In October, a U.S. Marines CH-53E helicopter was forced to make an emergency landing, igniting in flames within a U.S. military training zone in northern Okinawa, though no injuries were reported.

text: President Barack Obama is set to advocate for an increase in the budget for the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for the fiscal year 2017, as indicated by a White House representative on Monday. The proposed budget will suggest an 11 percent funding boost for the SEC, bringing its total to $1.8 billion, and a 32 percent rise for the CFTC, raising its budget to $330 million, according to economic adviser Jeffrey Zients in a blog entry on the White House’s website. "Last year, the Administration worked diligently to prevent Congressional Republicans from utilizing essential budget legislation to undo Wall Street Reform," he mentioned, alluding to the fiscal year 2016. "We also advocated for increased funding for financial regulators and aimed to preserve their autonomy. However, even these achievements fall short." "In addition to seeking additional resources for these regulatory bodies, the Administration will persist in opposing attempts to limit the funding autonomy of other financial regulators, such as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau," he added. The Congress, which is under Republican control, is expected to resist these and numerous other aspects of Obama’s budget proposal. Besides the suggested funding increases compared to the previous fiscal year, the budget will once again propose user fees to finance the CFTC similarly to other financial regulatory bodies, Zients remarked. "Implementing fee funding would transfer the financial burden of regulatory services offered by the CFTC from taxpayers to the firms that gain from the CFTC's oversight. This is a pragmatic adjustment that has been overdue," he stated. The budget will also aim to mitigate risk within the financial sector by imposing a fee on large financial entities based on their liabilities. "We learned the hard way in 2008 how detrimental risk and leverage can be in the financial system, and we’ve made significant efforts to reduce excessive risk on Wall Street since then," Zients noted, referencing the global financial crisis. "This fee represents another measure to advance those reforms, ensuring that taxpayers are not responsible for the risky endeavors on Wall Street." The federal fiscal year 2017 will commence on October 1 of this year.

text: A federal judge on Friday invalidated several Wisconsin voting restrictions enacted by the Republican-controlled legislature, mandating a revision of the state's voter identification rules, as these were found to disenfranchise minority voters. U.S. District Judge James Peterson, in a legal dispute brought forth by two liberal organizations, stated that he could not nullify the entire voter ID law due to a prior ruling from a federal appeals court that deemed such restrictions constitutional. However, in his 119-page decision, Peterson remarked that the stipulations requiring Wisconsin voters to present either a photo ID or undergo a special petition process had imposed an unfair burden on minorities and necessitated reform or replacement ahead of the presidential election in November. "To be frank, Wisconsin’s stringent voter ID law is a remedy that is worse than the ailment," the judge noted. Peterson maintained the voting regulations for the August 9 primary elections for federal, state, and local positions, explaining that alterations made less than two weeks before would be disruptive. Nevertheless, his ruling was anticipated to affect the November presidential election in Wisconsin, a state that could be pivotal for Democrat Hillary Clinton and Republican Donald Trump. Additionally, Peterson deemed unconstitutional the restrictions on in-person absentee voting, residency criteria, and the prohibition on using expired student ID cards. Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker expressed his disappointment in a tweet, referring to the ruling as that of an "activist federal judge" and indicated plans to appeal. A representative from One Wisconsin Institute, one of the groups that initiated the challenge, celebrated Peterson’s decision as "a significant victory not just for the plaintiffs but for democracy as a whole." Wisconsin is among several Republican-led states that have implemented such voter ID laws in recent years due to concerns over voter fraud by undocumented immigrants and others. Among the nine states with the strictest regulations requiring state-issued photo IDs for voters are Georgia, Indiana, Texas, and Virginia. Earlier this month, a U.S. appeals court judge ruled that the Texas law was discriminatory and referred the case back to the lower court to determine if the law had a discriminatory intent while also requesting a short-term solution for the upcoming general election in November. Republicans argue that voter ID laws are essential to combat voter fraud, while Democrats contend that these laws aim to create obstacles for low-income African-Americans and Latinos, who typically support the Democratic Party.

text: U.S. senators are urging President Barack Obama to implement sanctions against officials in the Democratic Republic of Congo who are linked to violence and human rights abuses amid escalating political tensions. On Friday, three of Obama’s fellow Democrats—senators Richard Durbin, Edward Markey, and Christopher Murphy—announced they had presented a Senate resolution earlier this week, which calls on the government of President Joseph Kabila to adhere to its constitutional obligation to ensure a democratic transition of power later this year. This initiative demonstrates the increasing international concern regarding the situation in the African country. text: Clinton willingly steps back from the national limelight, allowing Trump to take center stage. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - If there seems to be a lack of coverage regarding Hillary Clinton's perspective on a series of contentious remarks made by Donald Trump, which have sparked continuous discussion on cable news, it is intentional. Ever since she secured the Democratic nomination last month, Clinton has been visiting toy producers, touring tie manufacturers, and stopping by public health clinics, where her references to Trump, if any, are typically to highlight the differences in their policies. Her prompt denunciation during a campaign rally on Wednesday of Trump’s assertion that gun rights supporters could hinder her from nominating liberal justices to the U.S. Supreme Court was one of the rare moments she directly confronted her Republican opponent in the upcoming presidential race. According to her aides, Clinton’s approach is straightforward: allow Trump to be himself. In the past fortnight, Trump has encountered a number of blunders that extend beyond his comments regarding gun rights activists, which he later claimed the media had intentionally misconstrued. He has had disputes with party officials, argued with the parents of a deceased Muslim American Army captain, and this week accused Clinton, who previously served as secretary of state, and President Barack Obama of having 'founded' the Islamic State militant organization. On Friday, he stated he was merely being sarcastic with that comment. "There is an adage in politics: Don’t obstruct a train wreck," remarked Democratic strategist Bob Shrum, a senior aide for presidential candidates Al Gore in 2000 and John Kerry in 2004. Clinton's advisors believe there is little advantage in her engaging directly with Trump over every personal insult, which would generate quotes that could dominate cable news narratives. Instead, they are content to let him be embroiled in disputes while Clinton concentrates on policy matters. text: Armyworm invasion affects northern Cameroon, exacerbating food crisis. YAOUNDE (Reuters) - Fall armyworms, which feed on crops, have infested nearly 37,000 hectares of maize in northern Cameroon, officials reported on Wednesday, intensifying an already critical humanitarian situation caused by the cross-border insurgency of the Islamist militant group Boko Haram. Over twenty African nations have documented instances of this invasive pest, which originates from Central America and is more challenging to identify and eliminate than its African variant. The armyworms have now infiltrated all ten administrative regions of Cameroon, although maize crops in the Extreme North region have only faced significant damage since July, as stated by Deputy Agriculture Minister Clementine Ananga Messina to Reuters. The attack on maize threatens the entire sector and poses serious food insecurity risks, given that maize is the most widely cultivated cereal in Cameroon, she noted. The Extreme North region, which borders Chad and Nigeria, has been severely impacted by Boko Haram, whose violent campaigns and cross-border assaults have resulted in over 93,000 Nigerians fleeing to Cameroon, where approximately 235,000 individuals have also been displaced. According to the United Nations, around 1.5 million people in the Lake Chad region are facing a food crisis. Cameroonian officials have initiated an action plan to combat the infestation, but thus far, pesticides have proven ineffective in controlling it. "There are no efficient methods currently available in Cameroon to combat the armyworm," stated Agriculture Ministry specialist Andre Marie Elombat Assoua. "The chemical products currently employed by farmers are not effective and are prohibitively expensive." Approximately 12 million Cameroonians, more than half of the national population, regularly consume maize. It also serves as a key ingredient for the breweries in the central African nation and in the production of livestock feed. While the fall armyworm primarily targets maize, it also attacked sorghum and millet, two other staple crops of Cameroon, earlier this year.

text: (Reuters) - On Wednesday, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton asserted that President Donald Trump acted well within his authority by issuing his executive order concerning immigration, as he presented his arguments to a federal appeals court. Paxton, a member of the Republican Party, submitted a brief to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals located in California, seeking permission to advocate for Trump’s temporary travel ban affecting individuals from seven predominantly Muslim nations. Texas has become the first state to support Trump in this closely monitored legal battle. A coalition of 15 states along with the District of Columbia has filed documents with the appeals court backing Washington state's challenge to Trump’s order dated Jan. 27, arguing that it negatively impacts their educational systems and economies. Paxton urged the full court to reevaluate whether a lower court judge was warranted in blocking the ban. On Feb. 3, U.S. District Judge James Robart in Seattle halted Trump’s order nationwide. Washington state contended that the order infringed upon constitutional protections against religious discrimination. A three-judge panel from the 9th Circuit in San Francisco upheld that ruling last week, bringing up uncertainties regarding Trump’s next course of action. The appeals court is expected to soon deliberate on the possibility of reexamining the case with an 11-judge panel. Trump’s directive, which he claimed was essential for safeguarding the United States from assaults by Islamist militants, prohibited individuals from Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen from entering the nation for a period of 90 days. Refugees faced a 120-day prohibition, with the exception of those from Syria, who were banned indefinitely. These judicial rulings have put the order on hold pending court decisions on the fundamental issues at stake. Ultimately, the courts will need to tackle questions regarding the extent of presidential authority over immigration and national security concerns. Legal analysts have noted that judges have historically been very hesitant to interfere with the executive branch's powers in such matters. In his brief, Paxton stated that the order clearly aimed at national security, ensuring adequate vetting of foreigners seeking entry into the United States. It “reflects national-security interests involved in the ongoing War on Terror against radical Islamic terrorists.” Paxton dismissed any suggestion that the order discriminates against Muslims while preferentially treating Christian minorities. He argued that if such a claim were acknowledged, it would endanger the government’s capability to assist persecuted religious minorities abroad by granting them refugee status. Texas previously led the legal battle against President Barack Obama’s initiative to protect up to four million immigrants from deportation, joined by 25 other states controlled by the Republican Party. The challengers secured a nationwide injunction in February 2015 that blocked the program before it could be implemented. In June 2016, the Supreme Court reached a 4-4 deadlock in the matter, thereby upholding an appeals court decision favoring the states. A significant point of contention in that litigation was whether Texas possessed the legal standing to sue, a question that the Supreme Court did not address. In the brief submitted on Wednesday, Texas did not discuss whether Washington and other states had the standing to contest Trump’s ban.

text: The United States reports that an airstrike has eliminated over 100 militants in Somalia. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. armed forces announced that they killed more than 100 Islamist militants in Somalia on Tuesday during an airstrike targeting al Shabaab, a militant group linked to al Qaeda that seeks to overthrow the U.N.-endorsed government. The U.S. Africa Command stated that the airstrike occurred at a camp located 125 miles (201 km) northwest of Mogadishu, the capital, and affirmed that the U.S. will persist in its operations against militants. According to the Pentagon, this action was coordinated with the federal government of Somalia. While U.S. airstrikes resulting in such a significant number of militant deaths in Somalia are uncommon, they have occurred before. In March 2016, a U.S. airstrike eliminated over 150 al Shabaab fighters in Somalia. Somalia's state news agency SONNA reported late on Tuesday that around 100 militants were killed when U.S. aircraft and Somali commandos assaulted al Shabaab locations in the Bur Elay region of Bay. Abdiasis Abu Musab, a spokesperson for al Shabaab, refuted the claims about the attack, stating, "It is just...propaganda," he told Reuters from Somalia. Al Shabaab seeks to dismantle Somalia's Western-supported transitional federal government and impose its own governance in the Horn of Africa nation. Earlier this month, the U.S. government issued a warning regarding a potential threat to its diplomatic personnel in Mogadishu, advising all non-essential employees to exit the capital. Al Shabaab has lost dominion over the majority of Somalia's urban areas since being expelled from Mogadishu in 2011. However, it continues to maintain a significant presence in certain southern and central regions and executes gun and bomb assaults. The U.S. military statement noted that al Shabaab has explicitly vowed to plan and carry out attacks against the United States and its allies in the area. Al Shabaab's objective is to overthrow Somalia's government, expel African Union peacekeeping forces, and impose its stringent interpretation of Islamic law. Earlier this month, the U.S. military also conducted its initial strikes against Islamic State militants in Somalia, reporting the elimination of several terrorists.

Typically, the Electoral College vote is a straightforward procedure, but this year it gained additional attention after a coalition of Democratic activists sought to convince Republicans to defect and support Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton. At least four Democratic electors cast their votes for individuals other than Clinton, while two Republicans opted not to support Trump. With almost all votes tallied, Trump had achieved 304 electoral votes compared to Clinton's 227, as reported by an Associated Press count of the 538 electors nationwide. "I will work hard to unite our country and be the President of all Americans," Trump remarked in a statement addressing the results. The Electoral College allocates electors to each state equivalent to its number of congressional representatives and senators, with the District of Columbia also receiving three electoral votes. The official counting of these votes will take place during a joint session of Congress on January 6. The most recent occurrence of a "faithless elector" was noted in 2004, according to the Congressional Research Service. Such instances have been quite uncommon in contemporary history, with only eight such electors since 1900, each from different elections. "I stand with my conservative colleagues and Governor McCrory in seeking legislative measures to amend this radical direction," he continued. Civil rights organizations dismissed the public safety worries as exaggerated. They commended the council for enacting what they claimed was the first ordinance in the state that prohibits discrimination against individuals based on sexual orientation or gender identity in public facilities, such as restaurants, hotels, and taxis. text: (Reuters) - On Thursday, former FBI director James Comey disclosed that he had shared a memo detailing his discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump with a “close friend,” instructing him to relay its contents to a journalist. This announcement elicited strong condemnation from Trump’s attorney. During his testimony to the Senate Intelligence Committee, Comey expressed his desire to make his account of conversations with Trump public in hopes of triggering the appointment of a special counsel, which ultimately happened, to oversee the inquiry into Russia's alleged interference in the 2016 presidential election. One of the conversations involved Comey stating that he believed Trump had pressured him in February to halt the investigation into former national security adviser Michael Flynn as part of the wider Russia probe. Following his dismissal as director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation on May 9, Comey stated he asked “a close friend” who is a professor at Columbia Law School to help disseminate his story. Daniel Richman, a criminal law professor at Columbia, confirmed to Reuters that he was the individual mentioned in Comey’s testimony. Richman, identified as an adviser to Comey in his official biography on the university's website, did not respond to additional requests for comments. Throughout his presidency, Trump has expressed outrage towards the media and its reliance on anonymous sources. After Comey’s testimony, Trump’s personal attorney, Marc Kasowitz, harshly criticized Comey for disclosing what he termed “privileged communications” between the president and the former FBI director. Kasowitz attempted to associate Comey with other officials in the government who, he claimed, had selectively and unlawfully leaked classified information to damage the administration, suggesting that Comey may have violated the law. Kasowitz stated that it would fall to the relevant authorities to decide if the leak warranted investigation. Comey was unavailable for immediate comment. Some legal specialists argued that Comey’s actions did not violate any laws. Faiza Patel, co-director of the public policy organization Brennan Center for Justice, remarked that Comey testified to being cautious about not including classified information in the memos documenting his dialogues with Trump. Other experts contended that Kasowitz's assertion that Comey leaked “privileged” information was inaccurate, noting that Trump had previously disclosed details of his conversations with Comey. To share his memo, Comey selected someone who has publicly supported him before, including during the investigation into Hillary Clinton’s emails. Richman, a Yale Law School graduate from 1984, clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall. He served as the chief appellate attorney in the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan from 1987 to 1992, coinciding with Comey’s tenure as a prosecutor there. Richman later joined the faculty at Fordham University School of Law and transitioned to Columbia in 2007. He has also acted as a consultant for the U.S. Justice and Treasury departments on criminal issues and served on advisory boards for former New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg and New York state Governor Eliot Spitzer. Following Comey’s testimony, there was a notable increase in online searches for Richman, which appeared to crash the Columbia Law School’s website. “Columbia Law’s site is currently down. We are addressing the issue. Please stay tuned,” the school announced via a tweet.

text: Turkish officials have requested the detention of 133 individuals employed in the finance and labor ministries, according to the state-operated Anadolu news agency on Thursday. text: China is set to advocate for enhanced global collaboration in combating corruption and terrorism during the Interpol general assembly it will host next week, as reported by diplomatic sources acquainted with the situation, amid worries that China may be leveraging the organization for its own objectives. Last year, the global policing agency appointed Meng Hongwei, a senior Chinese public security official and Vice Public Security Minister, as its president, raising concerns among human rights organizations about whether Beijing might attempt to use this position to target dissidents abroad. For many years, Beijing has sought assistance from foreign nations to apprehend and deport individuals it accuses of crimes such as corruption and terrorism. According to three sources based in Beijing who are knowledgeable about the planning for the Interpol gathering, China is expected to concentrate on these two issues during the assembly. When Beijing requests the return of individuals wanted for alleged offenses in China, it has encountered hesitance, particularly in Western nations. Governments and judicial systems in these countries have expressed concerns that China does not provide evidence that meets the standards of Western courts, and that accused individuals may face mistreatment and lack a fair trial in China due to fears that the allegations could be politically motivated. Western diplomats who are familiar with China's requests note that China sometimes fails to grasp that in Western nations, it must pursue its demands through the legal system. "They’re often quite surprised to learn that we can’t just hand them over," remarked one diplomat, who chose to remain anonymous due to the sensitive nature of the topic. Nevertheless, officials from China's security sector have been striving to understand the legal prerequisites of developed nations and international organizations so that their requests for expedited action become more acceptable. Additionally, diplomats indicate that Beijing has been working to establish intelligence-sharing partnerships with Western nations in the battle against Islamist extremists, as China itself is contending with what it describes as Uighur militants operating in its far western region of Xinjiang. Last week, Li Shulei, who heads China’s initiatives to locate and repatriate individuals suspected of corruption residing abroad, emphasized the need for a reinforced global framework for anti-corruption cooperation. "We must create a new order to combat international corruption... sever escape routes for corrupt individuals," he stated at a meeting in Beijing. China has not provided extensive information regarding the upcoming Interpol general assembly, which will commence in Beijing on Tuesday with an address from Chinese President Xi Jinping. Concerning Meng's role within Interpol, diplomats observe that his position is primarily ceremonial. The Interpol headquarters in Lyon, France, states that its Secretary General, Jürgen Stock, a German citizen, serves as the organization’s full-time chief executive responsible for overseeing day-to-day international police cooperation. In 2014, China issued Interpol red notices for its 100 most-wanted corruption fugitives who have escaped abroad as part of Xi’s extensive anti-corruption campaign. According to the government, nearly half of these individuals have returned to China thus far, with some doing so voluntarily. Interpol clarifies that red notices are requests for the provisional arrest of suspects pending extradition and do not constitute international arrest warrants. It is at the discretion of a member state to act upon an Interpol red notice, which may be disregarded if a government deems the evidence insufficient to warrant action, diplomats report. There are no statistics available on how many red notices go unheeded. Furthermore, red notices are often not made public, and it is up to the issuing country to determine whether they are publicized. Requests are meticulously vetted to ensure they adhere to Interpol’s constitution, which prohibits "any intervention or activities of a political, military, religious or racial character," as stated by Interpol in a message to Reuters.

text: (Reuters) - A task force focusing on Puerto Rico's economic crisis has suggested that the U.S. Congress should rethink the benefits system for disabled individuals on the island, who currently receive minimal government assistance. The report, which was made public on Tuesday, referenced a December 9 Reuters investigation that highlighted the limited support available for residents of Puerto Rico dealing with severe mental and physical disabilities. The majority receive no assistance at all. Those who do receive aid get an average of $74 per month, which is roughly ten percent of the benefits provided to the disabled in the 50 states. The investigation by Reuters also uncovered significant variations in the support available across U.S. territories. For more details, see the Special Report here: reut.rs/2hg0vDR. Senator Orrin Hatch, a Republican from Utah and the leader of the bipartisan Congressional Task Force on Economic Growth in Puerto Rico, did not respond immediately to inquiries for comment on Wednesday. The task force has proposed that Congress consider extending the same Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits to Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories that are granted to the states. Since the SSI program began in the 1970s, four out of five U.S. territories, including Puerto Rico, Guam, American Samoa, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, have been excluded from receiving these benefits. The Northern Mariana Islands, the fifth territory, receives SSI benefits comparable to those of a state, averaging $560 monthly, largely due to its negotiations regarding territory status coinciding with Congress’ establishment of the SSI program. In stark contrast, disabled individuals in Puerto Rico receive significantly lower payments through a largely overlooked program managed by the Administration of Children and Families (ACF), a division of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Almost half of the disabled population in Puerto Rico lives in poverty, which is double the rate compared to those in the 50 states. Disabled residents in Guam receive an average of $164, while those in the Virgin Islands receive $176. American Samoa provides no benefits at all to its disabled individuals. SSI allows disabled residents in U.S. states to receive up to $733 monthly, with an average payout of $540. As an alternative to providing SSI benefits to the territories, the task force recommended that Congress increase funding through ACF. Federal funding for this program has been capped since 1996 and is not adjusted for inflation. The task force also urged ACF to publicly disclose current information regarding the benefits provided to disabled citizens in U.S. territories. When Reuters initially reached out for comments on benefits for the disabled in Puerto Rico, ACF did not make anyone available, citing that “no one is completely versed in all the details,” as stated by spokesman Pat Fisher. On Wednesday, Fisher declined to provide comments regarding the task force’s recommendations. “We cannot offer an opinion on proposed policy,” he stated. “We only carry out approved policy.” A 2014 report by the Government Accountability Office, which serves as Congress's investigative branch, indicated that if Puerto Rico were to receive SSI, the number of eligible individuals would increase significantly from nearly 34,500 in 2011 to 354,000. The annual federal payments to the island could soar from $24 million to as much as $1.8 billion. Additionally, the task force made suggestions aimed at enhancing healthcare in Puerto Rico, labeling it as “a serious and urgent issue.” For many years, the U.S. has provided lower reimbursements to Puerto Rico under federally funded Medicare and Medicaid programs, which cover the majority of island residents. For instance, the Medicaid program for low-income individuals has had its funding capped by federal authorities for decades, leading local officials to heavily rely on borrowing through municipal bonds. This has contributed to what is now recognized as the largest municipal debt crisis in U.S. history. It is estimated that around one-third of Puerto Rico’s $70 billion in outstanding debt originates from bonds issued to support healthcare funding. In October, Reuters reported that many physicians in Puerto Rico are leaving the financially troubled healthcare system in search of better-paying opportunities elsewhere.

text: Indonesian authorities have cautioned Islamist groups against conducting raids in pursuit of Santa hats. JAKARTA (Reuters) - On Thursday, Indonesian police urged for tolerance and respect towards the religious festivities of others after an Islamist organization threatened to inspect businesses for Muslims allegedly compelled to wear Santa Claus hats or other Christmas attire. The hardline Islamic Defenders Front (FPI) announced this week that it would launch extensive operations in the largest Muslim-majority nation in the world, asserting that coercing Muslims to don Christmas clothing infringes on their human rights. Indonesia is home to various religious minorities, such as Christians, Hindus, Buddhists, and adherents of traditional faiths. The constitution guarantees religious freedom in a state that is officially secular, although tensions among followers of different religions can sometimes escalate. "There should be no sweeping operations... members of the public must show respect for other religions celebrating their festivities," stated national police chief Tito Karnavian to police during a security drill in the capital city, Jakarta. The FPI expressed its intention to enforce a fatwa, or decree, issued by Indonesia's Islamic Clerical Council in 2016 that forbids business owners from compelling their employees to wear Christmas apparel. "We will raid businesses in anticipation of them being stubborn about this and we will be accompanied by police," declared Novel Bakmukmin, the head of the FPI's Jakarta chapter. He emphasized that employers who mandate their staff to wear Christmas clothing are infringing on their rights. "Businesses need to understand that there should be no coercion," he remarked. The decrees from the Islamic Clerical Council are not legally enforceable but act as guidelines for Muslims in Indonesia. Christmas is widely observed throughout Indonesia, and holiday decorations are prevalent, especially in shops, restaurants, and malls where many enthusiastic workers - including Muslims - don Santa hats or elf outfits. The FPI earned its reputation by conducting raids on restaurants and bars that served alcohol during the Muslim fasting month of Ramadan. In recent years, the group has shifted its focus to Christian celebrations. Additionally, the organization has called for the Jakarta city government to cease sponsorship of New Year festivities, which draw large crowds. Approximately 90,000 police officers will be deployed nationwide during the year-end holiday period, primarily to prevent militant attacks. Attacks on churches in Jakarta and other locations on Christmas Eve in 2000 resulted in nearly 20 fatalities. Since then, authorities have increased security measures at churches and tourist destinations for the holiday season.

text: U.S. senators have unveiled the final version of a sentencing reform bill. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A modified criminal justice reform proposal progressed closer to a complete vote in the U.S. Senate on Thursday, as it received backing from additional Republicans after being stalled in Congress for several months. In a move significant for President Barack Obama’s legacy, the bill's sponsors held a press conference in the Senate to announce four new Republican co-sponsors and an updated version of the legislation. As it stands, the measure now boasts 37 co-sponsors, as stated by Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Charles Grassley. Grassley indicated he was waiting for the bill to be finalized before requesting Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell to schedule it for a full Senate vote, but remarked that 'it is time for those discussions to start right now.' The revised bill continues to reduce mandatory minimum sentences for certain non-violent federal drug offenders; however, it no longer affects individuals convicted of serious violent felonies. This amendment was made in response to conservative critics of the legislation, which plays a crucial role in Obama's initiative to revamp the federal criminal justice system and alleviate prison overcrowding. This endeavor has been a rare instance of bipartisan agreement amid the divided Congress. Proponents of the bill have expressed hope that the new revisions and additional co-sponsors, including Republican senators Mark Kirk of Illinois and Steve Daines of Montana, will persuade McConnell to bring the bill to a Senate vote. Daines and Kirk provided their support after the inclusion of minor stipulations, such as a clause directing savings from the bill towards initiatives like combating nationally significant gangs. Following a statement made in January by a coalition of conservative Republican senators led by Tom Cotton of Arkansas, which suggested that the reforms would result in the release of violent felons, the authors of the bill began to remove elements that would have eased sentences for violent criminals. The current version of the bill introduces a new mandatory minimum sentence for offenses involving the opioid fentanyl, reflecting similar sentencing reforms awaiting a vote in the U.S. House of Representatives. Senator John Cornyn, a supporter of the Senate bill, mentioned at Thursday’s press conference that the House legislation is expected to include modifications to 'mens rea' laws that pertain to criminal intent. The Senate measure did not incorporate mens rea reform due to a lack of consensus among its authors. Generally, Democratic lawmakers are against enhancing mens rea requirements, arguing that it could facilitate corporate wrongdoing, given the challenges in proving a corporation's 'intent.' To eliminate violent criminals from the Senate bill, the authors removed a provision that would have reduced minimum sentences for unlawful gun owners with three prior convictions for violent felonies or serious drug offenses, referred to as 'armed career criminals.' Such offenders make up nearly one-fifth of the 12,908 current inmates who would have qualified for resentencing under the previous version of the bill, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission.

text: Venezuela's governors take their oaths, highlighting division within the opposition. CARACAS (Reuters) - In a further blow to the demoralized opposition in Venezuela, four out of five state governors broke away from their coalition's official position on Monday by taking their oaths before a pro-government legislative superbody. The Democratic Unity coalition entered the gubernatorial elections on October 15 as frontrunners, anticipating a significant victory over candidates backed by President Nicolas Maduro, fueled by public frustration over a severe economic crisis in the OPEC nation. However, they managed to secure only five out of 23 states. Initially claiming electoral fraud, the opposition later admitted that a lack of participation among their supporters significantly contributed to their defeat, casting doubt on their chances of defeating the ruling socialists in the upcoming presidential election next year. After the regional elections, the coalition declared that none of its victorious candidates would 'kneel' before the pro-Maduro Constituent Assembly, which they have refused to acknowledge since its formation following an election in July. Nevertheless, the newly elected governors of Tachira, Merida, Nuevo Esparta, and Anzoategui - all representatives of the Democratic Action party, one of the oldest and largest in Venezuela - took their oaths before the assembly officials as a requirement for assuming their roles. During the ceremony, Delcy Rodriguez, the head of the Constituent Assembly, reprimanded the lone opposition winner, Juan Pablo Guanipa from oil-rich Zulia state, who resisted. 'These actions will have consequences,' she warned. Maduro had previously cautioned that new elections could be held in any state where the victor fails to pledge loyalty to the assembly. Guanipa, affiliated with the Justice First party, known for its strong stance against Maduro, stated he would not legitimize the 'fraudulent' Constituent Assembly, whose election the opposition had boycotted. 'Zulia will never kneel before the dictatorship,' he remarked. Detractors view the establishment of the Constituent Assembly, which has overridden all authorities including the opposition-controlled congress, as solidifying dictatorship in Venezuela. Major Western and Latin American countries have declined to recognize its legitimacy. Conversely, Maduro argued that it was the only means to restore peace after four months of opposition demonstrations earlier this year, which resulted in 125 fatalities, numerous arrests and injuries, and extensive property and infrastructure damage. Appearing on state television late Monday, Maduro mentioned that he had congratulated the four Democratic Action governors via phone and would potentially meet with them as early as Tuesday. 'I told them: Let’s turn the page... and get to work,' he stated. Democratic Action is one of the largest parties within the opposition coalition, and its actions on Monday angered many opposition supporters who perceived it as a betrayal. This shift could indicate a complete restructuring or possible dissolution of the coalition, which comprises over two dozen parties and has long struggled with internal conflicts. 'We are going to see a new unity. In the most challenging crises and situations, opportunities always arise,' wrote opposition leader Henrique Capriles of the Justice First party, suggesting imminent changes. The coalition's most significant achievement was a decisive victory in the legislative elections of December 2015. However, it has been struggling since Maduro endured this year's protests, and many Venezuelans regard its leaders as elitist. To further weaken his adversaries, Maduro appointed five senior officials as 'protectors' for the states won by the opposition, diminishing their influence locally by providing new funding and parallel responsibilities to government figures in those areas.

text: A recent poll has revealed that nearly two-thirds of Germans perceive ongoing divisions between the former communist East and West, nearly three decades after the reunification of Germany. This finding, published in Bild newspaper on Monday, indicates that 64.6 percent of respondents recognized these divisions, whereas only 22.9 percent believed they had been resolved. The survey, conducted by the polling organization INSA, was released a day prior to Germany's reunification holiday, highlighting that 74 percent of individuals from the former East recognized this 'invisible barrier', in contrast to just 62.3 percent of those from the former West Germany. The persistent divisions were underscored during the national election on September 24, where mainstream parties faced their most significant setbacks since World War II, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secured 12.6 percent of the vote, marking its inaugural entry into parliament. Support for the AfD and its 'take your country back' agenda was notably strong in eastern Germany, stemming from frustrations over Chancellor Angela Merkel's 2015 decision to allow in a million predominantly Muslim migrants. Malu Dreyer, the Social Democratic premier of Rhineland-Palatinate in the west, described the election outcomes as a 'wake-up call' for major political parties regarding the ongoing, unaddressed issues of eastern Germans. 'We failed to recognize the extent of the pressure for transformation felt by east Germans and the challenges they faced in making reunification a tangible reality,' she stated in an interview with broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk on Monday. According to Iris Gleicke, the German government’s commissioner for eastern German affairs, while unemployment has decreased and average income has significantly risen in the region since reunification, the issue of population decline persists. Gleicke pointed out that glamorization and demographic shifts have intensified regional disparities, with the per capita gross domestic product trailing that of the west by 27 percent and industrial productivity lagging by 20 percent. She emphasized the need for enhanced efforts to guarantee essential services in the east and to prevent the rise of far-right extremism. 'Where government is absent, voids are inevitably filled by those with ill intentions,' she remarked. In a separate announcement, Research Minister Johanna Wanka unveiled a new initiative on Monday aimed at investigating how many former Nazis were allowed to continue their roles in East Germany's educational and research institutions following World War II.

On Friday, they presented their case to the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) in Bloemfontein, South Africa. Pistorius was sentenced to prison in July of the previous year after being found guilty on appeal of the murder of his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp, which occurred on Valentine’s Day in 2013. Women’s rights organizations in a nation struggling with high rates of violent crime against women claim that Pistorius has been afforded preferential treatment in comparison to non-white individuals and those lacking his financial means or global fame. Leading the prosecution, advocate Andrea Johnson argued that Masipa's sentence was excessively lenient, as it was less than half of the mandatory 15-year minimum sentence for murder in South Africa. Johnson pointed out that the High Court failed to outline the significant and compelling reasons for departing from the 15-year sentence and remarked that Pistorius had not demonstrated remorse for the murder. "There is no true, gut-wrenching remorse," Johnson stated. "It is shockingly lenient and has therefore resulted in an injustice," she added, referring to the sentence.
