text: BRASILIA (Reuters) - On Thursday, Brazil's Finance Minister Henrique Meirelles is set to engage with major credit rating agencies as the government works to prevent a downgrade of its sovereign debt, amid increasing skepticism about whether its proposed pension reform can control the escalating public debt. The vote on the contentious bill aimed at overhauling the social security system, deemed crucial for addressing the fiscal deficit, has been postponed until 2018 after failing to garner sufficient support in Congress. Legislators have cautioned that addressing this sensitive topic prior to the elections next year could diminish the likelihood of its passage. In a radio interview, Meirelles stated that he would inform the rating agencies that the postponement until February does not imply that pension reform will not be enacted. He mentioned to Radio Estad o that it would be "reasonable" for the agencies to hold off on a downgrade decision until after the bill is voted on. Lower house Speaker Rodrigo Maia indicated on Monday that it would be challenging to secure approval for pension reform if the bill is not passed by February. The initial vote was delayed last week and is now slated for February 19, following the Christmas-to-Carnival holiday break. At a news conference, Maia noted that there is potential to negotiate a longer transition period for public sector workers, including those who began their employment before 2003. Although this could increase future pension expenditures, Maia asserted that the government would not concede any further fiscal savings. The latest draft of the bill is projected to save 480 billion reais ($146 billion) over the next decade, as per government estimates, a reduction from the original proposal’s 800 billion reais, following compromises made to facilitate its passage. Brazil's overextended pension system, particularly generous to public sector employees, is the primary driver of a substantial budget deficit that resulted in Latin America's largest country losing its coveted investment-grade credit rating two years ago. The finance ministry announced that Meirelles will conduct conference calls with representatives from rating agencies on Thursday. Investors are concerned that a failure to reform social security could hinder Brazil's recovery from a severe economic recession, potentially compelling the central bank to increase interest rates from their record low, which might lead to further sovereign rating downgrades in 2018. Last week, Moody’s Investors Service characterized the delay in voting on the pension bill as "credit negative." This raises the likelihood that the reform may not be approved next year, given the political uncertainty surrounding the upcoming presidential elections, Moody's noted in a communication to clients.

text: Trump University has requested a postponement of a trial until after the inauguration. CHICAGO (Reuters) - Donald Trump, the U.S. President-elect, has sought to delay a trial regarding a lawsuit filed by former students of his now-defunct Trump University until after the presidential inauguration, as stated in a motion submitted by his attorney late on Saturday. A federal court trial in San Diego addressing the claims of former Trump University students, who allege they were defrauded through a series of real estate seminars, is set to commence on November 28. However, Trump’s attorney, Daniel Petrocelli, indicated that the president-elect must focus entirely on the transition process. Trump is scheduled to take office on January 20, 2017. "The 69 days leading up to the inauguration are vital and all-consuming," Petrocelli mentioned in the motion, arguing that the president-elect should not be obligated to participate in a trial during this period. At a hearing in San Diego on Thursday, Petrocelli had noted his intention to request the delay, although U.S. District Judge Gonzalo Curiel, who is presiding over the lawsuit, indicated that he was not inclined to further postpone the six-year-old case and urged the parties to reach a settlement. The lawsuit concerns students asserting they were enticed by false promises to pay as much as $35,000 to learn Trump’s real estate investing "secrets" from instructors he had "hand-picked." According to the students’ court filings, Trump possessed 92 percent ownership of Trump University and had authority over all significant decisions. The president-elect refutes these allegations and contends that he depended on others to run the business. Additionally, Curiel last week tentatively dismissed a request from the president-elect to exclude a broad array of statements made during the presidential campaign, which included criticisms directed at Curiel himself, from the fraud trial. Trump has criticized the judge as being biased against him, claiming that Curiel, who was born in Indiana but has Mexican heritage, could not be impartial due to Trump’s campaign promise to construct a wall between the United States and Mexico. Trump’s legal team has asserted that Curiel should prohibit references in the trial to Trump’s personal behavior, which includes alleged sexual misconduct, his taxes, and corporate bankruptcies, as well as his speeches and tweets. Curiel is overseeing two cases involving Trump and the university, with a separate lawsuit from New York’s attorney general still pending. While presidents enjoy immunity from lawsuits connected to their official duties, the U.S. Supreme Court has determined that this protection does not extend to actions allegedly occurring prior to taking office.

text: Trump mulls over a strategy to replace Tillerson with the CIA director: U.S. officials. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is weighing a plan to dismiss Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, whose rapport with the president has been strained due to the U.S. diplomat’s more lenient stance on North Korea, along with other disagreements, senior officials in the administration stated on Thursday. Under a proposal from the White House, Tillerson could be succeeded within weeks by CIA Director Mike Pompeo, a loyalist to Trump and a hardliner on foreign policy, marking the most significant personnel shake-up to date in the Trump administration. Republican Senator Tom Cotton, known as one of Trump’s strongest allies in Congress, is expected to be appointed to replace Pompeo at the Central Intelligence Agency, as per the officials who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity. It remains unclear if Trump has given his final approval to the reshuffle, but one official indicated that the president requested the plan be prepared. Tillerson’s anticipated exit would conclude a tumultuous tenure for the former Exxon Mobil Corp chief executive, who has found himself increasingly at odds with Trump on matters like North Korea and has faced criticism for proposed budget cuts at the State Department. In October, reports emerged that Tillerson had privately labeled Trump a “moron,” a characterization the secretary of state attempted to downplay. This came after Trump tweeted that Tillerson should not waste his time attempting to negotiate with North Korea regarding its nuclear and missile activities, which many interpreted as a sign of Tillerson's diminishing influence. Trump’s dissatisfaction with Tillerson has largely stemmed from the “moron” incident, his less confrontational stance on North Korea, and disagreements over the crisis involving Qatar, according to one senior U.S. official. Additionally, his slow pace in filling diplomatic vacancies at the State Department has contributed to the situation, another official noted. Trump tasked John Kelly, the White House chief of staff, with formulating the transition plan, which has been discussed with other officials, as indicated by one administration source. This plan, which has been in development for several weeks and was initially reported by the New York Times, is expected to be implemented around the end of the year or shortly thereafter, according to the official. When asked if he wished for Tillerson to stay in his position, Trump avoided a direct response, telling reporters at the White House: “He’s here. Rex is here.” State Department spokesperson Heather Nauert mentioned that Kelly informed Tillerson’s chief of staff on Thursday that the reports regarding Tillerson's replacement were inaccurate. Nauert also stated that Tillerson “serves at the president’s pleasure.” In response to inquiries about Tillerson, White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders affirmed that the secretary of state continues to hold his position. “When the president loses confidence in someone, they will no longer serve here,” she remarked. Pompeo, a former congressman, has risen to prominence as he has earned Trump’s confidence on national security issues. Tillerson, 65, has spent a significant portion of his time in office attempting to smooth the rough edges of Trump’s unilateralist “America First” foreign policy, with limited success. On multiple occasions, the president has publicly undermined his diplomatic efforts. A source familiar with Tillerson’s perspective revealed that the secretary of state’s initial intention upon taking the position was to resign in February. If enacted, the personnel changes would add to a series of firings or resignations within the Trump administration, which have already included the departures of the chief of staff, the national security adviser, and the FBI director. Pompeo, 53, has taken a hardline stance on foreign policy, particularly concerning Iran, and has spoken about making his agency more aggressive while focusing on deploying additional CIA operatives abroad. He has consistently praised Trump, despite the president’s criticisms of U.S. intelligence agencies, some of which determined that Russia engaged in an influence campaign aimed at supporting Trump during the 2016 presidential election. Tillerson has sometimes expressed his frustrations.

NEW YORK (Reuters) - Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton continues to hold a substantial advantage in her pursuit of the Electoral College and the U.S. presidency, as indicated by the most recent findings from the Reuters/Ipsos States of the Nation project released on Saturday. Over the past week, there has been minimal change. Clinton is ahead of Donald Trump in the majority of states that Trump would require to have any possibility of achieving the essential 270 votes for victory. The most probable result would show Clinton with 326 votes compared to 212 for Trump. Trump concluded his best debate performance of the campaign on Wednesday evening, yet the consensus from polling still indicated Clinton prevailing in the third and final televised debate. Trump contests these results. Additionally, while some national polls indicated a slight tightening of the race this week, others showed Clinton retaining her strong lead. Nonetheless, the project demonstrates that the overall situation remains grim for Trump with just 17 days remaining until the election on November 8. Trump did make gains in South Carolina, where his narrow lead from last week grew to seven points, solidifying it as his state from a toss-up. Unfortunately for him, he lost support in Arizona, which is now deemed too close to call. Furthermore, he faces competition for Utah’s six Electoral College votes from former CIA agent and Utah resident Evan McMullin. The independent candidate is drawing votes away from Trump in a state that is among the most Republican in the country. In certain polls, McMullin is even in the lead. text: The Muslim families of deceased U.S. servicemen are compelled to stand against Trump. NEW YORK (Reuters) - For over thirty years, Nazar Naqvi has consistently cast his vote for the Republican Party. However, following Donald Trump’s altercation with Muslim parents who lost their son in combat for the nation, he has pledged that no Republican will receive his support. Naqvi, 69, a retired engineer from the U.S. government residing in Newburgh, New York, belongs to a small group of Muslims who are considered Gold Star families in America, having lost loved ones in military service. His son, Mohsin Naqvi, originally from Pakistan, enlisted in the U.S. Army just four days after the events of September 11, 2001, and tragically lost his life in 2008 due to a roadside explosion in Afghanistan. Trump criticized Khizr and Ghazala Khan, the Pakistani American parents of the fallen U.S. Army Captain Humayun Khan, after they appeared at the Democratic convention in Philadelphia last week to express their discontent with the Republican presidential candidate's proposal for a temporary ban on Muslim immigration. "I’m going to vote for anyone but Republicans because of this one person, this man who has gone out of his mind," Naqvi stated this week. "No office should receive our vote. He has not been nominated by a single individual - the Republican Party put him forward." Naqvi mentioned that he is urging his fellow registered Republicans to follow suit. The Pentagon reports that 3,939 active duty service members identify as Muslim, which is less than 1 percent of the total 1.3 million active duty U.S. military personnel, but a Pentagon representative indicated that there is no record of the number of Muslims who have died in action. Reuters contacted a dozen Muslim Gold Star families who have lost someone in action since September 11, 2001. These families are not organized collectively, and some chose not to engage in conversation. However, those who did share their views concurred that Trump’s remarks disrupted their political allegiance and inspired them to take steps to register and mobilize other voters to ensure Trump does not occupy the White House in November. Nooshin Razani, 43, an Iranian-American pediatrician based in Oakland, California, whose 19-year-old brother Omead Razani was killed while serving as a U.S. Army medic in Iraq in 2004, revealed that Trump’s comments motivated her to speak to the media for the first time. "When I observed that there was an individual willing to misuse religion in such a negative manner, I chose to step forward," Razani explained. Trump criticized Khizr Khan for implying that he should read the U.S. Constitution and suggested that his wife Ghazala may have remained silent beside her husband because she might not have been "allowed" to speak. Although Trump referred to their son as a hero and expressed his intention to eliminate radical Islamic terrorism, the following backlash has led many Republicans to distance themselves from him and express support for the Khan family. Razani joined over 20 Gold Star families in signing an open letter demanding Trump apologize to the Khans and announced her intention to volunteer for voter registration, primarily due to Trump’s remarks about Ghazala Khan, which she described as an insult to all Muslim women. "I want to actively contribute to ensuring that people’s voices are heard. Even those whom Trump believes are voiceless," Razani stated. Trump’s ongoing conflict with the Khans has prompted Kevin Ahearn from Phoenix to take political action. text: Trump's challenge: slower job creation or increasing rates and inflation?. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The recent drop in the U.S. unemployment rate to its lowest level in nine years indicates a potential clash between President-elect Donald Trump’s intentions to stimulate the economy and the Federal Reserve’s attempts to slow down growth through higher interest rates. Following Trump’s election, officials at the U.S. central bank have tentatively suggested that his proposed spending and tax reductions could lead to a quicker implementation of rate hikes than the two increases currently anticipated for 2017. An increase is already on the horizon when the Fed convenes in two weeks. New economic forecasts, the first since the election, will also be released, and Fed Chair Janet Yellen will hold a press conference following the meeting on December 14. With the drop in November, the unemployment rate now stands below the most optimistic estimates from Fed officials regarding its year-end position. Should it continue to decline, Trump’s spending and tax cut strategies may be fueling an already full tank. Potential new restrictions on trade or immigration could tighten markets further, shifting the Fed's focus from concerns about deflation to combating rising prices before they spiral out of control. “There is much more than the Trump election driving the ... rally that started the day after the election,” stated Scott Anderson, chief economist at Bank of the West. “We are witnessing indications of a synchronized upswing in the global economy.” When Fed officials released their previous projections in September, the lowest forecast for the unemployment rate by year’s end was 4.7 percent. In November, this figure decreased by three-tenths of a percentage point to 4.6 percent. This decline was partially attributed to a decrease in the labor force participation rate, which officials have anticipated would begin to drop again due to an aging demographic with more retirees. Generally, a lower unemployment rate allows for a slower rate of job growth that the economy can sustain without causing wages and prices to rise too rapidly. Policymakers maintain that they still have the opportunity to raise rates to keep inflationary pressures in check. Several officials believe it might even assist in repairing some of the damage caused by the 2007-2009 recession if inflation temporarily exceeds the Fed’s 2 percent target. This could, for instance, enable stable wage increases to recover some of the losses experienced by workers. However, in recent months, even typically dovish officials, such as Boston Fed President Eric Rosengren, have warned that consistent rate increases might be necessary to avert the need for more aggressive hikes that could lead to a recession. “I view a small step up in interest rates as appropriate, not because I want to curtail the expansion, but because I believe it will help prolong the expansion,” Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank President Loretta Mester remarked on Wednesday. Trump’s victory amplifies the urgency of that discussion. His proposals for a substantial infrastructure spending initiative, tax reductions, and stricter immigration controls may test the boundaries of what the economy can handle before overheating. For the past year, Fed officials have indicated they expect job growth to decelerate as the economy approaches full employment. This has not yet occurred, suggesting that Trump will assume office at a potentially critical juncture: either job creation will slow down or inflation will rise sharply. Jed Kolko, chief economist at the Indeed job site, noted that the current rate of job growth and low unemployment rate “sets a baseline for the Trump administration.” “Recent wage increases and declines in unemployment create a challenging economic environment to improve upon,” he added.

text: Prominent U.S. legislators advocate for enforcement rather than abandonment of the Iran agreement. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Republican head of the U.S. House of Representatives Foreign Affairs committee stated on Wednesday that the international nuclear accord with Iran should be rigorously enforced by the U.S. in collaboration with its allies, without suggesting a termination of the pact. "Despite the deal's flaws, I believe we must enforce it to the fullest extent," Representative Ed Royce remarked during a hearing. U.S. President Donald Trump is anticipated to unveil a new approach regarding Iran on Friday, which may represent a preliminary move toward the U.S. withdrawing from the agreement. Royce, akin to all other Republicans in the U.S. Congress, opposed the nuclear accord established during President Barack Obama's administration, a Democrat, in 2015 and ratified by the United States, Iran, China, Russia, Britain, France, Germany, and the European Union. A number of Obama's fellow Democrats also expressed their opposition to the agreement, including Representative Eliot Engel, the leading Democrat on the foreign affairs committee. Engel remarked during the hearing that terminating the agreement would be a "serious error," as it is currently in effect and supported by U.S. allies and other nations. "We must collaborate with allies and partners on a common agenda that holds the Iranian regime responsible, rather than creating divisions between America and our closest allies worldwide," he stated. Trump is expected to reveal a "comprehensive Iran strategy," which may include a decision on whether to decertify the international agreement that limits Tehran's nuclear activities ahead of the October 15 deadline. The deal, under which Iran consented to suspend its nuclear activities for 15 years in return for easing sanctions, is regarded in Europe as a significant achievement of international diplomacy in the Middle East. Should Trump choose not to certify the Iran deal, it would initiate a 60-day period during which U.S. congressional leaders could swiftly move to reinstate sanctions on Tehran that were lifted under the agreement. This could serve as an initial step toward the U.S. withdrawing from the accord, a move that European allies strongly oppose. However, if Congress takes no action, the agreement would remain intact. Numerous congressional sources and those informed about the situation suggest that the Trump administration is contemplating utilizing decertification to amplify pressure on Tehran, rather than to terminate the deal. Iranian officials have stated that they will not enter into renegotiations.

text: Two women have pleaded not guilty to the murder of the estranged half-brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. KUALA LUMPUR (Reuters) - In a prominent murder trial that commenced in a Malaysian court on Monday, the two women are accused of killing Kim Jong Nam using a prohibited nerve agent. Siti Aisyah, 25, an Indonesian, and Doan Thi Huong, 28, a Vietnamese national, are charged with the murder that occurred at Kuala Lumpur airport on February 13, where they allegedly applied VX, a chemical poison banned by the United Nations, to his face. Both individuals were escorted into the courtroom on the outskirts of Malaysia's capital while wearing bullet-proof vests and could face the death penalty if found guilty. Authorities have also identified four North Koreans as suspects in the case, and an Interpol red notice, which serves as an international alert pending an arrest warrant, has been issued for these North Koreans, who remain unapprehended. The defense attorneys called on the prosecution to promptly disclose the identities of the four other suspects who have also been charged to facilitate their case preparation. "The charge must be clear," stated Siti Aisyah's attorney, Gooi Soon Seng. However, Judge Azmi Ariffin rejected their request. When the charges were read aloud by two interpreters, both women nodded and entered their pleas of not guilty. The prosecution argued that the actions of the women indicated a deliberate intent to kill the victim by applying the VX nerve agent to his face and eyes, a fact confirmed by a Malaysian autopsy. The women informed their legal representatives that they were unaware they were partaking in a lethal assault and believed they were merely engaging in a prank for a reality television program. Lead prosecutor Muhamad Iskandar Ahmad mentioned in his opening remarks that the prank conducted by the two accused, under the guidance of the four still at large, was a means to realize their shared goal of murdering the victim. The two women remained silent in the crowded courtroom. Siti was attired in a black floral outfit, while Huong wore a white long-sleeved shirt paired with jeans. Juliana Idris, an airport employee, testified in court that a man later recognized as Kim Jong Nam approached her and requested assistance to a police station. She recounted that the man, who communicated in English, stated that he had been "attacked from behind by a woman... another one closed his eyes." He was trembling slightly, the reason for which she could not ascertain. Police Lance Corporal Mohd Zulkarnain Sanudin, who was on duty at the airport, reported that Juliana had escorted Kim Jong Nam to him. Kim informed him that a substance had been applied to his face. Zulkarnain noted that Kim's eyes were red and he observed some liquid on his face. He also admitted to mistakenly documenting Kim Jong Nam’s nationality as South Korean. "The police report I made indicated South Korean nationality, while the passport stated DPR Korea, and I was not aware of what DPR meant. I only knew for certain that Korea referred to South Korea," he explained to the court. DPRK stands for North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Additional witnesses recounted that Kim Jong Nam experienced seizures at the clinic, with his eyes rolling back and saliva and mucus drooling. Medical assistant Rabiatul Adawiyah Mohd Sofi stated that Kim Jong Nam spent just over an hour at the clinic before being transferred to a hospital. By the time they arrived at the hospital's emergency department, they were unable to obtain a blood pressure reading, she said. "There was a high likelihood that either our monitor was malfunctioning or the patient had already passed away," Rabiatul remarked. The proceedings will continue on Tuesday.

text: Republican senator: Obama administration possesses funds for Zika. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A Republican Senate leader stated on Tuesday that the Obama administration does not currently require additional funding to address the Zika virus, as there are still unspent funds from the two-year Ebola outbreak response. As Zika continues to spread throughout South and Central America and the Caribbean, raising concerns about potential birth defects, lawmakers are discussing what resources are necessary. While Democrats have aligned with the administration in requesting over $1.8 billion in emergency funding, Republicans argue that immediate action is unnecessary and plan to conduct hearings on Capitol Hill, including a session with U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Sylvia Burwell on Tuesday. "We all agree this needs to be addressed," commented Senator Roy Blunt of Missouri, who is set to lead a hearing on Zika scheduled for Thursday. "There’s still funding available that was allocated for Ebola," Blunt informed reporters. "Therefore, there is no urgent financial shortage for the administration to undertake what they believe is necessary." He noted that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health have received extra funding. Most of the financial resources that Obama is requesting would be utilized within the United States for testing, surveillance, and response initiatives. A Republican aide indicated that as of December 31, 2015, the government had $1.49 billion remaining in Ebola funds. The Ebola outbreak commenced in West Africa in December 2013. According to the aide, the CDC received a funding increase of $272 million for 2016. Representatives from the Department of Health and Human Services were not immediately available for comments. Democrats dismissed the Republican plan for hearings and urged action on Obama’s proposal. "All the rhetoric in the world isn’t going to shield America from the Zika virus," stated Senator Charles Schumer of New York, the Senate’s No. 3 Democrat. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak an international health emergency on February 1, citing a “strongly suspected” link between Zika infection during pregnancy and microcephaly, a condition characterized by an abnormally small head size that can lead to developmental issues. Brazil is currently investigating over 4,000 suspected microcephaly cases and has found evidence of Zika infection in 17 of these instances. However, much remains uncertain regarding Zika.

text: Czechs cast their votes for a new parliament, with affluent entrepreneur Andrej Babis anticipated to be the next prime minister. PRAGUE (Reuters) - On Friday, Czechs participated in an election that is likely to grant authority to businessman Andrej Babis, who has garnered popular backing by vowing to dismantle traditional political parties, increase investment, and prevent the influx of refugees, despite being under investigation for alleged fraud. The central European nation has seen swift economic advancement, a balanced budget, and holds the lowest unemployment rate in the European Union, yet polls indicate significant voter backing for Babis's ANO party and other protest movements. (Graphic: Czech legislative election - tmsnrt.rs/2vO4hPW) Established and firmly regulated by the 63-year-old billionaire, ANO - translating to 'yes' in Czech - has gained support from both the right and left through its commitments to lower taxes, oust corrupt officials, and introduce business-like efficiency into governance. "We aim to establish a government that demonstrates to people that governance can operate differently than what they are accustomed to. We would connect with them (more)," Babis stated after casting his vote in the Prague suburb where he resides. Babis's backing has endured despite scrutiny over tax practices connected to his $4 billion empire, which encompasses food, chemicals, agriculture, and media, that he transferred to a trust fund earlier this year. Additionally, he has been accused by law enforcement of fraud for allegedly concealing ownership of a farm and a conference center to secure a €2 million subsidy in 2008. He refutes any allegations of misconduct. ANO has preserved its opposition rhetoric against the governing system, even while serving as a junior partner in the outgoing administration alongside Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka’s center-left Social Democrats and the centrist Christian Democrats. Final polls conducted before the polling blackout on Tuesday indicated that ANO had approximately 25-27 percent support, at least double that of the Social Democrats. "Previous administrations continually proclaimed the need for change but took no action," remarked Jarmila, a 66-year-old retired teacher in Prague, who chose not to disclose her last name. "He is logical and can articulate his thoughts clearly." Czech elections are conducted over two days, commencing on Friday at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) and concluding at 2 p.m. on Saturday. Although immigration to the Czech Republic is nearly nonexistent, anxiety surrounding it has significantly influenced the election campaign, with the majority of parties committing to resist any European Union efforts to compel Czechs to accept refugees distributed throughout the union. The anti-immigrant sentiment reflects similar trends in neighboring nations. Parties against immigration performed well in Germany's elections in September and in Austria's elections last week, and have fostered skepticism toward the EU across the 28-nation alliance. Babis's critiques of Brussels have sparked worries that he could steer the country toward a more confrontational stance with the EU, following in the footsteps of right-wing administrations in Poland and Hungary. Babis is against further EU integration and the adoption of the euro but has acknowledged the advantages of EU membership and asserts that the Czech Republic should take a more active role in reforming the union. Analysts suggest that the election might result in a coalition akin to the outgoing government but led by ANO, which would not signify a substantial shift in foreign policy. An agreement with ANO's current allies, or with center-right parties, could face hurdles due to their insistence that Babis personally remain out of the cabinet because of the police allegations. Several voters in Prague expressed skepticism towards Babis, who has been contending with accusations of collaboration with the secret police during the communist era. "For me, this election is centered on our position regarding the European Union, refugees, and primarily represents (an opportunity to vote) against Mr. Babis," stated Gabriela Kijova, 23, after voting for the small Pirate Party in central Prague. President Milos Zeman announced on Friday that he would request the leader of the largest party to initiate discussions on forming a new government. He mentioned that he would allow a month for negotiations prior to convening a session of the new parliament.

text: Trump's travel ban appears to be on firmer ground as the Supreme Court cancels its hearing. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Monday, the Supreme Court indicated it might dismiss a challenge against President Donald Trump’s contentious travel ban following the White House’s announcement of specific restrictions on eight nations that legal analysts believe are more likely to withstand judicial scrutiny. The high court has called off oral arguments that were set for October 10 to evaluate whether a March 6 executive order that temporarily barred travel from six predominantly Muslim countries was discriminatory. That ban concluded on Sunday. The president has issued a new proclamation that indefinitely prohibits travel from Iran, Libya, Syria, Yemen, Somalia, Chad, and North Korea. Additionally, some government officials from Venezuela will also face travel restrictions. This new ban, which is Trump’s third iteration, could impact tens of thousands of potential immigrants and visitors. Throughout much of the year, Trump has sought to establish a ban that would be legally sustainable. Scholars and other experts noted that the proclamation made on Sunday, which Trump stated is necessary to filter out threats to public safety or terrorism, might be less susceptible to legal challenges because it stems from a months-long evaluation of foreign vetting processes by U.S. officials. Furthermore, it could be more difficult to connect it to Trump’s campaign rhetoric that some courts perceived as prejudiced against Muslims. "The greater the impression that the policy is based on expert judgment and thoughtful consideration, the less likely courts are to second-guess the executive," remarked Saikrishna Prakash, a law professor at the University of Virginia, in an email. "It appears less to be an issue of bias or an attempt to fulfill a campaign pledge." "It has not yet demonstrated to be a capable threat against us right now ... we are still conducting the forensic analysis," Mattis informed reporters at the Pentagon. text: U.S. and Russia engage in extradition conflict over bitcoin fraud suspect in Greece. ATHENS (Reuters) - On Wednesday, a Greek court approved the extradition of a Russian national to Moscow, who is also at risk of being sent to the United States due to accusations of laundering billions in bitcoin. Alexander Vinnik, alleged to be the architect behind a $4 billion bitcoin laundering operation, is among seven Russians apprehended or charged globally this year under U.S. cybercrime legislation. Last week, judges determined that he should be extradited to the United States, a ruling that Russia condemned as unfair and unlawful, and which Vinnik is contesting at Greece’s highest court. If that court decides to maintain the extradition order to the United States, the ultimate decision will rest with Greece’s justice minister, who has the authority to approve extradition to one nation while denying it to another. Vinnik refutes all allegations against him. However, he has consented to be sent back to Russia where he will face lesser fraud charges. "That is his desire - to be extradited to Russia and to present his testimony before the Russian judicial system," stated Alexandros Lykourezos, the attorney representing Vinnik, to the media following the decision in Thessaloniki. In the United States, where he could face a maximum sentence of 55 years, Vinnik is charged with operating BTC-e, a digital currency exchange utilized for bitcoin transactions, to aid in various crimes ranging from computer hacking to drug trafficking since 2011. He has asserted to Greek judges that he served as a technical consultant for BTC-e but was not its operator. Vinnik was detained while vacationing in a coastal village in Greece in July. Subsequently, Russia sought his extradition, as it has done with other citizens pursued by the United States. The hearing at the supreme court is anticipated to occur within the next three weeks, according to Lykourezos.

text: The chief of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Scott Pruitt, will be subject to an investigation regarding his frequent trips to Oklahoma, as announced by the agency's Office of Inspector General on Monday, following requests from Congress. "Administrator Pruitt is traveling across the nation to engage directly with individuals affected by the EPA's regulations outside of the Washington bubble," stated Amy Graham, a spokesperson for the EPA. The records revealed that Pruitt personally funded some segments of the trips that were directly related to his visits home, although it was unclear if he covered all such segments. Pruitt has angered environmental advocates by expressing skepticism about climate change and committing to eliminate numerous regulations established during the Obama administration to benefit businesses. text: Trump's anticipated vice-presidential selection: a pro-coal advocate who opposed Obama's climate policies. WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - The announcement of Indiana Governor Mike Pence as Republican Donald Trump’s running mate was met with enthusiasm from the U.S. energy sector, while environmental advocates expressed disappointment, with both camps referencing Pence’s backing of coal mining and his resistance to President Barack Obama’s climate-change initiatives. As the leading Republican presidential candidate, Trump has labeled climate change a fabrication and vowed to dismantle U.S. environmental regulations to support the struggling oil and coal industries. A Trump-Pence partnership indicates that the New York businessman is unlikely to soften his position as the Nov. 8 election approaches. "Governor Pence has been a strong critic of the administration's Clean Power Plan," stated Laura Sheehan, spokesperson for the Washington-based lobbying organization American Council on Clean Coal Electricity. "We hope to see a continuation," she added. Trump revealed Pence as his running mate in a Twitter update on Friday morning, putting an end to days of speculation regarding his choice before the party’s national convention in Cleveland next week. Pence, 57, appears on Obama’s “call out the climate change deniers” website for claiming that the science surrounding climate change is not yet settled. In June 2015, Pence contacted Obama to inform him that Indiana, the eighth largest coal-producing state in the U.S., would not adhere to the Clean Power Plan aimed at regulating emissions from power plants, labeling it “ill-advised.” Indiana is among over 25 states that have contested the central element of the Democratic president’s environmental strategy. In 2014, Pence caused concern among local environmental organizations by repealing an energy efficiency initiative established by his Republican predecessor, Mitch Daniels, stating it was too costly for manufacturers in the state. The Indiana Public Utility Commission had projected that the initiative would generate over 18,600 jobs. "The selection of Pence indicates that Trump is not interested in reaching out to anyone beyond his extreme base and major polluters," remarked Clay Schroers, a director at the League of Conservation Voters environmental organization. Trump has consistently indicated his support for conventional energy production, which forms part of his broader appeal to blue-collar voters in America. In May, he detailed plans to eliminate environmental regulations introduced by Obama, abandon the Paris Climate Accord, and resurrect the Keystone XL pipeline project – actions that would reverse years of progress made by the environmental movement. Conversely, Trump’s Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton, has vowed to impose stricter regulations on the energy sector, promote the use of renewable fuels, and commit to international cooperation in addressing global climate change. Pence campaigned for governor in 2012 after his tenure in the U.S. Congress. His gubernatorial campaign received upwards of $850,000 from the energy sector, representing about 3 percent of his total campaign funds, according to finance reports. More than $300,000 of that funding was contributed by the billionaire Koch brothers, who are staunch advocates of limited government and fiscal conservatism and have shown support for Pence. Both David and Charles Koch have expressed that they will not back the Trump ticket. Trump has raised concerns among many figures in the Republican establishment due to his heated rhetoric on immigration and trade. However, a former high-ranking operative in the Koch political network, who maintains close ties with both brothers, stated that Pence could assist in making the donor network more amenable to Trump's campaign.

text: The commander of Myanmar's military urged on Thursday for individuals displaced by conflict in Rakhine State to return home and help rebuild their communities. However, he did not address the situation of the 422,000 Rohingya Muslims who fled to Bangladesh to escape military operations. During a significant address outlining his vision for Rakhine state, which marked his first trip there since the recent violence began, Senior General Min Aung Hlaing stated that the military had responded to the coordinated attacks by Rohingya insurgents on August 25 to the best of its ability. The United Nations has described the military's actions following the insurgent assaults as ethnic cleansing aimed at expelling the Rohingya Muslim population from predominantly Buddhist Myanmar. In contrast, Myanmar refutes this claim, asserting that its military is conducting a legitimate campaign against Muslim extremists who have been attacking and burning down the villages of Buddhists and other non-Muslims, with approximately 30,000 individuals being internally displaced. In his speech delivered to business leaders, officials, and some displaced individuals in Sittwe, the capital of the state, Min Aung Hlaing did not address the accusation of ethnic cleansing. He stated, "Regarding the restoration of villages for our national races, those who have fled their homes must first return to their original places." The term "national races" in Myanmar refers to members of officially recognized indigenous ethnic groups that contribute to the country's diversity. The Rohingya are not acknowledged as a "national race" and are thus perceived as illegal immigrants, denied citizenship. Tensions between Rakhine state's Buddhists and the Rohingya have historical roots but have intensified in recent years, partly due to a rise in Buddhist nationalism following nearly fifty years of stringent military governance. "The key issue is to have our people in the area. It's essential to maintain control of our region with our national races," Min Aung Hlaing remarked. "We cannot accomplish anything if there are no individuals from our national races... that is where they belong." He did not mention the return of Muslims to their homes in the northern part of the state, where nearly half of the villages have been deserted and destroyed. text: Protests against Donald Trump erupted in California's Bay Area late Tuesday following the Republican candidate's victory in the U.S. presidential election, according to a Reuters observer and local news outlets. Demonstrators set fire to an effigy of Trump, broke windows of shops, and ignited garbage and tires in downtown Oakland, which is located across the bay from San Francisco. A separate demonstration took place at the University of California, Davis, where students obstructed streets while marching and chanting anti-Trump slogans, including "You are not America, we are America," as shared on Twitter. text: (Reuters) - On Wednesday, the Communist Party of China revealed its key decision-making group, the Politburo Standing Committee, which is led by President Xi Jinping. Below is the list of the newly formed committee, composed entirely of men, arranged by their rank: - At 64, Xi Jinping is regarded as the most influential leader in China since Chairman Mao Zedong. Initially perceived as a dull 'princeling' from the elite class, Xi has risen to power since 2012, consolidating authority under his leadership while launching a notable anti-corruption campaign. His political ideology, known as 'Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era,' was incorporated into the Party's constitution on Tuesday. - Li Keqiang, aged 62, has served as the premier and has been in charge of China's economy for the past five years. He advanced from Hebei province, which encircles Beijing, and is a graduate of Hebei Normal University. Previously, he held the position of governor in Heilongjiang province and served as the party leader in Guizhou province. Li Zhanshu is viewed as one of Xi's closest confidants and frequently accompanies him on international visits. He holds a degree in philosophy from Peking University. - Han Zheng, aged 63, is the party chief of Shanghai, China's financial center, where he has spent his entire professional life. text: German voters are expressing their discontent with the Free Democrats (FDP) leader following the party's exit from three-way coalition negotiations last month, according to a poll released on Thursday. The recent survey indicated a decline in support for the FDP and a significant drop in the approval rating of its leader, Christian Lindner. In mid-November, the FDP abandoned exploratory discussions aimed at forming a coalition government alongside Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservatives and the environmentalist Greens. At that time, Lindner stated that it was preferable not to govern than to do so incorrectly. Some analysts speculated that the FDP's departure was premeditated to enhance its appeal among center-right voters and to demonstrate that the party prioritizes policy principles over the pursuit of power. However, the latest DeutschlandTrend survey, carried out by Infratest Dimap for ARD public broadcaster, revealed a 3 percentage point decrease in FDP support, bringing it down to 9 percent, making it the smallest party in the parliament. Merkel's conservatives saw an increase of 2 percentage points to 32 percent, while the Social Democrats (SPD) remained steady at 21 percent. The far-right Alternative for Germany registered at 13 percent, followed closely by the Greens at 11 percent and the Left party at 10 percent. Additionally, Lindner's approval rating fell sharply by 17 percentage points to just 28 percent. Merkel's popularity also decreased by 3 percentage points, landing at 54 percent, which is her lowest rating in this survey since October 2016. The most favored politician in Germany was SPD Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel, who surged by 8 percentage points to reach 65 percent approval. Greens co-leader Cem Ozdemir followed in second place, boasting an approval rating of 57 percent.

text: A prominent business organization from the U.S. expressed concerns on Tuesday regarding the lack of adequate preparations by President Donald Trump’s administration for upcoming discussions about economic discrepancies with China before his visit in November. Some members of the U.S. business sector fear that any agreements announced during the visit could divert attention from addressing long-standing grievances related to discriminatory Chinese practices and restrictions on market access. Zarit expressed his hope that the proposed agreements from the business delegation “do not overshadow the real necessity for structural reforms in the economic relationship.” Trump, who will visit five Asian nations on his inaugural trip to the region as president, is set to arrive in Beijing on November 8. Zarit mentioned that U.S. officials were “still waiting” for a response from China concerning issues that were raised during the U.S.-China Comprehensive Economic Dialogue in July, although he did not provide further details. He referred to Chinese officials as “master negotiators” and stated that the U.S. government and business community have historically maintained a less strategic perspective on the economic relationship. "And I think this administration is no exception,” Zarit remarked. He further stated that it was “not unreasonable” to anticipate more advancements 10 months into Trump’s presidency. Ross has indicated that the United States will be seeking “immediate results” and “tangible agreements” during Trump’s visit, while also recognizing that matters such as market access, intellectual property rights, and tariffs are more complex and will require more time to resolve. Washington and Beijing initiated a 100-day economic plan during Trump’s initial meeting with Xi in April, which included various industry-specific announcements, such as the revival of American beef exports to China. Nevertheless, U.S. business associations have voiced disappointment regarding the outcomes achieved. On Monday, Xi promised that China would implement additional measures to further open its economy. He made these statements during a meeting with members of an advisory board for Tsinghua University’s School of Economics and Management, which included Tim Cook, CEO of Apple Inc (AAPL.O), and Mark Zuckerberg from Facebook Inc (FB.O). According to the official China Daily newspaper, Xi stated that China will collaborate with the United States to “consider each other’s interests and concerns, resolve disputes and contradictions, and pursue win-win cooperation.” However, such frequently made promises have not alleviated the concerns of foreign companies regarding ownership limits in critical sectors like autos, securities, insurance, and information technology. U.S. business groups contend that their members face restrictions in these industries, whereas Chinese firms operate without hindrance in the U.S. market. They have also criticized Beijing’s “Made in China 2025” initiative, which provides government support for industries deemed strategic by the Chinese government. Particularly frustrating for foreign technology companies are new national security and cybersecurity regulations that require firms to store essential data within China and undergo security assessments that they argue could jeopardize their business secrets. "Essentially, when we analyze this situation, it boils down to a company competing against a country,” Zarit stated.

text: Kurdish parties opposing Barzani report attacks on their offices overnight. BAGHDAD (Reuters) - Political factions in Iraqi Kurdistan that are against regional leader Masoud Barzani reported that their offices were targeted in multiple cities during the night, just hours after Barzani declared his resignation, a consequence of a failed independence initiative. The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), the Movement for Change, and Gorran issued separate statements indicating that several of their offices in the Duhok area, located north of the Kurdish capital Erbil, were either looted or set ablaze overnight. No injuries were reported. The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), which is semi-autonomous in northern Iraq, stated it had instructed local police forces, known as Asayish, to intervene and halt the attacks. Barzani, aged 71, announced on Sunday his intention to step down as president effective November 1, following an independence referendum he advocated that backfired and led to military and economic repercussions from the Iraqi government. This long-time guerrilla leader has governed Iraq's Kurdish autonomous region since 2005, maintaining a strong grip as the region thrived while the rest of Iraq faced civil strife. However, in recent weeks, his push for the independence vote has led to his downfall, revealing significant divisions among the Kurdish factions. Armed demonstrators backing Barzani invaded parliament on Sunday as it convened to discuss his resignation. Opposition legislators who had been barricaded inside managed to exit later, as reported by their respective parties. The PUK, which has been Barzani's primary rival, the Kurdish Democratic Party (KDP), for many years, had supported his choice to conduct the independence referendum, though somewhat reluctantly. The reform-oriented Gorran party opposed the referendum, claiming the timing was inappropriate. In a televised address where he announced his resignation plans, Barzani accused supporters of his long-time opponent, PUK founder Jalal Talabani, who passed away in early October, of 'high treason' for surrendering the oil-rich city of Kirkuk to Iraqi forces without resistance two weeks prior. Kurdish troops known as Peshmerga had controlled Kirkuk, a key oil hub in Iraq, since 2014 when they took it over after government forces retreated amid an Islamic State advance. Although Kirkuk lies outside the official borders of the Kurdish autonomous region, Kurds regard it as the core of their homeland. Earlier this month, Prime Minister Haidar al-Abadi ordered his troops to reclaim it and all other disputed territories in retaliation following Barzani's independence referendum, which Baghdad deems illegal. The Iraqi authority responsible for overseeing media in Baghdad announced a ban on two prominent Kurdish TV stations aligned with Barzani's KDP: Rudaw and Kurdistan 24. The Baghdad-based Communication and Media Commission accused these channels of 'inciting violence and hatred.' In response, the management of Erbil-based Kurdistan 24 issued a letter to the International Federation of Journalists, stating, 'This is an assault on freedom of press and expression.' Rudaw alleged that Iranian-backed Iraqi paramilitary forces operating alongside government troops killed a Kurdish journalist, Arkan Sharif, in the Kirkuk region on Monday. While Iraqi Kurds have largely demonstrated external unity since Saddam Hussein's fall in 2003, there exists a longstanding history of conflict between Barzani's KDP and Talabani's PUK, which clashed in a civil war during the 1990s. The KDP is primarily based around Erbil, the regional capital, whereas the PUK garners support mainly from Suleimaniya, the other principal city in the region. Both political factions manage distinct units of Peshmerga, their former underground guerrilla forces that have transitioned into the official security apparatus of the Kurdish autonomous region. After the fall of Saddam, Barzani oversaw the Kurdish autonomous region while his adversary Talabani held the ceremonial presidency of all Iraq in Baghdad from 2005 to 2014.

The term "Indo-Pacific" has gained traction in diplomatic and security discussions within Australia, India, and Japan in recent years, serving as a shorthand for a broader, democratic-led region, countering the "Asia-Pacific" label, which some perceive as placing an authoritarian China at its core. China has been actively advocating for President Xi Jinping's Belt and Road initiative, a vast infrastructure endeavor aimed at reviving the ancient Silk Road, which connects Asia with the Middle East and Europe, though critics assert that it primarily serves to extend Chinese influence. China contends that it is merely a development initiative aimed at shared prosperity that welcomes participation from any country.

text: PARIS (Reuters) - In a coordinated counter-terrorism operation, French law enforcement apprehended nine individuals, while an additional person was detained in Switzerland. Among those detained in simultaneous French police actions tied to Islamist militant activities was a 27-year-old Swiss man, the officials reported. French police executed concurrent raids on locations in the eastern part of Paris as well as in the southeastern area adjacent to Italy and Switzerland, leading to the detention of nine individuals, according to a source within the French judiciary. text: The African National Congress (ANC), which governs South Africa, has passed a resolution that advocates for the nationalization of the central bank and land expropriation without compensation, as stated by a senior party official on Wednesday. The topic of nationalization often causes unease among investors in South Africa, particularly since the ANC's left-wing factions have also proposed that mines and banks be owned by the state. Land remains a sensitive issue more than twenty years after the end of apartheid, and the ANC faces pressure to address the racial imbalances in land ownership. Unlike the majority of central banks globally, the South African Reserve Bank has been privately owned since its founding in 1921. However, its shareholders do not influence monetary policy, banking regulation, or financial stability policy. After a gathering of party delegates, Enoch Godongwana, who leads the ANC’s economic transformation committee, informed the media that altering the ownership structure of the South African Reserve Bank would not compromise its independence. He noted that the party has also resolved to pursue constitutional amendments to facilitate land expropriation without compensation, although no specific timeline was provided. He emphasized that there would be no illegal land occupations. Following the ANC's proposal in July during a policy conference to nationalize the bank's shareholding, the South African Reserve Bank indicated that any change in its shareholding would not impact its mandate, which is defined by the constitution. Godongwana mentioned that no specific timeline has been established for the acquisition of shares in the central bank or for any parliamentary directives needed to amend the country’s laws to implement these changes. "No constitutional changes, no alterations to the Reserve Bank Act," he stated. "We have also asserted that it's unlikely to affect anything since shareholders in the Reserve Bank do not influence monetary policy whatsoever." Godongwana indicated that these changes would occur only after further preparations for the bank's nationalization are completed. In July, when the party expressed its desire for the central bank to become fully state-owned, initial investor concern led to a decline in the rand. Following Godongwana's announcement on Wednesday, the currency showed little fluctuation, but analysts predicted negative market reactions. "The SARB resolution will unsettle the markets, even if it is ultimately improbable to be enforced," remarked Anne Fruhauf, a political analyst from consultancy Teneo. Regarding the land issue, Godongwana mentioned that some delegates became unruly during an intense debate that almost derailed the conference. ANC officials dismissed claims that physical confrontations occurred among delegates during the discussion. Godongwana stated that the delegates ultimately consented to initiate constitutional amendments to enable land expropriation without compensation. He added that the condition is that it must be sustainable and should not negatively impact food production and security, reiterating that illegal land occupations should be avoided. When asked about potential market reactions, Godongwana expressed, "I suspect they will respond with shock and react negatively... if I were in the markets, I would likely hold off." Most land in South Africa continues to be owned by white individuals, even 23 years post-apartheid. Experts believe that the land expropriation plan in South Africa will not resemble the often violent land seizures seen in Zimbabwe, where the government confiscated white-owned farms for redistribution to landless blacks. Nonetheless, some economists and agricultural groups have warned that the reform might adversely affect investment and production. According to the government, approximately 8 million hectares (20 million acres) of land have been transferred to black ownership since the end of apartheid, which accounts for 8 to 10 percent of the land that was in white hands in 1994. This figure is merely one-third of the ANC's target of 30 percent by 2014.

text: WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. (Reuters) - On Monday, North Carolina Governor Pat McCrory acknowledged his defeat in the closely contested gubernatorial election against Democrat Roy Cooper, nearly four weeks after the November 8 vote, which many considered a referendum on a law restricting transgender bathroom rights. The Republican incumbent had been behind his opponent since election night, when Cooper declared victory with a margin of less than 5,000 votes. McCrory initially resisted conceding, pledging to pursue a recount and disputing the legitimacy of votes that his campaign suggested might include those cast by felons or deceased individuals. As of Monday, the unofficial election results indicated that Cooper's lead had expanded to 10,263 votes as counties continued to count ballots. McCrory was eligible for a recount only if his deficit was 10,000 votes or fewer. In a video message released by the governor’s office, McCrory acknowledged Cooper’s victory as “the closest North Carolina governor’s race in modern history.” “Despite ongoing concerns that deserve clarification regarding the voting process, I genuinely believe that the majority of our citizens have expressed their will,” said McCrory, who appeared on a couch with a Christmas tree visible in the video. Cooper’s victory over the one-term incumbent represents the only gubernatorial seat gained by Democrats nationwide, while Republicans secured additional governorships last month in New Hampshire, Missouri, and Vermont. Cooper, who serves as the state’s attorney general, remarked that being governor “will be the honor of my life.” “Even though this election season has been divisive, I still believe there is more that brings us together than separates us,” he stated following his opponent’s concession. The Democratic candidate’s campaign was bolstered by a backlash against McCrory after he enacted a state law in March that prohibits transgender individuals from using government-operated restrooms that align with their gender identity and restricts protections for LGBTQ individuals. This law, the only one of its kind in the United States, garnered national attention. It has been attributed to hundreds of millions of dollars in economic losses and the withdrawal of significant sporting events from the ninth most populous state in the country. Critics of this legislation, known as House Bill 2, indicated that a McCrory loss would have national repercussions. “McCrory’s obstinate and reckless backing of HB 2 cost him this election, and his defeat serves as a strong message to lawmakers nationwide that targeting LGBTQ individuals will not be accepted,” stated Chad Griffin, president of the Human Rights Campaign. LGBTQ stands for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (and/or questioning) individuals/identities.

text: Meals on Wheels America has experienced a significant increase in donations following the release of the U.S. budget. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Saturday, Meals on Wheels America, which oversees 5,000 providers of meal delivery services for seniors, announced that online contributions have surged since the White House unveiled a proposed budget that may result in a substantial reduction in its funding. The organization, which advocates for the national network, reported receiving approximately $50,000 on Thursday after the budget outline was made public, in contrast to the usual $1,000 received on an ordinary day. President Donald Trump’s initial budget proposal suggests a 17.9 percent decrease for fiscal year 2018 in funding for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which supplies the majority of government support for Meals on Wheels, according to the organization. The budget proposal did not clarify how this reduction would impact the Administration for Community Living, the HHS division that finances nutrition programs for seniors, stated Meals on Wheels spokesperson Jenny Bertolette. Meals on Wheels conveyed on its website that it is hard to envision a situation where the upcoming federal budget would not affect its services. "While Meals on Wheels America and local Meals on Wheels programs are experiencing an increase in donations, it does not substitute for federal funding," Bertolette mentioned in an email to Reuters. The White House directed inquiries regarding the HHS budget to the department itself. An HHS representative pointed to a statement from Secretary Tom Price that was issued earlier this week. "HHS is committed to achieving our department’s mission to enhance the health and well-being of the American population. This budget backs that mission and will help guarantee we are providing essential services to our fellow citizens," the statement indicated. Trump’s budget proposal advocates for a considerable rise in military expenditure, alongside a similar decrease in most discretionary non-defense programs, raising concerns among Democrats and some Republicans aligned with the president. Bertolette mentioned that the national Meals on Wheels association is uncertain if its local affiliates have experienced a similar surge in donations. According to the organization, one in six seniors "struggles with hunger," and it offers its services at no cost for those unable to pay. The organization, citing research from Brown University funded by AARP Inc., stated that seniors who receive fresh meals daily demonstrate greater health and well-being improvements compared to those who receive frozen meals weekly or those who do not receive meals at all. The website of Meals on Wheels America indicates that it operates a nutrition resource center with the assistance of federal funding.

text: At least eight individuals have died amid protests in Cameroon’s Anglophone regions. BUEA/BAMENDA, Cameroon (Reuters) - On Sunday, soldiers killed at least eight people and injured several others during demonstrations by activists advocating for independence from the predominantly Francophone country, according to officials and eyewitnesses. The protests coincided with the anniversary of Anglophone Cameroon’s liberation from British rule and occurred as a months-long campaign against perceived marginalization by the Francophone-led government intensified. These demonstrations, which started late last year, have become a focal point for opposition against President Paul Biya’s 35-year administration. Donatus Njong Fonyuy, the mayor of Kumbo, reported that five inmates died around 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) when a fire broke out at the prison where they were held. "We don’t know what caused the fire in the prison... But five prisoners were killed by soldiers. Two were shot and are currently hospitalized," he informed Reuters, also noting that two civilians sustained injuries. In separate incidents in Kumbo, soldiers shot and killed one protester and injured two others who displayed the blue and white flag associated with the Ambazonia separatist movement. Fonyuy mentioned that another woman was killed in her residence, without providing additional details. Police and military representatives were not available for immediate comment regarding the shootings. A security source, who wished to remain unnamed due to lack of authorization to speak with the media, stated earlier in the day, "We won’t resort to violence unless there is a significant cause. There are many risks, including terrorist threats. We are remaining calm." President Biya, in a post on his official Facebook account, denounced the violence, saying, "Let me make this very clear: voicing concerns is not prohibited in the Republic. However, no significant outcomes can be achieved through excessive language, public violence, or defiance of authority." The roots of Cameroon’s division trace back to the conclusion of World War One when the League of Nations partitioned the former German colony of Kamerun between the victorious French and British allies. Authorities had prohibited gatherings of more than four individuals, mandated the closure of bus stations, eateries, and shops, and restricted movement across various areas of the English-speaking regions prior to the protests. Additionally, the government ordered the closure of Cameroon’s border with Nigeria for the weekend. Access to major social media and messaging platforms, including Facebook, Twitter, and WhatsApp, was disrupted starting Friday. Communications Minister Issa Tchiroma Bakary on Sunday warned that any media outlets supporting separatists would face closure, stating they "must not support those who promote division and seek to destroy and destabilize our country." Businesses were closed in the main cities of the regions, Buea and Bamenda, with military helicopters flying above. The security presence included troops from the Cameroonian army’s Rapid Intervention Brigade, typically deployed to combat Islamist Boko Haram militants in the northern part of the country. One protester was fatally shot at the outskirts of Buea as security forces attempted to prevent pro-independence marchers from entering the city, according to three witnesses. Nevertheless, hundreds managed to navigate through the countryside to bypass the blockade and reach the city, where security forces deployed tear gas in an effort to prevent them from marching towards the regional governor’s office. A Reuters observer also reported hearing gunfire, but it was unclear if the shots were directed at the protesters or fired into the air. "The military, which is supposed to safeguard lives and property, has transformed into our worst nightmare," remarked a Buea resident who requested anonymity for fear of retaliation. In Bamenda, where a bomb attack attributed to separatists injured three policemen last week, young men wielding makeshift secessionist flags clashed with security forces who sought to disperse them using tear gas.

text: U.S. Vice President Joe Biden announced on Tuesday in Davos, Switzerland, that the United States would expedite the approval process for innovative drug combinations in a new initiative aimed at eradicating cancer "once and for all." This announcement follows the loss of his 46-year-old son Beau to brain cancer last year and comes a week after President Barack Obama appointed him to spearhead this effort at a World Economic Forum gathering of global cancer specialists. Combination therapy is increasingly recognized as crucial in combating tumors as researchers uncover various genetic elements that contribute to the growth of cancer cells; however, the pathway to market for these therapies can be lengthy and expensive. Biden mentioned hosting a meeting at his residence with three unnamed major pharmaceutical companies and the head of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), during which both parties committed to enhancing efforts to deliver novel cancer drug combinations to patients. "The FDA leader pledged that everyone would expedite the approval process for combinations," Biden stated. Additionally, he noted that the pharmaceutical executives expressed their willingness to explore alternative business approaches to ensure that effective drugs from different companies could be tested together as promptly as possible. Cancer specialists are particularly enthusiastic about the potential of new immunotherapy treatments that assist the body’s immune system in combating tumors, especially when used in conjunction with other medications. Francis Collins, director of the U.S. National Institutes of Health, labeled their potential as "breath-taking." Nevertheless, these immunotherapy treatments come at a high price, often exceeding $100,000 annually per patient, and pharmaceutical companies have historically been reluctant to share preliminary medical research. Obama's previous assertion to "make America the country that cures cancer once and for all" during his final State of the Union address was met with criticism from some scientists, who view it as an overly simplistic perspective on the complex disease. The new government initiative resonates with former President Richard Nixon’s unsuccessful "War on Cancer" from the 1970s, a period during which it became evident that cancer comprises hundreds of distinct diseases rather than a singular ailment, rendering the idea of a universal cure outdated. Biden recognized this complexity during his remarks in Davos, stating, "I’m not naive enough to think or suggest we are going to have a cure for every cancer in the world in the near term."

text: The United States has lost confidence in the government of South Sudan, as stated by U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley during her meeting with President Salva Kiir. Haley conveyed that the U.S. expects the country to work towards peace or risk diminishing support from Washington. She was the first high-ranking official from President Donald Trump’s administration to travel to South Sudan, a nation that descended into civil conflict in 2013, only two years post-independence from Sudan. Her one-on-one discussion with Kiir lasted approximately 45 minutes. Afterward, Haley informed reporters in Juba, the capital, that she emphasized the U.S. was at a pivotal moment and that future decisions would hinge on Kiir's choices. The United Nations has raised alarms that the ongoing violence in South Sudan has led to around 4 million individuals fleeing their homes and has created a risk of genocide. Kiir's administration has refuted U.N. claims of ethnic cleansing. Haley had to shorten her visit to a camp for those displaced by the conflict due to disruptive protests against Kiir. She remarked, "He recognized that Americans were dissatisfied with his governance in South Sudan, and I made that abundantly clear. He comprehended that the assistance or support he anticipates is not guaranteed." Haley did not specify what further steps the U.S. might take but affirmed that Kiir understood her message. On Monday, she mentioned that Washington was deliberating on methods to compel Kiir towards peace, while observing that withdrawing aid might not be effective. Last month, the Trump administration enacted sanctions against two high-ranking South Sudanese officials and the former army chief. The civil war was ignited by a conflict between Kiir, who is Dinka, and his former deputy Riek Machar, a Nuer, leading parts of the youngest nation in the world into famine. A delicate peace agreement collapsed last year, prompting Machar to flee the nation. Sources informed Reuters in December that he is currently detained in South Africa to prevent him from inciting unrest. Haley had to cut her visit to a camp in Juba, where U.N. peacekeepers are safeguarding around 30,000 displaced individuals, after hundreds of boisterous pro-Machar demonstrators obstructed nearby roads, chanting "Salva Kiir is a killer" and "Welcome USA." Protesters displayed a large banner stating, "South Sudan IDPs (internally displaced persons) and refugees appreciate President Trump, the peacemaker and advocate for human rights." A representative from the U.N. mission indicated that the protest gained traction after Haley departed, as IDPs expressed frustration over her inability to meet with them. text: PHILADELPHIA (Reuters) - On Wednesday, U.S. Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump lifted his previous prohibition on press credentials for certain media organizations, allowing them to cover his campaign events. This change includes outlets such as The Washington Post and Buzzfeed, which had faced significant backlash from advocates for press freedom due to the ban. At various points, the prohibition also extended to Politico and The Huffington Post, following their critical coverage of him. Although these banned media had continued to report on his campaign, they were unable to secure credentials to officially attend his events, including access to the media area at rallies. Campaign spokesman Hope Hicks confirmed that these outlets would now be permitted to obtain media credentials and travel alongside other reporters covering the Republican candidate. Advocates for press freedom had harshly criticized such restrictions. Reporters Without Borders stated that when The Post was banned in June, it represented an "act of hostility" towards the media and a significant infringement on press freedom. Marty Baron, Executive Editor of the Washington Post, expressed in a statement on Wednesday that “Revoking press credentials was imprudent, pointless and offensive from the start. We’re pleased to see the ban come to a long-overdue end.” Sam Stein, senior politics editor for The Huffington Post, tweeted that their outlet was no longer on the blacklist. He mentioned, “They even returned my email to confirm it,” referring to the Trump campaign. Journalists from the restricted organizations had frequently accessed Trump campaign events by queuing in the same lines as the general public, but they risked being removed by his security personnel if identified. Last month, Trump’s vice presidential candidate, Indiana Governor Mike Pence, indicated that the campaign was contemplating reversing the ban, although no official announcement was made until Wednesday. Trump, a businessman from New York, stated to CNN, "I figure they can’t treat me any worse," while declaring the end of the ban.
