WASHINGTON (Reuters) - With ample funds, political organizations outside the administration are energetically assisting President Donald Trump as he faces low levels of public approval, scrutiny regarding his campaign's connections to Russia, and a stalled legislative agenda. Through aggressive television advertisements and online initiatives typically reserved for election periods, these groups are enabling Trump to retaliate against his perceived adversaries and promote his agenda, enhancing the impact of his Twitter presence and the authority of the White House. On Tuesday, one such group, America First Policies, initiated an attack advertisement against a senator from Trump’s own Republican Party who had expressed hesitance regarding a Senate proposal to reform healthcare that would result in millions more Americans lacking insurance. This move upset Senate leader Mitch McConnell, who is having difficulty gathering the necessary votes for the proposal. This scenario marks the first instance in U.S. history where a sitting president has had Super PACs - political action committees that can collect unlimited funds and usually function during elections - or political non-profits, which are not required to reveal their donors or expenditures, actively working in his favor after the election campaign has ended. The pro-Trump organizations are not allowed to coordinate with the White House, which opted not to comment on this article. The New York Times noted that McConnell had expressed his concerns to White House chief of staff Reince Priebus regarding the advertisement from America First Policies. Subsequently, the group withdrew the ad. America First Policies along with other pro-Trump entities were established to advocate for Trump and his legislative priorities - including healthcare reform, the construction of a wall along the Mexican border, and the pursuit of tax cuts and deregulation. They operate independently of the Republican Party, which could create challenges for Republican leadership as demonstrated by Tuesday’s advertisement. With Trump's approval ratings declining and his agenda now overshadowed by a federal investigation into his 2016 campaign's links to Russia, these groups are investing heavily in safeguarding Trump's public image, vilifying his opponents, and amplifying his claim of being the target of a witch-hunt. "The establishment is shaken, angry, losing control," states another recent advertisement from America First Policies, which identifies itself on its website as a non-profit organization "supporting key policy initiatives." Background visuals include images of the U.S. Capitol, Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and liberal MSNBC host Rachel Maddow. "Desperately waging an all-out war to protect their interest," the narrator continues. "They lie, they leak, they leech onto power." America First Policies is made up of more traditionally conservative Republicans and was created after the election by a close associate of Vice President Mike Pence, Nick Ayers. The organization released a statement asserting their mission to advance Trump’s agenda and indicated their willingness to encourage House Republicans through grassroots efforts and advertising to back the healthcare reform. The transition of these groups from promoting policy to adopting an aggressive stance is not unexpected, according to Marjorie Hershey, a political science professor at Indiana University. "A significant amount of research indicates that negative advertisements are more likely to capture attention compared to positive ones, and since Super PACs themselves are not on the ballot, they can afford to risk the negative image that often accompanies such advertising," Hershey remarked. Strategists and political scientists find it challenging to ascertain whether these groups are genuinely influencing public sentiment. However, the organizations cite their fundraising achievements as a sign of their effectiveness – much of which comes not from affluent donors, but from small contributions from voters. "Great America Alliance" - which was established as a sister organization to a Super PAC formed by Trump supporters Rudy Giuliani and Newt Gingrich - has allocated $400,000 for an ad targeting former FBI Director James Comey, directly from the group.

text: The cabinet of Lebanon is set to convene on Tuesday for the first occasion since the nation fell into a political turmoil a month prior, following Prime Minister Saad al-Hariri's resignation announcement during a broadcast from Saudi Arabia. According to the media office of the cabinet, the meeting will commence at noon at the presidential palace. It is anticipated that the discussion will focus on Hariri's resignation, which has reintroduced Lebanon into a regional conflict between Riyadh and its primary adversary, Iran.
source_text: Lebanon's cabinet to meet Tuesday for first time since political crisis: media office. BEIRUT (Reuters) - Lebanon s cabinet will meet on Tuesday for the first time since the country entered a political crisis a month ago when Prime Minister Saad al-Hariri offered his resignation in a broadcast from Saudi Arabia.  The cabinet s media office said the session would begin at noon at the presidential palace. The meeting is expected to address Hariri s resignation which thrust Lebanon back into a regional tussle between Riyadh and its main regional foe, Iran.

text: UK Prime Minister Theresa May announced that the transition period for Brexit is expected to last approximately two years. Speaking in Florence, she stated that during this implementation phase, individuals will still have the opportunity to move to and work in the UK, although a registration system will be put in place as a necessary step towards the new framework. May indicated that current assessments suggest a transition period lasting around two years.
source_text: UK PM May says Brexit transition period to last around two years. FLORENCE, Italy (Reuters) - Prime Minister Theresa May said that a Brexit implementation period would last for around two years.  During the implementation period, people will be continue to be able to come and live and work in the UK but there will be a registration system, an essential preparation for the new regime,  May said in Florence.  As of today, these considerations point to a implementation period of around two years,  she said.

text: A woman reported to Reuters on Friday that she sustained injuries during a stampede at the Parsons Green underground station in London. According to a photographer from Reuters, armed police were present at the location. The London Metro newspaper mentioned on its website that an explosion occurred on an underground train at Parsons Green, causing some passengers to suffer facial burns at the station.
source_text: Witness says injured in stampede at London station: Reuters reporter. LONDON (Reuters) - A woman at London s Parsons Green underground train station told Reuters on Friday she was injured in a stampede.  Armed police were at the scene, a Reuters photographer said.  A blast on an underground train at Parsons Green left some passengers with facial burns at the station, London s Metro newspaper reported on its website.

text: MAR DEL PLATA, Argentina (Reuters) - Efforts to locate an Argentine navy submarine that has been missing in the South Atlantic with 44 crew members were complicated by a storm on Sunday, and satellite calls believed to have originated from the submarine did not assist search teams in pinpointing its location. The defense ministry reported that the ARA San Juan seemed to have attempted to connect through seven unsuccessful satellite calls on Saturday between late morning and early afternoon. The last known position of the vessel was 432 km (268 miles) off the coast of Argentina, early on Wednesday. As waves reached heights of 8 meters (20 feet) and winds hit 40 knots, the search operation at sea faced challenges, with authorities dedicating Sunday to analyzing data from the satellite calls without making significant headway, according to a navy official who spoke to reporters. "We examined these signals, which we know were weak and intermittent," stated Gabriel Galeazzi, a naval commander. "They could not assist in identifying a specific location on the map to facilitate the search." Iridium Communications Inc, a U.S. satellite communications firm called in to help assess the calls, indicated that they did not come from its device on the submarine and might have originated from equipment belonging to another satellite communications company. It noted that the last call detected from its device occurred on Wednesday, coinciding with the day the government reported the submarine's disappearance. Over a dozen boats and aircraft from Argentina, the United States, Britain, Chile, and Brazil have contributed to the search efforts. Authorities have primarily monitored the sea from the air as the storm hindered boat operations, navy Admiral Gabriel Gonzalez told reporters. "Regrettably, these conditions are expected to persist for the next 48 hours," Gonzalez stated from the Mar del Plata naval base, located approximately 420 km (240 miles) south of Buenos Aires, which was the destination the submarine was heading towards before it disappeared. The navy indicated that a power failure on the diesel-electric-propelled submarine may have disrupted its communications. Submarine protocol dictates that vessels must surface if they lose communication. Three boats departed from Mar del Plata on Saturday, equipped with radar detection probes and retracing the route the submarine would have taken to reach the base, Balbi explained. "These probes enable the boats to scan the ocean floor during their journey and attempt to create a three-dimensional map of the seafloor," Balbi noted. The U.S. Navy reported that its four aircraft were equipped with a submarine rescue chamber, developed during World War II, capable of reaching a grounded submarine at depths of 850 feet and saving up to six individuals at once. This chamber can seal over the submarine's hatch to facilitate the transfer of sailors between the vessels. Additionally, it brought along a remote-controlled vehicle that can be submerged and operated from the surface. The intense search operation has captured the attention of the 44 million people in the nation, which recently grieved the loss of five citizens who were killed when a truck driver drove through a bicycle path in New York City. Relatives of the crew members gathered at the Mar del Plata naval base, where the submarine was anticipated to arrive around noon on Sunday from Ushuaia. However, Balbi mentioned that delays caused by storms would not be unusual. At the entrance to the base, locals displayed signs with supportive messages for the crew and their families on a chain-link fence. "Strength for Argentina. We trust in God. We are waiting for you," read a message inscribed on a celestial blue-and-white Argentine flag hanging on the fence. "Let’s go, men of steel. We are waiting for you at home," was written on a picture of the submarine. Argentine-born Pope Francis included a mention of the missing submarine in his Sunday noon prayer. text: The U.S. Senate confirmed President Donald Trump’s appointment of David Friedman as ambassador to Israel on Thursday with a narrow vote of 52 to 46, primarily along party lines. Only two Democrats, Senators Robert Menendez and Joe Manchin, supported Friedman alongside Trump’s Republican allies. Such a level of dissent is quite rare for a candidate for the U.S. ambassadorship to Israel, a nation closely allied with the United States. Historically, nominees from both Democratic and Republican administrations have been approved without significant objection, often through unanimous consent or voice votes. Friedman, who lacks diplomatic experience, has been a longstanding associate of Trump and served as his bankruptcy attorney during his business career. He supports investments in Israeli settlements on land that Palestinians claim and advocates for the relocation of the U.S. embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This move is met with strong opposition from numerous U.S. allies, as both Israelis and Palestinians assert their claims to the city as their capital. Friedman is also recognized for his provocative rhetoric against political opponents, having referred to former President Barack Obama as anti-Semitic. Democrats have expressed concerns that his rhetoric may jeopardize security in a region marked by volatility. “Our ambassador should not be a person who uses language that incites violence, hatred, and instability,” stated Democratic Senator Brian Schatz on the Senate floor prior to the final vote on confirmation. Trump’s choice of Friedman illustrates his altered stance on Israel following years of tension between Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In contrast to Obama, Trump has shown flexibility regarding the U.S. dedication to a two-state solution, which has been a cornerstone of America’s Middle East policy, and has endorsed the embassy's relocation. When the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, also mostly along party lines, approved Friedman, Republican Senator Bob Corker, who chairs the committee, commended him as a passionate proponent for robust U.S.-Israeli relations. “He comprehends the intricacies of the issues at hand for the United States and the importance of supporting a democratic ally in a crucial and unstable region of the world,” Corker remarked. The outcome of Thursday’s vote ensures that Trump will have an ambassador appointed in time for the upcoming annual conference of the influential pro-Israel lobbying organization AIPAC in Washington next week.

text: HARARE (Reuters) - The leader of the Zimbabwe opposition, Morgan Tsvangirai, experienced severe vomiting following a meeting with his party and was airlifted to a hospital in Johannesburg, a senior source from the party reported on Saturday. Tsvangirai, who is set to run against President Robert Mugabe in the upcoming elections next year, was reported to be in stable condition, with the source rejecting media claims that his health was critically compromised. The 65-year-old's symptoms appeared suddenly during a Thursday evening gathering of his opposition coalition, the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), in Kadoma, a city located approximately 160 km (100 miles) southwest of Harare, according to the source. On Friday, two other political sources from Zimbabwe verified the details regarding his abrupt illness and subsequent airlift to South Africa. However, the MDC issued an official statement asserting that Tsvangirai was in South Africa for a routine medical procedure. The MDC statement emphasized, "Morgan Tsvangirai ... is in a very stable condition contrary to morbid media reports that he is critical and is battling for his life." This announcement followed a month after Vice President Emmerson Mnangagwa, considered a frontrunner to take over from the 93-year-old Mugabe, was also rushed to South Africa for urgent medical treatment. Mnangagwa, who has since returned, dismissed local media speculation suggesting that he had been poisoned. Last year, Tsvangirai disclosed that he was undergoing treatment for colon cancer. The party source clarified on Saturday that his recent illness was unrelated to that condition.

text: Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski from the Senate is indicating a favorable stance towards the tax reform budget. On Monday in Washington, U.S. Senator Murkowski mentioned that she is leaning towards a ‘yes’ vote on a budget resolution in the Senate aimed at making it easier to pass tax reform legislation later this year. ‘I am leaning ‘yes,’’ she told the press. However, she noted that her ultimate decision would hinge on the amendments included in the budget resolution prior to its final vote.
source_text: Senate Republican Murkowski leaning yes on tax reform budget. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski said on Monday that she was leaning toward a “yes” vote on a Senate budget resolution intended to facilitate the passage of tax reform legislation later this year. “I am leaning ‘yes,’” Murkowski told reporters. But she added that her final decision would depend on what amendments are added to the budget resolution before it comes up for final passage.

text: Russia has expressed its support for China's extensive Belt and Road initiative, which aims to establish trade and transportation connections across Asia and beyond. On Monday, it encouraged India to explore ways to collaborate with Beijing on this significant project. India has voiced strong opposition to a trade corridor that China is developing in Pakistan, which traverses the disputed region of Kashmir as part of the Belt and Road initiative. Notably, India was the sole nation to abstain from a summit in May hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, aimed at promoting the construction of railways, ports, and power infrastructure reminiscent of the ancient Silk Road. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov remarked that New Delhi should not allow political challenges to prevent it from participating in this initiative that involves substantial financial investments and potential benefits. Lavrov made these comments in the Indian capital following a trilateral discussion with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Indian Foreign Minister Sushma Swaraj, where he stated that India's concerns regarding the Chinese initiative were addressed. "I understand that India has issues, which we talked about today, regarding the concept of One Belt and One Road, but the specific difficulties related to this should not make everything else contingent on resolving political matters," he stated. He emphasized that Russia, along with all Central Asian countries and various European nations, had endorsed the Chinese initiative to enhance economic collaboration. "These are the facts," he added. "I am completely convinced that India possesses a sufficient number of astute diplomats and politicians who can devise a strategy that would enable you to gain from this process." Russia's comments, as a former ally of India during the Cold War, highlighted the disparities within the trilateral alliance established 15 years ago to counterbalance U.S. dominance in global matters. However, significant differences between India and China, particularly regarding longstanding border conflicts, have hindered any genuine cooperation among the three nations. Moreover, India has increasingly strengthened its ties with the United States in recent years, acquiring military equipment worth billions of dollars to modernize its predominantly Soviet-era armed forces. Swaraj noted that the three nations engaged in very productive discussions concerning economic matters and the battle against terrorism.

text: South Korea has stated that President Trump's warning to North Korea is 'firm and specific.' SEOUL/TOKYO (Reuters) - In his address to the United Nations, U.S. President Donald Trump cautioned that he would 'totally destroy' North Korea if it posed a threat, emphasizing the necessity for Pyongyang to abandon its nuclear arsenal, South Korea remarked on Wednesday. During a pointed speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump ridiculed North Korean leader Kim Jong Un by labeling him a 'rocket man' due to his ongoing ballistic missile tests. 'We interpret the speech as reflecting a firm and specific position on critical issues pertaining to maintaining peace and security that the international community and the United Nations face,' the office of South Korean President Moon Jae-in communicated in a statement on Wednesday. 'It clearly indicated the seriousness with which the United States government regards North Korea's nuclear program, as the president dedicated an unusual amount of time to addressing the issue,' the statement from the presidential Blue House expressed. Trump's address 'reiterated that North Korea must understand that denuclearization is the sole pathway to a future through maximum sanctions and pressure,' it added. Moon assumed office in May with a focus on increased engagement with North Korea. However, following Pyongyang's sixth and most significant nuclear test on September 3, Moon has indicated that the moment is not appropriate for dialogue. According to Moon's office, he and Trump are scheduled to meet in New York early on Wednesday U.S. time. Trump's most explicit military threat to strike North Korea represents his latest expression of concern over Pyongyang's continuous weapons tests. 'The United States possesses significant strength and patience, but if compelled to defend itself or its allies, we will have no alternative but to totally destroy North Korea,' Trump stated to the 193-member assembly. 'Rocket man is on a suicide mission for himself and his regime.' Japan, a U.S. ally that North Korea frequently threatens to annihilate, has consistently maintained a hardline stance on North Korea, advocating for heightened sanctions and pressure. 'We greatly value President Trump's strategy to transform North Korea's policy stance, promote denuclearization, and call upon the international community, including China and Russia, to cooperate in intensifying pressure on North Korea,' Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga informed reporters. Suga also expressed appreciation for Trump's mention of a Japanese girl abducted by North Korean agents in 1977. The issue of abductees is crucial for Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who has committed to rescuing them during his tenure, and it resonates deeply with the Japanese populace. North Korea admitted in 2002 to having kidnapped 13 Japanese individuals in the 1970s and 1980s for espionage training. Five of those abducted returned to Japan, but Tokyo suspects that many more may have been taken. North Korea, which has executed over 80 missile tests under the leadership of Kim, argues that it requires its weapons for self-defense against U.S. aggression. South Korea and the United States remain technically at war with North Korea since the Korean conflict from 1950 to 1953 concluded with a truce rather than a peace treaty. On Wednesday, U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis mentioned at an Air Force event that diplomatic efforts to address Pyongyang's actions are still ongoing, while acknowledging the 'somber reality' that the Pentagon must have military options prepared. U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Nikki Haley, during an interview with CBS News, noted on Wednesday that the United States has numerous military options available regarding North Korea that do not involve completely destroying the nation, stating: 'There are steps that lead up to that. No one desires war; the president does not want war. We have endeavored to accomplish this through dialogue, we have attempted this through sanctions, and we have exhausted every diplomatic measure possible. We are not abandoning diplomatic efforts,' she expressed. The U.N. His aides reiterated that discussions regarding NAFTA should be postponed until after the election scheduled for next year. Lopez Obrador, who is the frontrunner in most surveys ahead of the July election, presented a platform that proposed a frugal government aimed at eliminating corruption and reallocating funds towards public infrastructure and social initiatives without imposing new taxes or increasing the debt-to-GDP ratio. He countered assertions that he would implement socialist policies akin to those in Venezuela if he were to win. "Let’s be very clear, we are not inspired by any foreign governments, neither Maduro nor Trump," Lopez Obrador stated, referring to Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and U.S. President Donald Trump. Known popularly as AMLO, the seasoned leftist is attempting his third presidential run, this time aiming to cultivate closer relationships with the business sector while softening some policies to counteract opponents who argue he would devastate Mexico's economy. Lopez Obrador has largely refrained from engaging in public disputes with Trump, who is generally detested in Mexico for his anti-Mexican remarks. On Monday, he expressed his intention to foster amicable relations with the U.S. government while insisting on respect. His team reiterated his stance that negotiations to revise the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) should be halted until after the elections in Mexico, as the administration of President Enrique Pena Nieto would not adequately represent Mexico's interests. "A government like this ... lacks the necessary legitimacy to represent the interests of the country in this negotiation," commented Hector Vasconcelos, a former diplomat involved in drafting the government strategy, during the event. Currently, negotiators from the U.S., Mexico, and Canada are engaged in a fifth round of discussions in Mexico City, following Trump's insistence that the agreement be revised to favor the United States. These discussions are expected to conclude in early 2018. The two-time presidential runner-up's agenda also includes plans to explore the development of new oil refineries capable of processing 300,000 barrels daily. text: Philippine authorities have been compelled to cease drug surveys and testing in the largest and most populated region of the capital after a group of lawyers representing local residents lodged a petition with a court, a police official reported on Tuesday. A significant number of residents had undergone surveys, and several hundred had participated in testing as part of a door-to-door anti-narcotics initiative in two neighborhoods within Quezon City, Manila, since May this year, aligning with President Rodrigo Duterte's aggressive campaign against drugs. Human rights advocates and critics of Duterte have claimed that the tests carried out by law enforcement amounted to harassment that could jeopardize the safety of individuals who tested positive. Activists assert that numerous users have lost their lives amid the anti-drug initiative, frequently at the hands of unidentified gunmen. According to Guillermo Eleazar, the police chief of Quezon City, community representatives are still permitted to visit the city's 142 districts to solicit residents' participation in surveys regarding drug use and to undergo voluntary urine testing. "The police will no longer have an active role in the anti-drug activities," Eleazar informed Reuters, following a court session concerning the petition to terminate police testing. "Our uniformed personnel will now be restricted to providing security and visibility at the request of our barangay (community) officials. They will no longer engage in inquiries or collect urine samples," he stated. This decision arises as Philippine law enforcement faces heightened media scrutiny regarding their actions in an anti-narcotics campaign that has resulted in the deaths of thousands of Filipinos over the past 15 months, raising concerns among human rights observers. Activists and certain opposition figures have charged Duterte with implementing a lethal policy intended to eradicate alleged drug dealers instead of apprehending them. Both Duterte and the police deny these allegations, asserting that those killed had aggressively resisted arrest. Eleazar remarked that the drug tests administered by police were voluntary and not forced. He noted that the court did not issue a restraining order since he assured the judge that each community would determine its own programs, with police serving only in a supportive capacity. Eleazar acknowledged that some police personnel were "over-zealous" in conducting house-to-house surveys and tests, but he contended that the petitioners were incorrect to hold police accountable, as they were merely trying to assist. "The petitioners are barking up at the wrong tree," he expressed. "They should petition the court to prevent the barangays from conducting these anti-drug surveys and tests." The National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL) stated that they anticipated the police would shift the blame. "This sudden change in stance by the police is undoubtedly a response to public outcry and the legal action," the NUPL asserted in a statement.

text: BANGKOK (Reuters) - Authorities in Chonburi province, situated in southeastern Thailand, prepared for additional protests on Wednesday following a rare demonstration the previous day in which hundreds of irate residents expressed their dissatisfaction with bureaucratic inefficiency. Locals voiced their frustrations over lengthy wait times exceeding 12 hours and the overall disarray associated with the ceremonies commemorating the late King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who was cremated in Bangkok last week in a ceremony that cost $90 million. This protest took place in defiance of a junta-imposed restriction on gatherings of more than five individuals, a measure that has been enforced since the coup in May 2014. Additionally, it is uncommon to see such protests, as topics concerning the monarchy are particularly sensitive in Thailand; the royals benefit from strict lese-majeste laws that penalize any perceived disrespect toward them. However, the demonstrations in Chonburi were aimed at local officials rather than the monarchy itself. On Tuesday, protesters in the coastal province chanted "Get out!" while demanding the resignation of provincial governor Pakarathon Tienchai, citing inadequate organization of the funeral ceremonies. Many participants donned yellow, the color associated with the king. Similar demands for the resignation of the governor of Nonthaburi province, located north of Bangkok, have also surfaced. On Tuesday, Chonburi Governor Pakarathon addressed the crowd, asserting that his team had not mishandled the event. Prime Minister Prayuth Chan-ocha called on Thais on Tuesday to pardon those involved in organizing the funeral and to overlook any arising issues, stating, "The number of people who took part in the funeral caused a few problems." Hundreds of thousands of attendees came to pay their respects at King Bhumibol's funeral in Bangkok last week. The late monarch, who reigned for over seventy years, was regarded as a father figure. For those who could not travel to Bangkok, 85 miniature replicas of the cremation pyre were set up throughout Thailand, with hundreds of designated areas for mourners to lay flowers. Some argued that the organizational failures highlighted the stark class divide in Thailand. Chonburi protesters expressed dissatisfaction with the $90 million allocated for the funeral. The late king often emphasized self-sufficiency and was characterized as a modest individual despite his considerable wealth. Others contended that government officials received preferential treatment when it came to laying flowers, as noted by Tanarit Kumwivat from Chiang Mai in a Facebook post, stating, "Officials went first before the public." The Chonburi protest signifies the conclusion of an era. King Bhumibol, often referred to as "the people's king," was a rare symbol of unity in a politically fractured nation, and his passing has left many Thais apprehensive about what lies ahead.

text: Western nations are calling on Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi to advocate for an end to the violence. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Monday, leaders from Britain, France, and Australia urged Myanmar's leader Aung San Suu Kyi to take action to halt the military aggression against Rohingya Muslims. Meanwhile, her national security adviser indicated that those who have fled the country could return, but the details of this process need to be discussed. The military's response to insurgent attacks in the western part of Myanmar last month has caused over 410,000 Rohingya Muslims to escape to Bangladesh, fleeing what the United Nations has denounced as ethnic cleansing. The government reports that around 400 individuals have died in the conflict. "We will ensure that everyone who has left their homes can return, but this is a process that we need to talk about," Myanmar's national security adviser Thaung Tun told Reuters on Monday following a ministerial meeting focused on the crisis, which was organized by Britain alongside the United Nations General Assembly. "We want to guarantee that everyone requiring humanitarian support receives it, without bias. That is one of the agreements we reached," he stated. Nobel laureate Suu Kyi has encountered significant international backlash for her failure to curb the violence. She is scheduled to address the nation on Tuesday regarding the crisis, which the United States has termed a "defining moment" for Myanmar. "We anticipate a strong statement from Mrs. Aung San Suu Kyi tomorrow in this regard," French Foreign Minister Jean-Yves le Drian told reporters in New York. British Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson led a ministerial meeting aimed at discussing solutions to the Rohingya crisis, which involved ministers from Canada, Denmark, Turkey, Australia, Indonesia, Sweden, Bangladesh, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley, and a representative from the European Union. "Our aim is to achieve consensus that, firstly, the killings must cease, and the violence must end. We are looking not only to the military but also to Daw Suu to take the lead on this," Johnson remarked to Reuters prior to the meeting. After the meeting, Johnson expressed that while Myanmar has made commendable strides toward democracy in recent years, the circumstances in Rakhine, along with severe human rights violations and violence, tarnish the country’s image. "It is crucial for Aung San Suu Kyi and the civilian government to clearly communicate that these abuses must be halted," he stated. Johnson mentioned he was "encouraged by our discussion and the involvement of senior Burmese officials, but we now require concrete actions to stop the violence and facilitate immediate humanitarian access." China, which has sought to strengthen ties with Myanmar, a strategically significant nation in Southeast Asia, will not be present, citing a "really packed calendar" for Foreign Minister Wang Yi, as per a Chinese spokesperson. Turkish Foreign Minister Mevlut Cavusoglu informed Reuters before the British meeting that a sustainable political resolution must be established for the Rohingya in Myanmar. Prior to the recent unrest, nearly one million Rohingya were residing in Rakhine State. The majority face strict travel limitations and are denied citizenship in a nation where many Buddhists perceive them as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop stated to Reuters that she hopes to hear Suu Kyi propose a solution to what she described as a tragedy of immense scale. She noted that during the ministerial meeting in New York, there was unanimous agreement on the necessity for the violence to cease and for a ceasefire to be established. "We stressed the importance of humanitarian assistance being allowed through, and also that the Rohingya must have the opportunity to return home," Bishop said. The United States has urged the Myanmar government to terminate military operations in Rakhine state, provide humanitarian access, and commit to facilitating the safe return of civilians to their residences, as Haley articulated in a statement following the meeting. text: 'A surge of humanity' challenges aid organizations in Bangladesh. DHAKA/KUTUPALONG, Bangladesh (Reuters) - What is the best way to feed and provide shelter for nearly 500,000 distressed individuals who have arrived within a single month to a stretch of monsoon-drenched land already home to 300,000 refugees living in dire conditions? This is the dilemma faced by aid workers rushing to support the Rohingya Muslims now congregated in the Cox's Bazar area of southern Bangladesh after a wave of violence in Myanmar's Rakhine state drove them to flee across the border. According to Christopher Lom, Asia-Pacific spokesperson for the International Organization for Migration (IOM), nothing similar in terms of the rapid influx of people has occurred since 1994 in Rwanda. The United Nations estimates that around 480,000 men, women, and children have arrived in Cox's Bazar since late August, with most having arrived with little more than the clothing on their backs. Since their arrival, nearly 200 women have given birth, and another 20,000 are expecting. Addressing the needs of such a large population - indefinitely, as there is no alternative location for them - in one of the poorest regions of a struggling country presents a logistical challenge for the Bangladeshi government, U.N. agencies, and humanitarian organizations. A preview of what was to unfold occurred in October and November of the previous year when a smaller outbreak of violence led to an influx of 80,000 Rohingya. This prompted enhancements in infrastructure and coordination in Cox's Bazar, noted Robert Watkins, the United Nations' local chief coordinator. 'It was functioning exceptionally well,' he remarked. 'Then we encountered this surge of humanity, and we were inundated.' U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Filippo Grandi stated following a visit to Cox's Bazar this week that the most pressing requirements are shelter, clean water, and sanitation. 'The primary task, the foremost challenge, is to relocate people from the mud and despair in which they find themselves to a place where organized assistance can be rendered,' he expressed at a news conference in Geneva. 'The combination of inadequate health services, poor sanitation and hygiene conditions, and overcrowded sites... presents a dire risk for potential epidemics.' As of now, 475 tonnes of aid have been delivered to Chittagong airport, situated north of Cox's Bazar, much of which has come from Muslim-majority nations appalled by the violence and destruction of villages in northwestern Rakhine, which U.N. officials have labeled as ethnic cleansing. While the initial response was chaotic due to the overwhelming number of people arriving, according to aid specialists, Bangladesh has since received some commendation for its improvements in organization. During a meeting on September 14 at the prime minister's office in Dhaka, the authorities made 22 decisions aimed at alleviating logistical challenges. A document reviewed by Reuters indicated these included the construction of 14 storage facilities, regulating aid distribution, protecting orphans, building roads and power infrastructure, and establishing shelters for over 500,000 individuals. Mohammad Shah Kamal, the secretary of disaster management and relief for Bangladesh and the main coordinator of the aid initiative, mentioned that the armed forces are inspecting shipments of aid and transporting them from airports and ports to Cox's Bazar, where local officials oversee distribution. 'I believe everyone has been taken aback by the Bangladeshi government,' remarked Karim Elguindi, a senior World Food Program official in Cox's Bazar, highlighting that it was 'expediting everything,' providing police assistance, and resolving customs delays. However, the Inter-Sector Coordination Group, which is managing the humanitarian response to the influx of Rohingya, recently stated that basic coordination remains inadequate as staff and agencies have not been assigned to specific camps. Bangladesh aims to accommodate new arrivals by constructing a 2,000-acre camp in the Ukhia region of Cox's Bazar. The U.N. indicates that a significant portion of this area is not suitable.

text: Trump's recent appointment of Scaramucci makes a friendly start with the press. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - If President Donald Trump, who labels the media as "fake news," desires his team to adopt a more amicable stance towards journalists, new communications director Anthony Scaramucci might be initiating that change - at least for the time being. The Wall Street financier and Republican fundraiser entered the White House briefing room on Friday and immediately did what Sean Spicer, the previous press secretary, failed to do on his first day in January: interact, in a cordial manner, with reporters. Clad in a blue tie and an American flag pin on a dark suit, Scaramucci engaged in light-hearted exchanges with correspondents, committed to transparency, and even made courteous remarks about CNN, the cable channel with which Trump and Spicer have had ongoing disputes. He poked fun at himself, humorously referencing his height and offering apologies to Trump from the podium for having labeled the New York businessman a hack politician back in 2015. "He brings it up every 15 seconds, all right?" Scaramucci remarked, eliciting laughter, while referring to the president. "I should have never said that about him. So, Mr. President, if you’re listening, I personally apologize for the 50th time for saying that." Trump was likely attentive. Reporters bombarded Scaramucci with inquiries regarding press-related matters that have impacted the relationship between the Trump administration and the journalists covering it. When asked if he endorsed having briefings broadcast, he replied, "I obviously am committed to being transparent because I’m standing here. But I’d like to discuss that with the president." He pointed out that CNN had issued an apology when it reported something incorrect about him and that he had accepted that apology. "There feels like there’s a little bit of media bias, and so what we hope we can do is de-escalate that and turn that around. And let’s let the message from the president get out there to the American people," he stated. He also announced that the new press secretary to succeed Spicer, who resigned earlier that Friday, would be Sarah Sanders. Spicer’s first appearance at the White House podium in January included a lengthy reprimand of reporters for their depiction of the attendance figures during Trump’s Inauguration Day. When asked on Friday if he concurred with Trump’s assertion, for which there is no evidence, that 3 million individuals voted illegally in the 2016 election, Scaramucci responded cautiously. "So if the president says it, let me do more research on it, but my guess is that there’s probably some level of truth to that," he expressed. "I think what we have found sometimes is that when the president says things, some of you in the media believe it’s not true or it isn’t true, and it turns out it’s closer to the truth than people think."

text: TRIPOLI (Reuters) - On Thursday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian emphasized that Libya's competing factions should adhere to a United Nations peace initiative and prepare for elections scheduled for spring 2018, in an effort to reinvigorate stalled U.N. negotiations. The North African nation is currently divided between two rival governments: one located in the east and a U.N.-recognized administration in Tripoli, the capital of the west, amid ongoing conflict that originated from the ousting of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. France played a significant role in the NATO-led intervention against Gaddafi, deploying warplanes to target his military forces. In September, the United Nations initiated a fresh round of discussions in Tunis between the opposing factions to lay the groundwork for presidential and parliamentary elections in 2018; however, those talks were suspended after just one month. "I noted the desire from the Prime Minister (Fayez al-Seraj) to stick to the calendar. We have a total convergence of views to implement this agenda," Le Drian remarked following his meeting with the Tripoli-based prime minister in the Libyan capital. Later, Le Drian is set to travel to Benghazi, located in the east, to engage with the influential eastern military leader Khalifa Haftar, who declared on Sunday that the U.N.-recognized government and peace process are outdated. The U.N. negotiations have faced challenges regarding Haftar's potential role. He expressed on Sunday his intention to run as a candidate for the presidency. While Haftar enjoys popularity among eastern Libyans who are exhausted by the ongoing turmoil, he encounters resistance in western Libya. On Tuesday, the eastern-based House of Representatives deepened the rift between the east and west by endorsing a new governor for the central bank. Both the bank's headquarters in Tripoli and the U.N. have rejected this decision. text: The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Wednesday to support North Carolina's appeal to reinstate several voting restrictions for the upcoming elections in November, which included a stipulation requiring voters to present identification at polling stations. The eight-member court, which was largely split 4-4, dismissed a request from Republican Governor Pat McCrory following an appellate court's ruling last month that determined the 2013 legislation was discriminatory towards minority voters. An emergency request requires five votes to be approved. "We’re thrilled. Elections in North Carolina this fall are going to be conducted under a fair and nondiscriminatory election law scheme," stated Allison Riggs, an attorney representing the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, one of the civil rights organizations that contested the law. The U.S. Justice Department, which has actively opposed the legislation, did not provide immediate commentary on the ruling. McCrory expressed in a statement that the state "has been denied basic voting rights already granted to more than 30 other states to protect the integrity of one person, one vote through a common-sense voter ID law." The brief order indicated that three conservative justices on the court, including Chief Justice John Roberts, would have permitted the voter identification requirement and restrictions on early voting to remain in effect for the election. Justice Clarence Thomas concurred on that matter, but was the only justice to indicate he would have also allowed the requirement preventing pre-registration of 16-year-olds to remain intact. The lawyers for McCrory argued that the current situation should not be altered so close to the election, referencing judicial precedents that support their position. On July 29, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Richmond, Virginia, determined that the law was intentionally discriminatory against minority voters. That same court declined to pause its ruling for the election on November 8. Opponents argue that such laws, enacted in states governed by Republicans, complicate voting for minorities like African-Americans and Hispanics, who generally lean towards the Democratic Party. Proponents assert that these laws are essential to combat voter fraud. Following the death of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia in February, the court is currently one justice short, which likely prevented the conservative justices from obtaining the fifth vote required to approve the request. The Supreme Court may still be called upon to consider additional voting restrictions as the election approaches, with several cases awaiting resolution in lower courts.

text: The governor of Florida has dismissed a prosecutor who opposed the death penalty. TAMPA, Fla. (Reuters) - On Thursday, Florida Governor Rick Scott took action to replace a local prosecutor who announced her intention not to pursue the death penalty in a case involving a man accused of murdering an Orlando police officer and who also refused to step aside. In an executive order, Scott removed Aramis Ayala, the elected State Attorney for the Ninth Judicial Circuit in central Florida, and assigned the murder case to State Attorney Brad King from the adjacent Fifth Judicial Circuit. Earlier that day, during a press conference, Ayala stated that Florida's death penalty system resulted in “legal chaos” and indicated she would not pursue capital punishment against Markeith Loyd, who is charged with the shooting of the policewoman on January 9. Loyd was apprehended following a thorough manhunt that garnered significant public attention. Ayala's comments, made shortly after she took office this year, prompted outrage among law enforcement agencies, certain state legislators, and State Attorney General Pam Bondi. Conversely, groups such as Amnesty International USA and the NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund came to her support. In a statement, Scott remarked, “She has made it clear that she will not fight for justice and that is why I am using my executive authority to immediately reassign the case to State Attorney Brad King.” Following a conversation with Scott on Thursday afternoon, Ayala released a statement in which she expressed her willingness to have “a full conversation” regarding her decision, but noted that he “declined to explore my reasoning.” “Upon receipt of any lawful order, my office will follow that order and fully cooperate to ensure the successful prosecution of Markeith Loyd,” she stated. On Monday, Florida's governor enacted legislation that tightens state regulations to mandate a unanimous jury recommendation before judges can impose the death penalty. This law represents the state's latest attempt to resume its death penalty procedures, which faced suspension twice last year due to rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court and the Florida Supreme Court in different cases. Loyd was taken into custody on January 7 after a nine-day manhunt that ensued following the fatal shooting of Orlando police Master Sergeant Debra Clayton. Some of these inmates have been awaiting execution since the 1970s, as the appeals process for death penalty sentences can extend over many years.

text: U.S. military investigates additional potential civilian casualties in Yemen operation. DOVER AIR FORCE BASE, Del. (Reuters) - On Wednesday, the U.S. military announced that it was examining the possibility of more civilian deaths resulting from a raid on al Qaeda in Yemen that took place over the weekend, marking the first military action sanctioned by President Donald Trump as commander in chief. U.S. Navy SEAL William “Ryan” Owens lost his life during the raid targeting an al Qaeda faction, known as AQAP, in al Bayda province, with the Pentagon reporting that 14 militants were also killed. However, medics present at the site claimed that around 30 individuals, including 10 women and children, were killed. U.S. Central Command released a statement indicating that a team investigating the incident had “regrettably concluded that civilian non-combatants were likely killed” in the operation conducted on Sunday, noting that children might have been among the deceased. Central Command's assessment aims to ascertain whether there were any undetected civilian casualties during the intense firefight. U.S. military officials informed Reuters that Trump executed his first covert counterterrorism mission without adequate intelligence, ground support, or sufficient backup arrangements. Consequently, three officials reported that the SEAL team encountered a fortified al Qaeda stronghold, defended by landmines, snipers, and a larger-than-anticipated number of heavily armed Islamist fighters. The Pentagon deferred inquiries regarding the characterization of the raid by officials to U.S. Central Command, which only referred back to its statement made on Wednesday. “CENTCOM requests operations that we believe have a high likelihood of success, and when we seek authorization, we certainly believe there is a chance for successful operations based on our planning,” stated CENTCOM spokesman Colonel John Thomas. He added, “Any operation involving ground personnel carries inherent risks.” According to U.S. officials, the extremists’ location had been recognized as a target prior to the conclusion of the Obama administration on January 20, but then-President Barack Obama refrained from approving a raid before leaving office. A White House official conveyed that the operation had been thoroughly assessed by the previous administration and received approval from the former defense secretary in January. The raid was postponed for operational considerations, the official mentioned. Military officials who spoke to Reuters under conditions of anonymity indicated that “a brutal firefight” claimed the lives of Owens and at least 15 Yemeni women and children. text: Insults are rampant on the Republican campaign trail! WASHINGTON (Reuters) - For several months, candidates vying for the Republican presidential nomination have exchanged insults like "dummy," "jerk," and "loser." Recently, front-runner Donald Trump echoed a supporter’s term for Ted Cruz, referring to him as a "pussy." As the contest for the party's nomination heads into South Carolina with rising stakes, it appears that the most derogatory rhetoric of the November 8 election campaign may still be forthcoming. While this type of language might resemble that of schoolyard bullies, there is evidence that candidates are enjoying the attention it brings. The most severe attacks tend to provoke the greatest reactions at rallies, on social media, and on cable news. Trump, the wealthy former reality television star, ignited excitement at a rally in New Hampshire on Monday when he repeated the word "pussy" shouted by an audience member, effectively challenging Cruz’s masculinity. The following day, Trump secured victory in the state's primary, beating Cruz, who came in third, by a margin of 3-to-1. "It’s one of the reasons I won. You have to be yourself," Trump stated during an interview on NBC’s Today show. He later vowed to improve his use of language and adopt a more presidential demeanor. Historical trends indicate that the language could become even more vulgar as the Republican nominating contest in South Carolina approaches next Saturday. In that state, U.S. Senator John McCain of Arizona faced accusations in 2000 of having an illegitimate African-American child, and former Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney was accused in 2008 of endorsing polygamy. "These adults are behaving like elementary school children," remarked Leslie McRobbie, a former fifth-grade teacher from New Hampshire, regarding this year's Republican candidates. President Barack Obama, a Democrat, reflected this week on the sarcasm that marked a previous Republican race, recalling how rivals referred to Ronald Reagan as an "unshapely man" and a "yahoo" prior to his 1980 presidential election. Following the initial nominating contests in Iowa and New Hampshire, the seven remaining candidates for the Republican nomination are feeling the pressure to either distinguish themselves from the pack or hinder others from doing so. Insults can help achieve that. Former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, who has been derided by Trump as a "low-energy" candidate, has responded by tweeting that Trump is "not just a loser," but also a "liar and a whiner." This insult garnered nearly 3,000 retweets and over 4,000 likes. Cruz, reacting to Trump’s choice to skip a Fox News-hosted Republican debate, labeled his opponent "Ducking Donald" and launched a special edition filter on the Snapchat app that featured a duck with blonde hair and an exaggerated pout, intended to symbolize the real-estate mogul. "When we center so much of the modern campaign around the personalities involved rather than issues, the inevitable result is name-calling," commented political scientist Michael Artime. He noted that while disputes and name-calling have always been part of elections, this cycle has seen a significant increase in negativity. "In previous elections, if someone had made a statement like what Trump said the other night, it would have severely harmed their campaign," Artime explained. "The type of politics we engage in is the kind we deserve," he added. While many have watched with delight or indifference as candidates traded barbs, there are those who have criticized it. "Bullying can be quite effective and used for personal advancement," stated Bob Faris, an associate professor of sociology at the University of California-Davis, who studies aggressive behavior in young people. "And it is effective," he noted, "as long as children target the appropriate peers." For Trump, who is arguably the most boisterous of the candidates, the focus of his attacks is constantly shifting, with his poll numbers remaining stable as he criticizes opponents for being "stupid," "weak," and "pathetic." "He does appear to be a bully," Faris commented.

text: European nations urge U.S. to present comprehensive proposals for Middle East peace. UNITED NATIONS (Reuters) - On Friday, Britain, France, Germany, Sweden, and Italy urged the United States to deliver detailed peace proposals aimed at resolving the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians, criticizing President Donald Trump's decision to recognize Jerusalem as the capital of Israel as counterproductive. Trump's shift in U.S. policy on Wednesday ignited a Palestinian 'day of rage' on Friday, leading to thousands of Palestinians protesting, with numerous injuries reported and at least one death occurring during confrontations with Israeli forces. In response to the rising anger in the Arab world and apprehension among Washington's Western partners, the United Nations Security Council convened on Friday upon the request of eight of its 15 members - Britain, France, Sweden, Bolivia, Uruguay, Italy, Senegal, and Egypt. Following the meeting, Britain, France, Germany, Sweden, and Italy issued a joint statement declaring that the U.S. decision, which includes the intention to relocate the U.S. embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, was 'unhelpful' regarding the prospects for peace in the area. 'We are prepared to support all credible initiatives to revive the peace process, based on internationally accepted parameters leading to a two-State solution,' they stated. 'We urge the U.S. Administration to now present concrete proposals for an Israel-Palestinian settlement.' Egypt's U.N. Ambassador Amr Aboulatta remarked that the U.S. decision would have a 'grave, negative impact' on the peace process. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley asserted that Washington holds credibility as a mediator with both Israel and the Palestinians, while accusing the United Nations of undermining rather than fostering peace prospects through biased criticisms of Israel. 'Israel will never be, and should never be, coerced into an agreement by the United Nations, or any group of nations that have shown a lack of respect for Israel's security,' Haley stated. She emphasized that Trump is dedicated to the peace process and that the United States has not taken a stance on the borders or boundaries of Jerusalem and is not pushing for any alterations to the arrangements at the holy sites. 'Our actions are aimed at promoting the peace agenda,' she expressed. 'We believe we may be closer to that objective than ever before.' Earlier on Friday, U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, during a press conference in Paris, indicated that any ultimate decision regarding the status of Jerusalem would rely on negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians. United Nations Middle East envoy Nickolay Mladenov cautioned that there exists a risk of escalating violence. 'Today, there is a serious danger that we may witness a series of unilateral actions which can only take us further away from achieving our common goal of peace,' Mladenov informed the U.N. Security Council. Israel regards all of Jerusalem as its capital, while Palestinians seek the eastern portion of the city as the capital of a prospective independent state. The majority of nations view East Jerusalem, which was annexed by Israel following its capture in the 1967 Middle East War, as occupied territory, including the Old City, which houses sites sacred to Muslims, Jews, and Christians alike. A U.N. Security Council resolution passed in December of the previous year emphasizes that it will not acknowledge any modifications to the borders established on June 4, 1967, including concerning Jerusalem, except those agreed upon by the parties through negotiations. That resolution was adopted with 14 votes in favor and an abstention from the administration of former U.S. President Barack Obama, which resisted significant pressure from long-time ally Israel and Trump, who was then the president-elect, for Washington to use its veto.

text: Poll Indicates Gentiloni as Italy's Most Trusted Political Figure. ROME (Reuters) - Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni continues to be recognized as Italy's most reliable leader, while Luigi Di Maio of the 5-Star Movement has ascended to second place, surpassing former Prime Minister Matteo Renzi for the first time, as revealed in a poll released on Wednesday. The Ixe survey regarding the leaders of major political parties indicated that 39 percent of voters express confidence in Gentiloni, who assumed office in December after Renzi stepped down following a referendum defeat on constitutional changes. Italy is scheduled to conduct national elections by May, and Renzi has announced his intention to run for prime minister representing his Democratic Party (PD). Gentiloni, who is also affiliated with the PD, is anticipated to revert to the ranks upon the dissolution of parliament. In contrast, 27 percent expressed trust in Renzi, compared to 32 percent for Di Maio, who was selected as the prime ministerial candidate for the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement in September, enhancing his public profile and reputation. In the preceding Ixe leadership survey conducted in August, Gentiloni held an approval rating of 32 percent, Renzi was at 25 percent, and Di Maio recorded 18 percent. Roberto Weber, who conducted the Ixe poll, remarked on Rai Radio that people likely find Gentiloni's calm demeanor reassuring. Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right Northern League party, received a rating of 27 percent, while Giorgia Meloni, the head of the right-wing Brothers of Italy party, stood at 26 percent. Their ally Silvio Berlusconi, who considers himself the natural leader of the center-right coalition, was left behind with a rating of 21 percent. In the last survey, both he and Meloni were at 17 percent. Current opinion polls suggest that the 5-Star Movement and PD parties are nearly tied at approximately 27 percent, with the Northern League at 15 percent, Berlusconi's Forza Italia (Go Italy!) party around 13 percent, and Brothers of Italy just below 4 percent. A new electoral system that was legislated last month is expected to lead to a hung parliament in the upcoming election, with no single party or coalition likely to secure enough seats to govern independently.

text: Clinton aims to engage young voters through a new fundraising initiative. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Hillary Clinton, the leading Democratic candidate for president, initiated an effort on Thursday to attract young voters and small contributors to her campaign, focusing on the advantages of her competitor, Bernie Sanders, as she prepares for the general election. Named “for45” - referring to Clinton's goal of becoming the 45th president of the United States - the organization will provide associate level memberships starting at $250, as indicated in an invitation obtained by Reuters for an event scheduled in Philadelphia on April 25. “We will have an opportunity to fundraise and host low-dollar events, speaking to what we are passionate about and why we support her,” stated Akilah Ensley, a 32-year-old supporter of Clinton who plans to join the group. “It’s important that we engage.” The group conducted its inaugural conference call on Thursday, which included the Clinton campaign’s finance director, Dennis Cheng, along with other campaign officials, and actress Lena Dunham, according to an invitation for the call. The information sheet reviewed by Reuters reveals that the group consists of two additional tiers: a “member” level requiring a minimum fundraising of $2,500 and an “advisor” level necessitating at least $10,000 in fundraising. Neither the Clinton nor the Sanders campaigns responded to requests for comments. The creation of this group highlights the difficulties the former secretary of state faces in winning over young voters who have been instrumental in Sanders’ campaign. Younger voters represent a vital voting demographic and source of financial support should she secure the Democratic nomination for the presidential election on November 8. Clinton currently holds a significant lead in delegates over Sanders, the senator from Vermont, and bolstered her position by winning the primary in New York earlier this week. However, she has faced challenges in appealing to younger voters. Although she achieved a 16-point victory in New York on Tuesday, Sanders garnered 65 percent of Democratic voters aged 18 to 29, according to exit polls from Edison Research published in the New York Times. Younger voters have also shown greater support for Sanders in various other states. Sanders frequently highlights his average donation amount of $27, leading rally attendees to shout this figure alongside him. Steve Schale, a Democratic strategist based in Florida who does not have ties to the Clinton campaign, remarked that for45 is a “smart way” to start winning over Sanders’ supporters. He likened it to the “Gen44” group of young voters that rallied behind President Barack Obama. “Anything that encourages people to invest financially fosters a sense of ownership in the campaign,” he noted.

text: Saudi Arabia is planning to begin issuing tourist visas to international travelers next year, according to a high-ranking official speaking to CNN, as the nation aims to liberalize its traditionally conservative society and discover alternative revenue streams to diversify its economy. Currently, the entry of foreigners into Saudi Arabia is primarily limited to expatriate workers and their families, business visitors, and Muslim pilgrims who obtain special visas to visit sacred sites. "The focus is on individuals who wish to come and truly engage with this nation, exploring its grandeur," stated Prince Sultan bin Salman bin Abdulaziz, who leads the Saudi Commission for Tourism and Natural Heritage, during an interview aired late Wednesday. When questioned about the visa initiative, he expressed optimism for 2018, noting that the government plans to utilize online systems to simplify the visa application process. The 32-year-old Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, heir to the Saudi throne, is working to cultivate new sectors to reduce the country’s reliance on oil revenues. He has also initiated some measures to ease the stringent social regulations, including diminishing the influence of the religious morality police and announcing that women will be permitted to drive starting next year. Discussions about welcoming substantial numbers of international tourists have occurred for several years, often hindered by conservative viewpoints and bureaucratic obstacles; a similar initiative was proposed as far back as 2006 but did not materialize. This time, the government seems committed to implementing the change, partly in response to financial constraints. It aims to generate billions of dollars to address a state budget deficit resulting from decreased oil prices. Economic reforms are projected to boost total tourism expenditure in the country—from both local citizens and international visitors—to $46.6 billion by 2020, up from $27.9 billion in 2015. Prince Sultan mentioned that the commission is primarily concentrating on increasing the number of domestic tourists. The commission estimates that Saudi citizens spend over $20 billion each year on tourism outside the country, and encouraging more of them to vacation domestically could alleviate that economic outflow. However, Prince Sultan also informed CNN that his commission is preparing tourist attractions for international visitors. In August, the government revealed plans to develop resorts on approximately 50 islands along the Red Sea coast, with the initial phase of the project expected to be completed by 2022. The kingdom also plans to facilitate access to historical sites like Mada'in Saleh, a 2,000-year-old Nabatean city sculpted into the rock formations of the northern desert. Crown Prince Mohammed would mark the first ruler from a new generation since 1953, following six kings, all of whom were sons of the state’s founder, Abdulaziz ibn Saud. He has unveiled extensive proposals for social and political reforms within the kingdom, which operates as an absolute monarchy influenced by a powerful clergy that follows Wahhabism, a strict interpretation of Sunni Islam.

text: The European Union has set an absolute deadline of 10 days for Prime Minister Theresa May to enhance her Brexit divorce proposal, or she risks failing to convince EU leaders to initiate trade negotiations with Britain during the summit in December. Without an agreement next month, there will be limited time to finalize arrangements before the UK exits the EU in March 2019, placing additional pressure on businesses to prevent potential losses and relocate investments. European Council President Donald Tusk tweeted after a one-hour meeting with May in Brussels following an EU summit, stating, "We need to see progress from the UK within 10 days on all issues, including Ireland." The situation regarding the Northern Ireland border became unexpectedly more complicated on Friday as the Dublin government appeared on the verge of collapse. Tusk mentioned that it is still feasible for the other 27 EU leaders to determine at the summit on December 14-15 that Britain has made "sufficient progress" toward fulfilling three crucial conditions necessary for them to approve the start of trade negotiations in the coming year. However, the former Polish premier, who leads the bloc's summit meetings, added that it remains a significant challenge. EU officials anticipate that the critical moment will arrive when May meets with European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker and his chief Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier on Monday, December 4. According to an EU official, Tusk laid out the timeline with December 4 as the absolute deadline for the UK to make further efforts, allowing Barnier to be in a position to suggest sufficient progress. May accepted this timeframe. The UK must provide credible assurances on how to avoid a hard border by December 4, as the method for achieving this remains unclear, the official stated. An additional complication arises from Ireland, where Prime Minister Leo Varadkar, who has warned of a veto without significant British movement on the border issue, may call for a snap election next week over a different matter. Following her meeting with Tusk, May informed reporters that both sides are still working towards bridging gaps on a financial settlement, rights for expatriates post-Brexit, and how to prevent a hard border that could jeopardize peace in Northern Ireland. However, she noted, "There are still issues across the various matters that we are negotiating on to be resolved." She reiterated a statement she first made in September, asserting that Britain would "honour our commitments." Yet, there has been no indication of the specifics that EU counterparts are requesting regarding payments before they agree to London's request for discussions on a post-Brexit trade agreement. On the subject of the Irish border, May stated, "We and the Irish government continue to talk about solutions for that. We have the same desire. We want to ensure that movement of people and trade across that border can carry on as now." For months, the EU's demand for Britain to pay around 60 billion euros ($72 billion) has appeared to be the most challenging issue to resolve. However, EU negotiators have been buoyed by apparent leaks from the British media suggesting that May has gained support from Brexit hardliners in her cabinet to propose a substantial sum. Now, the situation regarding Ireland could prove to be a hurdle. "The Irish issue is very worrying. The likelihood of sufficient progress in December is only 50-50. Now maybe less," a Brexit talks official from one of the other 27 EU states told Reuters on the sidelines of Friday's summit. Barnier expressed the Union's strong support for Ireland on Friday, informing Irish Foreign Minister Simon Coveney that there is "strong solidarity for Ireland" and that "Irish issues are EU issues." Coveney, who condemned the government's opponents for irresponsibly calling a no-confidence motion for Tuesday over an unrelated topic, stated that Ireland would not consent to the commencement of EU trade discussions with Britain if it is dissatisfied with the border situation. May's pro-Brexit allies from Northern Ireland, who are crucial for her slim parliamentary majority, accused Dublin of attempting to compel Northern Ireland, or the entire United Kingdom, to remain in a customs union.

text: Senate to consider Puerto Rico debt legislation: McConnell. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - This month, the U.S. Senate will deliberate on a bill that received overwhelming approval in the House of Representatives and seeks to provide Puerto Rico with some relief from its $70 billion debt, as stated by Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell on Tuesday. McConnell’s statement followed a briefing by several House members who informed their Republican colleagues in the Senate about the bill's contents, which proposes creating a federal oversight board to handle the restructuring of Puerto Rican debt. Proponents of the House-approved legislation are optimistic that the Senate will approve it before July 1, when Puerto Rico must address a $1.9 billion debt obligation. Representative Rob Bishop, the chair of the House Natural Resources Committee that guided the bill through the House, informed journalists that Republican senators inundated him with inquiries regarding the composition and authority of the oversight board. He reassured senators that the legislation does not constitute a taxpayer-funded bailout for Puerto Rico and that it will not affect U.S. states. As a U.S. territory, Puerto Rico has faced criticism from some who worry that a control board appointed by Washington may not prioritize the island’s welfare. The bill also received a slight boost on Tuesday when Senate Finance Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch expressed conditional support for the House proposal. He mentioned that he was contemplating possible amendments to the bill but did not provide details. Hatch’s Finance Committee oversees the Puerto Rico debt legislation. A number of Senate Democrats have also raised concerns regarding the bill and suggested they might pursue amendments, although it remains uncertain if they will follow through. Any modifications made by the Senate to the House-passed legislation would require it to return to the House for approval, rejection, or further amendments. Bishop acknowledged the possibility that July 1 could arrive with Congress still deliberating on the Puerto Rico bill. "It’s not the end of the world," Bishop remarked regarding the chance of Congress finalizing the legislation in July. Puerto Rico, grappling with a poverty rate of approximately 45 percent, has been severely affected by its escalating debt issues, leading to the closure of some schools and medical facilities, while many residents are relocating to the mainland United States, where they often find employment, particularly in central Florida.

text: Peru has suggested initiating discussions to preserve the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) following Donald Trump's firm opposition. LIMA (Reuters) - Peru has put forward a proposal for renewed negotiations to ensure the implementation of the U.S.-initiated Trans-Pacific Partnership after Donald Trump pledged to pull the United States out of the extensive trade agreement on the inaugural day of his presidency. Trade Minister Eduardo Ferreyros, who previously called on the global community not to restrict Trump based on his campaign views regarding the TPP, remarked that the comments made by the President-elect on Monday significantly altered the situation. "However, I believe it doesn’t eliminate it. We can work on it, modify it" so that its execution isn’t dependent on U.S. ratification, Ferreyros stated during an interview late on Monday with local television network Canal N. The TPP, which was signed earlier this year by the United States, Peru, and ten other nations along the Pacific coastline, was constructed in such a way that it cannot come into effect without the ratification from the United States, which has framed the agreement as a strategy to counter China’s ascent in the rapidly expanding Asia Pacific region. "We can adjust that clause and also take the opportunity to amend other clauses that may be inconvenient for us," Ferreyros commented. When asked if China could potentially join the TPP, Ferreyros affirmed this possibility but indicated that Beijing would first need to express interest. China has been advocating for a competing regional free trade agreement, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), which includes India but is not anticipated to feature significant tariff reductions or strong safeguards for labor, environmental concerns, or intellectual property rights, according to the administration of outgoing U.S. President Barack Obama. Beijing stated on Sunday that stringent standards in multilateral trade agreements deter participation from developing countries. On Tuesday, Peru revealed that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with China to revise their six-year-old bilateral free trade agreement, which currently does not encompass the textile and garment industries. Trump, who has characterized multilateral free trade agreements as detrimental to U.S. manufacturing employment, on Monday officially announced his intention to withdraw from the deal on his first day in office, seemingly paving the way for China to take on a leadership role in trade and diplomacy within Asia.
