text: The offer from New Zealand to accept 150 refugees may assist Australia in resolving the standoff in Papua New Guinea. WELLINGTON/SYDNEY (Reuters) - Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand announced her intention to propose the acceptance of 150 refugees currently in Australian custody during her meeting with Malcolm Turnbull on Sunday, providing Canberra with a potential reprieve from the ongoing situation at a detention facility in Papua New Guinea. For over three days, around 600 men have barricaded themselves within a camp on Manus Island, resisting attempts by Australia and Papua New Guinea to close it, despite the lack of food and running water. On Friday, New Zealand became the first nation to publicly express a willingness to intervene, as Ardern stated she would propose taking 150 refugees from Australia’s two isolated Pacific detention centers during her discussions with Turnbull in Sydney. "I anticipate that the situation on Manus Island will be a topic of discussion in my meeting with Prime Minister Turnbull on Sunday," Ardern noted in an email. "I plan to reaffirm our offer when we convene." This offer could provide Turnbull with a partial resolution to the Manus Island standoff, which the United Nations recently characterized as an emerging humanitarian crisis. Australia had previously turned down a similar proposal from former New Zealand Prime Minister John Key, citing concerns over the potential for relocated asylum seekers to move freely to Australia. Residents of New Zealand have the right to live in Australia without the need for visas. However, the center-right Australian government is advocating for stringent new regulations to prohibit any asylum seekers who arrived by boat post-2013 from being permitted entry into Australia, even as visitors. Despite increasing criticism, Australia remains committed to its strategy to close the Manus Island facility, where it holds asylum seekers who arrive by boat, as part of its contentious immigration policies, along with another center located in Nauru. Heavy rainfall throughout Papua New Guinea on Thursday assisted in refilling water storage containers on Manus, but food scarcity remains a significant concern for the detainees, many of whom hail from conflict-ridden countries such as Afghanistan, Iran, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Syria. They have pledged not to leave, even as many begin to experience the adverse effects of several days without food. "We will never move to another prison," declared Behrouz Boochani, a Kurdish journalist from Iran. "We will never accept anything less than freedom. Only freedom."

text: Cuban opposition stumbles at the outset as Castro transition approaches. HAVANA (Reuters) - Leaders of the Cuban opposition reported that they were unable to secure any nominations for candidates in the municipal elections, marking a setback as the Communist-led nation enters a political phase that will conclude six decades of governance by the Castro brothers. The municipal elections occurring this month are the initial step in a process that will culminate with a new national assembly electing a president in February to succeed 86-year-old Raul Castro, who has committed to stepping down after two consecutive five-year terms. Some Cubans are optimistic that the transfer of authority from the 1959 revolution's leaders to a younger generation might foster greater political transparency. Conversely, others do not anticipate or desire significant changes, highlighting that Castro will remain the head of the Communist Party, the sole legal political entity in Cuba. In the one aspect of Cuba's political process where dissidents have a chance of being successful, neighborhood nomination assemblies have recently selected candidates for elections to 12,515 local positions across the nation of 11 million inhabitants. Hundreds of dissidents had sought nominations, an unprecedented figure, yet none advanced to the list of 27,221 candidates, according to opposition electoral platforms Otro18 and Candidates for Change. Opposition leaders attributed their lack of success partly to oppressive actions by the authorities but asserted that their efforts demonstrated the existence of viable political alternatives. 'The grassroots democratization process has begun,' stated Manuel Cuesta Morua, spokesperson for Otro18. The government did not respond to a request for comment. Reuters could not verify the opposition's statistics, and their attempts were not covered by state media, meaning that most ordinary Cubans were unaware of them. In Cuba's provincial and national elections, candidates are nominated by commissions made up of representatives from organizations controlled by the Communist Party, such as the trade union federation. Cuban leaders assert that their elections are more democratic than those in the West, which they claim are plagued by corporate influence and corruption. The divided opposition has historically labeled Cuban elections a sham and has boycotted them. Nevertheless, over the past few years, new opposition electoral platforms have surfaced, claiming that the moment is right to instigate change from within the system. The election occurs at a sensitive moment as Cuba strives to maintain a thaw in relations with the United States and sustain its economy amid declining support from its key ally, Venezuela. Several dissidents informed Reuters that the authorities barred them from attending or speaking at neighborhood nomination assemblies, altering the dates or attempting to intimidate them. 'State security threatened me,' remarked Abdel Legra, who opted not to put himself forward for nomination as he wished to avoid putting his neighbors, the majority of whom are state employees, in jeopardy by supporting him. 'The issue is that the voting is conducted by hand count; it's public.' The election cycle's postponement by a month, attributed by authorities to damages caused by Hurricane Irma, disrupted plans for several dissidents who had already arranged trips abroad. The Communist Party maintains that it does not interfere in elections. However, in a leaked video, First Vice President Miguel Diaz-Canel, who is expected to succeed Castro, indicated that the party would attempt to undermine 'counter-revolutionary' candidates. Cuba classifies all dissenters as mercenaries funded by foreign governments and exiles, intending to overthrow the government. In 2015, two dissidents managed to secure nominations but claimed that election officials modified their biographies to suggest they had connections to 'counter-revolutionaries' based or funded from abroad. One of them, Hildebrando Chaviano, stated he did not attend his assembly this year, expressing that he believed it would be a 'circus.' He reported that authorities visited his neighbors days prior, cautioning them against voting for him. That assembly ultimately nominated the current municipal delegate, a party veteran.

Guterres expressed these views to journalists following his meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in Tokyo, shortly after U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson proposed initiating direct discussions with North Korea without any preconditions. He further noted that unity within the Security Council is essential for enabling potential diplomatic engagement that could lead to denuclearisation. He remarked, "The worst possible thing that could happen is for us all to sleepwalk into a war that might have very dramatic circumstances." Japan currently believes that it is crucial to maintain maximum pressure on Pyongyang rather than initiate discussions regarding the North's missile and nuclear endeavors. Conversely, China and Russia have expressed support for Tillerson's approach. Abe, addressing the press alongside Guterres, reiterated the importance of ensuring that dialogue is substantial and focused on denuclearisation. He stated, "We fully agreed that the denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula is indispensable for the peace and stability of the region." text: A memo from the State Department reveals the unconstitutional nature of President Donald Trump’s travel ban, according to the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - The ACLU contended in court documents submitted late Thursday that internal instructions from the State Department for executing Trump’s temporary travel ban on individuals from six predominantly Muslim nations illustrate that the ban breaches the constitution. This assertion was part of the ACLU's ongoing lawsuit in federal court in California's Northern District on behalf of three holders of student visas, challenging Trump’s executive order from March 6, which prohibits travelers from Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen from entering the United States for a period of 90 days, along with a four-month suspension on refugees. The lawsuit, which seeks to achieve class-action status, claims that the order is discriminatory against Muslims. text: The Trump administration made a move on Wednesday to modify the commencement date of its proposed 90-day travel restriction affecting individuals entering the United States from six predominantly Muslim nations, aiming to sustain its ongoing legal struggle. This modification seems designed to prevent the administration's case at the U.S. Supreme Court from becoming irrelevant due to the expiration of certain elements of the executive order. Opponents of the travel ban, asserting that the order is meant to discriminate against Muslims, have indicated in legal documents that it should lapse on Wednesday, which marks 90 days after the executive order was slated to take effect on March 16. A memorandum released by the White House, coinciding with the Supreme Court's deliberation on two challenges to the ban, stated that portions of the order that are currently on hold would not lapse before they could be enacted, with the starting date to be determined once court injunctions were lifted. This action is part of the administration's strategy to secure a ruling from the Supreme Court affirming that the contentious travel ban should be enacted immediately following the obstruction of Trump's initial travel restriction attempts by lower courts. Omar Jadwat, a lawyer from the American Civil Liberties Union, which has contested the ban, remarked that the necessity for this amendment highlights the legal shortcomings of the ban. "And yet again, these revisions underline that the one thing the president has consistently wanted throughout is a Muslim ban," he stated. Lawsuits initiated by challengers from Hawaii and Maryland contended that the order contravened federal immigration legislation and a clause of the First Amendment of the Constitution, which forbids the government from favoring or disfavoring any specific religion. The Trump administration has maintained that the ban is essential for safeguarding national security. Shortly after the memo was issued, Acting Solicitor General Jeff Wall submitted court documents asserting that it clarified "any doubt" regarding the order's effective date. If the case were to become moot, the nine justices would lack grounds to make a ruling, leaving the lower court decisions against the administration in effect. On Tuesday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration additional time to submit responses to an appeals court ruling from Monday that upheld a suspension of the travel ban. This action by the court is likely to postpone any determinations regarding the administration's requests for the ban to be enacted until at least the following week. text: The director of the CIA announced on Thursday that a U.S.-Canadian couple, who had been abducted by Islamist militants in Afghanistan, was held for five years in neighboring Pakistan before their release. "We achieved a significant outcome last week when we succeeded in getting back four U.S. citizens who had been detained for five years in Pakistan," CIA Director Mike Pompeo stated during a talk at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank in Washington. Pompeo's comments seem to mark the first instance of a U.S. official publicly acknowledging that the couple and their children were kept in Pakistan during their captivity, which contradicts statements made by Pakistani officials. The military and government of Pakistan have suggested that Caitlan Coleman, a U.S. citizen, her Canadian spouse Joshua Boyle, and their children were rescued soon after they crossed into Pakistan from Afghanistan. The couple was taken hostage in 2012 while they were hiking in Afghanistan, and their children were born during their captivity. U.S. officials, who requested anonymity, previously indicated that there was no evidence to suggest that the hostages were in Afghanistan in the days leading up to their release. These officials believed that the hostages were likely held by the Haqqani militant group in or around its base in northwestern Pakistan the entire time. The Haqqani network is viewed as the most formidable and effective ally of the Taliban, receiving support from elements within Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence, a powerful military-run intelligence agency, according to U.S. officials. Pakistan has denied these claims. A senior security source from Pakistan stated last Friday that Pakistani military and intelligence personnel, acting on a tip from U.S. intelligence, located a vehicle transporting the family as they were being moved into the Kurram tribal area near Kohat, approximately 60 kilometers (37 miles) within Pakistan. Pakistani officials take offense at U.S. allegations that Islamabad is insufficiently addressing Islamist militants, particularly the Haqqani group. Following the family's release, Pakistani officials highlighted the significance of collaboration and intelligence sharing from Washington, which has warned of potential cuts to military aid and other punitive actions against Pakistan. However, two Taliban sources familiar with the family's captivity indicated that they had indeed been held in Pakistan in recent years. The Haqqani network operates across both sides of the porous Afghan-Pakistani border, but senior militants have acknowledged relocating a major operational base to the Kurram region. As part of a strategy introduced in August aimed at concluding the war in Afghanistan, the Trump administration is insisting that Pakistan stop providing what U.S. officials characterize as safe havens for militants, or face consequences. These consequences may include further reductions in U.S. aid and sanctions directed at Pakistani officials with ties to militant groups. Pompeo's statements came just before U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson's visit to Pakistan next week, where Tillerson noted on Wednesday that the United States anticipates decisive actions from Pakistan against terrorist organizations. A senior official from the Trump administration, also speaking anonymously, remarked on Thursday that the United States views the family's rescue as a "template for more cooperation" from Pakistan. "We consider this a first step and hope to build on it," the official expressed, adding that Washington is "very frustrated" that Taliban and Haqqani militants continue to find refuge in Pakistan. "It's the freedom of movement, the capacity to transport weapons and materials, and the ability to raise funds. This is what defines a sanctuary," the official elaborated. Pompeo stated that the United States would do everything in its power to bring the Taliban to the negotiating table in Afghanistan, but he noted that this could not be accomplished if the militants maintained safe havens.

Trump, who frequently condemns what he terms "fake news" in the U.S. media and recently targeted CNN, the New York Times, and the Washington Post, directed his ire on Thursday towards the hosts of the MSNBC show "Morning Joe," Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski. He also referred to former Republican U.S. Congressman Scarborough as "Psycho Joe." Trump is known for his extensive use of Twitter, where he often mocks his critics and adversaries, but his comments on Thursday elicited a particularly strong reaction. MSNBC’s communications office tweeted, "It’s a sad day for America when the president spends his time bullying, lying and spewing petty personal attacks instead of doing his job." "I don’t think it’s surprising to anyone that he fights fire with fire." The tweets sparked a commotion in Washington and diverted attention as Republican senators sought to reconcile differences within the party and reach an agreement on significant healthcare legislation. A wealthy businessman and former reality television star without prior governmental experience, Trump has been quick to react to criticisms of his presidency, attacking the media for its reporting on investigations into possible collusion between his campaign team and Russia, among other issues. He has occasionally targeted individual journalists, including a notable attack on former Fox News and current NBC journalist Megyn Kelly during his campaign. He confronted Kelly after she inquired during a presidential debate about his past descriptions of some women as "fat pigs, dogs, slobs and disgusting animals." Trump issued an apology last October, just prior to the election, following the emergence of a 2005 video in which he claimed he could grab women by their genitals whenever he wished because he was a star.

text: The dispute regarding restroom access looms large in the gubernatorial election of North Carolina. WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. (Reuters) - Amid a year marked by protests over police shootings, historic flooding from hurricanes, and conflicts over voting rights, the contentious issue of bathroom access could play a crucial role in the state’s governor race. This election is essentially a referendum on a law that prohibits transgender individuals from using public restrooms that correspond with their gender identity and restricts protections for LGBTQ individuals. Enacted by Republican Governor Pat McCrory in March, this law has been cited as a cause for significant economic losses amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars and the withdrawal of major sporting events from the ninth largest state in the U.S. Critics of the legislation argue that the outcome of Tuesday’s vote could also have ramifications on a national scale. Should McCrory be defeated by Democratic contender Roy Cooper, they assert that lawmakers in other states who support similar measures will encounter increased political jeopardy. "I believe a strong message has already been communicated to legislators nationwide," stated Chad Griffin, president of the Human Rights Campaign, the largest LGBTQ civil rights organization in the country. "I believe and hope an even more powerful message will emerge on Election Day." The advocacy organization has collaborated with Equality North Carolina to mount a comprehensive effort to enhance voter turnout and to oust McCrory along with other proponents of the law identified as House Bill 2. The groups are concentrating their efforts on approximately 400,000 voters who support equality in the state, including around 255,800 identified as LGBTQ voters, according to Griffin. The Human Rights Campaign indicated that this voting demographic could influence the results in a crucial presidential battleground state, where Democrat Barack Obama triumphed by roughly 14,000 votes in 2008 and Republican Mitt Romney led by about 92,000 votes in 2012. "There is no doubt that this will be a very closely contested race at the top of the ballot, and the LGBTQ voting bloc has the potential to significantly affect the election’s outcome," noted Chris Sgro, executive director of Equality North Carolina. A COMPETITIVE RACE Analysts regard the contest between McCrory and Cooper, one of 12 gubernatorial elections occurring on Tuesday, to be among the most fiercely competitive in the nation. Polls throughout the year have indicated close results, although the RealClearPolitics average of recent polling shows Cooper with a marginal lead. A Reuters/Ipsos survey discovered that among voters who plan to participate, 38 percent are less inclined to support McCrory’s re-election due to the law and its implications, while 32 percent are more likely to back him. This poll was conducted online in English from October 6 to October 19, involving 1,233 likely voters and possessing a credibility interval, which reflects accuracy, of 3 percentage points. Additional polls have revealed that a majority of residents believe the law is detrimental to the state. McCrory, who became North Carolina’s first Republican governor in two decades in 2012, has attributed the backlash against the law to national organizations attempting to alter perceptions of gender and "fundamental privacy standards." Cooper contends that the law is discriminatory and has made McCrory’s endorsement of it a key focus of his campaign. A recent advertising campaign initiated by the conservative NC Values Coalition charges Cooper, who has served as the state’s attorney general since 2001, with endangering women and children by not defending H.B. 2. "By failing to defend it, he is permitting men to enter women’s restrooms," said Tami Fitzgerald, the group’s executive director, in a phone interview. "We believe that crosses a line." "Equality NC and HRC have made North Carolina the epicenter of their extreme LGBTQ agenda," she continued. "However, I am confident that their efforts will not succeed." At early voting locations in North Carolina this week, the topic appeared to be energizing individuals on both sides. "I respect McCrory for standing by H.B. 2," expressed Republican Parker Umstead, 81, a certified public accountant who voted.

Critics from the West have accused Suu Kyi of failing to advocate for the Rohingya, who have been fleeing to Bangladesh following a military counter-offensive against militant assaults. In an open letter addressed to Suu Kyi, Tutu expressed: I am now elderly, frail and officially retired, but I am breaking my promise to remain quiet on public matters due to my deep sorrow concerning the situation faced by the Muslim minority in your country, the Rohingya. My dear sister: If the cost of your rise to the highest office in Myanmar includes your silence, then that cost is undoubtedly too high... We pray for you to advocate for justice, human rights, and the unity of your people. We pray for you to take action, Tutu stated. At 85 years old, Tutu has been battling prostate cancer for nearly twenty years and has predominantly stepped back from public engagement. The Rohingya people number approximately 1.1 million, having long voiced grievances of persecution, and are regarded by many in the predominantly Buddhist Myanmar as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. Earlier on Thursday, Suu Kyi remarked in a conversation with Reuters Television’s Indian affiliate, Asian News International, saying, We must care for our citizens, we must care for everyone in our country, regardless of their citizenship status. Although Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 1991 for her advocacy of democracy, did not specifically mention the mass departure of the Rohingya minority.

text: The Trump administration announced a final rule on Thursday that will reduce the enrollment period for Obamacare and provide insurers with what they claim they need in the individual insurance market, likely making it more challenging for certain consumers to obtain insurance, according to healthcare specialists. Experts also indicated that this could lead to increased out-of-pocket medical costs as it grants insurers greater leeway in defining the value of their coverage. The rule, set to take effect later this year, arrives as President Donald Trump and Congressional Republicans have revived efforts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, widely known as Obamacare, following the failure of a bill in the U.S. House of Representatives last month. This regulation, which was proposed in February by a sector of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, seeks to support insurers who have incurred hundreds of millions of dollars in losses in the individual insurance markets established by Obamacare. Several significant insurers, such as Humana Inc and Aetna Inc, have declared intentions to withdraw from certain state exchanges in 2018. While insurers have expressed approval of the rule, they also indicated that substantial uncertainty remains in the market. On Wednesday, Trump informed the Wall Street Journal of his consideration to withhold approximately $7 billion annually in Obamacare payments to insurers in order to compel Democrats to return to negotiations. Marilyn Tavenner, the president and CEO of America’s Health Insurance Plans, stated that it is essential for these payments to continue without interruption; otherwise, she warned that premiums could increase by 20 percent across the market and more insurers might exit the exchanges. The modifications outlined in Thursday’s final rule include a reduced open enrollment period for Obamacare plans and increased difficulty for individuals wishing to enroll outside of this timeframe, which is permissible under specific circumstances such as pregnancy or relocation. According to experts in the healthcare sector, the rule may also permit insurers to recover unpaid premium amounts and complicate the process for individuals to switch between insurance plans. Insurers have noted that 'gaming the system' has resulted in an unfavorable combination of healthy and sick clients. Additionally, the rule grants states greater authority by removing the federal government's involvement in regulating the doctor and hospital networks that are part of insurance plans. Republicans have asserted that any reform or overhaul of healthcare must provide states with more flexibility. The Affordable Care Act has allowed 20 million Americans to obtain insurance, primarily through the individual insurance markets created by the law or through an expansion of Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income and disabled individuals.

text: Legislation aimed at safeguarding the special counsel from being dismissed by Trump has been proposed by senators. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Thursday, senators from both the Republican and Democratic parties unveiled two legislative proposals designed to prevent President Donald Trump from terminating the special counsel who is investigating his connections to Russia, as Congress increasingly seeks to reinforce its policy-making power. Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have voiced worries that Trump might remove Robert Mueller, the special counsel tasked with determining whether there was any collusion between his 2016 presidential campaign and Moscow. On May 9, the Republican president dismissed FBI Director James Comey, who was in charge of the investigation. Additionally, he has recently criticized his attorney general, Jeff Sessions, for stepping back from the inquiry. In light of indications that Mueller’s investigation is ramping up, legislators aimed to safeguard the special counsel, who was appointed on May 17. Two individuals knowledgeable about the situation informed Reuters on Thursday that Mueller had assembled a grand jury in Washington to look into the claims of Russian interference. These individuals also reported that grand jury subpoenas had been issued concerning a June 2016 meeting that included Trump’s son, his son-in-law, and a Russian lawyer. Moscow has denied any attempts to sway the election, while Trump has contested any accusations of collusion involving his associates and Russia. "Our bill permits judicial review of any decision to terminate a counsel to ensure it is executed for the reasons specified in the regulations rather than for political reasons," stated Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who co-sponsored one of the proposals alongside Democratic Senator Cory Booker. A second, mostly similar, proposal was presented by Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democratic Senator Chris Coons. Coons indicated to reporters that he anticipated the two groups of senators would collaborate and seek additional co-sponsors from both parties to create a unified bill. He mentioned that they were engaged in talks with the leaders of the Senate Judiciary Committee, hoping they would consider the bill, which would be a step toward a vote in the full Senate. The proposals were introduced as the Senate was getting ready to leave Washington for its August recess, with lawmakers set to return in early September. Members of Congress, including several of Trump’s fellow Republicans, have recently been advocating for legislation aimed at enhancing Congress’ impact on U.S. policy. Last week, lawmakers voted nearly unanimously in favor of a comprehensive sanctions bill that granted Congress the authority to review any effort by Trump to relax or remove sanctions on Russia. Trump enacted that bill into law on Wednesday.

text: 'No doubt' Russia is responsible for hacks on U.S. election systems: senior Democrat. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A prominent Democratic legislator stated on Sunday that he has “no doubt” that Russia is behind the latest hacking efforts aimed at state election systems, calling on the Obama administration to publicly hold Moscow accountable for its attempts to erode confidence in the presidential election scheduled for Nov. 8. The comments from Representative Adam Schiff, who serves as the leading Democrat on the intelligence committee in the U.S. House of Representatives, arise amidst rising apprehensions among U.S. and state officials regarding the security of voting machines and databases, alongside unproven claims from Republican candidate Donald Trump that the election might be “rigged.” “I have no doubt [this is Russia]. And I don’t think the administration has any doubt,” Schiff stated during an appearance on ABC’s “This Week.” Schiff's demand to publicly condemn the Kremlin follows a week after Trump expressed skepticism about the widely accepted conclusions reached privately by the U.S. intelligence community, which holds Russia accountable for the hacking incidents. “It could be Russia, but it could also be China,” Trump remarked during a televised debate with Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton. “It also could be somebody sitting on their bed that weighs 400 pounds.” On Saturday, Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson mentioned that hackers have explored the voting systems of numerous U.S. states, although there is no indication that they have tampered with any voting data. Schiff expressed skepticism regarding the ability of hackers to manipulate vote counts in a manner that could influence the election's outcome. Officials and specialists have indicated that the decentralized and outdated characteristics of U.S. voting technology make such hacking efforts less probable. Nonetheless, Schiff asserted that cyber attacks on voter registration systems could “sow discord” on election day. He also mentioned that the release of altered emails would be challenging to disprove and could “be election altering.” Weeks ago, the National Security Agency, FBI, and DHS all reached the conclusion that Russian intelligence agencies were responsible for conducting, directing, or coordinating all significant cyberattacks on U.S. political entities, including the Democratic National Committee, and individuals, according to a U.S. official involved in the investigations who spoke on Sunday. However, the official noted that White House officials have been hesitant to publicly identify the Russians, as doing so might lead to an increase in cyberattacks, and because providing public, unclassified evidence of the allegation is deemed impossible. Schiff and Senator Dianne Feinstein, the leading Democrat on the U.S. Senate intelligence committee, indicated last month that they had determined Russian intelligence agencies were “making a serious and concerted effort to influence the U.S. election.”

Senior security staff held another meeting in the White House Situation Room on Saturday, and the FBI and National Security Agency were trying to identify the perpetrators of the massive cyber attack, said the official, who spoke on condition on anonymity to discuss internal deliberations.

text: The president of Tanzania has appointed tax law academic Florens Luoga as the new governor of the central bank. President John Magufuli announced this decision on Monday, indicating that Luoga would assume the role in December or January, following the conclusion of current governor Benno Ndulu's term. "I have chosen to appoint a new (central bank) governor from amongst the members of the committees that looked into the mining sector," stated Magufuli during a ceremony where he presented certificates of recognition to members of two presidential committees that investigated allegations of tax evasion concerning gold and copper concentrate exports in the East African nation. Luoga is presently the deputy vice chancellor at the University of Dar es Salaam (UDSM), which is the largest public university in the country. In July, he was also designated by Magufuli as the chairman of the board for the Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA). Magufuli acknowledged that many anticipated he would select an economist for the governor position. However, he pointed out that Luoga, as a taxation law professor, would assist in enhancing control over capital flight by certain foreign firms utilizing tax havens. The government, led by President Magufuli, alleges that mining companies are defrauding Tanzania of its rightful mineral wealth through tax evasion and smuggling, claims which the companies refute. Magufuli has directed the central bank to take action against capital flight from foreign investor firms. Additionally, the new Minister of Minerals, Angellah Kairuki, who spoke at the same event, emphasized the government's commitment to closing all gaps in the mining sector, including the illegal smuggling of minerals.

These remarks were made in parliament and followed last week's indication from Seoul that it was receptive to discussions regarding modifications to the five-year-old bilateral agreement, which U.S. President Donald Trump had previously threatened to cancel unless a renegotiation occurred. Dombrovskis mentioned during a standard news briefing that this matter is being addressed through dialogue, therefore, we are not currently conducting any evaluations regarding the possible economic implications.

This issue is being dealt with by dialogue, so currently we are not doing any assessments on the potential economic impact,  Dombrovskis told a regular news briefing.

text: Trump removes Steve Bannon from the National Security Council. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed his chief strategist Steve Bannon from the National Security Council, reversing his earlier controversial decision to grant a political adviser an unprecedented position in security deliberations. This alteration to the NSC, confirmed by a White House representative, also raised the profiles of General Joseph Dunford, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Dan Coats, the director of National Intelligence, who oversees all 17 U.S. intelligence agencies. The representative indicated that this adjustment returns the NSC "back to its core function of what it’s supposed to do." It also seems to signify a win for national security adviser H.R. McMaster, who had communicated to some national security experts that he felt he was in a "battle to the death" with Bannon and others within the White House staff. Vice President Mike Pence remarked that Bannon would still play a significant role in policy and downplayed the changes as standard procedure. "This is just a natural evolution to ensure the National Security Council is structured in a manner that best aids the president in addressing and making those challenging decisions," Pence stated on Fox News. Bannon, in a statement, expressed that he had successfully worked to restore the NSC to its traditional function of coordinating foreign policy instead of directing it. He referenced President Barack Obama’s national security adviser, Susan Rice, as a reason for advocating this adjustment. "Susan Rice operationalized the NSC during the last administration, so I was appointed to the NSC to ensure it was ‘de-operationalized.’ General McMaster has returned the NSC to its rightful role," he mentioned. The Trump administration has faced internal conflicts and intrigues that have hindered his nascent presidency. Recently, multiple senior U.S. officials in foreign policy and national security have noted that the frameworks for shaping the Trump administration’s responses to urgent issues such as Syria, North Korea, and Iran have yet to be established. Critics of Bannon’s position on the NSC argued that it granted excessive influence in decision-making to someone without foreign policy experience. Bannon, who served as chief executive of Trump’s presidential campaign leading up to his election in November, in many ways embodies Trump’s “America First” nationalist rhetoric, helping to fuel his anti-Washington sentiment and advocating for the president to occasionally distance himself from mainstream Republicans. Prior to his role in the Trump administration, Bannon led Breitbart News, a right-leaning website. U.S. Representative Adam Schiff, the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, described the change in the NSC as a favorable move that would assist McMaster in "gaining control over a body that was being politicized by Bannon’s involvement." "As the administration’s policy regarding North Korea, China, Russia, and Syria continues to meander, we can only hope this shake-up introduces some level of strategic clarity to the body," he stated. Bannon’s exclusion from the NSC could represent a potential decline in his influence within the Trump White House, where he has had a say in most significant decisions. However, a confidant of Trump asserted that Bannon remains as impactful as ever. "He is still involved in everything and retains the full confidence of the president, but to be fair, he can only handle so many tasks," the confidant said, speaking on condition of anonymity. The White House representative explained that Bannon was no longer deemed necessary on the NSC following the exit of Trump’s first national security adviser, Michael Flynn. Flynn resigned on Feb. 13 due to his communications with Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Sergei Kislyak, prior to Trump’s inauguration on Jan. 20. The representative noted that Bannon was originally placed on the NSC as a safeguard against Flynn and had only participated in one of the NSC’s routine meetings. text: The Constitutional Court of Spain has put a hold on a referendum law that the Catalan parliament passed on Wednesday, thereby preventing a vote on independence from Spain scheduled for October 1, according to a source from the court on Thursday. The law will be on hold while judges examine claims that the referendum violates the nation's constitution. Earlier on Thursday, Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy stated that he had requested the court to rule the referendum as illegal. The constitution asserts that Spain is indivisible.
source_text: Spain's constitutional court suspends Catalan referendum law: court source. MADRID (Reuters) - The Spanish Constitutional Court has suspended a referendum law that was approved on Wednesday by the Catalan parliament, blocking the way for an Oct. 1 ballot on independence from Spain, a court source said on Thursday. The law will be suspended while judges consider arguments that the vote breaches the country s constitution. Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy said earlier on Thursday he had appealed to the court to declare the referendum illegal. The constitution states Spain is indivisible.

text: ANKARA (Reuters) - On Sunday, Turkish President Erdogan declared that Turkey would not yield to what he described as U.S. 'blackmail' concerning the trial of a Turkish bank executive accused of circumventing U.S. sanctions on Iran. The relationship between NATO allies Ankara and Washington has become increasingly tense, particularly as Turkish-Iranian gold trader Reza Zarrab, who is collaborating with U.S. prosecutors, testified in court about a plan to bypass U.S. sanctions. Erdogan asserted that Turkey's activities were consistent with United Nations decisions, emphasizing that they did not contradict Ankara's alliance with Washington. 'What have we done, for instance? We acquired natural gas from a nation with which we have a contract to ensure our citizens remain warm in the winter. Like other nations, we are only bound by the UN's resolutions, and Turkey has adhered to them precisely,' he told members of his ruling AK Party in the eastern province of Mus. Over three days of testimony, Zarrab has implicated high-ranking Turkish officials, including Erdogan himself. Zarrab stated on Thursday that during Erdogan's tenure as prime minister, he had sanctioned a transaction aimed at assisting Iran in evading U.S. sanctions. Ankara has portrayed this testimony as an effort to destabilize Turkey and its economy, previously labeling it a 'clear plot' orchestrated by the network of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom they accuse of masterminding last year’s coup attempt. 'This case is merely the 17-25 December plot being transported across the ocean. Excuse us, but we will not submit to this blackmail,' Erdogan remarked, referencing the 2013 leaks concerning alleged government corruption that were attributed to his adversaries. While Erdogan has yet to address the assertions made in court, he has characterized the case as a politically motivated endeavor to topple the Turkish government led by Gulen. Turkey has persistently sought Gulen's extradition; however, U.S. officials have indicated that the courts need adequate evidence before they can proceed with extraditing the elderly cleric, who has denied any involvement in the coup. Gulen has been living in self-imposed exile in Pennsylvania since 1999.

text: A research report has indicated that Danish fishermen may face significant challenges due to Brexit. COPENHAGEN (Reuters) - The decision of Britain to exit the European Union could severely impact Danish fishermen if it results in limitations on their access to British waters, according to a report commissioned by the Danish government that was released on Wednesday. The fishing sector in Denmark holds considerable influence in Copenhagen and may urge the government to take a firm position during Britain's negotiations with the EU regarding a trade agreement following Brexit. Fishermen across Europe are advocating for Brussels to leverage its negotiating power—continued access to the crucial EU market—when discussing how to allocate fishing rights. The report from researchers at Copenhagen University suggested that Danish fishermen who primarily operate in British waters could see their catch reduced by more than half in the most adverse of four hypothetical scenarios. The actual impacts will rely on the outcomes of the talks between Britain and the remaining 27 EU nations, stated Minister for Fisheries Karen Ellemann. "We are collaborating with other nations that are affected to secure our fishing rights and access to British waters," she remarked in response to the report. From 2012 to 2016, Danish fishermen have consistently brought in fish from British waters valued between 700 million and 1 billion Danish crowns ($109-156 million) each year. This accounts for 34 percent of the total value of fish landed by Danish fishermen, and 45 percent of the total volume. Herring and mackerel are expected to be particularly impacted, which would also affect Denmark's domestic fish processing sector. The researchers noted in the report that Danish vessels might alter their operations in unforeseen ways, or new fishing opportunities could arise, such as in the Norwegian zone. Danish fishermen have contended that if British fishermen gain unrestricted access to sell their catch within the EU, then EU fishermen should likewise receive unrestricted access to the British fishing zones. Approximately 75 percent of the catch from Britain is imported by Europe. Following Brexit, Britain has stated its intention to permit foreign vessels to fish in UK waters while reserving the right to determine the level of access. Industry sources have informed Reuters that the EU will aim to sustain a situation similar to the current one.

text: Factbox: Raqqa - The Syrian headquarters of Islamic State has been conquered. BEIRUT (Reuters) - Militias in Syria, supported by the U.S., have proclaimed their victory over Islamic State in its capital, Raqqa, marking a significant achievement in the effort to dismantle the theocratic caliphate that was established in 2014. Below are details regarding Raqqa: Raqqa is located on the Euphrates River, approximately 90 km (56 miles) from the Turkish border in north-central Syria. The Sunni militant group Islamic State captured Raqqa in January 2014, taking control from rebel groups that opposed Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's regime. The United States has indicated that Islamic State organized and dispatched teams from Raqqa to execute attacks in cities such as Paris, Brussels, and Istanbul. THE ANTI-IS OFFENSIVE The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), an alliance predominantly consisting of Kurdish and Arab militias, commenced their advance toward Raqqa city in November 2016. After surrounding the city, they initiated an offensive to seize it, encountering significant resistance. The coalition led by the United States provided support to the SDF through airstrikes and the deployment of special forces on the ground. The conflict in Raqqa has had a devastating impact on civilians. In March, the United Nations reported that the city had a population of around 200,000, just shy of its pre-war figures. Since late last year, combat in and around Raqqa has led to the displacement of tens of thousands. Many have escaped the city to camps in nearby areas now under the control of the SDF and its key faction, the Kurdish YPG militia. Civilians trapped within the Islamic State-controlled area of the city faced dire conditions for months, suffering from a lack of water, electricity, food, and medical care. As the SDF took control of portions of Raqqa, these areas were mostly vacated of residents. Air strikes, ongoing fighting, and threats from Islamic State snipers and mines have resulted in the deaths of many hundreds. The coalition asserts that it takes precautions to prevent civilian casualties during its bombing operations in Syria and Iraq. However, the U.N. human rights office and the rights organization Amnesty International have expressed concerns regarding reports of significant civilian fatalities. Islamic State enforced its highly stringent interpretation of Islamic law on the inhabitants of Raqqa. The militants conducted public executions, lashings, and violent punishments for breaches of their regulations. The campaign for Raqqa has heightened tensions between the United States and its NATO ally Turkey. The potential influence of Kurdish forces in the predominantly Arab city is a sensitive issue for certain activists from Raqqa and for Turkey. The YPG has emerged as the principal U.S. ally in combating Islamic State in northern Syria. Ankara perceives it as a Syrian branch of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), which has been engaged in a decades-long insurgency within Turkey, and is apprehensive about the increasing Kurdish influence along its border. Political allies of the SDF have established a Raqqa Civil Council composed of local residents, which the SDF has stated it will transfer authority to following the defeat of Islamic State. This reflects a similar trend observed in other towns and cities captured by the SDF. The coalition led by the U.S. has assisted in training a new police force for Raqqa. Islamic State has antagonized multiple factions throughout the more than six-year Syrian conflict, with various offensives currently underway to eradicate it from its last strongholds in towns adjacent to the Euphrates River in eastern Syria near the Iraqi border. In addition to the U.S.-backed SDF, the Syrian army, supported by Russian airpower and Iranian-backed militias, is also conducting its own operations against Islamic State in eastern Syria. Raqqa, a contemporary provincial transport hub and marketplace, was established by the Abbasid Islamic Caliphate in the eighth century, at one time serving as its capital. It has been inhabited since ancient times and features significant archaeological and architectural sites. According to the United Nations, these sites have been extensively plundered during the conflict, and religious structures have suffered damage. In March 2014, Islamic State militants released footage of their destruction of a large section of the Uwais al-Qarani shrine complex.

text: According to the South Korean government, at least four individuals who have defected from North Korea may have been exposed to radiation. This statement was made on Wednesday, although it remains unverified whether this exposure is linked to Pyongyang's nuclear weapons initiatives. These four defectors are part of a group of 30 former residents from Kilju county, which encompasses the Punggye-ri nuclear test site, that have been evaluated by South Korean authorities since October, a month following North Korea's sixth and most powerful nuclear test, as stated by Unification Ministry spokesperson Baik Tae-hyun during a news conference. The exposure to radiation occurred between May 2009 and January 2013, and all four individuals had defected to South Korea prior to the latest nuclear test, a researcher from the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, which conducted the assessments, informed reporters. Since 2006, North Korea has executed six nuclear bomb tests, all taking place in tunnels deep within the Punggye-ri mountains, in defiance of United Nations Security Council resolutions and global criticism. The researcher emphasized that there are various ways in which individuals can be exposed to radiation and noted that none of the defectors who had actually resided in Punggye-ri displayed specific symptoms. Following the last test, which North Korea claimed was a hydrogen bomb, a series of minor earthquakes raised concerns that the mountainous region in the northwest corner of the country might have been compromised. Experts have cautioned that continued testing in this area could pose a risk of radioactive contamination. After the nuclear test on September 3, China’s Nuclear Safety Administration announced that it had initiated emergency radiation monitoring along its border with North Korea. Additionally, in early December, a state-run publication in China’s Jilin province, which shares borders with North Korea and Russia, issued a page of practical advice for readers on how to safeguard themselves from a nuclear weapons attack or explosion. The publication also included cartoon illustrations demonstrating methods to remove radioactive contamination, such as using water to rinse shoes and employing cotton swabs to clean ears, along with an image of a child vomiting to illustrate how medical assistance can facilitate the expulsion of radiation through stomach pumping and induced urination.

text: DUBLIN (Reuters) - The decision to feature Argentinian communist guerrilla leader Ernesto Che Guevara, a key figure in the Cuban revolution, on the new 1-euro postage stamp in Ireland is igniting debate both in the U.S. and Europe. This nation, historically Catholic and without a leftist government, only established diplomatic ties with Cuba in 1999, four decades after Guevara played a crucial role in the Cuban revolution alongside Fidel Castro. Notably, Guevara’s father, Ernesto Guevara Lynch, was an Irish-descended civil engineer, and the renowned red and black depiction of the long-haired Che, famous from t-shirts and posters worldwide, was created by Irish artist Jim Fitzpatrick. Consequently, Ireland’s postal service released this stamp featuring Fitzpatrick’s portrayal of Guevara to commemorate the 50th anniversary of his passing. The postal authority labeled Guevara, who was killed by CIA-supported Bolivian troops in Bolivia in 1967, as the quintessential leftist revolutionary. They noted that the demand for this stamp has matched that of its two previous top sellers, which honored the sinking of the Titanic and the 1916 Rising against British rule in Ireland. However, it quickly faced reminders that for many, Guevara symbolizes the violent repression associated with Cuba’s communist regime, with one Irish senator condemning him as a barbaric interrogator, jailer, and executioner of hundreds of so-called class enemies. "I firmly believe he is absolutely not a fitting choice for such an honor," stated Neale Richmond, a member of the ruling Irish party Fine Gael, in a letter to the country’s communications minister. Cuban-American radio personality Ninoska Perez Castellon also joined the discussion, urging her listeners to contact the postal service to request the withdrawal of the stamp. Fitzpatrick, whose 1968 artwork, based on a photograph by Cuban photographer Alberto Korda, became a symbol of rebellion for leftist students on merchandise, expressed that he was not taken aback by the backlash. Anti-communist activists in Ireland had previously threatened to break a shop window displaying his artwork when he first released it half a century ago. "This reaction isn’t entirely surprising. There was a revolution, and you have two opposing sides, similar to what we experienced after our Civil War," Fitzpatrick shared with Reuters at his Dublin residence, where his living room serves as a studio cluttered with sketches and old drawings. "I thought it was incredible that they (the postal service) wanted to create a stamp of Che, and it was a tremendous honor for me," he remarked. Fitzpatrick, who has crafted album covers for renowned Irish musician Sinead O’Connor and the band Thin Lizzy, indicated in 2011 that he sought to obtain copyright for his Che image to prevent its exploitation for commercial purposes. A representative from the postal service confirmed that neither Fitzpatrick nor Korda’s estate would receive compensation for the stamp’s use of the image.

source_text: Biden meets PM Abadi in Baghdad to discuss security: state TV. The trip is the first time that Biden, the point person for the White House on Iraq, has visited the country since the United States withdrew its forces in 2011. He is the third and highest-level U.S. official to visit Iraq this month.

text: European politicians express caution regarding the Republican convention due to Trump. BERLIN (Reuters) - Nigel Farage from Britain will be present at the Republican convention in Cleveland next week to share insights from his Brexit campaign. Geert Wilders, the leader of the Dutch Freedom Party, will also attend, viewing Donald Trump as a partner in his fight against the perceived ‘Islamization’ of the West. However, several mainstream European conservatives who have previously attended Republican events confess privately to being appalled at the idea of a Trump presidency and are opting out of this year's event, scheduled from July 18-21. Numerous center-right politicians traveling from Europe admit to quietly supporting Trump’s Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. They claim their purpose in attending is not to back Trump, but to see “the Donald” in person and witness what is anticipated to be one of the most tumultuous and unpredictable Republican conventions in years. "We will see if Trump can reinvent himself during the convention," Guenter Krings, a senior member of German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s conservative faction, remarked to Reuters, accompanying only one fellow Bundestag member. "One can only hope so, but I have my doubts." Every four years, politicians globally are invited to participate in the Republican and Democratic conventions through a structured visitors program that includes discussions with campaign leaders, pollsters, and foreign policy analysts. They also spend time in the primary convention hall. This year, around 120 center-right politicians from outside the U.S. are expected, with approximately half hailing from Europe. Trump's candidacy has placed European parties with historical ties to U.S. Republicans in a quandary. Many perceive his stances—on matters such as immigration, security, trade, and the contentious Brexit issue—as more aligned with the emerging far-right parties that they are striving to control. Four years prior, when Mitt Romney was the Republican candidate, the European People's Party (EPP), the largest faction in the European Parliament, dispatched eight members to Tampa. This year, there will be no EPP delegation as no members of the group expressed interest in attending. Despite their reservations, there remains a hesitance to criticize Trump overtly due to his well-known sensitivity, partly out of concern that he may win the election in November and retaliate against his international critics, similar to his prior warning to former British Prime Minister David Cameron when he denounced Trump’s suggestion for a temporary U.S. ban on Muslims as “divisive, stupid and wrong.” While the traditional conservative base is cautious, various nationalist and anti-immigration parties across Europe seem intrigued by Trump, even if some are hesitant to fully endorse the New York real estate mogul, who has pledged to “make America great again.” A representative from the UKIP party in Brussels confirmed that Farage would be attending to “provide them some lessons” regarding Brexit. Wilders informed Reuters that he plans to be in Cleveland and wishes to meet Trump there. "I hope Donald Trump becomes America’s next president," Wilders stated. "Such a victory would be beneficial for Europe. Both America and Europe face the same threat of cultural relativism and Islam." Austria’s far-right Freedom Party, France’s National Front, and the Alternative for Germany (AfD) have stated they do not intend to send representatives to Cleveland. "We are neutral," declared Freedom Party leader Heinz-Christian Strache when asked about his support for Trump. "He advocates for American interests. He is articulating points that need to be addressed." Additionally, Italy’s Northern League will also be absent, with its leader Matteo Salvini identifying as a fervent Trump supporter, although he discovered earlier this year that the admiration was not necessarily reciprocated. Salvini visited Pennsylvania in April to attend a Trump rally, where he was photographed shaking hands with the Republican candidate, and his party announced that Trump had indeed accepted his invitation.

text: The U.S. Senate has overwhelmingly approved Montenegro's entry into NATO. In a vote held on Tuesday in Washington (Reuters), the Senate expressed strong support for NATO's expansion, allowing Montenegro to become a member, signaling the U.S. commitment to counteract Russian attempts to strengthen its influence in Europe. The vote, which had been postponed for an extended period, concluded with a tally of 97-2 in favor of Montenegro joining the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. This result far exceeded the two-thirds majority necessary in the 100-member Senate for ratification of Montenegro’s membership. There has been no immediate indication regarding whether President Donald Trump will officially submit the ratification instrument, which is the final step in the U.S. ratification process. Nevertheless, his administration had endorsed NATO membership for the small Balkan state, one of the tiniest in Europe, even though Trump had occasionally criticized the alliance during his presidential campaign last year. During that campaign, Trump claimed that other NATO allies were not contributing their fair share while exhibiting a more accommodating attitude toward Russia. However, since taking office, Trump has reaffirmed his backing for the alliance. Last week, Reuters reported that Secretary of State Rex Tillerson communicated with Senate leaders earlier this month, asserting that Montenegro’s NATO membership was “strongly in the interests of the United States.” On Tuesday, the only two dissenting votes were cast by Republican Senators Rand Paul and Mike Lee, who had previously stalled the vote for several months by refusing to permit a swift decision. Senate leaders opted for a more protracted roll call vote this week following Tillerson’s correspondence. Paul expressed doubts about the prudence of allowing a nation with merely 650,000 inhabitants and an armed force of just 2,000 to join NATO, arguing that American taxpayers should not be obligated to finance Montenegro's defense in the event of an attack. Russia has opposed the expansion of NATO into the western Balkans. Proponents of Montenegro’s accession emphasized the necessity of supporting nations like Montenegro to uphold Western values and resist Moscow, which Montenegrin officials alleged was partially involved in a purported plot to destabilize their government during the elections of October 2016. Moscow has denied these allegations. “With nearly unanimous support, the Senate has conveyed a definitive message that it stands firmly alongside Montenegro and against the Kremlin’s intimidation tactics,” stated Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democratic member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. In order for Montenegro to officially join the alliance, all 28 NATO member states must ratify its accession. Washington is among the last to complete this process. text: Exclusive: Candidates for No.2 Fed role begin to surface, search to refine. (In this story dated Dec. 8, corrects Peters’ affiliation in paragraph 12 to reflect the change in company name) By Jonathan Spicer and Rob Cox NEW YORK (Reuters) - The Federal Reserve Bank of New York is poised to narrow its candidate search for what is regarded as the second-most influential position at the Fed, having explored a varied array of applicants, from a dean at a local business school to a former Fed governor. New York Fed President William Dudley is set to depart in mid-2018, and individuals familiar with the directors overseeing the search for his replacement indicate that they have reviewed several economists, academics, investors, bankers, and policymakers so far. "They are considering candidates outside the conventional profile" of an expert in banking, markets, or monetary policy, and aim to begin reducing a preliminary list of candidates in the coming days, one source in contact with the directors stated. The president of the New York Fed occupies a crucial role at the nexus of U.S. monetary policy and financial markets, overseeing Wall Street regulation and maintaining diplomatic relations with central bank leaders globally. Unlike other top positions that hold a permanent vote on policy matters, the New York Fed president is nominated by the bank’s board of directors rather than the White House and does not need Congressional approval. The successor to Dudley may have an even more significant influence in steering the Fed through a significant leadership transition, during which U.S. President Donald Trump has the opportunity to appoint six out of seven members to the Fed Board of Governors. So far, he has appointed Jerome Powell and Randal Quarles—both lawyers, not PhD economists—to key roles in Washington, with Powell taking over from Chair Janet Yellen, who, unlike her predecessors, will serve only a single term. Both Powell and Quarles advocate for the Republican agenda of Wall Street deregulation. However, their relatively limited background in monetary policy compared to their predecessors has raised concerns regarding the Fed’s plans for tightening and its ability to address any severe economic downturn. At this stage, the New York Fed directors have left open the question of what the ideal candidate profile should entail, according to sources knowledgeable about the search. Two of these individuals, who requested anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the process, stated that search firms have reached out to several candidates, including Peter Blair Henry, 48, the dean of New York University’s Stern School of Business, and former Fed governor Kevin Warsh. Warsh, 47, who was a contender for the Fed Chair position before Trump selected Powell last month, has reportedly opted out of consideration for the New York position. One of these sources mentioned that Henry seems to be the early favorite. Henry and a spokesperson for Warsh at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, where he serves as a visiting fellow, did not respond to inquiries for comments. The Fed governors with permanent voting rights require a nod from the White House and Senate confirmation. The other 11 district presidents cast votes every two or three years under a time-honored rotation designed to highlight New York's distinctive role as a counterbalance to the Washington-based board. The president of the New York Fed enjoys considerable independence and also acts as the vice chair of the central bank's rate-setting committee. (For a graphic showing the Fed's ideological doves and hawks, see: goo.gl/5BpTex) "It’s a vital role and arguably more significant than the Fed’s vice chair from a market perspective," Greg Peters, senior investment officer at PGIM Fixed Income, which manages $695 billion in assets, told Reuters. Nonetheless, the Fed’s Board of Governors would need to sanction the nominee selected by New York’s four-member search committee, which is led by directors with a liberal leaning, Sara Horowitz and Glenn Hutchins. Horowitz, who founded the Freelancers Union that advocates for independent workers, chairs the board of the New York Fed. Hutchins is a co-founder of the private-equity firm Silver Lake Partners and a recognized philanthropist in public policy. Several weeks prior to Dudley’s announcement of his resignation in early November, the two were already actively reaching out.

text: Boehner: Trump has been a 'total catastrophe'. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - According to John Boehner, a fellow Republican and former Speaker of the U.S. House, President Donald Trump's administration has been a "total catastrophe" except for matters related to foreign policy, which he discussed at an energy conference. The ex-congressman from Ohio shared that he has known Trump for 15 years but never anticipated that he would become the President. While he acknowledged Trump’s bold actions against the Islamic State militant group and other international initiatives, he expressed significant dissatisfaction with the president's other initial actions. "Everything else he’s done has been a total catastrophe," Boehner stated during the energy conference held in Houston on Wednesday, as reported by the energy outlet Rigzone. "He’s still figuring out how to be president." A representative for Boehner verified these statements. The White House did not promptly reply to a request for feedback regarding Boehner’s comments. The former House speaker, who stepped down from Congress in 2015, was also very critical of the administration and his previous Republican colleagues in Congress regarding their attempts to push through extensive healthcare and tax reform initiatives. He argued that Republicans should not have attempted to "repeal and replace" the Affordable Care Act, even after the House narrowly approved a reform proposal. The Senate is reviewing its own version of the bill. Moreover, he dismissed tax reform efforts, which are a key aspect of the Republican policy agenda, as "merely a lot of optimistic talk." While Boehner’s successor, Speaker Paul Ryan, is working to incorporate a border adjustment tax, a tax on imports, as a significant component of any tax code revision, Boehner described it as "deader than a doornail" due to resistance from fellow Republicans and the White House. Boehner also endorsed initiatives to "get to the bottom" of any possible connections between Trump associates and the Russian government. However, he characterized calls for Trump's impeachment as the domain of "the radical left-wing Democratic colleagues of mine." Democratic Representative Al Green has officially presented articles of impeachment against Trump, but this initiative has not been supported by most Democratic lawmakers as the investigation continues.

text: A heavy metal band from Virginia resonates with the anthem of Catalonia. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Deep within a small basement in a home located in the suburbs of Washington, D.C., the sounds of music from the Spanish region of Catalonia fill the air. A heavy metal version of the Catalonian national anthem, Els Segadors, also known as The Reapers, has transformed A Sound of Thunder, a band from Virginia that was relatively unknown, into notable figures in the politically charged area of northeastern Spain. Just days after its release, the track surpassed one million views on YouTube, becoming the band's most successful single since their inception in 2008. In October, thousands of Catalonians participated in a banned referendum for independence from Spain, which resulted in violence and led to a constitutional crisis in the fourth-largest economy of the euro zone. Back in Manassas, Virginia, Nina Osegueda, the lead vocalist of the band, quickly decided to upload a video of their version of Els Segadors to YouTube. Osegueda, whose mother hails from Catalonia, has a strong connection to the region and initially recorded the anthem as a dedication to her mother. The song was not meant to be released as a single, but instead was part of the band’s upcoming full-length album, It Was Metal, scheduled for release in March 2018. The violent events surrounding the referendum altered those plans. "We had a couple of other singles that we intended to release beforehand to showcase what the new album would sound like," she stated. "But then the vote occurred, and 800 individuals were injured by police attempting to vote. So I thought we should just release the song to demonstrate our support against police brutality." Suddenly, it began to gain traction everywhere... Then I realized that someone had shared our music on Twitter, and it turned out to be a Catalan politician, Osegueda recounted. Radio stations in Catalonia began to play the song, and Osegueda was featured on several radio programs. The interest she garnered extended to her family, as her uncle from Catalonia was also interviewed on local radio. On the band’s YouTube channel, fans have commented that they prefer the metal adaptation over the original, with many expressing that the song resonated with them emotionally. Osegueda recorded portions of the song in Catalan. Although she does not speak the language, she found the challenge of singing it with accurate pronunciation intimidating, yet she has expressed that the encouragement and backing from her new fans have been a humbling experience. "I think the most significant emotional reaction we've received has been, 'it brought me to tears, which is unusual for a heavy metal song.' So for us, that was a major deal," Osegueda remarked. "You know, we’re not signed to a label. We handle everything independently. So when we see this level of response from people, it’s quite overwhelming." The band, which has funded its albums through various Kickstarter campaigns, is set to tour Catalonia for the first time in December, just days ahead of the regional elections on December 21. They have scheduled performances in Barcelona, Tarragona, and other cities in Catalonia. For Osegueda, who has visited Catalonia multiple times, this upcoming trip feels different. "I have always loved going there for holidays. But now it carries a much deeper significance because there are so many individuals who view our song as a source of inspiration. I feel like I certainly have a stronger connection now," she reflected.

text: The United States and Germany urged China to promptly free a well-known human rights advocate who received an eight-year prison sentence on Tuesday for subversion, marking the most severe punishment in a recent crackdown on activism. Wu Gan, a blogger commonly recognized by his online alias Super Vulgar Butcher, frequently supported sensitive issues regarding government abuse of power through both online platforms and public protests. He was apprehended in May 2015 and charged with subversion. In another case on the same day, rights attorney Xie Yang avoided facing criminal penalties despite being found guilty of inciting subversion, as he acknowledged his wrongdoing. The U.S. and German embassies in China issued a joint statement urging Chinese authorities to release Wu without delay. They also called for Xie to be allowed to return to his professional duties without any conditions or limitations. China's Foreign Ministry did not respond immediately to a request for a statement, but Beijing often criticizes foreign concerns regarding human rights cases as meddling in domestic matters, asserting that China adheres to the rule of law. In a statement released by his legal representatives late on Tuesday, Wu expressed that he viewed the sentence as an 'honor' since it demonstrated that he had not become a 'slave' or 'accomplice' of China's autocracy. 'I received eight years, but I feel neither sorrow nor despair. This was my decision, as opposing autocracy means you are already on the path to imprisonment,' Wu stated. He further urged the global community to pay attention to the worsening human rights conditions in China. Wu's sentence is regarded as the harshest in what rights organizations have termed an unprecedented assault on rights advocates and lawyers, referred to as the 709 crackdown, which began in earnest on July 9, 2015. The stringent measures have shown no signs of easing as President Xi Jinping begins his second five-year term, raising significant concerns among Western nations. Germany has been particularly vocal, causing irritation in China. At a regular news conference on Wednesday, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Hua Chunying expressed dissatisfaction with remarks made last week by the German ambassador regarding China's failure to establish a previously agreed cyber consultation mechanism. Hua informed reporters that China had indeed invited Germany to send delegates for discussions, but the Germans continually postponed their participation. She added that China hopes the ambassador will refrain from making such 'irresponsible comments.'

BEIJING (Reuters) - The United States and Germany called on China to immediately release a prominent human rights activist who was jailed for eight years on Tuesday for subversion, the harshest sentence passed in a recent crackdown on activism. Wu Gan, a blogger better known by his online name  Super Vulgar Butcher , regularly championed sensitive cases of government abuses of power, both online and in street protests. He was detained in May 2015 and charged with subversion. In a separate case, also on Tuesday, rights lawyer Xie Yang avoided criminal punishment despite being found guilty of inciting subversion, because he admitted to his crimes.  We call on the Chinese authorities to release Wu immediately,  the U.S. and Germany embassies in China said in a joint statement.  As Xie has been exempted from punishment, we urge China to allow Xie to resume his professional activities without preconditions and be free of any restrictions.
