text: In a review concerning Afghanistan, President Trump's dissatisfaction echoes the challenges faced during Obama's administration. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Since assuming the presidency, Donald Trump has exhibited a tendency to respect, and perhaps even defer to, the military leaders in his Cabinet and at the White House, with one notable exception: the conflict in Afghanistan. Over a dozen interviews conducted with current and former U.S. officials familiar with the discussions indicate that the president is profoundly frustrated by the absence of viable strategies to achieve victory in the 16-year-old conflict, characterized internally as 'an eroding stalemate.' This debate mirrors the quandary Barack Obama encountered in 2009. As is the case now, officials, both current and former, predict that Trump will likely deploy additional troops. 'It’s the least worst option,' remarked one former U.S. official knowledgeable about the discussions, who requested anonymity but acknowledged that under Trump, a withdrawal cannot be entirely dismissed. Trump’s Secretary of Defense, retired Marine Corps General Jim Mattis, has possessed the authority for nearly two months to increase the troop count to thousands more than the approximately 8,400 currently stationed there (down from a peak exceeding 100,000 in 2011). In February, Army General John Nicholson, who commands U.S. forces in Afghanistan, requested additional troops. However, officials indicate that Mattis will refrain from exercising his authority until he secures Trump's agreement on a strategic vision for America’s longest conflict. The strategy, in addition to increasing troop levels in Afghanistan, is intended to tackle militant sanctuaries in neighboring Pakistan. This issue has also become contentious, with several members of Trump’s close circle divided on how aggressively to engage Islamabad. Discussions, which included a high-level meeting at the White House on Thursday, are expected to extend throughout the summer, surpassing a mid-July deadline to submit a war strategy to a Congress that is growing increasingly impatient. Following Thursday’s meeting, led by Vice President Mike Pence, sources familiar with the discussions informed Reuters that a conclusive decision did not seem to be forthcoming. Officials at the Pentagon have declined to comment on the internal discussions. The White House has also chosen not to provide comments prior to a decision regarding the strategy. While U.S.-backed forces are making progress against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, the same cannot be said for the battle against the Taliban in Afghanistan. U.S. intelligence agencies have evaluated that conditions in Afghanistan are likely to worsen through the next year, even with a modest increase in military support from the U.S. and its allies. During a meeting in the White House Situation Room on July 19, Trump suggested that Mattis and Marine General Joseph Dunford, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, might want to consider dismissing Nicholson, who was appointed by Obama in 2016 to lead the war effort and has gained the respect of Afghan leaders. 'We aren’t winning,' Trump reportedly said during the conversation. However, current and former officials assert that frustration has been building for months. As early as February, one former U.S. official stated that the discussions regarding Afghanistan were not intended to create a comprehensive set of options for Trump. Just before McMaster was scheduled to present his plan for Trump’s approval ahead of the May NATO summit, Secretary of State Rex Tillerson chose not to endorse it, indicating that Trump was not being provided with options, according to the former official and another current official. 'The absence of options meant that the only recommendation that was initially to be presented to the president was essentially the status quo,' the former official noted, downplaying the troop increase as a significant change in strategy. Nevertheless, in the intervening months, the potential for a complete withdrawal has been repeatedly suggested and refined alongside a genuine 'status-quo' option where no additional troops are deployed to Afghanistan, but none are withdrawn either. Nonetheless, it is believed that U.S. defense leaders do not favor these options.

text: U.S. President Donald Trump is set to launch a significant campaign next week aimed at persuading the public regarding the necessity of tax reform, as reported by The Financial Times on Friday. This shift in focus to fiscal policy is part of an effort to secure a substantial legislative achievement by the year's end. According to Gary Cohn, the director of the National Economic Council, Trump will kick off this initiative with a speech in Missouri next Wednesday, marking the beginning of a series of speeches designed to garner public backing for the reform. "We are fully committed to tax reform," Cohn stated in the FT interview. "Beginning next week, the president’s agenda and schedule will center around tax reform. He will start traveling to deliver significant speeches that explain the rationale behind tax reform." While Cohn emphasized that tax reform is a priority on Trump’s agenda, the Republican-led Congress has two urgent matters to address when it reconvenes after the August recess on September 5. Legislators need to authorize an increase in the U.S. debt ceiling to permit the federal government to continue borrowing and meet its financial obligations, including servicing its debt. Additionally, they must enact at least temporary spending measures to ensure the government remains operational. Deadlines for both issues will approach swiftly after lawmakers return from their break. When asked by the FT if the discussion surrounding the debt ceiling could hinder the tax reform initiative, Cohn responded that "ultimately, Congress must increase the debt ceiling - that is simply the reality." He further noted that this would occur in September, ahead of any tax reform legislation. "The pivotal point is this: tax reform is currently the White House’s top priority," he added. Cohn mentioned that officials at the White House have been collaborating with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, House Speaker Paul Ryan, and other key congressional Republicans to develop "an outline and framework" for the tax reform proposal, stating, "and we have a solid framework that we have agreed upon." The specifics Cohn shared aligned closely with those mentioned by Ryan during a meeting with Boeing employees the previous Thursday. When questioned about whether the emphasis on tax reform had been complicated by Twitter criticisms from the Republican president directed at McConnell and Ryan, Cohn remarked that White House officials have collaborated effectively with both leaders and "we have made substantial progress" on tax matters. He stated that the House Ways and Means Committee would provide more "details" on the tax reform plan once lawmakers return from the recess. Cohn expressed confidence that a bill could advance through tax committees in both legislative chambers and be approved by both the House and Senate by the end of 2017. Concerning individual taxpayers, Cohn indicated that the president’s reform strategy would safeguard the three major deductions that individuals can claim on their taxes: for home mortgages, charitable contributions, and retirement savings. Moreover, it would raise the limits for the standard deduction while removing most other personal deductions, according to Cohn. The proposal also intends to eliminate taxes on estates inherited after a person’s passing. For businesses, Cohn stated that the administration is looking to reduce corporate tax rates while also abolishing many of the deductions that corporations utilize to lessen their tax liabilities. When asked if the corporate tax rate could be reduced to 15 percent as Trump had previously suggested, Cohn replied, "I would like to set the tax rate as low as possible to encourage businesses to create jobs here." He also mentioned that the administration would advocate for a system whereby American companies would not incur additional taxes when repatriating profits earned overseas. "Currently, they frequently have to pay extra taxes for bringing profits back to the U.S.," Cohn explained. "Our existing system effectively penalizes companies for being headquartered in the U.S." He concluded by saying that the administration does foresee a one-time low tax rate on all overseas profits.

text: CAIRO (Reuters) - Sameh Shoukry, Egypt's Foreign Minister, is scheduled to travel to Addis Ababa next week for discussions with his Ethiopian counterpart, as announced by a spokesman from the foreign ministry. This visit aims to resolve a deadlock concerning a multi-billion dollar dam project on the Nile River. The contention, which also includes Sudan, revolves around the distribution of the Nile's waters, which extend for 6,695 km (4,184 miles) from Lake Victoria to the Mediterranean Sea, serving as the essential economic resource for all three nations. Egypt asserts that the dam poses a threat to water supplies that have historically supported its agriculture and economy for millennia. In contrast, Ethiopia maintains that the Grand Renaissance Dam, which it aspires will establish it as Africa's largest power exporter, will not significantly impact Egypt. Ethiopia accuses Cairo of exerting its political influence to discourage investors from supporting other energy projects in Ethiopia. Delegations from Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia convened in Cairo in November to endorse a study conducted by a French company, aimed at evaluating the environmental and economic implications of the dam. However, talks came to a standstill as they could not reach a consensus on the preliminary report, with each side attributing the lack of progress to the other. Moataz Moussa, Sudan's Irrigation Minister, indicated that Egypt was reluctant to accept modifications to the report suggested by Khartoum and Addis Ababa. He noted in November that Sudan and Ethiopia had raised concerns regarding various aspects, particularly the proposed baseline from which the study would assess the dam's effects. Another point of contention is whether Ethiopia intends to finalize construction before concluding negotiations about water distribution. Mahmoud Abou Zeid, Chair of the Arab Water Council and a former Egyptian irrigation minister, remarked that it is evident Ethiopia does not wish to quickly arrive at conclusions. He expressed belief that they may wish to commence filling the dam and finish construction while discussions are still ongoing, which he claimed would breach an agreement made by all three nations in Khartoum in 2015 to promote diplomatic collaboration and mitigate concerns over a resource conflict. Cairo is apprehensive that the 6,000-megawatt dam, being constructed by Italy’s leading construction company, Salini Impregilo SpA, and expected to be completed next year, will diminish the water flow critical for drinking and irrigation. Egyptian officials assert that protecting the nation’s share of Nile water is a matter of national security. "No one can touch Egypt’s water ... (which) means life or death for a population," President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi stated last month.

text: Connecticut's governor has stated that a return to the prosperity experienced before the recession is unlikely. NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Wednesday, Governor Dannel Malloy of Connecticut gave a grim speech, laying out strategies to cut government expenditures and acknowledging a "visceral feeling" that the state would not revert to the affluence of the pre-recession era. This brief and serious address followed a presentation by Malloy’s chief budget advisor, who advocated for $570 million in spending reductions for the upcoming year, in addition to prior years' significant cuts and tax increases. "Our national economy, while showing improvement since the Great Recession, has been fundamentally altered," Malloy, a member of the Democratic Party, remarked during his annual state of the state speech. "A changing labor market, the swift advancement of technology, and stagnant wage growth have made this recovery more challenging for everyone, everywhere." Connecticut has persistently fallen behind the national economic recovery and has experienced job losses in its vital financial and high-tech manufacturing sectors. The state possesses one of the least well-funded pension systems across the nation. With mandatory payments projected to surge to $6 billion by 2032, this system poses a considerable threat to the budget. "Connecticut is not returning to that pre-recession reality," Malloy conveyed to the legislature, which is dominated by Democrats. "It simply no longer exists." The difficulties faced by Connecticut illustrate the uneven way U.S. states have participated in the recovery since the financial crisis that occurred between 2007 and 2009. Andrew Cuomo, the governor of nearby New York, expressed enough confidence to promote a $100 billion infrastructure initiative in January. "It’s been a really hard recovery," remarked Douglas Offerman, an analyst at Fitch Ratings. "The previous assumption that every expansion would surpass previous peaks doesn’t seem to be holding true at this moment." Ben Barnes, Malloy’s leading budget official, indicated that the transition from higher-paying jobs to lower- and middle-wage employment has been a "major story" contributing to Connecticut’s budget challenges. Barnes suggested a 5.75 percent reduction in the budgets of state agencies, which could lead to the loss of several thousand jobs. He noted that discretionary spending cuts would total 15 percent over a two-year period. At the commencement of the legislative session, Malloy urged legislators to approve an early budget instead of waiting until the fiscal year's end on June 30. However, he stated he would not bypass the established process. The governor also proposed reforming the state’s budget management to align the process more closely with revenue projections, moving away from a "current services" framework. Additionally, he asserted that lawmakers should adopt a spending cap.

text: The German interior minister has called on the EU to create uniform standards for benefits provided to asylum seekers. De Maiziere suggested that a more unified system might include potential subsidies for migrants to help them manage higher living expenses in countries like Germany, in addition to a consistent amount established at the EU level. He also advocated for shared legal regulations, asserting: "Asylum seekers here can significantly prolong their deportation using various legal avenues more than they can in other places."

text: Tension envelops the Nigerian city as a separatist leader goes unaccounted for. UMUAHIA, Nigeria (Reuters) - A leader advocating for independence from Nigeria has been untraceable since an alleged military raid that occurred over two weeks ago, which left his residence in Umuahia peppered with bullet impacts, shattered windows, and doors hanging loosely. The vanishing of Nnamdi Kanu, following the army's claim that the raid did not take place, poses a risk of reigniting separatist turmoil that could destabilize southeastern Nigeria, a region that witnessed the deaths of one million individuals during the civil war from 1967 to 1970 over the brief Republic of Biafra. Kingsley Kanu, 48, recounted that he was with his brother Nnamdi, the leader of the Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB), at their family residence on the night of September 14 when soldiers burst in. They were shooting at everything in sight, he remarked, indicating the bullet marks on the walls and windows. They came here merely to kill everyone, he stated, adding that around 20 members of IPOB were gunned down, although most bodies were taken away by the soldiers. On September 27, Reuters reporters, including a journalist and a TV cameraman, observed six bodies with bullet wounds in a morgue, which IPOB claimed were their members. Two of the corpses resembled men in photographs displayed by grieving relatives who informed Reuters that their brothers perished during the raid, although the identities of the other four could not be confirmed. A military spokesperson declared to reporters in Abuja, the capital, that the military did not conduct a raid on Nnamdi Kanu's home. Nnamdi Kanu is not held by the military. This accusation and subsequent denial have become a significant point of contention amid a military deployment in the southeast that commenced in September. Observers from civil society and analysts assert that the military's presence, the recent classification of IPOB as a terrorist organization, and the leader's disappearance could lead to separatists abandoning their non-violent stance. President Muhammadu Buhari, a Muslim from the north, emphasized a crackdown on secessionists in his first address in August after returning from a three-month medical leave in Britain. He subsequently engaged in discussions with military leaders, and days later, Operation Python Dance was initiated, which the military claimed aimed to curb violent crime and separatist agitation. Armed soldiers are visible throughout Umuahia, the capital city of Abia state, in armored vehicles and at checkpoints where drivers are frequently questioned. Buhari is already dealing with the jihadist insurgency of Boko Haram in the northeast while attempting to uphold a ceasefire with militants in the oil-rich Niger Delta region to the south. However, some critics argue that the former military leader may be worsening the situation, as militant violence in the Niger Delta surged last year following troop deployments. HEAVY-HANDED? The government's aggressive tactics will only bolster local support for a radical faction that previously struggled to expand its following, stated Malte Liewerscheidt from global risk consultancy Verisk Maplecroft. Ryan Cummings, director of the Africa-focused risk management firm Signal Risk, indicated that the Igbo ethnic group, which predominates the area and has long expressed feelings of marginalization, feels specifically targeted. He noted that the government has allowed insecurity to flourish in other parts of Nigeria without similar military interventions, referencing attacks by Fulani herdsmen that have resulted in hundreds of deaths in central Nigeria in recent years. Following the arrival of troops in the southeast, tensions rose. The governor of Abia implemented a curfew in the city of Aba last month. Several days of conflict between IPOB members and soldiers led to claims from the group that Kanu's residence had been surrounded by military personnel, which the military refuted. Videos circulating on social media, including clips allegedly depicting troops in Abia using sticks to beat men stripped to the waist, which the army stated it was investigating, have intensified public outrage. The army's presence frightened our community. People recounted experiences from the Biafran war, stated Onyebuchi Ememanka, a special assistant.

The committee expressed worries about FEMA’s supervision of the Whitefish agreement. text: PHNOM PENH (Reuters) - A prominent deputy of Cambodia's imprisoned opposition leader departed the nation on Tuesday, expressing concerns for her safety following Prime Minister Hun Sen's warning of additional arrests targeting opposition figures. Kem Sokha, who heads the Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP), was detained on September 3 and charged with treason amid an expanding crackdown on Hun Sen's critics, which his adversaries argue is a strategy to secure victory in the upcoming election next year. "With no genuine opposition and a pervasive atmosphere of fear, there is no chance for free and fair elections in 2018," Mu Sochua, 63, stated to Reuters after exiting Cambodia, noting that she "did not feel secure." She added, "Democracy in Cambodia is swiftly deteriorating to a point where there are no opposing forces left to combat dictatorship." Government spokesperson Phay Siphan remarked that Mu Sochua had chosen to leave voluntarily and was uncertain if authorities had intended to arrest her. Mu Sochua, recognized globally for her efforts against sex trafficking and for promoting women's rights, has been one of the most vocal opposition leaders since Kem Sokha's arrest and allegation of conspiring to seize power with American assistance. Last week, she informed Reuters that nearly half of the CNRP's parliamentary members had fled the country out of fear. On Monday, Hun Sen, who has been in power for over thirty years, threatened further arrests of opposition members, labeling them as "rebels in the city" intent on initiating a "color revolution" despite past failures. Western nations have denounced Kem Sokha's detention and called for his release, asserting that the legitimacy of next year's election is questionable, yet they have not indicated any actions against the government. In contrast, China has expressed support for Hun Sen's administration, who is 65 and a former Khmer Rouge commander that later defected from the group responsible for the genocide that ravaged Cambodia in the 1970s. The CNRP's significant successes in local council elections in June had suggested a challenging contest for Hun Sen in the forthcoming general election. Despite consistent annual economic growth of about 7 percent, which has aided in transforming Cambodia from a failed state, public discontent has increased due to inequality and claims of cronyism. In his first remarks following his arrest, Kem Sokha stated on Facebook on Monday that he was pursuing positive change in Cambodia through elections rather than through revolution, as alleged. One of his three deputies remains in Cambodia. text: Trump and his political party: an American pair like no other. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, President Donald Trump took the opportunity to speak with journalists aboard Air Force One, where he notably praised Democratic congressional leaders he had met with earlier at the White House. This omission could be interpreted as a slight or simply an oversight - the White House did not clarify immediately - but given the recent circumstances, it served as a reminder of Trump's ongoing dissatisfaction with Republicans in Congress, even as he begins to collaborate with Democrats to overcome a legislative stalemate. Trump, who has labeled Democrats as obstructionists, on Wednesday supported a proposal from Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi for a three-month extension of the U.S. debt ceiling, turning down a Republican proposal for a longer extension. In contrast, during a meeting on Tuesday with McConnell, the Senate majority leader, and Ryan, the House speaker, both fellow Republicans, there was minimal personal engagement in front of the press. A close associate of Trump stated that the 71-year-old bold former reality television personality, who had never held public office prior to his inauguration in January, has yet to grasp the importance of mending his relationship with McConnell, a 75-year-old serious legislative strategist with over 30 years of experience in the U.S. Senate. Faced with the precariousness of his legislative agenda, Trump is feeling the strain to strengthen his rapport with McConnell and salvage what remains of an increasingly threatened agenda that encompasses healthcare reform, immigration, infrastructure, and tax legislation. "If you want to go after the majority leader, that’s your choice, but it won’t advance your agenda. To achieve results, you must maintain a good relationship with him," the source remarked. A Republican ally of the White House mentioned that Trump "doesn’t realize he depends on Mitch McConnell more than anyone else in Washington, as he oversees the Senate and dictates the agenda." "McConnell is an expert in the Senate and he could and should be Trump's most valuable asset," the Republican stated. Trump has spent recent months in conflict with McConnell. Following the failure of a healthcare reform initiative in the Senate in July, Trump and McConnell exchanged blame. McConnell remarked in his home state of Kentucky that Trump had "unrealistic expectations" about the speed at which things could be accomplished in Congress and hinted that Trump lacked experience. Clearly irritated, Trump cast doubt on McConnell’s effectiveness. "Senator Mitch McConnell claimed I had 'unrealistic expectations,' but I don’t believe that. "He simply dislikes being criticized and perceived McConnell’s remarks as belittling," the source explained. An associate of McConnell noted that he views the typical drama surrounding Trump as "completely irrelevant" to conducting business with him and that from a "practical standpoint," McConnell's sole focus is on accomplishing tasks. "He’s quite devoid of drama," the associate noted. "I have yet to encounter any instance where he allows personal feelings, animosity, or emotional reactions to influence his business dealings." McConnell, whose spouse, Elaine Chao, is Trump’s transportation secretary, has stated that he holds no grudges following Trump’s criticisms. text: A congressional intelligence committee in the United States harshly criticized former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden on Thursday. The report accused Snowden of leaking information that led to significant harm to U.S. national security, misrepresenting his background, and clashing with colleagues. Supported by both Republican and Democratic leaders, the House intelligence committee asserted that Snowden was "not a whistleblower," contrary to his claims. The majority of the materials he illegally acquired from the NSA did not pertain to privacy violations but instead disclosed intelligence and defense initiatives that are of considerable interest to America’s adversaries abroad, the report noted. While the committee acknowledged that the "full scope" of the damage from Snowden’s leaks is undetermined, it indicated that a review of the materials he reportedly compromised "clearly demonstrates that he disclosed secrets that safeguard American personnel overseas and intelligence critical for defending against terrorists and hostile nations." The committee published a four-page summary of what it described as a 36-page investigative report, which remains classified as Top Secret. Nonetheless, the summary included strong critiques regarding Snowden's actions and history. The findings introduce new allegations regarding Snowden and his potential motivations for leaking government secrets. The report claims that Snowden, who sought asylum in Moscow after fleeing to Hong Kong, "was and continues to be a habitual exaggerator and fabricator." It highlights discrepancies in his official employment history, stating that despite his assertions of leaving U.S. Army basic training due to broken legs, he actually "washed out due to shin splints." The report further states that while Snowden claimed to have obtained a high school equivalency diploma, he never actually did. Additionally, it mentions his assertion of working as a "senior advisor" for the CIA, while he was, in reality, an entry-level computer technician. Although the report states that Snowden "stole 1.5 million sensitive documents," other sources who have scrutinized the materials he provided to media outlets estimate the figure to be between 200,000 and 300,000 documents. Some U.S. officials involved in investigations related to Snowden admit that the government does not have a definitive count of how many documents he downloaded, acknowledging that the 1.5 million figure is merely an estimate. The report also challenges Snowden’s reasons for acquiring and leaking classified information, claiming he became involved in a "workplace disagreement" with NSA supervisors in June 2012 regarding computer updates. It mentions that a contracting officer reprimanded him for not adhering to proper grievance protocols, and he began downloading classified information just two weeks after that. However, in 2013, Reuters reported that U.S. officials and other sources familiar with the situation suggested that Snowden started downloading the data in April 2012, nearly a year earlier than previously indicated at that time. The release of the House committee report coincided with the debut of "Snowden," a film directed by Oliver Stone depicting him as a whistleblower and a hero. On Wednesday, leading human rights advocates called on President Barack Obama to pardon Snowden before he leaves office in January. U.S. officials have indicated that Obama is not contemplating a pardon for Snowden, who is facing criminal charges in the U.S. for providing classified information to unauthorized individuals. Ben Wizner, an attorney from the American Civil Liberties Union representing Snowden, criticized the House committee report as lacking depth. Wizner stated that the timing of the report's release, just a day before the film's opening, "is indicative that individuals within the intelligence community are taking us seriously, and they are worried that Oliver Stone’s movie will solidify Snowden’s representation as a genuine patriot, which he is not."

text: President-elect Donald Trump announced on Wednesday that he has engaged with several candidates to fill the long-standing vacancy on the U.S. Supreme Court and committed to making a decision on a nominee approximately two weeks after he assumes office on January 20. During a press conference held in New York, Trump emphasized the significance of selecting a successor for the late conservative Justice Antonin Scalia, who passed away on February 13 of last year. The Senate, controlled by Republicans, declined to consider President Barack Obama’s nominee for the position, appeals court judge Merrick Garland. "This will be a choice that I am very passionate about. I believe it is one of the reasons I was elected," Trump remarked, reiterating his earlier promise to select a judge akin to Scalia, a prominent conservative figure on the nine-member court. Trump indicated that he would likely announce his decision "probably within two weeks of the 20th ... likely in the second week." He refrained from naming any of the potential candidates or specifying how many had been interviewed, but noted, "We’ve met with numerous candidates. They were outstanding in every case." Trump mentioned he would be choosing from individuals recommended to him by conservative legal organizations. He stated that he has a list comprising 20 names, while the initial list released by his presidential campaign included 21 names. Trump specifically acknowledged contributions from the Federalist Society and former Republican South Carolina Senator Jim DeMint. The passing of Scalia resulted in a split in the U.S. Supreme Court, which now has four conservative and four liberal justices. Finding a replacement for Scalia could shift the ideological balance of the court for years, reinstating the historically conservative majority at a time when it seemed that liberals might gain an advantage on the bench. This decision could have significant implications for a variety of issues including abortion, the death penalty, religious freedoms, presidential authority, transgender rights, federal regulations, and more. According to the U.S. Constitution, the president is tasked with nominating members of the Supreme Court, while the Senate holds the power to confirm such selections. In a rare move in U.S. history, the Republican-led Senate opted not to consider President Obama’s nominee, asserting that the victor of the November 8 presidential election, between Republican Trump and Democrat Hillary Clinton, should be the one to make the appointment. The Supreme Court is currently in the midst of its term, which began in October and will conclude in June.

BELFAST (Reuters) - A spokesperson for the British government stated that legislation will need to be introduced to establish a budget for Northern Ireland if the political parties in the region fail to reach a consensus on reinstating their power-sharing government by Monday. Since the collapse of its regional administration in January, Northern Ireland has been without governing authority, which raises the possibility of direct rule being reinstated from London, potentially disrupting a fragile political equilibrium in the British province. Last week, the British minister responsible for the region, James Brokenshire, indicated that negotiations had stalled, with the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein party and the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) at an impasse over the rights of Irish language speakers. If an agreement is achieved by Monday, Brokenshire would head back to London to initiate the necessary processes to establish a new Northern Ireland Executive, the spokesperson noted. Conversely, if London imposes a budget, it would mark the closest Northern Ireland has been to a return to direct governance in ten years. Brokenshire cautioned the parties that they are on a trajectory toward increased intervention by the UK government. The DUP and Sinn Fein previously shared power in the last devolved administration, which was established following a peace agreement that ended three decades of conflict in the region. The leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), a smaller party in the area, stated that transferring budgetary control to London essentially amounts to direct rule and cannot be described otherwise. Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams remarked that a new round of discussions would commence if an agreement is not reached by Monday. 'If there is no arrangement finalized when the British minister proposes a budget, it will indicate that this round of talks - and there will inevitably need to be additional rounds - has been exhausted,' Adams told the Irish national broadcaster RTE. Irish Foreign Minister Simon Coveney, who is co-facilitating the discussions alongside Brokenshire, has expressed that reverting to direct rule would deal a 'devastating' blow to reconciliation efforts in the area. Coveney has also urged the parties to come to an agreement so that Northern Ireland can have a more significant role in Britain's negotiations to exit the European Union, which is anticipated to have a more substantial effect on the province than on any other part of the United Kingdom.

text: The White House defended President Donald Trump's invitation to Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte on Sunday, emphasizing the necessity of his cooperation in addressing the North Korean situation, even while the administration faced criticism regarding human rights concerns related to its outreach to Manila. Trump extended the invitation during a phone call with Duterte on Saturday evening, which the White House described as being "very friendly." Duterte has been accused by international human rights organizations of endorsing extrajudicial killings of drug offenders in the Philippines. White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus stated on ABC's "This Week" that "There is nothing right now facing this country and facing the region that is a bigger threat than what’s happening in North Korea," during a weekend in which Trump aimed to solidify support in Southeast Asia to assist in curbing North Korea's nuclear and missile activities. On Monday, North Korea indicated it would persist with its nuclear tests, asserting it would enhance its capabilities "to the maximum" in a "consecutive and successive way at any moment" in response to what it perceives as U.S. aggression and hysteria. Priebus emphasized that the engagement with Duterte "doesn’t mean that human rights don’t matter, but what it does mean is that the issues facing us developing out of North Korea are so serious that we need cooperation at some level with as many partners in the area as we can get to make sure we have our ducks in a row." Since assuming office last year, Duterte has frequently criticized Washington, his nation's long-time ally, while attempting to improve relations with China and has expressed interest in strengthening ties with Russia. Regarding his invitation from Trump on Monday, he remained non-committal, stating to reporters, "I’m tied up. I cannot make any definite promise. I am supposed to go to Russia and go to Israel," referencing previously scheduled trips. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Robespierre Bolivar remarked that a formal letter of invitation would be accepted once received. The invitation for Duterte to visit the White House at a yet-to-be-determined date appears to exemplify Trump's tendency to favor foreign leaders with questionable human rights records or autocratic backgrounds. For example, he has shown admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin during the 2016 presidential race, welcomed Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to the White House, and has spoken positively about Chinese President Xi Jinping, whom Trump is urging to take more action to restrain North Korea, its ally and neighbor. On Sunday, Trump also offered an invitation to Thai Prime Minister Prayuth Chan-ocha, a former general who leads a military government that assumed power following a coup in 2014. Prayuth’s administration has had a contentious relationship with Trump’s predecessor, Barack Obama. John Sifton, the Asia director of Human Rights Watch, criticized the invitation, stating, "Celebrating a man who boasts of killing his own citizens and inviting him to the White House, while remaining silent on his disgusting human rights record, sends a terrifying message. By effectively endorsing Duterte’s murderous ‘war on drugs’, Trump has made himself morally complicit in future killings," he added. However, a Trump administration official insisted that the invitation was not intended as a reward for Duterte or an endorsement of his policies, but rather a decision that engaging with the Philippines was preferable to withdrawal, which could "intensify bad behavior" from Duterte. "It’s not a ‘thank you’," the official clarified, requesting anonymity. "It’s a meeting." The official refuted a report from the New York Times which indicated that administration officials were surprised by the invitation to Duterte and were expected to protest it internally. "We were not surprised. The guys who prepared for the call were unified on this," the official stated. Priebus underscored that North Korea remains the top priority.

text: China has detained a Japanese national believed to be involved in espionage activities. BEIJING (Reuters) - On Monday, Chinese officials arrested a Japanese individual suspected of spying, as reported by local state media. The arrest took place in Dalian, a port city situated in the northeastern province of Liaoning, which shares a border with North Korea, according to an online report from the official Dalian Daily. The report indicates that Ken Higuchi is under investigation by the Dalian City National Security Bureau for alleged espionage against China, with prosecutors having sanctioned his arrest. The character attributed to Higuchi's first name may also refer to Takeshi or Takeru. However, the report did not clarify if Higuchi was a new case or if he had been previously detained, with this being his formal arrest. In 2010, four Japanese citizens were detained in China for allegedly entering a military area and photographing it without authorization. Furthermore, at least two Japanese nationals were arrested on espionage charges in 2015. Last year, China announced it was investigating a Japanese citizen for allegedly compromising national security.

text: NEW YORK (Reuters) - On Monday, Puerto Rico’s federal oversight board unanimously voted to endorse the government’s revised fiscal recovery plan, contingent upon modifications that would remove Christmas bonuses, enforce employee furloughs, and further decrease pension expenditures. This plan is a fundamental aspect of the PROMESA federal law aimed at rescuing Puerto Rico and will establish the groundwork for upcoming restructuring negotiations with creditors holding approximately $70 billion in debt, which has pushed the U.S. territory to the edge of economic disaster. The board indicated that the government could circumvent some austerity measures, which have led to protests among Puerto Ricans, provided it submits alternative cost-saving strategies by April 30. PROMESA mandates that Governor Ricardo Rossello deliver a recovery strategy that requires approval from the board. The initial draft was rejected by the board last week due to its reliance on “overly optimistic” economic forecasts. The revised version adjusted those figures, raising the island’s projected funding gap over the next decade to $67 billion from $56 billion and anticipating $39.6 billion in new cash flows from spending cuts and revenue measures, an increase from the previous plan’s $33.8 billion. This new iteration estimates that the island would have $800 million annually available for debt servicing, a reduction from $1.2 billion in the earlier draft. On Monday, Puerto Rico credit analyst Chas Tyson from KBW Inc remarked in a note that “the new plan is modestly worse than the old plan for creditors, as it implies larger haircuts.” The board’s approval came with stipulations: the government must cut pension costs by 10 percent starting in 2020, eliminate Christmas bonuses, and enforce employee furloughs no later than July 1 to prevent a short-term cash shortage. Protests against the austerity measures occurred outside the meeting venue in lower Manhattan, with teachers asserting that furloughs would effectively shorten the public school calendar by two months annually. The government can evade furloughs and bonus reductions if it presents the board with a strategy by April 30 that boosts liquidity by $200 million. Rossello expressed confidence that such cuts would not be necessary, stating, “I’m very confident we’ll have $200 million in reserve cash, so that we can jump over that obstacle” in an interview with Reuters following the meeting. The board announced it would enter negotiations with the government over the next 30 days regarding pension reductions, a sensitive topic on an island where retirement systems are nearly insolvent due to years of mismanagement and overly generous promises made to workers. After the meeting, board member Andrew Biggs, a pension specialist, told reporters, “All stakeholders have been forced to sacrifice, and no one is exempt from that.” He added that the cuts would be implemented “in a way that would spare the lowest-income people from any reductions.” Rossello assured that he would not support policies that would negatively impact the most vulnerable pensioners, stating, “I don’t see any way I can reduce pensions of people already having a hard time getting medications and things.” In a separate contentious decision, the board endorsed government efforts to pursue additional concessions from the bondholders of PREPA, Puerto Rico’s power utility, which is over $8 billion in debt. Although a tentative restructuring has been in place for more than a year, Rossello’s administration has indicated it will seek revised terms, leading to concern and frustration among PREPA’s creditors. Additionally, a subcommittee of the U.S. House Committee on Natural Resources announced a hearing scheduled for March 22 to discuss the status of the PREPA agreement, which currently entails creditors accepting a 15-percent reduction.

text: The campaign for U.S. Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump reached out to Capitol Hill on Monday, seeking support as his criticisms of the Muslim parents of a decorated American soldier who died in Iraq faced severe backlash from members of his own party. Trump's remarks directed at Khizr Khan and Ghazala Khan, who appeared at the Democratic convention the previous week, have raised alarm and disappointment among Republican lawmakers reacting to this latest Trump incident that has caught his party associates off guard. Republican Senator John McCain, a former prisoner of war and the most notable veteran in Congress, along with the leader of the Veterans of Foreign Wars, joined in the widespread disapproval, emphasizing the esteemed status that the military and its veterans hold in the United States. The conflict between Trump and the Khans has taken center stage in the presidential campaign in recent days, highlighting the fragile relationship many prominent Republicans have with the party's unconventional and free-spirited nominee for the election on November 8. Rob Wasinger, a former congressional candidate involved in outreach efforts for the Trump campaign, sent an email to senior aides in the Senate requesting assistance, stating, "We want to issue several member statements on this matter today and would greatly appreciate your support." A similar request was made to House Republicans, as mentioned by a senior aide. Accompanying the request were talking points for lawmakers to use in efforts to mitigate the escalating controversy following the Khans' appearance at the Democratic convention, where they spoke about their son, U.S. Army Captain Humayun Khan, who died from a bomb in Iraq 12 years ago. Hope Hicks, a spokesperson for Trump, indicated that the campaign appreciated congressional support and that Republicans were focused on preventing Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton from achieving the presidency. Wasinger declined to comment when reached by phone. However, the request did not yield any assistance for Trump. A senior aide to Republican senators, who wished to remain anonymous, noted that they were pleased with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s statement on Sunday, which referred to Captain Khan as "an American hero" and remarked that "a travel ban on all members of a religion is simply contrary to American values." Despite this, the aide suggested that the controversy likely would not lead Republican senators to retract their endorsements of Trump. During a speech at the convention, accompanied by his wife, Khizr Khan highlighted his son's military service and condemned Trump's proposal for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the United States, holding up a copy of the U.S. Constitution and encouraging Trump to read it. Subsequently, Trump expressed that he was "viciously" attacked by the couple and insinuated that Ghazala Khan might not have been "allowed" to speak, suggesting that her silence represented restrictions imposed on women by certain traditional Muslims. McCain, the 2008 Republican presidential nominee and current chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, released a detailed statement strongly criticizing Trump's remarks. "While our party has granted him the nomination, it does not come with an unrestricted license to slander those who are the best among us," stated McCain, who was a prisoner of war for five years during the Vietnam War. His counterpart on the House Armed Services Committee, Representative Mac Thornberry of Texas, supported McCain's sentiments, expressing in a statement that he was "dismayed at the attacks Khizr and Ghazala Khan have faced after discussing their son's service and sacrifice." The leader of the 1.7 million-member Veterans of Foreign Wars also indicated that Trump’s comments regarding the Khans were excessive. Both Trump and Clinton addressed the group’s national convention last week. "Regardless of the election year, the VFW will not stand for anyone disparaging a Gold Star family member for exercising their right to speech or expression," declared Brian Duffy, the national commander of the organization.

text: President Barack Obama is set to sign a bill aimed at addressing the widespread crisis of heroin and opioid addiction across the United States, as announced by the White House on Wednesday. Following extended negotiations, the Senate approved the legislation with an overwhelming vote of 92-2 on Wednesday, which had already received the backing of the U.S. House of Representatives. This initiative seeks to assist communities in establishing treatment and overdose prevention programs, especially given that less than half of the approximately 2.2 million Americans in need of support for opioid addiction are currently receiving assistance, as reported by the U.S. Centers for Human and Health Services. In a statement, the White House acknowledged that the bill "falls far short" of the required funding, but President Obama will sign it "because some action is better than none." Republican Senator Rob Portman from Ohio, a principal advocate for the bill, remarked that this represents "the first time that we’ve treated addiction like the disease that it is, which will help eliminate the stigma that has plagued addiction for far too long." Despite this legislation being a rare instance of bipartisan cooperation in an election year, Democrats raised concerns that it does not allocate sufficient resources to tackle the drug crisis effectively. Senator Charles Schumer of New York, the No. 3 Senate Democrat, criticized the bill, stating, "This bill is like a Hollywood movie set - something that appears real on the surface but has no substance and no life behind its facade." According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, drug overdose fatalities in the United States reached an unprecedented high in 2014, driven by the misuse of prescription painkillers and heroin. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services reported that 28,000 individuals succumbed to opioid overdoses in 2014, with at least half of those cases involving a prescription opioid. Common prescription medications include oxycodone, hydrocodone, and fentanyl, which are prescribed for pain management. The number of deaths linked to heroin has also surged dramatically, more than tripling since 2010, with over 10,500 fatalities attributed to heroin in 2014, according to the agency. The bill allocates $181 million annually for the new programs it establishes. Democrats expressed uncertainty about whether the funding included in the bipartisan legislation would actually be disbursed, given the ongoing disagreements in Congress regarding next year’s budget for the Department of Health and Human Services. They urged Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, a Republican, to complement this legislation with $600 million in immediate emergency funding. President Obama has sought $920 million for opioid treatment initiatives over a two-year period. If signed into law, the bill would also offer new training for emergency responders in the administration of drugs that can reverse opioid overdoses and assist communities in acquiring these medications.

text: Exclusive: Poll shows Clinton ahead of Trump in crucial swing states, likely to win election. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Should the U.S. presidential election take place today, Democrat Hillary Clinton is poised to secure victory in the pivotal swing states of Florida, Ohio, and Virginia, boasting a 95 percent likelihood of defeating Republican Donald Trump to become the first female president of the United States, as indicated by the Reuters/Ipsos States of the Nation project. This initiative merges opinion polling with an evaluation of voting behaviors across various election scenarios, revealing that Clinton currently leads Trump in the popular vote by six percentage points and is ahead in 19 states, including many of the more populous ones that significantly impact the election outcome. Presently, Clinton would garner at least 268 votes in the Electoral College, which is the entity that ultimately elects the next president, just two votes shy of the number required to claim the White House. On average, the former secretary of state would win by a margin of 108 electoral college votes. Trump, on the other hand, would secure at least 21 states, most of which have smaller populations, providing him with a minimum of 179 electoral votes. With the election still 10 weeks away, significant changes could occur before November 8. The candidates are nearly tied in eight states, including Pennsylvania, Michigan, and North Carolina, while the polling sample is insufficient to establish a clear leader in Alaska, Wyoming, and Washington D.C. However, for Trump to win the presidency, he would need to hold on to the 21 states currently in his favor and sweep all the remaining “toss-up” states. This presents a considerable challenge for Trump, whose combative, anti-establishment campaign has secured him the Republican Party’s nomination but has yet to generate widespread support among voters. According to the polling initiative, if Trump fails to attract significantly larger numbers of women, moderate Republican voters, and minorities, he is highly likely to lose the race for the White House. For instance, an ideal scenario for Trump would involve a high turnout of white men with below-average incomes on Election Day. This demographic strongly supports the real estate tycoon, but even if every one of them votes, it would not suffice for Trump to win any states currently leaning towards Clinton or any of the toss-up states. Clinton would still emerge victorious in the election. The Reuters/Ipsos States of the Nation project is based on an online survey that collects responses from approximately 16,000 individuals weekly. Participants provide information regarding their demographic details, party affiliation, and presidential preference. Responses are weighted according to the latest population estimates, and each respondent is assessed based on their likelihood to vote. Once the polling concludes, the project calculates the support levels and estimated error margins for both candidates and conducts numerous election simulations based on their respective support. Separate simulations are performed for each state and Washington D.C. The initiative executes over 25 million simulations to assess the probability of one candidate’s victory. Representatives from both the Clinton and Trump campaigns did not reply to inquiries regarding the project. A divisive figure, Trump has proposed a more extensive border wall with Mexico, a prohibition on Muslim immigration, and a rejection of international trade agreements. Since March, seven districts in the Tahoua and Tillabery regions have been in a state of emergency, with the government extending this status for an additional three months on September 18. French aircraft were able to evacuate the wounded, but it took two days for Nigerien soldiers to recover the body of one of the fallen soldiers. text: Republicans achieve victory in Obamacare legal dispute, raising insurer apprehensions. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A U.S. judge delivered a win for congressional Republicans on Thursday who contested President Barack Obama’s hallmark healthcare legislation, determining that his administration exceeded its constitutional authority concerning government expenditures. U.S. District Judge Rosemary Collyer, located in Washington, decided that the administration is not permitted to utilize billions in federal funding to grant subsidies under the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, to private insurance companies without Congress's consent. The case, initiated by the Republican-controlled House of Representatives, revolves around reimbursements to insurance firms intended to offset the reductions mandated by the law on customers’ out-of-pocket medical expenses. Although the ruling will not have an immediate impact on the legislation due to the judge placing the decision on hold while an appeal from the administration is anticipated, it contributes to the unpredictability surrounding the future of Obama’s key domestic policy initiative as the Nov. 8 presidential and congressional elections approach, including the question of whether there will be sufficient health insurers willing to stay in the program. Insurers have reported losses from their operations under Obamacare, claiming they have failed to attract a sufficient number of healthy clients to balance the costs incurred from sicker individuals. Two of the largest players in the market, UnitedHealth Group and Humana Inc, have already indicated they will not provide plans in numerous markets for the upcoming year. “If you’re going to lose more money, why participate?” inquired Steve Halper, an analyst with FBR Capital Markets. Shares of hospital operators like Community Health Systems Inc saw a significant drop, while stocks of insurers such as Aetna Inc, which intends to remain in at least 15 Obamacare markets next year, also fell. In legal documents, the administration cautioned that a triumphant court ruling for the House Republicans would result in a surge in insurance premiums for Americans and compel the government to disburse more in tax credits to insurance policyholders. As part of their appeal, the administration is expected to argue that the House lacks the legal standing to bring a lawsuit. “This suit marks the first instance in our nation's history where Congress has been allowed to sue the executive branch over a disagreement regarding the interpretation of a statute,” stated White House spokesman Josh Earnest to reporters. “It’s regrettable that Republicans have turned to a taxpayer-funded lawsuit to re-engage in a political battle they continue to lose,” Earnest added. “They’ve been on the losing side of this fight for six years, and they will again.” Since its enactment by Congress in 2010 amidst unified Republican opposition, conservatives have launched a series of legal challenges against the Affordable Care Act. Collyer was appointed by Republican former President George W. Bush. The law has provided insurance coverage to millions of Americans previously uninsured, subsidizing insurance costs through tax credits. Additionally, the federal government has assisted in mitigating consumers’ out-of-pocket expenses. House Republicans contended that the actions of the administration breached the U.S. Constitution, as it is the legislative branch, not the executive, that grants authorization for government spending. “BIG win for the Constitution,” House Speaker Paul Ryan tweeted. Jonathan Turley, the attorney who led the lawsuit, described the ruling in a blog post as “a resounding victory not just for Congress but for our constitutional system as a whole.” The appeals court in Washington may be more inclined to support the administration’s position, partly because seven of its 11 active judges are Democratic appointees, including four chosen by Obama. The case centers on a cost-sharing provision of Obamacare that mandates insurers to lower deductibles and co-pays. Insurers are expected to receive reimbursements for these expenses from the federal government. Cost-sharing is determined by the income of the policyholder and serves as a mechanism.

text: Kenya's President Uhuru Kenyatta asserted on Thursday that the Supreme Court of the country executed a 'coup' against the people's wishes by invalidating his victory in the presidential election held last month, marking his most forceful comments since the August 8 vote. These statements coincided with the announcement from the election board that the repeat election would be postponed until October 26. Kenyatta's remarks come amid rising political tensions in Kenya, reigniting concerns about potential political violence. Following a disputed presidential election in 2007, clashes resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,200 individuals.  In a televised gathering with supporters, primarily speaking in Kiswahili, Kenyatta declared, "A coup in Kenya has just been executed by the four members of the Supreme Court." He added, "(The court is saying) numbers don’t matter, it is processes that matter." After the court's unexpected ruling on September 1 to annul the election, Kenyatta had initially urged for calm and respect for the decision. However, he later began to voice criticism towards the court. This ruling, which annulled the election on procedural grounds, marked the first occasion in which a judicial entity nullified the election of an incumbent president in Africa. As a key ally to the West, Kenya boasts the largest economy in East Africa and serves as a center for diplomacy, security, and trade in a region frequently afflicted by conflict. Any indication of political instability can have reverberating effects throughout the region. Last month, the election board revealed that Kenyatta won the August 8 election by a margin of 1.4 million votes over his main rival, seasoned opposition leader Raila Odinga, who is contesting the outcome in court. Four judges, along with two dissenting judges, presented a comprehensive argument for either voiding or upholding the election during a lengthy 12-hour court session on Wednesday. Kenyatta stated in a televised press conference that the court failed to thoroughly investigate evidence that could have supported his victory. "The Supreme Court owes Kenyans an explanation of how such a monstrous injustice occurred," he remarked. He noted that the ruling could potentially plunge the nation into judicial turmoil, suggesting that lower courts might follow this precedent and overturn voters' decisions in other electoral races, including local or legislative positions, and indicated he had requested parliament to address the concerns raised by the ruling. On Thursday, the cabinet sanctioned 10 billion shillings ($97 million) to finance the repeat election. Odinga has stated he will not participate in the new election unless certain conditions are fulfilled, including the dismissal of some senior personnel at the election board. The court determined that there was no evidence of individual wrongdoing by the board's staff. The court mandated that the election must be conducted by the end of October. The detailed judgment issued by the court on Wednesday was based on the election board's failure to verify electronic tallies, which can be prone to errors, against paper forms designed as a backup before results were declared. The judges did not indicate they discovered evidence of vote tampering. Kenyatta expressed his intention to respect the court’s ruling but claimed it undermined the people's will. "We have reversed everything in this country by the decision of a few individuals. I am uncertain how history will assess these gentlemen," he stated. "The citizen has been told he does not have a voice... If that is not dictatorship, then I don't know what to say."

text: Syrian government troops intensified their offensive in Aleppo on Friday, engaging in ground combat and conducting air strikes as part of an operation aimed at reclaiming the entirety of the city’s eastern areas held by rebels, a move that would bring President Bashar al-Assad closer to achieving victory in the civil war. "The advance is proceeding as planned and at times is quicker than anticipated," a military source from Syria informed Reuters. According to the source, the Syrian army and its allies have regained control of 32 out of the 40 neighborhoods in eastern Aleppo, which amounts to approximately 85 percent of the territory. This military push was confirmed by Reuters reporters, rebel forces, and a monitoring group. However, there were no indications that the Syrian army had achieved substantial progress. Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov mentioned that the Syrian army had paused military operations to allow civilians to exit from areas held by rebels, as reported by the RIA news agency. The army and its allies attempted to advance on two fronts, as stated by a Turkish-based official associated with the Jabha Shamiya rebel faction. "The helicopters, warplanes, and rocket attacks continue as they do every day. Nothing has changed," the official remarked. Despite the ongoing bombardment, the official noted that "the guys are steadfast." During a visit to Old Aleppo on Friday, which had recently come under Syrian army control, Reuters reporters recorded the sound of nine air strikes over a span of about thirty minutes. Fighting was audible from adjacent areas. The Russian air force and Iran-backed Shi’ite militias are supporting the government’s efforts in Aleppo. Rebel leaders have shown no indication that they are considering withdrawal, as the civilian population is being confined to an increasingly smaller area. On Friday, Sergei Rudskoi from the Russian Defense Ministry stated that around 10,500 Syrians had fled from parts of eastern Aleppo still under rebel control in the past 24 hours. This claim remains unverified independently. In the last two weeks, Syrian government and allied forces have pushed rebels out of the majority of their territory in what was previously Syria’s largest city. The rebels have maintained control over the eastern section since 2012, and Assad stated in a Thursday interview that reclaiming Aleppo would alter the trajectory of the civil war across the entire nation. The Syrian government now seems closer to victory than ever before in the five years since protests against Assad escalated into armed conflict. The war has resulted in over 300,000 deaths and has left more than half of the Syrian population homeless. Outside of Aleppo, the Syrian army announced a ceasefire in several regions around Damascus and in the northwestern province of Idlib starting Friday evening, without specifying the duration of the ceasefire. There was no immediate response from the rebels. Nevertheless, there was no indication of any ceasefire within Aleppo. "There are aerial assaults on the city’s neighborhoods using highly explosive incendiary bombs, barrel bombs, and artillery fire," a fighter from the Nour al-Din al-Zinki rebel group on the eastern Aleppo front told Reuters. In Old Aleppo, newly reclaimed by the government, extensive damage was evident within the UNESCO World Heritage Site, with ancient buildings suffering fire damage, structures reduced to rubble, and spent munitions scattered everywhere. Alongside a road, a woman in her late 20s, veiled and dressed in black, sat weeping while holding her baby. "My son was born after three months of siege. There were no hospitals, no diapers, no milk," she lamented. "My milk is dry from fear and panic." A group of displaced civilians, including children, had gathered along the road with their belongings after escaping the Saliheen district, where fighting persisted. Nine-year-old Maher Tashtash expressed that the bombardment had been terrifying and revealed that rebels had warned them of death if they were caught by the army. His 12-year-old brother Mohammed shared that they had taken refuge in a cellar until the fighting subsided. Even the deceased were not spared from the devastation. In the Dar al-Islam cemetery near Ibn Sina street in al-Hamdaniya, graves were damaged, and people were burying bodies in open public spaces.

text: At least six individuals lost their lives during a protest in Colombia regarding the eradication of coca crops, which serve as the primary ingredient for cocaine. This was confirmed by President Juan Manuel Santos on Friday. Santos has mandated a more thorough investigation into the incident, which occurred on Thursday and resulted in 19 additional injuries. The confrontation took place in Narino province, close to Tumaco, an important area for coca cultivation. There were conflicting reports concerning the circumstances surrounding the deaths of the six individuals. The defense ministry stated that on Thursday, a breakaway faction of former fighters from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) coerced farmers into protesting against police efforts to remove coca crops. According to the ministry, the dissidents opened fire on law enforcement and launched homemade projectiles, which inadvertently struck the farmers. However, local agricultural organizations accused the police and military of targeting civilians to disperse the protest and facilitate the manual eradication of the crops. While the majority of FARC members have demobilized following a peace agreement signed last year, some dissident groups remain engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining. The FARC, which has transitioned into a political party, has distanced itself from these dissidents. "We are in the process of verifying the precise way in which events unfolded," Santos stated during a press conference. "We are conducting an investigation; I do not wish to commit to any narrative until these inquiries provide us with complete clarity regarding what transpired." The incident highlighted the substantial challenge that the drug trade poses to the peace process with FARC, as noted by the head of the United Nations mission in Colombia. "These events reinforce our belief at the United Nations in the imperative to provide coca farmers in affected areas with all necessary means to avoid the dire choice between severe poverty and illegality," mission chief Jean Arnault told reporters. Subsistence farmers are often compelled by rebel factions, paramilitary groups, and criminal organizations to cultivate and harvest coca. Additionally, some choose to grow coca because illegal entities offer higher compensation than what farmers can receive in the market for other crops—an alluring option amid extreme poverty. Last year, coca cultivation reached levels not seen in a decade after the government prohibited aerial spraying with glyphosate, a herbicide linked to cancer. This ban has drawn criticism from the United States, which is expected to provide over $400 million in aid to Colombia for the FARC agreement. Coca is cultivated on approximately 188,000 hectares (464,000 acres) throughout Colombia. The government aims to manually eliminate 100,000 hectares this year.

text: U.S. President Donald Trump embarked on a barnstorming tour on Wednesday in an effort to generate support for his initial legislative endeavor, a healthcare reform, by organizing a large rally in Nashville, Tennessee, which was reminiscent of his campaign gatherings. Meanwhile, Republican leaders on Capitol Hill were engaged in private negotiations, conducting media briefings, and participating in cable-news interviews as they sought to advance their initiative aimed at dismantling the Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare. Following the unveiling of the new plan by Republican House Speaker Paul Ryan last week, divisions surfaced within the party, as some conservatives argued that it did not go far enough, while others outright rejected it. In his speech on Wednesday night, Trump employed campaign-style rhetoric, vowing to "repeal and replace horrible, disastrous Obamacare." After the rally, while speaking to journalists aboard Air Force One, Trump conveyed a sense of optimism regarding the prospects of his plan in Congress. "We’re going to come up with something. We always do," he stated. Republicans now hold control of both Congress and the White House for the first time in ten years, yet the overhaul still encounters political hurdles that a president inexperienced in governance must navigate. Prior to the rally, White House spokesperson Sean Spicer informed reporters that the Trump administration had engaged in discussions with Ryan and congressional leaders, while also saturating the media with interviews featuring administration officials to facilitate the plan's progress. Ryan, the leading Republican in the House of Representatives, continued to advocate for the legislation, stating on cable news that he was open to making "improvements and refinements," but emphasized that "the major components are staying intact." He later announced at a press conference that the House would vote on repealing and replacing Obamacare, though he declined to specify a timeline. Last week, two House committees approved the provisions of the bill without alterations. The Budget Committee is set to attempt to consolidate the plan into a single bill for consideration on the House floor on Thursday. Republicans can only afford to lose three members from their ranks on the committee for it to successfully pass. Three Republicans on the committee are affiliated with the hardline conservative House Freedom Caucus. On Wednesday, indications arose that the White House was successfully persuading hesitant conservatives who had initially challenged the legislation on the basis that it closely resembled Obamacare, the hallmark domestic policy achievement of former President Barack Obama. The administration signaled its willingness to reconsider the plan's approach to Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income individuals, during a meeting with the party's conservative faction. Specifically, conservatives are advocating for the termination of Obamacare’s Medicaid expansion to occur earlier than outlined in the Ryan plan, and for the introduction of Medicaid work requirements for able-bodied adults without children. State governments manage Medicaid with federal reimbursements. Obamacare broadened its eligibility and enhanced funding, which allowed approximately 10 million previously uninsured Americans to secure health insurance. Earlier on Wednesday, Vice President Mike Pence promoted the plan behind closed doors with the Republican Study Committee, a significant group of House conservatives. After the meeting with Pence, Republican Representative Phil Roe indicated that the bill would likely be revised to accelerate the conclusion of the Medicaid expansion by one year, targeting 2019. The leader of the conservative group, Representative Mark Walker, informed reporters that the members were "very close to signing off" on the legislation. On CNN, Ryan spoke about "providing states with better opportunities for more flexibility with Medicaid," but did not elaborate further. Just as conservative members of the party began to express hope regarding the proposal's prospects, Republican moderates raised alarms concerning the tax credits currently included in the bill, which are intended to assist individuals in purchasing health insurance.

text: Republican legislators have sanctioned $1.1 billion in additional funding to combat the Zika virus. The House reached a funding agreement that had been settled on Wednesday by Republican members from both the House and Senate. Nonetheless, the bill’s prospects in the Senate remain uncertain, where the Democratic minority holds greater leverage to obstruct legislation, and Democratic leader Harry Reid has declared his disapproval. "This is a responsible plan that ensures the administration will retain the necessary resources to safeguard the public," stated Republican House Speaker Paul Ryan. Republicans indicated that the agreement encompasses funding for the fiscal years 2016 and 2017. However, the White House expressed that the allocation was inadequate. "This proposal from congressional Republicans is four months overdue and nearly a billion dollars less than what our public health experts have indicated is essential to do everything feasible to combat the Zika virus, and it diverts funding from other health priorities," White House press secretary Josh Earnest remarked in a statement prior to the House's vote. For months, Democrats have been pressing Republicans to consent to increased Zika funding, and the Obama administration has already diverted close to $600 million that was originally allocated for combating Ebola. House Democrats articulated their inability to support the agreement due to the $750 million in budget cuts elsewhere that Republicans intend to utilize to finance the Zika expenditures. Senate Democrats also expressed dissatisfaction, complicating the prospects for its passage. "A narrowly partisan proposal that restricts women’s access to birth control, underfunds veterans, and rescinds Obamacare funds to cover the costs is not a serious response to the Zika virus threat," Reid commented. According to House Appropriations Committee Chairman Hal Rogers, $543 million of the $1.1 billion would be sourced from unspent allocations intended for the implementation of Obamacare in U.S. territories, while $107 million would come from unused funds allocated to combat another virus, Ebola. He further noted that an additional $100 million would be drawn from unutilized administrative funds at the Department of Health and Human Services.

text: A mere 25% of Canadians believe that the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) is beneficial for their nation, and over a third advocate for its renegotiation, based on polling data released prior to a North American leaders’ summit scheduled for Wednesday. The Angus Reid Institute conducted the survey, published on Monday, amid rising protectionist attitudes in the United States, where voters from both major political parties are questioning the economic advantages of NAFTA. The U.S. Congress is currently reluctant to approve a new 12-nation trade agreement, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), which also includes Canada and Mexico. Trade discussions have traditionally been a key topic at the 'Three Amigos' summits involving NAFTA participants Canada, the United States, and Mexico, with this year's meeting taking place in Ottawa. The issue has also become a contentious topic in the election campaign to succeed U.S. President Barack Obama, who is urging Congress to ratify the TPP before his term concludes on January 20. Republican Donald Trump, the likely nominee for his party in 2016, has criticized the TPP and labels NAFTA as a failure that requires renegotiation or abandonment. Meanwhile, Democratic frontrunner Hillary Clinton has expressed her opposition to the TPP as well. The Angus Reid Institute's poll also indicated that one-quarter of Canadians believe NAFTA is detrimental to the country, while half are either uncertain or consider the agreement to have no significant effect. Shachi Kurl, the executive director of the institute, noted that this survey diverges from previous polls regarding other trade agreements, where Canadians tended to show greater support. "Is this merely an indication that policymakers have not sufficiently persuaded Canadians that this has been a beneficial arrangement?" she questioned. "Is NAFTA unique in that Canadians perceive this specific trade agreement as unfavorable? These are questions we must contemplate." Kurl further mentioned that the poll brings into focus whether Canadians are genuinely worried about the implications of NAFTA itself or if their views are influenced by the global trend of skepticism towards trade, referencing the anti-free-trade sentiments in the U.S. Angus Reid stated that it conducted the online survey with a representative sample of 1,519 Canadian adults who are members of the institute, with a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
