text: Franken and Franks step down as charges of misconduct shake Congress. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Democratic Senator Al Franken declared his resignation on Thursday following a wave of sexual misconduct accusations, while Republican Representative Trent Franks also announced his departure amid ethics allegations. Under pressure from fellow party members and facing weeks of sexual harassment claims, Franken stated on the Senate floor that he would resign in a few weeks, despite denying some accusations against him and questioning others. The 66-year-old former comedian from Minnesota was considered a promising figure within the Democratic Party. "I know in my heart that nothing I’ve done as a senator - nothing - has brought dishonor on this institution," he expressed. "Nevertheless, today I am announcing that in the coming weeks, I will be resigning as a member of the United States Senate." Shortly afterward, Franks revealed his resignation following complaints from two former staff members regarding conversations he had with them about his search for a surrogate mother. "I deeply regret that my discussion of this option and process in the workplace caused distress," said Franks, who first won his Arizona congressional seat in 2002 and has been a vocal opponent of abortion. Franks stated in a release that he and his wife "have long struggled with infertility." These events unfolded amidst a backdrop of widespread dissatisfaction with Congress among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos poll indicated that only 20 percent approved of Congress's job performance, with 70 percent disapproving. In recent weeks, numerous allegations of sexual misconduct have led to the fall of notable figures in entertainment, media, and politics. It is relatively uncommon for members of the Senate or House of Representatives to resign, but veteran Democratic Representative John Conyers also stepped down earlier this week in response to sexual harassment claims he has denied. The House Ethics Committee announced on Thursday that it was probing yet another legislator. Blake Farenthold, a Republican representative from Texas, faces accusations of sexual harassment, discrimination, and retaliation involving a former female staff member. Franken has been the most prominent lawmaker embroiled in allegations over the past few weeks. Reuters has not independently confirmed the claims against Franken, Franks, Conyers, or Farenthold. Franken’s seat will temporarily be filled by a Democrat appointed by Minnesota’s Democratic governor, meaning the slim Republican majority in the Senate will remain unchanged. Allegations that Franken had groped and attempted to kiss women without their consent began to emerge three weeks ago. Initially, he expressed embarrassment and shame over his actions but refused to resign. However, the majority of his Democratic Senate colleagues called for his resignation on Wednesday following a new allegation, which Franken denied. "Some of the allegations against me are simply not true. Others I remember very differently," Franken remarked on Thursday. With a tone of defiance, he sought to differentiate himself from two notable Republicans - President Donald Trump and Senate candidate Roy Moore. "I, of all people, am aware that there is some irony in the fact that I am leaving while a man who has bragged on tape about his history of sexual assault sits in the Oval Office and a man who has repeatedly preyed on young girls campaigns for the Senate, with the full support of his party," he stated. Trump was recorded boasting about kissing and forcibly touching women in a 2005 videotape that emerged last year during his presidential campaign. He apologized for those remarks but labeled them as private "locker-room talk" and asserted that he had not engaged in the actions he discussed. Trump also denied allegations from at least 12 women regarding past sexual advances and groping. Moore, a candidate for the Senate in Alabama, is facing accusations as he campaigns in a special election on Tuesday.

text: Investors and economists prepare for a new perilous challenge: interpreting Trump's language. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Step aside, Janet Yellen. The head of the Federal Reserve now faces competition for the title of the most analyzed speaker by Wall Street, and that competitor is Donald Trump. Every newly elected U.S. president is carefully observed by the financial sector for insights into how their policies may affect the markets. However, Trump's unique speaking style, which often includes incomplete sentences or enthymemes that allow for various interpretations, paired with ambiguous or contradictory campaign pledges, renders him particularly difficult to interpret. "His remarks are bizarre. He makes odd claims, such as constructing the wall and having Mexico finance it, which you know are simply unrealistic," remarked Allan Meltzer, a historian of the Fed and professor of political economy at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. "Yet, his actions, as opposed to his words, have been quite moderate," he added. The first example of how Trump keeps policymakers and investors hanging onto his every utterance occurred shortly after the Republican's conciliatory acceptance address early Wednesday. Bonds dropped while stocks rose as investors made cautious bets that Trump's somewhat ambiguous economic stimulus agenda would lead to corporate profits and increased inflation. The stakes are significant. With a Republican majority in both the House and Senate, Trump has the chance to fundamentally transform the American economy during his time in office. He has committed to substantial tax reductions, infrastructure investment, and easing economic regulations, and he aims to repeal Obamacare. He asserts that these initiatives will invigorate growth and assist in improving the wages of those who have been marginalized in a globalized economy where “middle-class” positions have been diminished. With the U.S. budget deficit at a mere 3.2 percent of gross domestic product, a drop from 9.8 percent in 2009, and interest rates at near-record lows, Trump has the capacity to pursue a significant fiscal expansion, at least temporarily. His measured acceptance address suggested that infrastructure would be a focal point. Trump stated he would "restore our highways, bridges, tunnels, airports, schools, hospitals (and) our infrastructure, which will, by the way, be second to none.” During his campaign, Trump's speeches were replete with superlatives and incomplete sentences that only served to confuse traders and observers of economic policy. These enthymemes reflect a rhetorical strategy at the core of a persuasive speaking style that has propelled the billionaire to the presidency. Attempting to decode his language is one challenge. However, committing capital based on his statements carries significantly more risk than usual, as noted by Brian Shapiro, CEO of SPAG Funds, a small global macro hedge fund based in New York. "I won’t react to it, but the world will," he stated. "I believe people will have a heart attack if they respond to every word." The economic advisory group Fathom Consulting labeled the election result "Trump Lite": a scenario in which as President-elect he would be either reluctant or incapable of implementing some of his more radical policies like constructing a wall at the Mexican border, mass deportations of immigrants, and extensive protectionist strategies. "Markets are awaiting to determine whether we will see the campaign Trump who spoke in rhetoric, or President Trump who will adopt a more pragmatic strategy," noted Komal Sri-Kumar, president of Sri-Kumar Global Strategies. Economists, fund managers, and even Fed policymakers are keenly observing which issues Trump will prioritize. So far, signs indicate he would pursue tax reductions, increased military expenditure, and a revision of President Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare. Chicago Fed President Charles Evans, addressing reporters while Americans cast their votes on Tuesday, expressed his intent to ascertain whether the new president’s fiscal policies "would be more stimulative, about the same, or worse," adding that the degree of market volatility would offer a hint.

text: President Donald Trump of the United States took action on Friday by signing an executive order aimed at extending offshore drilling for oil and gas into previously restricted areas. This initiative is intended to enhance domestic production, although it may not succeed due to the current low demand from the industry for these leases. The directive could potentially make vast areas of the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic oceans, along with the Gulf of Mexico, available for exploration, regions that former President Barack Obama had aimed to safeguard after the significant BP oil spill in 2010. "We’re opening it up....Today we’re unleashing American energy and clearing the way for thousands and thousands of high-paying American energy jobs," Trump stated while signing the order. During his campaign, Trump pledged to eliminate the environmental protections established during Obama's presidency, which he claimed were hindering energy development without yielding concrete benefits, a move that garnered support from industry stakeholders but angered environmentalists. However, the executive order, titled the America-First Offshore Energy Strategy, is being implemented at a time when low oil prices and increased onshore production have resulted in offshore lease demand reaching near record lows, leading to uncertainties about its effectiveness. A review by Reuters of governmental records indicated that the financial expenditures by oil companies during annual lease sales in the central Gulf of Mexico plummeted by over 75 percent from 2012 to 2017. Both the amount bid per acre and the percentage of acreage receiving bids saw declines of more than 50 percent. Similar trends were observed in the western Gulf of Mexico, the only other region that received offers for leases during this timeframe, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management. "The Trump administration’s hasty move today toward expanding offshore oil drilling ... defies market realities and is as reckless as it is unnecessary," commented David Jenkins, president of the non-profit conservation organization Conservatives for Responsible Stewardship. "Why on earth would someone choose to push drilling in the riskiest and most expensive places on the planet when the current oil glut will make such ventures unprofitable for the foreseeable future?" he questioned. The president of the American Petroleum Institute trade association expressed support for the order in a statement, while an official from the API noted that the order might benefit the industry in the long run. This official chose not to comment specifically on the current demand for offshore leases. "To satisfy U.S. energy requirements, it's essential to keep long-term options available, enabling the industry to plan and identify the best prospects before making necessary investments that the global economy will demand over time," the unnamed official stated. The order instructs the U.S. Department of Interior to evaluate and replace the Obama administration’s last five-year oil and gas development strategy for the outer continental shelf, which encompasses federal waters off all U.S. coastlines. Just before leaving office, Obama had prohibited new oil and gas drilling in federal waters in the Atlantic and Arctic oceans, safeguarding 115 million acres (46.5 million hectares) off Alaska and 3.8 million acres in the Atlantic from New England to the Chesapeake Bay. Besides mandating a new five-year drilling strategy, the order reverses Obama's decision to permanently restrict specific areas of the Arctic from drilling activities. It also instructs Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross to reassess the marine national monuments and sanctuaries designated by previous presidents. Jill McLeod, a partner at the international law firm Dorsey & Whitney, remarked that Trump’s order is a positive indication for the oil sector but is unlikely to lead to a significant increase in exploration in the short term due to the associated costs. "The lifting of the ban does not necessarily make drilling in the Arctic a compelling proposition," she added. Environmental organizations such as Oceana and the Center for Biological Diversity have expressed criticism.

text: The leader of Turkey's nationalist opposition stated on Thursday that the upcoming independence referendum proposed by Kurds in northern Iraq should be regarded by Ankara as a potential justification for war if deemed necessary. Turkey, which has been engaged in a Kurdish insurgency in its southeast for three decades, is apprehensive that the referendum could intensify separatist feelings among the 15 million Kurds residing in Turkey. On Wednesday, Foreign Minister Mevlut Cavusoglu traveled to Iraq, where he expressed to Iraqi Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani Ankara's apprehensions regarding the decision to proceed with the referendum, scheduled for September 25. Devlet Bahceli, the leader of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), who has aligned with the government in supporting the ruling AK Party's initiative during the April referendum aimed at enhancing President Tayyip Erdogan's authority, urged Ankara to take a stand against the vote. 'A firm stance must be taken against Barzani's preparations for an independence referendum that includes Turkmen cities,' Bahceli stated during a press conference in Ankara. 'This is a practice run for Kurdistan. If necessary, Turkey should consider this referendum as grounds for war,' he continued. Although Bahceli does not dictate policy, his views mirror those of a portion of Turkish society that is strongly opposed to the notion of an independent Kurdistan and is in favor of Iraq's Turkmen ethnic minority, which shares historical and cultural connections with Turkey. Kurds have been pursuing an independent state since at least the conclusion of World War One, when colonial powers partitioned the Middle East, leaving Kurdish-inhabited regions divided among present-day Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria. Similar to Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria all reject the notion of Iraqi Kurdish independence, apprehensive that it might incite separatism within their own Kurdish communities. The Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), which is classified as a terrorist organization by Ankara, the United States, and the European Union, has conducted a 33-year insurgency in southeast Turkey, resulting in over 40,000 fatalities. The United States and other Western nations are concerned that the vote in September could trigger a new conflict with Baghdad and potentially neighboring countries, distracting from the efforts against Islamic State militants in Iraq and Syria.

text: S&P Global Ratings increased the pressure on Alaska regarding its budget on Thursday. The rating agency cautioned that if state lawmakers do not reach an agreement on a budget addressing the long-term financial issues, the credit ratings for essential Alaska bonds may decline. Last month, Alaska Governor Bill Walker called a special legislative session with the goal of approving a budget for fiscal 2017 and addressing the state's nearly $4 billion deficit, a situation exacerbated by falling global oil prices. On Thursday, S&P placed the state’s AA-plus general obligation, AA appropriation, and A-plus moral obligation ratings for Alaska’s debt on CreditWatch with negative outlooks. The proceeds from the bonds are intended for various transportation projects. "The CreditWatch designation suggests that we might downgrade Alaska’s credit rating if state officials postpone implementing fiscal reforms to address the structural budget deficit," stated Gabriel Petek, a credit analyst at S&P Global Ratings. Since the special session commenced late last month, the legislature has approved a $4.4 billion spending plan for fiscal 2017 and a measure aimed at cutting the expenses associated with the state’s oil and gas tax credit program, according to S&P. However, it remains uncertain whether a contentious bill that seeks to divert funds from the state’s permanent fund to its general fund will overcome resistance in the House of Representatives. The bill, SB 128, proposes to decrease the annual payouts to residents from the fund. Even if it is enacted, S&P noted that it is unclear whether SB 128 and other fiscal reforms would be adequate to place Alaska’s financial structure on a sustainable path. "The passage of SB 128 on its own would reduce the deficit, but it would not eliminate it. To fully close the structural fiscal gap, additional actions – like introducing a new income tax or implementing further spending cuts – would also be required," S&P remarked. In spite of the budget deficit, S&P indicated that Alaska still possesses very strong credit quality due to the substantial reserves accumulated during periods of high oil prices.

text: Obama loosens restrictions on Cuba, removes caps on rum and cigars. WASHINGTON/HAVANA (Reuters) - Americans who visit Cuba will now be permitted to return home with increased quantities of the island's prized cigars and rum due to new regulations introduced by the U.S. government on Friday, aimed at further relaxing trade, travel, and financial limitations that have existed for many years. Cuba expressed appreciation for these developments, which are part of President Barack Obama’s initiative to make his groundbreaking engagement with Cuba 'irreversible' by the time he departs from office in January, although they indicated that the measures fell short. This latest set of rules, which follows a series of regulations since the two nations began normalizing relations in 2014, will enable Cubans to purchase specific U.S. consumer products online, allow Cuban pharmaceutical firms to engage in business within the United States, and facilitate collaborative medical research endeavors between Cubans and Americans. For U.S. travelers, the most significant alteration is the elimination of restrictions on the quantity of rum and cigars they can carry in their luggage for personal consumption. 'You can now celebrate with Cuban rum and Cuban cigars,' U.S. National Security Adviser Susan Rice humorously remarked while outlining the policy changes in a speech at a Washington think tank. Although U.S. law continues to prohibit general tourism to Cuba, the administration has utilized prior regulatory measures to simplify the process for Americans to visit the island under 12 officially approved categories. The recent actions are part of an executive order concerning Cuba, through which Obama aims to bypass the Republican-majority Congress that has opposed his efforts to lift the economic embargo that has been in effect for over 50 years. Republican opponents argue that Obama is granting too many concessions to Cuba without receiving adequate returns, particularly concerning human rights matters. 'After two years of President Obama’s Cuba policy, the Castro regime has benefited tremendously,' stated U.S. Senator Marco Rubio, a Cuban-American representative from Florida. The new measures permit Cuban pharmaceutical companies to seek U.S. regulatory approval, allow U.S. enterprises to enhance Cuban infrastructure for humanitarian reasons, and sanction them to provide safety-related aircraft services in Cuba, where U.S. airlines are starting regular flights. Additionally, under the revised regulations, certain foreign vessels carrying designated cargo will be able to travel directly to U.S. ports after docking in Cuba to load or unload goods. Previously, these ships were required to wait for 180 days, a limitation that Cuban officials claim obstructs their import-export activities. Josefina Vidal, the Cuban Foreign Ministry’s head of U.S. affairs, stated during a press conference in Havana that the measures were 'positive but of a very limited nature.' 'Today, I signed a Presidential Policy Directive that represents another significant step forward in our efforts to normalize relations with Cuba,' Obama declared in a statement. With less than a month remaining before the Nov. 8 presidential election, Obama affirmed that his aim was to 'make our opening to Cuba irreversible.' The latest set of changes, the administration’s sixth, is expected to be the 'final significant batch of alterations' during Obama’s presidency, according to a senior official who requested anonymity. Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton supports the policy of rapprochement with Havana. In contrast, Republican Donald Trump has pledged to reverse Obama’s executive measures. Vidal criticized Obama’s directive for explicitly stating that the U.S. intended to 'promote change in Cuba’s economic, political and social system,' which she argued disrespects its sovereignty. In March, Obama became the first U.S. president to visit Havana in 88 years. His visit was made feasible by his landmark agreement with Cuban President Raul Castro in December 2014, which aimed to end decades of animosity that began shortly after Cuba’s 1959 revolution. Since initiating this opening, Obama has consistently used his executive authority to ease trade and travel restrictions while urging Cuba to expedite market-oriented reforms and enhance political and economic liberties.

text: Candidates opposing the current president are aiming to shift Czech policy towards the West in the upcoming presidential election. PRAGUE (Reuters) - A number of pro-Western contenders submitted their nominations by Tuesday's deadline to compete for the position of Czech president, hoping to replace the incumbent Milos Zeman, who has favored Russia and China. While Czech presidents possess limited daily authority, they hold significant informal power and play a crucial role in government formation, which is currently ongoing following last month’s elections. The victor of the presidential election set for January will either bolster or mitigate the euroscepticism that has emerged despite the nation’s economic achievements and stability since its accession to NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004. Zeman, 73, a former leader of the Social Democrats and prime minister, is a prominent figure in the nation's contemporary history, alongside former presidents Vaclav Havel and Vaclav Klaus. According to bookmakers, he remains the frontrunner for a second five-year term, even though his public appearances have been limited in recent months due to diabetes and mobility issues. Currently, the most formidable challenger to Zeman is Jiri Drahos, a chemist and former head of the Czech Academy of Sciences, who is running as an independent candidate. Drahos, 68, is supportive of the EU and NATO and presents a composed and serious demeanor, which contrasts with Zeman’s tendency to lash out at the media and opponents. "If Drahos prevails, it would signify a pro-Western, pro-European direction," stated political analyst Josef Mlejnek Jr. "Under Zeman, our politicians frequently had to remind international partners that it is the government, not the president, that dictates foreign policy, which does not leave a favorable impression, especially amid the existing east-west discord between the two approaches." Zeman adopted a strongly anti-EU stance when he aligned with Russia regarding the Ukraine situation and opposed EU sanctions. Furthermore, he has taken a staunch anti-immigration position, labeling Islam as "anti-civilization." Zeman has also expressed support for Andrej Babis, a billionaire entrepreneur whose ANO party triumphed in the parliamentary elections last month, and whom Zeman pledged to appoint as prime minister. ANO did not nominate its own candidate for the presidency, which eliminates one potential challenge to Zeman. Another pro-Western candidate is Michal Horacek, 65, who established the betting company Fortuna, which he sold in 2004, and is known as a lyricist for popular music artists. Former center-right prime minister Mirek Topolanek, whose government fell during the nation’s EU presidency in 2009, also entered the race at the last moment. A eurosceptic, Topolanek's former aide, Marek Dalik, began a five-year prison term on Monday for corruption related to army procurement while Topolanek was in office. In a poll released on Monday, Zeman was leading with 34 percent, followed by Drahos with 22 percent and Horacek at 13 percent. Another poll conducted on Tuesday indicated Drahos holding a slight advantage of 51-49 percent over Zeman in a potential run-off.

text: The likelihood of victory for Donald Trump surged on betting platforms, according to recent reports. NEW YORK (Reuters) - The online trading site PredictIt and the bookmaker Paddy Power experienced a significant shift in fortunes for U.S. presidential candidates, Republican Donald Trump and Democrat Hillary Clinton, on Tuesday night, as the New York entrepreneur’s prospects of winning the presidency escalated on both platforms. Trump surprised numerous political analysts, gaining a slight advantage over Clinton in various swing states after polling had concluded in more than two-thirds of the 50 U.S. states. On Tuesday, Paddy Power estimated Trump’s chance of winning at 83.3 percent, while Clinton’s was at 22.2 percent. Earlier on Tuesday morning, the two candidates were in nearly opposite standings. Paddy Power is poised to incur a $4 million loss if Trump emerges victorious, as stated by Paddy Power spokesperson Féilim Mac An Iomaire, who noted that this sudden shift in odds is reminiscent of the dramatic changes seen during the “Brexit” vote on Britain’s exit from the European Union. “You could say it’s deja vu again,” remarked Mac An Iomaire. “Similar to Brexit, the early odds seemed to predict one outcome before a remarkable turnaround occurred.” Leading up to the June 23 referendum in Britain regarding EU membership, opinion polls fluctuated, favoring the “remain” campaign, yet Britons ultimately voted to leave by a margin of 52 percent to 48 percent. A comparable pattern was observed on the online trading platform PredictIt, which launched in 2014 and is jointly operated by Victoria University in Wellington, New Zealand, and the Washington-based political consulting firm Aristotle International Inc. Throughout the campaign, Clinton had consistently outperformed Trump in PredictIt’s market regarding the presidential race, but news of her Republican opponent's unexpected surge caused her winning chances to plummet by approximately 75 percentage points from Tuesday morning levels to just 5 percent. Conversely, Trump’s likelihood rose by over 40 percentage points, reaching about 65 percent. This marked the first occasion in the entire campaign where Trump had taken the lead over Clinton on the platform, according to a spokesperson for PredictIt. The British betting company Ladbrokes rated Trump’s chances of victory at around 85 percent Tuesday night, compared to 15 percent for Clinton. Earlier that day, Ladbrokes had assessed Clinton’s chance of winning at 76 percent and Trump’s at 24 percent, but company spokesperson Jessica Bridge indicated that this development “isn’t a surprise in the slightest,” given the substantial volume of trades placed on Trump since the market's inception in 2012. Approximately 75 percent of all wagers in Ladbrokes’ U.S. presidential betting have been made on Trump.

text: CHICAGO (Reuters) - On Monday, Illinois Governor Bruce Rauner announced a special legislative session set to commence on Wednesday, aiming to establish a school funding system prior to the commencement of classes next month. The Republican governor has established a deadline of July 31 for the implementation of a new funding formula, which excludes additional funding for Chicago Public Schools (CPS) teacher pensions that were part of a bill approved by the Democrat-majority legislature in late May. "We need to take action immediately, which is the reason I’m summoning lawmakers back to Springfield for a special session. Our schools need to open on schedule," Rauner stated in a release. During a press conference earlier on Monday, Rauner accused the Democratic legislators of "playing political games" with the educational needs of roughly 2 million school children in the state by failing to provide him with the education funding bill. The governor expressed his support for the bill’s creation of an evidence-based model that links public school funding to "best practices" designed to boost student performance. However, the proposal also addresses the issue of state funding inequality regarding CPS pensions, which Rauner has characterized as a bailout for a poorly managed retirement system. The state budget for fiscal year 2018, totaling $36 billion, was passed by the legislature earlier this month despite Rauner's veto and forbids the allocation of state funds to schools without an evidence-based funding model in place. Consequently, this has raised concerns that some school districts heavily reliant on state funding might not open their doors in August. Rauner rebuffed a suggestion from Democratic Senate President John Cullerton to convene with legislative leaders to allow the governor to make a "rational decision" regarding the bill. "I would like to engage in a discussion with Governor Rauner in hopes of gaining some clarity about what is truly happening," Cullerton mentioned in a statement on Monday. "We delayed the process in the Senate to provide everyone a chance to vent, politically speaking." Rauner, who insisted on receiving the bill for his review before engaging in any talks, refrained from elaborating on his plans for amendatory vetoes concerning CPS funding within the bill. Information available on his website suggested that the proposed $293 million funding increase for CPS state aid and pensions would be nearly halved, allowing $145 million to be redirected to other school districts. Rising pension payments have resulted in depleted reserves, increased debt reliance, and junk bond ratings for CPS, which is the third-largest public school system in the nation. The governor referred to the CPS pension funding as "a poison pill" within the legislation, asserting that it ought to be addressed independently.

text: A magnitude 5.2 earthquake occurred near Tehran, the capital of Iran, on Wednesday night, according to reports from state media. There were no immediate accounts of injuries or major damage. Previously, a 7.3-magnitude quake struck various villages and towns in Iran's Kermanshah province, located in the mountainous region bordering Iraq, resulting in 620 fatalities and numerous injuries. Officials indicated they were in the process of collecting data regarding the recent quake, which took place in the evening at a depth of 7 km (4 miles). They advised residents to stay calm while remaining alert for potential aftershocks. The earthquake's epicenter was situated 3 km from Malard and close to Meshkin Dasht, approximately 50 km to the west of Tehran, as reported by the state news agency IRNA. The tremor was also experienced in Alborz, Qazvin, Qom, Gilan, and Markazi provinces, according to state media. Behnam Saeedi, a spokesperson for Iran's National Disaster Management Organization, stated through the semi-official ILNA news agency that there were no reports of injuries or damage. In Tehran and other urban areas, residents poured into the streets and parks, anxious about a potential stronger aftershock. Some individuals set up tents to spend the night outdoors and kindled fires. The Tasnim news agency cited Minister of Sports Masoud Soltanifar stating that sports facilities in Karaj, located in Alborz province, and Eslamshahr in southern Tehran were made available to the public for overnight shelter. Additionally, some individuals sought refuge at the mausoleum of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the founder of the Islamic Republic, in southern Tehran. Minister of Energy Reza Ardakanian informed ISNA news agency that the Amirkabir Dam, situated one hour west of Tehran, remained undamaged and that the supply of water and electricity was uninterrupted. On Thursday, schools, universities, and government offices in Tehran, Alborz, and Qom provinces will be closed, as announced by state television.

text: U.S. presidential debates: from Kennedy-Nixon to Clinton-Trump. (Reuters) - On Monday, Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton will confront her Republican opponent Donald Trump in the inaugural event of a series of televised debates that could be pivotal in determining the victor of the White House on November 8. This first debate is set to occur at Hofstra University located on Long Island in New York state. The Commission on Presidential Debates has planned two additional presidential debates and one vice presidential debate for October. These rhetorical showdowns, which first aired on television in 1960, have delivered some of the most unforgettable moments and quotes in contemporary American political history. Below is a summary of the highlights spanning more than fifty years. 1960: The initial televised American presidential debate attracted seventy million viewers, featuring Republican Vice President Richard Nixon against Democratic candidate John F. Kennedy. Nixon was recuperating from a hospital stay and sported a five-o'clock shadow, having declined makeup. Conversely, Kennedy presented himself with a smooth and charismatic delivery. Audiences concentrated on visual impressions rather than auditory messages. Kennedy emerged victorious in the election. 1976: In the first televised debate in sixteen years, Democrat Jimmy Carter went head-to-head with unelected incumbent President Gerald Ford. This was also the debut of televised debates for vice presidential candidates, with Republican Senator Bob Dole facing off against Democratic Senator Walter Mondale. Ford's statement, "There is no Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, and there never will be under a Ford administration," benefited Carter as the media emphasized it as a significant gaffe, leading many analysts to believe it aided Carter's electoral success. 1980: Carter participated only in the second debate against Republican Ronald Reagan after boycotting the first due to the inclusion of third-party candidate John Anderson. In this debate, Carter accused Reagan of intending to reduce Medicare funding for the elderly. Reagan, who had expressed that Carter misrepresented his positions on various topics, replied with the phrase, "There you go again," which elicited laughter from the audience and became a memorable catchphrase. Reagan won the election, with this debate drawing an unprecedented 80.6 million viewers per Nielsen ratings. 1984: Reagan, aged 73, effectively addressed concerns about his age during the second debate with Democratic contender Walter Mondale, who was 56, by humorously stating, "I want you to know that also I will not make age an issue of this campaign. I am not going to exploit, for political purposes, my opponent’s youth and inexperience." Reagan was re-elected. 1988: The second presidential debate featuring Republican Vice President George H.W. Bush and Democratic challenger Michael Dukakis commenced with a question directed at the Massachusetts governor concerning his stance on the death penalty for someone who had raped and killed his wife. This question aimed to uncover the human aspect of a candidate labeled as "the Ice Man." However, his lengthy response to this emotional topic did the opposite. Bush won the election. The vice presidential debate gained momentum when Senator Dan Quayle, Bush’s running mate, likened himself politically to John F. Kennedy. In a measured, impactful tone, Democratic Senator Lloyd Bentsen responded, "Senator, I served with Jack Kennedy. I knew Jack Kennedy. Jack Kennedy was a friend of mine. Senator, you’re no Jack Kennedy." 1992: This election year’s three debates marked the first instance where three candidates - Bush, Democrat Bill Clinton, and independent Ross Perot - were on stage together. Clinton secured the election. 1996: In the second debate between Republican Bob Dole and Clinton, a student questioned Dole about whether, at the age of 73, he was too old to grasp the needs of younger generations. Dole asserted that his age brought wisdom through intelligence and experience. Clinton responded, "I can only tell you that I don’t think Senator Dole is too old to be president."

text: 'Catastrophic' conditions for migrants displaced due to clashes in Libya, according to an official. GHARYAN, Libya (Reuters) - Thousands of migrants who have been displaced by the ongoing fighting along Libya's northwestern coast urgently require medical assistance, stated the head of a detention facility in Gharyan on Thursday, characterizing their circumstances as tragic. Since the outbreak of clashes last month in Sabratha, a coastal city that used to serve as a major departure point for journeys to Italy, approximately 5,800 migrants have arrived at the center. Around 2,000 individuals have already been transferred from Gharyan to other facilities in the capital, Tripoli. 'The situation is extremely tragic... catastrophic. There is a significant lack of support,' remarked Abdulhameed Muftah, who manages the Al-Hamra detention center in Gharyan, located about 80 km (50 miles) south of Tripoli. The fighting in Sabratha led to the retreat of an armed group that had begun obstructing migrant departures from the area, responding to intense pressure from Italy. Previously, Sabratha was the primary hub for smuggling migrants attempting to traverse the Mediterranean. U.N. agencies have been facing challenges in providing assistance to thousands of mainly sub-Saharan African migrants left stranded after the conflict. Many have been relocated to facilities such as the one in Gharyan, which are nominally overseen by the U.N.-backed government but are infamous for their poor conditions and widespread abuse. Humanitarian workers have restricted access. Al-Hamra comprises roughly a dozen hangars, each designed to accommodate up to 150 individuals. According to Muftah, around 70 percent of the migrants brought to the center required medical care that they were not receiving. One migrant, grasping the bars of a hangar's door, pleaded as a reporter walked by, stating, 'Please. We’re dying, we’re dying.' Muftah noted that there were many children and some pregnant women in the facility, several of whom had given birth since their arrival. 'We urge all international organizations and the Libyan state to take into account the humanitarian plight of these migrants,' he urged. The conditions of migrants were also brought to the attention of Libyan officials by U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, Zeid Ra'ad Al Hussein, who visited Libya on Tuesday. 'I urge the government to establish alternatives to detention in Libya, to cease the practice of arbitrary detention, and to ensure accountability for the abuses inflicted upon migrants in detention facilities,' he stated in a Thursday announcement. He called for human rights monitors to be allowed access to detention centers where thousands of Libyans have been held for years without legal proceedings, referencing 'horrific reports' that have emerged from some of these locations.

"I’m optimistic about where we’ll end up," he remarked. "We’ve been through these periods before and we’ve always had a way to come out of it. I’m more optimistic than some." Trump, who became the first Republican president since Bush's departure from office, secured the November election after defeating 16 other candidates for the party nomination, including Bush’s sibling Jeb. Key figures within the Republican establishment, including both Bush and his father, former President George H.W. Bush, either distanced themselves or provided only lukewarm support for Trump. In a separate interview on NBC’s "Today" show on Monday, Bush expressed significant differences with Trump’s administration, advocating for a “welcoming” immigration stance and commending the media as "indispensable to democracy." Bush and his wife Laura conversed with People at their residence in Dallas. The revenues from the book, which showcases portraits of injured veterans, will support veterans’ healthcare and employment initiatives at the George W. Bush Presidential Center. The couple conveyed to the entertainment magazine that the center’s immigration ceremonies, reproductive health programs for women in Africa, and leadership training for Muslim women from the Middle East starkly contrast with Trump’s isolationist policies. "There’s a lot of ways to speak out," he added. "But it’s really through actions defending the values important to Laura and me. We’re a blessed nation, and we ought to help others." text: China expressed its respect for Robert Mugabe's choice to step down as Zimbabwe's president. On Wednesday, BEIJING (Reuters) reported that China acknowledged Mugabe's resignation, which occurred a week after Zimbabwe's military and Mugabe's former political allies acted to terminate his nearly 40-year rule. The 93-year-old Mugabe had held on for a week following a military takeover and ultimately resigned on Tuesday, just as the parliament initiated impeachment proceedings, resulting in celebrations in the streets of Harare, the capital. China maintains strong relations with Zimbabwe and historically with Mugabe, who is viewed in the West as a tyrant whose poor management of the economy and readiness to use violence to retain power devastated one of Africa's most promising nations. During a routine news briefing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lu Kang stated that China was pleased to observe Zimbabwe resolving the situation peacefully and appropriately through dialogue, affirming that its policy towards the nation would remain unchanged. "China respects Mr. Mugabe's choice to resign. He continues to be a good friend of the Chinese people," Lu remarked, adding that Mugabe had made a significant contribution to Zimbabwe's independence and liberation. The military took control after Mugabe dismissed his former vice president, Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was seen as the likely successor. Mugabe's decision appeared to be an attempt to clear a path for his wife Grace, 52, who has been nicknamed "Gucci Grace" by her detractors due to her alleged love for luxury shopping. Mnangagwa is anticipated to be inaugurated within days and will complete the remainder of Mugabe's term until the next election, scheduled to occur by September 2018. When asked about the U.S. urging for free elections in Zimbabwe, Lu responded that China believed it was capable of managing its own matters and hoped that other nations would refrain from interfering. China and Zimbabwe share a strong diplomatic and economic bond, with China supporting Mugabe's administration amid Western economic sanctions, investing in projects related to automobiles, diamonds, tobacco, and power generation. In August, Zimbabwe announced that a Chinese firm intended to inject up to $2 billion to revive operations at the Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Company (ZISCO), which halted production in 2008 during a severe economic crisis. That same year, China vetoed a proposed U.N. resolution backed by Western nations that aimed to impose an arms embargo on Zimbabwe and financial and travel restrictions on Mugabe and 13 other officials, arguing that it would "complicate" rather than alleviate conflict.

BOGOTA (Reuters) - On Wednesday, police recovered over 12 tons of cocaine linked to the country's leading criminal organization, representing the most significant capture in the ongoing battle against drug trafficking, according to President Juan Manuel Santos. text: Trump's 'America first' address raises concerns among U.S. allies. LONDON (Reuters) - Donald Trump’s initial significant foreign policy speech has caused alarm among American allies, who interpret the Republican frontrunner's frequent references to an 'America first' approach as a potential retreat from global engagement. Although most governments refrained from publicly commenting on a speech delivered by a U.S. presidential candidate, Germany’s foreign minister broke from that norm to express unease regarding Trump’s language. 'I can only hope that the election campaign in the USA does not lack the perception of reality,' remarked Frank-Walter Steinmeier. 'The global security framework has evolved and is no longer solely reliant on two pillars. It cannot be managed unilaterally,' he stated in reference to foreign policy in a post-Cold War context. 'No American president can bypass this evolution in the international security structure... 'America first' is truly not a solution to that.' Carl Bildt, a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden who acted as the UN envoy to the Balkans following the Yugoslav wars in the 1990s, noted that he perceived Trump’s speech as 'abandoning both democratic allies and democratic principles.' 'Trump did not utter a word against Russian aggression in Ukraine, yet he had plenty to say about past U.S. support for democracy in Egypt,' Bildt tweeted, alluding to parts of Trump’s address that criticized the Barack Obama administration for pulling support from autocrat Hosni Mubarak during the 2011 uprising. Trump's address, unusually delivered via teleprompter, appeared to aim at presenting a more serious demeanor from a politician who has indicated his intention to act more 'presidential' following months of primarily off-the-cuff remarks. He committed to a 'disciplined, deliberate and consistent foreign policy' in contrast to the 'reckless, rudderless and aimless' approaches of Obama and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who is anticipated to be his Democratic rival if he clinches the Republican nomination. The speech did not introduce any significant new policy proposals likely to create headlines, unlike his former calls to prohibit Muslims from entering the United States or to construct a wall along the border with Mexico. Where Trump was specific, such as in dismissing the terms of last year’s nuclear agreement with Iran, advocating for increased missile defense investments in Europe, and accusing the Obama administration of lukewarm support for Israel, he remained firmly aligned with the Republican mainstream. A prominent theme — that additional NATO allies ought to allocate at least 2 percent of their economic output to defense — is also one that has been echoed by the Obama administration itself, notably during the president’s recent visit to Europe last week. Nevertheless, Trump’s rhetoric has raised concerns among allied nations that depend on the superpower for defense, particularly the phrase 'America first', which was utilized by isolationists in the 1930s who aimed to keep the United States out of World War Two. Former South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Kim Sung-han, currently a professor at Korea University in Seoul, stated that Trump would be 'the first isolationist to be a U.S. presidential candidate, while in the post-war era all U.S. presidents have, to varying degrees, been internationalists.' 'To declare that the U.S. will no longer engage in anything that burdens its relationships with allies would nearly equate to abandoning those alliances,' he added. 'This will inevitably spur anti-American sentiment globally.' Xenia Wickett, head of the U.S. and Americas Programme at Britain’s Chatham House think tank, remarked that the speech 'indicates Trump would make America’s allies less secure rather than more secure.' 'He spoke about allies needing to be confident, yet all his rhetoric implied that America should be unpredictable and that America’s allies ought to fend for themselves.' text: Germany is contemplating a new strategy to enhance surveillance capabilities on vehicles and residences. BERLIN (Reuters) - The German administration is evaluating potential legal modifications that would require operators of vehicle and home alarm systems to assist law enforcement in their initiatives to monitor possible terrorists or criminals, a representative from the interior ministry stated on Friday. Interior Minister Thomas de Maiziere, a member of the conservative party, intends to discuss this matter with security officials nationwide next week, aiming to eliminate what he perceives as barriers to improved surveillance, according to the spokesperson. However, these proposals have already drawn criticism from the Social Democrats (SPD), who are coalition partners in the current German caretaker government and face pressure to revive the grand coalition that governed Germany for the last four years. The topic of surveillance is particularly sensitive in Germany, owing to the historical context of espionage by East Germany’s Stasi secret police and the Gestapo from the Nazi period. Boris Pistorius, an SPD member and the interior minister of Lower Saxony, remarked that de Maiziere’s proposals were hasty and ‘panicked,’ advocating for a more prudent approach. '2017 is not Orwell's 1984,' he stated in an interview with the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung, set to be released on Saturday. 'We require sensible judgment, not hyperbole.' Previously, law enforcement agencies have experienced challenges in setting up covert listening devices within vehicles and homes, as individuals were often alerted by security systems in internet-connected devices or received notifications when their vehicles were accessed. Authorities are now looking into legal amendments that would mandate alarm system operators to supply law enforcement with specialized tools to secretly disable and bypass alarm systems in cases of suspected terrorist actions or organized crime, the spokesperson mentioned. He clarified that officials are not seeking access to the computers, smartphones, or other electronic devices of suspects.

text: On Monday, a seasoned Republican antitrust expert was appointed to U.S. President-elect Donald Trump’s transition team for the Justice Department, a move that legal professionals interpret as indicative of a more lenient stance on antitrust enforcement in contrast to that of Democratic President Barack Obama. David Higbee, a partner at Hunton & Williams LLP, served in President George W. Bush’s administration from 2001 to 2005, spending his final year in the Antitrust Division. Since leaving, he has provided counsel on merger evaluations, antitrust lawsuits, and government inquiries. Higbee is joining Joshua Wright, an economist and former commissioner of the Federal Trade Commission, making them the sole members of Trump’s transition team with expertise in antitrust matters. The Obama administration has contested an unusually high number of mergers over recent years, which contributed to the failure of Halliburton Co’s acquisition plan for Baker Hughes Inc, among other cases. At present, the Justice Department is pursuing legal action against Anthem Inc to obstruct its acquisition of Cigna Corp and Aetna Inc’s attempt to purchase Humana Inc. Despite Trump’s populist campaign rhetoric regarding media mergers, such as AT&T Inc’s purchase of Time Warner Inc, and his specific mention of Amazon.com Inc for antitrust examination, Higbee's appointment indicates a shift back to a conventional Republican perspective on merger regulation, according to legal analysts. "Higbee will exercise prudent caution," remarked Bruce McDonald, another veteran from the Bush administration now with the law firm Jones Day. "He will exhibit greater trust in business and markets while being less assured that the government can effectively discern and resolve issues." According to McDonald, an antitrust division shaped by Higbee would adopt a stringent approach towards price-fixing and competitor mergers but would proceed with caution in challenging transactions involving companies acquiring suppliers or allegations of companies violating antitrust laws to eliminate competition.

text: Pence cautions North Korea about U.S. determination demonstrated in Syria and Afghanistan strikes. SEOUL/PYONGYANG (Reuters) - On Monday, U.S. Vice President Mike Pence issued a warning to North Korea, stating that recent military actions by the United States in Syria and Afghanistan demonstrated that President Donald Trump’s determination should not be doubted, while Pyongyang committed to continuing its missile and nuclear tests. Following a significant exhibition of missiles in Pyongyang and a failed North Korean missile launch over the weekend, U.S. officials commended China for increasing its efforts to control North Korea, its neighboring ally. Nevertheless, Pence and South Korea’s acting president, Hwang Kyo-ahn, confirmed plans to advance the early deployment of the U.S. THAAD missile-defense system in South Korea, despite objections from China. During an Easter celebration at the White House on Monday, Trump was asked if he had a message for North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, to which he replied: "Gotta behave." However, senior officials from North Korea remained resolute. North Korea’s deputy representative to the United Nations, Kim In Ryong, accused the U.S. of fostering “a situation where nuclear war could break out at any time” and stated that Pyongyang’s next nuclear test would occur “at a time and at a place determined necessary by our headquarters.” (Graphic - Carl Vinson strike group: tmsnrt.rs/2pqOMWA) (Graphic - North Korea's nuclear program: tmsnrt.rs/2n0gd92) North Korea’s Vice Foreign Minister Han Song-Ryol informed the BBC that missile tests would persist on “a weekly, monthly and yearly basis.” Kim Song Gyong, the director general of the European Department of North Korea’s Foreign Ministry, conveyed to Reuters in Pyongyang that if Washington made “the slightest movement” indicating a nuclear strike on North Korea, Pyongyang would respond preemptively and “destroy the aggressors without any mercy.” He elaborated that the arrival of a U.S. naval strike group led by the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier Carl Vinson in Korean waters would not be deemed sufficient to signify “the slightest movement.” Tensions on the Korean Peninsula have heightened following numerous North Korean missile tests and apprehensions that Pyongyang may soon execute a sixth nuclear bomb test in defiance of U.N. sanctions. Washington is increasingly concerned about North Korea's attempts to develop a nuclear-capable missile that could reach the U.S. mainland. While standing alongside Hwang, Pence remarked that the world has observed Trump’s determination over the past two weeks, which included a U.S. missile strike on a Syrian airfield and the deployment of a powerful non-nuclear bomb against the Islamic State in Afghanistan. “North Korea would be wise not to test his resolve or the strength of the armed forces of the United States in this region,” Pence stated during his first stop on a four-nation tour of Asia aimed at demonstrating that Trump is not neglecting this increasingly unstable region of the world. Pence, whose father fought in the Korean War from 1950 to 1953, visited the North-South border on Monday, asserting that Washington would uphold its “ironclad alliance” with South Korea. “All options are on the table to achieve the objectives and ensure the stability of the people of this country,” he told reporters, as faint propaganda music drifted across from the North Korean side of the so-called demilitarized zone (DMZ). The Trump administration has indicated that military action remains a potential strategy for addressing the North Korean situation. However, recognizing that such action could likely provoke significant retaliation and casualties in South Korea and Japan, as well as among U.S. forces stationed there, U.S. officials assert that the primary focus of the Trump administration is on implementing stricter economic sanctions to persuade Pyongyang to abandon its weapons programs. Trump himself, when questioned on Monday about the possibility of military action, told Fox News Channel that he did not wish to “telegraph” his intentions like the previous administration. “We’ll see what happens. I hope things work out well,” he stated, while noting that the United States has sought to engage the North Koreans in dialogue for an extended period.

text: Trump's adversaries quickly head to the courthouse to impede his actions. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Following President Donald Trump's announcement on October 12 that he would cease subsidies to health insurers vital to the Obamacare law, Democratic state officials responded promptly and predictably: a lawsuit was filed within 24 hours by 18 state attorneys general. The rush to the courthouse in reaction to presidential decisions has become a routine since Trump assumed office in January, with early judicial decisions in numerous cases temporarily hindering significant aspects of the president’s agenda. Many of the Republican president’s most notable executive actions, ranging from immigration and transgender rights to energy and environmental issues, have faced obstacles due to court decisions stemming from lawsuits initiated by Democratic state and local officials as well as progressive advocacy organizations. "We are more of a check on this administration than Congress," remarked Democratic New York state Attorney General Eric Schneiderman regarding the role of state attorneys general. Similarly, key executive actions taken by Trump’s Democratic predecessor Barack Obama were obstructed by lawsuits from Republican state attorneys general, including one case that ultimately reached the Supreme Court, aimed at safeguarding millions of undocumented immigrants from deportation. Since Trump took office, courts have temporarily blocked his initiatives to: **prohibit travelers and immigrants from several Muslim-majority nations **withhold federal funds from so-called sanctuary cities that do not comply with federal authorities on immigration enforcement **prohibit transgender individuals from serving in the military **postpone the implementation of a regulation introduced by the Obama administration that limits methane emissions **halt an Interior Department regulation mandating that energy companies pay increased mineral royalties on federal property **delay adherence to an Obama-era regulation designed to reduce emissions from natural gas drilling waste on federal land **and obstruct a detained undocumented immigrant teenager from obtaining an abortion. Trump has also claimed some judicial victories, such as on October 25, when a federal judge in California denied the request from state attorneys general to compel the government to maintain the subsidies to insurers under Obamacare, officially known as the Affordable Care Act, while the legal proceedings continue. That ruling was more of an exception than the standard. "President Trump remains dedicated to safeguarding our national security and eliminating burdensome regulations that, if enacted, would jeopardize jobs, harm consumers, and offer no substantial benefits," a White House official, who requested anonymity, stated in a comment provided to Reuters. "The Trump administration is assured of its legal stances and is eager to present its case – and succeed – before the federal judiciary," the official continued. In light of legal challenges, Trump has criticized the judiciary in manners that even his own Supreme Court appointee Neil Gorsuch described as disheartening and demoralizing. text: Reports indicate that the U.S. attorney's office in Manhattan is looking into Paul Manafort for possible money laundering. text: Before his discussions with Putin, Trump downplays election interference in the U.S. WARSAW (Reuters) - On Thursday, just a day prior to his inaugural meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump stated that it remains uncertain whether Moscow intervened in the 2016 U.S. election, although he expressed suspicion regarding Russian involvement. While addressing reporters in Poland, Trump minimized the evaluation from his own intelligence agencies, which concluded that Russia interfered in the election by hacking into Democrats' emails and disseminating propaganda online. "I believe it was Russia, but I also think it was likely other individuals and/or nations, and I see no issue with that assertion. The truth is, nobody really knows. Nobody can say for certain," Trump remarked at a press conference. Investigations led by special counsel Robert Mueller and various U.S. congressional committees are currently examining whether Russia intervened in the election and collaborated with Trump’s campaign. According to lawmakers and intelligence officials, these investigations are primarily centered on Moscow’s actions, and no public evidence has emerged implicating other nations. Moscow has denied any interference, and Trump asserts that his campaign did not collude with Russia. Trump, who triumphed over Democrat Hillary Clinton in the November election, is set to meet Putin on Friday during a G20 summit in Hamburg, Germany, marking their first official meeting. It remains uncertain if the Republican president will address the subject of election interference during their encounter. In a speech delivered in Warsaw, Trump reiterated the U.S. commitment to defend NATO allies and subtly criticized Russia. Throughout his election campaign, Trump often praised Putin as a strong leader and advocated for improved relations between the U.S. and Moscow, although he has since moderated that stance. Representative Adam Schiff, the leading Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, described Trump’s comments in Poland concerning the election as merely reinforcing "his own personal fiction." "The President’s remarks today, once more casting doubt on whether Russia was responsible for the obvious interference in our election and implying – contrary to his own intelligence agencies – that nobody truly knows, continue to directly harm U.S. interests," Schiff stated. "To start off, I heard it was 17 agencies. I said, wow, that’s quite a number, do we even have that many intelligence agencies? Let’s verify that. We conducted extensive research, and it turned out to be three or four. It wasn’t 17," Trump stated. The U.S. intelligence report released in January, which accused Russia of meddling in the U.S. election, was published by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which supervises the 17 U.S. intelligence agencies. However, the report acknowledges that it relies on assessments made by the CIA, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the National Security Agency, which held the critical classified information regarding Russian operations. Trump claimed that the CIA informed his predecessor, Democratic President Barack Obama, last August about the Russian interference in the election, but he took no action to prevent it. "I believe what transpired is that he assumed Hillary Clinton would win the election, and he thought, let’s not take any action. Had he believed otherwise, he would have acted," Trump said.

text: Venezuela may prohibit its primary opposition parties from participating in the presidential election. CARACAS (Reuters) - On Wednesday, the pro-government legislative superbody of Venezuela determined that parties which abstained from this month's local elections had forfeited their legitimacy, which could potentially disqualify the principal opposition factions from the 2018 presidential contest. The ruling by the Constituent Assembly—established through a controversial vote in July that the opposition boycotted and that faced widespread international criticism—outraged the opposition in Venezuela and drew rebuke from the United States. The U.S. Embassy stated on Twitter, "The Venezuelan government and its illegitimate Constituent Assembly are inventing rules as they go along. This is not democracy." The Justice First, Democratic Action, and Popular Will parties refrained from presenting candidates in this month's mayoral elections, protesting what they described as a skewed electoral system aimed at sustaining the dictatorship of leftist President Nicolas Maduro. Maduro had warned that this decision could hinder their participation in future elections, a stance echoed by the Constituent Assembly on Wednesday, which declared that these parties had lost their legal standing and must reapply to the National Election Board. Considering that the board is aligned with Maduro and that authorities frequently create barriers for the opposition, it is highly likely that these parties are now effectively barred from competing in the presidential election set to occur by the end of 2018. Maduro, aged 55, is anticipated to seek re-election despite the dire economic conditions in Venezuela, where countless citizens are missing meals and struggling to survive amid one of the highest inflation rates globally and widespread shortages of essential goods. Two of his potentially strongest opponents are already unable to challenge him: Popular Will leader Leopoldo Lopez is under house arrest, while Justice First leader Henrique Capriles is banned from holding political office. "We alert the world and all democratic nations that the prohibition of opposition political parties is yet another tactic by the dictatorship that merits rejection and condemnation," remarked Capriles' party associate Tomas Guanipa. Maduro and his supporters assert that the Constituent Assembly has restored peace to the OPEC country following months of opposition demonstrations earlier this year, during which over 125 individuals lost their lives. Protesters claimed they were fighting for freedom, but the government labeled them as violent subversives. "It’s time for the coupsters to confront the constitution. Let no one undermine the people's participation and the democratic system," stated Delcy Rodriguez, head of the Constituent Assembly, following the approval of Wednesday's measure.

text: The Afghan Taliban have dismissed allegations made by a Canadian individual regarding murder and sexual assault. PESHAWAR, Pakistan (Reuters) - On Sunday, a spokesperson for the Taliban refuted claims made by Joshua Boyle that during their captivity by militants in Afghanistan in 2012, one of his children was killed and his wife was assaulted. Boyle and his American spouse, Caitlan Coleman, were captured by the Haqqani network, a semi-autonomous faction of the Afghan Taliban, prior to their rescue last week by Pakistani forces in the northwest region of Pakistan, close to the Afghan frontier. Shortly after their return to Canada on Friday, Boyle informed reporters that their captors had killed one child and assaulted his wife. Taliban spokesperson Zabiullah Mujahid dismissed Boyle's statements as propaganda disseminated by Western nations that assisted in the family's rescue. "We strongly reject these fabricated and false accusations concerning this Canadian family, which is now under the influence of the enemy," he stated in a communication to the press. "Any statement the enemy wishes to force upon them is something the family is compelled to state." Boyle urged the Taliban to provide his family with the justice they are entitled to. Mujahid claimed that the couple was deliberately kept together to ensure their safety. He also denied the allegation of child murder but conceded that one child had fallen ill and died. "We were located in a remote area without access to a physician and medical supplies, which resulted in the child's death," he explained. Three children, all born during their captivity, were rescued alongside Boyle and Coleman. The U.S. government describes the Haqqani network as "the most lethal and sophisticated insurgent group" operating in Afghanistan. In 2015, its operational leader, Sirajuddin Haqqani, was appointed as deputy to the Taliban's newly designated leader, Mullah Akhtar Mohammad Mansour, strengthening the connection between the two factions. The Haqqani network previously held U.S. Army Sergeant Bowe Bergdahl, who was released in exchange for Taliban detainees in 2014, and is suspected of having two professors, one American and one Australian, who were abducted outside their university in Kabul in 2016. A high-ranking official from the Afghan government informed Reuters that American and Afghan special forces conducted two unsuccessful operations to rescue the professors in Afghanistan, but it is now believed that they have been taken to Haqqani hideouts across the border in Pakistan.

On Tuesday, he announced that the ongoing scandal would divert attention from more pressing matters. During a press conference held at a waterfront park close to his childhood residence, an emotional Murray refuted the accusations, which he characterized as politically driven, according to a video shared on the mayor’s Facebook page. Murray, a Democrat and the first openly gay mayor of the city, also implied that the allegations stem from negative stereotypes associated with gay men. He stated, "The mayor’s race must be focused on... issues, not on a scandal, which it would be focused on if I were to remain in this race," as he declared his exit from the election. Since taking office as mayor in 2014, Murray had previously advocated for gay rights and the legalization of same-sex marriage during his time as a senator in the Washington state legislature. A fourth individual, in a sworn court declaration, made similar claims against Murray, according to the Seattle Times. While Murray has repeatedly rejected the allegations as politically motivated, he has faced backlash for questioning the credibility of the accusers, whom the Seattle Times noted had criminal histories. An attorney representing the first accuser, Lincoln Beauregard, remarked on Twitter that his client viewed the mayor’s decision to withdraw from the race as "one step towards justice."

text: The ruling party of the Czech Republic asserts that enhancing wage growth should be the priority for the forthcoming government. PRAGUE (Reuters) - Lubomir Zaoralek, who will head the ruling Social Democrats in the upcoming election next month, stated on Wednesday that the next Czech administration ought to distribute the advantages of robust growth among workers and transition to a higher wage economy. (For graphic, click tmsnrt.rs/2xRMCax) The center-left party is trailing its coalition ally, the ANO movement, by significant margins ahead of the vote scheduled for October 20-21, but Foreign Minister Zaoralek believes it can appeal to voters who prioritize economic fairness. The Czech Republic has a highly industrialized economy with a substantial automotive sector. The strong growth rate, which reached 4.7 percent in the second quarter, has resulted in labor shortages and heightened wage expectations. Growth in private sector wages has prompted public sector employees to request increased compensation, and the government has responded by raising salaries for healthcare and education workers who have historically been underpaid. 'If society is to remain cohesive... during times of prosperity, it must be inclusive,' Zaoralek, 61, remarked in an interview. He identified his key focuses as wage growth, education, and improving living standards to match those in Western Europe. The outgoing administration has consistently raised the minimum wage annually, with the most recent increase setting it at 12,200 crowns ($561.23) per month, effective next year. They have also committed to enhancing teacher salaries, as educators are among the lowest-paid professionals compared to other skilled occupations in OECD nations. Zaoralek emphasized the necessity for a new economic framework that would enable the production of higher-margin goods, even if this means that some companies reliant on cheap labor may have to close. This transition would reflect trends in export sectors, where rising wages have compelled firms to innovate in order to preserve profit margins. Currently, Czech workers earn about one-third of what their German counterparts make. To align with its Western neighbors, the country must maintain cooperation with EU partners as the bloc discusses its future post-Brexit, he noted, adding that there is interest in obtaining observer status in the euro zone. However, he cautioned against a rapid push for euro zone membership, as this could face resistance from potential coalition partners. Zaoralek's views contrast with those of outgoing Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka, who advocates for the next government to establish a timeline for joining the euro zone. The majority of Czechs are opposed to entering the currency union. Zaoralek remarked that elections are often determined in the last moments of the campaign, so the Social Democrats could still secure the next government. No single party is anticipated to achieve an absolute majority, and past opinion polls have been shown to be unreliable. A significant concern for both ANO and any potential coalition allies is that parliament recently voted to permit police to charge ANO founder and chairman, billionaire Andrej Babis, with fraud regarding EU subsidies. He has denied any wrongdoing. Zaoralek indicated that he could not envision Babis being part of the next cabinet if he faces charges. However, he did not dismiss the possibility of forming a coalition with the ANO movement if Babis is not the prime minister. 'It is challenging to establish a coalition with someone who is under prosecution... That is inconceivable,' he stated.

text: On Thursday, nine U.S. senators representing states with oil refineries sent a letter to President Donald Trump, requesting modifications to the nation's biofuels policy and seeking a meeting to discuss the matter. This correspondence highlights escalating conflicts between refiners, who are against the U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard—a law mandating that they incorporate greater amounts of ethanol into the nation’s fuel supply each year—and the corn lobby in the Midwest that backs it. Last week, the Trump administration responded to mounting pressure from lawmakers in the Midwest, assuring them through letters and phone calls that it would abandon proposals, favored by the refining sector, aimed at revamping the biofuels policy. The senators warned that this decision could lead to job losses. "If your administration does not implement adjustments or reforms regarding the Renewable Fuel Standard, it will result in job losses across the country, especially within our states," the letter stated, which was endorsed by Texas Senator Ted Cruz, Oklahoma Senator Jim Inhofe, Pennsylvania Senator Pat Toomey, along with six other senators. In their letter, the senators requested a meeting with Trump within the next three weeks, which would include themselves, several lawmakers from the Midwest, and pertinent officials from the administration "to explore a forward path towards a mutually acceptable solution." A representative from the White House has not yet responded to the request for a meeting. The Renewable Fuel Standard was introduced by former President George W. Bush in 2005 to assist farmers, decrease imports, and tackle climate change. The oil industry has opposed this regulation primarily because the rising biofuels volume requirements encroach upon their market share of petroleum-based fuels. Several independent refiners, such as Valero Energy Corp, CVR Energy, and PBF Energy, have also openly criticized the regulation's demand that refiners either blend biofuels or buy credits from competitors that do, arguing that this obligation costs them hundreds of millions of dollars annually. CVR’s majority owner, billionaire Carl Icahn, served for several months as a senior advisor to Donald Trump on regulations and during that period advocated for transferring the blending responsibility from refiners to supply terminals or distributors. He stepped down from his advisory position this summer due to concerns regarding his conflicting roles as an investor and advisor. Last week, the Environmental Protection Agency stated that it did not find it suitable to move the blending responsibility away from refiners. The EPA also abandoned a proposal to reduce biofuels volume mandates, as well as another proposal to count ethanol exports against those mandates.

text: The White House announced on Monday that U.S. President Donald Trump has tentatively agreed to eliminate the weight restriction on warheads for South Korean missiles following North Korea's sixth nuclear test. In a conversation with South Korean President Moon Jae-in, Trump also provided preliminary approval for South Korea to procure billions of dollars worth of military equipment from the United States, according to a statement from the White House. Additionally, South Korea's presidential office indicated that both leaders reached a consensus to remove the weight limit and to impose the strongest possible sanctions and pressure on North Korea via the United Nations. In a different phone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the same day, Moon mentioned that the U.N. Security Council should explore methods to cut off North Korea's foreign currency revenue, which includes earnings from its overseas workers and oil imports, as stated in the South Korean announcement. Currently, the missile agreement between the United States and South Korea restricts Seoul's warheads to a maximum weight of 500 kg (1100 lb). This agreement, which was last revised in 2012, was being reconsidered following a series of missile launches by North Korea this year, subsequent to Moon's inauguration in May, which included two tests of intercontinental ballistic missiles. Allowing an unlimited warhead weight would provide South Korea with the capability to deliver a more powerful strike against North Korea in the event of military hostilities. However, the missiles would still be subject to a flight range limit of 800 km, and no modifications to the flight range were referenced in the Blue House statement. Most analysts and policymakers concur that halting oil supplies to North Korea would adversely affect its economy. It remains uncertain whether China, North Korea's primary ally and trading partner, would participate in such efforts.
