text: U.S. legislators are investigating cyber security incidents at the Federal Reserve, expressing 'serious concerns'. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A congressional committee in the United States has initiated an inquiry into the cyber security protocols of the Federal Reserve after a Reuters article disclosed over 50 cyber security breaches at the U.S. central bank from 2011 to 2015. On Friday, the House Committee on Science, Space and Technology sent a correspondence to Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen to articulate their 'serious concerns' regarding the central bank’s capability to safeguard sensitive financial data. The correspondence referenced the Reuters article, which was based on significantly redacted internal records from the Fed acquired through a Freedom of Information Act request. The redacted documents did not specify who compromised the bank's systems or if they accessed confidential information or embezzled funds. 'These reports highlight serious concerns regarding the Federal Reserve’s cyber security stance, particularly its ability to avert threats that could jeopardize highly sensitive financial information maintained on the agency’s systems,' stated the letter, which was endorsed by House Science Committee Chairman Lamar Smith, a Republican from Texas, along with Barry Loudermilk, a Republican from Georgia and the chairman of the oversight subcommittee. A spokesperson for the Fed indicated that the central bank had received the committee's letter and 'will respond to it.' The committee requested that the Fed’s national cyber security team - the National Incident Response Team - provide all cyber incident reports in their unredacted form from January 1, 2009, to the present. Additionally, it sought incident reports from the Fed’s local incident response teams. Global policymakers, regulators, and financial institutions have increasingly worried about the security of the international banking system following a series of cyber attacks on banks in Bangladesh, Vietnam, and other locations connected to fraudulent transaction messages transmitted via the global financial platform SWIFT. The investigation into the Fed’s security practices was prompted by a separate examination by the same committee regarding the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's management of the cyber theft of $81 million from one of its accounts associated with the central bank of Bangladesh. The committee asserted its jurisdiction over the Fed’s cyber security because it is responsible for overseeing the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, which is tasked with crafting federal cyber security standards and guidelines, under a federal information technology law enacted in 2014. The panel also asked for a 'detailed description of all confirmed cyber security incidents' from 2009 onward, all documents and communications pertaining to 'higher impact cases' managed by the Fed’s NIRT team, and all documents and communications with the Fed’s Office of Inspector General concerning confirmed cyber incidents, along with an organizational chart that outlines the Fed’s leading cyber security personnel. The committee requested a reply to its inquiry by June 17. (Click here to view the letter: tmsnrt.rs/1VBXvSz) The Fed’s computer systems contain confidential discussions regarding monetary policy that influences financial markets. According to the records acquired by Reuters, the central bank's staff suspected that many of the breaches were the work of hackers or spies. The Fed had chosen not to comment on the records, as they represent only a portion of all cyber attacks on the central bank since they only include incidents involving the Washington-based Board of Governors, a federal entity that is subject to public records regulations. (For a graphic on the Fed security breaches, see: tmsnrt.rs/1TxSu8R)

text: Chess federation reports that Israel has been barred from a match hosted in Saudi Arabia. Israel Gelfer, FIDE's vice president with the Secretariat located in Athens, informed Reuters via email that the Israeli players' visas have not been granted and will not be granted. "If they prevent chess players from various nations from participating, the event cannot be considered a world championship," Aizenberg told Reuters. Aizenberg asserted that FIDE should guarantee that Israeli players can engage in international competitions, and that the Israeli federation was weighing all possible actions, including legal measures and organizing an international tournament in Israel for competitors excluded from the Saudi event. In November, FIDE had stated it was making a significant effort to ensure that all players received the necessary visas. text: PHILADELPHIA (Reuters) - On Friday, Donald Trump aimed to persuade the American public regarding his stringent immigration policies by meeting in Philadelphia with the family of a woman who was murdered in a shooting incident in 2007 involving individuals who had entered the United States unlawfully. This week, Trump revealed a stringent immigration proposal that focused on the deportation of undocumented immigrants who commit offenses. His plan received applause from other critics of immigration, though some Hispanic supporters and moderate Republicans expressed that it showed a lack of empathy towards the millions of undocumented individuals in the country. Trump frequently cites instances of individuals harmed by undocumented immigrants to justify his firm stance, which also includes the construction of a wall along the Mexico border, despite some research indicating that immigrants are less prone to engage in serious criminal activities. On Friday, he met with the family of Iofemi Hightower, who was only 20 years old when she, along with two others, was shot dead in a Newark, New Jersey schoolyard. At least one individual convicted in the 2007 incident was reported to be in the U.S. illegally, according to a New York Times article from 2010 regarding the trials. Another individual was likely undocumented initially but later acquired legal status, as stated by the newspaper. "These are individuals who should not be in the country," Trump told the press. "Many people are unaware of the repercussions of these individuals entering." Shalga Hightower, Iofemi’s mother, 55, shared that her family spent seven years dealing with legal proceedings, in addition to experiencing homelessness and job loss. When asked if she would support Trump in his presidential bid, she affirmed her endorsement. text: SITTWE, Myanmar (Reuters) - A senior government official reported on Tuesday that thousands of Rohingya Muslims, who are currently in a precarious situation due to hostility from Buddhists in northwestern Myanmar, are not going to receive the safe passage they requested from two isolated villages, despite having sufficient food supplies. The Rohingya residents expressed their desire to leave but insisted they required protection from ethnic Rakhine Buddhists, who had made threats against their lives. They also mentioned that they have been facing food shortages since August 25, after Rohingya militants carried out deadly assaults in Rakhine state, leading to a severe crackdown by the Myanmar military. Since then, at least 420,000 Rohingya individuals have fled to neighboring Bangladesh to escape what a senior United Nations official described as a clear case of ethnic cleansing. Tin Maung Swe, the secretary of the Rakhine state government, stated that the requests for safe passage from the two villages had been declined, as the villagers had enough rice and were under the protection of a nearby police station. He remarked, "Their reasons were not acceptable. They must stay in their original place." Residents from Ah Nauk Pyin, one of the two Rohingya villages, expressed their hope to move to a relatively safer camp outside of Sittwe, the state capital. Approximately 90,000 Rohingya individuals displaced during prior violence in 2012 are currently confined to camps in Rakhine under dire conditions. However, state secretary Tin Maung Swe deemed such a relocation "impossible," as it could provoke Rakhine Buddhists and exacerbate communal strife. In a nationally broadcast address on Tuesday, Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi pledged to hold accountable those responsible for human rights abuses in Rakhine, but did not respond to U.N. allegations of ethnic cleansing by the military. The Nobel Peace Prize laureate noted that many Muslims had not fled and encouraged foreign diplomats to investigate why certain regions of Rakhine state have managed to maintain peace. "We can arrange for you to visit these areas and to ask them for yourself why they have not fled ... even at a time when everything around them seems to be in a state of turmoil," she stated. The Rohingya inhabitants of Ah Nauk Pyin claim they have no alternative but to remain, with their complicated relationship with their equally anxious Rakhine neighbors potentially reaching a breaking point at any time. About 2,700 individuals reside in Ah Nauk Pyin, which is partially concealed among fruit trees and coconut palms on a rain-drenched peninsula. The villagers reported that Rakhine men have made menacing phone calls and have recently gathered outside the village, shouting, "Leave, or we will kill you all." On Tuesday morning, Rakhine villagers forced two Rohingya men who were attempting to tend to their fields to leave, according to Maung Maung, the leader of Ah Nauk Pyin. The Rakhine community denies harassing their Muslim neighbors but wants them to depart, fearing collaboration with militants from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), which was responsible for the attacks on August 25. Khin Tun Aye, the chief of Shwe Laung Tin, a nearby Rakhine village, remarked that they expelled the two Rohingya men out of concern that they might be planning to assault or bomb their village. "They shouldn’t come close during this time of conflict," he stated. "People are living in constant fear." The Office of the United Nations Resident Coordinator in Myanmar informed Reuters that it is "aware and concerned" about the situation and is in discussions with the Myanmar government. State secretary Tin Maung Swe mentioned that Reuters could not access the area for security reasons but assured that authorities were evaluating the needs of the residents there. "If they need food, we are ready to send it," he said. "Don’t worry about it."

(Reuters) - At the Morgan County fair in McConnelsville, situated in a rural section of Ohio that strongly supported U.S. President Donald Trump in the previous election, ticket vendor John Wilson quietly lists several grievances with the man he helped to elect. The 70-year-old retired banker expressed his dissatisfaction with the internal conflicts and frequent staff changes within the White House. He is also critical of Trump’s tendency to frequent his personal golf resorts. Additionally, he wishes the president would take more action to reform the healthcare system, and he is concerned that Trump may not fulfill his commitment to expel illegal immigrants from the country. "Every president makes mistakes," Wilson remarked. "But if you keep piling them on, there's just a limit." According to the Reuters/Ipsos daily tracking survey, the Republican president’s approval is diminishing in small towns and rural regions, where 15 percent of the national population resides. The survey, which included over 15,000 adults from "non-metro" locations, revealed that the respondents are now just as likely to disapprove of Trump as they are to approve of him. In September, 47 percent of individuals in non-metro areas expressed approval of Trump, while another 47 percent disapproved. This marks a decline from Trump’s initial four weeks in office, during which 55 percent approved and only 39 percent disapproved. The poll indicated that support for Trump in rural areas has decreased among men, white individuals, and those without a college education. He has lost backing from rural Republicans and voters who supported him on Election Day. While Trump continues to receive relatively favorable ratings for his management of the economy and national security, rural Americans are becoming increasingly dissatisfied with his immigration policies, which were a core element of his presidential campaign. In September, only 47 percent of rural Americans approved of the president’s handling of immigration, a drop from 56 percent during his first month in office. Poll participants interviewed by Reuters cited various reasons for their discontent with the president regarding immigration. Some expressed frustration over the lengthy wait for Trump to fulfill his promise of constructing a wall along the southern border, while others felt uneasy about his administration's initiatives to limit travel into the United States. text: Democrats challenge U.S. housing nominee Carson regarding possible Trump conflicts. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Thursday, U.S. Senate Democrats interrogated Ben Carson, who has been nominated by Donald Trump to oversee housing policy, concerning potential conflicts of interest involving the agency he is expected to lead and properties that the president-elect might have financial ties to. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) allocates billions of dollars annually to developers and landlords. During his confirmation hearing, Democrats raised concerns to Carson that some of this taxpayer funding could inadvertently benefit Trump or his relatives. "The president-elect is concealing his family's business interests from you, me, and all of America," stated Senator Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts, a prominent critic of Trump, as she addressed Carson. "He can channel taxpayer funds into his own accounts without the American public being aware of it." Trump, a businessman from New York who began in real estate, has not disclosed his tax returns or provided comprehensive details about his global holdings. On Wednesday, he announced plans to transfer control of his business interests to his two eldest sons and place his assets into a trust. However, these actions have not alleviated concerns from critics who contend that as president, Trump will still possess undisclosed financial interests that may influence his policies. When pressed on the matter by Democrats, Carson at one moment promised he would keep an eye on any possible conflicts of interest but expressed uncertainty regarding how to proceed. When asked how he would prevent conflicts, the retired neurosurgeon and former Republican presidential candidate told the Senate Banking Committee, "I would hope that this committee could come up with a proposal that might be satisfactory to everyone involved." Reports indicate that Trump has a stake in the substantial Starrett City housing project located in Brooklyn, New York, which has received HUD funding. However, Trump's real estate career has primarily centered around luxury housing, commercial real estate, and resort properties. Earlier in the hearing, Carson was evasive when Warren questioned him about ensuring that no HUD initiatives would benefit Trump. "If there happens to be an extraordinarily good program that is working for millions of people and it turns out that someone you’re focused on is going to gain $10 from it, am I going to say, 'No, the rest of you Americans can’t have it?'" Carson replied. Carson is largely anticipated to be confirmed by the Senate committee, which is controlled by Republicans, and by the full Senate. Much of Thursday’s discussion centered around Carson’s long-held opposition to social-welfare programs, with some senators inquiring whether he truly supports HUD’s mission to provide housing assistance to millions of Americans. "I believe the rental assistance program is vital," Carson responded. He later added that social programs must function within financial limits. Much of Carson’s statements highlighted his well-known background of growing up in poverty in Detroit’s inner city, emphasizing that he learned early what "housing insecurity" entails. He offered limited specifics regarding U.S. housing policy or how he would reform the agency, merely suggesting an interest in enhancing its efficiency. If confirmed as HUD secretary, Carson would manage an agency with an approximate budget of $40 billion that not only aids the poor but also supports mortgage loans for middle-class households. HUD’s Federal Housing Administration (FHA) backs around one in five home loans and at least $1.1 trillion in debt—a figure Carson described as concerning. This week, outgoing HUD Secretary Julian Castro reduced HUD fees for mortgage default insurance, claiming it would save the average HUD-supported homeowner $500 annually. Carson indicated that he might contemplate reversing that unexpected decision. "Certainly, if confirmed, I will collaborate with the FHA administrator and other financial experts."

text: The Afghan Air Force has received its initial four UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters manufactured in the United States, as announced by officials on Tuesday. This acquisition is part of a strategy to replace the outdated fleet of Russian Mi-17 helicopters. The U.S. is set to provide a total of 159 Black Hawks to Afghanistan in the upcoming years, aiming to enhance the capabilities of the Afghan Air Force (AAF), which is regarded as one of the most effective components of the Afghan Defence and Security Forces. The first batch of UH-60s for the Afghan Air Force landed in Kandahar today. According to the NATO-led Resolute Support mission, these helicopters will assist in further developing a capable and sustainable AAF. The sturdy Soviet-era Mi-17 helicopters have been the backbone of the AAF, responsible for approximately 50% of all sorties in recent months, and are highly favored by Afghan pilots. These helicopters are utilized not only for transporting troops and casualties but also for delivering supplies to remote areas that are challenging to access by road. Additionally, they can be equipped with weaponry for close air support to ground units. Nonetheless, their age has rendered maintenance and replacements increasingly problematic, leading to plans for their gradual retirement over the next few years in favor of refurbished Black Hawks, which are a key component of the U.S. Army’s helicopter fleet. A report from July by the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan, a Congressional oversight body in the U.S., indicated that 19 out of the AAF's fleet of 46 Mi-17s were inoperable due to being under repair or overhaul. Beyond operational issues, the Pentagon has faced ongoing political pressure from Congress to redirect funding toward American-built aircraft. Enhancing the Afghan Air Force is a crucial aspect of President Ashraf Ghani’s four-year initiative aimed at strengthening Afghan security forces, which have faced challenges in managing the Taliban insurgency since the NATO-led coalition concluded its primary combat activities in 2014.

text: Russia aims to reach an agreement regarding debt repayment with Venezuela by the end of the year. MOSCOW (Reuters) - A senior official from the Russian finance ministry stated on Friday that they are seeking a resolution on how Venezuela will meet its debt obligations to Moscow by the close of this year. Konstantin Vyshkovsky, who leads the state debt department at the finance ministry, informed Reuters that Venezuela's debt to Russia exceeds $3 billion. Venezuela secured loans from Russia in late 2011 but was unable to maintain payment schedules starting in 2016 as the South American nation experienced a severe economic and financial crisis. 'Currently, we view it as a liquidity crisis rather than a financial solvency crisis,' Vyshkovsky remarked. He indicated that the finance ministry hopes to establish new terms for how Caracas will repay the debt by the end of 2017. He did not specify when he anticipates Caracas will begin repaying its debt. Venezuela's faltering socialist government is increasingly reliant on its ally Russia for the financial support and credit necessary for its survival, as reported in a special Reuters article published last month.

The relationship between North Korea and its primary ally and trading partner, China, has been strained due to its rapid development of weapons programs, with many of Pyongyang’s recent tests coinciding with significant Chinese events. Chinese President Xi Jinping did not mention North Korea during his extensive address, lasting over three hours, at the commencement of a crucial Communist Party Congress. Clinton asserted that China’s retaliatory measures concerning the deployment of a U.S. anti-missile system in South Korea, which target South Korean firms operating in China, would have been unnecessary if Beijing had effectively managed North Korea.

text: The attorney for Indonesia's parliament speaker asserted on Thursday that his client is not evading an anti-corruption investigation regarding a $170 million graft case, emphasizing instead that the politician has a packed agenda. Members of the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) attempted to apprehend speaker Setya Novanto at his residence in Jakarta on Wednesday evening but were unable to locate him, leading to speculation about his location. "He is not hiding," Novanto's lawyer, Fredrich Yunadi, informed Reuters via phone. "He is quite occupied, invited to numerous events and such. If he becomes aware of any legal infractions, he will confer with other officials," added Yunadi. He noted that Novanto, who leads Indonesia's second-largest political party, Golkar, remained in Jakarta. Novanto did not respond to requests for comments. He has previously denied any wrongdoing but has repeatedly missed KPK summons for questioning over the past few months, citing health issues and the need for heart surgery. The KPK is probing state losses around $170 million related to a national electronic identity card initiative, following claims that amounts between $5,000 and $5.5 million—resulting from inflated procurement costs—were distributed among parliament politicians. Due to these alleged embezzlement activities, many individuals have encountered extensive delays in receiving their cards or have been issued temporary documents instead of proper cards. Novanto was once again named a suspect in this case last week after he employed a controversial legal tactic, a pre-trial motion, to have earlier charges dismissed in the previous month. On Thursday, Yunadi mentioned that his client had been summoned by the KPK 11 times as both a witness and a suspect in the investigation. "We will submit another pre-trial motion, but the timing is yet to be determined," stated Yunadi. Vice President Jusuf Kalla, who is also affiliated with Golkar, remarked to reporters that Novanto ought to be prepared to engage with any legal proceedings if called to do so. Officials from the anti-corruption agency did not promptly respond to inquiries for comments. A spokesman for the KPK, Febri Diansyah, was cited in the Kompas newspaper as stating that the commission had a warrant for Novanto's arrest and urged him to turn himself in. For years, Novanto has faced allegations of corruption, yet he has never been prosecuted. In late 2015, a parliamentary ethics committee initiated an investigation following claims from a Freeport Indonesia executive that Novanto attempted to extort $1.8 billion worth of shares from the local division of the U.S. mining firm. Novanto refuted the claims but temporarily resigned from his position. He was reinstated as speaker a year later after being exonerated by an ethics panel. Transparency International reports that many Indonesians view parliament as one of the most corrupt entities in the country.

The Zarrab case represents a blatant scheme against Turkey, described as a political matter devoid of any legal foundation, stated government spokesperson Bekir Bozdag last week. Zarrab has been missing from recent court sessions. Last month, Atilla’s attorneys indicated that Zarrab, who was apprehended in Miami in March 2016, had essentially not engaged in the case, suggesting that Atilla might be the sole defendant present at trial. Yildirim remarked that the defendants are under duress and being compelled to make statements against our country, without providing further details. The case is particularly sensitive in Turkey because prosecutors allege that a Turkish government minister, Caglayan, was implicated in the supposed conspiracy to avoid U.S. sanctions. In a submission four weeks ago, prosecutors also included a transcript from an April 16, 2013 recorded phone call in which a person identified as Zarrab conversed with another co-defendant about his attempts to acquire a bank to create a channel for Iranian transactions. Prosecutors noted that Zarrab and Erdogan, who was then Turkey’s Prime Minister, had a conversation four days prior at a wedding. text: Trump's news conference ignites social media worldwide. NEW YORK (Reuters) - During his inaugural news conference following the election on November 8, President-elect Donald Trump set social media on fire with his comments on Wednesday, which included strong criticism of the media and a defense of his aim to strengthen relations with Russia. The event, conducted in the lobby of his Trump Tower office in Manhattan, was marked by several viral moments, including a confrontation with a reporter whom Trump labeled as disseminating "fake news." "I’m not going to give you a question," Trump said to the CNN journalist, who had reported the previous day that U.S. intelligence agencies had informed the Republican president-elect about claims that Russian operatives possessed compromising information regarding him. "You are fake news!" he stated, a remark that echoed across Twitter. Trump's assertion that journalists were "the only ones who care" about whether he would release his tax returns generated 165,000 tweets during the conference. Users on social media encouraged others to "retweet if you’re not a reporter and still care about seeing Trump’s tax returns." In Russia, the hashtag #TrumpPressConference was among the top trending topics throughout the news conference and for several hours thereafter. "If Putin likes Donald Trump, I see that as an asset, not a liability, because we have a terrible relationship with Russia," Trump, who assumes office on January 20, remarked in reference to the Russian leader. "I can’t say for sure that I will get along with Vladimir Putin. I hope to, but there’s a significant chance I won’t," Trump stated, leading to a surge of tweets from users in Russia. U.S. intelligence agencies have indicated that Russia was responsible for a hacking operation intended to support Trump’s presidential bid against Democrat Hillary Clinton. Approximately 80,000 tweets were recorded globally using the #TrumpPressConference hashtag during the hour-long event, which included around 250 journalists. According to Amobee, a global digital marketing technology firm, Twitter sentiment regarding Trump during this period was 14 percent positive, 63 percent neutral, and 23 percent negative. Additionally, Trump's remarks concerning the wall he has committed to constructing on the U.S.-Mexican border, which he intends for Mexico to fund, also sparked reactions on Twitter. He mentioned that he would not postpone construction for negotiations with Mexico, adding: "Mexico in some form ... will reimburse us." In response, former Mexican President Vicente Fox tweeted: "Neither today, nor tomorrow nor never Mexico will pay for that stupid wall."

text: Scotland has expressed regret to gay men for past convictions. EDINBURGH (Reuters) - On Tuesday, the devolved government of Scotland issued an apology to men who were historically convicted for engaging in same-sex relations and introduced a new law allowing them to exonerate themselves. "It is only right that we address this historic wrong," stated First Minister Nicola Sturgeon during a session of the Scottish parliament. She noted that discriminatory laws, despite being repealed, still affect individuals today. "The wrong has been committed by the state to them, not by the individuals," she emphasized. Furthermore, she stated: "I categorically, unequivocally and wholeheartedly apologize for those laws and for the hurt and the harm they did to so many." In the gallery, same-sex couples were seen weeping, holding hands, and applauding. In 1981, consensual sexual acts between men over the age of 21 in Scotland were decriminalized. A spokesperson for the gay rights organization Stonewall commented that the apology will provide significant comfort to many who faced unjust prosecution and will assist in closing a dark chapter in Scotland's history. The new legislation recognizes the wrongful nature and discriminatory impact of historical convictions for specific sexual offences by granting pardons to those convicted and establishing a legal avenue for these convictions to be disregarded. Earlier in January, the UK government enacted a comparable law for England and Wales.

Since 2014, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration has intensified oversight of non-profit organizations, alleging that they operate against India’s national interests. Numerous licenses of foreign-funded charities have been revoked due to inaccurate reporting of donations. However, detractors argue that the government has leveraged the foreign funding regulations as a means to suppress non-profit organizations that have highlighted the social repercussions of India's swift economic growth. Last year, the intelligence division of India’s home ministry prepared a memo on Bloomberg Philanthropies, expressing worries that the foundation was conducting a campaign to focus on Indian tobacco enterprises and was actively lobbying against the industry. Although the three-page memo, which was reviewed by Reuters, acknowledged that the Bloomberg initiative's stated goal of liberating India from tobacco is commendable, given the known dangers of tobacco, it also emphasized the significance of the industry, noting that it generates nearly $5 billion in yearly revenue for the government and sustains millions of livelihoods. The memo stated that foreign entities contributing funds for the aim of lobbying against an established economic activity raises numerous concerns, including an adverse economic effect on 35 million individuals. The memo, dated June 3, 2016, marked as SECRET, was circulated among senior government officials, including those in Modi’s office, and had not been previously disclosed. The investigation persisted until at least April of this year, as indicated by another government document. Rebecca Carriero, a spokesperson for Michael Bloomberg and the New York-based Bloomberg Philanthropies, declined to comment as they were not aware of any ongoing investigation. India is one of his focus countries, where tobacco causes 900,000 deaths annually. text: According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), there are approximately 10 million stateless individuals globally, with three million recognized officially. This lack of nationality results in the absence of identity, rights, and frequently employment opportunities. The largest stateless minority in the world is the Muslim Rohingyas in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, with around 600,000 having fled violence and oppression since the end of August, seeking refuge in Bangladesh. The U.N. agency released a report titled "This is Our Home - Stateless Minorities and their Search for Citizenship," urging governments to eliminate this discriminatory practice by 2024. "Living in this world without nationality means lacking an identity, documentation, and the rights and privileges that many of us take for granted, such as employment, education, and the assurance that your child belongs somewhere," stated Carol Batchelor, the director of UNHCR’s International Protection Division, during a press conference. UNHCR spokesperson Adrian Edwards noted that 3.2 million individuals across 75 nations are identified as stateless, having been officially registered or counted by their respective governments. However, the overall estimate stands at 10 million, which includes significant populations in nations such as Indonesia, Ivory Coast, Lebanon, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The UNHCR advocates that nationality should be granted to individuals born in a country if they would otherwise be stateless and encourages the naturalization process for long-term stateless residents. The report also mentions other stateless communities, many of whom have lived in their areas for generations, including Syrian Kurds, the Karana people in Madagascar, Roma in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, and the Pemba people in Kenya. "It is essential to guarantee that there is no intentional or arbitrary exclusion or deprivation of nationality," Batchelor emphasized. When asked if the Rohingya are among those who face deliberate exclusion from nationality, Batchelor responded, "We can only examine the outcome... Myanmar has a nationality law that specifies the categories of individuals recognized as citizens. The Rohingya are not included in that classification." Since 2012, around 30,000 stateless individuals in Thailand have obtained nationality, and last year, the Makonde community, numbering about 4,000, was recognized as Kenya's 43rd official tribe, as noted in the report. "We are observing declines in Thailand, Central Asia, Russia, and Western Africa. However, the reductions are not nearly significant enough to achieve the goal of eliminating statelessness by 2024," commented Melanie Khanna, who leads the UNHCR's section on statelessness.

text: Factbox: Nations that have expelled North Korean ambassadors following nuclear test. SEOUL (Reuters) - In reaction to Pyongyang's nuclear test on September 3, which was its most powerful to date, several nations have declared the expulsion of the North Korean ambassador assigned to their capitals. In spite of North Korea's growing isolation due to its ongoing breaches of international sanctions, the impoverished nation still maintains 49 diplomatic missions abroad and has relations with 160 countries, as reported by South Korea's Unification Ministry. In addition to its largest diplomatic missions located in Moscow and Beijing, North Korea also operates significant embassies in London, Rome, Stockholm, and Berlin, along with numerous smaller embassies throughout Africa and Asia. Below is a summary of the countries that have expelled North Korean diplomats following Pyongyang's sixth nuclear test: SPAIN, September 18, 2017 - The Spanish foreign ministry requested North Korean ambassador Kim Hyok Chol to depart the country by September 30, citing his nation's ongoing refusal to abandon its nuclear weapons program. KUWAIT, September 17, 2017 - Kuwait announced it had instructed North Korean ambassador So Chang Sik and four additional diplomats to exit within a month as the nation downgraded its diplomatic relations with Pyongyang. North Korea's Embassy in Kuwait City has been the sole diplomatic facility in the Gulf region for North Korea. PERU, September 11, 2017 - The government of Peru stated it was giving North Korean ambassador Kim Hak Chol five days to leave the country in response to North Korea's sixth nuclear test. MEXICO, September 7, 2017 - Mexico declared North Korean ambassador Kim Hyong Gil as persona non grata, requiring him to leave the country within 72 hours in protest of the North's sixth nuclear test, which it deemed a flagrant violation of international law and U.N. Security Council resolutions. The only nation to have entirely severed diplomatic relations with Pyongyang in recent years was Botswana, which ended ties following a United Nations investigation that uncovered severe and widespread human rights violations in North Korea. Security Council resolutions regarding the North's repeated missile launches. text: German authorities are searching for former members of the Red Army Faction (RAF) in connection with a suspected robbery. On Monday, police in Germany released video footage featuring three ex-members of the RAF militant organization, who were involved in an armed heist that took place in northern Germany in 2016. This leftist group emerged from the student protests of the late 1960s and is believed to have been responsible for the deaths of 34 individuals from 1972 to 1991. The RAF was officially disbanded in 1998, with many of its members returning to normal life. The three individuals being sought, which include two males and one female aged 49 to 63, have evaded capture for over 25 years. Since 2011, they have been implicated in robberies resulting in the theft of over 370,000 euros from various supermarkets and money transfer establishments. Newly released security footage from July 2016 captures two men entering a supermarket in Hildesheim, a central city, with their faces concealed, before they brandish a firearm at an employee and force him into a back room. Another video depicts the two individuals on a bus in Osnabruck, Lower Saxony, with noticeably heavy backpacks. German police have reached out to more than 4,000 car dealerships in an effort to locate the suspects, who tend to purchase inexpensive vehicles weeks prior to their heists. A reward of 80,000 euros is being offered for any substantial information leading to their capture. The RAF gained international attention in 1977 when they kidnapped and murdered industrialist Hanns Martin Schleyer, aiming to secure the release of their comrades imprisoned in a high-security facility in Stuttgart. Two decades ago, German officials stated their belief that the majority of RAF members were either deceased, incarcerated, or leading ordinary lives.

text: U.S. Congress validates Trump's Electoral College win. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Friday, the U.S. Congress confirmed the Electoral College results that awarded Republican Donald Trump his victory in the controversial 2016 presidential election following a lively half-hour joint session marked by Democratic opposition. The Republican businessman, making his initial attempt at public office through his presidential campaign, received 304 electoral votes, in contrast to the 227 secured by his Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton, as revealed by the vote tally announced by Vice President Joe Biden. The electoral votes were formally presented during a joint congressional session, a process generally regarded as a routine procedure for most presidential elections. Members of the House of Representatives raised objections to the electoral counts in states such as Alabama, Florida, Michigan, Texas, Mississippi, and the Carolinas, in a symbolic gesture that highlighted ongoing dissatisfaction with a divisive election campaign. Some representatives voiced concerns about lengthy lines at polling places, while others pointed to worries regarding Russian efforts to sway the outcome in Trump’s favor. “I object because people are horrified by the overwhelming evidence of Russian interference in our election,” stated Representative Barbara Lee from California before her objection was dismissed. Biden systematically rejected the challenges, often in a humorous manner, seemingly intent on concluding the tally. “It is over,” he remarked at one point, eliciting laughter from Republican members. None of the objecting representatives had a senator's support, which would have permitted them to pause the joint session and enable separate discussions in the House and Senate regarding the objections. Although Trump, who is scheduled to assume office on January 20, won the Electoral College vote that determines the election winner, Clinton surpassed him in the popular vote by nearly 3 million votes. The election has been overshadowed by worries about Russian hacking targeting Democratic organizations and other forms of interference throughout the campaign. Trump, who has consistently minimized the potential impact of Russian meddling, was expected to receive a U.S. intelligence report on the matter later that Friday. He remarked to The New York Times on Friday that the attention on the issue constituted a “political witch hunt.” The intelligence agencies did not determine that Russian hacking altered any vote counts. Nevertheless, House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi asserted that apprehensions regarding Russian interference tainted the perception of the 2016 election. “That’s why people have some level of dismay today on the vote ... about the Electoral College,” Pelosi expressed during a press conference. “How much is known about the foreign disruption of our election?”

text: WELLINGTON (Reuters) - According to the Electoral Commission, the ruling National Party of New Zealand secured 46.3 percent of the votes with 31.4 percent of the results counted in the general election held on Saturday, while the opposition Labour Party garnered 36 percent of the votes. The nationalist New Zealand First Party obtained 7.1 percent of the votes thus far, positioning it as a potential kingmaker within the German-style proportional representation framework. The Green Party received 6.2 percent of the vote. A historic 1.2 million ballots were submitted prior to election day, representing roughly one-third of the 3.3 million New Zealanders registered to vote. In previous elections, early voting has been a good predictor of the final outcomes.

text: Injuries and scars: Depictions of wounded Rohingya refugees. COX'S BAZAR, Bangladesh (Reuters) - Six-year-old Mohamed Heron and his four-year-old brother Akhter, both Rohingya Muslims, clung to each other while displaying burn injuries on their arms and torsos, which their uncle claims were caused by rockets fired by Myanmar's military at their village. According to their uncle, Mohamed Inus, two of their siblings—one aged seven and the other a 10-month-old infant—perished in the assault. Their father has been missing since he was taken by the military. "These two children survived when our village was struck by rockets," Inus shared with Reuters at the Kutupalong refugee camp near Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh. They were among several Rohingya individuals who revealed their injuries to a Reuters photographer who visited Kutupalong and other nearby camps such as Balukhali, Leda, and Nayapara. (Click reut.rs/2hBZZoK to see the photo essay) After fleeing with other villagers from their burned homes, the brothers made the journey to Bangladesh after three days of walking. At Kutupalong, they received treatment for their burns at a Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) clinic for three weeks. Since ethnic violence erupted at the end of August, thousands of Rohingya have been crossing the border weekly, often traveling for days or weeks, navigating through forests and mountains, with many risking dangerous river or sea crossings on the final leg of their escape to the fellow-Muslim country of Bangladesh. Bangladeshi hospitals and international humanitarian organizations are struggling to provide medical assistance to all the refugees, many of whom bear severe injuries and psychological scars. Since the onset of the crisis, Chittagong Medical College Hospital has admitted 261 patients with gunshot wounds or blast injuries, as reported by its director, Brigadier General Jalal Uddin. Sixteen individuals have succumbed to their injuries, and some have been left disabled. "We have had to perform amputations on some patients," Jalal Uddin stated. Sadar Hospital in Cox's Bazar has treated 1,467 Rohingya since the beginning of the exodus for various injuries, including gunshot wounds, fractures, and lacerations caused by knives or machetes, according to residential medical officer Shaheen Abdur Rahman Chowdhury. More than 600,000 Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh since Myanmar's military initiated what it described as "clearance operations" following a series of assaults by Rohingya militants on security posts in Rakhine state in late August. Human rights observers and fleeing Rohingya claim that the army, along with Rakhine Buddhist vigilantes, has conducted a campaign of arson aimed at expelling the Muslim population. The U.N. human rights agency termed it "a textbook example of ethnic cleansing." Myanmar, a predominantly Buddhist country, denies these allegations, asserting that its forces are targeting insurgents from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, whom they accuse of setting fires and attacking civilians. His resignation has thrown Lebanon back into the center of the Middle East's most intense rivalry, which pits a predominantly Sunni coalition led by Saudi Arabia and including the UAE against Shiite Iran and its affiliates. text: BRATISLAVA (Reuters) - On Friday, Slovak government officials reached an agreement to revise their coalition pact in an effort to bring back a junior party that had withdrawn its support three weeks prior, triggering a political crisis. The Slovak National Party (SNS), the junior participant in a three-party coalition, annulled the coalition agreement on August 7, demanding a new arrangement that would provide it with a greater influence in decision-making processes. Currently, the leaders of the three parties—Prime Minister Robert Fico of the leftist Smer party, Bela Bugar, the leader of the ethnic-Hungarian party Most-Hid, and Andrej Danko from the SNS—have come to a consensus to conduct regular weekly meetings to address the SNS's request for improved communication within the coalition. Danko expressed concerns on Thursday regarding the challenges of co-governing with Fico’s Smer, as both parties target the same electorate. As per a survey conducted by the Polis agency, support for the SNS declined to 7.2 percent in August from 8.6 percent during the March 2016 elections. The coalition requires the backing of all three parties to retain a majority in the 150-seat parliament, and Fico adopted a conciliatory approach on Friday, stating, "There is no alternative to this government. We must discover new methods of communication to enhance our mutual understanding," he told reporters. The SNS has advocated for increased government funding to rejuvenate thermal spa resorts and has proposed the establishment of a national airline, while Smer maintains that expenditures must not jeopardize the goal of achieving a balanced budget set for 2019. Opposition lawmakers have claimed that the SNS's exit from the coalition was a tactic to shift focus from a dispute regarding the allocation of 300 million euros ($351.69 million) in EU subsidies managed by the education ministry. The situation intensified last week when Fico called for the resignation of Education Minister Peter Plavcan over purported mishandling of the subsidies overseen by his department. Reports from Slovak media have indicated that the ministry selected various companies lacking a background in research or innovation as beneficiaries of EU funds intended to bolster science. SNS leader Andrej Danko contended that the claims regarding the misappropriation of funds were baseless but concurred to replace Plavcan.

text: MILWAUKEE (Reuters) - Donald Trump, the leading candidate for the Republican presidential nomination, forecasts a "very massive recession" looming in the United States. He cautioned that the combination of elevated unemployment rates and a stock market perceived as overvalued has set the groundwork for another economic downturn. In an interview with The Washington Post released on Saturday, the billionaire entrepreneur stated, "I believe we are sitting on an economic bubble. A financial bubble." Following a challenging week on the campaign trail marked by several missteps, Trump’s recent remarks have brought him back into the spotlight just ahead of Tuesday’s critical primary in Wisconsin, where he is currently trailing in the polls. The former reality television personality claimed that the actual unemployment rate in the U.S. is significantly greater than the five percent figure reported by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. "We’re not at 5 percent unemployment," Trump asserted. "The real number is probably in the twenties," he added, insisting that the official unemployment statistic is "statistically devised to make politicians — especially presidents — appear favorable." Trump expressed that "it’s a terrible time right now" for investing in the stock market, presenting a more pessimistic perspective on the U.S. economy compared to many mainstream economists. The interview was conducted by Robert Costa of the Post and the renowned Watergate journalist Bob Woodward. A real estate tycoon, Trump has focused on appealing to working-class voters as a key aspect of his campaign for the Republican nomination for the presidential election scheduled for November 8, frequently attributing unemployment to the relocation of American jobs and facilities to nations like China and Mexico. In the interview, Trump pledged to eliminate the more than $19 trillion national debt "over a period of eight years," aided by a renegotiation of trade agreements. "I’m renegotiating all of our deals, the major trade agreements that we are currently faring poorly on," he stated. After making contentious remarks about abortion last week, Trump has shown little willingness to heed the advice of fellow Republicans to adopt a more presidential demeanor to avoid alienating voters in the general election in November, should he secure the nomination. On Saturday, he criticized the close U.S. relationship with Saudi Arabia and reiterated accusations that U.S. allies are not contributing adequately within the NATO military alliance. During a campaign rally in Racine, Wisconsin, Trump remarked that NATO partners "are not paying their fair share" and labeled the 28-nation alliance as "obsolete." "Either they pay up, including for past deficiencies, or they need to exit. And if NATO breaks apart, it breaks apart," Trump declared. The Wisconsin nominating contest on Tuesday could serve as a pivotal moment in the Republican race. Trump, aged 69, is currently behind his main opponent, U.S. Senator Ted Cruz, 45, from Texas in the state. A victory for Cruz would complicate Trump’s path to amassing the required 1,237 delegates to secure the nomination before the Republican national convention in July. The winner will take all of Wisconsin’s 42 delegates.

text: The Italian administration successfully secured approval for all five confidence votes it initiated in the Senate on Wednesday concerning a new electoral law, which is unlikely to yield a definitive outcome in the national elections slated for next May. Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni introduced these five confidence motions to expedite the approval process despite fierce resistance from the anti-establishment 5-Star Movement and smaller leftist factions. Each of the five motions, addressing various components of the law, received solid majorities, even though numerous leftist allies abandoned the coalition. The legislation has already been approved by the lower house. Additionally, a sixth vote on a different article—though not tied to a confidence motion—was also approved. A concluding vote on the law is expected to take place on Thursday morning. The suggested voting framework benefits parties that establish pre-election coalitions and is supported by the leading parties within Italy's primary centre-left and centre-right groups. It will disadvantage entities wishing to operate independently, such as the 5-Star Movement. However, opinion polls suggest that the system, which combines proportional representation with first-past-the-post, is unlikely to result in a clear victor, as the vote appears to be divided among three factions: the left, the right, and 5-Star. A YouTrend poll conducted for the AGI news agency indicated on Wednesday that none of the three major parties is projected to achieve an absolute majority of seats. The survey noted that the only scenario in which this could occur would require one coalition to secure over 40 percent of the vote, which would lead to a significant shift. Currently, none of the three political entities is anticipated to gain more than 33 percent support. The 5-Star Movement has condemned the reform as an "institutional coup d'état," with its senators closing their eyes or donning blindfolds while casting "no" votes in the Senate. Hundreds of their supporters gathered in a central square in Rome to protest the legislation, shouting "honesty" and waving party banners. "This law is fraudulent for the people here. It disregards voting rights and instead benefits mergers and alliances," stated Rossano Cioccolini, a 56-year-old worker from Milan who took a day off to participate in the rally in Rome. He added, "The largest party in Italy, the 5-Star, will be sidelined because it refuses to enter alliances." The government's repeated use of confidence motions, first in the lower house and now in the Senate, has enabled the ruling centre-left coalition to limit debate regarding the bill and avoid numerous secret votes that might have allowed disenchanted lawmakers to oppose their party and disrupt the legislation. The administration maintains that the new law is essential to align the electoral processes for both the upper and lower chambers and to mitigate the risk of divergent majorities emerging in the two legislative bodies. All previous reform efforts this year have been unsuccessful. Detractors argue that the proposed legislation will empower political leaders to fill electoral lists nationwide with their most enthusiastic supporters, suppressing internal discussions within parties.

text: Republicans are opposing Trump's proposal to reduce foreign aid. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, fellow Republicans in Congress criticized President Donald Trump’s suggested reductions in the diplomatic and foreign aid budget, making it improbable that the cuts to global health, peacekeeping, and other initiatives will be implemented. Senator Lindsey Graham, who chairs the Senate subcommittee overseeing diplomacy and foreign aid expenditures, stated that Trump’s intention to slash the diplomacy and aid budget by one third would effectively "gut soft power." "If we were to adopt this budget, we would either need to withdraw from global engagement or endanger many lives," Graham informed reporters. "This budget is not going to progress." Congress holds the authority to set the federal budget, and both Republicans, who dominate both chambers, and Democrats have expressed opposition to such severe reductions. The proposed funding cuts in Trump’s plan for the fiscal year starting in October would signify a significant reduction in non-military U.S. government involvement overseas, as the administration adheres to Trump’s “America First” ideology. Officials from the Trump administration justify the cuts by asserting that other countries must contribute their “fair share” as the U.S. steps back from its historic financial commitments abroad. Overall, Trump’s proposal suggests a roughly 32 percent reduction in U.S. diplomacy and aid budgets, amounting to nearly $19 billion. The budget plan aims to decrease U.S. funding for global health initiatives, including those addressing HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria, by approximately one quarter, bringing it down to around $6.5 billion for 2018. This budget outline projects reductions to the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) program, a key component of U.S. global health aid that provides treatment, testing, and counseling for millions globally. Under Trump’s budget, PEPFAR funding would be $5 billion annually, compared to about $6 billion per year currently, according to the State Department. Officials noted that no patient currently receiving antiretroviral therapy for HIV through PEPFAR funding will lose access to that treatment. The budget proposal also entails significant reductions in support for international organizations, though it does not specify which entities may face funding losses. The NATO military alliance will continue to receive full funding. U.S. contributions to international peacekeeping efforts would drop to around $1.5 billion, representing over a 50 percent decrease from 2017 levels. The United States stands as the largest contributor to the United Nations, providing 22 percent of the $5.4 billion core budget and 28.5 percent of the $7.9 billion peacekeeping budget. "Considering the escalating threats we confront, we should be bolstering – not cutting – anti-terrorism, law enforcement, and humanitarian initiatives," stated Representative Ed Royce, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Trump’s budget would slash funding for educational and cultural exchange programs by 52 percent, including a 47 percent reduction to the Fulbright Program, which allows U.S. citizens to study abroad and attracts international students to the United States. The Trump proposal presumes that the State Department will retain its existing structure, even though Tillerson has indicated a desire to reorganize the agency and pursue efficiencies. Nonetheless, the budget introduces significant changes in certain funding areas. A primary $2.8 billion development account managed by USAID, which finances agricultural, water, sanitation, and other initiatives, would be merged with other funding sources to form the Economic Support and Development Fund. This new account would then experience a cut of approximately 45 percent compared to current funding levels.

text: Pope Francis encouraged Colombians who are doubtful about a peace agreement with guerrillas to embrace reconciliation with those who have expressed remorse, just hours after a prominent rebel leader sought the pope's forgiveness. "Dear people of Colombia: do not be afraid to ask for forgiveness and to give it," he remarked during a poignant gathering that united victims of the five-decade civil war with former guerrilla and paramilitary combatants. The Argentine pope, who leads the global Roman Catholic Church, is in Colombia promoting a message of national harmony as the nation seeks to mend the scars left by the conflict and contentious debates surrounding a peace agreement reached the previous year. Francis arrived in Villavicencio, located in Meta province, a significant cattle ranching region that was previously a center for right-wing paramilitary and Marxist guerrilla violence amid a conflict with various governments. Upon his arrival, Rodrigo Londono, the former leader of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and now the head of a new political party, penned an open letter to the pope requesting forgiveness for the pain caused by the group. "Your repeated expressions regarding God's infinite mercy inspire me to seek your forgiveness for any tears or suffering we have caused the Colombian people," Londono, who is known by the alias Timochenko, stated in the letter. Tens of thousands of enthusiastic individuals filled the roads in this humid savanna and shantytown area as the pope, seated in the front of a modest vehicle, made his way through after arriving from the capital, Bogota, on Friday morning. The pope's afternoon prayer gathering in Villavicencio with approximately 6,000 survivors of the harsh conflict was the highlight of his five-day visit to predominantly Catholic Colombia. He listened to personal stories from four individuals, including a woman who became part of a paramilitary group at the age of 16, a former FARC member, and two victims of the violence between guerrilla forces and paramilitary groups. One victim, Pastora Mira García, recounted the loss of her father, husband, and two children due to the conflict. To loud applause, she called for forgiveness to "break the cycle of violence" and expressed that she could now "name the unnamable and forgive the unforgivable." A destroyed statue of Jesus Christ, salvaged from a church that the FARC attacked in 2002 in the rainforest village of Bojaya, was displayed on the stage. Around 80 individuals were killed seeking refuge inside the modest church during rebel bombings. The plaster statue, missing arms and legs, has become a lasting symbol of the war. "As we gaze upon it, we remember not only the events of that day but also the vast suffering, the numerous deaths and shattered lives, and all the blood that has been shed in Colombia over these past decades," the pope remarked. The conflict involving right-wing paramilitary forces, Marxist rebels, and government troops since the 1960s has resulted in over 220,000 fatalities and has displaced millions. Currently, Colombians are highly divided as they prepare to integrate 7,000 former fighters, including Londono, into society. Many are outraged that under the peace deal from last year, FARC leaders accused of kidnapping and murder will evade prison sentences and may obtain congressional seats as members of a new political party. Francis addressed this reluctance directly, stating, "Undoubtedly, it is a challenge for each of us to trust that those who have caused suffering to communities and an entire nation can take a step forward. Let us heal that pain and welcome every person who has committed offenses, acknowledges their wrongdoings, is remorseful, and genuinely wishes to make amends." As he departed Villavicencio, he paused to pray at the Reconciliation Cross, a memorial dedicated to survivors and those who lost their lives during the war, and planted a tree as a symbol of peace. Earlier, Francis officiated a Mass for hundreds of thousands of attendees in a muddy field.

text: The Workers Party of Brazil officially endorses ex-president Lula. BRASILIA (Reuters) - On Saturday, Brazil's leftist Workers Party (PT) approved a resolution to formally back the candidacy of former President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, as the left in the nation continues to unite around the leader despite his corruption conviction. Lula, who previously led Brazil from 2003 to 2011 as a union leader, was sentenced in July for taking 3.7 million reais ($1.12 million) in bribes from an engineering company in return for public works contracts. A Datafolha survey published on December 2 indicated that if a presidential election were to occur today, Lula would secure at least 34 percent of the votes, which is double the backing of his closest competitor. "If they have the audacity to convict Lula, it will reveal the political nature of the whole process," read the PT resolution. ($1 = 3.29 reais)

text: (Reuters) - Just three days ahead of Puerto Rico’s Democratic presidential primary, Bernie Sanders launched a scathing critique of a restructuring bill currently advancing in the U.S. Congress and proposed a markedly different solution to address the territory’s $70 billion debt crisis. Sanders, a senator representing Vermont who is presenting a more formidable challenge to front-runner Hillary Clinton for the Democratic presidential nomination than anticipated, is set to officially present his legislation next week, according to a spokesperson on Thursday. In contrast to a bipartisan bill in the House of Representatives that aims to create a federal oversight board to renegotiate the considerable debt with creditors, Sanders’ proposal seeks to establish a “Reconstruction Finance Corporation of Puerto Rico” that would safeguard public pensioners from reductions and “concentrate losses among vulture funds,” as outlined in a summary. “It is morally reprehensible that Wall Street vulture funds are demanding that Puerto Rico fire even more teachers, close more schools, cut pensions and slash the minimum wage so that they can reap huge profits off the misery of the people of Puerto Rico,” Sanders remarked in a statement. The phrase vulture funds refers disparagingly to targeted investments in deeply discounted or distressed assets, usually bonds, acquired at low prices with the anticipation of profiting from a credit restructuring. Clinton has expressed support for the House bill. Last week, a House committee overseeing Puerto Rico approved a debt restructuring initiative that proponents aim to have enacted before July 1, when the island must fulfill $1.9 billion in debt payments. Sanders’ suggestion arrives as the presidential election nominating contests are nearing their conclusion. text: U.S. Democratic presidential hopefuls responded lukewarmly on Sunday to the possibility of former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg entering the 2016 race as an independent candidate. Bernie Sanders remarked that this would introduce another billionaire into the contest, similar to Republican Donald Trump. With just eight days remaining before Iowa conducts its inaugural nominating event leading up to the presidential election on November 8, Republican Senator Marco Rubio enjoyed the spotlight following an endorsement from the Des Moines Register, the largest newspaper in Iowa. The revelation over the weekend from a close source indicating that Bloomberg is preparing for a potential campaign, contingent on Democratic frontrunner Hillary Clinton's decline, sent shockwaves throughout the entire political landscape. Sanders, who identifies as a democratic socialist and is challenging Clinton in both Iowa and New Hampshire, stated on ABC’s "This Week" that Bloomberg’s involvement would mean a second billionaire in the race. Trump, a real estate tycoon, is currently at the forefront of the crowded Republican field. Throughout his insurgent campaign for the Democratic nomination, Sanders has criticized "millionaires and billionaires" and the influence they exert on politics. "That is not what, in my opinion, American democracy should embody, a competition among billionaires. If that occurs, I am confident that we will prevail," Sanders expressed. Numerous analysts speculate that Bloomberg’s entry could draw votes away from Democrats, representing another setback for Clinton, a former Secretary of State and spouse of ex-President Bill Clinton. A campaign as an independent would be quite challenging for Bloomberg. The last significant third-party candidate, Ross Perot, garnered 18.9 percent of the vote in 1992, which some believe allowed Bill Clinton to win against President George H.W. Bush. Hillary Clinton, who secured the Register’s endorsement on the Democratic side on Saturday, mentioned that she intends to counter Bloombergs rationale for entering the race. "He’s a good friend of mine, and I will do everything I can to secure the nomination and we’ll see what happens from there," she noted during an interview on NBC’s "Meet the Press." "From what I interpreted of his comments, he suggested that if I didn’t clinch the nomination, he would consider running. ... I will ensure that he does not need to do that," she added. Bloomberg, 73, a media mogul who has long been considering a presidential bid, was the mayor of New York from 2002 to 2013. He changed his party affiliation from Republican to independent in 2007 and has invested millions in recent years advocating for stricter U.S. gun laws and immigration reform. Trump remarked that he and Bloomberg have differing views on gun control and abortion, expressing his eagerness to compete against him. Bloomberg supports maintaining a woman’s right to choose regarding abortion. "I know Michael very well and would relish the chance to compete with him. He stands in stark contrast to me on guns and pro-life issues. ... I would be thrilled to have Michael enter the race," Trump stated during a CNN interview. Former Florida Governor Jeb Bush commented on the ABC program that Bloomberg had been an "excellent mayor," but is unlikely to enter the race unless Trump and Sanders become the nominees of their respective parties. "But that’s a long way off," Bush noted. Rubio, during a town hall gathering in Marion, Iowa, mentioned Bloomberg’s advocacy for increased gun control. He shared that he had been asked in a television interview about Bloomberg’s possible candidacy. "I said he’s not a candidate. If he decides to run, we will discuss his history and his disdain for the Second Amendment," Rubio said, referencing the constitutional amendment that protects Americans' right to bear arms. text: The leader of the New Zealand First Party, which has become the pivotal party following a weekend election that yielded no clear winner, announced on Wednesday that he would postpone any decision regarding the formation of the government until after the final vote count is released on October 7. There are still special votes to be counted, which include ballots from voters overseas and those who voted outside their home electorates, representing 15 percent of the total votes. Although these votes are not anticipated to alter the outcome, with the ruling National Party holding a solid 10-point advantage, they could potentially enhance the seat count for a prospective Labour-Green coalition, making it easier for New Zealand First to align with them, even though they did not secure the highest number of seats. "I can’t intelligently – nor can my colleagues – inform you of our course of action until we have all the facts," stated Winston Peters, the vocal leader of the New Zealand First Party, during a press briefing in Wellington. After conferring with his caucus, Peters revealed little regarding what his party might request in exchange for backing either Prime Minister Bill English or opposition Labour leader Ardern in forming a coalition government. Negotiations are anticipated to span several weeks, and those familiar with Peters suggest that the ultimate choice will rest solely with him. "No one knows what Winston Peters or NZ First will decide; at this moment, they are unsure of their next steps," tweeted Tau Henare, a former representative for both NZ First and National, on Wednesday. "But once Winston figures it out, they will have clarity." At 72, Peters, a flamboyant populist and ex-foreign minister, has a history of serving in both National and Labour administrations. In the recent election, the National Party secured 58 seats, surpassing the 52 seats won by the Green Party and Labour, leaving both still reliant on NZ First’s nine seats to achieve the necessary 61 votes to form a government. Recently, both parties have suggested they are prepared to offer Peters the deputy leadership as an incentive. Alternatively, Peters could opt for a confidence and supply arrangement, as he did in 2005, wherein New Zealand First would support vital legislation from the governing party, such as the budget, while remaining outside the cabinet. On paper, Peters aligns more closely with Labour’s policies, including immigration restrictions, and acquaintances of his indicate that he might find the prospect of serving as a senior cabinet member under relative newcomer Ardern, aged 37, appealing. He has also been critical of English’s leadership. Nevertheless, Peters has a history of siding with the party that garners the most votes during elections and has been less than favorable towards Labour’s minority partner, the Green Party. "Everything is negotiable," remarked NZ First MP Tracey Martin. "It hinges on how accommodating the National Party is willing to be, I suppose." Peters has been a member of parliament since 1978 and was associated with the National Party until he established New Zealand First in 1993. He was first recognized as a kingmaker in 1996 when he famously delayed coalition discussions the day after the election to go fishing.

text: Playing with danger: tens of thousands decline to evacuate homes near Bali volcano. KARANGASEM, Indonesia (Reuters) - Tens of thousands of residents on the Indonesian resort island of Bali are opting not to leave a 10-km (six-mile) danger zone surrounding an erupting volcano, entrusting their fate to the gods or choosing to remain to safeguard their homes and livestock. The 3,000-metre tall Mount Agung, revered as sacred by many on the Hindu-majority island, began emitting large plumes of ash over the weekend, and there have been ongoing tremors and volcanic mudflows since that time. Daily search and rescue operations in the area report that some individuals refuse to abandon their cattle, while others cite spiritual beliefs. The government has been explicit about evacuation orders, yet some individuals are hesitant to comply or prefer to stay, stated Gede Ardana, head of Bali's search and rescue agency. "We cannot compel them - but we will be held accountable, so it is necessary to persuade them." Cattle farmer Ketut Suwarte faced no dilemma about leaving. "Thick ash was falling around us, and we could detect sulfur in the air. We were frightened and decided to leave at once," said Suwarte, 47, who is currently residing in an evacuation camp just outside the danger zone. Suwarte's father recalls the last eruption of Mount Agung in 1963, which resulted in around 1,000 fatalities as pyroclastic flows - consisting of hot gas and volcanic materials - surged down the mountainside. Sutopo Purwo Nugroho from the disaster mitigation agency noted that approximately 43,000 individuals had followed advice to take refuge, but out of an estimated population of 90,000 to 100,000 in the danger zone, many had not evacuated. Ika Wardani, 33, spends the night with her family at an evacuation center but returns during the day to her cattle farm located about 10 km north of the volcano. "At least during the day we can see the volcano. However, we feel uneasy sleeping here at night because an earthquake or loud explosion could trigger panic," she explained. "We would have to ride our motorbikes at night, and the roads are narrow, so it’s safer to stay at the evacuation center overnight." She mentioned that there are individuals as close as five km from the crater who have chosen not to evacuate. "They are obstinate," she remarked. "Some of them survived the 1963 eruption, so they believe everything is fine now." The government has established radio stations and social media chat groups to alert people about the dangers. "Many individuals have chosen to remain within the exclusion zone, which is clearly very perilous," stated Sutopo Purwo Nugroho, a spokesperson for the disaster management agency. Officials also pointed out that others, including tourists, are taking unnecessary risks by attempting to capture selfies as close as possible to the volcano. Last month, a Frenchman posted a video of himself at the edge of the crater on social media. In September, when authorities first elevated the warning alert to the highest level, a 12 km exclusion zone was put in place, leading nearly 150,000 people to evacuate. However, when no significant eruption occurred, many returned, and the warning status was downgraded. When officials again raised the warning level this week, many were hesitant to relocate. "If (Mount Agung) continues its most common pattern, it is likely to escalate in explosivity, but the rate and magnitude remain uncertain," explained Dr. Carmen Solana, a volcanologist from the University of Portsmouth. On Wednesday, President Joko Widodo urged individuals to leave the exclusion zone before it becomes too late. "There must not be any casualties," he declared.

The glowing, 3,000-metre Mount Agung, considered sacred by many on the Hindu-majority island, started spewing huge columns of ash at the weekend and there have been constant tremors and volcanic mud flows since. Search and rescue teams making daily forays into the zone say some are refusing to leave their cattle unattended, while others have spiritual reasons.  The government has been clear about evacuation orders, but some people are slow to act or want to stay,  said Gede Ardana, head of Bali s search and rescue agency.
