text: From the plains to the White House: Within a Tribe's effort to halt a pipeline. CANNON BALL, N.D./WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Three days following an incident where guard dogs assaulted Native Americans protesting an oil pipeline initiative in North Dakota in early September, a historic occurrence unfolded at the White House. Brian Cladoosby, the president of the National Congress of American Indians, which advocates for over 500 tribes, addressed nearly a dozen of President Barack Obama’s Cabinet-level advisers during a meeting on September 6 of the Native American Affairs Council, which has been active for three years. This marked the first occasion that a tribal leader spoke at a council session, and Cladoosby was invited in his capacity as the leader of the Indian Congress. Cladoosby, a Swinomish Indian from Washington state, spoke two times during the one-hour roundtable discussion. He informed Reuters that he commended the Obama administration in his opening remarks for its history regarding Native American concerns, such as advocating for reforms in the Indian Health Service. However, in his closing remarks, Cladoosby made a heartfelt appeal to his listeners: to support Native Americans who have come together with the Standing Rock Sioux tribe to prevent the construction of the Dakota Access Pipeline, a 1,100-mile pipeline intended to transport oil from North Dakota to Illinois. This appeal represented one of the previously unreported pivotal moments in a situation that has unfolded since February and reached a significant turning point on September 9, when the U.S. government shifted from approving the pipeline to supporting a request from North Dakota’s Standing Rock Sioux to cease its construction. The tribe is concerned that sacred sites may be damaged during the pipeline's construction and that a potential oil spill could contaminate their drinking water. The recent victory for the tribe, which regulators could overturn, is a rare example of protests leading to swift federal response and the success of an uncommon coalition of environmentalists and Native Americans, both of whom claim they were empowered by the previous fall's defeat of the Keystone XL pipeline. Some tribal leaders stated that this was the most unifying movement in Native American politics seen in decades, as Crow, Navajo, Sioux, and other traditional rivals banded together to combat what they viewed as an attack on their lifestyle. Cladoosby did not hold a prominent role during the initial stages of the pipeline controversy. However, that day he addressed a high-ranking audience, including Secretary of the Interior Sally Jewell, director of the White House Domestic Policy Council Cecilia Munoz, and the leaders of the Departments of Energy, Agriculture, Education, Health and Human Services, and the Environmental Protection Agency, as per a senior administration official who wished to remain anonymous, as well as a photo of attendees reviewed by Reuters. "The world is watching," he stated in prepared remarks provided to Reuters. A few days prior, footage of security personnel at the pipeline in North Dakota using guard dogs and mace to disperse protesters gained widespread attention on social media. One of the initial videos was captured and shared on Facebook by Lonnie Favel, a member of Utah’s Ute tribe who journeyed to North Dakota to lend support to the protests. "I was receiving messages of encouragement from New Zealand, Europe, and all around the globe," Favel remarked. Until that moment, Obama had not publicly addressed the Dakota issue, even though he had personally visited Standing Rock in June 2014. Just one day after Cladoosby made his appeal to the administration, Obama attended a young leaders conference in Laos where a Malaysian woman inquired about the Dakota Access pipeline and how he intended to guarantee a clean water supply and safeguard ancestral land. Obama mentioned that he needed to consult with his staff for further information but praised his record of protecting Native Americans’ "ancestral lands, sacred sites, waters, and hunting grounds," adding, "this is something that I hope will continue as we move forward." In late 2014, the pipeline operator Energy Transfer Partners made a pivotal decision.

text: The struggle over President Donald Trump’s travel ban, which prohibits visitors from six mainly Muslim countries and has been halted by federal courts, is likely to escalate to the Supreme Court, where Trump’s appointee Neil Gorsuch could play a pivotal role in resolving the issue. On Thursday, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Richmond, decided not to lift an injunction imposed by a federal judge in Maryland that blocks the temporary travel ban Trump instituted on March 6. In response, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced that the administration plans to appeal to the Supreme Court. Additionally, a second federal appeals court conducted hearings on May 15 in Seattle regarding the administration's challenge to a ruling from a federal judge in Hawaii, who also blocked the ban. A decision from the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals is currently awaited. The Justice Department has yet to clarify when it will officially file its appeal or if it will wait for the 9th Circuit's ruling before proceeding. Should the case be accepted, the justices would need to determine whether courts ought to consistently defer to the president regarding the admission of certain individuals into the country, particularly when national security is cited as the rationale, as it is in this instance. They must also evaluate whether Trump’s directive contravenes the U.S. Constitution’s stipulation against government preference for one religion over another, as argued by the ban's opponents. Gorsuch’s confirmation in April by the Republican-controlled Senate, despite Democratic resistance, reinstated a 5-4 majority in the court, indicating that if all conservative justices side with the administration, the ban could be reinstated regardless of the votes from the four liberal justices. During his confirmation hearings, Gorsuch was asked about Trump’s critiques of judges who opposed the ban. He refrained from addressing the specific legal question, merely stating that he would not act as a 'rubber stamp' for any president. Although the justices could decide within the next few weeks whether to take up the case, it is likely that oral arguments would not occur until later in the year, with a ruling anticipated afterward. A conclusive resolution may not emerge until potentially a year following the issuance of Trump’s executive order. The justices are not obligated to hear the case, but it meets significant criteria noted by experts, including the fact that it involves an appeal from the federal government and pertains to a nationwide injunction. The administration might submit an emergency request aiming to implement the order while the legality of its enforcement is contested in court. For such a request to be approved, at least five justices must concur. While a 5-4 ideological division is possible, it is also conceivable that some conservative justices could align with the liberals in overturning the travel ban, as suggested by Ilya Somin, a libertarian law professor at George Mason University. He remarked, 'Conservatives in different situations often take a firm stance against any form of governmental discrimination based on race or religion, regardless of whether the intent is perceived as benign. Additionally, conservatives are concerned about government overreach into religious matters.' The 4th Circuit noted that the ban’s challengers, including refugee advocacy groups represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, are likely to prevail on their argument that the order breaches the Constitution's ban on governmental favoritism or disfavor towards any religion. In the ruling, which passed with a 10-3 vote, three judges appointed by Republicans expressed dissent. The directive from the Republican president on March 6, which replaced an earlier order from January 27 that was also blocked, mandated a 90-day prohibition on individuals from Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen while the government enhances its visa screening processes. It also called for a 120-day suspension of all refugee admissions. The opponents of the travel ban may find solace in the appeals court ruling's reliance on a concurring opinion from Justice Anthony Kennedy in a 2015 Supreme Court case concerning immigration.

text: TORONTO (Reuters) - On Tuesday, two Canadian organizations requested a court to annul a recent Quebec law that prohibits observant Muslim women from wearing a full-face veil while receiving or providing government services. The National Council for Canadian Muslims, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, and Quebec Muslim resident Marie-Michelle Lacoste have appealed to a provincial court to rule the law as invalid, contending that it discriminates against Muslim women and infringes upon the equality and freedom of religion protections established in both the Canadian and Quebec constitutions. The provincial Liberal government, which supported the legislation that was enacted on October 18, has dismissed allegations that it targets Muslim women, asserting that the prohibition on all face coverings is essential for security and to facilitate communication and the identification of individuals. The discussion has primarily centered on the niqab, a veil that covers the entire face except for the eyes, worn by a small portion of Muslim women. Critics of the legislation argue that it specifically targets a visible minority that has faced threats and violence in the predominantly French-speaking province. As of 2011, Statistics Canada reported that Quebec was home to approximately 243,000 Muslims. The government maintains that the law is constitutional and intends to defend it in court, according to Isabelle Marier St-Onge, a spokesperson for Quebec Justice Minister Stephanie Vallee, who spoke by phone on Tuesday. The law impacts teachers, police officers, hospital staff, and daycare workers within government agencies, as well as users of public services ranging from schools to mass transit systems. The groups' court submission declared that such overt and unwarranted infringements on religious freedom, alongside the equality protections of the Quebec and Canadian Charters, have no place in Quebec or Canada. Political scientist Emmett Macfarlane, who has extensively analyzed Canada's constitution and Supreme Court, indicated that the plaintiffs have a solid chance of success. 'It’s a pretty clear case, where we know who’s being adversely affected and we know it’s a distinct minority,' Macfarlane stated. In January, a gunman entered a mosque in Quebec City and fatally shot six individuals. A French-Canadian university student has been identified as the sole suspect. Other countries, including France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Bulgaria, and the German state of Bavaria, have enacted restrictions on wearing full-face veils in public areas. Denmark is also set to implement its own ban.

text: The European Union is preparing to implement an arms embargo against Venezuela and is contemplating additional sanctions due to the ongoing political turmoil in the South American nation, according to two EU diplomats. This action aligns the EU more closely with the United States, which initiated sanctions earlier this year, and indicates a shift in the EU’s stance, which had previously been hesitant to adopt a more stringent policy towards Caracas. The measures received approval today, setting the stage for endorsement by the bloc's foreign ministers next Monday, as stated by an EU diplomat, who mentioned that ministerial support is merely a formality. Spain has consistently advocated for sanctions targeting individuals associated with President Nicolas Maduro, who is accused by Washington of establishing a dictatorship; however, the EU has faced internal divisions regarding which individuals to sanction, particularly as Britain remains a prominent arms supplier to Venezuela. According to diplomats, a crucial moment for EU member states was last month’s regional elections, which seemed to favor Maduro’s ruling Socialist party. Although polls indicated that the opposition would likely secure a majority, they ultimately captured only a few governorships, as reported by the pro-government electoral board. Nonetheless, the decisions made by EU ambassadors during a Wednesday meeting merely lay the groundwork for sanctions without specifying any individuals. Travel bans and asset freezes on Venezuelan officials would only be enacted if the situation necessitates it, noted a second EU diplomat. Once finalized, the arms embargo will also include restrictions on the export of equipment that could be employed for internal repression, as well as surveillance technology, according to the diplomats. Critics have labeled it hypocritical for the EU to target Venezuela while European nations continue to sell arms to Saudi Arabia. U.S. philosopher and activist Noam Chomsky remarked, "The notion of enforcing an arms embargo on Venezuela while refusing to do the same for Saudi Arabia is absurd, especially considering Saudi Arabia’s brutal campaign in Yemen, which has resulted in one of the worst humanitarian crises globally." Chomsky added in an email to Reuters, "This is easily understood under the assumption that principles and values are merely for rhetoric, whereas what truly matters are tens of billions of dollars in arms sales." Since 2015, Saudi Arabia has been involved militarily in Yemen’s civil war, targeting Houthi militias and supporters of a former president believed to receive backing from Iran. The conflict has claimed the lives of over 10,000 individuals.

text: Google is intensifying its efforts to recruit more conservatives for its lobbying and policy department as President-elect Donald Trump organizes a technology meeting. SAN FRANCISCO/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Alphabet’s Google is striving to establish a presence in Trump's Washington after having enjoyed a notably close relationship with President Barack Obama’s administration. In the weeks following the November 8 election, Google has increased its initiatives to engage Republican lobbying firms and hire in-house lobbyists to alter the makeup of its Washington office, as reported by three lobbyists informed about the situation. Furthermore, the company has listed a job opening for a manager focused on conservative outreach and public policy collaboration, looking for a “liaison to conservative, libertarian and free market organizations.” Although this position is not a novel one, it presents Google with an opportunity to make a hire that aligns with the altered political landscape. Conservatives are already present within the office. A spokeswoman for Google opted not to provide comments for this article on the record. Alphabet’s Chief Executive Officer Larry Page is anticipated to attend a meeting on Wednesday convened by Trump, which will include leaders from some of the largest technology firms at Trump’s headquarters in New York. This assembly, organized by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, adviser Reince Priebus, and tech financier and Trump supporter Peter Thiel, is described as an introductory gathering that will not lead to any job or investment announcements, according to two sources briefed on the discussions. Other attendees will include Tim Cook, Chief Executive Officer of Apple Inc (AAPL.O), Sheryl Sandberg, Chief Operating Officer of Facebook Inc (FB.O), Jeff Bezos, CEO of Amazon.com (AMZN.O), Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla Motors Inc (TSLA.O), Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft Corp (MSFT.O), and Safra Catz, CEO of Oracle, as per sources acquainted with the meeting arrangements. The Information Technology Industry Council, a trade organization encompassing members like Google, Apple, Facebook, and Amazon, held a conference call last Friday to explore shared policy goals to propose to Trump, according to a source familiar with the call. Trump encountered conflicts with Silicon Valley on various topics during the election campaign, such as immigration, government surveillance, and encryption. His unexpected victory raised concerns among numerous companies, which worry he may act on his commitments. Trump has also expressed opposition to the “net neutrality” regulations established by the Obama administration in 2015, which aimed to reclassify broadband internet services to treat them similarly to public utilities. Reports suggest that this rule is now on track for a possible reversal. Silicon Valley, leaning liberal, heavily invested in the belief that Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton would win the presidency, and many tech firms are now scrambling in the aftermath of Trump’s election. However, Google, which cultivated strong connections with the Obama administration and was the largest corporate supporter of Clinton’s campaign, appears to have been particularly taken aback, according to those in Washington. Only 33 individuals from Google and its parent company Alphabet contributed $201 or more to Trump, amounting to a total of $23,300. In contrast, Clinton received financial support from 1,359 employees of Google or Alphabet, totaling $1.6 million. Google NetPAC, the political action committee of the company, directed 56 percent of its contributions to Republicans during the 2016 election cycle, based on data from the Center for Responsive Politics. During Obama’s time in office, more than 250 individuals transitioned between roles at Google or related entities and the federal government, national political campaigns, and Congress, as reported by the Campaign for Accountability, a watchdog organization. The company achieved several victories during the administration, including favorable net neutrality policies. Google appeared to be in a position to receive similar treatment under a Clinton administration, with Schmidt seen wearing a staff badge at Clinton’s election night celebration, indicating their close relationship.

This information was published on Tuesday by Reuters. The Journal, referencing sources familiar with the investigation, indicated that the interview took place in June or July. Special Counsel Robert Mueller is investigating claims of Russian interference in the 2016 elections, possible collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia, and whether Trump obstructed justice by terminating Comey in May. text: The U.S. government has stated that a payment made to Iran was used to facilitate the release of American detainees. On Thursday, the U.S. State Department announced that it disbursed $400 million in cash to Iran as part of a settlement with a tribunal, but only after confirming that American prisoners had been released and were on a plane. "The $400 million payment was not executed until the prisoners were freed," John Kirby, a spokesman for the State Department, informed reporters. "We utilized that opportunity to ensure we had the greatest possible leverage to secure our people's safe return," Kirby continued. This marks the first instance in which the administration has publicly confirmed that the payment was leveraged to guarantee the release of prisoners by Iran. Among the five prisoners released were Jason Rezaian, the Tehran bureau chief for the Washington Post; Saeed Abedini, an Idaho-based pastor; and Amir Hekmati, a former U.S. Marine from Flint, Michigan, along with some family members. The release was part of a prisoner swap that came after the lifting of most international sanctions against Iran, which followed a nuclear agreement established in 2015. Another detainee, Nosratollah Khosravi-Roodsari, opted to stay in Iran, while a fifth prisoner, American student Matthew Trevithick, was released on his own. Both U.S. President Barack Obama and Secretary of State John Kerry have asserted that the payment was not a ransom for the prisoners' release nor was it linked to the Iran nuclear agreement. On January 17, the White House disclosed it would be releasing $400 million in funds that had been frozen since 1981, along with $1.3 billion in interest owed to Iran, as part of a settlement concerning a long-standing Iranian claim at the Iran-U.S. Claims Tribunal in The Hague. These funds originated from a trust fund that Iran used prior to its 1979 Islamic Revolution to procure U.S. military equipment, which had been mired in litigation at the tribunal for decades. Because of international sanctions against Iran, the payment was made in cash by the United States. The administration has insisted that discussions surrounding the funds and the detainees were carried out independently and were not connected. Representative Jason Chaffetz, who chairs the House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, has requested that Kerry attend a future hearing to address the payment.

text: A federal judge in Washington ruled on Wednesday that Hillary Clinton, the Democratic presidential candidate, might need to provide testimony in a lawsuit concerning the private email server she utilized during her tenure as Secretary of State. U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan indicated that the involved parties, which include the State Department and the conservative watchdog organization Judicial Watch, reached an agreement regarding the extent of the testimonies from several of Clinton’s former senior aides in this case. These testimonies, referred to as discovery, are scheduled to occur over the next eight weeks and could potentially result in information necessitating Clinton's deposition, as stated by Sullivan in his order. Clinton has faced criticism for her use of a personal email account and server located at her residence in New York for official correspondence while serving as the nation’s top diplomat from 2009 to 2013. Detractors, including her probable Republican opponent in the presidential race, Donald Trump, argue that she jeopardized government secrets and circumvented laws regarding transparency, although the former First Lady asserts she has done nothing wrong. Judicial Watch initiated a lawsuit against the State Department to obtain records pertinent to the employment of a Clinton aide. Additionally, the Federal Bureau of Investigation is investigating her email setup. Tom Fitton, the president of Judicial Watch, remarked, "This is a very great victory for transparency and, despite the best efforts of the Obama administration and the Clinton camp, it looks like we might finally get some answers under oath about the Clintons’ illicit email system." Sullivan authorized Judicial Watch to gather testimony from close Clinton associate Huma Abedin and others. They may be questioned about the establishment and functioning of the private server, but the inquiries must be limited to "whether State conducted an adequate search" in response to Judicial Watch’s demand for the emails, as per the court's directive. It is uncommon for a judge to allow discovery to a plaintiff in a Freedom of Information Act case; however, Sullivan noted in the order that it remains uncertain whether the State Department has provided all pertinent documents to Judicial Watch.

text: Concerns are mounting over Malaysia's increasing 'Arabisation' as its relationship with Saudi Arabia strengthens. Kuala Lumpur (Reuters) - The deepening connections between Malaysia and Saudi Arabia, alongside its strict Salafi-Wahhabi Islamic principles, are facing renewed examination as fears rise regarding the dilution of traditional cultural and religious practices in the diverse nation. A series of recent incidents has intensified these worries. There has been a surge in animosity towards atheists, non-believers, and the LGBTQ+ community. Following objections from Islamic leaders, two annual beer festivals were called off. A controversial preacher, implicated in inciting hatred in India, has received official support. The government has endorsed a parliamentary proposal that would expand the shariah court's criminal jurisdiction over Muslims in the Kelantan state. Additionally, after religious authorities backed a laundromat exclusively for Muslims, Malaysia's largely ceremonial royalty intervened publicly, urging for religious harmony. Marina Mahathir, daughter of Malaysia's longest-serving prime minister, Mahathir Mohamad, has openly criticized the government for permitting the 'Arabisation' of Malaysia. Marina, who leads the civil rights organization Sisters in Islam, informed Reuters that the Saudi influence on Islam in Malaysia has been detrimental to traditional Malay culture. Her father, now 93, is currently at the helm of the opposition alliance. For decades, Saudi Arabia's extremist Wahhabi ideology has significantly impacted Malaysia and neighboring Indonesia, but this influence has notably intensified since Najib became prime minister in 2009 and nurtured closer ties with the kingdom. The relationship gained scrutiny when nearly $700 million was found in Najib's bank account in 2013. Najib claimed this was a donation from the Saudi royal family, countering accusations that it was money misappropriated from the 1MDB state investment fund he established and managed. Malaysia's attorney-general exonerated him of any misconduct. The shift towards a politicized interpretation of Islam in Malaysia, a developing middle-income market, has caused alarm among non-Muslims, particularly the ethnic Chinese, who make up a quarter of the population and dominate the private sector. This trend also raises concerns for foreign investors, who represent nearly half of the local bond market and have poured $8.95 billion into project investments in the first nine months of this year. The government refutes claims of actively endorsing Wahhabi-style Islamic conservatism. Najib has remained largely reticent about the recent religious issues. Critics have accused the prime minister, whose ruling coalition lost the popular vote in the last general election but maintained a simple majority in parliament, of exploiting anxieties that Islam and Malay political authority will diminish if the opposition prevails. An election is anticipated by mid-2018. Additionally, militancy has been escalating in Malaysia, where from 2013 to 2016, over 250 individuals with alleged connections to Islamic State were arrested, many of whom were indoctrinated with extreme interpretations of Islam. Following the Saudi monarch's visit this year, Malaysia revealed plans to establish the King Salman Centre for International Peace to unite Islamic scholars and intelligence agencies in a bid to combat extremist interpretations of Islam. The center, which will be constructed on a 16-hectare (40-acre) site in the administrative capital of Putrajaya, will utilize resources from the Saudi-funded Islamic Science University of Malaysia and the Muslim World League, a Wahhabi religious organization from Saudi Arabia. text: The UK’s highest court is seeking more precise direction from Parliament regarding its approach to rulings from the European Union following Brexit. LONDON (Reuters) - The Supreme Court of Britain desires clearer instructions from Parliament on how to handle decisions made by the European Union courts post-Brexit, as expressed by its newly appointed president on Thursday. The question of the significance, if any, of the European Court of Justice (ECJ) rulings within British law after the UK exits the European Union is among the numerous complex issues surrounding the Brexit discussions. Brenda Hale, who took office as president of the Supreme Court on Monday after a 13-year tenure as one of its justices, indicated that she and her fellow judges are in search of guidance from Parliament on this matter. "We hope that the European Union Act, once it is ultimately enacted, will clarify what our responsibilities will be—whether that means granting us the authority to consider these rulings, mandating that we must consider them, or instructing us to disregard them," she informed reporters. "Whatever Parliament decides we should do, we would appreciate being informed, as that would allow us to proceed accordingly." A government document released in August stated that the UK aims to exit the direct jurisdiction of the ECJ while also acknowledging that future civil judicial cooperation must take into account regional legal frameworks, including the ECJ. The European Union maintains that for specific matters, such as the rights of EU citizens residing in Britain, the ECJ should still play a role—an assertion firmly opposed by staunch Brexit supporters. Hale remarked that the government’s policy documents circulated during the summer were "at quite a high level of generality" and characterized them as aspirational. Nevertheless, she commended the wording used by Prime Minister Theresa May in a significant address on Brexit delivered in Florence on September 22. May expressed her desire for UK courts to be able to "take into account" ECJ rulings where there is ambiguity regarding EU law. "‘Take account’ is quite useful because it provides the authority to consider it, while also allowing the flexibility to state that, for valid reasons, we believe otherwise," Hale noted. Her deputy, Jonathan Mance, commented that the phrasing in the EU Withdrawal Bill currently being reviewed by Parliament represents "a weaker formula." The bill stipulates that British courts "need not have regard to anything done on or after exit day by the European Court ... but may do so if it considers it appropriate to do so."

text: Russia has accused the United States of training ex-Islamic State fighters in Syria, with the intention of causing instability in the region. In an interview with a newspaper, General Valery Gerasimov, the head of the Russian General Staff, made these allegations, focusing on the U.S. military installation at Tanf, which is a significant border crossing on a Syrian highway near Iraq in the southern part of the country. Russia claims that the U.S. base is unlawful and that it, along with the surrounding area, has turned into a 'black hole' where militants can operate freely. This year, the Islamic State has lost nearly all its territory in both Syria and Iraq. On Wednesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov stated that the main phase of the conflict against the Islamic State in Syria has concluded, as reported by the state-run RIA news agency. The United States, however, contends that the Tanf base is a temporary establishment meant for training allied forces to combat the Islamic State. Washington has dismissed similar accusations from Russia in the past, asserting its commitment to eliminating the Islamic State and preventing its establishment of safe havens. 'They are in reality being trained there,' Gerasimov remarked, adding that a significant number of militants and former Islamic State fighters were also present at Shadadi, where he indicated there was another U.S. base. 'They are practically Islamic State,' he asserted. 'However, after they receive training, they change their identity and assume a different name. Their objective is to disrupt the situation.' Although Russia has partially pulled back from Syria, Gerasimov indicated that Moscow's maintenance of an air base and naval facility in the region positions it well to address any emerging pockets of instability.

text: MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - A senior official announced on Thursday that Mexico has enhanced discussions with American businesses to advocate for stronger economic relations, aiming to counteract the anti-Mexican sentiments emerging from the U.S. presidential race. Donald Trump, the presumptive Republican candidate, has claimed that Mexico is harming U.S. trade, has threatened to construct a border wall to deter migrants, intends to restrict remittances sent back by Mexicans, and plans to increase tariffs on Mexico to protect American jobs. Although generally cautious in addressing Trump directly, officials from the Mexican government have cautioned that his suggested policies could inflict significant harm on the economies of both countries. Appointed in April, Paulo Carreno, Mexico’s new deputy foreign minister in charge of North America, is leading efforts to enhance Mexico's image in the United States. Since his appointment, Mexico's diplomatic channels in the U.S. have intensified outreach to business leaders, along with politicians and academics, according to Carreno, who emphasized that his government remains neutral in the presidential election. "They recognize the advantages of increased commercial integration, and they rely on it in a certain way," Carreno remarked. text: A suicide bomber from the Pakistani Taliban drove a vehicle into a police truck in the southwestern city of Quetta on Wednesday, resulting in the deaths of at least seven individuals, according to police reports. The incident claimed the lives of five police officers and two civilians on the outskirts of Quetta, as stated by police chief Abdur Razzaq Cheema. He also mentioned that 22 individuals sustained injuries, with eight in critical condition. Sarfraz Bugti, the home minister of Baluchistan province, where Quetta serves as the capital, informed Reuters that it was a suicide explosion. Quetta is located approximately 100 km (60 miles) east of the Afghan border. Bugti explained that the police truck was en route to the city to drop off officers at their respective posts when the bomber crashed into the vehicle. Images from television displayed the charred remains of the vehicles involved. The Pakistani Taliban, a coalition of various militant factions within Pakistan, which is loosely connected to the Afghan Taliban, released a statement taking responsibility for the attack. Baluchistan province has historically experienced an insurgency from separatists seeking a larger share of the region's resource wealth, which includes gas and minerals. These groups also accuse the central government of bias. In this strategically significant area, which borders both Iran and Afghanistan, the Taliban, Sunni Islamic militants, and sectarian organizations tied to al Qaeda and the Islamic State group are also active. The ongoing violence has raised alarms regarding the safety of initiatives within the $57 billion China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, a proposed transport and energy route that will connect western China to Gwadar, Pakistan's southern deep-water port. Earlier this month, a suicide bombing attributed to the Islamic State at a Sufi Muslim shrine resulted in 22 fatalities and more than 30 injuries. Ayub Qureshi, the provincial police chief, reported that a counter-terrorism officer was shot and killed in a different area of Quetta while officials were responding to the suicide blast. The militant sectarian group, Lashkar-e-Jhangvi al-Almi, took responsibility for the murder of the counter-terrorism officer and for a roadside bomb planted in a northwestern area that killed two soldiers. Security forces indicated that a remote-controlled explosive device detonated as an army vehicle passed by.

text: The White House assesses that the current nuclear threat from North Korea is manageable, according to U.S. Chief of Staff John Kelly. On Thursday, Kelly stated that the Trump administration believes that while North Korea's nuclear capabilities are a concern, it is crucial that Pyongyang does not gain the capacity to target the U.S. mainland. "A state that has developed a pretty good ICBM (missile) capability and is developing a pretty good nuclear re-entry vehicle, I would believe ... that that state simply cannot have the ability to reach the homeland," Kelly remarked. He added, "At this moment, we consider the threat to be manageable, but if it escalates beyond its current level, let’s hope that diplomatic efforts succeed," Kelly, a former Marine Corps general, concluded.
source_text: U.S. believes current North Korea nuclear threat is manageable: White House. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - White House Chief of Staff John Kelly said on Thursday the Trump administration thinks the threat posed by North Korea s nuclear weapons capability is currently manageable but Pyongyang cannot be allowed to develop the ability to strike the U.S. homeland.  A state that has developed a pretty good ICBM (missile) capability and is developing a pretty good nuclear re-entry vehicle, I would believe ... that that state simply cannot have the ability to reach the homeland,  Kelly said.  Right now we think the threat is manageable but over time if it grows beyond where it is today, well, let s hope that diplomacy works,  said Kelly, a retired Marine Corps general.

text: FBI Director Christopher Wray defended the agency's personnel on Thursday, responding to increasing accusations from Republicans, including President Donald Trump, regarding alleged political bias influencing their investigations. During his testimony before the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee, Wray expressed his belief that the FBI's reputation is not, as Trump recently claimed on Twitter, 'in tatters.' 'The agents, analysts, and staff of the FBI are grown adults. We recognize that criticism can come from all sides,' Wray stated. 'In my view, our reputation remains quite strong.' In recent weeks, Republican criticism of the FBI and Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is examining possible collusion between Trump campaign associates and Russia regarding the 2016 U.S. presidential election, has intensified. This criticism is broadly perceived as an effort to undermine Mueller's inquiry, which has to date resulted in criminal charges against four individuals close to Trump. This occurs as Republicans gear up for a potentially difficult midterm congressional election cycle in 2018. They have attempted to revisit issues surrounding the FBI’s investigation into Hillary Clinton's use of a private email server, questioning whether Justice Department officials provided her with favorable treatment by opting not to prosecute her. Additionally, they have reproached former FBI Director James Comey for publicly declaring a decision against recommending Clinton for prosecution and have inquired whether political bias influenced that decision. Wray assumed leadership of the FBI after Trump unexpectedly dismissed Comey earlier this year. Recently, Republicans obtained new grounds for criticism against Mueller and the FBI following media reports indicating that FBI agent Peter Strzok was removed from the Russia investigation due to private text messages that criticized Trump and supported Clinton. Strzok participated in both the investigations concerning Clinton's emails and the Russia inquiry. On Thursday, Wray confirmed that Strzok had been taken off Mueller’s team but clarified that he was reassigned rather than disciplined. 'We cannot allow the FBI—historically regarded as the leading law enforcement agency globally—to be compromised by politicization or the impression of a lack of impartiality,' stated Committee Chairman Bob Goodlatte. Wray consistently declined to comment on his predecessor’s management of the Clinton situation, deferring to Justice Department Inspector General Michael Horowitz, who is conducting an extensive review of the matter. Horowitz recently informed lawmakers that he anticipates completing his review by late winter or early spring. 'When those findings are presented to me, I will take appropriate action if deemed necessary,' Wray remarked. Meanwhile, Democrats urged Wray to resist pressure from the president. 'Your position demands that you have the courage to confront the president, Mr. Director,' stated the committee’s Ranking Democrat Jerrold Nadler. text: Senator Franken, addressing groping accusations, promises 'this will not occur again'. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Monday, U.S. Democratic Senator Al Franken returned to Congress to initiate what he described as a journey towards restoring trust that has been broken due to allegations of groping or inappropriate touching of women, asserting, “this will not occur again.” “I realize that I must be significantly more aware in these situations, more cautious, more attuned, and that this will not take place again moving forward,” he informed journalists outside his office on Capitol Hill. Franken faces accusations of sexual misconduct from Leann Tweeden, a radio personality who appeared with Franken in 2006 during an entertainment tour for U.S. troops deployed in conflict zones. Before securing his Senate position, Franken was a prominent comedian, television writer, and author. Another individual, Lindsay Menz, alleged that Franken touched her buttocks while they posed for a photo at the Minnesota State Fair in 2010. A remorseful Franken addressed a crowd of reporters outside his office on Monday, pledging to return to work after a week-long Senate Thanksgiving recess. “I understand that there are no magical phrases I can use to win back your trust, and I recognize that this will require time. I’m prepared to commence that journey, starting with my return to work today,” Franken stated, seemingly speaking to his constituents in Minnesota. First elected in 2008, Franken is not expected to seek a third Senate term until 2020. In the wake of sexual misconduct claims against film producer Harvey Weinstein, further allegations have surfaced concerning other prominent figures in entertainment and politics, including Republican U.S. Senate candidate Roy Moore from Alabama and Representative John Conyers from Michigan. All three individuals have denied the accusations, which Reuters has not been able to confirm, and Conyers has resigned from his role as the senior Democrat on the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee. In November 2008, Franken narrowly won the election in a contest so tight that recounts and judicial decisions were necessary before he was ultimately declared the victor the following July. Due to the narrowness of his election and his background in entertainment rather than public service, Franken entered the Senate declining most media interviews. He maintained a discreet presence as he sought to prove to his constituents that he was earnest about his political aspirations. Eight years later, Franken is once more tasked with demonstrating his commitment to Minnesotans. Acknowledging that his supporters had “relied on me to advocate for women,” Franken reiterated his apologies for his actions. When asked by a reporter, he expressed that he would be “open” to disclosing the outcomes of a Senate ethics investigation once that process is finalized.

NEW YORK (Reuters) - A group of six U.S. senators has requested President Barack Obama to make cybercrime a key focus at the upcoming Group of 20 summit in China this weekend, following the theft of $81 million from Bangladesh’s central bank, as per a letter accessed by Reuters. In a letter dispatched to the White House prior to the Sept. 4-5 summit, Sherrod Brown, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, along with five other Democratic senators, expressed their desire for the U.S. president to encourage leaders of the world's 20 largest economies to agree in joint statements to a “coordinated strategy to combat cyber-crime at critical financial institutions.” The letter, dated Monday, indicates that U.S. lawmakers are increasingly worried about the February incident when hackers infiltrated Bangladesh Bank’s systems and utilized the SWIFT banking network to request nearly $1 billion from an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Some of these requests were processed, resulting in the loss of $81 million, a significant portion of which ended up in casinos in the Philippines - leading to months of international blame, an ongoing investigation, and numerous calls from Congress members for explanations from both the Fed and SWIFT, the secure messaging service used by banks globally to transfer funds. “Our financial institutions are interconnected to facilitate global commerce, but cyber criminals - whether acting independently or sponsored by states - threaten this international system in a manner that few risks have,” the senators, led by Gary Peters of Michigan, stated in their letter to Obama. “We strongly urge you to collaborate with your counterparts and make this discussion a priority at the G20 leaders meeting in September,” the letter regarding the summit to be held in Hangzhou, China, added, stressing that “executive leadership circles around the world” must give greater attention to these risks. A senator from the Philippines has suggested that Chinese hackers were likely responsible for the Bangladesh Bank theft, referencing a network of Chinese individuals involved in funneling the stolen money through Manila. However, Beijing has rejected this assertion. Copies of the letter from the U.S. senators were also forwarded to Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen and U.S. Treasury Secretary Jack Lew. OBAMA-XI TALKS The other senators who signed the letter include Mark Warner and Martin Heinrich, both of whom are part of the Senate’s Select Committee on Intelligence; Kirsten Gillibrand and Debbie Stabenow, who is the ranking Democrat on the Senate’s Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. A senior administration official mentioned that the White House anticipates G20 members at the summit to “affirm their commitment to collaborate in the fight against cybercrime and to build confidence and trust in the digital economy.” When asked broadly about cybersecurity on Monday, White House spokesman Josh Earnest remarked during a press conference: “I would expect this issue generally to be on the agenda” when Obama meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping, the host of the G20 summit, later this week. At a summit in November, the G20 made a commitment not to engage in economically motivated cyber espionage, an agreement aimed at reducing the estimated hundreds of billions of dollars in commercial trade secrets stolen by foreign governments seeking to gain advantage for their own industries. Since then, the attack on Bangladesh Bank and other recently reported incidents are just a few examples of the threats posed by cyber criminals, according to the senators. Global regulators should “establish stronger defenses and collaborative frameworks to prevent and lessen the consequences of successful attacks,” the letter stated, pointing out that the measures already implemented by SWIFT are insufficient. Bangladesh has expressed support for raising this issue at the G20. “In most instances, cyber attacks and crimes originate from outside the country,” remarked Zunaid Ahmed Palak, a junior minister in the government for information and communications technology. “Thus, addressing the rapidly escalating cyber threats is crucial.

In the letter sent to the White House ahead of the Sept. 4-5 summit, Sherrod Brown, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, and five other Democratic senators say they want the U.S. president to press leaders from the world’s 20 biggest economies to commit in joint communiques to a “coordinated strategy to combat cyber-crime at critical financial institutions.” The letter, dated Monday, suggests that concern among U.S. lawmakers is growing over the February incident in which hackers breached Bangladesh Bank’s systems and used the SWIFT banking network to request nearly $1 billion from an account held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York

text: Mateusz Morawiecki took the oath of office as the new Prime Minister of Poland on Monday, amid ongoing tensions with the European Union. Donald Tusk, the President of the European Council, urged the new PM to work towards European unity. The Law and Justice Party (PiS), which governs Poland, is in conflict with the EU concerning various issues including immigration, logging in a historic forest, and government efforts to exert control over the judiciary and the media. Detractors argue that the policies of this eurosceptic party have undermined democracy and the rule of law. Additionally, there has been longstanding animosity between Tusk and PiS. Poland, under the direction of PiS leader and longtime Tusk opponent Jaroslaw Kaczynski, was the only one among the 28 EU nations to vote against Tusk's re-election in March. Morawiecki, aged 49, succeeds Beata Szydlo, who has now been appointed as a deputy prime minister. PiS dismissed the popular Szydlo last week in an effort to enhance Poland's reputation internationally and to prepare the conservatives for upcoming elections. Morawiecki will also retain his positions as finance minister and economy minister. All other current ministers will remain in their roles for the time being, though some changes are anticipated in the coming weeks. Morawiecki stated that his administration would carry on the initiatives of Szydlo. He is scheduled to present his policy agenda on Tuesday. Tusk, who served as Poland's prime minister prior to PiS's rise to power in 2015, expressed hope for effective collaboration. "Acting for Poland's strong position in the European Union and for the unity of all member states is the need of the moment," Tusk commented. Former Polish President Lech Walesa, a critic of PiS, remarked on Twitter: "The circus has stayed the same, only the clowns have changed their roles." Walesa was a key figure in the protests and strikes that challenged communist governance in the 1980s. Szydlo's administration was among the most favored in Poland since communism's fall in 1989, enjoying approximately 40 percent approval, attributed to low unemployment rates, an increase in public expenditure, and an emphasis on traditional Catholic principles in public life.

text: Hillary Clinton announced on Friday that she would establish an oversight committee aimed at protecting American consumers from significant price increases on long-established, life-saving medications if she is elected President. This committee would also have the authority to import alternative treatments when necessary, furthering her commitment to control overall drug costs. The Democratic presidential candidate intends to equip this panel with a "robust new set of enforcement mechanisms," which would include the power to impose fines and penalties on pharmaceutical companies that enact an "unjustified, outlier price increase" on generic or long-available drugs, as stated by her campaign. "In the past year, we’ve witnessed too many instances of pharmaceutical companies excessively raising prices on long-standing, life-saving treatments without any new innovation or research and development," Clinton remarked in her statement. Should Clinton prevail over Republican opponent Donald Trump in the election on November 8, she would require the backing of the U.S. Congress to execute critical aspects of her proposal, which is an extension of a broader initiative to control drug prices that she introduced a year earlier. Morningstar analyst Damien Conover indicated that while her latest plan may impact a limited number of firms, gaining Republican lawmakers' support could prove challenging, noting that a "Republican Congress would strongly oppose this." Clinton’s campaign pointed to Turing Pharmaceuticals LLC’s increase in the price of its AIDS medication Daraprim (pyrimethamine) and Mylan NV’s repeated substantial price hikes on EpiPen for severe allergy patients as "concerning" instances of price increases that have drawn bipartisan attention from Congress. Conover mentioned that Clinton’s approach to tackling unjustified price increases poses less of a threat to the pharmaceutical industry compared to her previous commitment to overall drug price reductions. Pharmaceutical companies have argued that lowering or capping drug prices would restrict their capacity to invest in research, resulting in fewer new therapies. The ARCA Pharmaceutical Index, which tracks major U.S. and European drug manufacturers, rose by 0.30 percent on Friday, mirroring the broader stock market's gains. Mylan's shares dropped by 4.6 percent to $40.00 on the Nasdaq, while the Nasdaq biotech index fell by 0.40 percent. This decline was minimal compared to the over 4.7 percent fall in the index recorded on September 21, 2015, when Clinton criticized "price gouging" in the specialty drug sector on Twitter, in response to reports that Turing had acquired Daraprim, an established antibiotic, and subsequently raised its price by 5,000 percent. Shortly after, Clinton unveiled a comprehensive strategy to reduce prescription drug expenses, including allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices and requiring higher rebates for prescription medications. Her initiative would also impose caps on monthly and annual out-of-pocket expenses for patients suffering from chronic or severe health issues. It aims to prevent manufacturers from compensating generic drug producers to postpone the introduction of their more affordable alternatives and would abolish corporate deductions for direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical marketing. Dr. Peter Bach, director of a nonpartisan health policy research organization at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, commented that Clinton’s announcement on Friday serves as a "signal" to drug manufacturers that her administration would be vigilant and responsive to significant price increases. "It’s a reaction to the wider industry trend of generating extra profits by elevating drug prices for which there is no competition," Bach stated, noting that the campaign is targeting a "sub-category" of manufacturers that have not heavily invested in drug development. Bach revealed that he was contacted by the Clinton campaign regarding his research on drug pricing but had not formally advised the campaign.

text: Saudi King Salman dismissed several high-ranking ministers on Saturday, assigning two new officials to critical security and economic roles, while also elevating the power of the young crown prince. The king declared the establishment of a new anti-corruption committee led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, which Al Arabiya TV reported has already apprehended 11 princes, four sitting ministers, and numerous former ministers, although the identities of the suspects were not disclosed. The reshuffle in the cabinet resulted in Prince Miteb bin Abdullah being succeeded by Khaled bin Ayyaf as the head of the National Guard, with Economy Minister Adel Fakieh being replaced by his deputy Mohammed al-Tuwaijri, as stated in a royal decree reported by state media. Prince Miteb, who was the favored son of the late King Abdullah, had been considered a leading candidate for the throne prior to the unexpected ascent of Prince Mohammed two years ago. He inherited leadership of the National Guard, an elite internal security force created from traditional tribal units, from his father, who managed it for fifty years. Prince Miteb was the last representative from Abdullah’s branch of the family to occupy a role within the upper tiers of Saudi Arabia's governance. This action further strengthens Crown Prince Mohammed's dominance over the kingdom's security apparatus, which has historically been overseen by distinct powerful factions within the ruling family. Prince Mohammed, the 32-year-old son of the king, is also the defense minister and was appointed as heir to the throne in a reshuffle in June that marginalized his older cousin, Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, who had previously held the role of interior minister. He has concurrently managed Saudi Arabia's military engagement in Yemen, shaped energy policies with global significance, and spearheaded initiatives for the kingdom's post-oil future. Crown Prince Mohammed, committed to combating corruption at the highest levels, will now also lead the new anti-corruption agency, which has been granted extensive authority to investigate cases, issue arrest warrants, impose travel bans, and freeze assets. "The homeland will not exist unless corruption is eradicated and the corrupt are held accountable," stated the royal decree. The newly appointed economy minister, Tuwaijri, is a former pilot in the Saudi air force and the ex-CEO of HSBC's operations in the Middle East, who has overseen the ministry's efforts to privatize around $200 billion of government assets. He takes over from Fakieh, who had been the key figure in the kingdom’s extensive economic reforms since his appointment as economy and planning minister in 2015. A former executive in the food industry known for implementing politically sensitive reforms, Fakieh had previously held positions as labor minister, health minister, and mayor of Jeddah. He faced significant resistance from the business sector during his tenure as labor minister when he introduced quotas for foreign workers to create job opportunities for Saudis. Under Prince Mohammed's guidance, Fakieh contributed to the creation of a national transformation plan and a privatization initiative launched last year to reduce the kingdom’s dependence on a fluctuating oil market. His replacement coincides with the kingdom’s modifications to that plan, a process referred to as NTP 2.0. The royal decree did not indicate if Fakieh would assume any other governmental role. Former ministers frequently take on advisory capacities after leaving their positions.

Lebanese Prime Minister Saad al-Hariri announced his resignation during a speech delivered from Saudi Arabia on Saturday and has not yet returned to Lebanon. In his televised speech, Nasrallah expressed his belief that Hariri is being held in Riyadh.

text: The Kremlin indicated on Wednesday that it is receiving mixed messages from the White House regarding the new sanctions on Russia that have been sanctioned by the U.S. Congress. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson mentioned that both he and President Donald Trump do not think the new sanctions would "be helpful to our efforts" in terms of diplomatic relations with Russia. However, the White House has also stated that Trump plans to enact the sanctions into law. When asked about Tillerson’s remarks, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov informed reporters: "We have not heard such statements. We observe that there is a certain inconsistency in the messages coming from the White House." He added, "Undoubtedly, it’s significant that the President of the United States is considering the current situation and the future of bilateral relations."

text: Republicans in the U.S. Senate are aiming to accelerate the confirmation of nominees put forth by President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, prominent Senate Republicans voiced their dissatisfaction regarding the sluggish pace of confirmations and proposed modifications to the Senate's procedures to hasten the approval process. "I think it is time to amend the Senate rules," remarked John Barrasso, Chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, while addressing the media, insisting that a method must be established to reduce debate durations. Trump has vocally criticized Senate regulations that impede the advancement of his agenda. Nevertheless, he has primarily targeted a specific Senate rule that necessitates 60 votes for the majority of legislation to progress in the 100-member Senate, known as the filibuster rule. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell asserted that Republicans are not inclined to alter the 60-vote requirement for legislative matters. However, following Barrasso's comments on Tuesday, McConnell indicated that there might be a possibility to decrease the time allocated for debates on judicial and other nominees once they pass an initial stage. At present, this debate time is limited to 30 hours. Republicans have consistently expressed concerns that Democrats are exploiting this time limit to prolong the confirmation of Trump's nominees. "Because of the Democrats’ obstruction, this administration has seen the lowest percentage of confirmed nominees of any administration in the last 30 years," Barrasso stated in a press release. At this same point during the term of Democratic President Bill Clinton, 76 percent of his nominees had been confirmed, and 67 percent of nominees for Democratic President Barack Obama had received confirmation, whereas Trump has managed to secure confirmations for less than 40 percent, according to Barrasso. He proposed that the Senate might consider reinstating a bipartisan agreement from a prior Congress, which permitted debate on Supreme Court nominees and Cabinet members to extend up to 30 hours, while other categories of nominees were allotted shorter periods: either eight or two hours. Two other prominent Republicans, Senators John Cornyn and Roy Blunt, indicated that Republicans could unilaterally amend the rules if the Democrats show no willingness to negotiate a change. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer evaded a question on the issue. "Senator McConnell does not approach the floor with a clean slate regarding these matters. He postponed and obstructed numerous Obama nominees; in fact, many of the judges currently being appointed should have been filled by Obama’s nominees," Schumer told reporters. Earlier this year, McConnell took steps to eliminate the 60-vote barrier on Supreme Court nominations to facilitate the confirmation of Neil Gorsuch to the court. Previously, when Democrats controlled the Senate, they abolished the 60-vote requirement for other executive branch nominations.

text: Timeline: Europe's lengthy pursuit of a unified defense. BRUSSELS (Reuters) - On Monday, France, Germany, and 21 other EU nations entered into a defense agreement, aspiring to usher in a new phase of enhanced military integration in Europe following Britain's exit from the union. Below is a chronology of milestones in European defense collaboration: 1949 - The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), a military alliance led by the United States, is established by the United States, Canada, and various European nations. 1950 - A proposal for the European Defence Community emerges as a continental counterpart to NATO, intending to include West Germany and establish a European army, a collective budget, and shared weaponry. 1954 - The French parliament votes against the European Army initiative. Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Britain create the Western European Union, a defensive coalition featuring a unified air force and shared command structure. 1993 - The Maastricht Treaty of the EU redefines the course of European integration and introduces a Common Foreign and Security Policy as one of its objectives, enabling European nations to act collectively in foreign affairs. 1998 - Britain and France reach an agreement on shared defense in the Saint-Malo Declaration, with London committing to play a pivotal role in the European Union's security and defense strategy. 2003 - The European Union initiates its inaugural independent military operation outside of Europe, Operation Artemis, with support from the United Nations, aimed at the Democratic Republic of the Congo. 2004 - Establishment of the European Defence Agency occurs to assist EU nations in enhancing their military capabilities. 2007 - Approximately 1,500 soldiers are organized into rapid-reaction forces known as EU Battlegroups, operating under the Council of the European Union's authority. However, these forces are never deployed. 2009 - The Lisbon Treaty bolsters the Common Foreign and Security Policy within the EU, leading to the establishment of a foreign policy chief. 2011 - France and Britain spearhead efforts to remove Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, yet are unable to enforce a no-fly zone without U.S. aircraft and munitions. 2017 - Over 20 EU nations sign a defense agreement aimed at integrating military planning, weapons development, and operations, underpinned by a defense fund valued at 5 billion euros ($5.83 billion).

text: Turkey expressed its dismay on Tuesday regarding the U.S. Department of Defense's position concerning an agreement between the Islamic State and the Syrian Kurdish YPG militia for the withdrawal of Islamic State fighters from Raqqa, Syria. A spokesperson for the YPG had indicated last month that Syrian Islamic State fighters were preparing to leave Raqqa under a deal made with U.S.-supported Syrian militias. A BBC report on Sunday indicated that approximately 4,000 individuals, including many foreign nationals, had been evacuated from Raqqa as part of this agreement, spreading across Syria and extending to Turkey. Turkey's Foreign Ministry stated that it was shocking that representatives from the international coalition against the Islamic State and the U.S. Department of Defense had neither refuted the existence of the agreement nor condemned it, but rather indicated they respected it. Ankara has been angered by Washington's backing of the YPG, which Turks view as a branch of the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), a group that has waged a long-standing insurgency in Turkey and is classified as a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States, and the European Union. The ministry labeled the exit of Islamic State militants from Raqqa as 'extremely troubling' and suggested it was a situation that 'should be noted.' The ministry added that this agreement serves as an illustration of how, when engaging with a terrorist organization, such groups may ultimately choose to collaborate with one another. Following the capture of Raqqa by the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) in October, Syria's military last week announced its triumph over the Islamic State, asserting that its takeover of the jihadists' last stronghold in Albu Kamal signified the end of their three-year hardline rule in the area.

text: Allied nations express outrage over Trump's remarks on Virginia violence. BERLIN/LONDON (Reuters) - On Wednesday, leaders from America’s closest allies issued strong and personal condemnations of U.S. President Donald Trump after he attributed some responsibility for the violent confrontations in Virginia to those protesting against armed neo-Nazis. British Prime Minister Theresa May, who has faced criticism domestically for nurturing a close relationship with Trump during his initial months in office, spoke out following the president's reiteration of his belief that both the white nationalists and counter-demonstrators share blame. "There is no equivalence; I see no equivalence between those who advocate fascist ideologies and those who oppose them, and it is crucial for all individuals in positions of authority to denounce far-right ideologies whenever we encounter them," May stated. text: THE HAGUE (Reuters) - On Friday, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court announced her intention to request authorization for a formal inquiry into claims of war crimes in Afghanistan, a case that may scrutinize the involvement of U.S. forces abroad. Fatou Bensouda stated in her announcement that there exists a reasonable basis to believe that war crimes and crimes against humanity have occurred, and that all parties involved in the conflict would be investigated. The focus of the prosecutor will be on offenses allegedly committed in Afghanistan since May 2003, as well as war crimes that are closely related to the situation in Afghanistan and allegedly committed in other countries since July 2002. The prosecutor did not specify any particular parties to be investigated on Friday. In a report released last year, ICC prosecutors highlighted potential cases involving three groups of alleged offenders: the Taliban and its affiliates, the Afghan authorities, and personnel from the U.S. armed forces and the Central Intelligence Agency. The report indicated there are preliminary grounds to suspect that U.S. forces committed war crimes in Afghanistan and at CIA detention sites elsewhere during 2003 and 2004. The alleged incidents occurred across all 34 provinces of Afghanistan, with a lesser number of offenses reported in Poland, Lithuania, and Romania, where suspected Taliban or Al Qaeda members were interrogated. Should the court's judges grant authorization, the prosecutors will conduct an investigation in an independent, impartial, and objective manner, focusing on crimes within the court's jurisdiction allegedly perpetrated by any participant in the armed conflict. The primary emphasis will be on those deemed most responsible for the gravest offenses, as noted in her statement. Established in 2002, the ICC serves as the world’s permanent tribunal for prosecuting the most serious war crimes, including genocide. It is supported by the European Union and numerous countries; however, several of the globe's most influential nations—especially the United States, Russia, and China—have never joined. Initial U.S. administrations voiced opposition to the court's creation, expressing concerns that American military personnel could face politically motivated prosecutions, although they later supported specific investigations. The ICC acts as a court of last resort, stepping in only when a national government is found unwilling or unable to prosecute. Its jurisdiction is restricted to crimes committed on the territory of member states or those referred to it by the U.N. Security Council, as occurred with Sudan regarding alleged genocide in Darfur in 2005. Nevertheless, crimes committed on the soil of member states by soldiers from non-member countries also fall within the court's jurisdiction under international law. A state may avoid having a case brought to The Hague if it can demonstrate that it has investigated and prosecuted the same crimes the ICC is examining. In a 2016 report concerning the preliminary examination of alleged crimes in Afghanistan, the prosecutor remarked that while the U.S. Department of Justice examined allegations of mistreatment of CIA detainees between 2009 and 2011, the investigation's scope was limited and two cases did not lead to prosecution.

text: Exiled Egyptian presidential candidate intends to return in the upcoming weeks: family. CAIRO (Reuters) - The most formidable potential opponent to Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi in the 2018 election aims to come back from exile soon, his daughter disclosed on Friday. Ahmed Shafik, a former air force leader and government official, announced earlier this week from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where he currently resides, that he plans to run for president. His daughter, May Shafik, informed Reuters on Friday that he was getting ready to leave, first heading to Europe and the United States. After that, he will return to Egypt to kick off his presidential campaign, she stated. Shafik had been barred from leaving the UAE in prior days but has now received guarantees that he can travel without restrictions, she mentioned, although she did not specify who provided those guarantees. The UAE refuted claims of imposing any travel limitations on Shafik, following a video aired by the Qatari-owned television channel Al Jazeera, in which he stated he had been prevented from traveling. May Shafik remarked that there was no plan to broadcast that video, and it had been leaked to Al Jazeera. She clarified that the video was recorded as a precaution. The UAE is a supporter of Sisi’s administration, which has remained officially silent regarding Shafik’s announcement of his candidacy. However, several commentators on Egyptian television have expressed opposition to Shafik, signaling the challenges he may encounter from state-associated media. Shafik represents the most significant potential adversary to Sisi thus far, who is anticipated to pursue a second term, although he has yet to declare his intentions to run. Sisi, as a military leader, was instrumental in the removal of former president Mohamed Mursi of the Muslim Brotherhood in 2013, before winning his own decisive election a year later. Supporters of Sisi view him as essential for maintaining stability following the prolonged and violent unrest that ensued after the 2011 Egyptian uprising that ousted president Hosni Mubarak. Sisi's government is currently combating an Islamist militant insurgency in the Sinai Peninsula and has implemented severe austerity measures over the past year, which critics argue have diminished his popularity. Shafik, who served as a minister under Mubarak, narrowly lost to Mursi in Egypt's 2012 election before escaping abroad.

text: Canadian authorities are looking into the unexplained deaths of billionaire pharmaceutical entrepreneurs Barry Sherman, who established Apotex Inc., and his spouse Honey. Their remains were discovered in their Toronto home on Friday. On Saturday, officials began conducting post-mortem examinations and are treating the fatalities as suspicious. A spokesperson for the Toronto Police indicated that no possibilities have been excluded in the investigation. Two Canadian publications reported that law enforcement is examining the case as a potential murder-suicide, referencing unnamed police sources. According to the Globe and Mail and the Toronto Sun, the bodies were discovered suspended from a railing near a basement swimming pool, as per police sources. The reports suggested that investigators are considering the hypothesis that Barry Sherman, aged 75, murdered his wife, hung her body, and subsequently took his own life at the pool's edge. Apotex issued a statement on Saturday expressing that the Sherman family was unsettled by the reports. "We are astonished and believe it’s irresponsible that police sources have purportedly informed the media of a theory that neither their family, friends, nor colleagues accept as true," stated the message attributed to Barry and Honey Sherman’s family. "We call upon the Toronto Police Service to carry out a comprehensive, thorough, and unbiased criminal investigation, and we encourage the media to refrain from further speculation regarding the reasons behind these tragic deaths until the investigation concludes," it continued. Toronto Police Constable David Hopkinson remarked that authorities are pending results from the post-mortem examinations, and no conclusions have been reached concerning the cause and manner of death. "There are numerous possibilities here. We are not dismissing any scenarios," he remarked. Approximately twelve police officers were seen interviewing neighbors for insights into the case on Saturday, while a forensic photographer captured images of the snow-covered property. The incidents have sent shockwaves through Canada’s political, business, and philanthropic circles, eliciting an outpouring of condolences from various business leaders and politicians, including Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. Barry Sherman was a significant benefactor to Canada’s governing Liberal Party, drawing from a wealth estimated by Forbes at $3.2 billion. The Canadian advocacy organization Democracy Watch criticized him last year for participating in a fundraiser for the Liberals while registered as a government lobbyist. Sherman founded the generic drug company Apotex in 1974, transforming it into one of the largest pharmaceutical enterprises globally. According to its website, the company generates annual revenues exceeding C$2 billion across more than 45 nations. He resigned as CEO in 2012 but continued to serve as chairman. Sherman was embroiled in multiple lawsuits, including a prolonged legal dispute with cousins who claimed he excluded them from the company that generated his wealth. Police became aware of the Shermans' deaths around midday on Friday in response to an emergency call. Authorities have yet to disclose who initiated the call, although Canadian media outlets reported that a real estate agent, who was assisting them in selling their home listed at C$6.9 million ($5.4 million), discovered their bodies. The real estate agent was unavailable for comment. The Shermans, parents to four children, contributed significantly to hospitals, universities, and Jewish organizations. Honey Sherman was a member of several boards for hospitals, charitable entities, and Jewish foundations, and she received a Senate medal for community service last month.
