text: Rainbow raids: Egypt initiates its broadest anti-gay crackdown to date. CAIRO (Reuters) - Sarah Hegazy has been imprisoned, assaulted by fellow inmates, and may face life imprisonment in an Egyptian jail if convicted of promoting sexual deviancy and other allegations related to her supposed offense: displaying a rainbow flag at a concert. The 28-year-old asserts she did not wave the flag but is among 57 individuals apprehended thus far in Egypt's most extensive anti-gay operation, a rapid zero-tolerance reaction to an uncommon public demonstration of support for lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) rights in the conservative Muslim nation. This crackdown occurs as Egypt, a vital Western ally in the Middle East, faces criticism over its human rights practices, with the United States withholding a portion of its $1.3 billion in annual military assistance. Hegazy, the sole woman captured in this three-week-long campaign, claims that police incited her fellow inmates to mistreat her during her initial night in custody, where she is held for 15 days and interrogated by special prosecutors typically focused on Islamist extremists. "This is the game they (police) always play, especially since she is a girl. They incite the other detainees and say this girl wants men and women to be gay so they harass her. I saw scratches on her shoulder; she appeared very disheveled and exhausted. She was beaten," stated Hegazy's attorney, Hoda Nasralla. A security official declined to comment on Hegazy's situation but refuted claims that police incite prisoners against one another or mistreat them in any manner. Legal representatives for other detainees indicated that their clients experienced similar treatment. Suspected gay male detainees are subjected to forced anal examinations to ascertain if they have engaged in homosexual acts, a procedure that human rights organizations argue constitutes torture. According to Amnesty International, at least five such examinations have been conducted. Judicial sources acknowledge that these examinations occur but assert they are conducted legally and do not constitute abuse. Egyptian authorities do not deny targeting homosexuals, and a report from the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR) shared with Reuters explicitly describes the police's campaign against homosexuals. Police, state-affiliated media, and the religious establishment all regard it as their public duty to combat the proliferation of homosexuality. Ten men have already been tried during this recent sweep and received prison sentences ranging from one to six years. On September 22, at a concert attended by 30,000 people featuring Mashrou Leila, a Lebanese alternative rock band with an openly gay lead singer, a small group of attendees displayed a rainbow flag, and within hours, the image went viral. Almost instantly, local media, primarily dominated by state-aligned television figures, launched a campaign against homosexuals, alleging they were receiving foreign support, and hosting callers who equated their threat to that of the Islamic State. Egypt's media regulator subsequently prohibited homosexuals from appearing in the media unless they were expressing repentance, labeling homosexuality a "shame and a disease that should be kept under wraps, not promoted" to safeguard public morality. Al-Azhar, Egypt's 1,000-year-old center for Islamic scholarship, declared it would oppose gays in the same manner it opposes Islamist extremists. One church organized an anti-gay conference. Public Prosecutor Nabil Sadek instructed the State Security Prosecution, which typically investigates terrorism and other national security issues, to probe the flag incident. At least four individuals, including Hegazy and 21-year-old Ahmed Alaa, were arrested for allegedly displaying the flag, although one man has since been released. However, the vast majority of those apprehended are not connected to the flag incident and have simply been detained based on their perceived sexual orientation in the ensuing days. Police have conducted raids on residences, parties, and utilized online dating applications to ensnare gay men—a common strategy in Egypt—to arrest many of them, according to their attorneys. In a Cairo courthouse, defendants were seen standing within a cage.

text: UNITED NATIONS (Reuters) - On Monday, the Democratic Republic of Congo was elected as one of 15 nations to serve a three-year term on the United Nations Human Rights Council, a development that has drawn criticism from Britain, the United States, and various human rights organizations following the vote by the 193-member General Assembly. Although Congo was elected unopposed to the 47-member council based in Geneva, it still required majority backing, securing 151 votes. The nation has been facing a resurgence of political and militia-related violence since President Joseph Kabila opted not to resign in December. British U.N. Ambassador Matthew Rycroft expressed disappointment on Twitter, stating, "What happened in DRC last year makes their election to the Human Rights council entirely disappointing." U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley, who has advocated for competitive voting within the Human Rights Council, remarked that Congo's entry undermines the council's credibility. "Countries that aggressively violate human rights at home should not be in a position to guard the human rights of others," Haley noted in a statement. The United States is currently reassessing its participation in the council. Although it is in the first year of a second term, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has called for reforms to address what it describes as a persistent anti-Israel bias. Alongside Congo, countries such as Angola, Senegal, Slovakia, Ukraine, Chile, Mexico, Peru, Afghanistan, Nepal, Pakistan, Australia, and Spain were also elected to the council on Monday, while Nigeria and Qatar secured second terms. Their terms are set to commence on January 1, 2018. To guarantee geographical representation, countries are categorized into five regional groups for nominations. Four of these categories had uncontested slates, whereas there were five candidates vying for four seats in the Asia Pacific region, in which Malaysia was unsuccessful. Members of the council are restricted to a maximum of two consecutive terms. The council has the authority to reprimand governments it identifies as violating human rights and to initiate investigations. Human Rights Watch has called for competitive elections. Louis Charbonneau, U.N. director at Human Rights Watch, stated, "The Democratic Republic of Congo's election to the Human Rights Council is a slap in the face to the many victims of the Congolese government’s grave abuses across the country." Over the past year, violence in eastern and central Congo has displaced more than 1.5 million people, reigniting fears of civil war in a nation where conflicts from 1996 to 2003 resulted in millions of fatalities and the emergence of numerous armed groups that exploit local populations and natural resources.

text: U.S. agency to open protest areas during Trump inauguration. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A significant federal land agency announced on Thursday that demonstrators will have access to public spaces for protests during Republican Donald Trump’s presidential inauguration, following threats of legal action from civil rights attorneys who claimed it was suppressing dissent. As many as 900,000 individuals are anticipated to descend upon the U.S. capital for the New York businessman's swearing-in ceremony on January 20, marking his entry into his first political office. Some individuals plan to voice their opposition to Trump's more contentious proposals, such as the intention to construct a wall along the Mexican border and to deport undocumented immigrants. Out of more than 30 organizations aiming to hold rallies either opposing or celebrating Trump’s election independently of the Trump Presidential Inaugural Committee, only three have been granted permits to utilize National Park Service land before, during, or after the inauguration. The agency indicated that it would start issuing permits for protest locations on park property in the upcoming days, a statement that followed shortly after the Partnership for Civil Justice Fund announced it would file a lawsuit if the permits were not released by Friday. "We view this as a significant win for free expression. They are acting under the pressure of a lawsuit," said Mara Verheyden-Hilliard, the fund’s executive director, in a phone conversation. The Park Service had asserted that it was adhering to a procedure established in 2008 by transferring control of locations, including those along the parade route from the Capitol to the White House, to Trump’s Presidential Inaugural Committee. Agency spokesperson Mike Litterst stated that the Park Service would regain authority over permits for the Ellipse, a park area located south of the White House, from the inaugural committee on January 21. Litterst mentioned in an email that the agency was collaborating with over 30 applicants for permits and was still accepting requests. The Park Service has been under a court mandate since 2008 requiring it to ensure free speech during presidential inaugurations. Three progressive organizations, the ANSWER Coalition, the American Constitution Society, and the Black is Back Coalition, have been authorized to hold events near the parade route, but only ANSWER received a permit for Inauguration Day, according to the Park Service permits website. Approximately 3,000 police officers and 7,000 National Guard personnel from outside the District are expected to be present to assist with security during Trump’s swearing-in, as stated by Chris Geldart, the District of Columbia’s homeland security director, in a phone interview. The largest inauguration protest, the Women’s March on Washington scheduled for January 21, will proceed regardless of the ongoing dispute regarding protest areas, as it will take place on city streets. At least one demonstration may be accompanied by marijuana smoke, as the DCMJ pro-cannabis lobbying organization, which led the campaign for the drug's legalization in Washington D.C. in 2015, intends to distribute 4,200 joints near the inauguration site. Consuming marijuana along the parade route would violate both District of Columbia laws - which permit it only in private settings - and federal regulations, which prohibit it entirely.

text: Rohingya Muslims facing persecution escape violence in Myanmar. (Reuters) - The assaults carried out by Rohingya Muslim militants against Myanmar's security forces in Rakhine State prompted a military response along with brutal actions from Buddhist vigilantes, so severe that a high-ranking U.N. official condemned it as a clear case of ethnic cleansing. In the days, weeks, and months following the violence on August 25, over 600,000 Rohingya sought refuge in Muslim-majority Bangladesh, traversing mountains and navigating through forests and rice fields flooded by monsoon rains. Many of the fleeing individuals were traumatized, fatigued, and starving, with some suffering from bullet, knife, or club wounds, and others bearing burns. Numerous women reported having been raped. All refugees recounted experiences of a violent campaign involving killings and arson perpetrated by Myanmar's security forces and Buddhist civilians, actions they believed were aimed at forcing them out of the country. The predominantly Buddhist nation of Myanmar refutes these allegations. (To view a photo essay on the Rohingya refugee situation, click on reut.rs/2jc8rZe.) Myanmar claims that the group behind the August 25 assaults on around 30 security posts and an army camp, known as the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, are terrorists and asserts that they were responsible for the majority of the violence and fires that turned numerous Rohingya villages nestled in lush green rice fields into ashes. The Rohingya have historically endured discrimination and oppression in Rakhine State, where a longstanding animosity with ethnic Rakhine Buddhists, resulting from reciprocal violence, has persisted for generations. The Rohingya are not recognized as an indigenous ethnic minority in Myanmar; the government even refuses to acknowledge the term Rohingya, instead categorizing them as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. Most Rohingya have been denied citizenship due to a law that ties nationality to ethnicity. They have lived under conditions resembling apartheid, with minimal access to the limited educational and employment opportunities available to their Buddhist neighbors in one of Myanmar's poorest areas. Prior to the recent violence, it was estimated that about one million Rohingya were residing in Rakhine State. Bangladesh already housed 400,000 Rohingya who had escaped prior repression. The new arrivals, many reaching by boat after being transported across a river at the border, crowded into existing refugee camps in the Cox's Bazar district, with many setting up makeshift shelters in the rain— fortunate ones managing to secure a piece of plastic—next to muddy paths. Initially, Bangladesh, one of the world's most impoverished and densely populated countries, declared that the Rohingya were unwelcome and instructed border guards to turn them away. However, it swiftly reversed its position in light of the magnitude of the exodus and began preparing, with assistance from U.N. and other aid organizations, to handle what has become the fastest-growing refugee crisis the world has witnessed in years. This crisis has raised serious questions about Myanmar's transition from a military-ruled pariah state to a developing democracy and about the commitment to human rights of its democratic leader, Aung San Suu Kyi, who has worked to end nearly five decades of oppressive military governance. The military retains complete authority over security under a constitution they created, even though Suu Kyi leads the government. Analysts suggest that Suu Kyi must tread carefully to avoid provoking the military and alienating her supporters by appearing to advocate for a Muslim minority that garners little sympathy in a nation experiencing a rise in Buddhist nationalism. Nonetheless, the Nobel laureate's failure to vocally defend the Rohingya has seemingly irreparably harmed her reputation abroad. The global community is insisting that the Rohingya be allowed to return home safely, and discussions between Bangladesh and Myanmar regarding repatriation have commenced, yet substantial doubts linger regarding the Rohingya's ability to return peacefully to restore their homes and cultivate their fields.

text: Mexico is not a 'back door' for Chinese products entering the United States, according to Mexican Economy Secretary Ildefonso Guajardo. In a live interview on CNBC on Tuesday, Guajardo acknowledged that the rules of origin under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) could be enhanced, but he refuted the notion that Mexico serves as a conduit for Chinese goods. He expressed optimism that there are opportunities to renegotiate NAFTA in a way that would be advantageous for the United States, Canada, and Mexico. However, he noted that Mexico's 'Plan B' would involve reverting to the World Trade Organization's tariff rates for exports to the U.S., such as the 2.5 percent tariff applied to passenger vehicles. 'Clearly, it’s a bit more expensive, but it’s not the end of the world,' he remarked. Guajardo pointed out that the proportion of Chinese content in vehicles traded among North American nations is minimal, approximately 3 percent, mostly consisting of components that are no longer manufactured in the area, like flat panel display screens and various electronic products. 'The concept that Mexico is being exploited as a back door for Chinese imports into the U.S. is incorrect,' he stated. According to the existing NAFTA framework, motor vehicles are required to contain 62.5 percent North American content, a threshold that U.S. Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross has indicated is insufficient and permits excessive content from outside regions to qualify for NAFTA's tariff-free advantages. Guajardo cautioned that excessively increasing the requirements for North American content could diminish the region's competitiveness. 'We can certainly strive to enhance that, no doubt about it. But if taken too far, it could backfire, as it would lead to a loss of competitiveness,' he commented. Discussions to update the 23-year-old NAFTA agreement are anticipated to commence after August 16, following a consultation period with U.S. lawmakers, industries, and the public. Guajardo also mentioned that he and Ross are nearing the announcement of an agreement concerning sugar trade between the two nations.

text: Obama confronts Communist-led Cuba with a plea for democracy. HAVANA (Reuters) - U.S. President Barack Obama confronted Cuba’s Communist regime with a heartfelt appeal for democratic governance and economic reforms on Tuesday, directly addressing the Cuban populace in a landmark speech broadcast across the island. Standing at Havana’s Grand Theater, with President Raul Castro present, Obama stated that his visit to Cuba was intended to extend a gesture of friendship and to 'bury the last remnant' of the Cold War in the Americas. However, he firmly advocated for economic and political reforms and increased transparency in a one-party system where dissent is suppressed, Internet access is limited, and the media is government-controlled. This address marked the pinnacle of a 48-hour visit that was made possible by his agreement with Castro in December 2014 to set aside decades of animosity that began shortly after Cuba’s 1959 revolution and to strive for normalized relations. Nevertheless, Obama issued a clear challenge to Castro, asserting that Cubans cannot achieve their full potential if the government does not permit change and loosen its control over Cuban politics and society. 'I believe citizens should be free to express their opinions without fear,' Obama stated to the audience on the last day of his trip. 'Voters should have the ability to select their governments through free and democratic elections.' 'Not everyone agrees with me on this, nor does everyone see eye to eye with the American people on this, but I hold that these human rights are universal. They are the rights of the American people, the Cuban people, and individuals worldwide,' Obama remarked. The carefully chosen audience responded with enthusiastic applause, particularly when he denounced the longstanding U.S. economic embargo against Cuba, praised the skills of Cubans, and acknowledged the nation’s successes in healthcare and education. The image of the leader of the United States, a superpower long criticized by Cuba’s government, standing in Havana and advocating for such transformations in a speech broadcast into homes throughout the island would have been unimaginable prior to the thawing of relations between the two nations 15 months ago. Since that time, Obama has consistently utilized his executive authority to ease trade and travel restrictions, while also urging Cuba to accelerate the cautious market-oriented reforms initiated by Castro and to permit greater political and economic freedoms. Castro has welcomed Obama’s initiatives while maintaining that a new rapport with the former adversary does not imply a change in Cuba’s political framework. The audience of over 1,000 attendees at Obama’s speech on Tuesday consisted of officials and business figures from both nations, U.S. lawmakers, and members of Cuba’s cultural elite. Obama received prolonged applause when he reiterated his appeal for the U.S. Congress to abolish the embargo, which he labeled as 'an outdated burden on the Cuban people.' However, the reaction was more subdued when he urged Castro to permit enhanced political freedoms. Following the speech, Obama proceeded directly to a private meeting with notable dissidents on the island, some of whom are critical of his engagement strategy. 'As far as I am concerned, nothing has changed; the repression continues,' stated Berta Soler from the Ladies in White group, who met with Obama at the embassy. The Cuban government regards the dissidents as mercenaries lacking public backing, but Obama commended their efforts and 'extraordinary courage.' Obama views his significant pivot away from a long-standing policy aimed at isolating and undermining Cuba as a narrative of success and seeks to cement it as an unchangeable part of his legacy before leaving office in January. Nonetheless, significant hurdles remain for the complete normalization of relations, particularly the disagreements over human rights, the Republican-controlled U.S. Congress's reluctance to lift the embargo, and Washington’s unwillingness to discuss the return of the U.S. naval base at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. Critics of Obama in the U.S. have condemned his trip to Cuba as an untimely reward for the Communist government.

text: PORTSMOUTH, N.H. (Reuters) - On Tuesday, Democrat Bernie Sanders publicly endorsed his former competitor Hillary Clinton for the presidency, showcasing a moment of party solidarity. He characterized her as the most qualified candidate to address the issues facing the United States and to defeat Republican Donald Trump in the upcoming election on November 8. Standing alongside Clinton, who nodded in agreement, Sanders put aside the contentious nature of their prior campaign for the Democratic nomination, stating that she would champion efforts to reduce economic inequality, enhance college affordability, and broaden healthcare access for all Americans. "This campaign is centered on the needs of the American populace and tackling the significant crises we encounter, and I have no doubt that as we approach November, Hillary Clinton is, by far, the most capable candidate to achieve that," he expressed to an enthusiastic audience in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, which included many passionate Sanders supporters. "I will do everything within my power to ensure she becomes the next president of the United States," declared the U.S. senator from Vermont. His endorsement came five weeks after Clinton was seen as the likely Democratic presidential nominee, bringing a key figure from the party’s progressive faction into her fold. Sanders offered his support less than two weeks ahead of the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, where she is set to receive her formal nomination. "I can’t help but think about how much more enjoyable this election will be now that we are united," Clinton remarked regarding Sanders. "Thank you, Bernie, for your endorsement, but even more so, thank you for your lifelong commitment to fighting injustice." Trump mocked the endorsement through a series of tweets, claiming that Sanders had forsaken the supporters who rallied behind his grassroots campaign aimed at regulating Wall Street and eliminating large contributions in politics. "Bernie Sanders endorsing Crooked Hillary Clinton is akin to Occupy Wall Street endorsing Goldman Sachs," Trump tweeted. The Trump campaign released a statement asserting that Sanders had now officially joined the manipulated system he had critiqued during his protracted primary contest with Clinton. "Bernie’s endorsement serves as Exhibit A in our rigged system - the Democratic Party is disenfranchising its voters to serve a select, privileged few," stated Stephen Miller, a senior policy advisor to Trump. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll published on Tuesday revealed that Clinton has widened her lead over Trump to 13 percentage points, up from a 10-point advantage at the end of the previous week. The former U.S. secretary of state hopes that her joint appearance with Sanders in Portsmouth will assist her in winning over his supporters, some of whom displayed Sanders signs during the rally and chanted his name. Recent Reuters/Ipsos surveys indicated that only around 40 percent of Sanders’ supporters expressed willingness to support Clinton, and the crowd at the rally demonstrated that she still has work to do. "I am absolutely certain I will not cast my vote for Hillary Clinton," stated Gale Bailey, a Sanders supporter and unemployed graphic designer from Rochester, New Hampshire, who wore a Sanders T-shirt to the rally. "She’s a crook, and I refuse to vote for a crook," Bailey asserted, adding that she planned to write Sanders’ name on the ballot in November. The joint appearance followed weeks of negotiations between their teams as Sanders sought compromises from Clinton regarding his progressive policy agenda. This occurred after Clinton integrated aspects of Sanders’ proposals for free in-state college tuition and expanded affordable healthcare coverage into her platform last week. Sanders also successfully advocated for a variety of progressive policy positions to be included in the Democratic platform, which was approved by a committee on Saturday. Although he did not succeed in all his policy battles, notably failing to gain support for halting a congressional vote on the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement, he told the Portsmouth audience that "our task now is to ensure that platform is enacted by a Democratic-controlled Senate, a Democratic-controlled House, and a Hillary Clinton presidency."

text: Supporters of neo-Maoism in China have expressed their approval of President Xi Jinping's new era of socialism, appreciating its renewed focus on equality. However, they are hesitant to elevate Xi to the same status as Mao Zedong, the founding leader of communist China. At a leadership conclave of the ruling Communist Party that concluded this week, Xi presented a bold vision for a strong and prosperous China, asserting the party's dominance and reinforcing his position as the most powerful leader since Mao assumed control in 1949 and proclaimed the establishment of modern China. Delegates paid tribute to Xi with honorifics reminiscent of the Mao era, and he became the first current Chinese leader since Mao to have an ideology named after him included in the party charter, indicating its continuation beyond his newly commenced second five-year term. Song Yangbiao, a freelance journalist based in Beijing with neo-Maoist tendencies, remarked to Reuters, "Their commonality lies in their desire to rejuvenate the Chinese nation and establish a new, independent, and strong China. Chairman Mao liberated the Chinese populace from Western oppression, while Xi Jinping is committed to amplifying China's voice internationally." Nonetheless, Song expressed that it is "not realistic" to reinstate Mao's title of party chairman for Xi, citing that this idea has been suggested by some leadership insiders. "Mao's authority was earned through a long and challenging struggle, whereas Xi's power is derived from the bureaucracy during a peaceful period. The historical contexts are entirely different," he added. Some prominent party officials at the congress did not share these concerns. Numerous attendees referred to Xi as a wise and great 'lingxiu,' a term traditionally reserved for Mao Zedong and his brief successor, Hua Guofeng. Bayanqolu, the party leader of Jilin province in northeastern China, even referred to Xi as the 'party helmsman,' a title that has not been commonly used in senior Communist Party circles since Mao, who was known as the 'Great Helmsman.' Sima Nan, a television commentator, blogger, and advocate for Mao and the Communist Party, stated, "Accepting Xi as a powerful leader and as the most influential leader since Mao is essential for Xi’s new era. Just consider how much he has articulated, how extensively he has written, and how many individuals he has engaged with—when does he find time to rest?" China navigates a complicated relationship with Mao's legacy. While the Party officially honors Mao as the founder, with his substantial portrait displayed over Tiananmen Square and his image on every yuan banknote, he is viewed unfavorably by many intellectuals and others in China, who hold him accountable for the disruptive Cultural Revolution and economic policies that resulted in widespread famine and millions of deaths. State media occasionally characterize Mao's actions as 30 percent negative and 70 percent positive. Neo-Maoists reject the criticisms leveled against Mao, labeling them as attacks from Westerners and revisionists, and they actively defend Mao and his strategies through online articles, sometimes publicly condemning those who undermine his legacy. In January, a professor in central China lost his university position following protests from Maoists over a social media remark attributing millions of deaths to Mao. Although Xi has not excessively praised Mao or his policies, he has acknowledged Mao's 'mistakes' and has drawn a firm line against efforts to alter the Party’s official history, which has pleased neo-Maoists. He has also utilized Maoist imagery, discourse, and initiatives to promote discipline among party members, attract public backing, and reinforce the party's leading position within society. "The Party leads everything—party, government, military, civilian, and academic, from east to west, south to north, and in the center," Xi stated during his address at the Congress opening.

text: Activists report that the Vietnamese authorities limited access to Facebook during President Obama's visit. SAN FRANCISCO (Reuters) - According to two activist groups, the Vietnamese government imposed restrictions on Facebook Inc access within Vietnam for several days this week as part of a wider initiative to crack down on human rights and political dissidents coinciding with President Barack Obama's visit. Representatives from Access Now, a digital rights organization, and Viet Tan, a pro-democracy group from Vietnam, stated on Thursday that the social media platform was restricted and occasionally inaccessible in Vietnam from Sunday to Wednesday. They based their claims on reports from individuals in the country on Twitter and from Access Now’s digital security assistance service. This action aligns with a pattern of Facebook restrictions in nations like China, Uganda, and Turkey during politically sensitive periods as the social media network, with 1.6 billion users, gains more influence. Obama concluded his three-day visit to Vietnam on Wednesday, primarily concentrating on normalizing relations with the country. However, he also advocated for human rights and expressed concerns regarding Vietnam's limitations on political freedoms after critics of its communist regime were barred from meeting him. Activists indicated that the Facebook restrictions were part of an intensified effort by the Vietnamese government to curb the use of the platform for political demonstrations. Earlier in the month, Facebook was blocked multiple times amid street protests triggered by an environmental crisis that led to widespread fish deaths, according to the two organizations. Additionally, the social media platform was unavailable in Vietnam prior to the parliamentary elections on Sunday, as pro-democracy activists urged a boycott, according to members of both groups. Facebook opted not to provide a comment. Vietnamese government representatives did not promptly respond to a request for comment submitted via a government website. In February, Uganda’s government restricted access to Facebook and Twitter Inc during presidential elections. Following a fatal bombing in Turkey in March, an Ankara court mandated a ban on Facebook and Twitter access. Furthermore, during the 2011 Arab Spring in Egypt, Tunisia, and Libya, social networks faced repeated shutdowns. Angelina Huynh, the advocacy director for Viet Tan, which has global membership including in Vietnam, noted in a phone interview that Facebook is frequently blocked in Vietnam during politically sensitive events. "People were utilizing Facebook to organize protests. They aimed to prevent people from taking to the streets," Huynh stated.

text: A bill has been put forward in the U.S. Congress that would prohibit American tourists from traveling to North Korea. On Thursday, lawmakers from both the Republican and Democratic parties introduced the legislation, which mandates that Americans must seek special authorization for any visits other than tourism. The North Korea Travel Control Act, proposed by Democrat Adam Schiff and Republican Joe Wilson, comes in response to the detention of at least 17 Americans in North Korea over the last ten years. The North Korean government has a history of using the detention of U.S. citizens as leverage to secure high-profile visits from the United States, despite the absence of formal diplomatic ties. "As tensions escalate in North Korea, the likelihood of Americans being detained for political motives is higher than it has ever been," the congressmen stated in a release. They emphasized that due to North Korea’s "proven readiness to use American visitors as negotiation tools to gain high-level meetings or concessions, it is fitting for the United States to implement measures to regulate travel to a country that represents a genuine and immediate threat to American interests." Currently, four Americans are held in North Korea amid rising diplomatic tensions with the U.S. Among them, two were detained in the last month and are connected to a private university located in the North Korean capital. According to a congressional source, the proposed legislation would completely prohibit tourist travel for Americans, while any other types of visits would necessitate a special license from the Treasury Department, which is overseeing a broad array of sanctions against North Korea due to its nuclear and missile initiatives. This month, North Korea claimed its right to "harshly punish" U.S. nationals it has apprehended for offenses against its government, stating that labeling these arrests as bargaining tactics is "sheer ignorance." On May 7, North Korea announced the detention of Kim Hake Song, an employee of the Pyongyang University of Science and Technology, on charges of "hostile acts." Another American, Kim Sang Dok, who was also associated with the same institution, was taken into custody in late April under similar allegations. The other two Americans include Otto Warmbier, a 22-year-old student arrested in January 2016 who received a 15-year hard labor sentence for trying to steal a propaganda banner, and Kim Dong Chul, a 62-year-old Korean-American missionary sentenced to 10 years of hard labor for subversion last year.

text: MECCA (Reuters) - As the haj comes to a close, over two million pilgrims who participated this week began their return to Mecca on Sunday for their concluding prayers, marking the end of the largest annual assembly of Muslims worldwide. High-ranking Saudi officials reported that this year's rituals, which have previously been marred by fatal stampedes, fires, and riots that posed challenges for authorities, proceeded without any incidents. The governor of Mecca province, Prince Khaled al-Faisal, who leads the central haj committee, declared this year's pilgrimage a success.  'I take pride today in having provided these services, and I am proud of all my brothers who took part, as well as each pilgrim who came to this land and contributed to the success of this season,' he stated to journalists in Mina, located east of Mecca. A large number of pilgrims engaged in the symbolic act of stoning the devil, which is a component of the haj rituals, at Jamarat before heading back to Mecca. By night, worshippers filled the Grand Mosque in Mecca. Saudi Arabia's reputation hinges on its stewardship of Islam's most sacred sites and the organization of the pilgrimage. This year, over 2.3 million pilgrims arrived in Saudi Arabia, with the majority coming from outside the country, for the five-day event. Attendance is considered a religious obligation for every capable Muslim who can afford it, to be fulfilled at least once in a lifetime. 'The organization was exceptional, and there was no overcrowding or any issues. Everything went smoothly, thanks to God,' commented Yemeni pilgrim Rashid Ahmed. This week, more than 100,000 security personnel and 30,000 health workers were deployed to ensure safety and offer medical assistance. A tragic incident in 2015 resulted in the deaths of nearly 800 pilgrims, according to Riyadh, when two large groups converged at a crossroads east of Mecca. Reports from countries of repatriated bodies indicated that over 2,000 individuals may have perished, including in excess of 400 Iranians. After boycotting the event last year due to a diplomatic dispute with Riyadh, Tehran sent nearly 90,000 pilgrims to the haj this year. Saudi Health Minister Tawfiq al-Rabeeah stated that the pilgrimage occurred without any disease outbreaks, which is a recurring concern. In an interview with Reuters late on Saturday, he noted that the ministry had also provided care for 400,000 individuals, which included 21 open-heart surgeries. 'We are dedicated to delivering outstanding service so that the pilgrims return home in good health after completing the haj,' he remarked.

text: PRISTINA (Reuters) - On Friday, Kosovo police apprehended three lawmakers, including the well-known opposition leader, who was detained in the street, after they did not show up in court regarding allegations of discharging tear gas in parliament during 2015 and 2016. For nearly two years, opposition lawmakers disrupted parliamentary proceedings by releasing tear gas in the chamber to protest a border agreement with Montenegro and an EU-mediated accord with Serbia. Albin Kurti, the head of Kosovo's largest opposition party Vetevendosje, was captured and handcuffed by police near the parliament building while en route to a regular session. Police utilized pepper spray to disperse several other lawmakers from Kurti's party who attempted to cling to him and obstruct the police from taking him away, as reported by Kosovo media. Ultimately, he was placed into a police vehicle. Kurti received more votes than any other political contender, and his party secured the top position in the June snap elections, but he did not join the ruling coalition. According to Dukagjin Gorani of Vetevendosje, all three MPs were sentenced to one month of detention later in the day. So far, numerous other MPs have been charged for the release of tear gas in the 120-seat parliament. This marks the continuation of a significant and extensive persecution against Vetevendosje, stated the party president, Visar Ymeri. Last week, a court in Pristina imposed prison sentences ranging from two to eight years on four individuals, including one parliament member, for their involvement in a grenade attack on the parliament building last year. All of them were supporters of Vetevendosje. Opposition parties criticize the border agreement with Montenegro, arguing that the nation of 1.8 million is surrendering land by transferring approximately 8,000 hectares (19,700 acres). They also oppose a 2013 agreement signed between Pristina and Belgrade as part of an EU-sponsored dialogue that would enhance rights for the local Serb minority. They contend that this deal will effectively fracture the economically challenged Balkan nation along ethnic lines. Kosovo proclaimed its independence from Serbia in 2008, nearly ten years after NATO airstrikes expelled Serb forces from the region.

text: TOKYO (Reuters) - U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson emphasized on Thursday the urgent need for a "new approach" in response to the rising threat posed by North Korea's nuclear ambitions, although he did not specify the plans of the Trump administration. This marked Tillerson's first interaction with the media since he began his role in early February, as he addressed reporters at a joint news conference in Tokyo following discussions with Japanese Foreign Minister Fumio Kishida. Tillerson, a former oil executive without previous diplomatic experience, stated that two decades of diplomatic efforts and U.S. aid to North Korea had not succeeded in denuclearizing Pyongyang. "We have 20 years of failed approach," he remarked. "That includes a period where the United States has provided $1.35 billion in assistance to North Korea as an encouragement to take a different pathway." He added, "In the face of this ever-escalating threat, it is clear that a different approach is required. Part of the purpose of my visit to the region is to exchange views on a new approach." A representative from the Japanese foreign ministry mentioned that U.S. officials had explored potential new strategies concerning North Korea, but he did not provide further details. As Tillerson urges China to take stronger action to control North Korea's nuclear and missile activities, he is anticipated to inform them of the U.S. plans to enhance missile defense in the region, despite strong objections from Beijing, according to a U.S. official in Washington. An advanced U.S. anti-missile system is currently being deployed in South Korea, and the official indicated that the Trump administration is keen to discuss similar upgrades with Japan. Later in the week, Tillerson will visit South Korea and China. Additionally, he is likely to discuss the possibility of implementing "secondary sanctions" on Chinese banks and businesses that engage with North Korea, as mentioned by the official, who requested anonymity. This consideration is part of a comprehensive review of North Korea policy expected to be finalized by late March or early April. State Department spokesperson Mark Toner stated on Wednesday that Tillerson will engage in "substantive, hard" discussions regarding next steps in addressing North Korea, but his trip is not expected to yield an immediate, specific outcome. In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Hua Chunying reiterated Foreign Minister Wang Yi's suggestion from the previous week that North Korea ought to halt its nuclear and missile testing, while South Korea and the United States should cease their joint military exercises and pursue dialogue instead. "We welcome all parties, including the United States, to come up with their own proposals," Hua said during a daily news briefing. "As long as these proposals are conducive to ameliorating the present tense situation on the Korean peninsula and are beneficial to maintaining regional peace and stability ... China will have an open attitude." Tillerson made it clear that he anticipates China, North Korea's primary ally, to increase its efforts. "We will be having discussions with China as to further actions we believe they might consider taking that would be helpful to bringing North Korea to a different attitude about its future need for nuclear weapons," he stated. Observers around the world closely monitored Tillerson's remarks in Japan for hints about their implications for the Trump administration's foreign policy. Japan is looking for insights into U.S. strategies regarding both North Korea and China's growing military and economic influence while aiming to avoid trade disputes. Tillerson also met with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and had dinner with Kishida. U.S. President Donald Trump made it a central theme of his campaign to urge allies, including Japan, to contribute more for the presence of U.S. forces and other aspects of American protection. Tillerson, however, conveyed a significantly softer message at this occasion.

text: HARARE (Reuters) - Newly inaugurated President Emmerson Mnangagwa articulated an ambitious plan on Friday aimed at rejuvenating Zimbabwe's devastated economy, pledging to govern for the benefit of all citizens. Just days following the ousting of Robert Mugabe, the 75-year-old former security chief promised to protect the rights of foreign investors and to re-establish relations with the West, confirming that elections would proceed next year as planned. During a 30-minute address to tens of thousands of supporters at Harare's national stadium, Mnangagwa reached out to his adversaries, seemingly seeking to mend the ethnic and political rifts that his predecessor exploited during his 37-year rule. "I intend, nay, am required, to serve our country as the president of all citizens, regardless of color, creed, religion, tribe or political affiliation," he stated, also declaring that the voice of the people is the "voice of god." However, behind the grand declarations, some Zimbabweans question if a man who faithfully served Mugabe for many years can instigate any real change within a ruling system accused of extensive human rights violations and poor economic strategies. He made it clear that the land reforms that led to the violent takeover of thousands of white-owned farms beginning in 2000 would remain intact, but he assured that those who lost their properties would be compensated. For some political rivals, the address marked a refreshing shift from Mugabe's usual confrontational style and seemed to draw on Mnangagwa's understanding of China's economic model. "His model has been the Chinese," remarked David Coltart, a former education minister and MP from the opposition Movement for Democratic Change. "He will work to make Zimbabwe a more appealing investment destination, and more effective, but similar to China, will not accept dissent. If you behave, you will be secure." Skeptics of the new president's dedication to reform question his involvement in the Gukurahundi massacres in Matabeleland in 1983, during which approximately 20,000 individuals were killed in a crackdown on Mugabe's opponents by the North Korean-trained Fifth Brigade. Mnangagwa was responsible for internal security at that time, although he has denied any involvement in the atrocities. Many Zimbabweans, particularly the ethnic Ndebele who suffered the most during the Gukurahundi violence, may perceive his call on Friday to "let bygones be bygones" as an effort to gloss over one of the nation’s most tragic periods. Some opponents have claimed that soldiers treated those opposing the military intervention last week harshly - characterized as a de facto coup against Mugabe, 93, and his 52-year-old spouse Grace. Former finance minister Ignatius Chombo was hospitalized due to injuries sustained from beatings during a week of military detention, his lawyer informed Reuters. "He was blindfolded throughout his time in custody," Lovemore Madhuku stated. "It was a very brutal and draconian way of dealing with opponents," he added. When asked for a comment, police spokeswoman Charity Charamba stated she had no information regarding Chombo. In a separate development, High Court Judge President George Chiweshe ruled the military intervention last week was legal, following a request made by two citizens who sought to confirm that the military acted justifiably. Since returning to Zimbabwe this month after escaping a purge led by Mugabe, Mnangagwa has been advocating for democracy, tolerance, and adherence to the rule of law. Alongside Mugabe, Grace - Mnangagwa's declared adversary - has been afforded immunity from prosecution and had her safety assured, part of an agreement that led to Mugabe's resignation on Tuesday, sources familiar with the negotiations reported. For many years, Mnangagwa served loyally under Mugabe, who faced widespread accusations of suppressing dissent and electoral fraud, and under whose leadership one of Africa's formerly most prosperous economies was devastated by hyperinflation and mass emigration. Mnangagwa earned the moniker "Ngwena."

text: Clinton's attorney criticizes the FBI following the release of a search warrant. NEW YORK (Reuters) - Hillary Clinton’s lawyer stated that the FBI behaved improperly by announcing the restart of its inquiry into her private email system just days before the presidential election on November 8. This declaration was made in light of search warrant documents unveiled on Tuesday. The sharp critique from attorney David Kendall came after federal court documents in Manhattan were made public, which related to an October search warrant aimed at emails connected to the Democratic presidential candidate. The warrant was issued two days post the notification from FBI Director James Comey, who had informed Congress via a letter on October 28 that new emails had been found that seemed “pertinent” to the investigation. Comey’s letter reignited scrutiny of Clinton’s use of the email server during her tenure as secretary of state from 2009 to 2013 and disrupted the campaign just 11 days before the election, which was ultimately won by Republican candidate Donald Trump. Clinton has attributed her loss to Comey and his letter. In an affidavit that was unsealed on Tuesday, an FBI agent indicated there was “probable cause” to suspect that emails involving Clinton were among the “thousands” discovered on a laptop belonging to an unrelated investigation that contained U.S. State Department communications. However, the documents did not suggest that the FBI had any evidence at the time of Comey’s letter indicating that any of the emails found on the laptop were classified correspondence with Clinton. Kendall remarked that the documents illustrated the “extraordinary impropriety” of Comey’s letter, which “inflicted devastating yet predictable political harm and was both legally unauthorized and factually unnecessary.” The FBI opted not to comment. The laptop in question belonged to former Democratic U.S. Representative Anthony Weiner, who is the estranged spouse of Clinton aide Huma Abedin and was under investigation due to reports regarding messages he sent to a 15-year-old girl through cellphone and online platforms. Randol Schoenberg, a lawyer based in Los Angeles, sought the release of the search warrant materials, arguing that transparency was vital due to the potential impact of the investigation on the election's outcome. In a statement, Schoenberg expressed that he found “nothing to indicate that there would be anything other than routine correspondence between Secretary Clinton and her longtime aide Huma Abedin.” Brian Fallon, who was the national press secretary for Clinton’s campaign, stated on Twitter that the search warrant “shows Comey’s interference in the election was as entirely unjustified as we suspected at the time.” In July, Comey recommended that no charges be filed regarding Clinton’s handling of classified information in the emails, although he characterized her and her associates as “extremely careless” in managing such information. This conclusion followed what the search warrant documents referred to as a “criminal investigation concerning the improper transmission and storage of classified info on unclassified email systems and servers.” In his letter to Congress, Comey mentioned that emails possibly related to the investigation had been found in an “unrelated case.” Federal agents obtained the warrant to analyze the emails on October 30. Two days prior to the election, Comey revealed that the emails did not alter his earlier recommendation.

text: Indonesian envoy to press Myanmar to cease violence against Rohingya Muslims. JAKARTA (Reuters) - Indonesian President Joko Widodo has dispatched his foreign minister to Myanmar to implore its administration to stop the violence directed at Rohingya Muslims, he announced on Sunday following an incident where a petrol bomb was launched at the Myanmar embassy in Jakarta. The attack on the embassy, which resulted in a minor fire according to police, occurred in the early hours of Sunday morning amidst growing frustration in Indonesia, which has the largest Muslim population in the world, over the mistreatment of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. A police officer on patrol near the embassy detected flames on the second floor of the property at approximately 0235 Jakarta time (GMT+7) and informed the officers stationed at the front entrance, as stated in a report by Jakarta police. Once the fire was put out, police discovered a broken beer bottle with a wick attached, and it was noted that the unidentified assailant likely fled the scene in an MPV vehicle. Jakarta police are looking into the incident, according to spokesman Argo Yuwono. On Saturday, a group of activists protested at the embassy, urging the Nobel Prize Committee to revoke the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi, as reported by state news agency Antara. Protests persisted on Sunday in the downtown area of Jakarta, with numerous individuals demanding that the Indonesian government take an active role in efforts to end human rights abuses against Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. President Widodo remarked that he has sent Foreign Minister Retno Marsudi to Myanmar to engage in "intensive communications" with relevant parties, including the United Nations. Earlier today, the Foreign Minister departed for Myanmar to request that the Myanmar government cease and avert violence, ensure the protection of all citizens, including Muslims within Myanmar, and grant access to humanitarian assistance, Widodo stated. Widodo further emphasized the necessity for concrete actions and expressed the Indonesian government's dedication to resolving the humanitarian crisis, noting that Marsudi will also visit Bangladesh to arrange additional aid for refugees there. The treatment of the approximately 1.1 million Muslim Rohingya, who are part of the Buddhist-majority Myanmar, poses the most significant challenge for leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who has been criticized by Western observers for failing to advocate for a minority that has long reported persecution. Aid organizations estimate that around 73,000 Rohingya have sought refuge in neighboring Bangladesh since the outbreak of violence in Myanmar last week.
